full.da-anterior:
What's tested
  • Where each surface's height of contour sits, and what over- or undercontouring does to the gingiva
  • The contact, embrasure and CEJ trends and their exceptions
  • Telling the incisors apart: maxillary central from lateral, mandibular central from lateral
  • Maxillary versus mandibular canine: crown, cusp ridges, lingual anatomy and roots; the longest tooth, crown and root

Surfaces, angles and lobes

A line angle is where two surfaces meet (mesiolabial); a point angle is where three meet (mesiolabioincisal). Teeth grow from lobes: anterior teeth from 4 (three labial lobes plus the cingulum). The labial lobes leave mamelons (three bumps on a new incisal edge that wear away) and two faint labial depressions. Perikymata are the fine wavy enamel ridges on newly erupted teeth. The cingulum is the lingual bulge in the cervical third of every anterior tooth.

Heights of contour

The height of contour is the crest of curvature of a surface. It deflects food over the gingiva. Overcontoured (too bulky): food skips the gingiva and plaque collects at the margin, so the gingiva becomes inflamed; this is the more common restorative error. Undercontoured (too flat): food is driven into the sulcus and the gingiva is injured.

SurfaceWhereNotes
Facial, every toothCervical thirdMnemonic: "none, they're all cervical"
Lingual, anterior teethCervical third (the cingulum)
Lingual, posterior teethMiddle thirdMandibular premolars: it overhangs the root outline
Mesial, incisors and mandibular canineIncisal thirdMaxillary canine: junction of incisal and middle thirds
Distal, anterior teethOne step more cervical than the mesialMaxillary incisors and mandibular canine: incisal-middle junction; maxillary canine: middle third
Mesial and distal, posterior teethOcclusal-middle junction or middle thirdNo height of contour is ever in the occlusal third alone

Contacts, embrasures and the CEJ

  • Contacts move cervically as you go back from the midline, and each tooth's distal contact is more cervical (and slightly more lingual) than its mesial. Exceptions: the mandibular central incisor (both contacts at the same level, incisal third), the mandibular first premolar (mesial more cervical) and the primary maxillary canine (mesial more cervical).
  • From the incisal view, anterior contacts are centered faciolingually; from the occlusal view, posterior contacts sit slightly buccal of center.
  • Each contact has four embrasures (facial, lingual, incisal or occlusal, gingival). Lingual embrasures are larger than facial ones, and incisal embrasures open up going distally. Contacts stabilize the arch, stop food impaction and protect the papilla.
  • The CEJ curves toward the apex on the facial and lingual and toward the incisal or occlusal on the proximal surfaces. The curve is deepest on the mesial of the central incisors, shallows going back, is similar on adjacent surfaces, and is greater on the mesial than the distal.

Maxillary incisors

  • Central: the largest incisor crown and the widest anterior tooth mesiodistally; trapezoidal labially, triangular proximally. The mesioincisal angle is sharp (almost square) and the distoincisal rounded; the mesial contact is in the incisal third, the distal at the incisal-middle junction. Cingulum slightly distal. One conical root with a blunt apex, a rounded-triangle cross-section, about 1–1½ times the crown.
  • Lateral: a smaller, rounder central with a deeper lingual fossa and stronger marginal ridges; the cingulum is centered and a lingual pit is common. Both incisal angles are more rounded (the distal most). A palatogingival groove (about 3%) runs from the cingulum onto the root and can hold a deep localized periodontal pocket. The root often bends distally and has more accessory canals. It is the second most variable tooth after the third molars (peg laterals, congenital absence).

Mandibular incisors

  • Central: the smallest permanent tooth and the most symmetric (hard to call right or left); the first succedaneous tooth; the tooth least prone to caries. Its contacts are at the same height. It occludes with only one opposing tooth (the maxillary central), as does the maxillary third molar.
  • Lateral: slightly larger, with a longer root; the cingulum is distal to center and the incisal edge has a distolingual twist that follows the arch, so from the mesial you see more lingual surface.
  • Both: incisal edge lingual to the root axis; little lingual anatomy; a ribbon-like root, narrow mesiodistally and broad faciolingually, with proximal depressions (deeper on the distal).

Canines

FeatureMaxillary canineMandibular canine
SizeLongest tooth overall (about 27 mm) and longest rootLongest crown; longest root in the mandible
CuspSharp, tip slightly labial to the root axis; cusp angle about 105°Blunter, tip on or lingual to the axis; flatter (about 120°)
Cusp ridgesMesial shorter than distalDistal about twice the mesial
Labial viewStrong labial ridge; distal outline bulgesMesial crown outline nearly straight in line with the root
LingualLarge centered cingulum and a lingual ridge that splits two fossae; pits commonFaint cingulum (slightly distal) and shallow fossae; no pits
ContactsMesial at the incisal-middle junction, distal in the middle thirdMesial in the incisal third, distal at the incisal-middle junction
RootMay curve in the apical third (usually distally); canine eminenceMesial groove; may bifurcate into labial and lingual roots

The maxillary canine is the "cornerstone": its long root in dense bone supports the corner of the mouth (the canine eminence) and makes it the best tooth to guide lateral movements. It erupts last among the anterior teeth (11–12 years), so it is often blocked out or impacted. Wear: maxillary canines wear on the mesial cusp ridge and lingual surface, mandibular canines on the distal cusp ridge and labial surface. A prominent cingulum is not a second cusp, and a flat mesial cusp ridge does not make a mandibular canine an incisor.
full.da-posterior:
What's tested
  • Which premolar or molar has which crown feature: cusps, ridges, grooves, outline
  • Root numbers, canals, root lengths and where the furcations are
  • First versus second (and third) molars, and maxillary versus mandibular
  • The exceptions: the mandibular first premolar's marginal ridge and contact, the maxillary first molar's lingual width

Premolars

Premolars develop from 4 lobes (3 buccal, 1 lingual); the three-cusp mandibular second premolar has 5 (two lingual lobes). Crowns taper to the lingual, and the buccal cusp is the larger. Maxillary premolar cusps sit over the root; mandibular premolar crowns tilt lingually.

ToothCrownRoot
Maxillary firstBuccal cusp about 1 mm taller; lingual cusp tip mesial of center; hexagonal outline; long central groove; mesial crown concavity and a mesial marginal ridge grooveTwo roots (buccal and palatal), two canals; deeper mesial depression; shortest premolar root
Maxillary secondRounder, cusps nearly equal in height; short central groove with many supplemental grooves; no mesial concavityOne root (one or two canals); deeper distal depression
Mandibular firstCanine-like: large buccal cusp, tiny lingual cusp; strong lingual tilt; mesiolingual groove; transverse ridge with two pits ("snake eyes"); diamond outline, more bulk distallyOne root, pointed apex; rarely bifid
Mandibular secondThree-cusp Y form most common (ML larger than DL, a lingual groove, the only premolar with a central pit); two-cusp forms H (more common) or UOne root, blunt apex; distal depression only, mesial surface flat
  • The mandibular first premolar is the only posterior tooth whose mesial marginal ridge is more cervical than its distal (it slopes about 45°, so you see more occlusal surface from the mesial), and its mesial contact is lower than its distal.
  • The maxillary first premolar's mesial concavity runs from the crown onto the root: hard to match with a matrix and to clean.
  • Most commonly rotated tooth: the maxillary second premolar.

Molars: class traits

Wider mesiodistally than tall, the shortest crowns occlusocervically, clinical crowns shrinking from first to third. Crowns taper buccal to lingual, except the maxillary first molar, which is wider on the lingual (its large distolingual cusp and the Carabelli cusp). Centric cusps: maxillary lingual, mandibular buccal; non-centric cusps protect the cheek (maxillary buccal) and tongue (mandibular lingual). Distal marginal ridges and contacts are more cervical than mesial. Root trunks lengthen and roots converge from first to third molar.

Maxillary molars

  • First molar: largest maxillary tooth; rhomboid outline (MB and DL angles acute, ML and DB obtuse). Cusps largest to smallest ML, MB, DB, DL, plus the Carabelli cusp on the lingual of the ML cusp. The ML cusp is the longest. The oblique ridge joins the DB and ML cusps (only maxillary molars have one) and is crossed by the transverse groove of the oblique ridge. Four fossae: central (largest), distal oblique, mesial triangular, distal triangular. The lingual groove and pit are caries-prone.
  • Second molar: DL cusp small or absent (a 3-cusp, heart-shaped form), Carabelli rare, less prominent oblique ridge, roots closer and more distally inclined with a longer trunk.
  • Third molar: most variable tooth and the most often missing; bulbous, wrinkled crown; roots short and often fused.
  • Roots: three (MB, DB, palatal). By length and bulk palatal > MB > DB. The broad MB root often holds two canals (the MB2), so the tooth usually has four canals. (One class guide gives the second molar four canals and the first three; the standard teaching is an MB2 in most first molars.) The first molar's roots flare most and its trunk is shortest.
  • Furcations: mesial about 3–4 mm from the CEJ (most coronal, entered from the palatal side), buccal about 4 mm, distal about 5 mm (most apical).

Mandibular molars

  • First molar: 5 cusps in 80–85% (MB, DB, D buccally; ML, DL lingually), pentagon outline, two buccal grooves and one lingual groove. MB is the widest cusp, ML the tallest and sharpest, D the smallest. The crown tilts lingually.
  • Second molar: 4 cusps, a "+" groove pattern (one buccal, one lingual groove), rectangular outline; a buccal cervical ridge on the MB cusp; roots closer and straighter.
  • Roots: two, mesial and distal. The mesial root is broader, more curved and has two canals (MB, ML), with a deeper distal-side depression; the distal root is straighter, usually one canal. A third, distolingual root occurs occasionally. The furcation is about 3 mm from the CEJ buccally and 4 mm lingually.
ToothRootsCanals (usual)
Maxillary first premolar2 (buccal, palatal)2
Maxillary second premolar11 (sometimes 2)
Mandibular premolars1 (first rarely bifid)1
Maxillary first and second molars3 (palatal longest)4 with MB2 (first molar)
Mandibular first and second molars2 (mesial broader)3 (two in the mesial root)
Mandibular canine1, occasionally 2 (labial, lingual)1–2

Longest roots in the maxilla: canine, then second premolar, then the first molar's palatal root. Distal root depressions are usually deeper than mesial ones (the maxillary first premolar is the exception, deeper mesially).

Quick ways to orient a posterior tooth

  • Maxillary or mandibular? Premolars: cusps centered over the root (maxillary) or crown tilted lingually (mandibular). Molars: three roots (maxillary) or two (mandibular).
  • Mesial or distal? Maxillary first premolar: the mesial concavity and marginal groove. Maxillary second premolar: the lingual cusp tip leans mesially. Mandibular first premolar: the mesiolingual groove and the larger distal fossa. Mandibular second premolar: the ML cusp is larger than the DL. Maxillary molars: the small DL cusp is distal, the Carabelli cusp mesial. Mandibular molars: the small distal cusp is distal, the crown tapers distally and the roots tilt distally.
  • Buccal or lingual? Two buccal roots on a maxillary molar; the crown tilts away from the buccal on a mandibular tooth.
full.da-anomalies:
What's tested
  • Naming an anomaly from a description or a radiograph: number, position, size, shape, root and structure
  • Fusion versus gemination versus concrescence, and how the tooth count tells them apart
  • The hereditary defects (amelogenesis and dentinogenesis imperfecta) against the acquired ones (fluorosis, tetracycline, Turner tooth)
  • Attrition, abrasion, erosion and abfraction
  • Identifying a permanent tooth step by step, right or left included

Anomalies are more common in the permanent dentition and in the maxilla.

Number and position

  • Anodontia: true (complete) anodontia is rare and goes with ectodermal dysplasia (hair, skin, sweat glands); partial anodontia (hypodontia) is one or more teeth missing; agenesis means the tooth never formed. Most often missing: third molars (maxillary more than mandibular).
  • Supernumerary teeth are often malformed. The mesiodens, between the maxillary centrals, is the most common; it can hold the centrals apart (a diastema) or block their eruption. A distomolar/paramolar sits in the third molar area; the mandibular premolar area is the other common site.
  • Malposition: impaction is most common in third molars, then maxillary canines (last anterior to erupt). Transposition: two teeth swap places (canine and first premolar). Rotation: most often the maxillary second premolar.

Size and shape

  • Microdontia (the peg lateral, a maxillary lateral formed from one lobe) and macrodontia.
  • Gemination: one tooth bud tries to split; a notched or bifid crown on one root and one canal; the count is normal when the double tooth is counted as one.
  • Fusion: two buds join through dentin; the count is one short; most common in the primary dentition and the mandibular incisor area.
  • Concrescence: two formed teeth joined by cementum only, usually maxillary molars.
  • Congenital syphilis: Hutchinson incisors (notched, screwdriver-shaped) and mulberry molars (constricted crowns with many small cusps).
  • Talon cusp: a claw-like extra cusp off the cingulum of an anterior tooth, often with a pulp horn; it can interfere with occlusion. Shovel-shaped incisors have heavy marginal ridges (more common in Asian, Arctic and Native American dentitions). Tuberculum intermedium: an extra lingual cusp between the ML and DL cusps of a mandibular molar. Tubercles are more common on mesial than distal marginal ridges.
  • Dens in dente (dens invaginatus): enamel folded into the tooth through a deep pit at the cingulum, most often a maxillary lateral; it decays early and the pulp can die.

Roots

AnomalyWhat it isClue
DilacerationSharp bend of the root, about 90° or moreTrauma during root formation; hard extraction and endodontics
FlexionA bend of less than 90°
TaurodontismTall pulp chamber, furcation moved apically, little CEJ constriction"Bull tooth" on a molar radiograph
Enamel pearlA blob of enamel on the root, usually at a molar furcationNo periodontal attachment there: a localized pocket
HypercementosisExtra cementum on the root after eruptionBulbous apex; trauma, heavy occlusion
Dwarfed rootsShort rootsResorption from trauma or orthodontic movement that is too fast
Accessory rootsExtra roots and canalsThird molars, then mandibular canines and premolars

Structure (dysplasias)

ConditionCauseLook
Amelogenesis imperfectaHereditary; enamel only; both dentitionsThin, soft, pitted or missing enamel; normal dentin and pulps
Dentinogenesis imperfectaHereditary; dentin; both dentitions (can go with osteogenesis imperfecta)Opalescent blue-gray or amber, enamel chips off, bulbous crowns, short roots, obliterated pulps
FluorosisToo much fluoride while enamel formsWhite to brown mottling, sometimes pitting; caries-resistant
Tetracycline stainingThe drug taken while teeth formGray-brown bands in the dentin matching when it was taken
High feverIllness while crowns formPits or a band on all teeth forming at that time
Turner toothInfection or trauma of the primary predecessorOne hypoplastic permanent tooth (often a premolar or maxillary incisor)

A defect on every tooth in both dentitions points to a hereditary cause; a band on the teeth forming at one age points to an event; a single tooth points to a local cause.

Changes after eruption

  • Attrition: tooth against tooth (bruxism, porcelain against enamel); flat, shiny, matching facets.
  • Abrasion: a foreign object: hard brushing and abrasive paste (cervical, worse on the side opposite the dominant hand), a pipe, pins or nails held in the teeth; rounded in cross section.
  • Erosion: acid without bacteria (citrus, soda, reflux, bulimia); smooth, dished-out, yellow dentin showing. Vomiting erodes the lingual of the maxillary anterior teeth.
  • Abfraction: enamel rods breaking at the CEJ as the tooth flexes under heavy lateral loads; V-shaped, in the cervical third.

Identifying a permanent tooth

  1. Class: no cusp = incisor; 1 cusp = canine (a big cingulum is not a second cusp); 2–3 = premolar; 4–5 = molar.
  2. Arch: maxillary incisors are wider with conical roots, mandibular ones narrow with ribbon roots; maxillary canines have stronger anatomy; mandibular premolars tilt lingually; maxillary molars have 3 roots, mandibular 2.
  3. Type: central or lateral, first or second (the traits in the earlier pages).
  4. Mesial and facial: find the landmark, such as the rounder distoincisal angle, the distal bulge of a canine, the maxillary first premolar's mesial concavity, the small distal cusp of a mandibular first molar, or the two buccal roots of a maxillary molar.
  5. Right or left: hold the facial toward you with the mesial at an imaginary midline; the side it lands on is the patient's side (the patient's right is on your left).
full.da-occlusion:
What's tested
  • Angle Class I, II (divisions 1 and 2) and III, by molar and canine
  • Centric and non-centric cusps, the curves of occlusion, and which teeth meet which
  • Centric relation, maximum intercuspation and centric occlusion, and the slide between them
  • Canine guidance, group function, mutually protected and balanced occlusion; working, nonworking and protrusive interferences
  • What makes cusps taller or shorter, and how ridge and groove directions change

Terms

Occlusion is the static relationship of the teeth; articulation adds the dynamic contacts during function. Teeth sit in the neutral zone, where the tongue's outward push balances the lips' and cheeks' inward push; restorations and denture teeth belong there too. Arch integrity depends on proximal and occlusal contacts; tipping, drifting and supereruption after a loss change it.

Alignment

  • Curve of Spee: seen from the side (sagittal), from the mandibular canine tip along the buccal cusp tips toward the condyle. Curve of Wilson: seen from the front (frontal), side to side across the arch, from the lingual inclination of the mandibular molars. Monson joined them into a sphere of about 4 inches' radius. A compensating curve is the one built into dentures.
  • Mandibular teeth incline mesially and lingually; maxillary posterior teeth incline buccally.
  • The occlusal table (between the buccal and lingual cusp tips) is about 50–60% of the buccolingual width.
Centric (supporting, stamp, holding)Non-centric (guiding, shearing)
WhichMaxillary lingual, mandibular buccalMaxillary buccal, mandibular lingual
Shape and positionBroad, rounded; about 1/3 of the way into the tableSharper; about 1/6 of the way in
JobHold the vertical dimension of occlusion; crush in the opposing central fossa lineShear, guide the mandible into MIP, keep the cheek (maxillary buccal) and tongue (mandibular lingual) off the table

Each tooth meets two opposing teeth (its namesake and a neighbor), except the mandibular central incisor and the maxillary third molar. Cusps contact in two kinds of places: marginal ridges (and embrasures) and fossae. Mandibular teeth sit slightly mesial and lingual to their maxillary partners. In a posterior crossbite the maxillary buccal cusps land in the mandibular central fossae, so non-centric cusps act as centric ones. Overbite is vertical overlap; overjet is horizontal overlap.

Angle classes

ClassMolar relationOther
I (about 70%)Maxillary first molar's MB cusp over the mandibular first molar's buccal groove; mandibular MB cusp in the embrasure between maxillary PM2 and M1; maxillary ML cusp in the mandibular central fossaMaxillary canine in the embrasure between the mandibular canine and first premolar. Crowding or rotations can still be present ("Class I malocclusion")
II (about 25%)Mandibular molar distal: the mandibular MB cusp in the maxillary first molar's central fossa; the maxillary MB cusp mesial of the buccal grooveDivision 1: proclined maxillary incisors, large overjet. Division 2: retroclined maxillary centrals (laterals often flared) and a deep overbite
III (about 5%)Mandibular molar mesial: the maxillary MB cusp over the embrasure between mandibular M1 and M2; the maxillary ML cusp in the mesial pit of mandibular M2Prognathic profile; anterior crossbite or edge-to-edge

CR, MIP and CO

  • Centric relation (CR): the condyles in their most anterosuperior position against the posterior slopes of the articular eminences, on the thinnest avascular part of the discs. It is set by the joints and muscles, not the teeth, it is reproducible, and it is the musculoskeletally stable position (older definitions said "most retruded").
  • Maximum intercuspation (MIP, ICP): the teeth fully interdigitated, wherever the condyles are. It is learned by the neuromuscular system and changes with the teeth.
  • Centric occlusion (CO): tooth contact with the condyles in CR. In the course, CO never means MIP.
  • About 90% of people have a slide from CR contact into MIP (about 1–1¼ mm); only about 10% close straight into MIP.

Optimal functional occlusion

  1. With the condyles in CR, even, simultaneous contact of all posterior teeth; the anterior teeth touch more lightly.
  2. Every contact loads the tooth along its long axis (cusp tips against flat fossae or marginal ridges); the PDL takes vertical force well and horizontal force poorly. Tripodization puts three contacts around each cusp tip; cusp-to-fossa point contacts are simpler and also axial.
  3. In a lateral excursion, working-side contacts immediately disocclude the nonworking side; canine guidance is preferred.
  4. In protrusion, the anterior teeth immediately disocclude all posterior teeth.
  5. In the upright head and alert feeding positions, posterior contacts are heavier than anterior ones.

This is mutually protected occlusion: the posterior teeth stop closure and protect the anterior teeth; the anterior teeth guide excursions and protect the posterior teeth.

Guidance schemes

  • Canine guidance: in a lateral excursion only the canines touch. Canines have the longest roots and the best crown-to-root ratio, sit in dense bone, and when only they touch, fewer elevator muscles fire.
  • Group function: several working-side teeth share the guidance, ideally the canine, the premolars and sometimes the MB cusp of the first molar, with nothing touching on the nonworking side.
  • Bilateral balanced occlusion: contact on both sides in every excursion; used for complete dentures, not natural teeth (it wears teeth and loads them sideways).
  • With no symptoms, copy the patient's existing guidance. Anterior guidance is the most important and most controllable determinant.
MovementContact (if it happens)Note
ProtrusiveDistal inclines of maxillary cusps against mesial inclines of mandibular cuspsRemove posterior protrusive contacts before anterior restorations
Working (laterotrusive)Lingual inclines of maxillary buccal cusps against buccal inclines of mandibular buccal cusps (and lingual-to-lingual)Buccal-to-buccal is the more acceptable
Nonworking (mediotrusive)Facial incline of the maxillary lingual cusp against the lingual incline of the mandibular buccal cuspThe most damaging: it raises elevator muscle activity

The paths an opposing cusp traces across a maxillary tooth: protrusive toward the mesial, working toward the buccal, nonworking toward the mesiopalatal; on a mandibular tooth each is reversed.

Determinants of occlusal morphology

Mandibular movement is set by a posterior determinant (the TMJ: condylar guidance, fixed; the dentist cannot change it) and an anterior determinant (anterior guidance, variable). The nearer a tooth is to one of them, the more that one shapes its cusps.

Taller cusps allowedShorter cusps needed
Steeper condylar guidance (articular eminence)Flatter condylar guidance
More vertical overlap (overbite)More horizontal overlap (overjet)
Occlusal plane less parallel to the condylar guidanceOcclusal plane more parallel to the condylar guidance
Flatter curve of SpeeMore acute curve of Spee (the posterior-most teeth)
Less lateral translation (Bennett) or immediate side shiftMore lateral translation or immediate side shift; a rotating condyle that moves upward

Horizontal determinants change the angle between the laterotrusive and mediotrusive grooves on a tooth: it widens the farther the tooth is from the rotating condyle and with more lateral translation, and it narrows with a greater intercondylar distance (the one that decreases it).

Numbers and concepts

  • The postural (rest) position is 2–4 mm below MIP; that gap is the freeway space (rest vertical dimension minus occlusal vertical dimension). The closest speaking space ("s" sounds) is about 1–2 mm.
  • Concepts: Bonwill (4-inch triangle, bilateral balance), Monson (sphere), gnathology and Stuart (canine disclusion), D'Amico (canine-protected). Most dentistry is conformative (work to the existing MIP); a reorganized approach builds a new occlusion at CR from a CR record.
  • Implants move 2–3 µm versus about 28 µm for a tooth: keep implant contacts light on tapping, even on clenching, and off posterior implants in excursions.
full.da-tmj:
What's tested
  • The TMJ's parts: the disc, the retrodiscal laminae, the two compartments and the ligaments
  • Which muscles open, close, protrude, retrude and move the jaw to each side
  • Posselt's envelope: rotation, translation and the numbers; the working and nonworking condyles; Bennett movement
  • Articulators, the facebow and the records
  • TMD causes and care, occlusal trauma and mobility, and wear

The joint

The TMJ is a ginglymoarthrodial joint (hinge plus gliding) and a compound joint: the condyle, the temporal bone's articular fossa and eminence, and the articular disc, which acts as a third, non-ossified bone. Its articular surfaces are covered with dense fibrous connective tissue, not hyaline cartilage, so they can repair.

  • Disc: dense fibrous tissue, avascular and non-innervated in its center. The intermediate zone is the thinnest (where the condyle sits in CR); the posterior band is the thickest.
  • Retrodiscal tissue (vascular, innervated, where pain comes from): the superior retrodiscal lamina is elastic and attaches the disc to the tympanic plate, pulling it back as the mouth opens; the inferior lamina is collagen and attaches the disc to the condyle, limiting its forward rotation.
  • Two compartments with synovial fluid: the lower (disc to condyle) is where rotation happens; the upper (fossa to disc) is where translation happens.
  • Superior lateral pterygoid: attaches to the disc and condylar neck and works on closing (the power stroke), stabilizing the condyle against the eminence.
LigamentWhat it does
Collateral (discal)Ties the disc to the condyle's poles, so the disc rides with the condyle; allows rotation in the lower compartment
CapsularEncloses the joint, holds the synovial fluid, gives proprioception
Temporomandibular, outer oblique portionLimits rotational opening: once it is taut (about 20–25 mm), the condyle must translate
Temporomandibular, inner horizontal portionLimits posterior movement of the condyle and disc, protecting the retrodiscal tissue
Stylomandibular (accessory)Limits excessive protrusion
Sphenomandibular (accessory)No significant limiting effect
MovementMuscles
Elevation (closing)Temporalis, masseter, medial pterygoid
Depression (opening)Inferior lateral pterygoid, suprahyoids (digastric) and infrahyoids
ProtrusionInferior lateral pterygoids (both), superficial masseter, medial pterygoids
RetrusionPosterior temporalis, deep masseter, digastric
To the rightRight temporalis and masseter; left inferior lateral pterygoid and left medial pterygoid

A lateral pterygoid acting alone pulls its condyle forward and medially, so the jaw swings to the opposite side. The temporalis has three parts: anterior (elevates), middle and posterior (retrudes).

Movement

  • Posselt's envelope (sagittal border movements, traced at the incisors): from CR the jaw first rotates (a pure hinge) to about 20–25 mm interincisal opening; then the condyles translate down the eminences to maximum opening, about 40–60 mm. Border movements are reproducible; functional movements (chewing, speech) happen inside the envelope.
  • In a lateral excursion the working (rotating) condyle turns about a vertical axis and shifts a little laterally (laterotrusion); the nonworking (orbiting) condyle moves forward, down and medially (mediotrusion).
  • Bennett movement (lateral translation) is the bodily shift of the mandible toward the working side. It may be immediate (a side shift, in millimeters, early in the movement) or progressive (the Bennett angle, the orbiting condyle's path against the sagittal plane, seen from above). More of it calls for shorter cusps and wider central fossae.
  • Function: the teeth meet in MIP only about 17.5 minutes a day (about 1,800 chewing strokes and 500 swallowing contacts). A normal adult swallow brings the teeth together to steady the mandible. The jaw rests (the postural position) a few millimeters below MIP; "s" sounds bring the teeth closest without touching; "f" and "v" put the maxillary incisal edges on the lower lip.

Articulators and records

KindWhat it can do
Nonadjustable (hinge)Accurate in one position only (the one it was mounted in); restorations need more adjustment in the mouth
Semi-adjustableSets the sagittal condylar inclination and the Bennett angle from a facebow and records; arbitrary values (about 30°) when no record is taken
Fully adjustableProgrammed from a pantograph and a kinematic facebow; least adjustment
  • Arcon: the condylar element is on the lower member, like the anatomy; non-arcon puts it on the upper member.
  • The facebow relates the maxillary cast to the hinge axis (an arbitrary facebow lands within about 2–5 mm of the true axis; a kinematic facebow finds it). The mandibular cast goes on with an interocclusal record.
  • A protrusive record sets the condylar inclination; lateral records set the Bennett angle. A cast mounted in CR can be closed into MIP, but a cast mounted in MIP can never find CR.

Temporomandibular disorders

  • Muscle disorders are the most common (about half), then intracapsular (joint) disorders (about a third). Okeson's five etiologic factors: occlusal conditions, trauma, emotional stress, deep pain input and parafunction.
  • Occlusion matters in two ways: an acute change (a high crown) triggers protective co-contraction and muscle pain; orthopedic instability (the joints and the teeth not stable at the same time, with a CR-to-MIP discrepancy greater than about 3–4 mm) loads the joint. Bruxism is centrally mediated; occlusion does not start it.
  • A disc displaced with reduction gives a click on opening and often on closing (a reciprocal click); without reduction (closed lock) limits opening to about 25–30 mm with deflection toward the affected side.
  • Treat with reversible care first (counseling, medication, physical therapy, a flat-plane stabilization splint); irreversible care (equilibration, crowns, orthodontics, surgery) only when needed. Prophylactic equilibration is not supported. The rule of thirds: a discrepancy in the first third of the tooth, selective grinding; the middle third, crowns or minor orthodontics; beyond, major orthodontics or surgery.

Trauma, mobility and wear

  • Primary occlusal trauma: excessive force on a normal periodontium. Secondary: normal or excessive force on a reduced periodontium. Signs: increasing mobility, a widened PDL space, fremitus. Trauma does not start gingivitis or periodontitis or cause attachment loss, and it is reversible; adjust the occlusion after the infection is treated.
  • A tooth intrudes about 28 µm under load; an implant moves 2–3 µm (no PDL). Miller's index: 0 none, 1 barely distinguishable, 2 horizontal up to 1 mm, 3 more than 1 mm or vertical (depressible).
  • Wear: attrition (tooth on tooth), abrasion (an outside agent; toothpaste abrasivity matters more than the brush), erosion (acid; palatal surfaces of the maxillary incisors with reflux or bulimia) and abfraction (flexure; not proven clinically).
  • Complete dentures use bilateral balanced or lingualized occlusion (the maxillary lingual cusps in the mandibular fossae), because stability matters most; denture teeth come anatomic (about 30–33°), semi-anatomic or flat (0°).
full.f1-biomol:
What's tested
  • Bond types and their strength, water's properties, pH, buffers and the bicarbonate system
  • Amino acid classes, the side-chain pKa values (histidine near 6), chirality and the four levels of protein structure
  • Fibrous and globular proteins: keratin and collagen, the four structural classes of globular proteins, what stabilizes a fold and why proteins have quaternary structure
  • Collagen: Gly-X-Y, the triple helix, vitamin C–dependent hydroxylation, the synthesis steps inside and outside the cell, and the collagen diseases
  • Hemoglobin: T and R states, cooperativity, the Bohr effect, CO2 and 2,3-BPG, fetal hemoglobin, and myoglobin for contrast
  • Carbohydrates: aldoses and ketoses, epimers and anomers, the disaccharides (sucrose and caries), glycogen, glycoproteins and GAGs
  • Lipids: fatty acids, triglycerides, membrane lipids, cholesterol, lipoproteins, β-oxidation and lipogenesis
  • Nucleic acids: purines and pyrimidines, nucleoside versus nucleotide, base pairing, antiparallel strands, chromatin packing

Chemistry that the rest depends on

An atom's valence electrons decide how it bonds: atoms share, gain or lose electrons to fill their outer shell. Covalent bonds (shared electrons) are the strongest. Electronegativity, an atom's pull on shared electrons, sets the type: equal sharing is nonpolar covalent (C–C and C–H, the carbon skeletons of biomolecules); unequal sharing is polar covalent (O–H), leaving partial charges; a difference big enough to strip electrons away makes ions, held by an ionic bond. The noncovalent forces are weaker and reversible; strongest to weakest, they are ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds (a hydrogen on N, O or F attracted to another N, O or F) and van der Waals forces (attractions between atoms whose electrons are unevenly spread). Covalent bonds build a cell's large molecules; noncovalent ones hold their shapes and let molecules recognize each other. Everything above a protein's primary structure is held by noncovalent forces, plus covalent disulfide bonds.

Water's O–H bonds are polar, so water is a good solvent for polar and charged molecules (it forms hydration shells around ions) and a poor one for nonpolar ones, which it pushes together (hydrophobic interactions, the reason lipids form micelles and bilayers). Its hydrogen bonds give it the properties that suit life: ice is less dense than liquid water (its hydrogen bonds are more ordered, so it floats), a high specific heat (1 cal/g/°C, so temperature stays steady), high surface tension (cohesion is water holding to water; adhesion is water holding to another substance) and its power as a solvent. They also give it a high boiling point (100 °C). Water is amphoteric (it can act as an acid or a base) and ionizes only slightly, into equal amounts of H3O+ and OH−.

Blood pH is held at 7.35–7.45, since small changes disturb protein structure. Metabolism makes mostly acid, and CO2 is the main acidic product. A buffer resists pH change best when the pH equals its pKa, works only over a limited range, and too much acid or base overwhelms it. The bicarbonate system is the main buffer of blood and extracellular fluid: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−. The first step can happen without an enzyme, but carbonic anhydrase in red cells and other tissues speeds it.

Amino acids and protein structure

An amino acid has an α carbon carrying an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen and a side chain (R). At physiological pH it is a zwitterion (NH3+ and COO−). All except glycine are chiral, and proteins use L amino acids (L and D name the configuration, not the direction a molecule turns polarized light). Peptide bonds are planar with partial double-bond character.

GroupAmino acidsSide-chain pKa
Acidic (negative)Aspartate (D), glutamate (E)3.9, 4.3
Basic (positive)Lysine (K), arginine (R), histidine (H)10.5, 12.5, 6.0
Other to knowCysteine (disulfides)8.3

Histidine's pKa near 6 lets it gain or lose a proton near physiological pH, so it buffers and works in active sites (and in hemoglobin's Bohr effect). The aromatic amino acids absorb UV light; tryptophan and tyrosine do most of the absorbing at 280 nm. Modified amino acids: hydroxyproline and hydroxylysine (collagen), γ-carboxyglutamate (vitamin K–dependent clotting factors), selenocysteine (selenoenzymes).

  • Primary: the amino acid sequence, joined by peptide bonds.
  • Secondary: backbone hydrogen bonds. The α-helix is right-handed, with 3.6 residues and 5.4 Å per turn (proline breaks helices); β-sheets are parallel or antiparallel (antiparallel is more stable); β-turns reverse the chain and are rich in proline and glycine.
  • Tertiary: the folded 3D shape. A protein folds into its most stable structure, driven by forming many intramolecular hydrogen bonds and by burying hydrophobic side chains inside, away from water, with polar ones outside. Helices and sheets make up the core, because their hydrogen bonds satisfy the backbone's polar N–H and C=O groups there. The fold is only marginally stable, so parts of a protein can flex, and that motion is what lets it bind ligands, catalyze and change shape. Proteins larger than about 250 amino acids usually fold into two or more domains, compact units that are stable on their own.
  • Quaternary: the arrangement of several chains (subunits), as in hemoglobin, a tetramer. A single-chain protein has none. Identical subunits make a homo-oligomer and different ones a hetero-oligomer (the Greek letters that name subunits have nothing to do with α-helices or β-sheets). Globular subunits are held together noncovalently, mostly by hydrophobic interactions; fibrous proteins are often joined covalently. Its advantages: stability (a lower surface-to-volume ratio buries surface that would face water), genetic economy and efficiency (small subunits are made more accurately than one huge chain), catalytic sites built where subunits meet, and cooperativity and regulation.

Fibrous proteins run mostly along one axis, are strong and insoluble, and do structural jobs; globular proteins are soluble and fold to maximize internal bonds and minimize contact with water (fibrous ones maximize contact between molecules). α-Keratin (hair) is a coiled coil: two right-handed α-helices twisted around each other in a left-handed supercoil, with side chains repeating every 7 residues; these build the 10 nm intermediate filaments. Silk fibroin and β-keratin (feathers) are stacked β-sheets with an alternating Gly-Ala/Ser sequence. Most globular proteins belong to one of four structural classes: all α, all β, α/β (helices and strands intermingled) and α+β (separate α-helical and β-sheet domains).

Diseases of protein structure and folding: a faulty subunit of a repeating structural protein (osteogenesis imperfecta, collagen), an unwanted polymer (deoxygenated sickle hemoglobin) and prions, misfolded proteins that make normal copies misfold (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease).

Collagen

The most abundant protein in the body (about a third of all protein), a fibrous protein laid down in the ECM by fibroblasts. There are 28 types; type I is over 90% (bone, dentin, PDL, skin, tendon, blood vessels). Type II is cartilage, type III is reticular fibers, blood vessels and granulation tissue (these three are fiber-forming), and type IV is the network collagen of basement membrane. The sequence repeats Gly-X-Y, X often proline and Y often hydroxyproline, and collagen has three unusual amino acids: 4-hydroxyproline, 3-hydroxyproline and 5-hydroxylysine. So much glycine, proline and hydroxyproline keeps each chain from forming an α-helix or β-sheet: it is an extended left-handed helix of 3.3 residues per turn. Three chains wind into a right-handed triple helix, tropocollagen (about 300 nm long and 1.4 nm wide). Every third residue faces the crowded center, where only glycine fits; proline and hydroxyproline suit the helix's angles, and hydroxyproline's hydrogen bonds between the chains hold it together.

Hydroxyproline's hydrogen bonds stabilize the triple helix, so without vitamin C the helix is weak: scurvy brings bleeding, swollen gums, loose teeth, poor wound healing and petechiae. Tropocollagens line up staggered, which gives fibrils a banded look with a 68 nm repeat; the dark bands are 40 nm gaps (hole zones) between molecules, which hold carbohydrate and are thought to be nucleation sites for bone mineral. The sugars on hydroxylysine help organize fibril assembly. Lysyl oxidase's cross-links, within and between molecules, give the fibers their strength. Osteogenesis imperfecta (mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2, the type I genes): brittle bones, blue sclerae, hearing loss and dentinogenesis imperfecta. Ehlers-Danlos: stretchy skin and loose joints.

Hemoglobin

Hemoglobin (α2β2), an O2 transporter, is the classic allosteric protein. It is 95% of a red cell's cytosolic protein, and red cells hold about 85% of the body's heme and 70% of its iron. It carries O2 on Fe2+ in heme, which has six ligands: four porphyrin nitrogens, the proximal histidine His F8 (the 8th residue of the F helix, the same in every globin) as the fifth, and O2 as the sixth. In deoxyhemoglobin the iron sits about 0.06 nm out of the heme plane; O2 binding pulls it about 0.04 nm toward the plane, dragging His F8 and the F helix with it, which breaks salt bridges at the subunit interfaces: one αβ pair turns about 15° against the other, and the tetramer shifts from the T (tense, deoxy) to the R (relaxed, oxy) state. That makes binding cooperative (each O2 bound makes the next bind more easily) and the curve sigmoidal, so hemoglobin fills in the lungs (pO2 about 100 mmHg) and gives up O2 in capillaries (about 40 mmHg). P50, the pO2 at half saturation, is 26 mmHg for HbA; a higher P50 means a lower affinity. Myoglobin is a monomer that stores O2 in muscle, with a hyperbolic curve and a higher affinity at every pO2, so it would release little O2 in capillaries.

Right shift (lower affinity, more O2 released)Left shift (higher affinity)
↑ H+ (lower pH: the Bohr effect), ↑ CO2, ↑ 2,3-BPG, ↑ temperatureFetal hemoglobin (α2γ2, binds 2,3-BPG poorly), carbon monoxide, ↓ temperature, alkalosis

The Bohr effect: deoxyhemoglobin binds H+ more tightly than oxyhemoglobin, so protons lower O2 affinity and O2 binding lowers proton binding. In tissues, CO2 hydration and glycolysis make H+, which hemoglobin takes up as it releases O2 where it is needed most; in the lungs, turning bicarbonate back into CO2 to breathe out uses up H+, which helps hemoglobin load O2. Chloride ions also lower affinity. 2,3-BPG is an allosteric effector: a very negative molecule that binds away from the iron, in the central cavity between the two β chains of deoxyhemoglobin, held by positive residues (His 2, Lys 82, His 143 and the amino terminus). Fetal γ chains have serine in place of His 143, so HbF binds 2,3-BPG less tightly and holds O2 more tightly, pulling it across the placenta from the mother's HbA. Sickle cell disease comes from glutamate → valine at position 6 of β-globin (HbS): deoxygenated HbS polymerizes and blocks small vessels. Thalassemias make too little of one chain; Cooley's anemia (β-thalassemia major) has no β chains.

Carbohydrates

Simple carbohydrates are (CH2O)n with n of 3 or more, named by their number of carbons (triose, pentose, hexose) and by their carbonyl: aldoses (aldehyde) or ketoses (ketone). Glycosidic bonds join them: two units make a disaccharide, 3–10 an oligosaccharide, more than 10 a polysaccharide. Isomers share a formula: positional isomers differ in where a group sits, geometric isomers in the arrangement at a rigid part, and optical isomers at a chiral carbon (one with four different groups). Enantiomers are mirror images (D and L) with the same physical and chemical properties but different biological ones; they turn polarized light in opposite directions. Epimers differ at only one chiral carbon (not the carbonyl carbon): glucose and galactose at C-4, glucose and mannose at C-2. In solution the carbonyl reacts with one of the sugar's own OH groups to close a ring (a hemiacetal, or a hemiketal for a ketose): a six-membered pyranose (glucose in solution, a C-1–O–C-5 ring) or a five-membered furanose (fructose, C-2–O–C-5). The open chain is under 0.01%. Ring closure makes C-1 a new chiral, anomeric carbon, giving the α and β anomers, which interconvert (mutarotation, sped by acid or base). Sugars with a free anomeric carbon are reducing sugars. A reducing sugar's carbonyl can join the amino group of a protein's lysine as a Schiff base: glycation, which is nonenzymatic and distinct from enzymatic glycosylation. Glycation products cross-link proteins, build up when blood glucose runs high and are thought to underlie some of diabetes's damage (HbA1c is glycated hemoglobin).

  • Sucrose (glucose α1→β2 fructose) is nonreducing, since its bond ties up both anomeric carbons. Streptococcus mutans ferments it to lactic acid and uses it to build sticky, water-insoluble extracellular glucans (dextran-based, with α-1,3 bonds) for plaque.
  • Lactose (galactose β-1,4 glucose) is split by lactase from the intestinal villi (too little lactase is lactose intolerance); maltose (glucose α-1,4 glucose) comes from starch digestion.
  • Glycogen: glucose in α-1,4 chains with α-1,6 branches, the store in liver and muscle. Cellulose: β-1,4 glucose (plants), which humans can't digest: insoluble dietary fiber. Chitin: β-1,4 N-acetylglucosamine (fungal walls, insect and crustacean shells).
  • Sugars attach to other molecules by N-glycosidic bonds (to an –NH, as in nucleotides) or O-glycosidic bonds (to an –OH); every sugar–sugar bond is O-glycosidic. The glycoconjugates are glycoproteins, glycolipids (blood group and tumor antigens, gangliosides) and proteoglycans.
  • Glycoproteins: glycosylation is the most common change made to a protein after translation. Most plasma proteins are glycoproteins (albumin is not); membrane glycoproteins serve in cell recognition and as antigens, and mucins, about one-third serine and threonine, are heavily O-glycosylated lubricants of the gut and urogenital tract. N-linked glycans go on asparagine in an Asn-X-Ser/Thr sequence, from a dolichol-linked precursor added in the ER, then are trimmed and built up in the ER and Golgi. O-linked glycans are added one sugar at a time to serine or threonine, mostly in the Golgi, starting with GalNAc (the Tn antigen, high on tumor cells). Mannose-6-phosphate sends enzymes to lysosomes.
  • ABO blood groups are sugars on red cell glycoproteins and glycolipids: the A allele makes a glycosyltransferase that adds GalNAc to the H antigen, the B allele one that adds galactose, and O alleles an inactive enzyme, so the H antigen stays as it is.
  • Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs): unbranched, negatively charged chains of repeating disaccharides, one sugar an amino sugar: hyaluronic acid, chondroitin sulfate, keratan sulfate, dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate and heparin (released by mast cells and basophils; an anticoagulant). They bind large amounts of water, making the ECM's gel and a molecular sieve, and give synovial fluid and the vitreous their resilience. On a core protein, linked through a galactose-galactose-xylose trisaccharide to serine, they form proteoglycans (about 95% carbohydrate; glycoproteins carry much less). In cartilage, monomers such as aggrecan (with keratan and chondroitin sulfate chains) bind one hyaluronic acid noncovalently, held by link proteins, in large aggregates.

Lipids

Lipids are a varied group defined by dissolving in nonpolar solvents (ether, chloroform) and hardly at all in water, because they are mostly hydrocarbon (nonpolar C–H bonds); unlike the other biomolecules, they don't form one kind of polymer. They store energy, form membranes, insulate and lubricate, and act as hormones. A fatty acid is a carboxyl group on a hydrocarbon chain, usually 16–20 carbons: the chain is hydrophobic and the carboxyl hydrophilic (it gives up a proton), so a fatty acid is amphipathic, one molecule with both a hydrophobic and a hydrophilic part. Fatty acids are saturated (no double bonds, the most hydrogens; they pack tightly) or unsaturated (one or more cis double bonds, which kink the chain and lower the melting point). Triglycerides are glycerol (a three-carbon alcohol) with three fatty acids joined by ester bonds: the main energy store, kept in adipose tissue, and about 35% of the calories in a Western diet. Membrane lipids are amphipathic, which lets them form bilayers: phospholipids (glycerophospholipids are the most abundant; sphingolipids are built on sphingosine instead of glycerol), glycolipids (only on the outer leaflet, as recognition markers) and cholesterol, the most rigid and hydrophobic, which steadies fluidity. The bilayer is a two-dimensional fluid in which lipids and proteins diffuse sideways. Carotenoids (β-carotene, a provitamin turned into vitamin A) and steroids (four fused rings: cholesterol and the sex hormones) are built from isoprene units. Chylomicrons carry dietary fat from enterocytes through the lymph; LDL carries cholesterol to tissues; HDL brings it back to the liver.

Lipolysis splits triglycerides (lipases). Fatty acids enter the mitochondrion on the carnitine shuttle and undergo β-oxidation in the matrix to acetyl-CoA. Lipogenesis runs in the cytosol of the liver when carbohydrate is plentiful; acetyl-CoA leaves the mitochondrion as citrate.

Nucleic acids

The central dogma: DNA copies itself (replication), is transcribed into mRNA, and mRNA is translated into protein. Nucleotides also carry energy (ATP, GTP) and serve in signaling, coenzymes and metabolic regulation; kinases add the phosphates that turn NMPs into NDPs and NTPs. A nucleotide is a pentose, a phosphate and a nitrogenous base; a nucleoside is the base and sugar without the phosphate. Purines (adenine, guanine) have two rings and break down to uric acid; pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have one. Phosphodiester bonds link the 5′ phosphate of one nucleotide to the 3′ OH of the next, making a sugar-phosphate backbone with the bases off to the side; a strand runs from its 5′ end (free phosphate) to its 3′ end (free OH). The two DNA strands are antiparallel and complementary, each pair a purine with a pyrimidine: A–T with two hydrogen bonds, G–C with three (so GC-rich DNA is harder to separate). DNA versus RNA: DNA has deoxyribose (no 2′-OH), thymine and two strands; RNA has ribose, whose 2′-OH makes it easier to hydrolyze (RNA is made to be used and broken down), uracil in place of thymine, and usually one strand. About 6 feet of DNA fits in each cell as chromatin: DNA wraps around an octamer of histones (four kinds, two of each, with H1 outside) as the nucleosome, then the 10 nm "beads on a string" (nucleosomes joined by linker DNA), the 30 nm fiber and the mitotic chromosome (46 in a human cell). Bacterial DNA is one circular, supercoiled double-stranded chromosome with little protein, in the nucleoid, plus plasmids, small circles that replicate on their own and can pass genes between bacteria.

What's tested

  • The cytoskeleton, the cell cycle and apoptosis (caspases)

  • Ion channel gating, equilibrium potentials (Nernst), the resting potential and the Na+/K+ pump

Cells and organelles

Prokaryotes (bacteria) have no nucleus or membrane-bound organelles: a nucleoid, ribosomes, storage granules, a cell wall, often flagella (for movement only) and pili. Eukaryotes (human cells, fungi such as Candida albicans, parasites) have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Every cell has DNA, cytosol, ribosomes (not membrane-bound) and a plasma membrane. All human cells are eukaryotic; pathogens can be prokaryotic (bacteria), eukaryotic (fungi, parasites) or neither (viruses, which are not cells). Cell walls differ: peptidoglycan in bacteria (Gram-positive bacteria stain purple, Gram-negative pink), chitin in fungi, cellulose in plants; human cells have none.

Endocytosis takes material in: phagocytosis (pseudopods engulf large particles such as bacteria into phagosomes), pinocytosis (small pits take in fluid) and receptor-mediated endocytosis (ligand-bound receptors in clathrin-coated pits, as for LDL; the vesicle becomes an endosome, and the receptor is often recycled while the cargo is degraded). Exocytosis sends material out, as when pancreatic acinar cells release their stored proenzymes.

The cytoskeleton is three protein polymers held together by noncovalent bonds so it can rebuild quickly. Microtubules (tubulin, about 24 nm, the thickest and most rigid) grow from microtubule organizing centers (centrioles, basal bodies): motor-protein highways (in axons they carry vesicles from the cell body to the terminal), the mitotic spindle and the core of cilia and flagella. Actin filaments (microfilaments, polymerized G-actin, about 7 nm, the thinnest) support microvilli and the cell surface, drive cell movement and, with myosin, muscle contraction; defects in the actin-binding protein dystrophin cause most muscular dystrophy. Intermediate filaments (about 10 nm; all related to keratin, with a kind for each cell type: cytokeratins, vimentin, desmin, the nuclear lamins) are rope-like, take tension, link the nucleus to the membrane and anchor desmosomes and hemidesmosomes; defects in some cause severe skin blistering. The extracellular matrix (collagen, elastin, fibronectin, laminin, proteoglycans, hyaluronic acid), made by fibroblasts, attaches to the cell's actin through integrins.

The cell cycle: G1 (growth; a cell that stops dividing rests in G0 until signaled back), S (DNA replication), G2 (proofreading, repair and growth), M (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, then cytokinesis); checkpoints and outside signals control the passage. Apoptosis is programmed, active, non-inflammatory death carried out by caspases, which digest DNA, proteins and organelles; the plasma membrane stays intact until the end and macrophages eat the remains. Necrosis, death from acute injury, spills the cell and inflames. Too much cell death or too little (cancer) causes disease.

Cells signal directly (through gap junctions, or one cell's membrane protein binding another's receptor) or by releasing a signal (hormones act at very low concentrations, transmitters at high local ones). Only a cell with the matching receptor responds; the signal is relayed by phosphorylation and second messengers (cAMP, Ca2+), often ending at transcription factors that change which proteins the cell makes. Tight junctions (zonula occludens) seal neighboring epithelial cells; gap junctions (connexons of six connexins) pass ions and molecules under about 1,000 Da and electrical current from cell to cell; desmosomes hold cells together and hemidesmosomes attach them to the basal lamina.

Membranes and transport

Homeostasis keeps the internal environment steady by negative feedback: sensors monitor a regulated variable, a comparator checks it against the set point (the middle of the normal range), and effectors push it back. Body water is about 60% of body weight in a man (42 L at 70 kg), about 50% in a woman and up to 75% in an infant, roughly two-thirds inside cells (ICF) and one-third outside (ECF: interstitial fluid and plasma). ECF is rich in Na+ and Cl−; ICF in K+, Mg2+, phosphates and protein anions (ICF Na+ 15, K+ 120, Cl− 20 mM; interstitial fluid Na+ 145, K+ 4.5, Cl− 116 mM). Water crosses freely, so osmolality is the same in every compartment; plasma osmolarity is about 290 mOsm/L (normal 285–295).

The fluid mosaic membrane: a phospholipid bilayer (amphipathic lipids, hydrophilic heads out and hydrophobic tails in, which reseal a small tear by themselves) with integral (transmembrane) and peripheral proteins, cholesterol (cuts permeability to small water-soluble molecules, steadies the outer leaflet and keeps the membrane fluid in the cold), carbohydrates on the outer face only (glycoproteins and glycolipids form the glycocalyx, used for cell recognition and adhesion), and lipid rafts rich in cholesterol and sphingolipids that act as signaling platforms. The two leaflets differ in composition. Membrane proteins (up to half the membrane) serve as channels, carriers and pumps, receptors, enzymes and structural links.

Diffusion is passive and downhill, driven by random thermal motion; with no gradient there is no net flux. For an uncharged solute (Fick's law) the rate rises with surface area, the concentration gradient and lipid solubility, and falls with molecular size and membrane thickness; a voltage across the membrane doesn't affect it. Gases and small uncharged or lipid-soluble molecules cross the bilayer easily; ions, other charged molecules and hydrophilic molecules larger than about 4 Å (glucose, amino acids) need a protein. A charged solute follows its electrochemical gradient (concentration and voltage together), so it doesn't always move down its concentration gradient. Osmosis is water moving toward the side with more osmotically active particles; it is always passive (there are no water pumps), through the bilayer and aquaporins. Osmotic pressure (van't Hoff: π = gσRTC) depends on the number of particles, not their size or mass (g, particles per molecule: NaCl 2, MgCl2 3, glucose 1), and on how well they cross, the reflection coefficient σ: 0 means the solute crosses freely and draws no water; 1 means it is impermeant and exerts its full pressure. Normal saline (0.9% NaCl, 154 mM) is about 286 mOsm/L.

  • Hypotonic solution: water enters, the cell swells (and can lyse). Hypertonic: water leaves, the cell shrinks. Isotonic: no change. Pure water given into a vein is hypotonic and lyses red cells.
  • Tonicity is a solution's effect on cell volume, so it counts only the solutes that can't cross the membrane; osmolarity counts every particle.
  • The Na+/K+ pump keeps cell volume: trapped protein anions draw water in, and the pump balances them by keeping Na+ (and with it Cl−) out. Block it (ouabain) and the cell gains NaCl and water and swells. Red cells that can't stretch (the small spheres of hereditary spherocytosis) burst more easily.

A carrier never opens to both sides at once: it binds the solute and cycles through shape changes, so it is slower than a channel and saturates. An ion channel is a gated pore with a selectivity filter. Its gating (opening and closing) responds to voltage (voltage-gated), a ligand outside (a transmitter: ligand-gated) or inside (Ca2+, second messengers, phosphorylation), or stretch (mechanically gated); leak channels stay open. Activation is opening in response to the stimulus; inactivation is a separate closing while the stimulus lasts.

Epithelial cells sit on a basal lamina, are joined by tight junctions (which seal the sheet, keep apical and basolateral proteins apart and set how leaky the path between cells is) and move solutes in one direction (vectorial transport), through the cells (transcellular) or between them (paracellular). The apical (luminal, brush border) and basolateral membranes carry different transporters: in the small intestine the basolateral Na+/K+ pump keeps cell Na+ low, apical SGLT1 brings glucose in uphill with Na+, and basolateral GLUTs let it out downhill. A transepithelial potential is the voltage between the lumen and the blood side; it drives charged solutes, as in Cl− secretion, where a lumen-negative potential pulls Na+ through the paracellular path and water follows.

Membrane potentials

Bulk solutions are electrically neutral; only a thin layer of charge at the membrane is separated (the membrane acts as a capacitor, ion channels as resistors). A membrane potential needs an ion gradient and a membrane permeable to that ion. The equilibrium (Nernst) potential of an ion is the voltage that exactly balances its concentration gradient, so it has no net movement: E = (60/z) log([out]/[in]) at 37 °C (2.3RT/F is about 60 mV; 61.5 mV more exactly). A tenfold gradient of a monovalent ion is worth 60 mV: with 100 mM inside and 10 mM outside, E(K+) is −60 mV; the same gradient of Cl− (z = −1) gives the opposite sign, and Ca2+ uses z = 2. With the body's concentrations E(K+) is about −85 to −90 mV and E(Na+) about +60 mV. Depolarization makes the inside less negative, hyperpolarization more negative, and repolarization brings it back toward rest.

A membrane permeable to several ions sits between their equilibrium potentials, nearest the one it conducts best. A resting nerve's K+ conductance (through K+ leak channels that are always open) far exceeds its Na+ conductance, so the resting potential (about −70 mV; −10 to −100 mV across cell types) sits close to E(K+). In the pump-leak model the Na+/K+ pump builds the gradients and the leaks spend them; its own electrogenic current adds only a few millivolts, so blocking the pump lets the potential fall only slowly, as the gradients run down.

The action potential

  • Threshold (about −55 mV): a stimulus opens enough voltage-gated Na+ channels that Na+ entry depolarizes the membrane further and opens more (positive feedback). Below threshold, potentials are graded (their size follows the stimulus); a hyperpolarizing stimulus never fires one.
  • Upstroke and overshoot: Na+ conductance peaks and the potential heads toward E(Na+) but doesn't reach it, about 100 mV above rest. All-or-none: a bigger stimulus doesn't make a bigger action potential.
  • Repolarization: Na+ channels inactivate and slower voltage-gated K+ channels (delayed rectifiers) open, so K+ leaves (negative feedback).
  • Afterhyperpolarization: K+ channels are slow to close, so the potential dips below rest.

The voltage-gated Na+ channel has two gates. The activation (m) gate is closed at rest and opens fast on depolarization; the inactivation (h) gate is open at rest and closes more slowly, ending the Na+ current even while the membrane stays depolarized, and stays shut for a few milliseconds. The channel can open again only after repolarization has reset both gates. The delayed-rectifier K+ channel opens slowly and closes only when the voltage returns to rest.

During the absolute refractory period the Na+ inactivation gates are closed and no stimulus can fire another action potential. The relative refractory period follows and overlaps the afterhyperpolarization: some Na+ channels are still inactivated and K+ channels are still open, so only a larger-than-normal stimulus works. An action potential spreads by local currents that bring the next patch of membrane to threshold; the patch behind it is refractory, so conduction runs one way, from the cell body to the terminals. Myelin (about 80% lipid, 20% protein) insulates the axon. It is made by oligodendrocytes in the CNS (one cell wraps segments of many axons, up to about 30) and by Schwann cells in the PNS (one cell, one segment of one axon). The action potential jumps from one node of Ranvier, where the voltage-gated Na+ channels are concentrated, to the next (saltatory conduction); larger diameter also speeds it.

Plasma K+ is normally 3.5–5.0 mmol/L. Hyperkalemia shrinks the K+ gradient, so E(K+) and the resting potential become less negative (raising outside K+ from 4.5 to 5.2 mM moves E(K+) from about −85 to −81 mV). A mild rise brings the membrane closer to threshold, but enough hyperkalemia locks the Na+ channels in the inactivated state, so nerve and muscle can't fire: weakness or paralysis (as in hyperkalemic periodic paralysis) and dangerous heart rhythms. Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes (2.2 mM outside gives about −104 mV), so a bigger stimulus is needed to reach threshold and excitability also falls.

Tetrodotoxin (pufferfish) blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels from outside, so threshold is never reached. Tetraethylammonium (TEA) blocks voltage-gated K+ channels: the action potential broadens, repolarizes more slowly and loses most of its afterhyperpolarization. Local anesthetics such as lidocaine cross the axon membrane as the uncharged base, pick up a proton inside, and the charged form blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels from the cytoplasmic side: a low dose slows the upstroke, a higher one stops action potentials. In inflamed, acidic tissue more of the drug is charged outside the nerve and less gets in, so the block is weaker.

Synapses and neurotransmitters

The CNS (brain and spinal cord) receives sensory (afferent) input from the PNS and sends motor (efferent) output through it: to skeletal muscle by the somatic system (voluntary) and to smooth muscle, heart and glands by the autonomic system (involuntary: sympathetic, parasympathetic and enteric). Sensory neurons are mostly unipolar, motor neurons multipolar, and interneurons lie within the CNS. A neuron has dendrites (input), a cell body (integration), an axon (conduction) and terminals (output). Electrical synapses pass current through gap junctions: very fast, two-way, mostly excitatory, coordinating cardiac and some smooth muscle. Chemical synapses are the most common, one-way with a short delay, and can excite or inhibit: the action potential opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the terminal, Ca2+ binds synaptotagmin, and the SNARE proteins (synaptobrevin on the vesicle, syntaxin and SNAP-25 on the membrane) fuse docked vesicles, releasing transmitter in quanta. It crosses the cleft (about 20 nm), binds receptors and is removed by reuptake or breakdown. What a transmitter does depends on its receptor, not on the transmitter itself. Ionotropic receptors are ion channels (fast); metabotropic receptors always act through a G protein and second messengers (cAMP, Ca2+, IP3), so they are slower. Small-molecule transmitters (amino acids, biogenic amines, purines, acetylcholine) are made and packaged in the terminal; neuropeptides (3–36 amino acids, such as substance P, enkephalin and vasopressin) are made in the cell body and carried down the axon along microtubules (fast axonal transport).

EPSPs depolarize (Na+ entry, usually glutamate); IPSPs hyperpolarize (Cl− entry, usually GABA or glycine; K+ exit does the same). Both are graded (their size follows the amount of transmitter) and local, and they add up at the axon hillock: temporal summation adds potentials that arrive one after another at one synapse; spatial summation adds potentials that arrive at the same time from different synapses. At skeletal muscle a motor unit is one motor neuron and all the fibers it supplies (a few for fine eye movements, hundreds or more for postural and power muscles). Acetylcholine opens nicotinic receptors at the motor end plate, and the graded end-plate potential triggers the muscle action potential.

What's tested
  • Replication: semiconservative, leading and lagging strands, the enzymes and their jobs, prokaryotes versus eukaryotes, telomeres and telomerase
  • RNA: how it differs from DNA, the RNA types and their share of cell RNA, ribosome sizes, nucleases
  • Prokaryotic transcription: RNA polymerase subunits (σ), promoters, termination, the lac operon
  • Eukaryotic transcription: the three RNA polymerases, TFIID and the TATA box, enhancers, acetylation and methylation
  • RNA processing: cap, splicing, poly(A) tail, editing, export and decay
  • Translation: tRNA charging, the ribosome's A, P and E sites, factors, wobble, bacterial versus eukaryotic
  • Mendel's laws, the test cross, modes of inheritance and pedigree risk; types of mutation, mutagens and the Ames test, and the classic mutation diseases, those of the teeth included
  • Oncogenes, tumor suppressors (two hits), DNA repair genes, inherited cancer syndromes, benign versus malignant

DNA replication

The two strands are antiparallel and complementary, so double-stranded DNA always has as much A as T and as much G as C (Chargaff's rule): DNA that is 30% A is also 30% T, and the other 40% is 20% G and 20% C. Replication is semiconservative (each daughter has one old and one new strand) and happens in S phase. It starts at origins (one in bacteria, many in eukaryotes) and runs both ways from each. Polymerases add only to a free 3′-OH, so new DNA grows 5′ → 3′. The leading strand is made continuously toward the fork; the lagging strand is made away from it in short Okazaki fragments, each also built 5′ → 3′.

DNA polymerases need a template and a primer (none can start a chain on its own), add nucleotides only to the 3′ end, and proofread: a 3′ → 5′ exonuclease backs up and removes a mismatched base, so they err only about once in 10 million nucleotides. Splitting off and hydrolyzing pyrophosphate drives each addition.

ProteinJob
DnaA (bacteria)Initiator: binds the origin first so helicase and primase can load
Helicase (DnaB)Breaks the hydrogen bonds and opens the fork
Single-strand binding proteinKeeps the separated strands from re-annealing
Topoisomerase (gyrase in bacteria)Relieves the overwinding ahead of the fork (fluoroquinolones block gyrase)
Primase (DnaG)Lays down the short RNA primer (5–10 nucleotides) that polymerases need
DNA polymerase III (bacteria)Main replicating enzyme, held on the DNA by the β sliding clamp; 3′ → 5′ exonuclease proofreading
DNA polymerase I (bacteria)Removes RNA primers (5′ → 3′ exonuclease), fills the gaps and also proofreads (3′ → 5′); polymerase II is a backup
DNA ligaseSeals the nicks between Okazaki fragments (phosphodiester bond)

Eukaryotes: many origins (up to about 100,000 in the human genome), slower (50–100 nucleotides a second versus about 1,000 in bacteria), polymerase α (with primase) starts each fragment, δ and ε do most of the copying and proofread, PCNA is the sliding clamp, RNase H (with a flap nuclease) removes primers. Linear chromosomes lose a little at each end every round, so they end in telomeres (TTAGGG repeats in humans). Telomerase, a reverse transcriptase carrying its own RNA template, extends them; it is active in germ cells, some adult stem cells, epidermal cells and activated lymphocytes, and in most cancers. Without it, short telomeres stop cell division, a limit on divisions that may guard against cancer.

The nature of RNA

RNA has ribose with a 2′-OH next to its 3′-OH, so dilute base hydrolyzes it (into a mix of 2′- and 3′-nucleotides) while DNA, lacking that OH, resists; RNA does resist dilute acid. That fits their jobs: the genetic material must last, while RNA is made, used and broken down. RNA uses uracil instead of thymine and is usually single-stranded.

RNAShare of cell RNAJob
rRNAAbout 80%Scaffold and catalyst of the ribosome (ribosomes are about two-thirds rRNA)
tRNAAbout 15%Carries one amino acid on its 3′ CCA end; cloverleaf in 2D, L-shaped in 3D
mRNAAbout 2–5%Carries the code; short-lived in bacteria (half-life about 2–3 minutes)
snRNASmallSplicing (in snRNPs)
Small non-coding RNAs (miRNA, siRNA)SmallPost-transcriptional silencing

Ribosomes: bacterial 70S = 30S (16S rRNA) + 50S (23S + 5S); eukaryotic 80S = 40S (18S) + 60S (28S, 5.8S, 5S). Bacterial mRNA is polycistronic (several proteins per message) with no introns; eukaryotic mRNA codes one protein and is spliced.

Nucleases (DNases and RNases) are phosphodiesterases that cut nucleic acids with water. Endonucleases cut inside a chain; exonucleases trim from an end (snake venom phosphodiesterase from the 3′ end, spleen phosphodiesterase from the 5′ end). Pancreatic RNase A is an endonuclease that cuts after pyrimidines (C or U).

Prokaryotic transcription

One RNA polymerase makes all RNA. The holoenzyme (α2ββ′σ) starts transcription; σ recognizes the promoter's −35 (TTGACA) and −10 Pribnow box (TATAAT) sequences. β and β′ form the catalytic site; rifampin binds β. RNA polymerase needs no primer, builds 5′ → 3′, opens about 14 bp (closed → open complex), and after 7–12 nucleotides σ leaves and the core enzyme elongates. It errs about once in 10,000 bases, far more often than DNA polymerase, which is tolerable because each gene is read into many transcripts. Termination is rho-dependent (rho, an ATP-dependent helicase) or intrinsic (a GC-rich hairpin followed by a run of U's, which pulls the RNA off).

The lac operon: lacZ, lacY, lacA share one promoter and operator. Negative control: the lacI repressor binds the operator; allolactose (from lactose) pulls it off. A lacI mutant with no working repressor makes the lac enzymes all the time (constitutive expression). Positive control: when glucose is low, cAMP rises and the CAP–cAMP complex binds upstream, bends the DNA and recruits polymerase. Transcription is highest with lactose present and glucose absent; glucose and lactose together give only low expression (catabolite repression).

Eukaryotic transcription

DNA wraps histone octamers (two each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4; H1 links nucleosomes into the 30 nm fiber). Histones are rich in positive lysine and arginine.

  • RNA polymerase I: the large rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S) in the nucleolus. II: mRNA (and most snRNA), blocked by α-amanitin. III: tRNA and 5S rRNA.
  • General transcription factors build the pre-initiation complex; TFIID carries the TATA-binding protein, which binds the TATA box about 25 bp upstream.
  • Enhancers bind activators and work at a distance, upstream, downstream or in introns, in either orientation.
  • Histone acetylation loosens chromatin and turns genes on; DNA methylation (at CpG) recruits deacetylases and silences genes.

RNA processing (in the nucleus)

  • 5′ cap: 7-methylguanosine joined by a 5′–5′ triphosphate bond. Needed for export, translation and stability. RNA polymerase I and III products are uncapped.
  • Splicing starts while transcription continues. The spliceosome (snRNPs U1, U2, U4, U5, U6, each a small RNA with proteins; its assembly uses ATP) removes introns, which begin with GU and end with AG. U1 binds the 5′ splice site and U2 the branch point, 18–40 nucleotides upstream of the 3′ splice site; the branch-point A's 2′-OH attacks the 5′ splice site to form a lariat, the exons are joined and the lariat is degraded. The snRNAs, not the proteins, catalyze the transesterifications. Alternative splicing (and different promoters or poly(A) sites) gives several proteins from one gene, often differing by tissue; in constitutive splicing every exon is kept.
  • Poly(A) tail: after the AAUAAA signal the transcript is cut 10–30 nucleotides downstream and poly(A) polymerase adds about 200–250 A's with no template. Poly(A)-binding protein protects the message and helps translation.
  • Editing changes single bases by deamination: A → I (ADAR, on double-stranded RNA; I pairs like G) and C → U. In the gut, C → U turns apoB's CAA codon into a UAA stop, so the intestine makes the short apoB-48 for its lipid particles while the liver makes the full apoB-100 for VLDL. Editing can change an amino acid, add a stop or move a splice site.
  • Export and decay: the capped, tailed mRNA leaves the nucleus 5′ end first. In the cytoplasm the cap-binding eIF4E and eIF4G and the tail's PABP bend the message into a loop that favors translation and guards both ends, so anything that slows translation speeds decay; decay usually starts when a poly(A) nuclease shortens the tail. Bacterial mRNAs last minutes; most eukaryotic mRNAs last over 10 hours, but those for regulatory proteins can last 30 minutes or less.

Translation

Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach each amino acid to its tRNA's 3′ end using ATP, and an editing site removes a wrong, smaller amino acid: this charging is the main fidelity step. The genetic code has 64 codons: AUG starts (methionine; formyl-Met in bacteria) and UAA, UAG, UGA stop. The code is degenerate, and wobble at the codon's third base lets one tRNA read several codons. The reading frame is kept by starting at AUG and moving exactly three nucleotides each step.

The ribosome has three sites: A (incoming aminoacyl-tRNA), P (the tRNA holding the growing chain) and E (exit). The peptidyl transferase is the large subunit's rRNA, so the ribosome is a ribozyme.

Initiation factorsIF-1, IF-2 (a G protein carrying fMet-tRNA), IF-3Many eIFs
ElongationEF-Tu delivers tRNA, EF-Ts recharges it with GTP, EF-G translocateseEF1A, eEF1B, eEF2 (diphtheria toxin inactivates eEF2)
