Classical genetics

Alleles are versions of a gene; the genotype is the allele combination (homozygous or heterozygous), the phenotype is the trait. Segregation: the two alleles separate into different gametes. Independent assortment: alleles of different (unlinked) genes sort independently. Multiply probabilities for "and", add them for "or". A monohybrid cross of heterozygotes (Tt × Tt) gives genotypes 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt and phenotypes 3 : 1 (75% dominant); a dihybrid cross gives 9:3:3:1. A test cross mates an individual showing the dominant trait with a homozygous recessive one: if every offspring shows the dominant trait it is homozygous (true-breeding); any recessive offspring mean it is heterozygous.

ModePedigree clueExamples
Autosomal dominantEvery generation; males and females alike; an affected child has an affected parent; 50% risk per childHuntington disease, familial hypercholesterolemia (LDL receptor), Marfan syndrome (fibrillin 1: long limbs, weak aorta, lens dislocation), neurofibromatosis 1 (benign nerve tumors under the skin), brachydactyly
Autosomal recessiveSkips generations; unaffected carrier parents; 25% risk when both carrySickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, albinism
X-linked recessiveMostly males; through carrier mothers; never father to sonHemophilia A (factor VIII), Duchenne muscular dystrophy (dystrophin, often a gene deletion)
X-linked dominantAn affected father passes it to all daughters and no sons
Y-linkedFather to every son
MitochondrialMother to all her children; never through the fatherEnergy-failure diseases of muscle and nerve

An unaffected sibling of someone with a recessive disease (both parents carriers) has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier.

Mutations

  • Point mutations: a transition swaps purine for purine or pyrimidine for pyrimidine; a transversion swaps a purine for a pyrimidine. By effect: silent (a synonymous codon: AAA and AAG both code lysine), missense (another amino acid, with a severe, mild or no effect; sickle cell, Glu → Val, mRNA GAG → GUG, a transversion), nonsense (premature stop, truncated protein; some cystic fibrosis alleles) and splice-site (an intron is kept in the message or an exon is skipped).
  • Insertions or deletions: not a multiple of three shifts the frame (frameshift); a multiple of three adds or removes whole amino acids (the common cystic fibrosis mutation removes one phenylalanine).
  • Expanding triplet repeats: more repeats mean earlier, more severe disease in later generations (anticipation): Huntington disease (CAG), fragile X syndrome, Friedreich ataxia and myotonic dystrophy (CTG: 5–37 copies normal, 50–1,000 in disease; 40 or more are unstable).
  • Spontaneous (de novo) mutations come from replication errors, about 1 in 100,000 per gene per round. Induced ones come from mutagens (a mutagen that causes cancer is a carcinogen): alkylating agents damage and remove a base, so a wrong one can go in (a substitution); intercalating agents (acridine dyes) add or remove a base (a frameshift); ionizing radiation, including X-rays, breaks the sugar–phosphate backbone (double-strand breaks); ultraviolet light makes thymine dimers. Examples: aflatoxin B (fungi on peanuts), nitrosamines (cigarette smoke), UV (sunlight, tanning beds). The Ames test screens a chemical with Salmonella that can't make histidine: only bacteria the chemical mutates back can grow, and liver extract is added to mimic human metabolism. Somatic mutations affect only the person's own cell line; germline mutations can pass to children.

One gene, several diseases: different β-globin mutations give sickle cell disease or β-thalassemia (too little β-globin, so excess α chains damage red cells; worse in homozygotes), and different collagen mutations give osteogenesis imperfecta (one type I α1 allele inactivated, collagen halved: brittle bones, blue sclera, deafness), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (stretchy, easily scarred skin and lax joints) or Alport syndrome (type IV collagen: deafness and inflamed kidneys). The reverse happens too: many different LDL receptor mutations all cause familial hypercholesterolemia.

Inherited diseases of the teeth: amelogenesis imperfecta (abnormal enamel: small, discolored, pitted or grooved teeth that wear and break), dentinogenesis imperfecta (abnormal dentin: blue-gray or yellow-brown, translucent, weak teeth) and ectodermal dysplasia (skin, hair, nails, sweat glands and teeth: missing teeth, or small, pointed ones).

Genetics of cancer

Cancer is uncontrolled growth from accumulated somatic mutations in genes that control the cell cycle or repair DNA. About 10% of cases are single-gene disorders and 90% involve several genes, and it takes years (often over 20): initiation (a mutation sets one cell proliferating), promotion (its clone keeps dividing) and progression (more mutations, four or more in all, make it malignant). Benign tumors are encapsulated, well differentiated, with rare mitoses, slow and don't metastasize; malignant ones are unencapsulated, invade, are poorly differentiated with variable anaplasia (reversion to an immature form), divide often and metastasize. Tissue goes hyperplasia (more cells) → dysplasia (abnormal, less mature cells) → carcinoma in situ → invasive cancer.

  • Oncogenes: a mutated proto-oncogene (normally pro-growth) becomes overactive ("stepping on the gas"; over 100 are known); one mutated copy is enough. Activated by amplification (HER2/ErbB2 in breast, stomach and brain cancers, with a poorer prognosis, and the target of the antibody trastuzumab (Herceptin); N-myc in neuroblastoma), a point mutation that leaves the protein always on (RAS), a translocation making a fusion protein (BCR-ABL: ABL moves from chromosome 9 onto BCR on chromosome 22, the Philadelphia chromosome of chronic myeloid leukemia; imatinib (Gleevec) blocks its ATP pocket, and resistance comes from mutations that reshape the pocket), or extra transcription when a virus or a move (insertional mutagenesis) puts it next to a strong promoter.
  • Tumor suppressors ("removing the brakes"; over 30 are known): both copies must be lost, Knudson's two-hit hypothesis; the loss is usually a deletion, sometimes a point mutation, and DNA tumor viruses (HPV, SV40, adenovirus) bind their proteins. RB (retinoblastoma: sporadic cases need two somatic hits; inherited cases need one more hit beside the inherited one, so they are found earlier and are often in both eyes, and the susceptibility passes to half of an affected parent's children), p53 (stops the cycle or triggers apoptosis after DNA damage; abnormal in over half of cancers; an inherited TP53 mutation is Li-Fraumeni syndrome, many cancers at young ages), APC (colon: an inherited APC mutation is familial adenomatous polyposis, hundreds to thousands of polyps).
  • DNA repair genes (mismatch, excision and double-strand break repair): BRCA1/2 (double-strand break repair; breast cancer susceptibility inherited as a dominant trait, though each cell still needs a second hit, so BRCA1 acts recessively in the cell) and the mismatch repair genes of Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer, with other cancers too).
  • An inherited first hit is in every cell, gametes included, so cancer comes earlier and more often, and the tumor grows wherever the second hit happens. High-risk HPV (types 16 and 18) causes oropharyngeal and cervical cancer: its E6 protein degrades p53 and E7 inactivates RB.
  • Cancer cells stop answering their neighbors' growth signals, lose contact inhibition (they pile up), dedifferentiate, mutate faster, turn on telomerase, induce angiogenesis (VEGF from oxygen-starved cells), invade and spread by blood, lymph, nerves (perineural) and across body cavities (transcoelomic). A tumor outgrows its tissue because a larger share of its cells are dividing, not because each divides fast: some cancers divide more slowly than some normal cells.

What's tested
  • Endocrine, paracrine and autocrine signaling; the chemical classes of hormones; how hormones are regulated and measured
  • Peptide hormones: synthesis, transport, cell-surface receptors, the cAMP–PKA and IP3/DAG–Ca2+–PKC pathways, insulin and GLUT4
  • Steroid hormones: cholesterol to pregnenolone, P450 enzymes, carrier proteins, nuclear receptors, the three classes and their disorders; the calcium hormones
  • Metabolism: catabolic versus anabolic, NAD+ versus NADPH, ATP coupling, which tissues burn which fuel
  • Thermodynamics: the three laws, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, exergonic versus endergonic, the ΔH/ΔS table
  • Enzymes: catalytic power, specificity, activation energy, cofactors and coenzymes, the six classes, Km, Vmax, kcat, kcat/Km, bisubstrate reactions, induced fit, and inhibition on a Lineweaver-Burk plot

Hormones: the basics

The endocrine system signals chemically through the blood: slower than the nervous system, but longer lasting. The two overlap (the adrenal medulla releases norepinephrine; the hypothalamus is neural tissue that makes hormones that control the pituitary, the "master" gland). Endocrine hormones travel in blood (growth hormone, insulin), paracrine ones act on neighbors (testosterone from Leydig cells in the testis), autocrine ones act on the cell that made them (estradiol).

  • Chemical classes: amino acid–derived (thyroxine and catecholamines from tyrosine), peptides and proteins (insulin, oxytocin, growth hormone), steroids (from cholesterol), fatty acid–derived (eicosanoids).
  • Regulation: rate of synthesis; rate of release (insulin is biphasic, some hormones pulsatile, cortisol diurnal); half-life (short half-life = tight control); negative feedback (cortisol suppresses ACTH); opposing hormones (insulin versus glucagon); bioavailability (only free hormone acts).
  • Measuring them is hard: tiny blood levels, binding proteins and changing release. Methods: sandwich ELISA (a capture antibody and an enzyme-linked detection antibody) and mass spectrometry (the usual test for testosterone).
PeptideSteroid
Made asPreprohormone → prohormone; stored in granulesMade on demand from cholesterol; not stored
Solubility and transportPolar; small ones travel free, large ones on carriersNonpolar; mostly protein-bound in blood
ReceptorCell surface, second messengersInside the cell; the complex binds DNA (hormone response elements) and changes transcription
SpeedFastSlower, longer lasting
By mouthNo (digested)Often yes

Peptide hormone signaling

G protein–coupled receptors: the hormone changes the receptor's shape, the G protein swaps GDP for GTP, and its α subunit acts on an enzyme.

  • Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A. PKA is two regulatory and two catalytic subunits; cAMP binds the regulatory subunits (four sites in all) and frees the active catalytic ones. Phosphodiesterase breaks cAMP down (caffeine blocks it). Gs examples: glycogen breakdown in liver, fat breakdown in adipose tissue, water conservation in the kidney (ADH). Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase (slows the heart).
  • Gq activates phospholipase C, which splits PIP2 into IP3 (releases Ca2+ from the ER) and DAG (with Ca2+ activates protein kinase C).
  • Each step amplifies the signal: one epinephrine molecule releases a flood of glucose from the liver.

Insulin: pancreatic β cells make preproinsulin on the ER; the signal peptide is cut to proinsulin, which the Golgi cleaves to insulin plus C-peptide and packs in granules. Glucose entry raises ATP, and Ca2+ influx triggers exocytosis. Its receptor is a receptor tyrosine kinase (two α and two β subunits); the cascade moves GLUT4 to the membrane of skeletal muscle and fat cells, so glucose enters and blood glucose falls. Glucagon does the opposite in the liver.

Steroid hormones

Three types: glucocorticoids (carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism; immunosuppression), mineralocorticoids (salt and water recovery by the kidney) and sex steroids (androgens and estrogens: the sex organs and their function; pregnancy). Made in the adrenal cortex (glomerulosa: aldosterone; fasciculata: cortisol; reticularis: androgens) and the gonads (testosterone mostly from the testes, with some from the ovaries and adrenals; estrogen mostly from the ovaries, with smaller amounts from fat, liver and breast). ACTH from the anterior pituitary drives the adrenal synthesis of cortisol and androgens. The first and rate-limiting step, in mitochondria, cleaves cholesterol's side chain (side-chain cleavage, desmolase) to make pregnenolone. Over a dozen enzymes take part, most of them cytochrome P450 mixed-function oxidases whose main job is to modify cholesterol's tail: the synthesis is an oxidation that needs O2 and NADPH (from the pentose phosphate pathway).

Transport and action: steroids are insoluble in plasma and ride on carriers. Transcortin (corticosteroid-binding globulin) holds about 75% of cortisol and albumin the rest. SHBG, made mainly by the liver, binds testosterone and estradiol and keeps them out of cells, so its level sets how much is bioavailable (free plus loosely albumin-bound). About 2% of testosterone is free in both sexes, but women carry much more of theirs on SHBG (about 78% against 44% in men), so less of it is bioavailable. The free hormone crosses the membrane and binds its receptor inside the cell; the complex binds hormone response elements (enhancers) in DNA, and the receptor's N-terminal transactivation domain changes transcription.

ClassMain hormone and actionsToo muchToo little
GlucocorticoidCortisol (stress): gluconeogenesis and high blood glucose, protein and fat breakdown, immunosuppression, less bone formationCushing syndrome, most often iatrogenic (glucocorticoid drugs), otherwise an adrenal or pituitary cause: weight gain with central obesity, moon face, insulin resistance and hyperglycemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, poor healing; hyperpigmentation when ACTH is high (pituitary cause)Addison disease (primary adrenal insufficiency, usually autoimmune, sometimes infection): fatigue, hypotension, hyperpigmentation of skin and oral mucosa from high ACTH; adrenal crisis under stress
MineralocorticoidAldosterone: Na+ (and water) retained, K+ secreted in the distal tubule and collecting duct; raises blood volume and pressureConn syndrome (an adrenal adenoma or idiopathic): hypertension with low K+Addison disease: salt loss, high K+, low blood pressure
Sex steroidsTestosterone: muscle, bone density, sex organ maturation. Estrogen: uterus and breast maturation, less bone resorption, more clotting, more HDLAnabolic steroid abuseMenopause: estrogen replacement eases symptoms

Calcium hormones: PTH raises blood Ca2+ (osteoclast resorption through osteoblast signals, kidney Ca2+ reabsorption, more calcitriol); calcitriol (active vitamin D) raises gut absorption of Ca2+ and phosphate; calcitonin from the thyroid lowers Ca2+ by inhibiting osteoclasts. Osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts resorb it, osteocytes signal when to do which.

Metabolism

  • Metabolism is the sum of a cell's chemical reactions. Its four jobs: make ATP, break nutrients down (catabolism), build macromolecules (anabolism), and take part in signaling and gene control (metabolites such as acetyl-CoA are substrates for protein modifications and epigenetic marks).
  • Oxidation is the loss of electrons, reduction the gain; passing electrons between carriers lets the cell move energy in small steps. NAD+/NADH works mostly in catabolism, NADP+/NADPH mostly in anabolism; FAD and FMN are other carriers.
  • Catabolic pathways break molecules down: oxidative, exergonic, and they reduce NAD+ to NADH. Anabolic pathways build: reductive, endergonic, and they spend NADPH and ATP.
  • Major pathways: glycolysis (glucose to pyruvate, with ATP and NADH), the citric acid cycle (acetyl-CoA to CO2, with NADH, FADH2 and GTP), oxidative phosphorylation (electrons to O2, most of the ATP), gluconeogenesis (new glucose, used by the brain), the urea cycle (ammonia into less toxic urea), fatty acid β-oxidation (fatty acids to acetyl-CoA) and the pentose phosphate pathway (NADPH for synthesis and the sugars for nucleotides).
  • ATP from catabolism powers anabolism and the rest of the cell's work (ion transport, synthesis of macromolecules, DNA and RNA, signaling, contraction, neurotransmission), and ATP is also an allosteric regulator of enzymes (more under Thermodynamics).
  • The liver is the metabolic hub: it stores glucose as glycogen and makes fuel for the brain, muscle and other organs. The brain runs almost entirely on glucose (fatty acids don't cross the blood–brain barrier), and red blood cells use only glucose, by glycolysis (no mitochondria). Heart and skeletal muscle burn mainly fatty acids, and skeletal muscle switches to glucose in intense exercise; the liver and adipose tissue burn mainly fat. Muscle protein is used as fuel only in fasting. The general order of preference is glucose, then fat, then protein.
  • Pathways are controlled by compartments, substrate and product levels, energy charge, enzyme amount and allosteric effectors.

Thermodynamics

Systems are isolated (no exchange), closed (energy only) or open (energy and matter: living cells). First law: energy is neither created nor destroyed; ΔE = q + w (the heat absorbed plus the work done on the system), and internal energy is a state function (it depends on the state, not the path). Second law: every real energy transfer increases the entropy of the universe. Third law: a perfect crystal has zero entropy at 0 K. Energy units: joules (SI) or calories (1 cal = 4.184 J).

  • Enthalpy (H = E + PV) is the heat content: at constant pressure, as in the body, ΔH = q, the heat absorbed, measured with a calorimeter. In biology it reflects bonds, van der Waals interactions, hydrogen bonds and electrostatic interactions.
  • Entropy measures how dispersed energy is, the number of microstates (S = k ln W, k Boltzmann's constant). In biology it reflects the solvent and ions and how freely molecules can rotate and move.

ΔG = ΔH − TΔS at constant temperature and pressure. ΔG < 0: exergonic, spontaneous. ΔG > 0: endergonic, needs coupling to an exergonic process. ΔG = 0: equilibrium. A process is spontaneous when the system gives up energy (ΔH negative), gains disorder (ΔS positive) or both, and the more negative ΔG, the more work it can do: oxidizing glucose to CO2 and water has ΔG = −686 kcal/mol (−2,870 kJ/mol); photosynthesis, the endergonic reverse, runs on sunlight. ΔG says nothing about speed: ΔG°′ = −RT ln K′eq links it to the equilibrium constant, while the free energy of activation (ΔG‡) sets the rate constant. Unfolding a protein absorbs heat (ΔH positive) and raises entropy.

ΔHΔSSpontaneous?
− (exothermic)+At every temperature

++Only at high temperature

ATP is the cell's energy shuttle: ATP + H2O → ADP + Pi has ΔG°′ of about −30.5 kJ/mol (−7.3 kcal/mol). The energy comes from the products' lower free energy, not from the phosphate bonds themselves. ATP has four ionizable protons and in cells is bound to Mg2+, which stabilizes its phosphates. Phosphoryl transfer has a high activation energy (200–400 kJ/mol), so ATP keeps until an enzyme uses it. Energy coupling: an exergonic process (ATP hydrolysis) drives an endergonic one, for the cell's three kinds of work: mechanical (muscle contraction, cilia), transport (across membranes) and chemical (nonspontaneous synthesis, such as making proteins). The body holds only about 50 g of ATP and ADP but turns over about 65 kg of ATP a day, so each molecule is recycled nearly 1,300 times a day.

Enzymes

Enzymes have catalytic power (the ratio of the catalyzed to the uncatalyzed rate, up to about 10^16), specificity (choosing the right substrate and giving yields often above 95%, set by the structure of the active site, the pocket where the substrate binds and the reaction happens) and regulation (substrate and cofactor supply, allosteric control, how much enzyme is made and broken down). They lower the activation energy (ΔG‡) by binding the transition state most tightly; they don't change ΔG or the equilibrium. Keep the two apart: ΔG is related to the equilibrium constant (how far a reaction goes), ΔG‡ to the rate constant (how fast). Lock and key was the first model of specificity (a rigid site that fits the substrate); induced fit is more accurate: substrate binding changes the enzyme's shape and favors the transition state; in hexokinase two domains close around glucose to form the catalytic site. Enzymes work in a pH range (ionizable side chains) and speed up with temperature, roughly doubling every 10 °C, until they denature (activity falls above about 50–60 °C). Not all enzymes are proteins: ribozymes are catalytic RNAs (RNase P, the ribosome's peptidyl transferase), and abzymes are antibodies raised against a transition state.

  • Cofactors are usually metal ions (Mg2+ for hexokinase, K+ for pyruvate kinase, Zn2+ for DNA polymerase). Coenzymes are organic, often from vitamins (NAD+ from niacin, FAD from riboflavin, TPP from thiamine), and carry groups or electrons. A tightly bound one is a prosthetic group. The protein alone is the apoenzyme; with its cofactor or coenzyme it is the holoenzyme.
  • Six classes: oxidoreductases (redox), transferases (move a group), hydrolases (split with water), lyases (add to or form double bonds without water or ATP), isomerases, ligases (join molecules using ATP).
  • Bisubstrate reactions: single-displacement (sequential: both substrates bind before any product leaves; ordered or random, as in creatine kinase) and double-displacement (ping-pong: the first product leaves before the second substrate binds, through a covalently modified enzyme, as in glutamate–aspartate aminotransferase). On Lineweaver-Burk plots, sequential reactions give lines that cross to the left of the 1/v axis; ping-pong reactions give parallel lines.

Michaelis-Menten (E + S ⇌ ES → E + P): v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]). Km = (k−1 + k2)/k1 is the [S] that gives half of Vmax and, under true Michaelis-Menten conditions, estimates the enzyme–substrate dissociation constant; a low Km means tight binding (high affinity). At low [S] the rate is first order in substrate; at saturating [S] it is zero order and approaches Vmax, a theoretical maximum that is approached but never reached (it would need every enzyme molecule bound to substrate) and that rises with the amount of enzyme. kcat (turnover number) = Vmax / [enzyme]: substrate molecules converted per enzyme per second at saturation. kcat/Km is catalytic efficiency at low [S]; its ceiling is the diffusion limit (about 10^8–10^9 per molar per second). The ES complex reaches a steady state.

Lineweaver-Burk is the reciprocal of Michaelis-Menten: 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. Plotting 1/v against 1/[S] gives a straight line: y-intercept 1/Vmax, x-intercept −1/Km, slope Km/Vmax. The Hanes-Woolf plot ([S]/v against [S]) is more reliable, because its errors are smaller and more even across the plot.

Examples. Competitive: malonate at succinate dehydrogenase (the classic case: it resembles succinate), methotrexate with dihydrofolate at dihydrofolate reductase, statins at HMG-CoA reductase, and sildenafil, which resembles cGMP, at phosphodiesterase 5 (more cGMP relaxes vascular smooth muscle). Uncompetitive: lithium at inositol monophosphatase, its target in bipolar disorder. Pure noncompetitive inhibition (equal binding to E and ES) is uncommon. Irreversible inhibitors bind for good, usually covalently: penicillin is a suicide inhibitor of the bacterial transpeptidase that cross-links the cell wall, aspirin acetylates cyclooxygenase, organophosphates block acetylcholinesterase. Allosteric enzymes give sigmoidal curves, not Michaelis-Menten.
full.f1-carbmet:
What's tested
  • Glycolysis: the ATP it spends and makes, its three irreversible enzymes, and PFK-1 control
  • Pyruvate's fates: lactate, the PDH complex and its five coenzymes, carboxylation
  • Citric acid cycle products and its rate-limiting enzyme
  • Electron transport chain: complexes, proton pumping, inhibitors and uncouplers; ATP per glucose
  • Glycogen synthesis and breakdown and their hormonal control
  • Gluconeogenesis: bypass enzymes, precursors, the Cori and alanine cycles

Glycolysis (cytosol)

Glucose (6 carbons) is split into 2 pyruvate (3 carbons each) in every cell, with or without oxygen, in ten steps whose enzymes are all in the cytosol. The preparatory phase (the first five steps) spends 2 ATP to make fructose 1,6-bisphosphate and splits it into two trioses; the payoff phase makes 4 ATP and 2 NADH. Net: 2 ATP, 2 NADH, 2 pyruvate. ATP is made by substrate-level phosphorylation at phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase. NADH comes from glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase, which needs a steady supply of NAD+.

EnzymeReactionControl
Hexokinase (glucokinase in liver and pancreatic β cells)Glucose → glucose 6-phosphate (spends ATP)Hexokinase is inhibited by glucose 6-phosphate; glucokinase (high Km, induced by insulin) is not
PFK-1 (rate-limiting)Fructose 6-phosphate → fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (spends ATP)On: AMP, fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, Pi. Off: ATP, citrate, H+ (low pH)
Pyruvate kinasePEP → pyruvate (makes ATP)On: fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (feed-forward). Off: ATP, alanine; glucagon phosphorylates and inhibits it in liver

Fructose 2,6-bisphosphate is made by PFK-2. Insulin raises it and glucagon lowers it (cAMP and protein kinase A phosphorylate the bifunctional enzyme). It switches PFK-1 on and fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase off, so glycolysis and gluconeogenesis never run full speed at once. Together, PFK-1's effectors report the cell's energy state (ATP, AMP, Pi), its pH (H+), other fuels such as fatty acids and ketone bodies (citrate) and the insulin/glucagon ratio (fructose 2,6-bisphosphate).

What happens to pyruvate

  • No oxygen or no mitochondria (red cells, sprinting muscle): lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate and regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue. Lactate goes to the liver (Cori cycle).
  • With oxygen: pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix, where the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex makes acetyl-CoA, CO2 and NADH. The step is irreversible, so acetyl-CoA can't become glucose. Five coenzymes: thiamine pyrophosphate (B1), lipoic acid, CoA (B5), FAD (B2), NAD+ (B3). It is three enzymes in one complex. Its products acetyl-CoA and NADH, and ATP, turn it off, mainly by activating PDH kinase, which phosphorylates the E1 enzyme (phosphorylated PDH is inactive); a phosphatase turns it back on, and pyruvate, ADP, NAD+ and CoA keep it active. Thiamine deficiency and arsenic (which binds lipoic acid) block it.
  • Fasting liver: pyruvate carboxylase turns it into oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis.
  • Transamination turns it into alanine.

Citric acid cycle (mitochondrial matrix)

Acetyl-CoA + oxaloacetate → citrate (citrate synthase). Per acetyl-CoA: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP, 2 CO2; double it per glucose. The rate-limiting enzyme is isocitrate dehydrogenase (on: ADP, NAD+, Ca2+; off: ATP, NADH). The cycle's two other regulated steps: citrate synthase (off: ATP, NADH, succinyl-CoA) and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase (off: NADH, succinyl-CoA; on: AMP). With PDH, these set the cycle's pace. α-Ketoglutarate dehydrogenase uses the same five coenzymes as PDH. Succinyl-CoA synthetase makes the GTP. Succinate dehydrogenase, the cycle's only membrane enzyme, is also Complex II and makes FADH2. The cycle needs oxygen indirectly, to regenerate NAD+ and FAD, and its intermediates also feed synthesis (citrate → fatty acids, succinyl-CoA → heme).

Electron transport and oxidative phosphorylation (inner membrane)

ComplexElectronsH+ pumped per pairBlocked by
I, NADH dehydrogenaseNADH → coenzyme Q4Rotenone
II, succinate dehydrogenaseFADH2 (succinate) → coenzyme Q0Malonate
III, cytochrome bc1Coenzyme Q → cytochrome c4Antimycin A
IV, cytochrome c oxidaseCytochrome c → O2 (makes water)2Cyanide, carbon monoxide, azide
V, ATP synthase (F0 channel, F1 head)Protons flow back in and drive ATP synthesis—Oligomycin
  • Mobile carriers: coenzyme Q (lipid-soluble, inside the membrane) and cytochrome c (water-soluble, in the intermembrane space). Electrons fall in energy along the chain, from carriers with a more negative reduction potential (NADH) toward the most positive: oxygen is the final electron acceptor. Complex I passes electrons from NADH through FMN and iron-sulfur centers to coenzyme Q; Complex III passes them to cytochrome c by the Q cycle; Complex IV (hemes a and a3 and two copper centers) reduces O2 to 2 H2O with four electrons.
  • Chemiosmosis: pumped protons build a gradient (the proton-motive force) whose flow back through ATP synthase makes ATP. Protons pass through the F0 channel and turn its ring of c subunits (the rotor), and each of the F1 head's three catalytic sites cycles through ADP + Pi bound, ATP bound and empty (the binding-change model, rotational catalysis). About 4 protons per ATP (3 through the synthase, 1 to bring in phosphate and ADP through their translocases), so the P/O ratio (ATP per electron pair passed to oxygen) is about 2.5 for NADH (10 H+) and 1.5 for FADH2 (6 H+, because Complex II pumps none).
  • Inhibitors stop electron flow and oxygen use, and cells switch to glycolysis (lactic acidosis). Blocking ATP synthase also slows electron flow, because the gradient backs up.
  • Uncouplers (2,4-dinitrophenol, high-dose aspirin, thermogenin/UCP1 in brown fat) let protons leak back; the chemical ones are hydrophobic weak acids that ferry protons across the membrane. Oxygen use goes on or rises, ATP falls, and the energy becomes heat.
  • Cytosolic NADH can't cross the inner membrane, so shuttles carry its electrons in: the malate-aspartate shuttle delivers them to NADH in the matrix (2.5 ATP), the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle to FAD (1.5 ATP).

Glycogen

Liver glycogen keeps blood glucose up; muscle glycogen fuels the muscle itself. The liver stores more per gram (up to about 10% of its weight, against 1–2% in muscle), but there is so much more muscle that it holds about twice as much glycogen in all. Chains are α-1,4 with α-1,6 branches every 8–10 residues; the many branch ends give phosphorylase and glycogen synthase many places to work, and each molecule has a single reducing end, attached to glycogenin.

  • Synthesis: glucose 6-phosphate → glucose 1-phosphate (phosphoglucomutase) → UDP-glucose ("activated glucose", made from UTP; hydrolysis of the pyrophosphate released makes the step irreversible) → glycogen synthase (rate-limiting; adds glucose in α-1,4 links to the nonreducing ends of chains, starting from glycogenin, a primer protein that attaches the first glucose residues to one of its own tyrosines) → branching enzyme (once a chain is at least 11 residues long, moves a block of about 7 to make each α-1,6 branch).
  • Breakdown: glycogen phosphorylase (rate-limiting) cleaves α-1,4 links at the nonreducing ends with phosphate (phosphorolysis, unlike the gut's α-amylase, which hydrolyzes them), releasing glucose 1-phosphate, and stops 4 residues from a branch (the limit dextrin). The debranching enzyme moves 3 of them, then frees the last as free glucose (α-1,6-glucosidase). Liver's glucose 6-phosphatase releases glucose to the blood; muscle has none.
  • Control: glucagon (liver) and epinephrine (liver and muscle) → cAMP → protein kinase A → phosphorylase kinase → phosphorylase a (phosphorylated, active); protein kinase A also phosphorylates glycogen synthase (less active). Insulin's protein phosphatase-1 reverses both. Phosphorylase kinase is itself switched on by protein kinase A and by Ca2+, so in contracting muscle Ca2+ speeds breakdown; muscle phosphorylase b is also activated directly by AMP (blocked by high ATP), and liver phosphorylase is inhibited by glucose. Protein phosphatase-1 works only while bound to glycogen: insulin activates it, and protein kinase A releases it.

Gluconeogenesis

Mostly in the liver (a little in the renal cortex, more in long fasts), from lactate, pyruvate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids (alanine and glutamine above all, the main carriers of amino groups to the liver). Glycerol enters as dihydroxyacetone phosphate (glycerol kinase, then glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase), so the glycerol of fat can make glucose. Never net glucose from even-chain fatty acids or the purely ketogenic amino acids leucine and lysine. Liver glycogen lasts 12–24 hours into a fast; after that gluconeogenesis supplies the tissues that live on glucose (brain, red cells, kidney medulla, lens, cornea, testis). Seven of its ten steps are glycolysis run backward; its three bypasses replace glycolysis's irreversible steps. It costs 4 ATP, 2 GTP and 2 NADH per glucose.

Glycolysis stepGluconeogenesis enzymeNotes
Pyruvate kinasePyruvate carboxylase (mitochondria, biotin, ATP; activated by acetyl-CoA), then PEP carboxykinase (GTP, Mg2+)Oxaloacetate has no carrier, so it leaves the mitochondria as malate or aspartate and is remade in the cytosol (or a mitochondrial PEP carboxykinase makes PEP there)
PFK-1Fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase (rate-limiting)Off: fructose 2,6-bisphosphate, AMP
HexokinaseGlucose 6-phosphatase (ER)Liver and kidney only, not muscle; a glucose 6-phosphate translocase brings its substrate into the ER, and a defect in either causes von Gierke disease (glycogen piles up in the liver, with fasting hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis)
  • Reciprocal control in a fast: acetyl-CoA from fat oxidation turns pyruvate carboxylase on and PDH off; the extra citrate slows PFK-1; protein kinase A phosphorylates and inhibits liver pyruvate kinase; glucagon lowers fructose 2,6-bisphosphate; and high ATP with low AMP favors fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase over PFK-1.
  • Cori cycle: lactate from red cells and muscle → liver → glucose → back to the tissues. The liver spends 6 ATP per glucose and the tissue gets back only 2, so the cycle costs energy; it needs no oxygen or mitochondria in the tissue.
  • Alanine cycle: muscle sends alanine to the liver, which makes pyruvate (then glucose) and turns the nitrogen into urea (4 ATP per urea, so about 10 ATP spent in the liver per glucose). The tissue needs mitochondria and oxygen, because it can't use pyruvate to regenerate NAD+, and it gains 6–8 ATP per glucose, more than in the Cori cycle.
full.f1-innate:
What's tested
  • Innate versus adaptive immunity, how immune cells communicate (cytokines, chemokines); the innate cells and their jobs
  • Hematopoiesis and the cell markers (CD numbers); primary and secondary lymphoid organs, lymph and the lymphatics
  • Barriers, pattern recognition receptors (TLRs, NLRs, RLRs), PAMPs and DAMPs
  • Phagocytosis and the respiratory burst
  • Complement: the three pathways, what each fragment does, key deficiencies
  • Inflammation: mediators, leukocyte extravasation and the order cells arrive, kinds of cell death, M1 and M2 macrophages, fever and the acute phase response
FeatureInnateAdaptive
SpeedMinutes to hoursDays on first exposure (a fully active response takes 10–14 days)
ReceptorsAbout 100 invariant, germline pattern recognition receptors (everyone inherits the same genes for them)Rearranged BCRs and TCRs, unique to each clone; soluble BCRs are antibodies
RecognizesLarger molecular patterns shared by microbes and uncommon on host cells (PAMPs), and damage signals (DAMPs)Epitopes: very small parts of an antigen (for example 8–12 amino acids of a protein)
Where it startsIn the peripheral tissues: resident sentinel cells and cells recruited from the bloodIn secondary lymphoid tissue, where B and T cells are activated
MemoryNone: it responds the same way every timeYes: it adapts and improves with each exposure
CellsEvery immune cell except B and T cells (NK cells included)B cells (plasma cells are B cells) and T cells
ResponsesPhagocytosis, inflammation, complement, the acute phase, the interferon responseAntibody-mediated and cell-mediated effector functions

The immune system has three layers: barriers, then innate immunity, then adaptive immunity. Its four functions are recognition, effector functions (containing and destroying invaders), regulation (mostly the adaptive response's job; when it fails, autoimmunity and allergy follow) and memory (adaptive only). Infection is a microbe invading and replicating in a host; disease is when that infection damages tissue and disrupts normal function. Immune responses damage tissue as they clear a pathogen, so resolution matters as much as activation.

Cells talk by direct contact (receptor–ligand binding, such as PRRs and antigen receptors) and by soluble cytokines (interleukins, interferons, TNF): very small, short-lived proteins, made by immune and non-immune cells, that tell cells what to do, acting on the same cell, a neighbor or a distant one. Chemokines are the cytokines that tell cells where to go: cells with the matching receptor move toward them. One cytokine can have many effects (pleiotropy), several can have the same effect (redundancy), and they can work together for a greater effect (synergy) or oppose each other (antagonism).

Innate cells

Hematopoiesis, in the bone marrow, is the development of each kind of blood cell from a pluripotent progenitor: all blood cells come from hematopoietic stem cells (CD34+), through a myeloid or a lymphoid progenitor. Cells are told apart by function, by shape and by surface proteins, many named with a CD (cluster of differentiation) number. Granulocytes, also called PMNs (polymorphonuclear leukocytes), have multilobed nuclei and granules of degradative enzymes, lipid mediators, antimicrobial peptides, cytokines and chemokines.

CellWhereMain job
NeutrophilMyeloid granulocyte; the most abundant blood leukocyte; multilobed nucleusShort-lived first responder to bacteria; phagocytosis, degranulation; dies in tissue as pus; NETs
Monocyte → macrophageMyeloid; monocyte in blood, macrophage in tissue (some tissue macrophages are residents seeded before birth)Sentinel in tissue; phagocytosis, cleanup, the main source of inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-12), antigen presentation; M1 (inflammatory) or M2 (repair)
Dendritic cellMostly myeloid; in tissues, then lymph nodesCarries antigen to the node; best activator of naive T cells; plasmacytoid DCs make type I interferon
Mast cellMyeloid; granules but a round nucleus; lives in tissue near vessels and mucosa; long-livedStarts inflammation and allergy: histamine, heparin, leukotrienes
BasophilMyeloid granulocyte; circulates, short-livedLike mast cells; enters tissue when called
EosinophilMyeloid granulocyte; bilobed nucleusHelminths, too big to engulf (major basic protein, which also makes mast cells release histamine and constricts the bronchi); asthma and late allergic reactions
NK cellLymphoid lineage, innate function; granules, but not a granulocyte; CD16, CD56Kills cells missing MHC I and IgG-coated cells (ADCC); makes IFN-γ

Adaptive cells: every T cell carries CD3. CD4 helper T cells direct responses with cytokines; CD8 T cells kill abnormal cells (activated, they are cytotoxic T lymphocytes, CTLs). B cells (CD19, CD20) present antigen and secrete antibody but aren't phagocytic. A plasma cell is a terminally differentiated B cell: it no longer carries a BCR, can't be activated again and only secretes antibody.

CellMarker

Dendritic cellCD11c

Lymphoid organs

  • Primary (where immune cells develop): the bone marrow (B cells and every other immune cell except T cells) and the thymus (T cells).
  • Secondary (where naive lymphocytes meet antigen and are activated; other immune cells are activated in the tissues where they live): lymph nodes (filter lymph), the spleen (filters blood; red pulp removes old red cells, white pulp holds lymphocytes; no afferent lymphatics), and MALT, less organized lymphoid tissue in the mucosa of the gut, airways and urogenital tract (tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix). Each keeps separate B-cell and T-cell zones, so antigen and APCs arriving in the lymph meet the right cells, and activated B cells can then meet T cells.
  • Lymph is interstitial fluid collected from the tissues. Lymphatic vessels carry it, with lymphocytes and APCs, to the local lymph nodes, and it returns to the blood through the left and right subclavian veins. B and T cells circulate through both the blood and the lymph and are the main cells in lymph, hence the name lymphocytes.

Barriers and pattern recognition

Barriers are the first line of defense. Skin is hostile to microbes: its epidermis is mostly keratinocytes, dead cells are shed all the time, and it is dry and salty, with sebum keeping its pH low. Mucosa is epithelium joined by tight junctions (which keep molecules from slipping between the cells) and bathed in mucus made of mucins, glycoproteins the epithelium secretes. Mechanical clearance: mucociliary clearance and the flow of tears and saliva.

Chemical barriers, secreted by the epithelium: defensins (α and β), amphipathic antimicrobial peptides made in skin and mucosa that disrupt the membranes of bacteria and of enveloped viruses such as influenza and herpesviruses; lysozyme, an enzyme in saliva, tears and respiratory mucus that cleaves the peptidoglycan of the bacterial cell wall so the cell lyses; and protease inhibitors (α2-macroglobulin), which stop a pathogen's proteases from breaking down host tissue so it can't spread; also stomach acid and lactoferrin. The microbiota of skin and mucosa is the microbiological barrier. Innate sentinel cells in the tissues, such as resident macrophages, act as a barrier too: they detect microbes and damaged cells.

ReceptorWhereSensesResult
Toll-like receptors (TLRs)Cell surface (TLR4: LPS; TLR2: lipoteichoic acid; TLR5: flagellin) or endosome (TLR3: dsRNA; TLR7/8: ssRNA; TLR9: CpG DNA)PAMPsNF-κB → inflammatory cytokines; IRFs → type I interferon
NOD-like receptors (NLRs)CytosolDegraded pathogen components, DAMPsNF-κB → inflammatory cytokines (they back up the TLRs); some form inflammasomes → caspase-1 → IL-1β, IL-18; pyroptosis
RIG-I-like receptors (RLRs)CytosolViral dsRNANF-κB → inflammatory cytokines, and IRFs → type I interferon (signaling through mitochondrial MAVS)
C-type lectin receptors (CLRs)Cell surface; soluble ones are mannose-binding lectin and the lung's surfactant proteins (SP-A, SP-D)Carbohydrates of fungi, mycobacteria, viruses and parasitesA strong trigger of phagocytosis; cytokines

PAMPs are conserved microbial molecules (LPS, peptidoglycan, flagellin, dsRNA, unmethylated CpG). DAMPs come from damaged host cells (HMGB1, ATP, uric acid, heat shock proteins). Each person has about 100 kinds of PRRs, all invariant (everyone inherits the same genes for them), and together they bind all four classes of biomolecules. Every PRR family can induce cytokines, but each has its strength: CLRs and TLRs are strong triggers of phagocytosis (as are scavenger, complement and Fc receptors), while TLRs, NLRs and RLRs turn on NF-κB, the transcription factor that is crucial for proinflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6). The antiviral PRRs (RLRs, TLR3, TLR7/8) also make type I interferon. Soluble PRRs include mannose-binding lectin and C-reactive protein.

Phagocytosis and the respiratory burst

The most phagocytic cells are neutrophils, macrophages and dendritic cells. Opsonins (C3b, IgG) speed uptake. The phagosome fuses with a lysosome, whose proteases are switched on by the change in pH. The respiratory burst (in neutrophils, macrophages and eosinophils) is a brief rise in oxygen use: NADPH oxidase makes superoxide, which becomes hydrogen peroxide; neutrophil myeloperoxidase turns that into hypochlorite (bleach). These reactive oxygen species kill ingested bacteria but can diffuse out and damage host cells; catalase limits the damage by breaking down hydrogen peroxide. Macrophages also make nitric oxide. Granulocytes also degranulate: they empty their granules into the phagosome, or outside the cell to kill microbes there. Chronic granulomatous disease (NADPH oxidase defect): recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms (S. aureus, Aspergillus) and granulomas.

Complement

Complement is a set of proteins in the blood and tissue fluid, made by hepatocytes and epithelial cells, that is always on: a passive surveillance that needs no cell to respond. Its jobs are lysis, opsonization and inflammation and chemotaxis. Each pathway builds enzymes (convertases) that cleave C3 and then C5.

PathwayStarts whenNotes
AlternativeC3 breaks down spontaneously on a microbial surface (factors B and D, properdin)Usually acts first, because C3 is in every tissue (any pathway can start at any time); no antibody needed
LectinMannose-binding lectin binds mannose on microbesUses C4 and C2
ClassicalC1q binds IgM or IgG on a pathogen or in an immune complex, or CRP bound to phosphocholine on bacteriaNeeds antibody; held in check by C1 inhibitor

C3 is the key: it links the three activation pathways to everything complement does. All three build a C3 convertase (they meet at C3), so a great deal of C3 is cleaved; then a C5 convertase; then the one terminal pathway, the membrane attack complex.

  • C3b (the large fragments, C3b and C5b, act on the microbe): opsonization through complement receptors on phagocytes, and clearing immune complexes.
  • C3a, C5a (the small fragments): anaphylatoxins that bind receptors on endothelial cells (vessels dilate and leak) and make mast cells degranulate; C5a also draws neutrophils.
  • C5b–C9: membrane attack complex, which lyses bacteria, fungi and enveloped viruses (Neisseria especially).
  • Host cells protect themselves with DAF (CD55), CD59 and factor H.
  • Deficiencies: C1 inhibitor → hereditary angioedema (low C4, bradykinin, nonitchy swelling, often after dental work; antihistamines don't help); C3 → severe pyogenic infections; C5–C9 → recurrent Neisseria; early classical (C1q, C2, C4) → lupus-like disease.

Inflammation

Acute inflammation is the response of vascularized tissue to infection, toxins or damage that brings cells and molecules of host defense out of the blood to where they are needed. It runs through initiation, effector actions and resolution; acute inflammation that isn't resolved becomes chronic. Signs: redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function.

It starts when tissue-resident sentinel macrophages (and mast cells) bind microbes or damage through their PRRs. Macrophages are the main makers of the proinflammatory cytokines: TNF-α and IL-1 strongly activate the endothelium (and cause fever), and IL-8 (CXCL8) calls neutrophils. Other mediators are histamine, complement (C3a, C5a) and the lipids prostaglandins and leukotrienes: they activate endothelium (vessels dilate and leak), draw cells and contract smooth muscle. Prostaglandins and leukotrienes are potent proinflammatory mediators made from arachidonic acid in membrane phospholipids, prostaglandins by cyclooxygenase (blocked by NSAIDs) and leukotrienes by lipoxygenase.

Leukocyte extravasation: rolling (selectins bind mucin-like CAMs, which are glycoproteins) → activation by chemokines → tight binding (integrins bind Ig-superfamily CAMs: LFA-1 on neutrophils, Mac-1 on monocytes; in inflammation LFA-1 binds ICAM-1) → diapedesis between endothelial cells (PECAM-1) → chemotaxis up the chemokine gradient (IL-8, C5a, leukotrienes, bacterial peptides). Cells enter in order: neutrophils first (their numbers in the blood rise fast), then monocytes (which become M1 macrophages), then basophils, eosinophils and lymphocytes. A CD18 integrin defect (leukocyte adhesion deficiency) means no pus and severe early periodontitis.

Macrophages through the response: resident sentinel macrophages detect the problem and make the first cytokines; monocytes recruited early become M1 (inflammatory) macrophages, and those recruited later become M2 macrophages that help resolution and tissue repair.

KindInflammatory?Features
ApoptosisNoProgrammed, caspases; shrinkage, rounding, chromatin condensation, DNA fragments, blebs; DAMPs stay sequestered, so it is immunologically silent
NecrosisYesUnprogrammed: the cell ruptures after overwhelming injury (infection, trauma); DAMPs released
NecroptosisYesProgrammed; happens when apoptotic signaling is blocked: pores form in the membrane, then the cell and its organelles burst, releasing many DAMPs
PyroptosisYesNLRs sense PAMPs or DAMPs → inflammasome and caspase-1; releases IL-1β and IL-18 with the cell's contents
NETosisYesUnique to neutrophils: after their PRRs bind bacteria (gram-positive or gram-negative) or fungi, they cast out their chromatin as a net that traps and destroys microbes

Macrophage cytokines also act on the whole body: fever and the acute phase response. Molecules that cause fever are pyrogens: IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-α act through prostaglandins in the hypothalamus. The acute phase response is a change in the levels of certain serum proteins, made mostly by hepatocytes, driven largely by IL-6 (with IL-1 and TNF-α, the master inflammatory regulators): the liver makes more CRP (opsonin, activates classical complement), mannose-binding lectin, fibrinogen (raises the ESR) and serum amyloid A, proteins that enhance phagocytosis and inflammation.

Cytokines to know

  • TNF-α and IL-1: activate endothelium, fever; TNF-α in excess drives septic shock.
  • IL-6: the acute phase response; IL-8 (CXCL8): the main neutrophil chemokine.
  • IL-12: from macrophages and dendritic cells; activates NK cells and pushes CD4 cells toward Th1.
  • Type I interferons (IFN-α, IFN-β): antiviral state; IFN-γ: activates macrophages.
  • IL-10 and TGF-β: calm inflammation down and favor tolerance.

Antibodies

Two identical heavy chains and two light chains (κ or λ), held by disulfide bonds. Each light chain has one variable and one constant region; each heavy chain has one variable and 3–4 constant regions. The Fab arms carry the variable regions of both chains, whose hypervariable regions (CDRs) touch the epitope and set the specificity; antibodies bind epitopes on proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids. The heavy-chain constant region (the Fc tail) decides the isotype, its structure and its effector functions, and binds Fc receptors and C1q; κ or λ doesn't change function. Antibodies aren't cytotoxic themselves: they flag targets for other cells through neutralization, opsonization, complement activation and ADCC. Fc receptors: FcγRs bind IgG (phagocytes, NK cells), FcεRs bind IgE (mast cells, basophils), and FcRn (neonatal) carries IgG across the placenta. IgG, a monomer whose Fc many cells' FcγRs can reach, is the most versatile antibody.

IgGMonomerMost abundant in serum; main antibody of the secondary response; crosses the placenta (FcRn); opsonizes, ADCC

How diversity is made

  • V(D)J recombination (somatic recombination) in developing lymphocytes, at random and before any infection: heavy chains join V + D + J; light chains join V + J only. RAG1 and RAG2 cut the DNA at recombination signal sequences; TdT adds random nucleotides at the joints; heavy and light chains pair in many combinations. These are the only site-specific DNA rearrangements known in vertebrates. Each B cell has one unique BCR, and the antibody it secretes has exactly the same specificity. A pathogen selects the few cells that fit, and they multiply (clonal selection and expansion).
  • RNA splicing, not DNA recombination, lets a naive B cell make IgM and IgD together: no switch region separates the μ and δ genes, so one transcript is spliced either way. Splicing also decides whether a heavy chain keeps its membrane-insertion piece (the BCR) or is secreted (antibody).
  • Class switching in activated B cells changes the constant region, not the specificity. It needs CD40 on the B cell binding CD40L on a helper T cell, which turns on the enzyme AID, and cytokines from the T cell, which pick the class (IL-4 → IgE; TGF-β → IgA) by opening switch regions for transcription. The DNA between the switch regions is cut out, so a switch can't be undone. A CD40L defect gives hyper-IgM syndrome.
  • Somatic hypermutation (also AID) makes point mutations in the rearranged VJ and VDJ regions as germinal-center B cells multiply; a clone's affinity can rise, fall or turn self-reactive. Follicular dendritic cells hold antigen, and only clones with high-affinity BCRs can bind it and survive: affinity maturation. The specificity stays the same, and the selected cells can then switch class.

MHC and antigen presentation

The TCR is built like an antibody's Fab arm, by the same V(D)J recombination (RAG1, RAG2, TdT): α chains join V + J, β chains V + D + J (γ like α, δ like β). Classic α/β T cells recognize only protein; the minority γ/δ T cells are specialized cells that recognize nonpeptide antigens such as lipids. The TCR chains bind peptide and MHC but don't signal: the CD3 complex (γ, δ, ε) and ζ chains do, and CD4 or CD8 steadies the contact. A TCR sees peptide only when its own body's MHC presents it (MHC restriction), and each TCR fits one peptide. Unlike a BCR, a TCR is never secreted, has one antigen-binding site (an antibody has two) and has a simple constant region (no class switching).

MHC genes (the HLA complex, on chromosome 6) are polygenic (several genes make nearly identical molecules: HLA-A, B, C and DP, DQ, DR), polymorphic (many alleles in the population, such as HLA-A1 and A5, differing mostly in the peptide-binding groove; the most polymorphic genes in the genome) and codominant (both parents' alleles are expressed). Each MHC molecule binds hundreds of different peptides, so more alleles show more peptides to more T cells. Most cells show both parents' class I; APCs show both parents' class I and class II.

Rule of 8: CD4 × II = 8, CD8 × I = 8. An MHC molecule is stable on the surface only with a peptide in its groove, so cells show self peptides all the time, and foreign ones join them in an infection. Dendritic cells can also cross-present engulfed antigen on MHC I to prime CD8 T cells.

B-cell activation

  • T-independent antigens (any kind of molecule) activate B cells without T-cell help. TI-2 antigens have repeating epitopes, often polysaccharides, that cross-link many BCRs; TI-1 antigens (mitogens), often microbial wall parts such as LPS, bind a PRR such as a TLR as well as the BCR. Both give low-affinity IgM with little switching or memory; polysaccharide responses are weak in children under 2.
  • T-dependent antigens (proteins only): the B cell takes the antigen in through its BCR (receptor-mediated endocytosis; B cells aren't phagocytic but are professional APCs) and presents peptide on MHC II to a Tfh cell in a secondary lymphoid organ. The B and T cells see the same antigen but different epitopes (linked recognition). The Tfh cell gives CD40L and cytokines (IL-21); germinal centers then run somatic hypermutation, affinity maturation and class switching, making high-affinity switched plasma cells and many memory B cells.
  • The BCR is membrane antibody plus Igα/Igβ; CR2 (CD21) binding complement C3d on the antigen lowers the threshold.

T-cell activation and helper subsets

Naive T cells are activated only in secondary lymphoid tissue (the draining lymph node), where dendritic cells, the best activators of naive T cells, bring antigen from the infected tissue. The dendritic cell gives signal 1 (peptide–MHC to TCR and CD4/CD8), signal 2 (B7 = CD80/86 binding CD28) and signal 3 (cytokines: IL-2, which the T cell both makes and uses through its high-affinity receptor, whose α chain is CD25, drives clonal expansion). Signal 1 without signal 2 gives anergy. CTLA-4 and PD-1 later turn the response off. Afterward most effector cells die by apoptosis and memory cells remain. The cytokines the dendritic cell makes decide the helper subset; effector Th cells then go back to the infected tissue, where dendritic cells, macrophages or B cells showing the same peptide set off their cytokines.

SubsetMade underFactorSecretesJob
Th1IL-12T-betIFN-γActivates macrophages and CD8 T cells against phagocytosed and intracellular microbes
Th2IL-4GATA-3IL-4, IL-5, IL-13IgE, eosinophils; helminths, allergy
Th17TGF-β + IL-6 (kept by IL-23)RORγtIL-17, IL-22Neutrophils; extracellular bacteria and fungi
TregTGF-β + IL-2FoxP3TGF-β, IL-10Suppress self-reactive cells, keep tolerance, prevent autoimmunity; TGF-β and IL-10 are anti-inflammatory

CD8 cytotoxic T cells are activated in two steps. Priming, in secondary lymphoid tissue, needs peptide–MHC I with the TCR, costimulation and cytokines from CD4 T cells; the dendritic cell gets the peptide by cross-presentation. Killing, in the tissue, needs only the TCR binding its peptide on the target's MHC I, with no costimulation. The CTL kills with perforin (built like C9; it lets the other granule contents in) and granzymes (serine proteases; granzyme B starts apoptosis) or Fas–FasL, and it makes IFN-γ.

Antiviral defense

  • Type I interferons (IFN-α, IFN-β) come from infected cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells after RIG-I-like receptors (dsRNA in the cytosol), TLR3 (dsRNA) or TLR7/8 (ssRNA) in endosomes sense viral nucleic acid and turn on IRF transcription factors. Through JAK-STAT signaling they put the infected cell and its neighbors into an antiviral state (protein synthesis blocked), raise MHC I and activate NK cells. IFN-γ (type II) comes from Th1, NK and CD8 cells and activates macrophages.
  • NK cells (large granular lymphocytes, CD16 and CD56) have no TCR and need no priming by an APC. Their receptors are inhibitory (ITIM motifs) or activating (ITAM motifs), and they kill when activating signals outweigh inhibitory ones. Many inhibitory receptors bind MHC I, so a cell that loses MHC I ("missing self") is killed; NK cells sense how much MHC I a cell has, not which peptide it shows. CD16 (an FcγR) lets them kill IgG-coated cells (ADCC). They kill with the same perforin, granzymes and Fas–FasL as CTLs. IFN-α/β and IL-12 activate them; they make IFN-γ, which activates macrophages, an inflammatory feedback loop.
  • Later: CD8 T cells and neutralizing antibody. Viruses escape by hiding MHC I (herpesviruses), changing antigens (influenza) or latency.

Memory and vaccines

Memory belongs to B and T cells: after a primary response the innate system resets and answers about the same way the next time (innate memory is less well understood). Most effector cells die after an infection; memory B and T cells remain. They are more numerous (about 1 in a thousand cells instead of 1 in a million), live in peripheral tissues as well as lymphoid organs, and are easier to activate: memory T cells need fewer peptide–MHC contacts and no costimulation, and memory B cells have higher-affinity BCRs, many of them class-switched. The secondary response is faster and larger, mostly high-affinity IgG (the primary is mostly lower-affinity IgM). Vaccines usually aim for protective immunity (milder disease) rather than sterilizing immunity (no infection at all).

TypeExamplesNotes

Adjuvants are needed for protein subunit, toxoid and conjugate vaccines, because purified proteins don't trigger PRRs. Aluminum salts (alum) are the most common; newer ones (monophosphoryl lipid A, CpG) target TLRs. They help the antigen persist and activate APCs, raising their costimulatory molecules. Live, whole, mRNA and viral vector vaccines generally don't need one. Protection lasts longest when a vaccine looks like the pathogen, follows its route of infection and the pathogen changes little.

Influenza protection is short: antibody falls quickly, the vaccines make few memory T cells, and the virus changes. Antigenic drift is gradual change from copying errors in its genes; antigenic shift is a sudden new protein from reassortment of genome segments with an influenza virus of another species (avian, swine), one no immune system has seen. Original antigenic sin (immune imprinting): antibody and memory B cells from the first strain met suppress naive B cells, so later responses stay aimed at that strain's epitopes and protection against variants erodes.

Herd immunity: when enough people are immune, by vaccination or infection, a disease can't spread to those who can't be vaccinated or don't respond.

Dental personnel get the hepatitis B series and an anti-HBs test 1–2 months later: 10 mIU/mL or more means protected; a nonresponder repeats the series once.

Mucosal immunity

The systemic and the mucosal immune systems are two semi-autonomous parts of one immune system: the systemic one defends against pathogens that enter through the skin, the mucosal one against those that breach a mucosal surface. Mucosal surfaces, needed for gas exchange, absorption and reproduction, are permeable and far larger than the skin, so most infections start there. Most of what is known comes from the gut; the eye's and the mouth's mucosa are built differently but share many of its components.

  • Barrier: goblet cells secrete mucins, the glycoproteins of the mucus layer. Sialic acid gives mucins a negative charge, so positively charged effector molecules stay in the mucus: defensins and other antimicrobial peptides (which lyse microbes) and secretory IgA (which neutralizes them). Tight junctions keep molecules from slipping between epithelial cells, which would set off inflammation.
  • Secretory antibody: plasma cells in the lamina propria make dimeric IgA. The poly-Ig receptor on the epithelium binds the J chain of polymeric antibody and carries it across the cell; part of the receptor stays on as secretory component, protecting it from proteases. So pentameric IgM, which also has a J chain, can be carried out too, while monomeric IgA, with no J chain, can't. IgA dominates secretions only because most mucosal plasma cells make IgA. TGF-β drives IgA switching.
  • Constant sampling: M cells over Peyer's patches (the gut's MALT) carry molecules and microbes from the lumen to the immune cells on their basolateral side, and dendritic cells reach between epithelial cells to sample the lumen. Antigen sampled in this immunosuppressive setting keeps the dendritic cells tolerant.
  • A ready defense: healthy mucosa is crowded with effector cells, much like inflamed tissue elsewhere. Epithelial cells are a bridge: their PRRs detect commensals, and they answer with antimicrobial peptides, cytokines and surface proteins that signal to immune cells.
  • Tolerance (inflammation only when absolutely needed, to spare the barrier): epithelial cells release TGF-β, IL-10, retinoic acid and short-chain fatty acids, which keep dendritic cells and macrophages tolerant. Tolerant dendritic cells secrete TGF-β, which drives naive CD4 T cells to become Tregs (CD4+, CD25+, FoxP3+); Tregs are plentiful and make IL-10. Mucosal macrophages are highly phagocytic but hyporesponsive to PAMPs and DAMPs: they destroy what they eat in lysosomes with no respiratory burst, make no proinflammatory cytokines, carry no activation or costimulatory molecules and favor Tregs. Monocytes recruited to replace them take on the same anti-inflammatory character.
  • When the barrier is breached, the mucosa switches to an active state: dendritic cells present more antigen, raise their costimulatory molecules and secrete cytokines that make Th1 and Th17 cells, and macrophages make proinflammatory mediators. This contains the pathogen but damages the epithelium, so it is the last resort. Systemic responses are reactive (inflammation clears the pathogen at a destructive cost); mucosal responses are proactive and non-inflammatory.
  • The microbiota (the microbiome is the catalogue of these microbes and their genes) lives in symbiosis with us and is needed for the mucosal tissues and their lymphoid cells to develop and work. It makes essential metabolites, breaks down complex molecules, inactivates toxins, takes up the space pathogens would use and influences the epithelium, and it induces tolerance and limits inflammation. Oral tolerance is a specific, peripheral unresponsiveness to a protein antigen introduced by mouth. Dysbiosis, a disturbed microbiota (antibiotics kill helpful microbes along with pathogens), breaks down the mucus layer and the epithelium and sets off inflammation; it is linked to Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, food allergy, asthma and C. difficile infection.
  • Selective IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency; often mild (secretory IgM, carried out by the poly-Ig receptor, can partly stand in), with a risk of reactions to blood products.

What's tested

Lymphocyte development

All lymphocytes come from hematopoietic stem cells in the marrow. B cells mature in the bone marrow; T-cell precursors move to the thymus.

  • Pro-B: the heavy chain rearranges (D–J, then V–DJ).
  • Pre-B: the new μ heavy chain pairs with a surrogate light chain and Igα/Igβ (the pre-BCR), a check that it works and can signal. Its signal stops the other heavy-chain allele from rearranging (allelic exclusion), and the light chain (κ or λ) rearranges; once one light chain works, the other light-chain genes stop too, so each B cell has one specificity.
  • Immature B: surface IgM, tested in the marrow against self-proteins that the marrow's stromal cells make. Strong binding → receptor editing (only the light chain can be swapped) → apoptosis if still self-reactive. Weak binding of soluble self → anergy. Cells that pass leave the marrow.
  • Mature naive B: finishes maturing in the spleen and lymph nodes and carries IgM and IgD at once, the only B-cell stage with two isotypes. RNA splicing of one transcript, not DNA recombination, decides IgM versus IgD.
  • Double negative thymocytes (CD4−CD8−) rearrange the β chain (pre-TCR), then the α chain.
  • Double positive (CD4+CD8+) cells undergo positive selection in the cortex: the TCR must bind self-MHC weakly. No binding → death by neglect (most thymocytes). Binding class I → CD8; class II → CD4.
  • Negative selection, at the single-positive stage, mainly in the medulla (epithelial cells using AIRE, a transcription factor that switches on proteins from tissues all over the body, and dendritic cells): binding self peptide or self-MHC too strongly → apoptosis, or for some, becoming a Treg.
  • Single-positive naive T cells that pass leave the thymus. The thymus is fully formed before birth and starts to shrink within the first year; T-cell output falls further around puberty, but immunity holds because mature T cells are long-lived. B cells, by contrast, are made in the marrow for life.

Tolerance

  • Central tolerance happens in the primary organs as lymphocytes develop. AIRE lets the thymus show proteins normally made elsewhere (insulin, parathyroid and adrenal proteins). AIRE loss = APS-1 (APECED): chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency.
  • Central tolerance isn't perfect (editing or deletion can fail, or a self-antigen is shown too little), so peripheral tolerance catches cells that escape: traffic limits (naive T cells stay in the secondary lymphoid organs; only effector cells enter tissues), anergy (antigen without costimulation: an ordinary cell such as a kidney cell shows self-peptide without B7, so a naive T cell that sees it shuts down; later in a response CTLA-4 helps turn T cells off), activation-induced cell death (Fas and FasL appear on B and T cells late in a response; loss of survival signals at the end of an infection also kills them, leaving a few memory cells) and Tregs (CD4+CD25+FoxP3+; natural ones from the thymus, induced ones made from naive T cells in the periphery by TGF-β and IL-2; they suppress with IL-10 and TGF-β, by soaking up IL-2 and with CTLA-4 stripping B7 from APCs). Tregs handle most self-reactive cells that escape.
  • FOXP3 loss = IPEX (early severe autoimmunity); Fas loss = autoimmune lymphoproliferative syndrome.
  • Immune-privileged sites (brain, eye, testes, the pregnant uterus and fetus) limit immune responses that would damage them. The privilege is not mainly keeping immune cells out: it is active local suppression of responses to the tissue's own antigens, through TGF-β, IL-10 and high Fas ligand, which kills entering lymphocytes. Injury that releases their hidden antigens can start autoimmunity (sympathetic ophthalmia).

How autoimmunity starts

Central tolerance misses some cells and Tregs handle most of them, so autoimmunity needs more: genes plus a trigger, usually infection or inflammation.

  • Genes: MHC (HLA) differences sit mostly in the peptide-binding groove, so an allele decides which peptides are shown and how strongly T cells respond. HLA-B27: ankylosing spondylitis, carried by about 90% of patients: inflamed entheses (where ligaments and tendons insert) of the spine, which fuses, and uveitis in about half. HLA-DR4 (DRβ1*04): rheumatoid arthritis. Peptidyl arginine deiminases (PADs) turn arginine into citrulline as cells die; the immune system normally never sees it because phagocytes clear apoptotic cells, but when clearance fails, citrullinated joint proteins (vimentin, collagen, fibrinogen) bind DR4's groove better and CD4 T cells respond. HLA-DQ2/DQ8: celiac disease (gluten deamidated by tissue transglutaminase). DR3/DR4: type 1 diabetes. Each is a correlation, not a cause. Sex and hormones matter too: most autoimmune diseases are more common in women.
  • Molecular mimicry: a microbial epitope looks like self, so B and T cells made against the microbe cross-react; in acute rheumatic fever, antibodies against group A β-hemolytic streptococci cross-react with heart (myocardial) proteins.
  • Bystander activation: an infection's inflammation activates dendritic cells that are presenting self peptides, and with their new costimulation they activate self-reactive T cells in the lymphoid tissue by mistake.
  • Cryptic antigens and neoantigens: damage releases proteins that normally stay sequestered inside cells, with epitopes T cells were never tested against, or a chemical change creates new ones (citrullination; a drug bound to a protein).
  • Epitope spreading: the response starts on one epitope of a molecule and moves to other epitopes of the same molecule, then to other molecules. Pemphigus vulgaris, the most serious bullous disease (type II: IgG and C3 on the cadherins of keratinocyte desmosomes; oral ulcers and skin blisters), starts with antibodies to desmoglein 3 (mouth) and later adds desmoglein 1 (skin); the spread tracks the disease getting worse.

Hypersensitivity

Hypersensitivity is an excessive or aberrant immune response to an antigen that poses little or no threat (or, when tolerance fails, to self: autoimmunity). The four types are classed by how the tissue-damaging reaction starts.

TypeEffectorTimingMechanismExamples

  • Type I: allergens are soluble proteins or glycoproteins with many epitopes (often proteases or carrying PAMPs) that cross mucosa in tiny amounts; atopy is a predisposition to become IgE-sensitized to them. Sensitization: first exposure → Th2 cells, IL-4 → IgE that settles on the high-affinity FcεRI of tissue mast cells and blood basophils. Re-exposure cross-links it and the mast cell degranulates. Immediate phase (within 30 minutes): preformed granule contents, mainly histamine (made from histidine by histidine decarboxylase), with tryptase and heparin: vasodilation, leaky vessels, bronchospasm, itch, wheal (serum leaking into the skin) and flare (redness from dilated vessels). Late phase (4+ hours): chemokines and cytokines from the first wave recruit eosinophils, basophils, Th2 cells and monocytes. Eosinophils lead it: their major basic protein and eosinophil cationic protein keep mast cells degranulating, and leukotrienes (from LOX) and prostaglandins (from COX), made from arachidonic acid, swell tissue and contract smooth muscle. IL-4 keeps up Th2 cells and IgE switching, IL-5 keeps eosinophils alive and active (eosinophilia), and IL-13 drives mucus and tissue remodeling. The late phase is the same recruitment as inflammation from infection or injury, set off by an allergen; eosinophils also drive chronic allergic inflammation (eosinophilic esophagitis).
  • IgE and mast cells exist to fight helminths and other parasites too big to phagocytose, which must be expelled; without infection the same response is aimed at harmless allergens (the hygiene hypothesis is one idea for why). Anaphylaxis is the systemic form: foods trigger most in children, teenagers and young adults, stings and drugs in older adults. Treat with intramuscular epinephrine first (0.3–0.5 mg in an adult, in the thigh); antihistamines are second-line.
  • Type II: mostly IgG on a cell-surface protein. The cell dies by complement's membrane attack complex (IgG or IgM), by phagocytosis or ADCC through Fc receptors (NK cells), or it loses function. Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn: a first Rh-positive pregnancy sensitizes an Rh-negative mother, whose first anti-RhD is IgM, which can't cross the placenta; in a later pregnancy her memory B cells switch to IgG, which does, and destroys fetal red cells. Anti-RhD is the most dangerous; other blood-group antigens (Kell, Rh c and E) can do it too if they raise IgG. Anti-D immune globulin (RhoGAM) is anti-RhD IgG: fetal red cells coated with it don't activate her naive B cells. A drug such as penicillin stuck to red cells makes a neoantigen (drug-induced hemolytic anemia). In myasthenia gravis the antibody blocks the acetylcholine receptor without complement or Fc receptors: loss of function.
  • Type III: IgG binds soluble antigen, and the small complexes are cleared poorly, lodge in small vessels and fix complement; the inflammation makes vessels leaky and destroys the tissue around them, and phagocytes can't engulf complexes stuck to a wall (frustrated phagocytosis), so it is hard to resolve. Localized: the Arthus reaction, 4–8 hours after antigen enters the skin of someone who already has IgG to it: a large red, swollen area (some insect bites; rarely a tetanus or diphtheria vaccine). Systemic: serum sickness, from foreign serum proteins (antivenom in the past, drugs now): an itchy rash, arthritis and fever days to weeks later; and SLE, where antinuclear antibodies (probably from poorly cleared apoptotic cells; anti-dsDNA is highly specific) form complexes that deposit in tissues.
  • Type IV: T-cell initiated, mostly Th1 cells (IFN-γ activates macrophages), with CD8 CTLs that lyse cells. Sensitization takes at least 7 days; the effector reaction comes 24–72 hours after re-exposure. Contact hypersensitivity, the most common type IV: small chemicals (nickel, urushiol from poison ivy, glove accelerators) bind skin proteins and make neoantigens; Langerhans cells carry them to the node. The tuberculin test is read at 48–72 hours; its firm red lump is mostly macrophages, not neutrophils. Persistent microbes (M. tuberculosis) keep macrophages activated: they turn epithelioid and fuse into multinucleated giant cells, forming granulomas that wall the organism off but damage tissue. Celiac disease: CD4 T cells react to deamidated gluten peptides (a neoantigen) in the gut's lymphoid tissue, and the macrophages they activate destroy the epithelium. Type 1 diabetes: CD8 T cells lyse the insulin-making β cells, helped by CD4 T cells and macrophages.

In the dental clinic

  • Gloves: natural rubber latex proteins cause type I reactions (hives, swelling, wheezing in minutes); accelerators in gloves cause type IV contact dermatitis (1–2 days later); irritant dermatitis isn't immune at all.
  • Penicillin can cause all four types: its reactive bond (the β-lactam ring) binds host proteins and makes neoantigens, so it can cause anaphylaxis (I), hemolytic anemia (II), serum sickness-like illness (III) and rashes (IV).
  • True allergy to amide local anesthetics is rare; ester anesthetics (broken down to PABA) and the sulfite preservative in solutions with epinephrine are the usual culprits.

Looking at tissue

Light microscopes resolve about 0.2 µm; transmission electron microscopes show inner detail and scanning ones show surfaces. Bright-field microscopy needs stained tissue; phase-contrast and differential interference contrast microscopy show living, unstained cells (cell culture); fluorescence microscopy shows molecules that give off light.

  • Fixation stabilizes proteins, carbohydrates and lipids so the tissue doesn't decompose: formalin for light microscopy, glutaraldehyde and osmium tetroxide for electron microscopy.
  • Dehydration (alcohol or acetone), then clearing (xylene) and embedding: paraffin for light microscopy, epoxy resin for electron microscopy.
  • Sectioning: a microtome cuts 5–10 µm sections for light microscopy; an ultramicrotome cuts 50–100 nm sections for electron microscopy.
  • Staining with dyes (below). Immunohistochemistry tags an antibody against one antigen with a dye or a heavy metal (a fluorescent tag in immunofluorescence) to show where that molecule sits in the tissue.

Germ layers

Gastrulation (days 15–16) makes the three germ layers and puts them in place: ectoderm outside, endoderm inside and mesoderm between. Forming tissues is histogenesis.

  • Ectoderm: epidermis, hair, nails, enamel, the nervous system and the sensory placodes; neural crest forms much of the face and the dentin, pulp, cementum and PDL.
  • Mesoderm: connective tissue, cartilage, bone, muscle, heart, blood, kidneys, gonads, the linings of body cavities.
  • Endoderm: the lining of the gut and airways, lungs, liver, pancreas, thyroid, parathyroids.

The four basic tissues

  • Epithelium: covers surfaces, lines cavities, forms glands; cells packed close with little matrix.
  • Connective tissue: supports and connects; scattered cells in a lot of matrix.
  • Muscle: contracts (skeletal, cardiac, smooth). Nervous tissue: signals (neurons and glia).

A white cell leaving a vessel rolls on selectins (weak adhesion), then sticks firmly and squeezes out between the endothelial cells through integrins.

Epithelium

Epithelium covers body surfaces and lines cavities, a border between two environments, and forms glands. It comes from all three germ layers (the epidermis from ectoderm, endothelium and mesothelium from mesoderm, the gut lining from endoderm). It is polarized (an apical domain facing the lumen and a basolateral domain on the basement membrane), avascular (fed by diffusion from the connective tissue), tightly joined, and sits on a basement membrane: the basal lamina (lamina lucida with laminin; lamina densa with type IV collagen), made by the epithelial cells, plus a reticular lamina of type III collagen from the connective tissue. Seen together by light microscopy, the two layers are the PAS-positive basement membrane. In the glomerulus and the lung's alveolar wall, two cell layers share one fused basal lamina.

  • The basal lamina binds the epithelium to the connective tissue, lets nutrients in and metabolites out, filters selectively (the glomerulus), and binds growth factors that steer cell growth and repair.
  • Jobs of epithelium: protection (epidermis), absorption (gut), secretion (glands), excretion (kidney), lubrication (mesothelium of the pleura, pericardium and peritoneum), sensation (taste buds, retina) and reproduction (sperm are modified epithelial cells).
  • Renewal is fast in some places (the intestinal lining is replaced about weekly) and slow in others (large glands). In stratified epithelium only the basal layer divides; daughter cells move up and differentiate, so damage is repaired quickly.

It's named for its number of layers (simple, pseudostratified, stratified), the shape of its surface cells (squamous, cuboidal, columnar) and its surface specializations.
