  • Microvilli: short, still, with a core of actin filaments only, anchored in the terminal web; high-capacity absorption (the brush border).
  • Stereocilia: much longer microvilli, also still, their actin cross-linked by α-actinin; found only in the male reproductive tract (epididymis) and the inner ear's hair cells.
  • Motile cilia: long enough to see by light microscopy; an axoneme of 9+2 microtubules (9 doublets around 2 central ones) rising from a basal body, moved by dynein, covered by the cell membrane; they move mucus, fluid or cells across the surface. A dynein defect (primary ciliary dyskinesia) causes sinus and lung infections. A primary cilium is a single, nonmotile sensory antenna on most cells.
  • Basal (and lateral) infoldings: folds of the membrane, packed with mitochondria, that add surface (striated ducts, kidney tubules).

All glands come from epithelium that grows down into the connective tissue and stay lined by it: exocrine glands keep a duct to the surface; endocrine glands lose it and secrete into the capillaries around them. Goblet cells are one-cell glands. Exocrine glands are classed three ways. By structure: a simple gland has an unbranched duct and a compound gland a branched one, and the secretory units are tubular (straight) or acinar (rounded), and may coil or branch. By product: serous, mucous or mixed. By mode of secretion: merocrine by exocytosis, usually of proteins, the way most glands secrete (salivary glands, pancreas, eccrine sweat glands); apocrine, losing a bit of membrane-wrapped apical cytoplasm, usually with lipid droplets (mammary lipid, while its proteins leave by exocytosis; apocrine sweat glands); and holocrine, the whole cell filling with product and breaking down (sebaceous glands of hair follicles). Serous cells make watery, enzyme-rich fluid and look dark and full of granules (parotid); mucous cells make mucins and look pale and hollow (minor palatal glands); the submandibular gland is mixed, mostly serous, and the sublingual mixed, mostly mucous.

A salivary gland shows the parts of a compound gland: secretory acini drain into intercalated ducts (simple cuboidal), then striated ducts, whose basal infoldings packed with mitochondria pump ions to make the saliva hypotonic, then the larger excretory ducts (stratified cuboidal or columnar). Myoepithelial cells around the acini contract to squeeze the product out.

Connective tissue

  • Mostly from mesoderm, by way of embryonic mesenchyme. Connective tissue gives the body its shape, supports and packs the other tissues, stores fat, signals to cells through the matrix, defends, and heals wounds. It carries the blood vessels and nerves (cartilage has none). In an organ, the cells doing its main job are the parenchyma (hepatocytes in the liver); the connective tissue framework that supports and feeds them is the stroma.
  • Resident cells: fibroblasts, adipocytes, pericytes, mast cells, tissue macrophages and stem cells. Transient cells: white blood cells (and the plasma cells they become) that arrive as needed for defense.
  • Fibroblasts, the main cell, make the collagen, elastic and reticular fibers and the ground substance. They rarely divide, but resume mitosis to heal a wound. A resting fibroblast (fibrocyte) is small and spindle-shaped; an active one is larger, with more rough ER.
  • Pericytes wrap small vessels, most of all postcapillary venules. They can become other cell types, steady and mature the endothelium, and contract or relax to set capillary blood flow.
  • Mast cells come from the bone marrow and finish maturing in the connective tissue, where they live a long time (basophils, with similar granules, circulate and are short-lived). They are large (20–30 µm) and packed with basophilic granules of heparin (a local anticoagulant), histamine (leaky vessels, smooth muscle contraction) and chemotactic factors; they also make leukotrienes and prostaglandins. Antigen binding IgE on their high-affinity Fc receptor sets off degranulation: immediate hypersensitivity.
  • Macrophages phagocytose bacteria and debris; those called in come from blood monocytes, while most resident ones descend from precursors seeded before birth. Plasma cells, terminally differentiated B cells, only secrete antibody; they have an off-center "clock-face" nucleus and basophilic cytoplasm packed with rough ER.
  • Fibers: collagen type I (the most abundant: skin, bone, dentin, tendon, PDL), type II (cartilage), type III (reticular fibers of lymph nodes, spleen and marrow, wrapped by the reticular cells that make them; early wounds), type IV (a sheet in the basal lamina) and type VII (anchoring fibrils that tie the basal lamina to the connective tissue). Types I, II and III form fibrils. Collagen synthesis needs vitamin C (scurvy: bleeding gums). Elastic fibers: fibroblasts make tropoelastin, and elastin covalently cross-linked on a fibrillin scaffold stretches and recoils like a rubber band. They are thinner than collagen fibers and hard to see without a special stain (fibrillin-1 defect: Marfan syndrome).
  • Ground substance, a clear, hydrated, semi-fluid gel: glycosaminoglycans (unbranched, acidic sugar chains: hyaluronic acid and chondroitin, dermatan, keratan and heparan sulfate), proteoglycans (GAGs on a protein core) and multiadhesive glycoproteins (fibronectin, laminin, chondronectin, osteonectin).
  • Types: loose (areolar, the lamina propria), dense irregular (dermis, capsules), dense regular (tendons, ligaments); specialized: cartilage, bone, blood, adipose, reticular tissue.

Blood is a specialized connective tissue whose cells form in the bone marrow; an adult has about 5–6 L. It is plasma (about 55%: water; albumin, the most abundant plasma protein; immunoglobulins and complement; lipoproteins; transport proteins such as transferrin and haptoglobin; fibrinogen and the other clotting factors; hormones, electrolytes and nutrients) plus cells (about 45%). The hematocrit, the packed red cell volume, is about 39–50% in men and 35–45% in women; white cells and platelets are only about 1% of blood volume. Serum is plasma without the clotting factors. Red cells and platelets stay in the vessels; white cells can leave for the tissues, and only lymphocytes return to the blood. White cells from most to fewest: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils. Blood carries gases, nutrients, hormones and wastes, buffers the pH at about 7.4, helps control body temperature, defends and clots.

Adipose: adipocytes are large (up to about 100 µm), and their lipid is not wrapped in a membrane. They store energy, insulate, cushion organs and secrete hormones. White fat is unilocular (one big droplet). Leptin, the adipocytes' hormone, lowers appetite; obese people have high levels but respond poorly to it. Insulin drives the cells' uptake and synthesis of triglycerides. Brown fat is multilocular, full of mitochondria, and uses thermogenin (UCP1) for heat without shivering; it is greatest at birth, scant in adults, and can grow with cold adaptation.

Cartilage, bone, muscle and nerve

  • Cartilage: chondrocytes sit in lacunae, often in isogenous groups, in a matrix of type II collagen (with elastic fibers in elastic cartilage) and proteoglycans that gives up water under pressure and takes it back (a shock absorber). A perichondrium surrounds it, and it has no blood vessels, nerves or lymphatics. Hyaline is the most common (nasal septum, joint surfaces, ribs); elastic cartilage is hyaline enriched with elastic fibers (external ear, larynx); fibrocartilage has rows of chondrocytes in a more fibrous matrix (intervertebral discs, tendon and ligament attachments).
  • Bone: highly ordered type I collagen with little ground substance, and calcium phosphate making up about 50% of the matrix; it is alive, highly vascular and always remodeling. It supports, protects, moves the body, stores calcium and holds the marrow. Osteoblasts lay down osteoid, osteocytes maintain the matrix (neither divides), and osteoclasts, large multinucleated cells of the monocyte line, resorb it. Compact bone is built of osteons (Haversian systems); cancellous (spongy) bone is trabeculae around the marrow, strong without the weight.

Supporting cells: Schwann cells and satellite cells in the PNS; astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia (neuroglia) in the CNS.

What's tested
  • Reversible versus irreversible cell injury, and the nuclear changes of cell death
  • The six necrosis patterns and the organ or disease each one belongs to (coagulative heart and kidney, liquefactive brain and abscess, caseous TB, fat necrosis pancreas)
  • Apoptosis versus necrosis, and the intrinsic (cytochrome c) and extrinsic (Fas) pathways, which both end in caspases
  • How cells are injured: ATP loss in hypoxia, free radicals and the enzymes that clear them, reperfusion injury
  • The four adaptations with an example of each, intracellular accumulations, and dystrophic versus metastatic calcification
  • Acute inflammation (vascular changes, exudate versus transudate, leukocyte recruitment, the main mediators, neutrophils versus macrophages) and chronic inflammation (M1 and M2 macrophages, granulomas, the morphologic patterns, repair and scar problems, the acute-phase response)
  • Neoplasia: naming, benign versus malignant, grade versus stage

Cell injury: reversible or not

Reversible injury goes back to normal if the cause is removed. The first sign is cell swelling (the ATP-driven sodium pump fails and water follows sodium in). Others: plasma membrane blebs, dilated ER with ribosomes falling off, swollen mitochondria, fatty change, myelin figures and clumped chromatin. The organ is heavier and firmer.

Irreversible injury ("the point of no return") comes from four failures: mitochondria can't make ATP again, membranes lose integrity, lysosomal enzymes leak and digest the cell, and DNA and chromatin break down. The nucleus shows it: pyknosis (shrinks and turns dark blue, basophilic), karyorrhexis (fragments) and karyolysis (nucleases from the lysosomes digest the DNA, so the nucleus fades); the cytoplasm turns pink (eosinophilic) as its proteins denature. Proteins that leak out of necrotic cells help diagnosis: troponin from heart, alkaline phosphatase from liver.

The changes are seen in order: biochemical, then electron microscopy, then light microscopy, then the gross organ. Heart muscle cut off from its blood stops contracting in 1–2 minutes, dies at 20–30 minutes (troponin appears in the blood), shows changes by electron microscopy at 2–3 hours and by light microscopy at 6–12 hours. How long cells survive ischemia depends on the cell: brain about 4 minutes, heart about 30 minutes, skeletal muscle about 3 hours. Injury also depends on its duration and severity and on the cell's type, nutrition, hormones, adaptability, genes and temperature.

Mitochondria are the first organelle hit by hypoxia: less oxidative phosphorylation means less ATP, so the cell switches to anaerobic glycolysis, lactic acid builds up and the pH falls (that is what clumps the chromatin).

MechanismKey points
Hypoxia and ischemiaIschemia = a blocked artery or vein, or blood loss; hypoxia = too little oxygen (high altitude, anemia, carbon monoxide). ATP falls: the Na+/K+ pump fails (swelling) and protein synthesis stops; severe, lasting ischemia finally breaks the mitochondrial and lysosomal membranes (necrosis)
Oxidative stressFree radicals (one unpaired electron: superoxide, hydroxyl radical, peroxynitrite from nitric oxide; hydrogen peroxide is a source) made faster than removed. Made by mitochondrial respiration, the phagocytes' respiratory burst, reperfusion and ionizing radiation; they damage lipids (peroxidation), proteins and DNA. Cleared by superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase
Ischemia-reperfusionRestoring blood flow to ischemic but viable tissue adds injury (more radicals and inflammation), e.g., after a heart attack, a stroke or a kidney transplant
ToxinsDirect-acting ones bind a vital molecule or organelle (chemotherapy drugs, microbial toxins); latent ones are converted (often by P450) to reactive metabolites that make radicals (pesticides, carcinogens, mycotoxins; asbestos can cause cancer decades later)
ER stressMisfolded proteins pile up; the unfolded protein response adds chaperones, and if that fails the cell dies by apoptosis
DNA damageRadiation, chemotherapy, radicals. p53 arrests the cycle to repair or triggers apoptosis

Endogenous pigments: lipofuscin (wear and tear), melanin (brown-black, made by melanocytes against UV light), hemosiderin. Exogenous: carbon (anthracosis, a smoker's lung), poisons such as lead, tattoo ink.

  • Metastatic calcification: high serum calcium (hyperparathyroidism, bone destroyed by cancer such as metastatic carcinoma, vitamin D excess, kidney failure), deposits in normal tissue (vessels, kidneys, the lungs' alveolar septa, stomach).

Acute inflammation

The five signs: pain, swelling, redness, heat and loss of function, all from the vascular changes and the leukocytes. Acute inflammation starts in minutes to hours, is mainly neutrophils, and its tissue injury is usually mild and self-limited; chronic inflammation starts over days, is macrophages and lymphocytes, and can be severe and progressive. Causes: infection, necrosis, foreign bodies (splinters, sutures, urate and cholesterol crystals), immune reactions (hypersensitivity, autoimmunity). Macrophages and dendritic cells recognize microbes with toll-like receptors, every cell has cytosolic sensors for molecules released by damage (DAMPs), and plasma proteins such as complement recognize microbes in the blood. Vessels: brief vasoconstriction, then histamine vasodilation (heat, redness), then leaky endothelium (endothelial cells retract under histamine and bradykinin, fast and short-lived; more transport across them too), then stasis (congestion) as fluid leaves, with neutrophils marginating to the vessel wall. Exudate = high protein and cells (inflammation; pus if full of neutrophils, debris and often microbes). Transudate = low protein, few cells (high hydrostatic or low oncotic pressure, e.g., heart failure). Edema is excess fluid in the tissue or a serous cavity, either kind. Lymphatics drain it and can become inflamed themselves (lymphangitis, red streaks up a limb; lymphadenitis in the nodes).

  1. Rolling: selectins.
  2. Firm adhesion: integrins (on the leukocyte) binding ICAM-1 and VCAM-1.
  3. Transmigration: PECAM-1 (CD31).
  4. Chemotaxis: chemokines, C5a, leukotriene B4, bacterial products.

TNF and IL-1 from macrophages make the endothelium put out selectins and integrin ligands; chemokines raise the integrins' grip and set the leukocyte's direction. Most mediators come from macrophages, dendritic cells and mast cells at the site and are short-lived.

Neutrophils dominate early; monocytes follow and become macrophages in the tissue (within about 48 hours). They kill by phagocytosis (recognition and attachment, engulfment into a phagosome, fusion with a lysosome into a phagolysosome) with reactive oxygen species (the phagocyte or NADPH oxidase makes superoxide and H2O2, and myeloperoxidase turns H2O2 into hypochlorite), nitric oxide (iNOS) and lysosomal enzymes. Outcomes: complete resolution (a limited, short injury with little tissue lost), healing by scarring (tissue that can't regenerate, or a lot of fibrin), or chronic inflammation (the agent persists or healing is disturbed).

Morphologic patterns (acute and chronic): serous (cell-poor fluid under a surface epithelium or in a serous cavity: a blister, an effusion), fibrinous (fibrinogen leaks and fibrin lines the pericardium or pleura; fibrinolysis and macrophages clear it, or it leaves adhesions), purulent (suppurative: neutrophils and liquefied debris of necrotic cells, from pyogenic bacteria such as staphylococci and streptococci; e.g., acute appendicitis, bacterial meningitis), abscess (pus localized in a tissue: a necrotic center with a rim of inflammatory cells), ulcer (a crater where inflamed necrotic tissue sloughs off a surface: mouth, gut, genitourinary tract, and the legs with poor circulation; acute and chronic inflammation together, a scar if it lasts; e.g., acute necrotizing ulcerative stomatitis) and granulomatous (below).

Chronic inflammation and repair

  • Causes: persistent infection (mycobacteria, some viruses, fungi, parasites), hypersensitivity (autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis or multiple sclerosis; allergy such as asthma), long toxic exposure (silica in silicosis; cholesterol in atherosclerosis). Histology: lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells, tissue destruction and fibrosis, so function is lost (acute = neutrophils, congestion and edema, tissue preserved, can resolve). Macrophages are the dominant cell: they phagocytose, secrete cytokines and growth factors (TNF, IL-1), activate T cells, and both drive inflammation and start repair.
  • M1 (classical) macrophages: switched on by microbial products and IFN-γ from CD4 T cells; make ROS, NO, IL-1, TNF, IL-6, IL-12; kill microbes. M2 (alternative): switched on by IL-4 and IL-13; secrete IL-10 and TGF-β; repair: new vessels, fibroblasts, collagen; anti-inflammatory. T cells and macrophages drive each other: T cells recruit macrophages (TNF, IL-17, chemokines) and switch them on (IFN-γ); macrophages present antigen and make IL-12 for the T cells, a cycle that keeps chronic inflammation going. Activated B cells and plasma cells are often there too. Eosinophils fight parasites (IgE). Mast cells act in both acute and chronic inflammation: antigen binds the IgE on their Fc receptors and they degranulate (histamine, prostaglandins), as in food and drug allergies and anaphylaxis.
  • Granulomas (granulomatous inflammation, a chronic pattern that walls off an agent that is hard to clear): epithelioid macrophages and multinucleated giant cells with a lymphocyte rim. Immune granulomas come from a persistent T-cell response: caseating in TB; noncaseating in sarcoidosis, Crohn disease and syphilis. Foreign-body granulomas form around fairly inert material (sutures, splinters, talc) with no T-cell response.
  • Repair: a platelet plug stops the bleeding and gives a scaffold → inflammation (about 1–2 days) → proliferation of epithelium, endothelium and fibroblasts (up to 1–2 weeks) with granulation tissue (new small vessels, edema, loose matrix, fibroblasts, macrophages, little collagen) → healing by regeneration (remaining cells regrow after a mild injury, no scar) or by scarring (remodeling after a bigger or chronic injury: collagen gives the tensile strength; a trichrome stain colors it blue). Fibrosis is heavy collagen in an organ: the heart after an infarct; the lung, liver (cirrhosis) and kidney after chronic inflammation. Labile tissues (blood-forming cells; skin, gut and genitourinary epithelium) always divide; stable (liver, kidney, pancreas) wait in G0 and can re-enter the cycle; permanent (neurons, heart muscle) heal only by scar. First intention (primary union) = a well-apposed surgical incision, minimal scar; second intention = a larger wound, healed by regeneration and scar together, with more granulation tissue and contraction.
  • Slow healing: infection (prolongs inflammation), protein or vitamin C deficiency, steroids (less TGF-β and fibrosis, so a weak scar), pressure or torsion, poor blood flow (arteriolosclerosis, diabetes), foreign bodies. Scar problems: hypertrophic scar (raised, inside the wound, can regress), keloid (grows past the wound edges, doesn't regress), exuberant granulation, contracture (the wound shrinks too much and deforms, as after burns).
  • Acute-phase response (cytokine-driven, whole body): fever (exogenous pyrogens such as bacterial lipopolysaccharide → endogenous pyrogens IL-1 and TNF → prostaglandins set the hypothalamus higher; NSAIDs such as aspirin block it; with a faster pulse, higher blood pressure, shivering, poor appetite and sleepiness), leukocytosis (normal white count 4,500–11,000/µL; often 15,000–20,000/µL in inflammation; 40,000–100,000/µL is a leukemoid reaction, which can mimic leukemia: first the marrow releases stored cells, including immature ones, then colony-stimulating factors make more), and liver proteins: CRP (binds microbial walls and complement, an opsonin; heart-attack risk marker), fibrinogen (sticks red cells together, raising the sedimentation rate), serum amyloid A (opsonin; long exposure causes secondary amyloidosis), hepcidin (holds iron: anemia of chronic disease). Sepsis is a severe acute-phase response to bacterial infection that can bring septic shock: low blood pressure, disseminated intravascular coagulation, metabolic trouble such as insulin resistance.

Neoplasia

A neoplasm ("new growth") is monoclonal (one transformed cell that keeps gathering mutations) and no longer answers normal growth controls. "Tumor" (a swelling) is used for it in the clinic, and a cancer is a malignant neoplasm. It has parenchyma (the neoplastic cells, which set its behavior and give it its name) and stroma (connective tissue and blood supply). Dysplasia is disordered, premalignant growth, usually in epithelium (cervix, oral mucosa; an adenoma in the gut), with more, disordered proliferation (more Ki-67 staining). The patient's cancer risk is higher, but the lesion may not progress.

GrowthUsually slowUsually faster (the less differentiated, the faster), with many exceptions; may outgrow its blood supply and necrose; still takes years to show

  • Benign or malignant is the most important clinical question: it decides conservative or wide excision, whether to check the lymph nodes (staging), and chemotherapy or radiation.
  • Function usually follows differentiation, but unexpected products can appear: ectopic hormones, fetal proteins.
  • Clinical: cachexia (lost body fat, weakness, anorexia, anemia, more infections, taste changes, a higher metabolic rate; worse with a bigger tumor); paraneoplastic syndromes (about 10–15% of patients; symptoms the tumor's spread can't explain: endocrine such as SIADH or excess cortisol, nerve and muscle disorders, blood and vessel changes such as thrombosis).
  • Diagnosis: biopsy (a tissue diagnosis), exfoliative cytology (Pap smear, bronchial brush), fine-needle aspiration (cytology). Tumor markers (PSA, CEA, alpha-fetoprotein) screen for or follow a tumor; they don't diagnose it.
  • Grade = differentiation under the microscope (1 = well differentiated). Stage = extent: TNM (T = tumor size and invasiveness, N = nodal metastases, M = distant metastases), AJCC stage 0 (carcinoma in situ) to IV; any distant metastasis makes it stage IV. Stage predicts prognosis better than grade.

What's tested

  • The Baltimore classes, which viruses bring their own RNA polymerase or reverse transcriptase, and the six steps of the life cycle
  • The human herpesviruses HHV-1 to HHV-8: their diseases and where each stays latent
  • HPV, adenovirus, parvovirus B19 and the poxviruses; the RNA viruses (how positive- and negative-sense genomes make mRNA; picornaviruses, coronavirus, measles, RSV, rabies, influenza drift and shift, the hemagglutination inhibition test)

Virus basics

Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites: a DNA or RNA genome (never both) in a protein capsid, sometimes wrapped in a lipid envelope taken from the host membrane (lipids, proteins and glycoproteins, with a matrix protein lining its inside). One particle is a virion. Viruses make no energy, have no metabolism, make no nucleotides or amino acids and encode no ribosomes; they are assembled from parts, not divided, and pass through filters that hold back bacteria ("filterable agents"). Bacteria, by contrast, make their own energy and proteins, carry dsDNA and divide by binary fission. Capsids are helical or icosahedral (20 triangular faces and 12 vertices, built from 60 identical subunits: a very stable shape); in human viruses a helical nucleocapsid is always enveloped. Viral attachment proteins (the envelope glycoproteins on an enveloped virus) bind host receptors, and which cells carry the receptor sets the host range and the tissue and cell tropism (HIV gp120 needs CD4; influenza hemagglutinin needs sialic acid).

EnvelopedNaked (non-enveloped)
Survives drying, acid, detergentPoorly: must stay wet; most can't survive the gutWell: survive the gut and stay infectious when dry
SpreadBlood, sex, respiratory dropletsFecal-oral, fomites
ReleaseBudding or exocytosis (cell often survives)Lysis of the host cell
ExamplesHerpesviruses, HIV, HBV, HCV, influenza, measles, coronavirusHAV, HEV, HPV, adenovirus, polio, parvovirus

The Baltimore classification sorts viruses by how they make mRNA, not by shape, envelope or disease: every strategy ends in mRNA that host ribosomes read. Humans have no RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), so a virus whose RNA genome isn't mRNA ((−)ssRNA, dsRNA) must carry its RdRp in the virion, while a (+)ssRNA virus makes its RdRp after entry by translating its genome.

IdsDNAHost RNA polymerase makes mRNAHerpes, adeno, HPV, polyoma, pox

V(−)ssRNAMust carry its own RdRp; genome not infectiousMeasles, RSV, rabies, influenza

Life cycle: attachment (adsorption) → entry → uncoating → transcription, replication and translation (every virus uses host ribosomes) → assembly → release. Entry: naked viruses enter by receptor-mediated endocytosis; enveloped ones fuse their envelope with the plasma membrane or, after endocytosis, with the endosome's membrane, where the low pH changes the shape of the viral proteins. Uncoating frees the genome, sometimes with the help of host endosomal proteases. DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus, except the poxviruses, which bring their own enzymes and replicate in the cytoplasm. Most RNA viruses stay in the cytoplasm. Assembly (building the capsid and packaging the genome) is usually spontaneous. Naked viruses assemble in the cytoplasm or nucleus and are usually released by lysis; enveloped ones take their envelope at the plasma membrane (released by budding) or at the ER or Golgi (released by exocytosis), usually without killing the cell.

One-step growth curve: right after infection, infectious virus in the culture falls (the eclipse period: the virions have entered and uncoated, so they are no longer infectious); new infectious virions appear only after replication and assembly, then rise to a plateau set by the burst size (virions made per cell). Bacteria instead grow by division, doubling exponentially.

How viruses cause disease and spread

A virus is selected to spread, not to kill: a dead host is a dead end. Much of the disease is collateral damage from the immune response (fever, lethargy, loss of appetite, rash, liver damage), on top of cells killed directly by the virus's replication. Starting an infection takes three things: an inoculum with enough live virus, susceptible cells it can reach and grow in, and innate and existing adaptive immunity too weak to stop it at once. The incubation period (to the first, prodromal symptoms) runs from days to years (HIV); the telling signs, such as a rash or paralysis, can come later. Virus spreads locally from the entry site, then through the blood: a primary viremia seeds organs such as the liver and spleen, where more replication makes a larger secondary viremia that carries it to its target organs (such as the skin or brain).

  • Human to human: respiratory droplets and aerosols (from breathing, speaking, singing, coughing and sneezing, even by people with no symptoms, as with SARS-CoV-2), the fecal-oral route, sex, saliva, skin contact, blood (needles) and mother to child. Mother-to-child spread (across the placenta, at birth or in breast milk) is vertical; spread between people otherwise is horizontal.
  • Animal to human: arthropod vectors (mosquitoes, ticks, fleas), other invertebrates (shellfish) and vertebrates (zoonoses from mammals and birds, such as rabies).
  • Stopping spread: staying home when sick (isolation and quarantine), hand hygiene, covering a sneeze, masks and distancing for respiratory viruses, mosquito control, education for sexually spread viruses (HIV, HSV) and, above all, vaccines.

DNA viruses

  • Herpesviruses: large enveloped dsDNA. Immediate-early, early (DNA polymerase), then late (structural) genes; capsids assemble in the nucleus and bud through the nuclear envelope. The hallmark is latency: the genome sits as a circular episome until it reactivates. Drugs such as acyclovir (a nucleoside analog activated by the viral kinase) stop replication but can't touch latent virus.
  • HPV (papillomavirus): naked, circular dsDNA; infects basal epithelial cells. Low-risk types (6, 11) cause warts and papillomas; 12 high-risk types cause cancer, with 16 and 18 the most important (then 31). The Gardasil vaccine is the L1 capsid protein as virus-like particles (no viral DNA): it covers 6, 11, 16 and 18, and Gardasil 9 adds 31, 33, 45, 52 and 58, preventing over 90% of HPV-related cancers. Polyomaviruses: large T antigen binds p53; JC virus causes PML, and Merkel cell polyomavirus causes Merkel cell carcinoma; serious mainly in the immunocompromised.
  • Adenovirus: naked, linear dsDNA; respiratory illness (military recruits), conjunctivitis ("shipyard eye"), gastroenteritis; tough in pools and on fomites; no antiviral.
  • Poxviruses: large, brick-shaped, cytoplasmic; smallpox (eradicated) and mpox, live vaccinia vaccine. Chickenpox is not a poxvirus.
  • Parvovirus B19: tiny naked ssDNA; grows in erythroid precursors in the marrow; fifth disease (slapped cheeks, rash from the immune response) in children, polyarthritis in adults; no vaccine.

Alpha herpesviruses (HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV) hide in neurons; beta (CMV, HHV-6, HHV-7) and gamma (EBV, HHV-8) in white cells. HSV hides from immunity by lowering MHC class I; its lesions are intraepithelial vesicles with multinucleated giant cells.

RNA viruses

  • (+)ssRNA: naked (icosahedral: picornaviruses, norovirus) or enveloped (coronavirus, rubella); every genome is linear, with a 5′ cap or a VPg protein on its end. The genome is mRNA, so it is infectious by itself and is translated as soon as it enters; no polymerase comes in the virion. It is self-replicating: it encodes its replication enzymes (RdRp first), proteins that block the innate immune response and the structural proteins. Then two steps: RdRp copies the genome into a full-length (−) antigenome, the template for new genomes and mRNAs; some (coronaviruses) also make shorter subgenomic mRNAs for single genes. Replication runs in cytoplasmic "viral factories" (inclusion bodies that shield it from host defenses); its dsRNA intermediates are what the sensors RIG-I and MDA5 detect.
  • Picornaviruses (small, naked): the genome is read as one long polyprotein that viral proteases cut into each protein, so every protein is made in equal (1:1) amounts. VPg, a small viral protein that the polymerase (3Dpol) tags with uridines, primes the copying of the genome (pairing with its poly(A) tail) and of the antigenome. They shut off the host's cap-dependent translation. Diseases: polio (fewer than 2% of infections reach the CNS, where it can paralyze, even the breathing muscles; vaccine; eradicated from the United States and most of the world), rhinovirus (colds), coxsackie A (herpangina and hand-foot-and-mouth disease) and HAV.
  • Coronaviruses: the largest RNA viruses (26–32 kb genomes), enveloped, with a helical nucleocapsid. SARS-CoV-2 first infects ciliated cells of the nasopharynx and trachea; its spike binds ACE2 and is cut by TMPRSS2. The genomic mRNA is translated into the ORF1a and ORF1b polyproteins, cut into 16 nonstructural proteins that build the replication complex (with RdRp); the structural and accessory proteins come from subgenomic mRNAs. Severe disease comes from immunothrombosis in the alveoli.
  • (−)ssRNA: all enveloped with helical nucleocapsids; the genome is linear (paramyxo-, pneumo- and rhabdoviruses) or segmented (influenza). It can't be read as mRNA, so the genome alone is not infectious: humans have no RdRp, and the virion carries its own (L, with its cofactor P) on the genome, which nucleocapsid protein (N) coats; matrix (M) lines the envelope and the glycoprotein (G) attaches. mRNA is made in one step. The RdRp starts at the genome's 3′ end and makes one capped, polyadenylated mRNA per gene, stopping at each gene junction (stuttering there adds the poly(A) tail) and scanning on for the next start. It often falls off at a junction and must restart at the 3′ end (attenuation), so genes near the 3′ end make the most mRNA: gene position sets expression. Nonsegmented viruses cap their own mRNAs; influenza takes caps from host mRNAs (cap snatching). While free N is low, the polymerase makes mRNAs; once N builds up, it makes full-length, N-coated antigenomes, the templates for new genomes. One gene can make more than one protein by alternative splicing, alternative initiation (leaky scanning) or ribosomal frameshifting (−1 at an RNA fold, +1 at a rare codon; not only in these viruses).
  • Measles (paramyxovirus; H and F glycoproteins; nonsegmented; kills cells and fuses them into syncytia): extremely contagious by aerosols and droplets (it stays in the air up to 2 hours) and infectious before symptoms; the "3 Cs" (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), then rash; Koplik spots (blue-white specks on red buccal mucosa) come first; MMR live attenuated vaccine, with outbreaks where vaccination is low.
  • RSV (pneumovirus; G and F; syncytia): bronchiolitis; the most common cause of pneumonia and of fatal acute respiratory infection in infants under 1 year; about 75% of infants are infected by age 1 and nearly all by 2; spread by droplets and fomites. A vaccine given in pregnancy passes maternal antibody that protects the baby for about its first 6 months.
  • Rabies (rhabdovirus; bullet-shaped; one glycoprotein, G; infects neurons of many mammals): animal bite → replication in muscle → up the axons of motor neurons by retrograde axonal transport → spinal cord and dorsal root ganglia → brain. Negri bodies (masses of nucleocapsid in the neurons' cytoplasm) are its main diagnostic sign. The long incubation lets post-exposure vaccine work.
  • Influenza (orthomyxovirus; spherical; 8 segments; RdRp and the nuclear export protein are packaged in the virion): hemagglutinin (HA) binds sialic acid to attach; neuraminidase (NA) cleaves sialic acid to free new virus (blocked by oseltamivir, zanamivir and peramivir). HA and NA are the main antigens. The sialic acid–galactose link differs by species: human strains bind α2,6, bird strains α2,3, and pigs carry both, so they can be infected by both and mix them; the HA sequence decides which species a strain infects. Drift = point mutations, above all in the antigenic sites around HA's receptor-binding site; gradual, in all strains, yearly epidemics and the reason the vaccine is updated. Shift = segments swapped (reassortment) between strains; sudden, a new HA or NA, influenza A only, pandemics.
  • Hemagglutination inhibition (HI): red cells alone settle into a tight dot (a button) at the bottom of a well; influenza HA cross-links them into a diffuse mat (hemagglutination). Antibody against HA in a serum sample blocks that, so the dot comes back. The HI titer is the highest dilution of serum that still blocks hemagglutination: a high titer against a strain means neutralizing antibody and protection, and a low titer against a new strain (after drift or shift) means vaccinated people are poorly protected.

Retroviruses and HIV

Enveloped, two copies of (+)ssRNA. Genes: gag (matrix, capsid p24, nucleocapsid), pol (protease, reverse transcriptase, integrase), env (gp120 binds, gp41 fuses), plus Tat, Rev and accessory proteins. Cycle: gp120 binds CD4 then a coreceptor (CCR5 or CXCR4) → fusion → reverse transcription to DNA (the provirus) → integrase inserts it → host RNA polymerase II transcribes → budding → protease cuts Gag so the particle matures and becomes infectious. Lentiviruses (HIV) have long incubations; the other retrovirus groups can cause cancer.

  • Spread: sex (more with genital lesions), mother to child (mostly at delivery; antiretrovirals prevent most), blood, shared needles. Needlestick risk is about 0.3%, versus about 1.8% for HCV and up to 30% for HBV.
  • Stages: acute (flu-like, rash, sore throat; CD4 drops and partly recovers) → clinical latency (years, CD4 falls, symptoms start below 500) → AIDS at CD4 below 200/µL (or an AIDS-defining illness); untreated adults reach AIDS in 5–10 years, infants in 3–5 years.
  • Tests: antibody or antigen-antibody (p24) screening; plasma HIV RNA is the most sensitive and tracks treatment; CD4 count stages the disease.
  • Drugs target entry (CCR5), reverse transcriptase, integrase, protease (maturation) and capsid. Even treated patients carry more heart, liver, kidney and cancer risk; the gut lymphoid tissue never fully recovers.
  • Oral signs: candidiasis, oral hairy leukoplakia (EBV), Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8), linear gingival erythema, necrotizing periodontal disease, HPV warts. No vaccine: fast mutation, sugar-shielded gp120, latency.

Oncogenic viruses

About 8–12% of cancers worldwide. Cancer follows years of persistent infection plus other factors; it is a side effect, not part of the virus's cycle. There are seven confirmed human tumor viruses.

  • Structures outside the wall (capsule, pili, fimbriae, flagella, axial filaments), endospores, plasmids and 70S ribosomes as drug targets

  • Growth needs (temperature, pH, osmotic pressure), DNA replication (leading and lagging strands) and why oxygen kills anaerobes
  • Gene transfer: transformation, transduction and conjugation
  • Steps of pathogenesis, virulence factors, biofilms, and exotoxins versus endotoxin with the classic toxins
  • Types of infection (acute or chronic, localized or systemic), antibiotic resistance and its alternatives
  • Oral biofilms: coaggregation, the shift to caries, and how fluoride and arginine work
  • Staphylococcus (abscess, coagulase, MRSA, toxin syndromes) and Streptococcus (pyogenes, pneumoniae, mutans, viridans)

The envelope and the gram stain

Gram stain: crystal violet → iodine → alcohol (decolorizer) → safranin. The alcohol step decides it: a thick peptidoglycan wall holds the violet (gram-positive, purple); a thin wall under an outer membrane lets it wash out, and the counterstain makes it pink (gram-negative). Shape and arrangement (cocci in clusters or chains, rods, spirals) complete the first identification.

FeatureGram-positiveGram-negative
Peptidoglycan (NAG-NAM chains cross-linked by peptides)Thick (20–80 nm; about half the cell's weight), outside the one membraneThin, in the periplasm between two membranes
Special moleculesTeichoic and lipoteichoic acids: wall teichoic acids are bonded to NAM and strengthen the wall; they aid adhesion and coaggregation (TLR2); M protein in S. pyogenesLipopolysaccharide: lipid A (endotoxin), core, O antigen; porins; lipoproteins
Outer membraneNoneYes: blocks many drugs; efflux pumps add resistance
EndotoxinNoYes (lipid A)

  • Exceptions: mycobacteria have waxy mycolic acids (acid-fast stain; resist drying, drugs and host defenses); Mycoplasma has no wall (sterols in its membrane); Chlamydia and Rickettsia are obligate intracellular and stain poorly. Archaea differ from bacteria by branched, ether-linked membrane lipids and no peptidoglycan.
  • Drug targets: wall building has three phases, all blockable. β-lactams block the transpeptidases (penicillin-binding proteins) that cross-link the wall; vancomycin binds the D-Ala-D-Ala ends (changing that last amino acid stops it binding). Resistance: β-lactamase, or PBP2a from the mecA gene (MRSA). 70S ribosomes (50S + 30S) are targets too; DNA itself isn't, but replication enzymes are.
  • The bacterial plasma membrane carries the respiratory chain (ATP is made there) and is negatively charged, so cationic antimicrobial peptides target it. The chromosome is one circular, supercoiled DNA; plasmids carry toxin and resistance genes.

Structures outside the wall

  • Capsule (glycocalyx; tight capsule or loose slime layer): antiphagocytic, aids adherence. S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, Klebsiella.
  • Fimbriae and pili (pilin): stick to host cells; the sex (conjugation) pilus links bacteria to pass DNA.
  • Flagella: filament (seen by TLR5), hook, basal body; mono-, amphi-, lopho- or peritrichous. Axial filaments in spirochetes run between the membranes and make the cell corkscrew into tissue.
  • Endospores (Bacillus, Clostridium): dormant, resist heat, drying, disinfectants and antibiotics; germinate when conditions improve. Inclusion bodies store glycogen and other materials.

Growth, metabolism, genetics

Bacteria divide by binary fission: the chromosome (and plasmids) is copied and split between two daughter cells, and the wall is remodeled with new peptidoglycan, which is why β-lactams act on dividing cells. DNA replication starts at one origin and runs both ways around the circle (about 40 minutes in E. coli): the leading strand is made continuously and the lagging strand in Okazaki fragments, whose RNA primers are removed (RNase H) before DNA ligase joins them; topoisomerase separates the two finished chromosomes. Growth curve: lag → log (exponential; drugs work best) → stationary → death.

Physical needs: temperature, pH and osmotic pressure. Most pathogens grow best at body temperature and near pH 7. T. pallidum (syphilis) and M. leprae (leprosy) prefer cooler tissue, so their lesions start on the lips, tongue and genitals or on the face, ears, hands and feet. H. pylori survives stomach acid for a time by making urease (its ammonia neutralizes the acid around it) and living in the mucus layer; vaginal lactobacilli thrive at about pH 5. Outside the host the wall protects the membrane from osmotic stress. Chemical needs: carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus, plus potassium, magnesium, calcium and iron.

GroupMetabolismExamples
Obligate aerobeNeeds O2; no fermentationM. tuberculosis, Neisseria
Facultative anaerobeRespiration with or without O2, or fermentationE. coli, S. aureus, streptococci
MicroaerophileLow O2H. pylori, B. burgdorferi
Obligate anaerobeO2 is toxic; fermentation and anaerobic respirationBacteroides, Clostridium, Porphyromonas
  • Aerobic respiration: glycolysis (in the cytoplasm), TCA cycle and electron transport (at the plasma membrane); final electron acceptor O2; most ATP (38 per glucose). Every route needs a final electron acceptor to regenerate NAD+ and FAD.
  • Anaerobic respiration: same pathways; final acceptor an inorganic or other molecule (nitrate, sulfate, carbonate, fumarate); less ATP.
  • Fermentation: glycolysis only; pyruvate is reduced to an organic end product (lactic acid, ethanol and others, which also help identify species) to regenerate NAD+; 2 ATP.
  • Why oxygen kills obligate anaerobes: O2 forms toxic superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, hydroxyl radicals and singlet oxygen. Aerobes and facultative anaerobes turn them into water and O2 with superoxide dismutase, catalase and peroxidase; obligate anaerobes lack these enzymes.
  • No nucleus, so transcription and translation are coupled, and many ribosomes read one mRNA.

Pathogenesis

Commensals (the microbiome, largest in the gut) protect by crowding out pathogens, killing them with hydrogen peroxide and bacteriocins, priming immunity and making vitamins (K and B). Opportunists (P. aeruginosa in the eye, C. albicans in the mouth) cause disease only when defenses drop: children, the elderly, the immunocompromised, after trauma or antibiotics. A strict pathogen causes disease whenever it is present. Infections are exogenous (food, water, air, fomites, sex), endogenous (normal flora in the wrong place, such as gut E. coli in the urinary tract, or reactivated tuberculosis) or nosocomial (a catheter-linked UTI; S. aureus and P. aeruginosa lead). Routes: contact, droplets, fomites, airborne, fecal-oral, vectors. Endemic = steady low level; epidemic = sudden rise; pandemic = across continents.

  1. Adherence: adhesins, pili and fimbriae, flagella, capsule and biofilm sugars; keeps bacteria from being washed away.
  2. Invasion and damage: toxins and enzymes; secretion systems (mostly gram-negative) inject toxins.
  3. Colonization and spread: biofilms (matrix mostly water; on teeth, lenses, devices; resist drugs and immunity; disperse when nutrients run out) and iron scavenging (siderophores, hemolysins).

Extracellular bacteria must avoid opsonization by antibody and complement; intracellular ones must survive the phagolysosome. Polymicrobial synergy: S. mutans with C. albicans makes more acid and more caries. Antagonism: bacteriocins, hydrogen peroxide, nutrient hoarding, surface blanketing. Disease mostly comes from the host's own inflammation, toxins and slow tissue destruction.

Kinds of infection: acute (sudden onset, fast course, then healing: a dental abscess, bacterial conjunctivitis) or chronic (slow onset and course, hard to treat and drug-tolerant, steady destruction, often polymicrobial: periodontitis); localized (one site) or systemic (spread to several regions). A dental abscess is a polymicrobial pocket of pus (streptococci and strict anaerobes) from an untreated cavity, a failed root canal or a hard-to-clean third molar; it is treated with antibiotics and root canal treatment.

Antibiotic resistance: efflux pumps (membrane proteins, overexpressed, that export the drug), target change (altered PBPs that penicillin can no longer bind) and drug inactivation (β-lactamase cleaves the β-lactam ring). Resistance genes spread on plasmids by conjugation and by transduction; overuse and misuse, farm use and poor infection control drive it. Antibiotics act only on actively growing cells, not dormant persisters. Alternatives: phage therapy (species-specific), small-molecule inhibitors of virulence factors, and vaccines (killed or live attenuated bacteria, or a bacterial part).

Gram-positive cocci

  • Staphylococci: clusters, catalase-positive, tough on fomites. S. aureus is coagulase-positive; carried by most people at some point; invades through broken skin or mucosa. Virulence: coagulase (fibrin wall), protein A (binds the Fc of antibody, blocking opsonization), leukocidin (kills neutrophils), hemolysins. When neutrophils can't clear it, the body walls it off: an abscess (liquefactive necrosis in a fibrous capsule) that must be drained, since drugs can't get in. About 90% of strains make β-lactamase; methicillin resists that, but mecA (PBP2a) gives MRSA, treated with vancomycin.
  • S. aureus toxin syndromes: food poisoning (preformed, heat-stable enterotoxin; vomiting within hours), scalded skin syndrome (exfoliative toxins split desmosomes; infants), toxic shock syndrome (TSST-1 superantigen, cytokine storm; hypotension kills).
  • S. epidermidis: coagulase-negative skin flora; biofilm on catheters, prosthetic joints and valves; sepsis, endocarditis.
  • Streptococci: chains, catalase-negative. S. pyogenes (group A): M protein (antiphagocytic), pharyngitis, scarlet fever (pyrogenic exotoxin), necrotizing fasciitis, strep toxic shock, then rheumatic fever (cross-reactive antibodies hit the heart) or glomerulonephritis. S. pneumoniae: lancet-shaped diplococci with a thick capsule; the leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia, often after a viral infection; lobar consolidation, high fever, productive (rusty) sputum; vaccines cover its capsule types. Viridans streptococci (S. mutans, S. sanguinis, S. gordonii, S. mitis): caries and infective endocarditis after bleeding in the mouth, linked to poor oral hygiene. S. mutans is acidogenic and aciduric (acid-tolerant down to about pH 4.4) and its glucosyltransferases cleave sucrose outside the cell to build sticky glucans.

Oral and eye flora, biofilms and caries

  • Gram-positive oral flora: Streptococcus, Actinomyces, Corynebacterium, Rothia and lactobacilli. Plaque is a structured, polymicrobial biofilm: anaerobes inside, aerobes and facultative anaerobes at the edge. It is built by coaggregation, specific binding between different species: teichoic acids of S. mitis and S. oralis bind lectins on the fimbriae of Actinomyces naeslundii.
  • Caries is a polymicrobial biofilm disease driven by diet: frequent sucrose is built into extracellular glucans and fructans and fermented to lactic acid. Healthy plaque balances acid makers and alkali makers (early colonizers go with health); frequent sugar shifts it to acidogenic, aciduric species (S. mutans, lactobacilli, Actinomyces, bifidobacteria) with less diversity. Supragingival plaque goes with caries; subgingival gram-negative anaerobes go with periodontitis.
  • S. mutans is a late colonizer. Its cariogenic factors: acid making and acid tolerance, extracellular and intracellular polysaccharides, glucan-binding proteins, adhesins for other bacteria and for collagen in dentinal tubules, and mutacin, a bacteriocin that kills competing species.
  • Prevention: brushing removes some biofilm, never all, and is hard for children and the elderly. Fluoride mainly slows demineralization and boosts remineralization; it kills little biofilm, though it blunts acid production and acid tolerance. Alkali raises plaque pH: arginine as a prebiotic (the arginine deiminase system of S. gordonii and Actinomyces makes ammonia) and urea (urease makes ammonia and CO2).
  • Eye: conjunctival flora is sparse (corynebacteria, Propionibacterium, coagulase-negative staphylococci). Tears carry lysozyme, which digests peptidoglycan; gram-positives resist it by acetylating NAM.

Gram-negative rods and spirochetes

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa: gram-negative rod and non-fermenter (it respires with O2, or with nitrate when O2 is absent; the course's slide calls it a facultative anaerobe), everywhere in the environment, opportunistic, multidrug-resistant; the second leading cause of nosocomial infection (catheters, endoscopes, ventilators); cystic fibrosis lungs, third-degree burns, ICU infants, diabetes, HIV, and long-wear soft lenses (the leading cause of contact-lens ulcerative keratitis); aminoglycosides, which block protein synthesis.
  • Klebsiella pneumoniae: non-motile, thick capsule, facultative, mucoid lactose fermenter; necrotizing pneumonia with abscesses and thick, bloody sputum (25–50% mortality), sepsis, UTI, meningitis; often multidrug-resistant. Acinetobacter baumannii: opportunistic, nosocomial, multidrug-resistant rod; recurrent wound infections (veterans of Iraq and Afghanistan). The ESKAPE pathogens, highly virulent and drug-resistant: Enterococcus faecium, S. aureus, Klebsiella, Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas, Enterobacter; four of the six are gram-negative.
  • Gut (contaminated food and water, fecal-oral): secretory diarrhea comes from toxins that cut sodium absorption and raise chloride secretion (V. cholerae; enterotoxigenic E. coli, traveler's diarrhea); pili attach the bacteria to the gut; treat with fluids. EHEC O157:H7 (undercooked meat, vegetables): Shiga toxin (stops protein synthesis, breaks down vessel linings) → bloody diarrhea, hemolytic uremic syndrome (kidney failure). Vibrio cholerae: comma-shaped, facultative, brackish water and shellfish; cholera toxin raises cAMP → up to 20 L a day of watery diarrhea; stomach acid protects, so it takes a large dose; oral rehydration is enough. Other E. coli: gut commensal and the usual cause of UTIs (female anatomy, catheters, incomplete bladder emptying). Salmonella: typhoid (enteric, systemic) fever, self-limited enterocolitis, and bacteremia as its complication. H. pylori: helical, flagellated (it swims through the mucus), microaerophilic, makes urease; ulcers and gastric cancer.
  • Identification: the gram stain (shape and gram type, fast), analytical profile strips (biochemical tests of enzymes and sugar use, overnight at 37 °C; fast species ID), selective and differential media, and sequencing or PCR (highest resolution but costly: research and outbreak tracking). MacConkey agar: bile salts stop gram-positives, so only gram-negatives grow; lactose fermenters are pink (E. coli, Klebsiella), non-fermenters pale or yellowish (Pseudomonas, Salmonella). Mannitol salt agar (high salt) sorts staphylococci: S. aureus ferments mannitol, S. epidermidis grows without fermenting it.
  • Periodontitis (chronic): gram-negative subgingival anaerobes; chronic inflammation, bone loss and tissue damage. The red complex = Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, Treponema denticola. T. denticola (a strict anaerobic spirochete) destroys gingival tissue with proteases and hydrogen sulfide. Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans: localized aggressive periodontitis.
  • Borrelia burgdorferi: microaerophilic, motile spirochete; Lyme disease from ticks; rash, flu-like illness, facial palsy, meningitis, arthritis, chronic infection; treat early, with 2 weeks of doxycycline. Eye: conjunctivitis ("pink eye": allergic, chemical or infectious) versus keratitis (the cornea). To know: gonococcal conjunctivitis (gram-negative diplococci; newborns infected at birth, ophthalmia neonatorum, and more adults now; corneal ulcers and blindness if untreated), trachoma (Chlamydia trachomatis, obligate intracellular, binds sialic acid receptors, spread by close contact; chronic and blinding) and Pseudomonas keratitis.

What's tested
  • The fungal cell (chitin wall, ergosterol membrane) and what antifungals target; yeast, mold and dimorphic forms
  • Endemic mycoses by region (Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides) versus opportunists (Candida, Aspergillus, Mucor, Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis); the five classes of mycoses; the medically important phyla
  • Tuberculosis: spread, latent versus active disease, the granuloma, IFN-γ and the macrophage, the skin test and the IGRA, why treatment takes months and the standard regimen; nontuberculous mycobacteria
  • Anaerobes: clinical clues, how to sample, the key organisms (Actinomyces, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides, Clostridium) and drugs
  • Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma (no wall), Rickettsia (Rocky Mountain spotted fever), Chlamydia (elementary and reticulate bodies), Neisseria (gonorrhea versus meningococcus) and syphilis
  • The five tissue reactions to infection and the lab tests (stains and preparations such as KOH, India ink and dark-field; culture, serology, antigen, skin test, PCR)

Fungi

Fungi are eukaryotes, distinct from plants and animals, with a thick cell wall of chitin, β-glucans and mannoproteins (chitin closest to the membrane, proteins on the outside) and a plasma membrane made with ergosterol, not cholesterol. Ergosterol is in the membrane, not the wall. They are heterotrophs with no photosynthesis: saprobic (living on dead matter), parasitic (as when they infect us) or mutualistic; hyphae secrete enzymes onto their food and absorb what they release. Drugs: amphotericin B and nystatin (polyenes) bind ergosterol and punch holes; amphotericin also binds our cholesterol, more weakly, hence kidney toxicity. Azoles (fluconazole, itraconazole, clotrimazole) and allylamines (terbinafine) block steps of ergosterol synthesis; echinocandins block glucan synthesis in the wall.

  • Yeasts: single oval or round cells that reproduce asexually by budding (the buds are blastoconidia); buds that stretch out and stay attached are pseudohyphae. Molds: multicellular filaments (hyphae, which grow at their tips; septate, with cross walls, or coenocytic, without them and multinucleate) forming a mat, the mycelium; they reproduce by spores (teleomorph = sexual, anamorph = asexual). Fleshy fungi are the mushrooms. Most fungi keep one form (monomorphic); dimorphic fungi switch with temperature: mold in the environment (the saprobic phase), yeast at body temperature (the parasitic phase). Thermal dimorphism is the mark of the true pathogens.
  • Five classes of mycoses: superficial (the outermost skin and hair; nondestructive and cosmetic only: pityriasis (tinea) versicolor from Malassezia furfur, tinea nigra), cutaneous (the keratinized layers of skin, hair and nails; the fungi are keratinophilic and keratinolytic: dermatophytes such as Trichophyton and Microsporum; ringworm, athlete's foot, scaling, broken hairs, ring-shaped patches, thick discolored nails), subcutaneous (deeper skin, cornea, muscle and connective tissue, usually after trauma: sporotrichosis from a thorn, chromoblastomycosis; abscesses, nonhealing ulcers and draining sinus tracts that rarely spread), endemic (the true pathogens, below) and opportunistic. The first three are localized, noninvasive and rarely life-threatening, and aren't counted as true pathogens.
  • Medically important phyla: Ascomycota (sac fungi: about 80% of medically relevant fungi, including every true pathogen, Candida and Aspergillus), Basidiomycota (club fungi, named for the club-shaped basidium: most edible mushrooms, and opportunists such as Cryptococcus), Mucoromycota (Mucor, Rhizopus: rare opportunists with a high mortality), Microsporidia (once classed as protists; opportunists in AIDS and other immunosuppression) and the Entomophthorales (mostly in Africa; subcutaneous mycoses).

Endemic (true) pathogens infect healthy people who breathe in spores, are limited to certain regions (Histoplasma and Blastomyces follow the Mississippi River and its tributaries) and are thermally dimorphic. Most fungal infections are opportunistic: they come from our own commensals or the environment, strike the immunocompromised (almost any fungus can), are usually not dimorphic and are mostly not communicable. (Histoplasma is a true pathogen that is much worse in the immunosuppressed.) How fungi reach us: inhaled (Histoplasma), inoculated into the skin (Sporothrix), invading from our own flora (Candida) or by contact with an infected host (dermatophytes). How tissue reacts: an acute pyogenic abscess (Candida), a chronic granuloma (Histoplasma), a mixed pus-and-granuloma reaction (Blastomyces), a chronic localized infiltrate in the dermis (dermatophytes), vessel invasion with thrombosis and infarction (Mucor; Aspergillus too), or allergy without a tissue reaction (Aspergillus). Oral candidiasis: white plaques that wipe off leaving a red base, or red atrophic forms under dentures and in angular cheilitis; risks are antibiotics, steroid inhalers, dentures, diabetes, dry mouth and HIV. With S. mutans it raises caries risk.

Mycobacteria

  • M. tuberculosis is an aerobic rod, nonmotile, with no spores, very slow-growing (20–24 hours a generation) and so rich in lipids (up to 60% of its dry weight: mycolic acids linked to arabinogalactan, and waxes) that it is not gram-positive: it is acid-fast, holding red fuchsin through an acid-alcohol wash, against a methylene blue counterstain. Koch's postulates were worked out on TB, and TB is still the leading infectious killer (about 1.3 million deaths a year), with drug-resistant TB a growing share.
  • Spread: airborne, person to person; the lungs in about 90% (nodules, cavities, fibrous scars on x-ray). Symptoms: cough (sometimes bloody), fever, night sweats, weight loss, chest pain, often mild for months. One active case can infect 10–15 people a year; untreated, about 45% of HIV-negative and nearly all HIV-positive patients die. Most infected people (about 90%) hold it as a latent infection; about 5% get active TB within 2 years and another 5% later in life. Outside the lungs: miliary TB (many small lesions like millet seeds), TB meningitis, osteomyelitis, intestinal and renal TB, scrofula (swollen, nontender cervical lymph nodes) and erythema nodosum (a sign of a primary infection held in check by strong cell-mediated immunity).
  • Pathogenesis: alveolar macrophages in the airways take up the bacilli first and carry them into the lung tissue; the bacilli block phagolysosome maturation and grow inside a modified phagosome; they later escape by killing the cell (necroptosis). CD4 Th1 cells make IFN-γ (driven by IL-12), which activates the macrophages (M1) to acidify the phagosome to about pH 4.5 and make ROS and NO. The result is the caseating granuloma. Defects in the IL-12/IFN-γ loop, HIV, malnutrition, age, male sex and immunosuppression allow disease or reactivation of latent infection.
  • Tests: the tuberculin skin test (purified protein derivative, PPD: a delayed-type hypersensitivity) and the interferon-γ release assay (IGRA), a blood test whose antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10) are missing from BCG, so a past BCG vaccine doesn't make it positive; it also needs one visit, gives a result within 24 hours and doesn't boost later tests. For disease: the acid-fast smear, culture and PCR (to confirm M. tuberculosis).
  • Why treatment takes months, with several drugs at once: bacilli hide in granulomas, out of the drugs' reach; the waxy outer membrane has very low fluidity and permeability, the main reason for its intrinsic resistance (β-lactams such as penicillin, vancomycin, macrolides, tetracyclines and sulfonamides don't work); slow, drug-tolerant persisters; and resistance. A lung cavity holds about 10^9 bacilli, while resistance to one drug arises in 1 in 10^5–10^8 (rifampin 1 in 10^8), so any single drug selects resistant mutants (streptomycin alone failed within a year); resistance to isoniazid and rifampin together arises in only 1 in 10^13–10^14. Standard regimen for drug-susceptible TB: isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months (about 90% cured; about 50% of MDR-TB, 25% of XDR-TB and 70% of TB with HIV). A vaccine (BCG) exists.
  • Nontuberculous mycobacteria (about 200 kinds) live in soil and water (showerhead biofilms, dust) and come from the environment, not other people; only a few cause serious, often opportunistic, disease. They are rising and hard to treat (intrinsic resistance to many antibiotics), and a problem in cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis: M. abscessus, one of the most drug-resistant, causes lung, skin and mucosal infections (clarithromycin, amikacin and cefoxitin; engineered phages have cleared it).
  • Dental note: active TB means delaying elective care and airborne precautions; the bacilli survive chlorhexidine, quaternary ammonium compounds, iodine and alkali; oral TB is a chronic painless ulcer, often on the tongue, and scrofula a nontender neck swelling.

Anaerobes

Obligate anaerobes can't survive in oxygen (they grow below about 1% O2), unlike facultative anaerobes, which grow with or without it; pH and the oxidation-reduction potential matter too. Superoxide dismutase (SOD) and catalase break down oxygen's harmful products, and the more pathogenic anaerobes make some SOD, so they survive until conditions suit them. They are normal flora on almost every mucosa (mouth, colon, vagina), so infections are mostly endogenous and mixed: facultative partners use up the oxygen and make β-lactamase; a capsule (B. fragilis) blocks phagocytosis and promotes abscesses; toxins kill host cells, white cells included. Oral anaerobes spread to the brain (abscesses, often with Streptococcus anginosus) and, by aspiration, to the lungs (lung abscess). Suspect them with foul-smelling discharge, a site near a mucosal surface, gas in tissue, or an abscess. Sample by aspirate or tissue, never a swab (subgingival plaque by paper point or scaler), straight into anaerobic transport (periodontal samples need special containers; a large piece of tissue stays anaerobic longer); culture on rich media with hemin, vitamin K or blood, with a plate containing an aminoglycoside to hold back facultative organisms, incubated without oxygen (a jar or an anaerobic chamber). A gram stain can't tell anaerobes from aerobes. Treat with drainage (source control) plus metronidazole, clindamycin or penicillin G, covering the aerobes in the mix too (some Bacteroides and Prevotella make β-lactamase); aminoglycosides don't work on anaerobes. Susceptibility tests aren't routine. Toxin diseases also get antitoxin.

  • C. difficile: carried by 10–50% of people as inactive spores; antibiotic-associated diarrhea and pseudomembranous colitis after broad-spectrum antibiotics that kill the gut's anaerobes; toxins A and B (hypervirulent strains overproduce them: severe disease such as toxic megacolon). Diagnose from stool with PCR (very sensitive, but also positive in carriers) or a toxin enzyme immunoassay (specific for disease, less sensitive), not culture (3–5 days, too slow). Infants carry it without disease (no toxin receptors).
  • C. tetani: an active wound infection that makes its toxin in the body; tetanospasmin is an A-B toxin (B binds motor neurons; A goes in and blocks release of the inhibitory transmitters glycine and GABA): spastic paralysis, lockjaw; generalized, localized or neonatal.
  • C. botulinum: an A-B toxin that blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction: flaccid paralysis. Preformed toxin: food-borne (canned foods) or inhaled (a bioterror select agent). Toxin made in the body: infant botulism, the most common form in the US (swallowed spores, as in honey, grow in the gut), and wound botulism. Diagnose by finding the toxin or the organism in stool or serum; treat with antitoxin, then antibiotics.
  • C. perfringens: cellulitis and gas gangrene (myonecrosis, H2 and CO2 in tissue) from alpha toxin (phospholipase C, the one toxin every type makes; it destroys cell membranes); also food poisoning (an enterotoxin).

Mycoplasma and Rickettsia

  • Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma (class Mollicutes): smallest free-living bacteria (0.2–2 µm), permanently without a cell wall (sterols stiffen the membrane), so most stains miss them and β-lactams and vancomycin are useless; they also resist trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and rifampin. Use macrolides, tetracyclines or fluoroquinolones (about 15% of M. pneumoniae in the US now resists macrolides). M. pneumoniae: "walking," atypical pneumonia, mostly in children and adolescents (peak 5–15 years; children, often mildly ill, are the reservoir) and the main syndrome in young adults; droplets, with high household spread; incubation 9–13 days (up to 3 weeks); gradual onset, low fever, headache, myalgia, dry cough, patchy infiltrates rather than lobar consolidation; P1 adhesin binds sialic acid; CARDS toxin strips cilia. Outside the lungs: the skin in about 25% (rashes up to Stevens-Johnson syndrome), mucositis (oral erosions) and conjunctivitis, meningoencephalitis, Bell palsy, myocarditis and cold-agglutinin hemolysis. NAAT/PCR is the most sensitive test (better than antigen tests); serology needs paired sera (antibodies at about 1 week, peaking at 3–6 weeks); culture takes 3 weeks or more. M. salivarium is normal oral flora that can worsen gingivitis and periodontitis in the immunocompromised (also a submasseteric abscess and TMJ pain). Genital: M. genitalium (sexually transmitted urethritis, often silent; about half resist azithromycin) and Ureaplasma (urease-positive: urethritis, epididymo-orchitis, stones) are linked to miscarriage, stillbirth and preterm birth; M. hominis to bacterial vaginosis and postpartum fever; newborns are often colonized at birth.
  • Rickettsia: tiny obligate intracellular gram-negative bacteria (peptidoglycan and LPS) that stain poorly with the gram stain but show with Giemsa; spread by arthropods (ticks, lice, fleas, mites). They infect endothelial cells, escape the phagosome and spread cell to cell on actin tails (the spotted fever group; the typhus group lyses the cell instead), causing necrotizing vasculitis, leaky vessels and possibly DIC, with damage to the brain, eyes, muscles, joints and lungs. Rocky Mountain spotted fever (R. rickettsii, dog and wood ticks; the most common rickettsial illness in the US): about a week after the bite, fever, headache, myalgia, then a petechial rash starting at the wrists and ankles that spreads inward and reaches the palms and soles late; about 23% fatal untreated. Tests (NAAT of blood or a skin biopsy, IgM and IgG serology, immunohistochemistry) need a sample taken while the patient is sick; give doxycycline at once, since confirmation by rising titers comes too late to wait for. Murine typhus (R. typhi, rats and rat fleas) is milder: a rash in only about 18%, on the trunk and limbs, sparing palms and soles.

Chlamydia and Neisseria

  • Chlamydia: obligate intracellular, cannot make its own ATP; gram-negative-type envelope without much peptidoglycan, so penicillins fail. Cycle: the elementary body (infectious) enters by endocytosis → becomes a reticulate body that divides inside an inclusion → turns back into elementary bodies released at about 48-72 hours. C. trachomatis: the most common bacterial STI, mostly silent, causes infertility; serovars A-C trachoma (a leading infectious cause of blindness), L1-L3 lymphogranuloma venereum (painless ulcer, buboes, proctitis). Test with NAAT; treat with doxycycline (azithromycin in pregnancy). C. pneumoniae: atypical pneumonia; C. psittaci: from bird droppings (psittacosis).
  • Neisseria: gram-negative diplococci, aerobic, oxidase- and catalase-positive, fast-growing, humans only.

Syphilis

Treponema pallidum is a spirochete that can't be grown in culture (dark-field or serology: RPR or VDRL, confirmed with a treponemal test). Primary: painless, firm chancre (can be on the lip or tongue). Secondary: rash on palms and soles, oral mucous patches. Tertiary: gumma (palatal perforation), aorta, nervous system. Congenital: notched incisors, mulberry molars. Treat with penicillin G.

Lab, each test with what it finds: the gram stain (gram-positive cocci such as Staphylococcus, gram-negative rods); the acid-fast stain for M. tuberculosis; a KOH preparation for fungi in a scraping (oral thrush); India ink for Cryptococcus's capsule in CSF; dark-field microscopy for Treponema pallidum; on biopsy, PAS and silver (GMS) for fungi (silver also H. pylori); culture, on media chosen for the organism sought (tell the lab when you suspect something unusual); serology (antibodies: exposure), most useful for organisms that can't be grown or grow slowly (Rickettsia, Mycoplasma, hepatitis viruses); antigen detection by ELISA, immunofluorescence or immunohistochemistry (Histoplasma, Aspergillus, Cryptococcus, Legionella, SARS-CoV-2); skin testing (PPD, a delayed-type hypersensitivity, for TB); PCR/NAAT, the test of choice for genital chlamydia and gonorrhea ("CT/NG"), also used for respiratory viruses, C. difficile, Trichomonas and to confirm M. tuberculosis.

What's tested
  • Potency versus efficacy, affinity and intrinsic activity, the kinds of agonists and antagonists, the therapeutic index and window, and pharmacodynamic interactions
  • The four receptor families and how fast each acts
  • Absorption and distribution: bioavailability, first-pass metabolism, ion trapping, protein binding, volume of distribution
  • Half-life, clearance, steady state, loading dose, first- versus zero-order elimination, AUC, Cmax and Tmax
  • What metabolism does, phase I and II, CYP450 inhibitors and inducers, CYP polymorphisms, drug transporters
  • Drug terms and kinds: indication, side effect and adverse event, generic and trade names, OTC and legend, orphan drugs
  • The phases of drug development, the IND and the NDA

Dose and response

Pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body; pharmacokinetics is what the body does to the drug (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion). On a graded dose-response curve, potency is how much drug is needed for an effect (read from the EC50: the lower the EC50, the more potent), and efficacy is the largest effect the drug can produce however much is given (Emax). A curve further left is more potent; a taller curve is more efficacious. Efficacy usually matters more in the clinic, since a weak but potent drug still can't do more than its ceiling.

Two properties of a drug decide what it does at a receptor. Affinity is how tightly it binds, measured by the dissociation constant KD, the concentration that fills half the receptors (affinity = 1/KD, so the smaller the KD, the higher the affinity). Intrinsic activity (α) is how well the bound drug activates the receptor: 1 for a full agonist, between 0 and 1 for a partial agonist, 0 for an antagonist. So full agonists, partial agonists and antagonists all have affinity, and a partial agonist has high affinity but low intrinsic activity. Potency reflects both and largely sets the dose. For most drugs the maximal response comes before every receptor is filled; the receptors left unbound are spare receptors.

A quantal curve plots the share of a group that responds at each dose. From it come the ED50, the TD50 and, in animals, the LD50. The therapeutic index is TD50/ED50 (LD50/ED50 in animal work): the larger it is, the safer the drug. Warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin and theophylline have narrow indexes and need blood levels or monitoring (the INR for warfarin). The therapeutic window is the range of plasma levels from the minimum effective concentration (MEC) to the minimum toxic concentration (MTC): the range in which most patients get the effect with few adverse effects.
