Physiologic antagonistActs on a different receptor with the opposite effectNot on the same curveEpinephrine against histamine in anaphylaxis
Chemical antagonistBinds the drug itselfRemoves the drugProtamine for heparin

Tolerance shifts the curve to the right: more drug for the same effect, from receptor desensitization (internalization, fewer working receptors) or faster metabolism, and it can carry over to related drugs (cross-tolerance). Tachyphylaxis is tolerance that develops within a few doses. Sensitization is the left shift: a bigger response to the same dose, as with repeated amphetamine. One drug can cause tolerance to some of its effects and sensitization to others. Dependence is the body's adaptation to a drug, so stopping it brings withdrawal; addiction is the behavior: craving and not being able to stop despite the harm.

Pharmacodynamic interactions: additive when the combined effect equals the sum (oxycodone with acetaminophen); synergistic when it is greater than the sum (alcohol with a benzodiazepine: deep CNS depression); potentiation when a drug with no effect of its own increases another's; antagonism when the second drug lowers the first one's effect.

Receptor families

FamilySpeedExamples
Ligand-gated ion channelMillisecondsNicotinic ACh receptor, GABA-A
G protein-coupledSecondsMuscarinic, adrenergic, opioid; Gs raises cAMP, Gi lowers it, Gq raises IP3, DAG and calcium
Enzyme-linked (receptor tyrosine kinase)MinutesInsulin, growth factors such as EGF
Nuclear (intracellular)Hours to daysCortisol, aldosterone, thyroid hormone, sex steroids, vitamin D: lipid-soluble ligands that act as transcription factors; the only family not in the cell membrane

Absorption and distribution

  • Most drugs cross membranes by passive diffusion of the un-ionized, lipid-soluble form. At a pH equal to a drug's pKa, half of it is ionized. A weak acid (aspirin) is un-ionized in acid, so much of an oral dose is uncharged in the stomach; a weak base (local anesthetics, amphetamine) is un-ionized in alkaline fluid.
  • Ion trapping: alkalinizing the urine with sodium bicarbonate ionizes a weak acid so it can't be reabsorbed, which speeds the clearance of aspirin and phenobarbital. Acidifying the urine does the same for a weak base such as amphetamine. Inflamed, acidic tissue ionizes local anesthetics, which is why they work poorly in an abscess.
  • Bioavailability (F) is the fraction that reaches the circulation unchanged, the extent of absorption rather than its rate: 100% for IV by definition, 75–100% for IM or subcutaneous, anywhere from 5% to nearly 100% by mouth. Poor absorption and first-pass metabolism in the gut wall and liver lower it (oral nitroglycerin and lidocaine lose most of the dose). Sublingual, IV, inhaled and transdermal routes avoid first pass, and rectal partly does. Switching IV to oral: oral dose = IV dose ÷ F.
  • Protein binding: acidic drugs bind albumin, basic drugs bind α1-acid glycoprotein. Only free drug crosses membranes, acts and is filtered by the kidney. Low albumin (liver disease, malnutrition, old age) or a displacing drug raises the free fraction of a highly bound drug such as warfarin or phenytoin.
  • Volume of distribution = amount in the body ÷ plasma concentration. It is often given per kilogram (gentamicin about 0.25 L/kg): multiply by body weight. About 3–5 L: the drug stays in plasma (large, hydrophilic or highly protein-bound: heparin, warfarin). About 12–14 L: extracellular fluid (aminoglycosides). About 42 L: total body water (ethanol). Far more than body water: the drug is held in tissues or fat (small, lipophilic drugs: digoxin, tricyclics such as amitriptyline, amiodarone at about 5,000 L). A large Vd means high tissue binding relative to plasma and a low plasma level.

Elimination and dosing

  • First-order kinetics: a constant fraction is removed per unit time (most drugs). Zero-order: a constant amount per unit time, because the enzymes are saturated (ethanol, high-dose aspirin, phenytoin). In first order the half-life stays the same at every level; in zero order it has no fixed meaning.
  • Half-life = 0.693 × Vd ÷ clearance: a larger Vd or a lower clearance lengthens it. Clearance = ke × Vd (ke, the elimination rate constant, = 0.693 ÷ t½), in mL/min or L/h; it sets the maintenance dose. A short half-life means frequent doses (ibuprofen every 4–6 hours); a long one (warfarin, digoxin), once a day.
  • With regular dosing, steady state comes after about 4–5 half-lives. After stopping, each half-life halves the level (50%, 25%, 12.5%, 6.25%, about 3% left), so about 4–5 half-lives clear about 94–97% of the drug, and falling to a quarter of a level takes two half-lives.
  • Loading dose = Vd × target concentration (÷ F). Maintenance dose rate = clearance × target concentration (÷ F).
  • AUC (the area under the concentration–time curve) is the total exposure. Cmax is the peak level and Tmax the time it comes; Cmin is the trough, the lowest level, at the end of a dosing interval. After an IV dose the level falls fast at first as the drug moves into tissues (distribution), then more slowly as it leaves the body (elimination).
  • Elimination is metabolism plus excretion. The kidney filters free drug (the GFR is about 120 mL/min, about 180 L a day), secretes some drugs actively (penicillin; probenecid blocks this and prolongs it) and reabsorbs lipid-soluble ones. A renal clearance above the GFR means the drug is also secreted; below it, some is reabsorbed. Dose by creatinine clearance in kidney disease. Drugs excreted in bile can be reabsorbed from the gut (enterohepatic recirculation), which keeps them in the body longer; volatile drugs (isoflurane, alcohol) leave through the lungs.

Metabolism

Metabolism turns drugs into more polar, water-soluble products, never more lipid-soluble ones, so the kidney or bile can remove them. About 70% of marketed drugs are cleared by metabolism, most of them by CYPs; the rest leave unchanged in urine or bile. The liver does most of it (high blood flow, many enzymes); the gut, lung and kidney do some. The product can be inactive (most drugs), an active metabolite of an active drug (diazepam → oxazepam), the active form of a prodrug (codeine → morphine) or a toxic product (acetaminophen → NAPQI).

PhaseWhat happensPoints to know
Phase IOxidation (hydroxylation is the most common CYP reaction), reduction or hydrolysis, mostly by CYP450 in the liver's smooth ER, with NADPH-CYP reductase as the electron source; adds or uncovers a polar group. Other phase I enzymes: alcohol and aldehyde dehydrogenase (disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase), MAO, esterases (procaine, enalapril)Products can be active or toxic: codeine → morphine (CYP2D6), acetaminophen → NAPQI (CYP2E1). Declines with age.
Phase IIConjugation by transferases: glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, glutathione. The drug needs a group to bond to, so many go through phase I firstMakes a water-soluble, usually inactive product. Newborns glucuronidate poorly (gray baby syndrome with chloramphenicol). Slow acetylators: more isoniazid, hydralazine and procainamide toxicity.

CYP3A4 handles about half of all drugs. The most polymorphic enzymes are CYP2D6 (codeine, tramadol), CYP2C9 (warfarin), CYP2C19 (omeprazole) and, in phase II, N-acetyltransferase. Prodrugs become active only after metabolism (codeine, tramadol, valacyclovir, enalapril). CYP2D6 variants matter in dentistry: a poor metabolizer gets little pain relief from codeine, and an ultrarapid metabolizer can build up dangerous morphine levels, which is why codeine and tramadol are not given to children under 12. CYP2D6 activity falls into four groups: poor, intermediate, normal and ultrarapid metabolizers.

Transporters move drugs too: P-glycoprotein (P-gp, MDR1, an ABC efflux pump) pushes drugs back out of cells such as the gut lining, and OATP uptake carriers bring statins into liver cells. Interactions can be pharmaceutical (incompatible outside the body), pharmacokinetic (absorption, protein binding, enzyme or transporter inhibition or induction, renal excretion) or pharmacodynamic (at the target).

DrugsDental consequence
Inhibitors (raise other drugs' levels)Erythromycin and clarithromycin, azole antifungals, ritonavir, grapefruit juice, cimetidine, amiodarone; metronidazole and fluconazole (CYP2C9); fluoxetine and paroxetine (CYP2D6)Bleeding with warfarin, muscle injury with simvastatin, deep sedation with triazolam or midazolam
Inducers (lower other drugs' levels)Rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, St. John's wort, griseofulvin, chronic alcohol (CYP2E1), smoking (CYP1A2)Oral contraceptive or warfarin failure; more NAPQI from acetaminophen in heavy drinkers

Terms and kinds of drugs

  • A drug is defined by its intended use (to diagnose, treat, mitigate or prevent disease, or to change the body's structure or function), not by its source, amount or cost. A poison has almost only harmful effects, though any substance harms at a high enough dose; a toxin is a poison made by a living thing.
  • An indication is an approved reason to use a drug; a contraindication is a condition in which it shouldn't be used, relative or absolute. A boxed (black box) warning is the FDA-required box on the label for a serious, possibly life-threatening reaction.
  • A side effect is an unintended effect of the drug at a usual dose, predictable from its actions: usually unwanted, sometimes useful and a reason for off-label use (minoxidil, an antihypertensive, grows hair). An adverse event is any harmful occurrence during or after use, whether or not the drug caused it.
  • The chemical name describes the structure; the generic (nonproprietary) name, such as acetaminophen or atorvastatin, is the official one; the trade (brand) name, such as Tylenol or Lipitor, is the maker's. Over-the-counter drugs (acetaminophen, ibuprofen) need no prescription; legend (prescription) drugs (amoxicillin, morphine) do. Controlled substances fall into DEA schedules I–V (F2-7). An orphan drug treats a rare disease (fewer than 200,000 people in the US), and its maker gets tax and patent incentives.

Drug development

PhaseWhoMain question
PreclinicalCells and animals: two species, one not a rodentPharmacology, pharmacokinetics and toxicity (the LD50); the first human dose is about 1/10–1/100 of the safe animal dose. Then the IND (Investigational New Drug application) goes to the FDA before anyone is dosed
Phase I20–100 healthy volunteers (patients for very toxic drugs such as cancer drugs)Safety first, with the dose range and some pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics
Phase II100–500 patients who have the diseaseDoes it work (efficacy), and what are the side effects?
Phase III1,000–5,000 patients, often at many centersSafety and efficacy at scale, often against standard treatment, and the dosing; then the NDA (New Drug Application) asks the FDA for approval
Phase IVEveryone who uses it after approvalLong-term safety, rare adverse effects and new indications (postmarketing surveillance)
full.f2-autonomic:
What's tested
  • How the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems are wired, and which receptor sits at each site
  • Cholinergic agonists, cholinesterase inhibitors and organophosphate poisoning
  • Antimuscarinic drugs, their uses and their side effects
  • Adrenergic agonists: epinephrine, norepinephrine, α1, α2 and β2 drugs, and indirect sympathomimetics
  • α- and β-blockers and their dental interactions
  • Which system sets the tone at rest, smoking-cessation drugs, and the autonomic drugs used in the eye

The wiring

  • Both divisions use two neurons. Every preganglionic fiber releases ACh onto nicotinic (NN) receptors in the ganglion.
  • Parasympathetic (craniosacral: cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4) postganglionic fibers release ACh onto muscarinic receptors.
  • Sympathetic (thoracolumbar, T1–L2) postganglionic fibers release norepinephrine onto α and β receptors, with exceptions: sweat glands (sympathetic fibers that release ACh onto M3), the eccrine sweat glands (sympathetic fibers that release ACh onto muscarinic receptors, for temperature control; the apocrine "stress" sweat glands use α instead), the adrenal medulla (preganglionic fibers end on it directly, and it releases mostly epinephrine into the blood) and renal vessels (dopamine on D1).
  • Somatic motor nerves are one neuron releasing ACh onto NM receptors at the neuromuscular junction.
  • Who sets the tone at rest: most organs that get both supplies are run by the parasympathetic side at rest, and the two sides usually oppose each other. The exceptions: the heart's ventricles are mainly under sympathetic tone, and most blood vessels have sympathetic nerves only, so resting vascular tone is set by α1. The muscarinic (M3) receptors on vessel endothelium make nitric oxide, which relaxes the muscle beneath; they have no parasympathetic nerves and answer only ACh carried in the blood.
  • ACh is made from choline and acetyl-CoA, packed into vesicles, released when calcium enters and SNARE proteins fuse the vesicle (botulinum toxin cleaves them), and broken down by acetylcholinesterase.
  • Norepinephrine: tyrosine → DOPA (tyrosine hydroxylase, the rate-limiting step) → dopamine → NE, and epinephrine in the adrenal medulla. Its action ends mainly by reuptake (blocked by cocaine and tricyclics), then breakdown by MAO and COMT.
ReceptorG proteinMain effects
M1GqCNS, ganglia, gastric acid
M2GiHeart: slower SA node, slower AV conduction
M3GqGlands (saliva, sweat, tears); contraction of bronchi, gut and bladder detrusor; relaxation of GI and bladder sphincters; miosis (iris sphincter), accommodation and more aqueous humor outflow (ciliary muscle); nitric oxide from vessel endothelium
α1GqVasoconstriction (sets resting vascular tone), mydriasis (iris radial muscle), contraction of GI and bladder (internal urethral) sphincters and of the prostate

β2GsBronchodilation, skeletal muscle vasodilation, uterine relaxation, liver glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis (raises blood glucose in hypoglycemia), more aqueous humor made, tremor
β3GsLipolysis, detrusor relaxation (mirabegron is a β3 agonist)

Cholinergic drugs

  • Direct muscarinic agonists: bethanechol (urinary retention, ileus), carbachol (glaucoma drops, and miosis during eye surgery), pilocarpine (glaucoma drops; in open-angle glaucoma they lower pressure by contracting the ciliary muscle, which opens the trabecular meshwork so aqueous humor drains out, and the small pupil is only a side effect), and pilocarpine and cevimeline tablets for dry mouth from Sjögren syndrome or radiation, as long as some gland tissue remains. Side effects follow DUMBBELSS: diarrhea, urination, miosis, bradycardia, bronchospasm, emesis, lacrimation, salivation, sweating.
  • Reversible cholinesterase inhibitors: neostigmine and pyridostigmine (charged, stay out of the brain: myasthenia gravis, reversing neuromuscular block), physostigmine (enters the brain: antimuscarinic poisoning), donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine (Alzheimer disease).
  • Organophosphates (insecticides, nerve agents) inhibit cholinesterase irreversibly: DUMBBELSS plus twitching, then paralysis, and seizures. Treat with atropine for the muscarinic effects and pralidoxime to regenerate the enzyme before the bond "ages".
  • Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release (SNARE cleavage): used for dystonias, spasticity, drooling, sweating, migraine, wrinkles and masseter hypertrophy.
  • Nicotinic drugs and smoking cessation: nicotine itself (patch, gum, lozenge) is replacement therapy; varenicline is a partial agonist at brain nicotinic (α4β2) receptors, the subtype that drives the reward center (smoking cessation). Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker (malignant hyperthermia risk); rocuronium and vecuronium are nondepolarizing blockers, reversed by neostigmine (given with glycopyrrolate) or sugammadex.

Antimuscarinic drugs

DrugMain use
AtropineBradycardia, drying secretions, organophosphate poisoning
ScopolamineMotion sickness (patch); enters the brain: sedation, amnesia
GlycopyrrolateDrying secretions before surgery, drooling; stays out of the brain
Ipratropium, tiotropiumCOPD (inhaled)
Oxybutynin, tolterodine, darifenacin, solifenacinOveractive bladder
Tropicamide, cyclopentolateEye exams: dilation and cycloplegia
BenztropineParkinson tremor

Side effects are DUMBBELSS in reverse: dry mouth (caries, candidiasis), dry eyes, dilated pupils with blurred near vision (and a risk of angle-closure glaucoma), fast heart rate, urinary retention, constipation, no sweating (overheating) and confusion in older adults. First-generation antihistamines, tricyclics and phenothiazines have the same effects.

Adrenergic agonists

DrugReceptorsUses and notes
Epinephrineα1, α2, β1, β2 (β at low dose, α at high)Anaphylaxis (IM 0.3–0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL in adults), cardiac arrest, with local anesthetics

Glaucoma drops use both systems: timolol (nonselective β-blocker) and betaxolol (β1-selective, safer in lung disease) cut aqueous humor production; brimonidine (α2 agonist) cuts production and raises outflow; pilocarpine and carbachol (muscarinic agonists) open the outflow path; latanoprost (a prostaglandin analog) raises outflow. Antimuscarinics and α1 agonists dilate the pupil and can set off angle-closure glaucoma.

Indirect sympathomimetics: amphetamine releases NE and dopamine from vesicles, cocaine blocks their reuptake (and blocks sodium channels, so it numbs and constricts vessels), and ephedrine and pseudoephedrine act both ways.

Epinephrine in dentistry: 1:100,000 is 0.01 mg/mL, about 0.018 mg per 1.8 mL cartridge. The usual ceiling is 0.2 mg for a healthy adult and about 0.04 mg (two cartridges) for a patient with heart disease or on a nonselective β-blocker. Avoid it after recent cocaine or methamphetamine use and in uncontrolled hypertension.

Blockers

  • α1 blockers (-osin): prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin (hypertension, BPH), tamsulosin (α1A, BPH). Main problem: orthostatic hypotension, worst after the first doses, so raise the chair slowly. Phentolamine (reversible, nonselective) treats epinephrine extravasation and reverses soft-tissue numbness after dental work. With an α blocker, epinephrine can lower blood pressure (β2 effect unopposed: "epinephrine reversal").
  • β-blockers (-olol): β1-selective atenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol, esmolol, betaxolol; nonselective propranolol, nadolol, timolol; α1 plus β carvedilol and labetalol. Uses: hypertension, angina, after MI, heart failure, arrhythmias, migraine prevention, tremor, performance anxiety, glaucoma. Harms: bradycardia, bronchospasm (nonselective), fatigue, masked warning signs of hypoglycemia, rebound if stopped abruptly.

full.f2-painrx:
What's tested
  • The arachidonic acid cascade and what each eicosanoid does
  • COX-1 versus COX-2; aspirin, NSAIDs and acetaminophen, their harms and interactions
  • Opioid receptors, full and partial agonists and antagonists
  • Toxidromes and their antidotes
  • The parts of a prescription, common abbreviations and DEA schedules

Eicosanoids

Membrane phospholipids are cut by phospholipase A2 (inhibited by corticosteroids) to free arachidonic acid. Cyclooxygenase (COX) turns it into prostaglandins, prostacyclin and thromboxane; 5-lipoxygenase turns it into leukotrienes (zileuton blocks the enzyme; montelukast blocks the receptor). Blocking COX can shunt arachidonic acid toward leukotrienes, which is why NSAIDs can trigger asthma in aspirin-sensitive patients.

EicosanoidMain effectsDrugs
PGE1, PGE2Fever, pain sensitization, vasodilation; gastric protection (less acid, more mucus and bicarbonate); keeps the ductus arteriosus open; relaxes the corpora cavernosa; contracts the pregnant uterusPGE1: misoprostol (prevents NSAID ulcers; it also induces abortion, so it is avoided in pregnancy), alprostadil (erectile dysfunction; keeps a ductus open in some congenital heart defects), lubiprostone (constipation, irritable bowel syndrome). PGE2: dinoprostone (labor or abortion)
PGF2αContracts the pregnant uterus, vasoconstriction, bronchoconstriction, lowers intraocular pressure, grows eyelashesCarboprost (abortion, postpartum hemorrhage); latanoprost, travoprost, bimatoprost, tafluprost, unoprostone (glaucoma eye drops; longer lashes, darker iris)

Aspirin, NSAIDs and acetaminophen

  • Aspirin acetylates COX irreversibly. Platelets can't make new enzyme, so 81 mg a day blocks thromboxane for the platelet's 7–10-day life. The drug itself has a half-life of about 15 minutes: the effect outlasts it because the platelets can't recover, which is why aspirin is stopped 7–10 days before surgery with a high bleeding risk. Harms: GI ulcers and bleeding, Reye syndrome in children with a viral illness, asthma and nasal polyps in sensitive people (someone whose asthma flares with aspirin avoids the other nonselective NSAIDs too; acetaminophen is the usual choice), tinnitus at high levels, and a chemical burn if a tablet is held against the gingiva. Overdose: respiratory alkalosis, then metabolic acidosis and fever; treat with urine alkalinization.
  • Nonselective NSAIDs block COX reversibly: ibuprofen (400–600 mg every 6 hours for dental pain; also given IV), naproxen (half-life about 14 hours, twice daily; reaches the CNS well, good for headache and migraine), ketorolac (strong, oral, IV or IM, 5 days at most), diclofenac (also a gel, solution or patch for osteoarthritis and sprains), indomethacin (gout, closing a patent ductus), meloxicam (half-life about 15 hours, once daily). Very long half-lives mean once-daily dosing: piroxicam (about 57 hours), oxaprozin (55) and nabumetone (26). All NSAIDs are weak acids except nabumetone. Three carry their own warning: fenoprofen is the one most linked to interstitial nephritis, mefenamic acid can cause seizures, and sulindac can cause rash and Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Ophthalmic NSAID drops (ketorolac, bromfenac, nepafenac) are used around cataract surgery. Ibuprofen taken just before aspirin can keep aspirin from reaching platelet COX-1.
  • Celecoxib is COX-2-selective: fewer ulcers and no antiplatelet effect, but more heart attacks and strokes (it cuts endothelial PGI2 while platelet TXA2 goes on) and the same kidney and blood pressure effects as other NSAIDs; it is a sulfonamide.
  • NSAID harms and interactions: ulcers and bleeding (worse with warfarin, steroids, SSRIs); kidney injury, since prostaglandins keep the afferent arteriole open (worst with ACE inhibitors or ARBs plus a diuretic); salt and water retention and a blunted effect of blood pressure drugs; higher lithium and methotrexate levels; avoided late in pregnancy (they close the ductus and can delay labor).
  • Acetaminophen isn't counted as an NSAID: it blocks prostaglandin synthesis centrally, so it relieves pain and fever but barely touches inflammation or platelets and spares the stomach and kidneys. It is preferred over an NSAID for pain without inflammation. Too much saturates the safe pathways, CYP2E1 makes more NAPQI, glutathione runs out and liver cells die. Keep the total at or under 4 g a day (lower with liver disease or regular alcohol use: alcohol induces CYP2E1 and uses up glutathione, so acetaminophen with alcohol is the pairing most dangerous to the liver). The antidote, N-acetylcysteine, replenishes glutathione.
  • For most acute dental pain, an NSAID, alone or with acetaminophen, works as well as an opioid or better. NSAIDs have a ceiling for pain relief: past the usual dose, more drug adds side effects, not relief.
  • Topical capsaicin (a cream, or an 8% patch approved for neuropathic pain) overstimulates TRPV1 receptors on peripheral nerve endings until they are desensitized; the cream can take about 2 weeks to work. Like acetaminophen, it relieves pain with no anti-inflammatory effect.

Opioids

Opioid receptors are Gi-coupled: they close presynaptic calcium channels (less transmitter release) and open postsynaptic potassium channels, hyperpolarizing spinal and supraspinal neurons so pain signals don't reach the brain. Their own ligands are endorphins (mu), enkephalins (delta) and dynorphin (kappa). Mu gives analgesia, sedation, euphoria, respiratory depression (a blunted response to CO2, the cause of overdose deaths), miosis, constipation and dependence; kappa gives analgesia, sedation and dysphoria; delta gives analgesia and also slows the gut. Other effects: itching, bradycardia and low blood pressure (morphine also releases histamine), prolonged labor, lower libido, and chest wall rigidity with fast IV fentanyl. Tolerance builds to most effects but not to miosis or constipation. Withdrawal (dilated pupils, yawning, tearing, runny nose, goosebumps, chills, aching muscles, diarrhea, cramps) is miserable but rarely deadly.

EffectMechanism
Respiratory depressionBrainstem respiratory centers respond less to CO2
Nausea and vomitingDirect stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone
MiosisParasympathetic excitation of the iris
Cough suppressionDirect effect on the medulla's cough center
Worse gallbladder disease (biliary pain)Constriction of the sphincter of Oddi
Urinary retentionThe voiding reflex is inhibited and the external sphincter tightens
ConstipationLess propulsion and secretion, more water absorbed, a tighter anal sphincter
EuphoriaNucleus accumbens (the reward pathway)

Tolerance (a bigger dose needed for the same effect) and physical dependence (withdrawal when the drug stops or an antagonist is given) can happen in any patient and are not signs of addiction; addiction is compulsive use and drug seeking, a disorder of dopamine reward in the nucleus accumbens. The boxed warnings on opioid agonists: addiction and misuse, respiratory depression, interactions with other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, alcohol), accidental exposure (children; patches and films) and neonatal withdrawal. Use them with caution in asthma, COPD or a GI obstruction. Their uses: moderate to severe pain, cough and diarrhea; long-acting ones (methadone) for opioid use disorder. By source, opioids are natural (morphine, codeine), semisynthetic (heroin, hydromorphone, oxycodone, hydrocodone) or synthetic (fentanyl, methadone, meperidine, tramadol). By action: full agonists (morphine, codeine, hydrocodone, oxycodone, hydromorphone, oxymorphone, fentanyl and its relatives, meperidine, methadone, levorphanol, tramadol, tapentadol), partial agonists (buprenorphine, butorphanol, nalbuphine, pentazocine) and antagonists (naloxone, naltrexone).

Toxidromes

Naloxone, a potent opioid antagonist, starts working in about 2 minutes IV, 2–5 minutes IM or subcutaneous and 8–13 minutes intranasal, and lasts 30–120 minutes, shorter than many opioids, so redosing is common; support breathing as needed. Medication for opioid use disorder pairs psychosocial support with methadone (full agonist), buprenorphine (partial agonist) or naltrexone (antagonist).

Other antidotes: acetaminophen → N-acetylcysteine; aspirin → sodium bicarbonate; methotrexate → leucovorin; heparin → protamine; warfarin → vitamin K; local anesthetic toxicity → lipid emulsion; methemoglobinemia from prilocaine or benzocaine → methylene blue.

Writing a prescription

As Dr. Fasinu lays it out, a prescription has a heading (superscription: the prescriber's name, qualification, address and phone, so the pharmacist can call; the date, which sets when it expires; the patient's name, date of birth and address, to verify the patient), a body (inscription: Rx; the drug, its strength and form; Disp: the quantity; Sig: the directions) and a closing (subscription: refills, any warning such as an allergy or storage, the signature, and the license, NPI and DEA numbers). Write the generic name (a brand that must not be swapped is marked "do not substitute", or DAW, dispense as written), and never abbreviate a drug's name (HCTZ, MSO4). Write a leading zero (0.8 mL, not .8 mL, which reads as 8 mL) and never a trailing zero (5 mg, not 5.0 mg, which reads as 50 mg). Spell out "units" (U reads as 0 or 4), "international units" (IU reads as IV or 10) and "micrograms" (µg and mcg read as mg); write "morphine sulfate" or "magnesium sulfate" in full (MS, MSO4 and MgSO4 get confused); write "daily" and "every other day", not q.d. and q.a.d. Write a specific quantity, not just a number of days, and a controlled drug's quantity in numbers and words.

Controlled drugs: the prescriber registers with the DEA and puts the DEA number on the prescription; never presign prescriptions; no refills for Schedule II; never prescribe one to keep an addiction going, for office use, or outside the scope of your license. The commonest prescription errors are missing information (which eye? for how long?), illegible writing with confusing abbreviations or zeros, look-alike drug names and the wrong drug; e-prescribing cuts them.

Abbreviations: Rx (take), po (by mouth), prn (as needed), q6h (every 6 hours), bid, tid, qid (2, 3, 4 times a day), hs (at bedtime), qhs (every night at bedtime), ac and pc (before and after meals), stat (at once), disp (dispense), sig (label: the directions), gtt (drops), OD, OS, OU (right eye, left eye, both eyes), qs (a sufficient quantity), tab, cap, susp, supp. On the do-not-use list: U, IU, µg and mcg, q.d., q.a.d., tsp and tbsp (write 5 mL and 15 mL). Conversions: 1 teaspoon = 5 mL, 1 tablespoon = 15 mL, 1 ounce = 30 mL, 20 drops = 1 mL, 1 grain ≈ 65 mg (often rounded to 60 mg), 1 kg = 2.2 lb.

full.f2-antiinf:
What's tested
  • Bactericidal versus bacteriostatic drugs, the goals of treatment, resistance and combinations
  • Cell wall drugs: β-lactams, β-lactamase inhibitors and vancomycin
  • Protein synthesis, DNA, folate, membrane and tuberculosis drugs: targets and signature harms
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental care
  • Antivirals (herpes, influenza, HIV, hepatitis) and antifungals: targets, uses and interactions
  • Chemotherapy principles, classic and targeted cancer drugs: mechanisms, dose-limiting toxicities and oral effects

Principles

  • Bactericidal drugs kill: β-lactams, vancomycin, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole, rifampin and the membrane disruptors (polymyxin B, daptomycin). Bacteriostatic drugs stop growth and leave the rest to the immune system: tetracyclines, macrolides, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, sulfonamides, linezolid. Bactericidal drugs are preferred in immunocompromised patients, and killing matters most in endocarditis and meningitis too. Combine like with like: two bactericidal drugs or two bacteriostatic ones.
  • Goals of treatment: prophylactic treatment prevents infection in someone at high risk (immunosuppressed patients; amoxicillin before dental care for a prosthetic valve); pre-emptive treatment starts when an infection is found on monitoring, before symptoms (cytomegalovirus after a transplant); empirical treatment covers the likely organisms before the cause is known; definitive (targeted) treatment aims at an identified, susceptible organism, often narrowing an empirical start once cultures return; suppressive treatment (secondary prophylaxis) keeps a treated or chronic infection from flaring, as in AIDS and after transplants.
  • β-lactams and vancomycin kill best by staying above the MIC (time-dependent); aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones by high peaks (concentration-dependent).
  • Resistance takes three routes: the drug fails to reach its target (less entry through the membrane, more efflux pumps), it is inactivated by an enzyme (β-lactamase), or its target is altered (PBP2a in MRSA, D-Ala-D-Lac in vancomycin-resistant enterococci) or overproduced. The genes are often carried on plasmids.
  • Synergy: a β-lactam plus an aminoglycoside; trimethoprim plus sulfamethoxazole. Antagonism: a static drug with a β-lactam.
  • Odontogenic infections are mixed streptococci and anaerobes. Drainage and treating the source come first; an antibiotic is added for spreading infection or systemic signs (penicillin VK or amoxicillin first; azithromycin or clindamycin for a penicillin allergy; add metronidazole when it isn't improving).

Cell wall drugs

Cell wall drugs are selective (human cells have no wall) and bactericidal. They act at three stages: making the precursors in the cytoplasm (fosfomycin, for bladder infections; cycloserine, for tuberculosis), moving them across the membrane into the growing chain (bacitracin, used on the skin and eyes; vancomycin), and cross-linking the chains outside the membrane (β-lactams). Only penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems and the monobactam aztreonam have the β-lactam ring; vancomycin, bacitracin and fosfomycin don't.

β-lactams irreversibly bind penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) and stop peptidoglycan cross-linking. β-lactamase inhibitors (clavulanate, sulbactam, tazobactam, avibactam) are added to a β-lactam to stop the bacteria's β-lactamase from destroying it. Penicillin harms: allergy in about 1% of patients (anaphylaxis in about 0.05%), rash with ampicillin or amoxicillin, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, C. difficile, a lower seizure threshold, neutropenia with nafcillin and liver injury with oxacillin. Cephalosporins share the allergy risk (some cross-allergy) and can harm the kidneys. The kidney secretes penicillins (probenecid slows this).

GroupDrugsNotes
Natural penicillinsPenicillin VK (oral), penicillin G (IV, IM; benzathine penicillin G for syphilis)Streptococci and other Gram-positive cocci, Gram-positive and many oral anaerobes; strep throat; destroyed by β-lactamase

Vancomycin, a glycopeptide (not a β-lactam), binds the D-Ala-D-Ala end of cell wall precursors and blocks their polymerization (transglycosylation): serious Gram-positive infections only, IV for MRSA, by mouth for C. difficile (it stays in the gut); flushing with a fast infusion, kidney and ear toxicity, so it is used with care in kidney disease or hearing loss. Telavancin, oritavancin and dalbavancin are longer-acting lipoglycopeptides.

All four for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin for at least 4 more

Antibiotic prophylaxis (AHA 2021)

For a prosthetic valve or valve repair material, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease, or a heart transplant with valve disease, before any procedure that manipulates the gingiva or periapical tissue or perforates the mucosa. One dose, 30–60 minutes before (or up to 2 hours after if missed). Prosthetic joints generally need none.

SituationAdult dose
StandardAmoxicillin 2 g by mouth (children 50 mg/kg)
Penicillin allergy without anaphylaxis, angioedema or hivesCephalexin 2 g
Any penicillin allergyAzithromycin or clarithromycin 500 mg, or doxycycline 100 mg
Can't take by mouthAmpicillin 2 g, or cefazolin or ceftriaxone 1 g, IM or IV

Clindamycin was dropped from the list in 2021 because of C. difficile risk. A patient already taking an antibiotic for another reason should get prophylaxis from a different class, since the oral flora may already resist the first.

Antivirals

  • Acyclovir, valacyclovir, famciclovir: guanosine analogs activated by viral thymidine kinase, then stopping viral DNA polymerase (HSV, VZV). Valacyclovir is a prodrug of acyclovir that is absorbed much better by mouth (famciclovir is the prodrug of penciclovir). For cold sores, valacyclovir started at the first tingle, or a cream: penciclovir 1% or docosanol 10% (docosanol blocks the virus from entering cells). IV acyclovir needs hydration (kidney crystals). Foscarnet, a pyrophosphate analog given IV, blocks viral DNA polymerase without needing thymidine kinase, so it treats acyclovir-resistant HSV and VZV, but is hard on the kidneys.
  • Ganciclovir treats CMV and suppresses the marrow. Cidofovir, a cytosine analog, and foscarnet are the alternatives for CMV.
  • Influenza: the neuraminidase inhibitors oseltamivir (by mouth), zanamivir (inhaled; can trigger bronchospasm) and peramivir (IV) stop new virions from leaving infected cells; started within 48 hours, a 5-day course shortens the illness and viral shedding. Amantadine and rimantadine block the M2 ion channel, so they work only on influenza A (influenza B has no M2), with CNS side effects. Baloxavir, one dose by mouth, blocks the viral polymerase complex.
  • HIV: nucleoside or nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs: tenofovir, emtricitabine, abacavir; can cause lactic acidosis), non-nucleosides (NNRTIs: efavirenz, nevirapine), integrase inhibitors (-tegravir: dolutegravir, bictegravir; bound by antacids, calcium and iron, so doses are taken apart) and protease inhibitors (-navir: lopinavir, ritonavir). Entry blockers: maraviroc (the CCR5 co-receptor), ibalizumab (binds CD4 and blocks entry after attachment) and enfuvirtide (fusion). Treatment is offered to everyone with HIV, whatever the CD4 count; a first regimen is an integrase inhibitor with 1 or 2 NRTIs, and it needs over 95% adherence. Ritonavir strongly inhibits CYP3A4: no triazolam or oral midazolam. Oral signs that suggest poorly controlled HIV: candidiasis, hairy leukoplakia, Kaposi sarcoma, linear gingival erythema and necrotizing periodontal disease.
  • Hepatitis: hepatitis C is treated to eradicate it. Direct-acting antivirals aimed at the virus's own proteins (NS3/4A protease inhibitors, -previr; NS5A inhibitors, -asvir, such as ledipasvir and velpatasvir; the NS5B polymerase inhibitor sofosbuvir) cure most cases in 8–12 weeks and replaced interferon with ribavirin. Hepatitis B is rarely cured: the goal is to suppress its DNA to undetectable levels, with nucleoside or nucleotide analogs (tenofovir, entecavir, lamivudine) or pegylated interferon. Hepatitis A needs only supportive care. Ask about liver function before giving acetaminophen or other drugs the liver clears.

Cancer drugs

Principles: combination chemotherapy pairs drugs that each work against the tumor but by different mechanisms, with different dose-limiting toxicities and no cross-resistance. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy comes before surgery, to shrink a locally advanced tumor (and show whether it responds); adjuvant chemotherapy comes after it, to kill what is left and lower recurrence; palliative therapy extends life without cure; supportive therapy reduces toxicity. Tumors grow along a Gompertzian curve: a small tumor has a high growth fraction and a short doubling time, so it responds best, while a large one slows and has fewer dividing cells to hit; this is why adjuvant chemotherapy starts soon after surgery. Cell cycle–specific drugs act in one phase: antimetabolites in S, bleomycin in G2, vinca alkaloids and taxanes in M, topoisomerase inhibitors in S and G2. Cell cycle–nonspecific drugs, the alkylating agents and platinums, act in any phase.

Head and neck cancer (mostly squamous cell carcinoma): tobacco and alcohol multiply each other's risk (over 100-fold together); HPV is linked to about half to two thirds of tonsil cancers, EBV to nasopharyngeal cancer and sunlight to lip cancer. Drug regimens pair cisplatin or carboplatin with 5-FU or a taxane, add cetuximab (also given with radiation), or use the PD-1 inhibitors pembrolizumab and nivolumab.

Checkpoint inhibitors: immune checkpoints keep T cells from attacking indiscriminately. PD-1 on activated T cells binds PD-L1, which many tumors overexpress, and CTLA-4 on T cells binds B7 on antigen-presenting cells; both switch the T cell off. Antibodies against PD-1, PD-L1 or CTLA-4 release the brake, so the T cells attack the tumor again. The HPV vaccines (Gardasil, Cervarix) prevent HPV-driven cancers; sipuleucel-T, made from the patient's own dendritic cells, treats prostate cancer.

Dental care: see the patient before chemotherapy or head and neck radiation and remove sources of infection. Mucositis peaks about 1–2 weeks after a cycle, and low counts bring candidiasis, herpes and bleeding, so check counts before invasive care (roughly neutrophils above 1,000/mm³ and platelets above 50,000/mm³, with the oncologist). Bisphosphonates, denosumab and antiangiogenic drugs carry a risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw, mostly after extractions. NSAIDs, penicillins and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole raise methotrexate levels.
full.om-caries:
What's tested
  • The order of plaque formation: pellicle, reversible then irreversible attachment of pioneer streptococci, coaggregation (F. nucleatum as the bridge), maturation, dispersal
  • S. mutans virulence: adhesins to salivary Gp340, acid production and acid tolerance, glucosyltransferases (GTFs) that turn sucrose into sticky glucans, stored intracellular polysaccharide
  • Why sucrose is special, and soluble α1,6 versus insoluble α1,3 glucans
  • The Stephan curve, the critical pH of 5.5 and the ecological plaque hypothesis
  • Which organism goes with which lesion (S. mutans, Lactobacillus, Actinomyces, Candida) and fluoride's three actions

The oral microbiome

The mouth holds the body's second largest microbial community, after the gut. It was the first human microbiome to be sequenced, and the results are kept in the Human Oral Microbiome Database (HOMD): about 700 species, with Streptococcus the most abundant genus; only about 58% have formal names and about 26% have never been grown in culture.

  • Microscopy shows shape, not species: a Gram stain gives morphology, fluorescence shows plaque in 2D, confocal laser scanning in 3D, and electron microscopy the ultrastructure.
  • Culture on selective media (does it grow?) and differential media (what does it metabolize?).
  • 16S rRNA sequencing of a housekeeping gene identifies organisms that cannot be cultured; it is reliable but costly, and it is how HOMD was built.

The flora is acquired soon after birth and first resembles the mother's; it drifts away as teeth erupt and solid food starts, and its diversity falls in old age. A sucrose-rich diet favors S. mutans; smoking kills commensals while periodontal pathogens survive it; alcohol-containing mouthwash kills normal flora.

Building the biofilm

Dental plaque is a biofilm: microbes in a matrix of exopolysaccharides (such as glucans), proteins, water, host products and extracellular DNA, which cross-links and strengthens it. Bacteria in a biofilm tolerate antimicrobials far better than free-floating cells.

StageWhat happens
1. Acquired pellicleWithin minutes a film of salivary glycoproteins, mucins, immunoglobulins and enzymes (under 1 µm thick) coats a clean tooth. Gp340 is the key receptor.
2. Reversible attachmentPioneer bacteria carried by saliva are held by weak, long-range forces (van der Waals).
3. Irreversible adhesionAdhesins on the pioneers bind pellicle receptors. The pioneers are commensal Gram-positive streptococci (S. sanguinis, S. oralis, S. mitis) and Actinomyces.
4. CoaggregationSecondary colonizers bind bacteria already attached, often through lectin-like adhesins. F. nucleatum is the bridge between early colonizers and the Gram-negative late colonizers.
5. MaturationThe matrix thickens, oxygen falls and Gram-negative anaerobes such as P. gingivalis (tertiary colonizers) settle in.
6. DispersalCells detach, often by degrading their own adhesins, and seed new sites.

Commensals and how microbes interact

  • Mitis group streptococci make hydrogen peroxide, which keeps competitors down and gives alpha (green) hemolysis.
  • Salivarius group: Gram-positive cocci that dominate the healthy tongue, make bacteriocins (salivaricins) and are not linked to disease.
  • Synergy: C. albicans binds streptococcal adhesins and builds a stronger mixed biofilm. With S. mutans it worsens early childhood caries (more acid); with S. oralis it promotes oral candidiasis.
  • Antagonism: one species suppresses another by making an inhibitor (bacteriocins, H₂O₂), hoarding nutrients, or blanketing the surface so others can't attach. The first colonizer has the advantage.
  • Nitrate–nitrite–nitric oxide pathway: commensals reduce dietary nitrate (leafy greens) to nitrite, which becomes nitric oxide or other products that kill pathogens; NO absorbed systemically helps lower blood pressure.

Systemic links taught: infective endocarditis from oral streptococci entering the blood after dental procedures (antibiotic prophylaxis for the highest-risk heart patients); P. gingivalis gingipains found in Alzheimer brain lesions; F. nucleatum in colorectal cancer and preterm birth (its Fap2 lectin binds tumor cells); S. salivarius and S. parasanguinis as the main streptococci in stable cystic fibrosis lungs.

Caries: which organism, which lesion

LesionMain organismsNote
Smooth-surface and pit-and-fissure enamel cariesS. mutans (and S. sobrinus)Initiates the lesion; usually more than 10% of the flora over early lesions
Deep, cavitated dentin cariesLactobacillusDrives progression, not initiation; thrives at low pH
Root-surface cariesActinomyces (A. viscosus/naeslundii), with S. mutans and lactobacilliOlder patients with recession and dry mouth
Early childhood cariesS. mutans with Candida albicansFrequent sugary drinks; the yeast boosts acid production

ICDAS grades lesions by what you see: codes 1–2 are initial enamel changes (white spots, seen dry or wet), 3–4 moderate (enamel breakdown, or a dentin shadow), and 5–6 extensive (a cavity with visible dentin, the largest reaching toward the pulp). G.V. Black's classes I–VI describe location.

S. mutans: why it causes caries

  • Adhesion: surface proteins anchored to the cell wall by the enzyme sortase bind Gp340 in the pellicle. This first attachment does not need sucrose.
  • Acidogenic: ferments sugars to lactic acid.
  • Aciduric: its acid tolerance response keeps its own pH steady by changing membrane proton permeability and fatty acids and making neutralizing ammonia and CO₂.
  • Glucans from sucrose through GTFs: GtfB makes insoluble α1,3 glucan, GtfC both, GtfD only soluble α1,6 glucan.
  • Intracellular polysaccharide (glycogen-like storage) lets it keep making acid between meals.
  • Bacteriocins (mutacins) suppress competitors.

Evidence for its role: it is nearly always found over small lesions, sound sites usually lack it, and longitudinal studies show it appears before caries develops. Keyes' triad: caries needs a susceptible tooth, fermentable carbohydrate and cariogenic bacteria (and time).

Sucrose, glucans and the Stephan curve

Sucrose is split into glucose and fructose. Inside the cell these are fermented (2 ATP per glucose, lactic acid under anaerobic conditions) or stored. Outside the cell, GTF uses the energy of sucrose's high-energy glycosidic bond to chain glucose into glucans; fructosyltransferase (FTF) makes fructans, which are soluble storage and don't help adhesion.

LinkagePropertyRole
α1,3 (and α1,4)Insoluble, stickyMakes attachment irreversible; the cariogenic matrix
α1,6Soluble, not stickyEnergy storage; little cariogenic effect

Grown on glucose plus fructose alone, S. mutans still grows but cannot clump or stick: without sucrose's bond energy it can't make glucans.

Stephan curve: within minutes of a sugar exposure plaque pH drops below the critical pH of 5.5, where enamel starts to dissolve, then recovers over 30–60 minutes as saliva's bicarbonate buffers it. Frequent exposures keep the plaque acidic longer, so how often matters more than how much.

  • Acidogenic (chemoparasitic) theory: plaque bacteria ferment sugar to acid that dissolves enamel.
  • Ecological plaque hypothesis: frequent sugar keeps the pH low, which kills acid-sensitive commensals and selects acid-tolerant species; low saliva flow makes it worse.
  • Quorum signal autoinducer-2 at high levels inhibits commensals, so an older biofilm drifts toward pathogens.

Prevention and fluoride

  • Cut sucrose (especially how often), lower S. mutans (antimicrobial rinses, sealants), experimental vaccines, and replacement therapy with a strain lacking lactate dehydrogenase.
  • Fluoride works three ways: forms fluorapatite, which resists acid (critical pH about 4.5); promotes remineralization of incipient lesions; and inhibits the bacterial glycolytic enzyme enolase, so less acid and less energy.
  • Fluoride does not inhibit lactobacilli, so its antibacterial effect matters mostly in early, noncavitated lesions dominated by S. mutans.
  • History: McKay and Black linked mottled enamel to fewer caries; Dean found the benefit without mottling at lower levels (about 1 ppm). Community water fluoridation cut caries by about 60%.
full.om-perendo:
What's tested
  • The red complex (P. gingivalis, T. forsythia, T. denticola) and its link to deep pockets and bleeding; the orange complex (F. nucleatum) as the bridge that comes first
  • The plaque hypotheses: nonspecific, specific, ecological/keystone (P. gingivalis as the keystone pathogen)
  • P. gingivalis traits and virulence factors (gingipains); A. actinomycetemcomitans and its leukotoxin in molar-incisor (localized aggressive) periodontitis
  • Host response and bone loss: antigen presentation, cytokines, RANKL and osteoclasts; the three routes to systemic disease
  • Pulp infection: routes, dentinal tubule size, the shift to obligate anaerobes, E. faecalis in persistent infection, and which treatment fits which stage

Periodontitis in one paragraph

Periodontitis is chronic, bacteria-driven inflammation that destroys periodontal connective tissue and alveolar bone; bone resorption is its hallmark. It is the main cause of tooth loss in adults and affects about half of adults 30 and older. Caries and gingivitis are driven by supragingival plaque; periodontitis by subgingival plaque.

The plaque hypotheses

HypothesisClaim
NonspecificThe total mass of plaque (a consortium of subgingival bacteria) causes disease, not any single species.
SpecificDisease comes from a shift to particular pathogens that are absent or rare in health. Socransky's 1998 study of over 13,000 subgingival samples grouped them into color-coded complexes.
Ecological / keystoneA synergistic, dysbiotic community causes disease. A low-abundance keystone pathogen (P. gingivalis) remodels a benign community into a destructive one.
  • Red complex: P. gingivalis, T. forsythia, T. denticola; strongest relationship with pocket depth and bleeding on probing.
  • Orange complex (F. nucleatum, Prevotella intermedia and others) colonizes before the red complex and bridges early colonizers to it.
  • Red complex paradox: red complex organisms are found in healthy mouths, disease can start without them, the flora is more diverse than thought, and P. gingivalis is often scarce in diseased plaque. P. gingivalis is easiest of the three to grow in the lab, not more important.
  • As keystone pathogen, P. gingivalis delays neutrophil recruitment and subverts complement so the whole community overgrows, shifting it toward anaerobes; it cannot cause periodontitis without commensal bacteria.

Two organisms to know cold

P. gingivalisA. actinomycetemcomitans
Shape and oxygenGram-negative, nonmotile rod, obligate anaerobeGram-negative coccobacillus, facultative anaerobe
Lab cluesBlack-pigmented colonies on blood agar; needs iron (hemin); asaccharolytic (ferments amino acids, not sugar)Capnophilic (likes CO₂)
DiseaseChronic (adult) periodontitis; red complexLocalized aggressive periodontitis, now the molar-incisor pattern: teens and young adults, bone loss at first molars and incisors with little plaque
Key virulenceGingipains (arginine- and lysine-specific proteases), fimbriae, LPS, capsule, Ig and complement proteases, collagenaseLeukotoxin A, which kills neutrophils and monocytes; cytolethal distending toxin

P. gingivalis virulence factors by job: colonize (fimbriae, hemagglutinins, outer membrane proteins, vesicles); evade the host (LPS, capsule, Ig and complement proteases); multiply (gingipains, hemolysins for iron); destroy and spread (gingipains, collagenase, trypsin-like and other hydrolytic enzymes). It is a weak trigger of inflammation, which helps it hide. Other members: T. forsythia (proteases), T. denticola (a motile spirochete; hydrogen sulfide).

Host response and bone loss

  • Neutrophils are the first line in the sulcus; neutrophil defects predispose to severe disease.
  • Innate cells capture pathogens and present antigen with costimulatory signals to naive T cells, which release proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-17); prostaglandin E₂ and matrix metalloproteinases destroy tissue.
  • Cross talk between immune cells raises RANKL, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors; OPG is the decoy that blocks it. More RANKL than OPG means bone resorption. This field is osteoimmunology.

Three links to systemic disease: bacterial dissemination (bacteremia, inhalation, swallowing); dissemination of inflammatory mediators, with trained myelopoiesis (innate immune memory) amplifying later responses; and oropharyngeal aspiration and oro-digestive translocation.

Pulp infection

Pulp necrosis is an anaerobic, polymicrobial, endogenous infection (the patient's own flora). The main cause is pulp exposure: caries, trauma, restorative procedures, attrition or abrasion, a periodontal pocket, or a developmental anomaly. Canal bacteria feed on necrotic pulp, tissue fluid seeping in through the apical and lateral foramina, saliva entering coronally, and each other's products.

  • Routes: from the mouth through dentinal tubules (main route), from the periodontium through lateral or apical foramina, and from the blood through the apex (anachoresis).
  • Tubule size: widest near the pulp (about 2.5 µm), narrowest near enamel or cementum (about 0.9 µm); most oral bacteria are 0.2–0.7 µm, so even the narrow ends admit them. Most are nonmotile and are pushed in by cell division and hydrostatic pressure.
  • Sequence: biofilm on enamel, acid reaches dentin, bacterial products diffuse to the pulp and inflame it, bacteria meet the pulp directly, host and microbes battle, and if the host loses the pulp becomes necrotic and colonized.
  • Ecological shift: crown, aerobes and anaerobes; pulp chamber, facultative bacteria at first; root canal after days or weeks, as oxygen and blood supply go, obligate anaerobes dominate, and they dominate the periapical bone too.
  • E. faecalis: Gram-positive facultative coccus of persistent or failed root canals; drug resistant, survives starvation and calcium hydroxide, invades tubules.
  • In primary molars the infection tends to show at the furcation (accessory canals, large pulp); in permanent teeth, at the apex.

Diagnosis and treatment

Diagnosis weighs severity (reversible or not, necrosis?), duration (acute or chronic), symptoms and vitality, from history, pain features, the exam (discoloration, palpation, percussion, pulp tests, mobility, bite test), swelling or sinus tract, and a periapical radiograph.

  • Pulp polyp (chronic hyperplastic pulpitis): a red, fleshy mass of inflamed pulp filling a large open cavity, bleeds easily, chronic and usually painless; young patients.
  • Space infection of dental origin: spread past the apex into fascial spaces or sinuses; mostly anaerobes; swelling and pain; a true emergency because it can reach the brain.
How far the infection has goneTreatment
Just reached the pulpDirect or indirect pulp cap
Coronal pulp onlyPulpotomy
Into the canals, mature toothPulpectomy (root canal treatment)
Immature tooth, pulp still vitalApexogenesis: keep the pulp alive so the root keeps forming
Immature tooth, pulp necroticApexification (artificial apical barrier, calcium hydroxide or MTA) or a regenerative procedure: disinfect with triple antibiotic paste, induce apical bleeding, seal with MTA or Biodentine
Past the apex, spreadingAntibiotics and drainage or extraction

Regeneration depends on stem cells (DPSCs, SHED, SCAPs, PDLSCs, BMSSCs), a scaffold and signaling molecules. Terms: revascularization restores blood supply to an immature tooth; revitalization is ingrowth of vital tissue unlike the original; regeneration restores the original structure and function.
full.om-viral:
What's tested
  • Culture media (blood agar, Rogosa SL, mitis-salivarius, Gold's agar) and Gram/colony features of common oral organisms
  • The herpesviruses: latency sites, oral signs and cancers (HSV-1, VZV, EBV, CMV, HHV-6/7, HHV-8)
  • HPV: papillomas, Heck disease, HPV-16/18 in oropharyngeal cancer, E6 and E7
  • RNA viruses with oral signs: coxsackievirus (hand, foot and mouth; herpangina), mumps, measles (Koplik spots), rubella
  • Cancer basics (oncogenes, tumor suppressors, two-hit) and bacteria tied to cancer (F. nucleatum, P. gingivalis, H. pylori)

Techniques in oral microbiology

The two basic tools are the direct smear and the culture plate. Advanced methods: PCR and DNA sequencing, biochemical tests, advanced microscopy, omics and bioinformatics.

A differential count (200 cells per field) goes in order: Gram-positive cocci and rods, Gram-negative cocci and rods, filaments, fusobacteria, spirilla, spirochetes.

Virus basics

A virus is packaged nucleic acid that needs a host cell. Steps: receptor-mediated entry, genome replication, translation of viral proteins, packaging into virions, and escape.

The herpesviruses

Large, enveloped, linear dsDNA viruses with an icosahedral capsid and a tegument layer. They replicate and assemble in the nucleus. Infection is lytic (kills the cell, makes lesions) or latent (lifelong); stress, UV light, hormones, other infections or immune suppression reactivate it. All eight human herpesviruses can affect the mouth; PCR tells them apart.

VirusLatencyOral and head-and-neck picture
HSV-1 (and HSV-2)Trigeminal ganglion (HSV-2: sacral)Primary herpetic gingivostomatitis in children; recurrent herpes labialis; herpetic whitlow on a finger. Spread by saliva during lytic shedding. Treat with antivirals (polymerase inhibitors such as acyclovir).
VZV (HHV-3)Sensory (dorsal root and cranial) gangliaChickenpox; shingles in older or immunosuppressed patients: painful unilateral vesicles in one dermatome, stopping at the midline, oral lesions on lip and palate. Ramsay Hunt syndrome (facial palsy with ear vesicles) is VZV in the geniculate ganglion. Vaccines exist for both.
EBV (HHV-4)B cells; oral epithelium and tonsilInfectious mononucleosis (saliva, 'kissing disease'); oral hairy leukoplakia; Burkitt lymphoma (with malaria), Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma. About 90% of Americans are seropositive by 25.
CMV (HHV-5)Monocytes, salivary glandSpread by saliva, urine, sex and mother to fetus; congenital infection causes enamel hypoplasia; common in HIV; no vaccine.
HHV-6 and HHV-7Salivary glandsSpread by saliva; no oral lesions; HHV-6 reactivation can cause encephalitis or pneumonitis in the immunosuppressed.
HHV-8 (KSHV)B cellsKaposi sarcoma in immunosuppressed patients: blue-red-purple lesions, classically at the hard–soft palate junction or on the gingiva.

Other DNA viruses

  • HPV: small, nonenveloped, circular dsDNA; replicates in basal squamous cells and assembles as they mature. Spread by direct contact. Oral lesions: squamous papilloma (finger-like, rough surface) and multifocal epithelial hyperplasia (Heck disease), soft painless nodules that regress on their own. About 20% of oral squamous cell carcinomas contain HPV, but tobacco and alcohol are the usual cause in the mouth proper.
  • Mpox: large dsDNA, brick-shaped virion; oral lesions are often the first to appear; a vaccine exists.

RNA viruses

VirusGenomeOral signPrevention
Enteroviruses: coxsackievirus A16 and A6, enterovirus 71(+) ssRNA, nonenveloped, hard to kill; fecal-oralHand, foot and mouth disease; herpangina (vesicles on the soft palate and pillars). Self-limited but very contagious.No vaccine or antiviral
Mumps (paramyxovirus)(−) ssRNAPainful parotid swelling; respiratory spreadHighly effective vaccine
Measles (paramyxovirus)(−) ssRNAKoplik spots: tiny white spots on red buccal mucosa, before the rash; extremely contagiousHighly effective vaccine
Rubella (German, 3-day measles)(+) ssRNA, envelopedRed macules and inflamed tonsils; congenital rubella causes missing teeth and enamel hypoplasiaHighly effective vaccine

Oral infection and cancer

  • Cancer cells divide without control, lose differentiation and contact inhibition, grow new vessels, invade, metastasize, hide from immunity and use nutrients differently.
  • Oncogene activation ('stepping on the gas'): a proto-oncogene gains function; dominant, one copy is enough.
  • Tumor suppressor loss ('removing the brakes'): usually both copies must go. Knudson's two-hit hypothesis: in inherited cancer every cell, gametes included, carries the first hit, and the tumor arises where the second hit happens.
  • About 90% of cancers involve several genes; about 10% are single-gene disorders.
AgentCancer link
HPV-16 and HPV-18Oropharyngeal (tonsil, base of tongue), cervical, anal, penile, vaginal; E6 degrades p53 and E7 inactivates Rb. All approved vaccines cover 16 and 18.
EBVNasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt and Hodgkin lymphoma, gastric cancer; linked to childhood ALL
H. pyloriChronic gastritis and ulcers, the strongest risk for gastric adenocarcinoma; the mouth and tonsils are reservoirs for reinfection
F. nucleatumEnriched in oral and colorectal tumors; enters cells through its FadA adhesin and turns on pro-tumor signaling
P. gingivalisRaises proliferation, invasion and metalloproteinases in oral cancer cells; linked to colorectal and pancreatic cancer
E. faecalisFound in oral cancer tissue; endodontic organism

Head and neck cancers are about 3% of new cancers. Oral and oropharyngeal cancer: twice as common in men, varied in appearance, usually found at stage III or IV; 5-year survival about 64%, and early diagnosis raises it to about 90%. Risk factors: tobacco (about 85% of head and neck cancers, including smokeless and secondhand), alcohol and HPV.
full.ns-anat:
What's tested
  • Glial cells and what each does; neuron shapes and axonal transport
  • Meninges, the dural reflections, herniation, and the three intracranial bleeds (source, space, shape on imaging)
  • The cavernous sinus and what runs in it; CSF flow through the ventricles
  • Lobes, sulci and the key cortical areas (motor, sensory, Broca, Wernicke, visual, auditory)
  • Development: germ layers, neural tube and crest, brain vesicles, neural tube defects and folate
  • Spinal cord levels, horns and funiculi, blood supply and the cord syndromes; spinal reflexes
  • Brainstem parts, the "rule of 4", medial and lateral medullary syndromes
  • Each cranial nerve's job, its parasympathetic ganglion and the lesion sign; thalamic and hypothalamic nuclei

Cells of the nervous system

  • Neurons: most CNS neurons are multipolar; bipolar neurons sit in the retina and olfactory epithelium; pseudounipolar neurons are the sensory neurons of the dorsal root and cranial ganglia. Nissl bodies are the neuron's rough ER. Anterograde transport (kinesin) carries cargo from the soma to the terminal; retrograde transport (dynein) carries it back to the soma, the route rabies, herpes and tetanus toxin use.
  • Astrocytes: the most numerous glia; take up K⁺ and glutamate, help form the blood-brain barrier, regulate blood flow and synapse formation, form the glial scar.
  • Oligodendrocytes myelinate many CNS axons (lost in MS); Schwann cells myelinate one PNS axon segment each (lost in Guillain-Barré) and help peripheral nerves regenerate.
  • Microglia: CNS macrophages (from mesoderm, not neural tube). Ependymal cells line the ventricles; the choroid plexus makes CSF. Satellite cells surround cell bodies in PNS ganglia.
  • Nerve wrappings: epineurium (whole nerve), perineurium (each fascicle), endoneurium (each fiber).

Meninges, bleeds and the cavernous sinus

The dura has a periosteal layer (on the skull, sensory supply from CN V, blood from the middle meningeal artery) and a meningeal layer that folds into the falx cerebri, falx cerebelli, tentorium cerebelli and diaphragma sellae, and splits to form the venous sinuses. The tentorium divides the skull into supratentorial (cerebrum) and infratentorial (cerebellum, brainstem) spaces; the brainstem passes through the tentorial notch. Herniation is brain pushed past a dural fold by raised pressure (bleed, tumor, trauma). The arachnoid is avascular; its villi and granulations return CSF to the venous sinuses. The pia follows every gyrus.

BleedSourceSpaceImaging and story
EpiduralMiddle meningeal artery (enters by foramen spinosum)Skull–duraLens-shaped (biconvex); temporal blow, lucid interval
SubduralBridging veinsDura–arachnoidCrescent-shaped; elderly, alcohol use, slower onset
SubarachnoidRuptured berry aneurysm (circle of Willis)Subarachnoid space (CSF)"Worst headache of my life"; blood in the sulci and cisterns

The cavernous sinus sits beside the sella turcica. The internal carotid artery and CN VI run through the sinus itself; CN III, IV, V1 and V2 run in its lateral wall. A spreading infection from the face's "danger triangle" can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis, and CN VI is often the first nerve hit (the eye cannot abduct).

Ventricles and cortex

CSF flows: lateral ventricles → interventricular foramen → third ventricle → cerebral aqueduct → fourth ventricle → median and lateral apertures to the subarachnoid space (and the central canal). The central sulcus separates frontal from parietal lobe, the lateral (Sylvian) fissure separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes, and the parieto-occipital sulcus separates parietal from occipital. White matter: association fibers (front to back, same hemisphere), commissural fibers (side to side, corpus callosum) and projection fibers (up and down, internal capsule).

AreaWhereLesion
Primary motorPrecentral gyrus (frontal)Contralateral weakness
Primary somatosensoryPostcentral gyrus (parietal)Contralateral sensory loss
Broca (speech output)Inferior frontal gyrus, dominant (usually left)Non-fluent aphasia, comprehension kept
Wernicke (comprehension)Posterior superior temporal gyrus, dominantFluent but meaningless speech
Primary visual (V1, area 17)Occipital lobe, calcarine sulcusContralateral visual field loss
Primary auditorySuperior temporal gyrus (Heschl)Hearing processing deficits
Frontal eye fieldsFrontal lobeEyes deviate toward the lesion

Development

  • Gastrulation makes three germ layers; the notochord (mesoderm) induces the overlying ectoderm to become the neural plate by blocking BMP.
  • Neurulation: the plate folds into the neural tube (brain and spinal cord); neural crest cells leave its edges and form the PNS: dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, adrenal medulla, melanocytes, and in the head much of the face and teeth (odontoblasts, dental pulp).
  • Failure of the anterior neuropore to close gives anencephaly; failure of the posterior neuropore gives spina bifida. Folic acid before and in early pregnancy lowers the risk.
  • Vesicles: prosencephalon → telencephalon (cerebrum, lateral ventricles) and diencephalon (third ventricle); mesencephalon → midbrain (aqueduct); rhombencephalon → metencephalon (pons, cerebellum) and myelencephalon (medulla), both on the fourth ventricle.
  • Later steps: neurogenesis and migration (failure: lissencephaly, smooth brain; periventricular heterotopia), synaptogenesis, then apoptosis and pruning, then myelination, which continues into adulthood. Synapse-refinement errors are linked to autism and schizophrenia.

Spinal cord and reflexes

31 segments (8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal). The cord ends at about L1–L2 (conus medullaris); below it the cauda equina floats in the lumbar cistern, which is why a lumbar puncture goes in at L3–L5. Enlargements: cervical C5–T1 (arms), lumbosacral L1–S3 (legs). The dorsal horn is sensory, the ventral horn holds lower motor neurons, and the lateral horn (T1–L2) holds sympathetic preganglionic neurons. White matter shrinks toward the sacral cord. Blood: one anterior spinal artery (anterior two thirds: corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts) and two posterior spinal arteries (dorsal columns); the artery of Adamkiewicz (around T9–T12) feeds the lower cord.

  • Anterior cord syndrome (anterior spinal artery): bilateral weakness and loss of pain and temperature below the lesion; vibration and position sense spared.
  • Brown-Séquard (hemisection): ipsilateral weakness and loss of fine touch, vibration and proprioception; contralateral loss of pain and temperature starting a level or two below.
  • Stretch reflex: monosynaptic; muscle spindle → Ia afferent → alpha motor neuron, with reciprocal inhibition of the antagonist. Golgi tendon organ: Ib afferents sense tension and relax the muscle. Withdrawal reflex: polysynaptic, flexes the stimulated limb and extends the opposite one. Gamma motor neurons set spindle sensitivity. Motor units are recruited smallest (slow) to largest (fast): the size principle.

Brainstem and the rule of 4

Midbrain (from the mesencephalon) has the colliculi (superior: visual reflexes; inferior: auditory), substantia nigra, red nucleus and cerebral peduncles; the pons has the locus coeruleus (norepinephrine) and crossing pontine fibers; the medulla has the pyramids (corticospinal decussation), olives and the area postrema (vomiting center, weak blood-brain barrier). The reticular formation keeps us awake; raphe nuclei make serotonin.

Rule of 4: four nerves above the pons (I–IV), four in the pons (V–VIII), four in the medulla (IX–XII). Four medial "M" structures: motor (corticospinal) tract, medial lemniscus, medial longitudinal fasciculus, motor nuclei III, IV, VI, XII. Four lateral "S" structures: spinocerebellar tract, spinothalamic tract, sensory nucleus of V, sympathetic pathway.

  • Medial medullary syndrome (anterior spinal or vertebral branches): contralateral weakness and loss of vibration/position sense, tongue deviates toward the lesion (XII).
  • Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome (PICA or vertebral): ipsilateral face pain/temperature loss with contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), ipsilateral ataxia, vertigo, and hoarseness and trouble swallowing (nucleus ambiguus, IX and X).

Cranial nerves

NerveKey jobsLesion sign
III OculomotorMost eye muscles, levator; pupil constriction (ciliary ganglion)Eye "down and out", ptosis, dilated pupil
IV TrochlearSuperior obliqueVertical diplopia, worse going downstairs
V TrigeminalFace sensation; V3 muscles of masticationV3 lesion: jaw deviates toward the lesion
