"Upper-half" pain (above the eyes) is mostly primary headache, glaucoma, giant cell arteritis or pseudotumor; "lower-half" pain is most often dental, then TMD and burning mouth; sinus disease (overdiagnosed), cardiac pain referred to the jaw, atypical facial pain and trigeminal neuralgia can be either. Red flags: thunderclap onset, new headache after 50, papilledema, fever, visual loss.

Facial trauma and reconstruction

  • Wound care: copious irrigation, exploration, remove debris (road grit tattoos the skin), check the facial nerve, parotid duct and nasolacrimal duct, early debridement, remove only free bone pieces under 1 cm without periosteum, drains for hematoma.
  • Grafts: autograft (same person, the gold standard), allograft (another person), xenograft (another species), alloplast (synthetic). Bone-graft healing: phase I (first 4 weeks) bone made by cells transplanted with the graft, disorganized; phase II (starts about 2 weeks, peaks about 6) bone made by host cells, with resorption and remodeling that continue indefinitely.
  • Orbit: seven bones; the optic nerve lies about 40–45 mm behind the infraorbital rim. Fracture complications: diplopia, enophthalmos, infection, ectropion, rarely blindness.
  • Superior orbital fissure syndrome: a fracture into the fissure injures III, IV, VI and V1 → ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, proptosis, a fixed dilated pupil, forehead numbness and lost corneal reflex. Orbital apex syndrome = the same plus blindness (optic nerve).
full.ns-dis:
What's tested
  • Multiple sclerosis: who gets it, its courses, how it is diagnosed (dissemination in time and space, MRI, oligoclonal bands) and treated
  • Seizures: generalized versus focal, absence, automatisms, status epilepticus; antiseizure drugs and their dental side effects
  • Alzheimer disease: plaques and tangles, the stages, other dementias, the drugs; Parkinson drugs and dental care
  • Sleep: stages, obstructive sleep apnea and oral appliances, narcolepsy and cataplexy, the circadian clock
  • Reward and addiction: VTA → nucleus accumbens, how each drug acts, treatments
  • Schizophrenia: symptoms, dopamine pathways, antipsychotics and their side effects; autism in brief
  • Memory and plasticity: declarative versus procedural memory, LTP and LTD; aphasia and neglect

Multiple sclerosis

A chronic immune-mediated demyelinating disease of the CNS (white and gray matter) with axon loss. Typical patient: a young adult woman (onset 20–40, about 2:1 female), white, raised far from the equator (risk rises with latitude; vitamin D, smoking and Epstein-Barr virus play a part). Common first events: limb numbness, optic neuritis (painful loss of vision in one eye), double vision (INO), weakness.

  • Courses: relapsing-remitting (most; stable between attacks), secondary progressive (RRMS that turns into steady worsening), primary progressive (worse from the start, more often men and older onset).
  • Diagnosis: a typical demyelinating event plus dissemination in time and space and no better explanation. MRI shows periventricular plaques (gadolinium-enhancing = active, new); CSF shows oligoclonal bands and a raised IgG index; evoked potentials are slowed.
  • Treatment: high-dose IV methylprednisolone to shorten a relapse; long-term disease-modifying immunotherapy to cut relapses and MRI activity; symptom care (bladder, fatigue, spasticity, pain, depression).
  • Dental: trigeminal neuralgia in a patient under 40 or on both sides suggests MS; patients on immunosuppressants or long steroids may need infection precautions; keep visits short and cool.

Seizures and epilepsy

A seizure is one event of excessive synchronized neuronal firing; its signs are stereotyped (the same each time). Epilepsy: at least two unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, or one with a high risk of more. Generalized-onset seizures start in thalamocortical circuits of both hemispheres (more common in children): tonic-clonic, absence (brief staring with a quick return, 3 Hz spike-and-wave on EEG), myoclonic, atonic, tonic. Focal-onset seizures start in one area and may spread; awareness may be kept or impaired; automatisms (lip smacking, chewing) point to the temporal lobe. Frontal: motor, brief, nocturnal; parietal: sensory; occipital: visual. Status epilepticus is 5 minutes or more of seizure, or repeated seizures without recovery: an emergency. Mimics include syncope, hypoglycemia and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures. Most patients become seizure-free on the first or second drug; after two failures, a third rarely works, so surgery (for focal epilepsy, 50–75% seizure-free), vagus nerve stimulation or a ketogenic diet are considered.

DrugMain actionDental relevance
PhenytoinNa⁺ channel blockGingival overgrowth (also with cyclosporine and nifedipine); good plaque control
CarbamazepineNa⁺ channel blockFirst line for trigeminal neuralgia; agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia (check counts), CYP inducer
ValproateSeveral (Na⁺, T-type Ca²⁺, GABA)Low platelets and platelet dysfunction → bleeding; liver toxicity; teratogen
EthosuximideT-type Ca²⁺ channel blockAbsence seizures
LamotrigineNa⁺ channel blockStevens-Johnson rash (oral ulcers)
Benzodiazepines (midazolam, diazepam, lorazepam)GABA-ARescue for status epilepticus

A seizure in the chair: stop treatment, clear instruments, protect the patient from injury (nothing in the mouth), time it, give oxygen; if it lasts 5 minutes, call EMS and give a benzodiazepine (for example midazolam intranasal, buccal or IM). Ask about triggers, control and missed doses before treating.

Dementia and Alzheimer disease

Dementia is a symptom (cognitive loss that interferes with daily function, a decline from before); Alzheimer disease is a specific disease and its most common cause. Pathology: extracellular amyloid-β plaques (start years before symptoms, drive the process) and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau (start in the medial temporal lobe, track the symptoms). Loss of the cholinergic nucleus basalis of Meynert. APOE ε4 is the largest genetic risk for late-onset disease; early-onset familial forms (under 50) are rare. Stages: preclinical (biomarkers only) → mild cognitive impairment → dementia. Early sign: trouble forming new episodic memories, then word-finding, apraxia, getting lost, and poor insight.

  • Other dementias: vascular (stepwise decline), Lewy body (fluctuating attention, visual hallucinations, parkinsonism), frontotemporal (younger onset, early personality and behavior change with relatively intact memory).
  • Drugs: cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) and memantine (NMDA antagonist, moderate to severe) ease symptoms for a time but do not stop the disease; anti-amyloid antibodies (lecanemab) slow decline in early disease and can cause brain swelling or bleeding (ARIA), more with APOE ε4.
  • Dental: short morning visits, involve the caregiver and confirm consent, aggressive prevention (fluoride) as self-care slips; cholinesterase inhibitors can slow the heart and increase saliva, while many other drugs dry the mouth.

Parkinson disease drugs and the dental patient

All current drugs raise dopamine signaling; none slows the disease (exercise may). Levodopa crosses the blood-brain barrier and becomes dopamine; carbidopa blocks peripheral decarboxylase so more reaches the brain and nausea falls; long use brings dyskinesias and on-off swings. Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) cause sleepiness and impulse-control problems. MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline) and COMT inhibitors (entacapone) slow dopamine breakdown; MAO-B inhibitors interact with meperidine and tramadol (serotonin syndrome). Amantadine and anticholinergics (benztropine, which dries the mouth) help tremor and dyskinesia. Dental: orthostatic hypotension (sit up slowly), tremor and rigidity make hygiene hard (power brushes), xerostomia, drooling and aspiration risk; limit epinephrine with levodopa or COMT inhibitors; schedule about an hour after a dose, when movement is best.

Sleep and circadian rhythm

  • Stages: NREM about 75% (N1 and N2 light, N2 has spindles and K-complexes; N3 deep slow-wave sleep, mostly in the first half of the night); REM about 25% (dreams, every muscle paralyzed except the eyes and diaphragm), first at about 90 minutes and longer through the night.
  • Obstructive sleep apnea: airway collapse with continued breathing effort; loud snoring, witnessed apneas, morning headache, daytime sleepiness. Risks: obesity (strongest), male over 50, postmenopause, thick neck, retrognathia or micrognathia, crowded oropharynx, alcohol and sedatives. Diagnosed by polysomnography. Treatment: weight loss, avoid sleeping supine, CPAP (first line), and a mandibular advancement oral appliance for snoring and mild to moderate OSA, or moderate to severe OSA when CPAP is refused or not tolerated (best in thin patients whose OSA is worse supine). Avoid benzodiazepines.
  • Narcolepsy: loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus; REM intrudes into waking: excessive sleepiness, cataplexy (sudden loss of tone with laughter or strong emotion, eyes and breathing spared), hallucinations at sleep onset, sleep paralysis. Nap test: falls asleep within 8 minutes with REM in at least two naps. Treatment: scheduled naps, modafinil, stimulants, sodium oxybate (cataplexy), pitolisant.
  • Circadian clock: the suprachiasmatic nucleus, set mainly by light through melanopsin-containing retinal ganglion cells (blue light), drives melatonin from the pineal gland. Molecular loop: CLOCK and BMAL1 switch on Per and Cry, which shut CLOCK and BMAL1 off. Morning light advances the clock, light at night delays it; shift work raises the risk of obesity and diabetes. Sleep hygiene: dark, quiet, cool, regular hours, short naps.

Reward and addiction

Reward runs on dopamine from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens (the mesolimbic pathway). Every drug of abuse raises dopamine there. Cocaine blocks the dopamine (and norepinephrine and serotonin) transporters; amphetamine reverses them. Opioids act on mu receptors (Gi/o) of GABA interneurons, releasing VTA dopamine neurons from inhibition. Alcohol boosts GABA-A and blocks NMDA; nicotine acts on α4β2 nicotinic receptors; marijuana on CB1 (anandamide). Addiction: tolerance, craving, withdrawal, use despite harm; genetic risk is polygenic. Treatment: behavioral therapy (CBT, contingency management, 12-step), nicotine replacement and varenicline, naltrexone or disulfiram for alcohol, methadone, buprenorphine or naltrexone for opioids. Dental: no epinephrine within 24 hours of cocaine use (arrhythmia, hypertensive crisis); methamphetamine causes rampant caries; for patients recovering from opioid use, plan non-opioid analgesia.

Schizophrenia and autism

Psychosis (hallucinations, delusions, disorganized thought) is a symptom with medical, drug and psychiatric causes. Schizophrenia: at least two of delusions, hallucinations (usually auditory), disorganized speech, disorganized or catatonic behavior, negative symptoms, for 6 months with 1 month of active symptoms. Positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions) track excess striatal (mesolimbic) dopamine; negative (flat affect, poverty of speech, withdrawal) and cognitive symptoms track low cortical dopamine and NMDA hypofunction (ketamine can mimic psychosis). Risk: genes, developmental insults, cannabis.

  • All antipsychotics block D2. First generation (haloperidol): extrapyramidal effects (acute dystonia within days, akathisia, parkinsonism within weeks) and tardive dyskinesia (orofacial movements after months to years, which can loosen dentures). Low-potency agents (chlorpromazine) are more anticholinergic: dry mouth, sedation, hypotension. Second generation: fewer motor effects, more weight gain and diabetes. Clozapine works in treatment-resistant cases but causes agranulocytosis (monitor counts) and drooling.
  • Blocking dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway raises prolactin (galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastia).
  • Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: fever, rigidity, altered mental status, unstable vitals; stop the drug, emergency care.
  • Autism spectrum disorder: deficits in social communication plus restricted, repetitive behaviors and sensory over- or under-reactivity. Models include weak central coherence, executive dysfunction, reduced social reward and theory-of-mind deficits. Dental: predictable routine, desensitization visits, low sensory load.

Memory, plasticity and cortex

Declarative memory (facts and events) needs the hippocampus (CA1) for consolidation; damage gives anterograde amnesia with old memories kept. Procedural memory (skills, habits) uses the striatum, motor cortex and cerebellum; emotional memory uses the amygdala. LTP: high-frequency input with depolarization relieves the NMDA Mg²⁺ block, the large Ca²⁺ rise activates CaMKII, and more AMPA receptors are inserted (silent synapses wake up); late LTP needs CREB and protein synthesis. LTD: low-frequency input, a small long Ca²⁺ rise, phosphatases, AMPA receptors removed. Cortex: a dominant (left) hemisphere stroke gives aphasia (Broca: non-fluent, aware and frustrated; Wernicke: fluent nonsense, unaware); a right parietal stroke gives left neglect and anosognosia.
full.cr-cardiac:
What's tested
  • How cardiac and smooth muscle start a contraction (troponin C vs calmodulin and MLCK), the sarcomere and the intercalated disc, and why the heart can't be tetanized
  • The heart's layers and the conduction pathway in order, with its slowest and fastest parts
  • Vessel and heart wall histology: the three tunics, arteries versus veins, and the three capillary types
  • Ventricular and SA node action potentials: each phase and the channel behind it, and how the autonomic nerves change them
  • ECG waves and intervals, heart rate from the strip, and how to tell the AV blocks apart
  • The cardiac cycle: valve events, heart sounds, the dicrotic notch, the jugular venous pulse and the pressure–volume loop
  • Hemodynamics: flow, resistance, Poiseuille's law, velocity, compliance, mean arterial pressure and pulse pressure
  • Cardiac output, stroke volume, ejection fraction, Frank–Starling, venous return and the cardiac and venous return curves

The big picture

The heart is two pumps in series: the right heart sends blood through the lungs at low pressure (the right ventricle peaks near 25 mmHg) and the left heart through the body at high pressure (the left ventricle peaks near 120 mmHg, so its wall is thicker). At steady state their outputs match, and cardiac output equals venous return, about 5 L/min. The organs are arranged in parallel. The aorta damps the pulse, arterioles are the resistance vessels that set total peripheral resistance (TPR), capillaries have the largest total cross-sectional area, for exchange, and veins are the capacitance vessels that hold about 70% of the blood at low pressure (the unstressed volume; the blood in the arteries is the stressed volume). Chordae tendineae and papillary muscles keep the AV valves (tricuspid and mitral) from everting when the ventricles contract; the semilunar valves (pulmonic and aortic) stop backflow from the arteries.

Cardiac and smooth muscle

All muscle contracts when Ca2+ lets myosin bind actin. What differs is the switch.

FeatureSkeletalCardiacSmooth
Ca2+ bindsTroponin CTroponin CCalmodulin, which turns on myosin light-chain kinase (MLCK); no troponin
Where the Ca2+ comes fromSarcoplasmic reticulum (SR)Some enters through L-type channels and opens the SR's ryanodine receptors for more (Ca2+-induced Ca2+ release); T-tubule and SR meet in a diad at the Z lineMostly from outside the cell, plus a small SR; no T-tubules
Cell linksNone; each fiber has its own nerve endingBranching cells joined by intercalated discs: fasciae adherentes and desmosomes (transverse portions) hold them together; gap junctions (lateral portions) pass the impulse, so the cells beat as one (a functional syncytium)Gap junctions in single-unit (visceral) muscle
Striated?YesYesNo: thin filaments anchor to dense bodies (like Z lines)
Tetanus?YesNo: the refractory period lasts until the muscle relaxesSlow, sustained tone (latch state)
NucleiMany, at the edgeOne (or two), centralOne, central (spindle-shaped cell)
RepairSome (satellite cells)Almost none (under 1% of cells divide a year): hypertrophy only, so an infarct scarsHypertrophy and hyperplasia

Smooth muscle relaxes through myosin light-chain phosphatase; nitric oxide raises cGMP, which favors relaxation (how nitrates work), and beta agonists and prostaglandins raise cAMP, which inhibits MLCK and speeds Ca2+ uptake into the SR. Heart muscle relaxes as the SR pump (SERCA) takes Ca2+ back and the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger moves it out. Digoxin blocks the Na+/K+-ATPase: more Na+ stays in the cell, the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger removes less Ca2+, and the extra Ca2+ strengthens contraction (a positive inotrope, used in heart failure).

The sarcomere runs from Z line to Z line: the A band is the length of the thick (myosin) filaments, the H band thick filaments alone and the I band thin filaments alone. The thin filament is actin with tropomyosin and troponin: TnC binds Ca2+, TnI inhibits the actin–myosin bond and TnT attaches to tropomyosin. In contraction the filaments slide, so the I and H bands narrow, but neither filament changes length and the A band stays the same. Each cardiac fiber contracts all-or-none. Heart cells, packed with mitochondria, burn mainly fatty acids, aerobically. Right atrial myocytes store atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) in granules and release it when stretched.

Layers of the heart

From outside in: the tough fibrous pericardium, the parietal serous pericardium, the pericardial cavity with a little fluid, the visceral serous pericardium (which is the epicardium), the myocardium (the thick muscle) and the endocardium (the inner lining, which also covers the valves). Fluid or blood in the pericardial cavity squeezes the heart: tamponade, with low BP, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds.

Under the microscope the epicardium is a mesothelium (simple squamous) over connective tissue with fat, nerves and the coronary vessels. The myocardium's fibers wind in spirals, so a contraction wrings the blood out. The endocardium (endothelium on thin connective tissue, like a vessel's intima) forms the valves, and the subendocardium under it carries nerves, vessels and the branches of the conduction system (the Purkinje fibers).

Vessel walls

Vessels larger than capillaries have three layers: the tunica intima (endothelium; arteries add an internal elastic lamina), the tunica media (smooth muscle) and the tunica externa or adventitia (collagen and elastic fibers). Arteries have the thicker tunica media, so their wall is thick for their lumen (a high wall-to-lumen ratio); a vein of the same size has a thin wall, a wide lumen and its thickest layer in the externa. The vasa vasorum feed the outer wall of large vessels and are better developed in veins, whose blood carries less O2.

VesselWall
Elastic artery (aorta and its largest branches)Media full of elastic laminae: stretches in systole and recoils in diastole, holding diastolic pressure up
Muscular artery (most named arteries)Thick media, up to 40 layers of smooth muscle; clear internal and external elastic laminae
Arteriole (resistance)1–3 layers of smooth muscle; no external elastic lamina
Capillary (7–9 µm)One layer of endothelium on a basal lamina, with contractile pericytes outside, which can become smooth muscle and new vessels after injury
VenuleVery thin; a few smooth muscle cells or pericytes; the externa is thickest
Vein (capacitance)Thin intima and media, thick externa; valves (folds of intima), most numerous in the limbs
TypeWallWhere
Continuous (the most common)No pores; tight junctions; some carry pinocytotic vesiclesMuscle, connective tissue, glands, nervous tissue
FenestratedPores with thin diaphragms; continuous basal laminaKidney, intestine, endocrine glands
SinusoidalWide and winding (slow flow); large pores without diaphragms; discontinuous basal lamina; very leakyLiver, bone marrow, spleen, some endocrine glands

Lymphatic capillaries are endothelium on a discontinuous basal lamina; they take up fluid that leaks into the tissues and carry it one way, back to the blood at the subclavian veins.

The conduction system

SA node → atrial muscle → AV node → bundle of His → right and left bundle branches → Purkinje fibers → ventricular muscle. The SA node is the pacemaker because its phase 4 rises fastest (about 70–80 a minute; the AV node's own rate is 40–60). The AV node is the slowest part: its delay (over 0.1 s) lets the atria finish emptying and shows as the PR interval. Purkinje fibers are the fastest, so the ventricles contract together.

Action potentials

PhaseVentricular muscle (and Purkinje)SA and AV nodes
4 (rest)Stable near −90 mV (K+)No stable rest: from about −65 mV it drifts up to threshold through the funny current (If, Na+ through HCN channels, which repolarization opens and cAMP boosts), then T-type Ca2+
0 (upstroke)Fast Na+ inflow (threshold about −70 mV, peak about +20 mV)L-type Ca2+ inflow (a slow upstroke)
1Brief K+ outflow (the notch)None
2 (plateau)L-type Ca2+ in, balanced by K+ out; triggers contractionNone
3 (repolarization)K+ outflowK+ outflow

The plateau makes the refractory period almost as long as the contraction, which is why heart muscle can't be tetanized. In the absolute refractory period the Na+ channels' inactivation gates are still shut, so no stimulus can fire the cell. Sympathetic input (norepinephrine on beta-1 receptors) raises cAMP, which speeds If and phase 4 and raises the L-type Ca2+ current: a faster rate, faster AV conduction and stronger beats. Vagal acetylcholine on M2 receptors lowers cAMP and If and opens ACh-gated K+ channels that hyperpolarize the cell, so the SA node takes longer to reach threshold, and it slows conduction through the AV node. At rest the SA node is under vagal (parasympathetic) control. Calcium channel blockers slow the nodes because their upstroke is carried by Ca2+.

The four "-tropy" words: chronotropy = rate, inotropy = contractility, dromotropy = conduction speed (mostly at the AV node), lusitropy = relaxation. Sympathetic stimulation raises all four.

The ECG

PartWhat it showsNormal
P waveAtrial depolarization0.08–0.10 s; upright in lead II
PR intervalAtrial depolarization plus the AV node delay0.12–0.20 s
QRS complexVentricular depolarization (atrial repolarization is hidden in it)0.06–0.10 s
ST segmentVentricles fully depolarized (the plateau)Flat (isoelectric), about 0.08 s; raised in a transmural MI
T waveVentricular repolarizationUpright in most leads
QT intervalAll of ventricular depolarization and repolarization0.20–0.40 s; longer with slow rates and some drugs
R-R intervalOne cardiac cycle (the cycle length)Regular in sinus rhythm; gives the heart rate

The paper runs at 25 mm/s: a small (1 mm) box is 0.04 s and a large (5 mm) box is 0.20 s; 10 mm of height is 1 mV. Heart rate = 1,500 ÷ the small boxes between two R waves (or 300 ÷ the large boxes): 20 small boxes is 75 a minute. Normal sinus rhythm: a P wave before every narrow QRS and a regular R-R interval. Over 100 a minute is a tachycardia (sinus tachycardia in exercise, fright or hyperthyroidism), under 60 a bradycardia (sinus bradycardia from vagal tone, as in trained athletes). Sinus arrhythmia is normal: the rate rises with inspiration and falls with expiration.

A wave points up when depolarization travels toward a lead's positive electrode, down when it travels away and is flat when it runs at right angles; more muscle mass, a bigger wave. Of the 12 leads, six are limb leads in the frontal plane (I, right arm to left arm; II, right arm to left leg; III, left arm to left leg; the right leg is the ground; plus aVR, aVL and aVF; lead II is the usual rhythm strip) and six are chest leads, V1–V6 (V1–V2 over the septum, V3–V4 the anterior wall, V5–V6 the lateral wall). The mean electrical axis is normally −30° to +105°: left axis deviation points to left ventricular hypertrophy (from the afterload of systemic hypertension), right axis deviation to right ventricular hypertrophy (from pulmonary hypertension). The ECG shows only electrical activity, nothing about pumping.

  • First-degree AV block: PR over 0.20 s, every P conducted; usually harmless (β-blockers, high vagal tone).
  • Second-degree, Mobitz I (Wenckebach): the PR grows longer beat by beat until a QRS drops; at the AV node, usually benign.
  • Second-degree, Mobitz II: QRS complexes drop suddenly with a fixed PR; below the AV node, it can progress to complete block and often needs a pacemaker.
  • Third-degree (complete): P waves and QRS complexes beat independently, with a slow escape rhythm.
  • Atrial fibrillation: many atrial sites fire instead of the SA node: no P waves, an irregularly irregular rhythm, and a risk of clots, stroke and heart failure (hence anticoagulants).
  • Ventricular tachycardia from an ectopic ventricular focus (up to about 300 a minute) can drop cardiac output to nothing and degrade into ventricular fibrillation and sudden cardiac death.
  • Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome is pre-excitation: an accessory pathway (the bundle of Kent) lets the impulse skip the AV node's delay.

The cardiac cycle

One cycle lasts 60 ÷ heart rate seconds: 0.8 s at 75 a minute, about 0.3 s of systole and 0.5 s of diastole. A faster rate shortens diastole much more than systole. Follow the left ventricle around its pressure–volume loop:

  • Mitral valve closes (S1) → isovolumetric contraction: all valves closed, pressure rises, volume holds at end-diastolic volume (EDV).
  • Aortic valve opens when LV pressure passes aortic pressure (about 80 mmHg) → ejection.
  • Aortic valve closes (S2; the dicrotic notch on the aortic tracing) → isovolumetric relaxation: all valves closed, pressure falls, volume holds at end-systolic volume (ESV).
  • Mitral valve opens when LV pressure falls below left atrial pressure → rapid filling, slow filling (diastasis), then the atrial kick, only 10–20% of the filling at rest (about 40% in exercise).

Heart sounds: S1 = mitral and tricuspid closure; S2 = aortic and pulmonic closure (it splits on inspiration); S3 = early rapid filling (normal in children, young adults and pregnancy; in older adults a sign of a dilated, failing ventricle); S4 = atrial contraction into a stiff, noncompliant ventricle (hypertrophy, ischemia). On the PV loop the width is stroke volume: more preload widens it to the right, more afterload makes it taller and narrower (end-systolic volume rises), and more contractility moves the end-systolic corner left. Chronic aortic stenosis raises end-systolic volume and lowers stroke volume; chronic aortic regurgitation greatly raises end-diastolic volume and stroke volume.

The jugular venous pulse has three waves: a = atrial contraction; c = the closed tricuspid valve bulging back into the right atrium during isovolumetric contraction; v = the atrium filling against the closed tricuspid valve, just before it opens. On the ECG the QRS comes just before LV pressure rises and the T wave during the late (reduced) ejection phase. A pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, from a catheter wedged in a small pulmonary artery branch, approximates left atrial pressure.

Hemodynamics

  • Flow = pressure difference ÷ resistance. For the whole body, MAP − central venous pressure = CO × TPR; central venous pressure is near 0, so MAP = CO × TPR (TPR is also called systemic vascular resistance, SVR).
  • Poiseuille: R = 8ηL/πr⁴. Radius is the strongest lever: halve it and resistance rises 16-fold. Viscosity and length raise resistance in a straight line. Red cells set most of blood's viscosity, which climbs steeply (faster than in a straight line) as hematocrit rises: polycythemia raises resistance and the left ventricle's afterload, and anemia lowers viscosity.
  • Resistances in series add; vessels in parallel lower the total (each organ is a parallel branch).
  • Velocity = flow ÷ total cross-sectional area: blood moves slowest in the capillaries (their combined cross-section is about 1,000 times the aorta's), giving time for exchange. The biggest pressure drop is across the arterioles, the high-resistance vessels.
  • Compliance = volume ÷ pressure: veins are far more compliant than arteries, so they store most of the blood at low pressure; venoconstriction lowers their compliance and moves blood toward the heart. Arteries stiffen with age.
  • Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic. Stroke volume is its main determinant, and it widens as the arteries stiffen and lose compliance (aging).
  • MAP ≈ diastolic + one third of pulse pressure: 120/80 gives about 93 mmHg. Diastole is about two thirds of the cycle at rest, so the mean sits nearer diastolic.
  • Flow is normally laminar and silent. Turbulent flow is noisy (a bruit or murmur) and comes with narrowed arteries, stenotic valves, branch points, high flow and low viscosity (anemia).

Cardiac output and venous return

CO = HR × SV, about 5 L/min at rest. SV = EDV − ESV, about 70 mL. EF = SV ÷ EDV, normally 55–70%, the bedside index of contractility. Stroke volume depends on three things:

  • Preload (end-diastolic stretch): more filling, more forceful ejection. This is the Frank–Starling law: within limits the heart pumps out what comes in, which keeps the two sides matched.
  • Contractility: raised by sympathetic stimulation, digoxin and more Ca2+ in the cell; lowered by heart failure, β-blockers and acidosis.
  • Afterload (the load the ventricle ejects against: mainly aortic pressure and TPR for the left ventricle, pulmonary artery pressure for the right; raised by hypertension and aortic stenosis): higher afterload, less stroke volume and a larger end-systolic volume.

A very fast heart rate shortens diastole, so filling and stroke volume fall. Venous return = (venous pressure − right atrial pressure) ÷ resistance to venous return. The gradient is small (about 7 mmHg in the veins to about 0 in the right atrium), so a few mmHg change it a lot. It rises with more blood volume, venoconstriction, the skeletal muscle pump and inspiration (intrathoracic pressure falls and draws blood into the chest), and it falls with a higher right atrial pressure, venodilation, standing still, a Valsalva maneuver and a vena cava compressed in late pregnancy. The mean systemic filling pressure (about 7 mmHg) is the pressure everywhere if the heart stopped, where venous return is zero; blood volume sets it.

At steady state cardiac output equals venous return: the point where the cardiac function curve (cardiac output against right atrial pressure, the Frank–Starling curve) and the venous return curve cross. More blood volume shifts the venous return curve right, so cardiac output and right atrial pressure both rise (blood loss: both fall). A positive inotrope, a faster rate or less afterload lifts the cardiac function curve: cardiac output rises and right atrial pressure falls. A higher TPR lowers the cardiac curve and rotates the venous return curve down: cardiac output falls with right atrial pressure unchanged. Myocardial O2 demand rises with heart rate, contractility and afterload, much less with preload; when supply falls short, ischemia brings angina and, if it lasts, infarction.
full.cr-bp:
What's tested
  • Short-term BP control: the baroreceptor reflex, its nerves, and the responses to standing, fainting and hemorrhage
  • Long-term BP control: the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, ADH and the natriuretic peptides
  • Local control of blood flow: autoregulation, the myogenic response, hyperemia, and the endothelium's nitric oxide and endothelin
  • Special circulations (coronary, brain, lungs, muscle, skin), the microcirculation and edema
  • Hypertension stages and damage, atherosclerosis, aneurysms, vascular malformations, vasculitis and venous thrombosis
  • Shock: its signs, stages, types by their hemodynamics, and treatment
  • Ischemic heart disease and MI, valve disease, and infective endocarditis with its prophylaxis
  • Heart failure types, cardiomyopathies, pericardial disease and Marfan syndrome
  • Dental decisions: blood pressure cutoffs, orthostatic hypotension, timing after an MI

Short-term control: the baroreceptor reflex

Stretch receptors in the carotid sinus (signals in the glossopharyngeal nerve, CN IX) and the aortic arch (vagus, CN X) fire faster as pressure rises and slower as it falls, reporting to the nucleus tractus solitarius in the medulla. When MAP falls, firing falls, so the medulla withdraws vagal tone and raises sympathetic tone: a faster, stronger heartbeat and constricted arterioles and veins. The reflex acts in seconds but resets if pressure stays high, so it doesn't set long-term BP. Sympathetic nerves raise heart rate, contractility and AV conduction and constrict both arterioles (resistance) and veins (capacitance, so venous return rises). The vagus mainly slows the rate and AV conduction: it barely changes ventricular contractility, has no effect on veins and dilates vessels in only a few organs.

  • Standing up: blood pools in the legs, venous return and BP fall, and the reflex speeds the heart and constricts vessels. When that fails (older patients, α1-blockers, diuretics and other antihypertensives, dehydration, a long reclined appointment), the patient gets orthostatic hypotension. Raise the chair slowly and let the patient sit for a minute before standing.
  • Hemorrhage: less stretch → more sympathetic tone (a fast, weak pulse and cool, pale skin), plus RAAS and ADH to save volume.
  • Vasovagal syncope, the most common emergency in the dental office: pain or fear fires the vagus and withdraws sympathetic tone, so both HR and BP fall. Lay the patient flat with the legs raised.
  • Cushing reflex: raised intracranial pressure → hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing.
  • The carotid and aortic bodies beside the baroreceptors are peripheral chemoreceptors: a low PO2, a high PCO2 or a low pH raises sympathetic output (vasoconstriction) and breathing. The central chemoreceptors in the medulla sense brain H+ made from CO2 and do the same.
  • Ischemic brain reflex: too little blood to the brain (MAP under about 60 mmHg, or a blocked cerebral vessel) sets off an intense sympathetic discharge that drives MAP up. Pain reflex: the chest pain of angina or an MI raises sympathetic tone: higher BP, a fast pulse and sweating.

Long-term control: volume

Renin comes from the juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole when renal perfusion falls, the macula densa senses less NaCl, or sympathetic nerves fire (beta-1). Renin turns angiotensinogen (from the liver) into angiotensin I, and ACE, mostly on lung capillary endothelium, makes angiotensin II. Angiotensin II constricts arterioles (and the efferent arteriole, holding GFR), releases aldosterone (Na+ and water kept, K+ and H+ lost at the collecting duct) and ADH, and causes thirst. ACE also breaks down bradykinin, which is why ACE inhibitors cause cough and angioedema.

ANP from stretched atria and BNP, mainly from the ventricles, do the opposite: Na+ and water loss, vasodilation (through cGMP), and less renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone. Neprilysin breaks ANP down, so blocking it (sacubitril) lowers BP. BNP is a blood test for heart failure. ADH (vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary rises with high plasma osmolality, low atrial stretch, angiotensin II and sympathetic input: through V2 receptors the kidney keeps water, and through V1 receptors, at high levels, vessels constrict.

Local control of blood flow

  • Autoregulation: an organ keeps its flow steady when perfusion pressure changes, through the myogenic response (stretched arteriolar smooth muscle contracts as Ca2+ enters; less stretch relaxes it) and the washout or buildup of metabolites. The kidney, heart and brain autoregulate best.
  • Active hyperemia: more flow when a tissue works harder. Reactive hyperemia: a surge of flow after a blocked vessel reopens. Both come from metabolites that built up and dilate the arterioles.
  • Tissue dilators: low O2 (it dilates every bed except the lungs, where it constricts), adenosine (key in the heart), CO2, H+, K+, lactate and phosphate; histamine (dilates arterioles through NO and makes capillaries leaky) and bradykinin.
  • Endothelium: nitric oxide, released by the shear stress of flow, is the most important dilator in normal flow and also keeps platelets and leukocytes from sticking; prostacyclin (PGI2) dilates and is made by COX, so aspirin and ibuprofen lower it; endothelin-1 constricts (raised by angiotensin II and ADH; part of pulmonary hypertension).
  • Arteriolar diameter is set by basal tone, local metabolites and sympathetic α1 nerves; venous diameter by sympathetic nerves, the pressure inside and compression from outside.

Special circulations

BedMain controlTestable point
CoronaryLocal metabolites (adenosine, NO)About 80% of LV flow comes in diastole, when the muscle stops squeezing its vessels; O2 extraction is already high at rest, so more demand needs more flow
BrainPCO2; strong autoregulationHigh CO2 dilates; hyperventilation constricts
LungsAlveolar O2Hypoxia constricts, sending blood to ventilated alveoli; systemic vessels dilate to hypoxia
Skeletal muscleSympathetic at rest; metabolites in exerciseIn exercise, adenosine, K+, lactate and CO2 override sympathetic tone; at rest α1 nerves constrict, and β2 receptors dilate with epinephrine. About 20% of cardiac output at rest, over 80% in hard exercise
SkinSympatheticTemperature control: cold constricts skin vessels through α1 nerves; heat withdraws that tone and sympathetic cholinergic nerves dilate them actively

Microcirculation and edema

Arterioles are the main resistance, venules and small veins hold the blood volume, and capillaries exchange. Continuous capillaries (muscle, lung, connective tissue) are tight; fenestrated ones (kidney, intestine, choroid plexus, endocrine glands) have pores; sinusoids (liver, bone marrow, spleen) have large gaps and an incomplete basement membrane. Lipid-soluble gases diffuse through the endothelial cells, water-soluble solutes pass between them, and large molecules cross in vesicles. Fluid moves by the Starling forces: net filtration pressure = (capillary − interstitial hydrostatic pressure) − (capillary − interstitial oncotic pressure); with a capillary pressure of 30, an interstitial pressure of 1, a plasma oncotic pressure of 26 and an interstitial oncotic pressure of 3 mmHg, it is (30 − 1) − (26 − 3) = +6 mmHg, pushing fluid out, while a lower hydrostatic or higher oncotic pressure makes it negative and fluid returns. Of about 20 L filtered a day, 16–18 L is reabsorbed and 2–4 L returns as lymph, through blind-ended lymphatics with one-way valves.

Fluid leaves capillaries when capillary hydrostatic pressure rises (heart failure, venous obstruction), plasma oncotic pressure falls (low albumin: cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, malnutrition), capillaries leak (inflammation, burns) or lymphatics are blocked (lymph nodes removed or irradiated, parasites, standing still). A higher plasma oncotic pressure protects against edema.

Hypertension and vascular disease

  • Stages (2017 ACC/AHA, unchanged in 2025): normal, under 120/80; elevated, 120–129 with diastolic under 80; stage 1, 130–139 or 80–89; stage 2, 140/90 or higher; crisis, above 180/120. It is the "silent killer": many patients don't know they have it or have stopped their drugs. About 90–95% is primary (essential): genes, salt, obesity, inactivity, smoking, diabetes and aging vessels, with the kidney excreting less Na+ than is taken in. Secondary causes: kidney disease, renal artery stenosis, primary aldosteronism, Cushing syndrome, pheochromocytoma, hypothyroidism, preeclampsia, coarctation of the aorta, sleep apnea.
  • Damage: thickened, narrowed arterioles and faster atherosclerosis lead to LV hypertrophy and heart failure, coronary disease, stroke, chronic kidney disease, aortic dissection and atrial fibrillation. The eyes often show it first: hypertensive retinopathy (narrowed arterioles, AV nicking and copper wiring; then flame hemorrhages, cotton wool spots and hard exudates; a swollen optic disc in malignant hypertension). In the mouth: more periodontal disease, slower healing, and the drugs' dry mouth and gingival overgrowth.
  • Atherosclerosis, the main cause of cardiovascular disease: endothelial injury → LDL enters the intima and oxidizes → monocytes become macrophages and then foam cells (the fatty streak) → smooth muscle migrates in, collagen and calcium are laid down, and a fibrous cap forms over a lipid core that can become necrotic. A cap that ruptures → thrombus → MI or stroke. Risk factors: hypertension, high LDL, diabetes, smoking, obesity, inactivity and family history. A calcified carotid plaque can show on a panoramic radiograph, xanthelasma (yellow plaques at the inner eyelids) and corneal arcus point to high cholesterol, and periodontal disease is linked to atherosclerotic events. Most often hit: abdominal aorta, coronary, popliteal and carotid arteries.
  • True aneurysm: all three layers bulge (an abdominal aortic aneurysm, mostly from atherosclerosis, with smoking and male sex; rupture risk rises above 5.5 cm). False aneurysm: a wall defect with a hematoma outside the vessel that still connects to the lumen. Dissection: blood splits the intima from the media through an intimal tear, making a false lumen (hypertension is the top risk; Marfan syndrome too), with tearing chest pain to the back; an ascending one needs surgery, a descending one is usually treated medically. A berry aneurysm is a congenital outpouching of a cerebral artery, more common with polycystic kidney disease, Marfan syndrome and coarctation; smoking and hypertension add risk.
  • Vascular malformations: a port-wine stain is a flat red-purple capillary malformation that never fades and grows with the child; a stork bite (nevus simplex) is dilated capillaries that usually fade. An arteriovenous malformation joins arteries straight to veins, skipping the capillaries: it can bleed, and a large one makes the heart pump extra volume (high-output heart failure). On the face, either raises the bleeding risk of dental treatment, so plan it with oral surgery, sometimes in a hospital.
  • Vasculitis (inflamed vessel walls) narrows the lumen and often shows a rash (palpable purpura). It is infectious (organisms invade the wall, which can weaken into an aneurysm or clot; untreated syphilis's aortitis is the classic) or immune (immune complexes as in lupus or drug reactions, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), anti-endothelial antibodies or T cells). Giant cell (temporal) arteritis, the most common vasculitis in older adults (rare under 50; more women), is granulomatous: headache, a tender temporal artery, jaw pain on chewing, fever, fatigue and weight loss, a dental look-alike. Sudden vision loss is the danger, so refer the same day; a biopsy confirms it and corticosteroids treat it.
  • Venous thrombosis: deep vein thrombosis (over 90% of cases) forms in the deep leg veins, is often silent or only swells the leg, and can break off to the lungs as a pulmonary embolism. Risks: immobility (bed rest, long trips), surgery, heart failure, pregnancy, oral contraceptives, obesity, age over 60, cancer, a central line and inherited clotting defects (factor V Leiden). Superficial thrombophlebitis is a clot in an inflamed vein under the skin (varicose veins, IV lines): a warm, tender red streak that settles in 1–2 weeks.

Shock

Shock is generalized hypoperfusion: O2 delivery falls short of what the tissues need. Signs: hypotension (MAP under about 70 mmHg with a fast pulse), cold, clammy skin, little urine, confusion, and a blood lactate over 2 mmol/L as cells turn to anaerobic metabolism. It moves through four stages: initial (anaerobic metabolism, often no signs yet), compensatory (the baroreceptor reflex, RAAS, ADH and the chemoreceptors raise HR, SVR and volume), progressive (decompensated: acidosis, less flow to the heart and brain, clots in small vessels) and refractory (irreversible organ failure: subendocardial necrosis in the heart, acute tubular necrosis in the kidney, diffuse alveolar damage in the lungs, centrilobular necrosis in the liver, mucosal necrosis in the gut, and adrenal hemorrhage with adrenal failure, Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome, in severe bacterial infection). About 30% of patients in shock die.

TypeCardiac outputSVRWedge pressureSkin
Hypovolemic (bleeding, burns)↓↑↓Cold, clammy
Cardiogenic (MI)↓↑↑Cold, clammy
Obstructive (PE, tamponade, tension pneumothorax)↓↑VariesCold
Septic (distributive; the most common)↑ early↓↓Warm, flushed
Anaphylactic (distributive)↑ or normal↓↓Warm, hives
Neurogenic (spinal cord injury)↓↓↓Warm, with a slow pulse
  • Causes: hypovolemic, lost volume (bleeding, burns, vomiting, diarrhea); cardiogenic, pump failure (MI, arrhythmia, valve disease, cardiomyopathy), with chest pain and raised neck veins; obstructive, blocked filling (tamponade, tension pneumothorax, PE), with distended neck veins and pulsus paradoxus (systolic pressure falling more than 10 mmHg on inspiration); distributive, widespread vasodilation, the most prevalent type.
  • Distributive: dilated venules and splanchnic beds hold the blood, so venous return and preload fall; septic shock's output is often high early, then falls. Septic shock, its most common cause, adds fever and warm skin. Anaphylactic shock (IgE, histamine) adds airway and facial swelling. Neurogenic shock (spinal cord or brain injury) loses sympathetic tone: warm skin and a slow pulse.
  • Treatment fits the cause: fluids, and blood if over 20% of the volume is lost; treat the heart and give inotropes (dobutamine, dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine) in cardiogenic shock; relieve the obstruction; epinephrine first for anaphylaxis, with fluids and corticosteroids; fluids and vasoconstrictors for neurogenic shock; antibiotics and fluids for sepsis.

Ischemic heart disease

  • Stable angina: a fixed narrowing; chest pain on exertion, relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. Unstable angina and NSTEMI: a ruptured plaque with a partial clot and pain at rest; an NSTEMI is a subendocardial infarct. STEMI: complete occlusion, a transmural infarct and ST elevation. During any of these acute coronary syndromes, no elective dental care.
  • MI territories: ST elevation in II, III and aVF = inferior wall, usually the right coronary artery (which also feeds the SA node in most people and the AV node in about 80%, so bradycardia and heart block go with it); V1–V4 = anterior wall and septum, the LAD, the artery most often blocked; I, aVL and V5–V6 = lateral wall, the circumflex.
  • Marker: troponin, which rises within hours and stays up for 7–10 days.
  • The infarct over time: reversible for about 20 minutes; necrosis begins at 20–40 minutes; a pale infarct shows by 4–6 hours; the muscle is softest at 3–10 days; a dense scar forms by 6–8 weeks.
  • Complications by time: arrhythmia in the first day (ventricular fibrillation, the main cause of early death); left ventricular failure and pulmonary edema; fibrinous pericarditis at 1–3 days; rupture of the free wall (tamponade), septum or a papillary muscle (acute mitral regurgitation) at 3–10 days, when the dead muscle is softest; a mural thrombus that can embolize to the brain or the retina; aneurysm and Dressler syndrome (autoimmune pericarditis) weeks later.
  • Elective dental care is put off after an MI and planned with the cardiologist: Dr. Anderson's slides say 6 months; newer guidance allows about 30 days for a stable patient. Then short morning visits, good anesthesia, limited epinephrine. After a stent, patients take aspirin plus clopidogrel for at least 12 months: never stop them without the cardiologist (the stent can clot), and control bleeding with local measures.
  • Emboli to the eye (from a mural thrombus, atrial fibrillation or aortic valve disease): a central retinal artery occlusion is sudden, painless loss of vision in one eye with a cherry-red spot, the eye's equivalent of a stroke and an emergency; brief episodes (amaurosis fugax) point to a carotid or cardiac source.

Heart failure, cardiomyopathy and the pericardium

  • HFrEF (systolic failure): EF under 40%, a dilated, flabby ventricle; ischemia is the most common cause (also dilated cardiomyopathy, myocarditis, alcohol, doxorubicin). HFpEF (diastolic failure): EF 50% or more, a thick, stiff ventricle that can't fill; hypertension is the most common cause, often in older women.
  • Left-sided failure backs blood into the lungs: breathlessness, orthopnea, pulmonary edema with pink frothy sputum. Right-sided failure backs it into the body: distended neck veins, leg edema, an enlarged liver, ascites. Most right-sided failure comes from left-sided failure. Treat these patients semi-reclined. With a pacemaker or implanted defibrillator, the slides say to avoid ultrasonic scalers and electrosurgery.
  • Cardiomyopathies: dilated (low EF; idiopathic in about half, alcohol, viral myocarditis, pregnancy, Chagas disease, doxorubicin); hypertrophic (autosomal dominant sarcomere mutations, an asymmetric septum that can block outflow; the leading cause of sudden death in young athletes; diuretics and vasodilators worsen the obstruction); restrictive (a stiff ventricle of normal size and EF: amyloidosis, which can also enlarge the tongue; sarcoidosis, which can also cause uveoparotid fever, with uveitis, parotid swelling and facial palsy; hemochromatosis; radiation).
  • Pericarditis (viral, often coxsackievirus; uremia; Dressler syndrome): pleuritic chest pain, a friction rub and diffuse ST elevation. Tamponade: fluid squeezes the heart, giving Beck's triad of hypotension, distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds.
  • Marfan syndrome (FBN1, fibrillin-1): tall, long fingers, loose joints, a high-arched palate and a dislocated lens; the aortic root dilates, with aortic regurgitation and dissection.

Valves and endocarditis

  • Aortic stenosis: a crescendo–decrescendo systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border, radiating to the carotids; syncope, angina and breathlessness on exertion (once they start, median survival is 2–3 years without a valve replacement); calcification after 65, a bicuspid valve in younger adults. In the chair: a risk of hypotension, so limit epinephrine.
  • Mitral regurgitation: holosystolic at the apex, toward the axilla. Mitral valve prolapse: myxomatous leaflets billow into the left atrium: a mid-systolic click; the most common valve abnormality (2–3% of people), usually benign. Aortic regurgitation: an early diastolic murmur and a wide pulse pressure. Mitral stenosis: an opening snap and diastolic rumble, usually after rheumatic fever; left atrial pressure rises, atrial fibrillation and clots follow, so these patients are often anticoagulated. A stenotic valve puts a pressure load, and a leaky one a volume load, on the chamber upstream.
  • Infective endocarditis: damaged endothelium or turbulent flow collects a sterile platelet–fibrin clot, and bacteremia (a dental procedure) seeds it into an infected vegetation. Viridans streptococci from the mouth on damaged valves (subacute, after bleeding dental care); S. aureus on normal valves (acute; the tricuspid valve in people who inject drugs); S. epidermidis on prosthetic valves; the HACEK group. Signs: fever, a new murmur, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions (painless, palms and soles: septic emboli), Osler nodes (painful, finger pads: immune complexes), Roth spots, an embolic stroke, and petechiae, including on the palate, which can be the first sign. The mitral valve is most often involved.
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental care that manipulates the gingiva or the periapical tissue (current AHA guidance): prosthetic valves or valve repair material, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease, and a heart transplant with valve disease. Not for rheumatic heart disease, mitral valve prolapse or a murmur alone. Adult dose: amoxicillin 2 g by mouth 30–60 minutes before.

Blood pressure in the dental chair

Take BP at every visit and repeat a high reading after a few minutes of rest. At 180/110 or higher, put off elective care and refer the patient to a physician, urgently if there is chest pain, a severe headache, confusion or a change in vision. Below that, treat with care: short, calm visits, good anesthesia, limited epinephrine and a referral when BP is uncontrolled.

What's tested
  • Each antihypertensive class: how it works, its signature side effect, and what matters in the dental chair
  • Diuretics and their electrolyte effects
  • Heart failure drugs: digoxin, the drugs that lower mortality, and those that only ease symptoms
  • Antiarrhythmic classes (Vaughan Williams) and amiodarone's toxicity
  • Nitrates for angina, and the chest-pain steps in the chair
  • Lipid drugs: mechanisms, side effects and interactions
  • Epinephrine limits for cardiac patients, and the drug interactions a dentist can cause

Antihypertensives

Two dental interactions come up again and again. NSAIDs taken for more than a few days block renal prostaglandins and blunt ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics and β-blockers; with an ACE inhibitor, ARB, loop diuretic or spironolactone they also raise the risk of acute kidney injury and high K+. A short course for dental pain is generally fine. Nonselective β-blockers leave epinephrine only alpha-1 receptors to act on, so BP rises and the baroreceptors slow the heart; with propranolol, nadolol or timolol use fewer cartridges, aspirate and inject slowly. A rough guide to selectivity: A to M are beta-1 selective (atenolol, bisoprolol, esmolol, metoprolol), N to Z nonselective (nadolol, propranolol, timolol). β-blockers also hide the warning signs of hypoglycemia and slow recovery from it in a diabetic patient on insulin, the nonselective ones most: make sure the patient has eaten. Drug-influenced gingival overgrowth comes from calcium channel blockers (nifedipine most), phenytoin and cyclosporine. With a calcium channel blocker it affects about 6–34% of patients, mild to severe: collagen breakdown slows (less matrix metalloproteinase activity) and fibroblasts multiply. Treatment is meticulous plaque control, a drug change by the physician and surgical excision when needed.

Epinephrine in local anesthetic

1:100,000 epinephrine is 0.01 mg/mL, so a 1.8 mL cartridge holds 0.018 mg (1:200,000 holds 0.009 mg; 1:50,000 holds 0.036 mg). The usual ceiling is 0.2 mg for a healthy adult and 0.04 mg for a patient with significant heart disease, about two cartridges of 1:100,000. Avoid it in unstable angina, an MI in the last 30 days or so, uncontrolled arrhythmia or uncontrolled hypertension, and keep it out of retraction cord in cardiac patients.

Heart failure

  • Drugs that lower mortality (reduced ejection fraction): an ACE inhibitor, ARB or sacubitril–valsartan; an evidence-based β-blocker (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol); an aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone, eplerenone); an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin); hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate in Black patients.
  • Sacubitril–valsartan (an ARNI) pairs the ARB valsartan with sacubitril, a neprilysin inhibitor that raises the natriuretic peptides (more Na+ and water lost, less fibrosis). It beats an ACE inhibitor or ARB alone on death and heart failure admissions. Adverse effect: hypotension. Contraindicated in pregnancy and after angioedema from an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors (-flozins: dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) block Na+–glucose cotransport in the proximal tubule, so Na+ and glucose leave in the urine. Used in type 2 diabetes, heart failure and chronic kidney disease. Adverse effects: low volume, urinary tract infections, mild weight loss, acute kidney injury.
  • Drugs that ease symptoms only: loop diuretics (congestion) and digoxin; a thiazide can be added.
  • Digoxin inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase, so Na+ builds up inside the cell, the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger removes less Ca2+, and contraction is stronger. It also raises vagal tone, slowing the AV node (rate control in atrial fibrillation). Its window is narrow: low K+ (from diuretics), low magnesium, high calcium, kidney failure, and drugs such as amiodarone, verapamil and the macrolides raise toxicity. Signs: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, yellow-green halos and blurred vision, arrhythmias. Antidote: digoxin immune Fab. Now seldom used; it doesn't lower mortality but may improve quality of life.
  • Spironolactone with an ACE inhibitor raises K+; check potassium.

Antiarrhythmics

ClassActionExamplesPoints
INa+ channel block (slower phase 0; widens the QRS the most)IA quinidine, procainamide; IB lidocaine, mexiletine; IC flecainide, propafenoneIC blocks Na+ the most, IB the least; procainamide: lupus-like syndrome; lidocaine IV for ventricular arrhythmias; flecainide and propafenone for rhythm control

Rate control in atrial fibrillation uses class II and IV drugs (β-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem); rhythm control uses class I and III drugs (dofetilide, ibutilide, propafenone, amiodarone, flecainide); either way with an anticoagulant. Any antiarrhythmic can cause new arrhythmias (proarrhythmia), hypotension and bradycardia. Amiodarone has a very long half-life and inhibits CYP enzymes, raising warfarin and digoxin levels. Epinephrine and albuterol speed the sinus rate; β-blockers (timolol eye drops too), calcium channel blockers and digoxin slow it. Amiodarone, dofetilide, sotalol, some antibiotics (the macrolides), ondansetron and haloperidol lengthen the QT and can bring on torsades de pointes; avoid stacking them. Lidocaine is itself a class IB drug, so its Na+ channel block adds to a class I antiarrhythmic's.

Nitrates and angina in the chair

Nitroglycerin releases nitric oxide → cGMP → smooth muscle relaxation, mostly in veins: less preload means less O2 demand, and coronary vessels dilate too. It is given under the tongue (0.4 mg tablet or spray), because swallowed nitroglycerin is destroyed by first-pass liver metabolism. Side effects: headache, flushing, hypotension and reflex tachycardia. Don't give it after a PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil, tadalafil) in the last 24–48 hours, with a systolic BP below 90 mmHg, or in a right ventricular MI. For chest pain in the chair: stop, sit the patient up, give nitroglycerin; if the pain isn't better 5 minutes after the first dose, call EMS, repeat every 5 minutes up to three doses and have the patient chew aspirin. Isosorbide dinitrate and mononitrate are the long-acting forms, which need a nitrate-free period each day to avoid tolerance.

The dental interaction: clarithromycin and erythromycin strongly inhibit CYP3A4, which clears simvastatin, lovastatin and atorvastatin, so statin levels and myopathy risk rise. Azithromycin barely affects CYP3A4; pravastatin and rosuvastatin depend least on it. Grapefruit and azole antifungals raise those statins too. Two more for the chair: omega-3 fatty acids add to bleeding, and bile acid sequestrants bind drugs taken at the same time. Statins, ezetimibe, bile acid sequestrants and PCSK9 inhibitors are the cholesterol (LDL) drugs; fibrates, niacin and omega-3 fatty acids are the triglyceride drugs.
full.cr-blood:
What's tested
  • Primary hemostasis (the platelet plug) and its disorders: von Willebrand disease, Bernard–Soulier, Glanzmann, thrombocytopenia
  • The clotting cascade: tissue factor and factor VII, the cofactors, the vitamin K–dependent and liver-made factors
  • The lab tests (PT/INR, aPTT, platelet count, the mixing study) and which disorder or drug lengthens which
  • Clotting disorders: factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, a lack of protein C, protein S or antithrombin, and DIC
  • Anticoagulants, antiplatelets and thrombolytics: targets, monitoring and reversal
  • Dental management of a patient on an anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug
  • Hemoglobin, the hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell disease, HbC and HbSC disease, the thalassemias) and their dental signs
  • Anemias and the hematopoietic drugs, including the drugs that lower vitamin B12

Hemostasis in two steps

Primary hemostasis builds the platelet plug: the vessel constricts; von Willebrand factor (vWF) links platelet GpIb to exposed collagen (adhesion); platelets release ADP and thromboxane A2 (activation); and GpIIb/IIIa binds fibrinogen to link platelets (aggregation). Its defects (of the platelets or the vessel wall) cause quick, oozing bleeding from mucosa and small cuts (gums, nose, heavy periods), petechiae (pinpoint bleeds), purpura (larger ones) and ecchymoses (large bruises after slight trauma), with a long bleeding time; inherited ones show up more in women. Vessel-wall causes are rare: Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (collagen), Marfan syndrome (fibrillin) and scurvy (no vitamin C to make collagen).

Secondary hemostasis is the cascade that makes fibrin to hold the plug. Its defects cause delayed bleeding, deep bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis), muscle and body cavities, and bleeding after surgery and dental procedures; inherited ones are mostly in men (the X-linked hemophilias).

The cascade

  • Tissue factor (factor III) exposed by injury binds factor VII: this starts clotting in the body (the extrinsic pathway, tested by the PT; "37 cents" for III and VII).
  • The intrinsic pathway (XII, XI, IX, VIII; "not $12.00 but $11.98"; tested by the aPTT) amplifies it. In the body, kallikreins and thrombin activate XI, and VIIa also activates IX; factor XII is needed only in the test tube, so its lack lengthens the aPTT but causes no bleeding.
  • Both meet at the common pathway: X → thrombin (II) → fibrin (I), with factor XIII cross-linking the fibrin (the "five and dime, $2 or $1 on the 13th" mnemonic: V, X, II, I, XIII). Calcium (factor IV) is needed throughout.
  • Factors V and VIII are cofactors, not enzymes (Va helps Xa; VIIIa helps IXa).
  • Vitamin K–dependent: II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S. The liver makes nearly all factors (not factor VIII or vWF, which come from endothelium). Factor VII has the shortest half-life, so liver failure, vitamin K lack and early warfarin show up first as a long PT.
  • Natural brakes: antithrombin (boosted by heparin; it inactivates thrombin and factors IXa, Xa, XIa and XIIa), proteins C and S (protein C is the enzyme, S its cofactor; they inactivate Va and VIIIa; a lack causes clots, not bleeding), and plasmin, which breaks fibrin down (fibrinolysis) once tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) has made it from plasminogen.
TestNormal (about)MeasuresLong in
PT / INR11–13.5 s; INR 1.0Extrinsic + common (VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen)Warfarin, liver disease, vitamin K lack, factor VII lack
aPTT25–35 sIntrinsic + common (XII, XI, IX, VIII)Heparin; hemophilia A, B and C (factors VIII, IX, XI); factor XII lack (no bleeding); sometimes von Willebrand disease
Both long—Common pathwayFactor X, V, II or fibrinogen lack; DIC; severe liver disease
Platelet count150,000–450,000/µLNumber of plateletsLow in ITP, leukemia, chemotherapy, liver disease (spleen), heparin-induced thrombocytopenia

Mixing study: the patient's plasma is mixed with normal plasma. If a long PT or aPTT corrects, a factor is missing; if it stays long, something is inhibiting the cascade (such as an antibody against a factor).

Bleeding disorders

  • Von Willebrand disease: the most common inherited bleeding disorder, usually autosomal dominant. vWF in the vessel wall binds platelet GpIb (and GpIIb/IIIa once platelets are activated); type 1 is a mild lack of vWF, type 2 a faulty vWF, type 3 a severe lack. Mucosal bleeding; desmopressin (DDAVP) releases stored vWF.
  • Hemophilia A (factor VIII) and B (factor IX, Christmas disease), the common inherited factor disorders: X-linked recessive, so boys are affected; bleeding into joints; long aPTT, normal PT and platelets. Dental surgery is planned with the hematologist: factor replacement, local hemostatics and antifibrinolytics; an inferior alveolar block needs factor cover.
  • Hemophilia C (factor XI) is rare and not X-linked: long aPTT, normal PT. The other rare factor lacks: VII (long PT only), XII (long aPTT, no bleeding), and V, X or fibrinogen (both long).
  • Bernard–Soulier syndrome (no GpIb, so platelets can't bind vWF) and Glanzmann thrombasthenia (no GpIIb/IIIa, so they can't bind fibrinogen): rare (about 1 in a million), autosomal recessive and usually severe. Platelet aggregation studies tell them apart: Bernard–Soulier has giant platelets and no response to ristocetin (which makes vWF bind GpIb); Glanzmann has normal-sized platelets that respond to ristocetin and to nothing else. Platelet granule (storage pool) defects are rare; dense granule defects are mild unless aspirin is added.
  • Thrombocytopenia, the most common cause of platelet bleeding: platelets are transfused below 10,000/µL even without bleeding, below 20,000/µL when the bleeding risk is high, and below 50,000/µL for active bleeding, surgery or an invasive procedure, so most dental surgery wants 50,000/µL or more. Causes: too few made (aplastic anemia, marrow infiltration, B12 or folate lack, alcohol), destruction (immune thrombocytopenia, ITP, treated with steroids; drugs; heparin; DIC), the spleen holding them, or a massive transfusion; pseudothrombocytopenia is platelets clumping in the tube. Liver or kidney failure, aspirin, other drugs and some herbs impair platelet function at a normal count.

Clotting disorders

  • Inherited (thrombophilia): factor V Leiden (factor V resists activated protein C; the most common), prothrombin G20210A (too much prothrombin), and a lack of protein C, protein S or antithrombin (a homozygous antithrombin lack is incompatible with life; antithrombin also falls in liver disease and nephrotic syndrome).
  • Acquired risks: immobility, surgery (hip, knee, pelvic), long-bone fractures, pregnancy, oral contraceptives and hormone therapy, smoking, cancer and antiphospholipid syndrome. Clots show as deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, retinal or mesenteric thrombosis and lost pregnancies.
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), most often from sepsis (also trauma, burns, cancer, childbirth): clotting inside the vessels blocks small vessels and uses up the factors and platelets, so the patient clots and bleeds at once; PT and aPTT long, platelets low. It is very hard to treat.
