Warfarin blocks VKORC1 (vitamin K epoxide reductase), so active vitamin K isn't regenerated to finish factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S. It starts slowly (2–7 days, while the finished factors run out), lasts long (half-life 1.5–2 days) and has a narrow therapeutic index. Protein C falls first, so the first days carry a clot risk (skin necrosis, more with protein C lack): heparin or LMWH is overlapped at the start (bridging). It causes fetal bleeding, birth defects and fetal death. It is the oral anticoagulant for a mechanical heart valve; the direct oral anticoagulants are for venous clots and for atrial fibrillation without a mechanical valve or moderate to severe mitral stenosis.

Why warfarin interacts so much: it is 99% protein-bound, broken down in the liver (CYP2C9; CYP2C9 and VKORC1 gene variants change the dose), long-acting and narrow. Metronidazole and fluconazole block CYP2C9 and raise the INR, and macrolides raise it too; some antibiotics (2nd- and 3rd-generation cephalosporins; also amoxicillin) raise it by cutting the gut bacteria's vitamin K; regular acetaminophen near 4 g a day raises it; NSAIDs, antiplatelets and other anticoagulants add bleeding; rifampin induces the liver enzymes and weakens it.

Heparin (IV or under the skin) makes antithrombin work about 1,000 times faster. Unfractionated heparin acts at once IV, wears off in about 2 hours, varies from patient to patient and is followed with the aPTT; LMWH (enoxaparin) is predictable, weight-dosed, lasts 12–24 hours, usually needs no monitoring and needs a lower dose in kidney failure. Both prevent and treat DVT and PE and are used in atrial fibrillation, acute coronary syndrome, dialysis and heart surgery. Side effects: bleeding, hypersensitivity, osteoporosis and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT): in 1–4% (very rare with LMWH), usually on days 5–10, antibodies to heparin bound to platelet factor 4 both clear platelets and activate them, so the count falls while clots form. Stop heparin and switch to a direct thrombin inhibitor (bivalirudin), fondaparinux or a direct oral anticoagulant.

Antiplatelets prevent arterial clots (MI, stroke, stents); anticoagulants treat venous and arterial clots; thrombolytics dissolve them. Aspirin's side effects: bleeding, GI upset, gout flares and allergy. Aspirin plus a P2Y12 blocker is dual antiplatelet therapy after an acute coronary syndrome or a stent. Ticagrelor is broken down by CYP3A4, so strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin) and strong inducers are contraindicated with it; clopidogrel's activation by CYP2C19 varies with genes. Cangrelor is the IV P2Y12 blocker; GpIIb/IIIa blockers are rarely used. Tenecteplase, a modified tPA, binds fibrin in the clot and turns the plasminogen there into plasmin: for an acute MI when angioplasty can't be done in time, a massive pulmonary embolism or an acute ischemic stroke; its main risk is bleeding.

Dental management

  • Warfarin: check the INR within 24 hours of surgery (up to 72 hours if it has been stable). At an INR of 3.5 or less, most office extractions go ahead without stopping the drug; above that, consult the physician. Target INRs: 2–3 for atrial fibrillation and venous clots, 2.5–3.5 for a mechanical mitral valve.
  • Direct oral anticoagulants: no INR; simple extractions usually go ahead, timed late in the dosing interval; for higher-risk surgery the physician may hold a dose.
  • Antiplatelets: don't stop aspirin or dual therapy for routine dental surgery, and never after a recent stent without the cardiologist.
  • Local measures: pressure, oxidized cellulose or collagen, sutures, and a 4.8% tranexamic acid rinse (a lysine analog that blocks the lysine-binding sites on plasminogen and tPA, so they can't dock on fibrin; in a bleeding disorder it is given with the missing factor).
  • NSAIDs are avoided in patients on an anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug: even a few days raise the bleeding risk, and some NSAIDs blunt aspirin's antiplatelet effect. If one can't be avoided, give the lowest dose for the shortest time, with stomach protection. Acetaminophen at usual doses is safer.

Hemoglobin and the hemoglobinopathies

Hemoglobin has four globin chains, each with a heme holding iron, and always two α chains. Adult hemoglobin is 95–98% HbA (α2β2), 2–3% HbA2 (α2δ2) and under 1% HbF; fetal hemoglobin (HbF, α2γ2) binds O2 more tightly, is 50–80% of a newborn's and falls to adult levels after about 6 months. Oral signs of the hemoglobinopathies: mucosal pallor, delayed tooth eruption, enamel and dentin mineralization defects, changes in the tongue's surface, hypercementosis, and periodontitis unusual for a child's age.

  • Sickle cell disease: valine replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of β-globin (HbS). Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes into rigid crystals; the cells sickle, block small vessels and hemolyze. Autosomal recessive and most common in people of African ancestry: sickle trait (HbAS) is usually silent and is the most common hemoglobinopathy in the US (about 8% of African Americans); the disease (HbSS) shortens life (median survival into the 40s). Vaso-occlusive crises: pain (sickling in bone), acute chest syndrome, stroke, priapism, and autosplenectomy, which leaves infection (pneumococcus, Salmonella osteomyelitis) and sepsis. Triggers: low O2, dehydration, acidosis, cold, fever, infection, stress. Radiographs: a stepladder trabecular pattern and a "hair-on-end" skull. In the chair: short morning visits, good pain control, stay well oxygenated, treat infection promptly. Treatment: transfusion, red cell exchange and hydroxyurea, which raises HbF. Carriers of sickle trait or thalassemia get milder malaria.
  • HbC (lysine for glutamic acid at β6) forms crystals and target cells: mild hemolytic anemia and splenomegaly, no pain crises, usually no treatment. HbSC disease is milder than HbSS: mild hemolysis, fewer and less painful crises, a modestly shorter life, and hip pain from aseptic necrosis of the femoral head; the smear shows target and sickle cells.
  • α-thalassemia (gene deletions; the α gene is doubled, so there are four): one gone, a silent carrier with normal labs; two, trait (mild microcytic anemia); three, HbH disease (β4 tetramers that precipitate: moderate hemolysis; more common in Southeast Asians); four, Hb Barts (γ4), whose O2 affinity is so high it can't unload O2, so the fetus dies of hydrops fetalis.
  • β-thalassemia (point mutations that make the β-chain mRNA unstable: less β chain, β+, or none, β0; Mediterranean ancestry): the unpaired α chains precipitate and destroy red cells in the marrow and the blood. Minor (one abnormal gene): mild microcytic anemia with a high HbA2. Major (both genes abnormal): shows up in early childhood, after about 6 months, with severe transfusion-dependent anemia and high HbA2 and HbF; it expands the marrow (maxillary overgrowth, "chipmunk" face, hair-on-end skull) and leads to iron overload.
  • Thalassemias and iron deficiency are both microcytic and hypochromic.

Anemias and the hematopoietic drugs

  • Iron deficiency, the most common anemia (blood loss from heavy periods, ulcers, gastritis or NSAIDs; pregnancy): microcytic and hypochromic. Low ferritin (storage iron) is the most sensitive test, with low serum iron and transferrin saturation; ferritin rises with inflammation. Pallor, a sore smooth tongue (atrophic glossitis), angular cheilitis, pica and ice craving, spoon nails. Oral iron, 150–200 mg of elemental iron a day in 2–3 doses: ferrous sulfate is the cheap, common one (GI upset, constipation, dark stools; liquid iron can stain teeth; antacids, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones bind it). IV iron is for when oral iron fails (iron dextran carries the most anaphylaxis and needs a test dose; iron sucrose is used in dialysis), not during an active infection. Iron overload (transfusions, poisoning) is treated with deferoxamine, which binds iron.
  • B12 and folate deficiency: both macrocytic and megaloblastic. B12 absorption needs stomach acid (to free it from food), intrinsic factor from the parietal cells and the terminal ileum. B12 lack comes from pernicious anemia, stomach or ileal disease or surgery, celiac disease, a vegan diet, alcohol use and drugs: proton pump inhibitors and H2 blockers (less acid), metformin, long-term antibiotics and nitrous oxide, which inactivates B12. It also raises methylmalonic acid and damages nerves (numbness, tingling, memory loss, psychosis), for good if not treated early; folic acid alone fixes the blood but not the nerves. Cyanocobalamin is given by injection (when there are nerve symptoms), by mouth or by nasal spray. Folate lack (alcohol use, pregnancy, a poor diet, methotrexate) raises homocysteine only; folic acid 1 mg a day for about 4 months fixes it (the hematocrit rises within 2 weeks), and folic acid lowers phenytoin levels. Folic acid before and early in pregnancy prevents neural tube defects (spina bifida, anencephaly).
  • Epoetin alfa, darbepoetin (longer-acting, more glycosylated): red cells, for the anemia of chronic kidney disease (the renal cortex makes about 85% of erythropoietin), chemotherapy and zidovudine in HIV; risks: hypertension (very common), clots and stroke, flu-like symptoms. Filgrastim (G-CSF) drives neutrophils and sargramostim (GM-CSF) several white cell lines, for neutropenia after chemotherapy or a bone marrow transplant; bone pain. Platelets: romiplostim (under the skin) and eltrombopag (by mouth), thrombopoietin receptor agonists for chronic ITP that steroids, IV immunoglobulin or splenectomy didn't fix, and oprelvekin (interleukin-11) to prevent low platelets during chemotherapy.
  • Polycythemia at altitude or in chronic hypoxia comes from more erythropoietin.
full.cr-resp:
What's tested
  • Thoracic and airway anatomy (landmarks, pleura, the intercostal bundle, phrenic nerve) and airway histology
  • Lung volumes and capacities, and which ones spirometry can't measure
  • Mechanics: pleural pressure, compliance, surfactant and Laplace's law, airway resistance
  • Ventilation and gas exchange: dead space, alveolar ventilation and PaCO2, the diffusion barrier, V/Q and shunt
  • O2 and CO2 transport and the oxyhemoglobin curve
  • Control of breathing
  • Obstructive versus restrictive disease, and the main lung diseases and infections
  • Asthma, COPD, antibiotic and allergy drugs, with their dental effects

Anatomy

  • The sternal angle (T4–T5 level) marks the second rib, the tracheal bifurcation and the start and end of the aortic arch. The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so aspirated objects (a dropped crown) usually go right.
  • The intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the costal groove under each rib, between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles, so a chest needle goes over the top of a rib.
  • The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) gives the diaphragm, the main muscle of quiet breathing, its motor and sensory supply, and senses the mediastinal pleura and pericardium. With one phrenic nerve paralyzed, that half of the diaphragm rises on inspiration instead of falling. The IVC passes the diaphragm at T8, the esophagus at T10 and the aorta at T12.
  • Pleura: visceral pleura covers the lung and has only visceral (autonomic) afferents, so it isn't sensitive to sharp pain. Parietal pleura lines the chest wall and is somatic, so pleuritis gives sharp pain with each breath: the intercostal nerves supply its costal part (pain felt over the chest wall), and the phrenic nerve its mediastinal and central diaphragmatic parts (pain referred to the C3–C5 dermatomes, the side of the neck and above the clavicle). In an upright patient, fluid collects in the costodiaphragmatic recess, which the lung enters only in deep inspiration. Air in the space is a pneumothorax; fluid is an effusion (drained by thoracentesis); lymph is a chylothorax.
  • Lungs: the right lung has three lobes (an oblique and a horizontal fissure) and three lobar bronchi; the left has two lobes (an oblique fissure only), two lobar bronchi and the lingula. Each segmental (tertiary) bronchus serves a bronchopulmonary segment, about 10 a lung, the smallest part that can be removed on its own. The bronchial arteries (from the aorta, about 1% of cardiac output) feed the conducting airways, the lung's supporting tissue and the visceral pleura, not the alveoli; part of their blood drains into the pulmonary veins, a small normal shunt.
  • Breathing muscles: the diaphragm does most of quiet inspiration, helped by the external intercostals, which raise the ribs (pump-handle movement widens the chest front to back, bucket-handle movement side to side); the scalenes and sternocleidomastoids join in forced inspiration. Forced expiration uses the abdominal muscles and the internal intercostals. The intercostal nerves are T1–T11 (the subcostal nerve is T12); the T4 dermatome is at the nipple and T10 at the umbilicus (T2 at the sternal angle).

Histology

The conducting zone (nose to terminal bronchioles, airway generations 0–16, about 150 mL) warms, filters and moistens air but doesn't exchange gas; it is the anatomic dead space. The respiratory zone (generations 17–23: respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs and alveoli) starts where alveoli first open off the respiratory bronchioles. Each branching adds total cross-sectional area, giving about 70 m² of exchange surface.

Most of the conducting airways, from the nasal cavity through the bronchi, are lined by respiratory epithelium, a ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium of ciliated cells (the most numerous), mucus-making goblet cells and basal cells (the stem cells). The trachea is held open by C-shaped rings of hyaline cartilage, closed behind by the trachealis smooth muscle. Cartilage is gone by the bronchioles; the terminal bronchioles have a simple cuboidal lining with no cartilage or goblet cells, and their club (Clara) cells secrete defensive proteins, break down mucus and detoxify. Goblet cells and submucosal glands make the mucus, and the cilia sweep it up to the pharynx: the mucociliary escalator, which smoking paralyzes. Particles over about 10 µm stop in the nose, 2–10 µm ride the escalator, and under 2 µm reach the alveoli, where alveolar macrophages (dust cells) engulf them.

The alveoli are lined by simple squamous epithelium. Type I pneumocytes cover about 95% of the alveolar surface for gas exchange; type II pneumocytes are cuboidal, cover about 5%, store surfactant in lamellar bodies and replace type I cells. The very thin blood–air barrier is a type I cell, the fused basal laminae and a capillary endothelial cell.

Volumes and capacities

MeasureMade ofAbout
Tidal volume (TV)One quiet breath500 mL
Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV)Extra breath in above TV3 L
Expiratory reserve volume (ERV)Extra breath out below TV1.2 L
Residual volume (RV)Left after a full exhale1.2 L
Inspiratory capacityTV + IRV3.5 L
Functional residual capacity (FRC)ERV + RV; the resting volume2.4 L
Vital capacity (VC)IRV + TV + ERV4.6–4.8 L
Total lung capacity (TLC)VC + RV6 L

Spirometry can't measure RV, FRC or TLC, because RV never leaves the lung; they need helium dilution, nitrogen washout or body plethysmography. Helium dilution counts only the gas that reaches the airways; body plethysmography (Boyle's law) counts all of it, so in obstructive disease, with air trapped behind closed airways, plethysmography gives the larger FRC. Then RV = TLC − VC, or FRC − ERV.

Forced vital capacity (FVC) is all the air breathed out as hard and fast as possible from TLC, normally within 3 seconds; FEV1 is the part out in the first second, normally 70–85% of FVC (FEV1/FVC above 0.7). Volumes are read as a percentage of predicted: a TLC below 80% of predicted points to restrictive disease, and above 120% to obstructive disease with air trapping.

Mechanics

  • At FRC the lung recoils inward and the chest wall springs outward; the pleural pressure between them is about −5 cm H2O, and alveolar pressure equals atmospheric (0), so no air moves. On inspiration the diaphragm contracts, pleural pressure becomes more negative, transpulmonary pressure (alveolar minus pleural) rises, alveolar pressure dips below 0 and air flows in until it is back to 0 at the end of the breath. Quiet expiration is passive: elastic recoil makes alveolar pressure positive. Forced expiration uses the abdominal muscles and internal intercostals and makes pleural pressure positive. If air enters the pleural space (pneumothorax), pleural pressure goes to 0: the lung collapses and the chest wall springs out.
  • Compliance (change in volume ÷ change in pressure) runs opposite to elastic recoil: it is high in emphysema (lost elastic fibers) and old age, and low in fibrosis, edema and surfactant lack.
  • Surfactant (mostly DPPC, from type II cells) lowers surface tension. It raises compliance, keeps alveoli of different sizes stable and keeps the alveoli dry. By Laplace's law (P = 2T/r), small alveoli would empty into large ones without it; as an alveolus shrinks, its surfactant concentrates and surface tension falls further. Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome: type II cells mature at about 35 weeks, so babies born before then lack surfactant; alveoli collapse (atelectasis), compliance falls and the baby turns cyanotic. Treatment is surfactant and ventilation until the lungs mature; steroids given to the mother before a preterm birth speed maturity.
  • Airway resistance follows Poiseuille's law: it rises with airway length and gas viscosity and falls with the fourth power of the radius. It is highest in the larger airways, the first seven or so generations (medium-sized bronchi most); the small airways are so many, in parallel, that their total resistance is low. Radial traction from the alveolar walls holds airways open at high lung volumes (lost in emphysema), so resistance falls as volume rises. The vagus releases acetylcholine onto M3 receptors (bronchoconstriction, more secretions); sympathetic beta-2 stimulation dilates the bronchi. Sympathetic signals also constrict pulmonary vessels, and parasympathetic ones dilate them.
  • Dynamic compression: in a forced expiration, positive pleural pressure squeezes the airways. Normally the pressure inside them, kept up by the lung's recoil, holds them open, and cartilage props the large ones. In emphysema, lost recoil leaves the airway pressure too low, the pressure across the larger airways reverses and they collapse, trapping air; pursed-lip breathing raises airway pressure and keeps them open. The work of breathing (about 5% of resting energy use) rises in fibrosis from extra elastic work and in COPD from extra resistive work.

Ventilation and gas exchange

  • Minute ventilation = tidal volume × rate (a normal rate is 12–20 a minute). Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − physiologic dead space) × rate. Physiologic dead space = anatomic (about 150 mL) + alveolar dead space (ventilated but poorly perfused alveoli, about 20–50 mL), about 175 mL in a healthy adult. By the alveolar ventilation equation (alveolar ventilation = CO2 production × 863 ÷ PACO2), PaCO2 varies inversely with alveolar ventilation: double the ventilation, halve the PaCO2; halve it, and PaCO2 doubles. If CO2 production doubles (exercise), alveolar ventilation must double to hold PaCO2 at 40 mmHg.
  • The alveolar gas equation gives alveolar PO2: PAO2 = FiO2 × (760 − 47) − PACO2 ÷ 0.8, or 0.21 × 713 − 40 ÷ 0.8 ≈ 150 − 50 = 100 mmHg at sea level (47 mmHg is water vapor; 0.8 is the respiratory quotient, CO2 made ÷ O2 used). So hypoventilation lowers PAO2 as PACO2 rises. Humidified inspired air has a PO2 of about 145–150 mmHg and a PCO2 of about 0. Mixed venous blood arrives at a PO2 of 40 and a PCO2 of 45 mmHg and leaves the capillary at 100 and 40, the same as alveolar gas, having come to balance in the first third of the capillary.
  • O2 crosses the fluid and surfactant lining, the type I epithelium, the fused basement membrane, the capillary endothelium, the plasma and the red cell membrane. By Fick's law (rate = pressure difference × area × diffusion coefficient ÷ thickness), diffusion falls with less area (emphysema) or a thicker barrier (fibrosis, edema); both lower DLCO. CO2 is more than 20 times as soluble as O2, so it diffuses about 20 times faster. A red cell spends about 0.75 s in the capillary at rest; in hard exercise this falls below 0.4 s, and blood can leave before it is fully loaded (diffusion-limited).
  • V/Q: for the whole lung, about 4 L/min of alveolar ventilation over 5 L/min of blood gives a V/Q of about 0.8. In an upright lung the apex alveoli are already stretched (pleural pressure is more negative there) and expand little, while the base alveoli start small and ventilate best; perfusion rises toward the base even faster. So ventilation and perfusion are both greatest at the base, but perfusion more so: V/Q is lowest at the base and highest at the apex. V/Q of zero is a shunt (blocked airway: atelectasis, pneumonia, a mucus plug): alveolar gas comes to the mixed venous values (PO2 40, PCO2 45), and the hypoxemia barely responds to 100% O2. An anatomic shunt (a septal defect, an artery-to-vein connection) bypasses the alveoli altogether. V/Q near infinity is dead space (pulmonary embolism): alveolar gas stays at inspired values (PO2 about 150, PCO2 0). Low alveolar O2 constricts pulmonary arterioles (hypoxic vasoconstriction), matching blood to air.
  • Pulmonary blood flow runs at low pressure (a mean of about 16 mmHg) through very compliant vessels. Gravity makes three zones: zone 1 (alveolar pressure > arterial > venous) has no flow; it is normally absent but appears at the apex with hemorrhage, low blood pressure or positive-pressure ventilation (alveolar dead space). Zone 2 (arterial > alveolar > venous) has flow set by arterial minus alveolar pressure. Zone 3, at the base (arterial > venous > alveolar), has the most flow. Pulmonary vascular resistance is lowest near FRC, in quiet breathing: at low volumes the extra-alveolar vessels are squeezed, and near TLC the alveolar capillaries are stretched thin.

Gas transport

Blood carries about 20 mL O2 per dL (about 1.34–1.39 mL per gram of hemoglobin × 15 g/dL), about 98% bound to hemoglobin and only about 0.3 mL/dL dissolved, so hemoglobin raises O2 content more than anything else. Each of hemoglobin's four hemes holds O2 on ferrous (Fe2+) iron, and each O2 bound raises the affinity of the rest, so the curve is sigmoid: flat above about 60 mmHg (saturation stays about 90–100% from 100 down to 60 mmHg) and steep below it, where the tissues unload. Mixed venous blood (PO2 40) is about 75% saturated. Right shift (less affinity, more unloading): more CO2, acid, 2,3-BPG (also called 2,3-DPG; it binds deoxyhemoglobin), exercise and heat. Left shift: carbon monoxide, fetal hemoglobin (two gamma chains, which bind 2,3-BPG weakly), alkalosis, cold, less 2,3-BPG. Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin about 200–250 times more tightly than O2, lowering content with a normal PaO2 and a falsely normal pulse oximeter, and shifts the curve left; treat with 100% O2.

CO2 is far more soluble than O2 and travels about 60% as bicarbonate, 30% as carbamino compounds (on hemoglobin's amine groups) and 10% dissolved (other texts put bicarbonate as high as 70–90%; it is always the main form). In the red cell, carbonic anhydrase turns CO2 and water into carbonic acid, which splits into H+ and bicarbonate; bicarbonate leaves in exchange for chloride (the chloride shift), and hemoglobin buffers the H+, which also helps it unload O2. In the lung all of this runs backward. A rise in PaCO2 lowers pH (respiratory acidosis: hypoventilation, V/Q mismatch, a thickened barrier); a fall raises it (respiratory alkalosis: hyperventilation from anxiety, high altitude). At altitude, low PO2 drives faster breathing, more 2,3-BPG and, over weeks, more red cells (polycythemia).

Control of breathing

  • Medulla: its two groups set the rhythm together. The dorsal respiratory group drives inspiration (the diaphragm) and takes in sensory signals about PaCO2 and PaO2; the ventral respiratory group runs the accessory muscles of forced inspiration and expiration and the upper-airway dilators, and is nearly quiet in quiet breathing. Pons: the pneumotaxic center limits inspiration and so helps set the rate, and standard texts have the apneustic center prolong inspiration; their roles in normal breathing aren't well established. The cerebral cortex can override the brainstem (breath holding, voluntary hyperventilation).
  • Central chemoreceptors in the medulla, behind the blood–brain barrier, control breathing at rest. CO2 crosses the barrier but H+ and bicarbonate don't; in the CSF, CO2 forms H+, and the CSF has little protein to buffer it, so a small rise in PaCO2 drives breathing hard. CO2 is the main minute-to-minute drive: ventilation rises in a straight line as PaCO2 rises above its resting 40 mmHg, and falls when PaCO2 drops below 40. In chronic CO2 retention (severe COPD), the choroid plexus secretes bicarbonate into the CSF, its pH returns toward normal, and the center resets to the higher PaCO2. Peripheral chemoreceptors (type I glomus cells of the carotid bodies, signaling by CN IX, and of the aortic bodies, by the vagus) sense PaO2, PaCO2 and pH. A fall in PaO2 from 100 to 60 mmHg changes breathing little, because the CO2 drive dominates; below about 60 mmHg they drive breathing hard. Chronic CO2 retainers depend more on this hypoxic drive.
  • Lung receptors, carried mostly in the vagus: stretch receptors in airway smooth muscle (at a large tidal volume, the Hering–Breuer reflex ends inspiration and lengthens the breath out), irritant receptors in the large airways and C fibers in the alveolar walls (smoke, dust, pollen, ammonia, cold air: cough, bronchoconstriction, mucus) and J receptors by the alveolar capillaries (congestion, edema, injury: bronchoconstriction and rapid shallow breathing).
  • Exercise: ventilation rises with O2 demand (up to about 15 times in trained athletes), yet mean arterial PO2 and PCO2 stay about normal; strenuous exercise can lower pH with lactic acid. Joint and muscle receptors raise breathing early, and the oxyhemoglobin curve shifts right to unload more O2.

Obstructive versus restrictive disease

FeatureObstructiveRestrictive
FEV1/FVCLow (under 0.7)Normal or high
TLC, RVHigh (air trapping)Low
ComplianceHigh in emphysemaLow
ExamplesAsthma, chronic bronchitis, emphysema, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosisFibrosis, sarcoidosis, asbestosis and other pneumoconioses, obesity, neuromuscular disease
  • Asthma: chronic airway inflammation, a type I hypersensitivity (IgE, mast cells, eosinophils), with bronchospasm, mucus and overreactive airways; obstruction that reverses with a bronchodilator, the key difference from COPD; Curschmann spirals and Charcot–Leyden crystals. Triggers: allergens, cold air, exercise, respiratory infections, and aspirin and NSAIDs: in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (Samter's triad: asthma, nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity) they can set off severe bronchospasm, so acetaminophen is the analgesic to use. Status asthmaticus is an attack that won't respond to usual treatment.
  • Chronic bronchitis (the "blue bloater"): a productive cough for 3 months in each of 2 years in a row; mucous gland hyperplasia (Reid index above 0.4). Emphysema (the "pink puffer"): permanent enlargement of the airspaces past the terminal bronchioles, with lost alveolar walls and elastic recoil, barrel chest, pursed lips, low DLCO; centriacinar from smoking (upper lobes), panacinar from alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (lower lobes). Alpha-1 antitrypsin normally blocks neutrophil elastase; its lack is the most common genetic cause of emphysema under 45, and the same protein builds up in the liver (hepatitis, cirrhosis), so emphysema with liver disease in a nonsmoker suggests it.
  • Bronchiectasis: permanently dilated bronchi from repeated infection and inflammation, with copious purulent sputum; cystic fibrosis is the main cause in young people (others: after TB or pertussis, immunodeficiency, Kartagener syndrome). Cystic fibrosis (CFTR on chromosome 7, faulty chloride transport): thick secretions, Pseudomonas and S. aureus lung infections, pancreatic insufficiency, male infertility and a high sweat chloride; its altered saliva brings a high caries risk.
  • Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: progressive, irreversible scarring with honeycombing on CT and bibasilar "Velcro" crackles; median survival 2–3 years untreated. Pneumoconioses: coal dust (anthracosis, a black lung); silica, the most common occupational lung disease worldwide (eggshell calcification on the chest film, a higher TB risk); asbestos (fibrosis with ferruginous bodies, and a higher risk of mesothelioma and lung carcinoma, multiplied by smoking). Connective tissue diseases (Sjögren syndrome, scleroderma, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus) can scar the lung too, and their drugs (methotrexate, azathioprine, mycophenolate) raise infection risk.
  • Sarcoidosis: noncaseating granulomas in many organs (lungs and hilar nodes, eyes, skin, liver, CNS), most often in young adults and African American women; high serum ACE, hypercalcemia (granuloma macrophages activate vitamin D) and high lysozyme; systemic steroids when an organ is threatened. In the mouth: parotid enlargement (consider it with unexplained swelling of both parotids), gingival enlargement, mucosal nodules and radiolucent jaw lesions. Heerfordt syndrome = parotid enlargement + uveitis + facial nerve palsy. Uveitis in a young adult calls for a chest film and an ACE level.
  • Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA): a vasculitis of small and medium vessels in the upper airway, lungs and kidneys. "Strawberry" gingivitis (red, granular, friable gingival overgrowth) + sinusitis + kidney disease = GPA: biopsy and refer rather than treating it as periodontitis, because the kidneys can fail within weeks. Its treatment (rituximab or cyclophosphamide with steroids) leaves the patient immunosuppressed.
  • Lung cancer: adenocarcinoma is the most common, usually peripheral, and the type seen in nonsmokers and women (EGFR mutations, which drugs can target); squamous cell is central, in heavy smokers, with keratin pearls and hypercalcemia; small cell is central, in smokers, fast-growing and neuroendocrine, with paraneoplastic syndromes (SIADH, ectopic ACTH, Lambert–Eaton weakness). Asbestos causes mesothelioma of the pleura 20–40 years after exposure. A Pancoast tumor at the apex invades the sympathetic chain: new Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) in a smoker needs chest imaging. The cancer itself rarely shows in the mouth; its treatment does (radiation: xerostomia, mucositis, radiation caries, osteoradionecrosis; chemotherapy: mucositis, bleeding and infection risk; EGFR inhibitors: aphthous-like ulcers).
  • Tuberculosis: acid-fast, lives in macrophage phagosomes, caseating granulomas; the Ghon complex is the primary subpleural lesion plus its calcified hilar node. Reactivation goes to the apex, where O2 tension is highest, and causes most clinical disease. Active TB (a productive cough over 3 weeks, sometimes bloody, with fever and night sweats) spreads by airborne droplets: elective dental care waits, and urgent care uses airborne precautions with N95 respirators.

Infections

Community-acquired pneumonia: S. pneumoniae most often; Mycoplasma for "walking" pneumonia in young adults (no cell wall); Legionella from water systems, with low sodium; Pneumocystis in HIV with a CD4 count below 200; S. aureus after influenza; oral anaerobes in aspiration (right lower lobe). Epiglottitis in an unvaccinated child: H. influenzae type b. Bronchiolitis in infants: RSV. Patterns: lobar consolidation (S. pneumoniae), patchy bronchopneumonia (S. aureus, Klebsiella, H. influenzae) and interstitial "walking" pneumonia (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila, viruses). Hospital-acquired pneumonia (more than 48 hours after admission) and ventilator pneumonia need drugs for MRSA (vancomycin) and Pseudomonas (piperacillin–tazobactam or levofloxacin). Most sinusitis is viral. Otitis media (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae) and bacterial sinusitis: amoxicillin or amoxicillin–clavulanate, with clarithromycin or azithromycin for penicillin allergy. Acute bronchitis: azithromycin, clarithromycin or TMP-SMX.

Influenza drugs help only when started within 48 hours of symptoms (or in severe illness or a patient at high risk). Neuraminidase inhibitors, which keep new virus from leaving infected cells: oseltamivir (oral, 5 days), zanamivir (inhaled; can cause bronchospasm, so not for asthma or COPD) and peramivir. The M2 channel blockers amantadine and rimantadine work on influenza A only (B has no M2), cause CNS effects, and resistance is now common. Baloxavir blocks the viral polymerase in a single oral dose.

Drugs and the dental chair

  • Asthma and COPD: albuterol (short-acting beta-2 agonist; tremor and a fast heart rate) for attacks and the emergency kit; inhaled steroids as the main asthma controller, which cause oral candidiasis (white plaques on the palate or oropharynx) and hoarseness (use a spacer, rinse and spit); salmeterol and formoterol never alone in asthma; ipratropium and tiotropium (antimuscarinics, the mainstay for COPD), which, like the long-acting beta-2 agonists, dry the mouth and raise caries risk; montelukast (blocks leukotrienes); theophylline, with a narrow window (erythromycin and fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin raise it); omalizumab (anti-IgE). High-dose or systemic steroids also bring cataracts, glaucoma, delayed healing and bone loss, and a recent prednisone burst can suppress the adrenals.
  • In the chair: ask how often the rescue inhaler is used, what sets off attacks and about hospital stays, and have the inhaler at hand for every visit. COPD: seat the patient semi-reclined (lying flat worsens breathlessness), ask about home oxygen and how far they can walk, and avoid nitrous oxide (it collects in the dead space, and the added oxygen can blunt the drive to breathe); nitrous oxide may be used in well-controlled asthma. COPD and chronic hypoxia go with more periodontal disease and blue lips and nails. Postpone elective care during an acute respiratory infection. Maxillary sinusitis can mimic tooth pain, and chronic sinusitis can be odontogenic even without caries: pulp tests and a CBCT tell them apart.
  • Antibiotics: β-lactams cover the typical organisms; macrolides, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones the atypical ones. Tetracyclines and doxycycline (protein synthesis, bacteriostatic) stain developing teeth (avoid in pregnancy and under age 8), are chelated by calcium, aluminum and magnesium, and can harm the vestibular system and liver. Respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin; DNA gyrase) carry boxed warnings for tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy and CNS effects such as seizures, so they are a last resort; they also lengthen the QT, are avoided in children (cartilage) and in myasthenia gravis. Macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) lengthen the QT, and erythromycin and clarithromycin inhibit CYP3A4. Vancomycin covers MRSA. TB: rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin for at least 4 more; rifampin turns secretions orange and, as a CYP inducer, weakens warfarin and oral contraceptives; isoniazid causes hepatitis and neuropathy; ethambutol causes optic neuritis (lost acuity, red-green color vision).
  • Allergy drugs: histamine acts at H1 (itch, vasodilation and leaky vessels, bronchoconstriction, gut contraction) and H2 (stomach acid). First-generation H1 blockers (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine, promethazine) cross the blood–brain barrier and also block muscarinic and alpha receptors: sedation (a caution for driving), dry mouth and orthostatic hypotension; they also treat motion sickness, nausea and insomnia. Second-generation ones (cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine) are less fat-soluble, pumped out of the brain by P-glycoprotein and more selective, so they barely sedate; they treat allergic rhinitis and hives. Topical ones (olopatadine, azelastine, ketotifen) go in the eye or nose. Cromolyn keeps mast cells from releasing histamine. H2 blockers (famotidine; cimetidine also inhibits CYP enzymes) lower stomach acid. Anaphylaxis (most often from penicillins, aspirin and NSAIDs, or insulin): stop the drug, lay the patient flat with the legs raised, call for help and give epinephrine 0.3 mg IM (1 mg/mL, the 1:1000 strength) at once. Epinephrine opposes histamine through alpha-1 (vasoconstriction), beta-1 (heart rate and force) and beta-2 (bronchodilation) receptors, and can't be given by mouth (gut MAO destroys it). Antihistamines (diphenhydramine 25–50 mg) and oxygen only help afterward, with itching and hives.
full.rn-filtration:
What's tested
  • The kidney's jobs, where it sits, and the paths of blood and urine through it
  • The nephron's parts, the glomerular filtration barrier and the juxtaglomerular apparatus
  • Bladder innervation and the micturition reflex
  • Renal blood flow, renal plasma flow, GFR and filtration fraction; Starling forces; what afferent and efferent resistance do; autoregulation
  • Clearance: the formula, inulin, creatinine and PAH, and what a clearance ratio says
  • Body fluid compartments, their ions, plasma osmolarity, fluid shifts and IV fluids

What the kidneys do

  • Excrete metabolic wastes (urea, creatinine, uric acid, hormone metabolites) and foreign substances such as drugs.
  • Regulate water and electrolytes, ECF volume, plasma osmolarity (with ADH), blood pressure (renin and angiotensin II) and acid-base balance (pH about 7.35–7.45).
  • Make hormones: erythropoietin from interstitial cells of the cortex when local O2 falls; renin from juxtaglomerular cells; and active vitamin D. Cholecalciferol (from skin exposed to UV light, or the diet) is 25-hydroxylated in the liver; the kidney then makes either the inactive 24,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol or, by 1α-hydroxylase in the proximal tubule, the active 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol). Low plasma Ca2+, high PTH and low phosphate turn 1α-hydroxylase on (FGF23 turns it down).
  • Metabolism: gluconeogenesis in the cortex during fasting (about 10%; most is the liver's) and ammoniagenesis from glutamine in the proximal tubule, which buffers urinary H+ and makes new HCO3−.

The four processes: filtration (glomerular capillaries into Bowman space), reabsorption (tubular fluid back to the peritubular blood), secretion (peritubular blood into the tubular fluid) and excretion (what leaves as urine). Key relationship: filtered − reabsorbed + secreted = excreted.

Anatomy

  • Paired retroperitoneal organs at about T12–L3; the right kidney sits lower because of the liver. An adrenal gland caps each upper pole.
  • Relations: right kidney – liver, duodenum, IVC; left kidney – spleen, stomach, pancreas. Posteriorly the subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves cross the posterior abdominal wall, a concern in a posterior surgical approach.
  • Blood path: renal artery → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular (cortical radiate) → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries (and vasa recta for juxtamedullary nephrons) → renal vein.
  • Urine path: collecting duct → renal papilla (tip of a pyramid) → minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter → bladder → urethra.
  • Nephron (the functional unit): renal corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman capsule) → proximal tubule → loop of Henle (thin descending, thin ascending, thick ascending) → distal convoluted tubule → collecting duct. Several nephrons drain into each collecting duct. Most nephrons (80–90%) are cortical, with short loops that stay in the outer medulla; juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops that reach the inner medulla, with vasa recta, and build the concentrating gradient.

The filtration barrier and the JG apparatus

  • Three layers, all negatively charged: fenestrated endothelium (large fenestrae, many aquaporin-1 channels), the glomerular basement membrane and podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms. Proteins of about 70 kDa and up, such as albumin and hemoglobin, are held back by size, and negatively charged ones by charge too; the few grams that leak each day are taken up by endocytosis in the proximal tubule.
  • Mesangial cells sit inside the glomerulus, support the capillary loops and can contract.
  • Juxtaglomerular apparatus: the macula densa (tubule cells where the thick ascending limb meets the distal convoluted tubule, touching its own glomerulus) senses NaCl (mainly the Cl− entering through NKCC2) and releases adenosine; JG (granular) cells in the afferent arteriole wall secrete renin; extraglomerular mesangial cells lie between them.

Bladder and micturition

  • Ureters and bladder are lined by urothelium (transitional epithelium), impermeable to water and NaCl, which flattens as the bladder fills. The trigone lies between the two ureteric openings and the urethral opening. The detrusor is the bladder's smooth muscle.
  • The internal sphincter is involuntary (autonomic); the external sphincter is voluntary (somatic).
  • Sympathetic: relaxes the detrusor and contracts the internal sphincter – storage.
  • Parasympathetic (S2–S4): contracts the detrusor through muscarinic receptors and relaxes the internal sphincter – voiding.
  • Somatic (pudendal nerve, S2–S4): keeps the external sphincter closed voluntarily; voiding starts when this drive is inhibited.
  • Micturition reflex, a spinal reflex: at roughly 300 mL (the bladder holds about 500–600 mL), stretch receptors signal the sacral cord and the detrusor starts to contract. The pontine micturition center (PMC) decides: if voiding is inconvenient, it suppresses the reflex; if voiding is allowed, the pudendal nerve is inhibited (the external sphincter relaxes) and parasympathetic output contracts the detrusor and relaxes the internal sphincter.

Blood flow and filtration

  • The kidneys get 20–25% of cardiac output (about 1–1.2 L of blood a minute; all the blood passes through them every 4–5 minutes). Renal plasma flow is about 600–650 mL/min.
  • GFR is about 100–125 mL/min (normal range about 97–140). The course's GFR lecture rounds it to 100 mL/min, or 144 L/day; its introduction uses 180 L/day, of which about 178 L is reabsorbed and about 2 L becomes urine.
  • Filtration fraction = GFR / RPF, normally about 20%.
  • Starling forces: GFR = Kf × [(PGC − PBS) − πGC]. Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (PGC, about 45 mmHg) pushes fluid out; Bowman space hydrostatic pressure (PBS, about 10 mmHg) and glomerular capillary oncotic pressure (πGC) oppose it; Bowman space oncotic pressure is about zero. The class example: (45 − 10) − 19 = 16 mmHg net.
  • Why GFR is so high: the glomerular filtration coefficient (Kf), water permeability times surface area, is about 100 times that of systemic capillaries (a large surface, fenestrae, aquaporin-1 in the endothelium), and PGC stays about 45 mmHg along the whole capillary because the efferent arteriole sits downstream.
  • Oncotic pressure rises along the capillary (from about 19 to about 35 mmHg) as protein-free fluid leaves, until it matches the net hydrostatic pressure (45 − 10 = 35 mmHg) and net pressure reaches zero (filtration equilibrium). A higher renal plasma flow makes it rise more slowly, so filtration goes on along more of the capillary and GFR rises; a lower flow does the opposite. The protein-rich blood leaving in the efferent arteriole gives the peritubular capillaries a high oncotic pressure, the main force for proximal reabsorption.

Efferent arteriole constricts (angiotensin II)↓↑ (moderate)Pressure builds up in the glomerulus; filtration fraction rises

  • Regulators: sympathetic nerves constrict both arterioles and lower RBF and GFR; angiotensin II constricts the efferent more and holds GFR up when perfusion falls; prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) dilate the arterioles and protect flow in hemorrhage or heart failure (NSAIDs remove this protection); low-dose dopamine dilates.
  • Autoregulation keeps RBF and GFR nearly constant from about 80 to 200 mmHg (below about 80 they fall steeply) by adjusting afferent and efferent tone, through two mechanisms: the myogenic response of the afferent arteriole and tubuloglomerular feedback – more NaCl at the macula densa → adenosine → afferent constriction → GFR back down. Sustained changes in NaCl delivery also change renin release. Caffeine blocks the adenosine (A1) receptors: the afferent arteriole stays open and tubular Na+ reabsorption falls, so urine flow and Na+ excretion rise.

Clearance

  • C = (U × V) / P: the volume of plasma cleared of a substance per minute (U, urine concentration; V, urine flow; P, plasma concentration).
  • Inulin: freely filtered, neither reabsorbed nor secreted, so its clearance equals GFR (the gold standard).
  • Creatinine: made from creatine phosphate by muscle at a steady rate and freely filtered, with a little secretion, so its clearance slightly overestimates GFR; it's the clinical marker (eGFR also uses cystatin C). Plasma creatinine varies inversely with GFR: if GFR halves, plasma creatinine doubles at steady state. Normal plasma creatinine is about 0.6–1.2 mg/dL in men and 0.5–1.1 mg/dL in women.
  • Its limits: production depends on muscle mass, so age and sex change what is normal. Creatine supplements and a high-meat diet raise plasma creatinine and make eGFR read low without kidney disease; a vegan diet lowers it. Inulin, the ideal marker, has to be infused.
  • PAH: filtered and secreted almost completely in one pass (renal vein PAH ≈ 0), so its clearance, the highest of any substance, estimates renal plasma flow. Then RBF = RPF ÷ (1 − hematocrit): an RPF of 600 mL/min with a hematocrit of 0.40 gives an RBF of 1,000 mL/min.
  • Clearance ratio (Cx / Cinulin): = 1, filtered only; > 1, filtered and secreted (PAH, organic acids and bases); < 1, filtered and reabsorbed (Na+, Cl−, K+, urea) or not filtered. Two substances normally have a clearance of 0: albumin, which the filter holds back, and glucose, which is filtered and then all reabsorbed. The highest possible clearance equals renal plasma flow (PAH).

Body fluid compartments

  • 60–40–20: total body water is about 60% of body weight (50–70%: lower with more body fat, so lower in women and older adults, and higher in infants); ICF 40% (two-thirds of body water); ECF 20% (one-third). The course splits the ECF 80% interstitial fluid and 20% plasma (many references round it to 3/4 and 1/4). In a 70-kg man: TBW 42 L, ICF 28 L, ECF 14 L, interstitial fluid about 11 L, plasma about 3 L (2.8 L by the course's 20%, 3.5 L by a quarter).
  • 1 kg of water is 1 L, so a sudden change in weight is a change in body water: losing 2 kg overnight is losing about 2 L.
  • Plasma is 55% of blood volume (hematocrit about 45%; proteins are about 7% of plasma volume); interstitial fluid is an ultrafiltrate of plasma without its proteins and cells. The water inside red cells counts as ICF.
  • ECF ions: Na+ (main cation), Cl− and HCO3−. ICF ions: K+ and Mg2+, with proteins and organic phosphates (ATP, ADP) as the anions.
  • Plasma osmolarity ≈ 2[Na+] + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8; normal about 275–290 mOsm/kg. At steady state ICF and ECF osmolarity are equal; water moves until they match.

  • Darrow-Yannet diagrams draw these shifts as two boxes, ICF on the left and ECF on the right: width is volume, height is osmolarity; the solid line is the normal state and the dashed line the new one. Work them in three steps: what changed in the ECF; whether ECF osmolarity rose, fell or stayed the same; which way water then moves so that ICF and ECF osmolarity match. Volume contraction moves the ECF edge in, expansion moves it out; a line above normal is hyperosmotic, below it hypo-osmotic.
  • IV fluids: normal saline (0.9%, 154 mEq/L NaCl, about 308 mOsm/L) stays in the ECF, the best plasma volume expander (volume depletion, maintenance); half-normal saline (0.45%) is hypotonic: it lowers ECF osmolarity, so some water enters cells (used when ICF is depleted, as in diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemia); D5W becomes free water once the glucose is used, spreads over both compartments, expands them more than half-normal saline does, and treats hypernatremia from a water deficit. Plain water is never given IV: it would lyse red cells.
full.rn-tubule:
What's tested
  • Epithelial transport: apical and basolateral sides, transcellular and paracellular paths, cotransporters and exchangers
  • The proximal tubule: Na+-coupled reabsorption, HCO3− and Cl− handling, glucose and its transport maximum, water, glomerulotubular balance
  • The loop of Henle: what each limb does with water and NaCl, NKCC2, countercurrent multiplication, urea recycling and the vasa recta
  • The distal tubule and collecting duct: NCC, principal and intercalated cells, aldosterone and ADH
  • Which diuretic acts on which segment

Ground rules

  • The apical membrane faces the lumen; the basolateral membrane faces the interstitium and blood. Solutes cross transcellularly (through the cell) or paracellularly (between cells, through tight junctions).
  • A cotransporter (symporter) moves two solutes the same way (SGLT2, NKCC2, NCC); an exchanger (countertransporter) moves them opposite ways (Na+/H+ exchanger).
  • Everything is powered by the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase (3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in), which keeps cell Na+ low so Na+ flows in across the apical membrane and drags other solutes with it. The apical carriers use no ATP of their own: Na+ moving down its gradient carries the other solute up its gradient, which is secondary active transport.
  • To read any transport-cell drawing, find the apical (lumen) side first, then ask whether each solute is reabsorbed or secreted and whether it crosses through the cell or between cells.
