Proximal tubule

  • Reabsorbs about two-thirds of filtered Na+, Cl−, K+ and water, about 80–85% of HCO3−, most phosphate, and nearly all glucose and amino acids. Reabsorption is iso-osmotic: water follows solute through aquaporin-1 and between the cells. Its cells are built for bulk transport: a brush border of microvilli (up to 36 times the surface), basolateral infoldings packed with Na+-K+-ATPase, many mitochondria, endocytosis for filtered protein and leaky tight junctions.
  • Early proximal tubule: the apical Na+/H+ exchanger secretes H+, which reclaims filtered HCO3− with the help of carbonic anhydrase; HCO3− leaves basolaterally on a Na+-HCO3− cotransporter. Glucose enters with Na+ on SGLT2 and leaves on GLUT transporters; other apical Na+ cotransporters carry amino acids, phosphate, lactate and citrate. Bringing Na+ in without Cl− makes the early lumen slightly negative.
  • Along the proximal tubule (tubular fluid ÷ plasma concentration): Na+ stays at about 1, because water follows it, so osmolarity stays about 1 too; glucose, amino acids and HCO3− fall toward 0 as they are taken back; Cl− rises above 1, because HCO3− is reclaimed first.
  • Late proximal tubule: early on, Na+ went back with HCO3− and organic solutes rather than Cl−, and water followed, so Cl− is now concentrated in the lumen. It is reabsorbed with Na+ through apical Na+/H+ and Cl−/formate exchangers (Cl− leaves the cell through a basolateral Cl− channel) and paracellularly, down its gradient. The lumen here is positive, which also pushes Na+ between the cells.
  • Glucose transport maximum (Tm): there are only so many SGLT2 carriers, so reabsorption saturates. Below about 200 mg/dL of plasma glucose, all filtered glucose is reabsorbed. Above about 200 mg/dL (the threshold) some carriers are full and glucose starts to appear in the urine; at about 350 mg/dL every carrier is saturated and reabsorption levels off at Tm. The bend between the two is splay, which is why glucose spills before Tm is reached. What isn't reabsorbed is excreted – glycosuria with an osmotic diuresis.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors (the "-flozins": empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) block SGLT2 but not the gut's SGLT1, causing glycosuria on purpose to treat type 2 diabetes. On their own they don't cause hypoglycemia; they also lower weight and blood pressure and are used in heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction, with or without diabetes. Watch for genital yeast infections, UTIs (rarely Fournier's gangrene), volume loss and euglycemic ketoacidosis.
  • Glomerulotubular balance: when GFR rises, the proximal tubule reabsorbs more, keeping the fraction reabsorbed about constant (a higher filtration fraction raises peritubular oncotic pressure, which pulls more fluid back). ECF volume expansion works the other way: peritubular hydrostatic pressure rises and oncotic pressure falls (dilution), so the proximal tubule reabsorbs less and the extra NaCl and water are excreted; volume contraction raises proximal reabsorption.
  • The proximal tubule also secretes organic anions and cations: PAH, penicillin, uric acid, many drugs (probenecid competes with them).
  • Proximal diuretics: acetazolamide (oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor: the Na+/H+ exchanger has less H+ to secrete, so HCO3−, Na+ and water stay in the lumen; alkaline urine, mild hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, hyponatremia and calcium phosphate stones; used for altitude sickness, to alkalinize the urine and for glaucoma, where the eye drops dorzolamide and brinzolamide act the same way; no longer used for hypertension or heart failure) and mannitol (given IV; an osmotic agent filtered but not reabsorbed, holding water in the lumen; lowers intracranial and intraocular pressure and flushes nephrons blocked by hemoglobin or myoglobin; can cause dehydration and hypernatremia).

Loop of Henle

  • Thin descending limb: permeable to water (aquaporin-1; about 10% of filtered water) and to small solutes such as urea, not to NaCl. Water leaves into the salty medulla and urea enters, so the fluid becomes more concentrated going down.
  • Thin ascending limb: impermeable to water; NaCl leaves passively, so the fluid becomes more dilute going up.
  • Thick ascending limb (TAL): NKCC2 (Na+-K+-2Cl−) moves salt into the cell; K+ leaks back to the lumen through ROMK, making the lumen positive, which pushes Ca2+ and Mg2+ (and some Na+) between the cells. Impermeable to water, so it is the diluting segment: fluid leaving it is hypo-osmotic (about 100 mOsm/kg). Reabsorbs about 25% of filtered Na+, and more when more is delivered (load-dependent).
  • Loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, torsemide) bind NKCC2's Cl− site and block it: the medullary gradient collapses, so urine can be neither concentrated nor fully diluted; K+, Ca2+ and Mg2+ are lost too. NKCC isoforms in the inner ear and in the salivary and lacrimal glands explain their tinnitus and dry mouth and eyes. They are used for edema in heart failure and to lower a high Ca2+ or K+, and they can raise uric acid (hyperuricemia).

Making concentrated urine

  • Countercurrent multiplication: the TAL pumps NaCl into the interstitium without water, and the opposite flows in the two limbs multiply this small step into a gradient from about 300 mOsm/kg in the cortex to about 1,200 at the papilla with ADH (about 600 without it). About half of the 1,200 is NaCl and half is urea. Without the TAL's active NaCl transport there would be no gradient.
  • Urea recycling: ADH makes the cortical and outer medullary collecting ducts permeable to water but not urea, so urea concentrates in the duct; in the inner medullary collecting duct ADH also inserts urea transporters, urea diffuses into the interstitium and supplies much of the inner medulla's osmolarity. Some urea re-enters the thin descending limb from the ascending vasa recta and is recycled. A low-protein (vegan) diet makes less urea, so the urine can't be concentrated as much.
  • Vasa recta: hairpin capillaries that act as countercurrent exchangers; their slow flow keeps the gradient from being washed away. Very high water intake or tubular flow causes medullary washout, lowering the maximum urine concentration for a while.

Distal tubule and collecting duct

  • Distal convoluted tubule: starts at the macula densa; water-impermeable; NCC (Na+-Cl− cotransporter) reabsorbs about 5% of filtered NaCl. Ca2+ enters through an apical channel (TRPV5) and leaves through a basolateral Ca2+-ATPase and Na+/Ca2+ exchanger; PTH increases it. Thiazides block NCC and increase Ca2+ reabsorption.
  • The collecting duct system: connecting tubule, then the cortical, outer medullary and inner medullary collecting ducts. Several nephrons drain into one collecting duct: their connecting tubules merge at the cortical collecting duct. It reabsorbs only about 4–5% of filtered Na+, but it is the segment hormones tune.
  • Principal cells (about 60%): Na+ in through apical ENaC, K+ out to the lumen through apical ROMK (renal outer medullary K+ channel); respond to aldosterone and ADH. Na+ entry makes the lumen strongly negative (about −50 mV), which drives K+ secretion and paracellular Cl− reabsorption, so the more Na+ is reabsorbed, the more K+ is secreted.
  • Aldosterone enters the cell, binds an intracellular mineralocorticoid receptor and, over hours, raises the number of ENaC channels, Na+-K+-ATPase pumps and K+ channels: more Na+ reabsorbed, more K+ (and H+) secreted.
  • ADH binds basolateral V2 receptors → adenylyl cyclase, cAMP and protein kinase A → aquaporin-2 inserted in the apical membrane (and, over the long term, more aquaporin-2 made). Without ADH the duct stays nearly water-tight. The V1 receptors of vascular smooth muscle are the ones that constrict vessels. ADH also raises urea permeability in the inner medullary duct and NKCC2 activity in the TAL.
  • Intercalated cells (about 40%): α-intercalated cells secrete H+ (apical H+-ATPase and H+-K+-ATPase, which also reabsorbs K+) and return HCO3− to the blood through the basolateral Cl−/HCO3− exchanger AE1; β-intercalated cells secrete HCO3− through apical pendrin (a Cl−/HCO3− exchanger) and put H+ into the blood through a basolateral H+-ATPase. Both types are rich in carbonic anhydrase II.
  • K+-sparing diuretics: amiloride and triamterene block ENaC; spironolactone and eplerenone block the aldosterone receptor. Less Na+ entry means a less negative lumen and less K+ secretion, so the risk is hyperkalemia. The duct handles only 4–5% of filtered Na+, so their diuresis is mild and they are mostly paired with a thiazide or loop diuretic to offset its K+ loss. Spironolactone also treats hyperaldosteronism.
full.rn-balance:
What's tested
  • Water balance: hypo- and hypernatremia, where ADH is made, osmotic and non-osmotic control, SIADH and central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
  • Sodium balance: the volume sensors, the sympathetic nerves, the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and ANP; responses to hypo- and hypervolemia
  • Potassium: shifts into and out of cells, renal handling, what raises and lowers K+ secretion
  • Magnesium, calcium and phosphate: where each is reabsorbed; PTH, vitamin D and FGF23; diuretic effects
  • Acid-base: the HCO3−/PCO2 ratio, HCO3− reabsorption, titratable acid and ammonium, the four simple disorders and their compensation

Water balance and ADH

  • Hyponatremia is plasma Na+ below 135 mmol/L (too much water for the sodium); hypernatremia is above 145 (too little water). Plasma Na+ reflects water balance; total body Na+ sets ECF volume.
  • ADH (arginine vasopressin) is made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. Its three actions: through V2 receptors it raises the collecting duct's water permeability (aquaporin-2) and the inner medullary duct's urea permeability; through V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle it constricts arterioles and raises blood pressure.
  • Osmoreceptors sit in the OVLT and subfornical organ, which lack a blood-brain barrier; when hypertonic plasma shrinks them, stretch-sensitive cation channels open and they fire. Their axons reach the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei and the cortex's thirst areas (insula, anterior cingulate gyrus). Normal plasma osmolality is 275–290 mOsm/kg. A 1–2% rise releases ADH; thirst needs about 2–3%, so ADH responds first. Below the threshold (about 275–280 mOsm/kg) ADH is fully suppressed.
  • Non-osmotic control: a 5–10% fall in blood volume or pressure, sensed by the left atrium, carotid sinus and aortic arch, releases ADH. Volume wins: hypovolemia resets the osmostat so ADH is released even at a low osmolarity. Nausea, pain, motion sickness, hypoxia, insulin-induced hypoglycemia, strenuous exercise and drugs (morphine, nicotine, MDMA) also release ADH; alcohol and opiate antagonists such as naloxone suppress it. Thirst also rises with a 10–15% fall in blood volume and with angiotensin II acting on the subfornical organ.
  • Water loss → osmolarity up → ADH and thirst → aquaporin-2 in the collecting duct → small volume of concentrated urine. Water load → the reverse: large volume of dilute urine.
DisorderADHPlasma Na+UrineCausesTreatment
SIADHHigh, unregulatedLowInappropriately concentratedSmall cell lung cancer and other tumors, CNS disease, drugs, pain and nausea after surgeryChronic: fluid restriction. Acute: IV furosemide with 3% saline
Central diabetes insipidusLowHighLarge volume, dilutePituitary or hypothalamic lesion, surgery, head trauma, inheritedDesmopressin
Nephrogenic diabetes insipidusNormal or high, no effectHighLarge volume, dilute; no response to desmopressinLithium (most common: about half of patients on it; it blocks aquaporin-2 insertion), V2 receptor or aquaporin-2 mutationsThiazide, amiloride (lithium), NSAIDs, low-salt, low-protein diet

Telling water deprivation from SIADH: both make concentrated urine, but plasma osmolarity is high with water deprivation and low with SIADH.

Acute hyponatremia (a large water load, often with an ADH stimulus such as MDMA, or in an endurance runner who drinks avidly) swells the brain: headache, confusion, seizures. It is treated urgently with 3% hypertonic saline, which draws water out of the brain.

Sodium balance

  • Na+ (with the Cl− that follows it) is the main determinant of ECF volume. The kidneys match Na+ excretion to intake (a Western diet has about 120–140 mEq a day; excretion can range from about 20 to over 1,000 mEq a day), driven mainly by changes in vascular volume, blood pressure and cardiac output.
  • Sensors: low-pressure receptors in the atria and pulmonary vessels; high-pressure baroreceptors in the carotid sinus (CN IX) and aortic arch (CN X); in the kidney, the afferent arteriole (perfusion pressure) and the macula densa (NaCl delivery). A 5–10% change is needed to respond.
  • Renal sympathetic nerves: constrict both arterioles, the afferent more (GFR and filtered Na+ down), release renin, and raise NaCl reabsorption in the proximal tubule, TAL and collecting duct.
  • Renin is released by JG cells for low afferent pressure, sympathetic (β1) activity and low NaCl at the macula densa (signaled by prostaglandins); a rise in afferent pressure inhibits it. This macula densa signal to renin is separate from tubuloglomerular feedback, where the macula densa adjusts the afferent arteriole through adenosine. Renin: angiotensinogen → angiotensin I; ACE (on the endothelium of the lungs and kidneys) → angiotensin II.
  • Angiotensin II: arteriolar constriction (efferent more than afferent), more proximal Na+ reabsorption (Na+/H+ exchanger), aldosterone release, ADH release, thirst and salt appetite. Aldosterone, a steroid from the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex, raises Na+ reabsorption in the collecting duct, the segment that matches Na+ excretion to intake day to day.
  • ANP from atrial myocytes, released by atrial stretch (volume expansion): dilates the afferent and constricts the efferent arteriole (GFR up), inhibits renin, aldosterone and ADH, and reduces Na+ reabsorption in the collecting duct → natriuresis. It opposes RAAS.
  • Hypovolemia: the baroreceptors raise renal sympathetic activity, RAAS up, ADH up, ANP down → Na+ and water kept (over hours to days). Hypervolemia: the reverse.
  • Heart failure: the excess fluid is Na+ and water retained in the interstitial compartment (about three-quarters of the ECF), where the baroreceptors can't sense it, and blood pressure is often low from the weak heart. The effective circulating volume is low, so the sensors keep signaling depletion, the kidney keeps retaining Na+ and the edema worsens. Cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome do the same.

Potassium

  • About 98% of K+ is inside cells. Plasma K+ is normally 3.5–5.0 mEq/L: hypokalemia below 3.5, hyperkalemia above 5.0. Both disturb nerve, muscle and heart rhythm.
  • Into cells (plasma K+ falls): insulin (after a meal, through the Na+-K+-ATPase), β2 agonists such as epinephrine and albuterol, α-adrenergic blockers, alkalosis, aldosterone. Excess aldosterone (primary aldosteronism) causes hypokalemia.
  • Out of cells (plasma K+ rises): insulin deficiency (type 1 diabetes), β-blockers, α-adrenergic agonists (epinephrine's α effect, mainly in the liver), acidosis, hyperosmolarity, cell lysis (burns, rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis, chemotherapy), strenuous exercise (hyperkalemia in someone on a β-blocker or with poor kidney function). Low aldosterone (Addison disease) causes hyperkalemia.
  • Renal handling: freely filtered; the proximal tubule reabsorbs about 67% and the TAL about 20%, whatever the diet. The kidneys excrete 90–95% of dietary K+: urine K+ is normally about 15% of the filtered load, can exceed 100% on a high-K+ diet and falls to about 1% on a low one. The collecting duct sets excretion: principal cells secrete K+; α-intercalated cells reabsorb it on a low-K+ diet (H+-K+-ATPase).
  • K+ secretion rises with a high-K+ diet, aldosterone, alkalosis and high tubular flow or Na+ delivery (loop and thiazide diuretics → hypokalemia). It falls with acute acidosis, low aldosterone, K+-sparing diuretics and low GFR.
  • Aldosterone raises K+ secretion mostly through its effect on Na+: more ENaC channels let more Na+ into the principal cell, the lumen turns more negative, and K+ is secreted. It also adds Na+-K+-ATPase pumps and apical K+ channels.
  • NSAIDs and CKD: NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that signal renin release at the macula densa, so renin and aldosterone fall and less K+ is secreted. With a low GFR, and more so with ACE inhibitors or spironolactone, this causes hyperkalemia, so CKD patients limit K+ intake and avoid NSAIDs.

Calcium, phosphate and magnesium

IonProximal tubuleThick ascending limbDistal tubuleExcreted
Ca2+ (99% in bone)about 65%, paracellular with Na+ and waterabout 20–25%, paracellular (lumen-positive)about 5–10%, transcellular, raised by PTH and thiazidesabout 1–2%
Mg2+ (mostly bone and cells)about 30%about 60%, the main site, paracellularabout 5–10%about 5%
Phosphate (85% in bone)about 80–85%–littleabout 15%; a urinary buffer
  • Loop diuretics raise Ca2+ and Mg2+ excretion: blocking NKCC2 stops K+ recycling, so the lumen-positive voltage that drives their paracellular reabsorption in the TAL is lost. Thiazides lower Ca2+ excretion: with less Na+ entering the DCT cell, the cell reabsorbs more Ca2+ (hypercalcemia can follow). ECF volume expansion raises Ca2+ excretion.
  • PTH is released when plasma Ca2+ falls (and when phosphate rises). It frees Ca2+ and phosphate from bone, raises Ca2+ reabsorption in the DCT, lowers phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule (phosphaturia) and stimulates 1α-hydroxylase. Net: Ca2+ up, phosphate down.
  • Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), made in the proximal tubule: its most important action is Ca2+ absorption from the gut (duodenum); it also raises gut phosphate absorption and the renal reabsorption of both, inhibits PTH and stimulates FGF23. PTH stimulates its synthesis; FGF23 inhibits it.
  • FGF23, from osteocytes and osteoblasts, is released when phosphate and calcitriol are high. It lowers proximal phosphate reabsorption and lowers calcitriol synthesis and PTH secretion.
  • A sudden fall in plasma Ca2+ is buffered mostly from bone.

Acid-base

  • The pH follows the ratio of HCO3− to PCO2: more HCO3− raises it, more CO2 lowers it. Normal: pH 7.35–7.45, PCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3− 24 mEq/L. The lungs set PCO2 (volatile acid); the kidneys set HCO3− and excrete the fixed acids (sulfuric and phosphoric acid from protein metabolism, about 1 mEq/kg a day).
  • Defense in three steps: buffers (immediate), lungs (minutes), kidneys (hours to days).
  • Reclaiming filtered HCO3− (proximal tubule, about 85%; the kidneys reclaim nearly all, 99.9%, of it): secreted H+ meets filtered HCO3− in the lumen → H2CO3 → CO2 + H2O (carbonic anhydrase); CO2 enters the cell, is turned back into H+ and HCO3−, and the HCO3− goes to the blood. No net acid is excreted.
  • Making new HCO3−: each H+ excreted on a urinary buffer adds a new HCO3− to the blood. Titratable acid is H+ on filtered buffers, mainly phosphate (also urate and creatinine). Ammonium: the proximal tubule turns glutamine into NH4+ (secreted) and α-ketoglutarate, which yields new HCO3−. Ammonium is the part that grows in chronic acidosis.
  • Net acid excretion = NH4+ + titratable acid − excreted HCO3−; at steady state it equals fixed acid production.
DisorderPrimary changeCompensationExamples
Metabolic acidosisHCO3− ↓Hyperventilation (PCO2 ↓)Diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure, aspirin overdose (high anion gap); diarrhea, acetazolamide (normal gap)
Metabolic alkalosisHCO3− ↑Hypoventilation (PCO2 ↑)Vomiting, loop and thiazide diuretics (contraction alkalosis), excess aldosterone, antacid or bicarbonate intake
Respiratory acidosisPCO2 ↑Kidneys make and keep HCO3− (days)Hypoventilation: COPD, pneumonia, pulmonary edema; airway obstruction (aspiration, sleep apnea); weak respiratory muscles (ALS); opioids, sedatives or anesthetics depressing the medullary respiratory center
Respiratory alkalosisPCO2 ↓Kidneys excrete HCO3− (days)Hyperventilation: anxiety, pain, hypoxemia (high altitude, pneumonia), stroke, early aspirin overdose
  • To read a blood gas: look at the pH; find which of PCO2 or HCO3− moved in the direction that explains it (the primary change); the other one moving the same direction is compensation. A quick check by the arrows: when PCO2 and HCO3− move opposite to the pH, the disorder is respiratory; when they move the same way as the pH, it is metabolic.
  • Acidosis and alkalosis name the process; acidemia and alkalemia name the blood's pH.
  • Anion gap = Na+ − (Cl− + HCO3−), normally about 8–12; a high gap means an added acid (ketoacids, lactate, salicylate, toxic alcohols, uremia).
  • Acid-base and K+ move together: acidosis drives K+ out of cells (hyperkalemia); alkalosis drives it in (hypokalemia). Vomiting gives metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia, kept going by volume contraction: proximal HCO3− reabsorption rises, angiotensin II and aldosterone drive H+ secretion, so the alkalosis lasts until volume is restored. Without volume contraction the kidney corrects an alkalosis by excreting HCO3− (β-intercalated cells secrete it). Severe diarrhea does the opposite: a normal-gap metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia (K+ lost in the stool, aldosterone up).
full.rn-disease:
What's tested
  • Chronic kidney disease: definition, causes, the five eGFR stages, eGFR and uACR
  • End-stage renal disease, azotemia versus uremia, and how uremia arises
  • What CKD does to the body: anemia, hypertension, hyperkalemia, acidosis, bone and mineral disease, bleeding, and the mouth and eyes
  • Glomerular disease: nephritic versus nephrotic syndrome and the classic examples of each
  • Tubular and interstitial disease, stones, obstruction, cystic disease and kidney tumors

Chronic kidney disease

  • CKD: abnormal kidney structure or function present for 3 months or more, with effects on health. The leading causes are diabetes mellitus, then hypertension; it is more common with age. End-stage disease also comes from chronic glomerulonephritis and polycystic kidney disease.
  • eGFR (from serum creatinine or cystatin C) is the chief measure of function and sets the stage. uACR (urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio) picks up damage even when eGFR is above 60; under 30 mg/g is normal.
  • Function is kept near normal until more than about 50% of nephrons are lost, because the survivors hypertrophy and hyperfilter. Lost nephrons are not replaced; end-stage kidneys are small, scarred and nodular.
  • Slowing progression: control of glucose and blood pressure, a low-protein, low-salt diet, ACE inhibitors or ARBs and SGLT2 inhibitors (both lower the pressure inside the glomerulus; ACE inhibitors and ARBs also lower albuminuria), finerenone (a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor blocker) and semaglutide (a GLP-1 agonist that dampens inflammation and fibrosis in the kidney).
StageeGFR (mL/min/1.73 m²)Meaning
190 or moreNormal filtration, but other signs of kidney damage (albuminuria, imaging)
260–89Mild loss
330–59Moderate loss (split into 3a, 45–59, and 3b, 30–44); complications start to show
415–29Severe loss; plan for dialysis or transplant
5under 15Kidney failure; dialysis or transplant

Azotemia and uremia

  • Azotemia is a lab finding: non-protein nitrogen (urea, creatinine) builds up in the blood because filtration has fallen. It may cause no symptoms.
  • Uremia is the clinical illness of kidney failure, the stage azotemia leads to: nausea, vomiting, fatigue and muscle cramps, with signs in nearly every system. The oral and eye signs below are the ones to know.
  • Uremia comes from three things: retained products the kidney should excrete (nitrogen wastes), normal products in excess (hormones such as PTH), and loss of products the kidney makes (erythropoietin, calcitriol). Failing excretion also retains Na+ and water and causes hyperkalemia.

Complications of CKD

  • Anemia: normocytic, from low erythropoietin; it rises steeply from stage 3 on. Treated with erythropoietin analogs (epoetin, darbepoetin) and iron.
  • Hypertension (Na+ and water retention, renin), and cardiovascular disease, the leading cause of death in CKD.
  • Hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis as excretion falls.
  • Hypoglycemia in a diabetic on insulin: the failing kidney clears less insulin, so the same (or a lower) dose acts longer.
  • Edema: albumin lost in the urine lowers plasma oncotic pressure, so fluid filters out of the capillaries; Na+ and water retention adds to it.
  • CKD mineral and bone disorder: falling GFR retains phosphate → FGF23 rises and calcitriol falls → less Ca2+ absorbed → plasma Ca2+ falls → secondary hyperparathyroidism (seen from stages 3–5) → renal osteodystrophy: bone resorption, demineralized jaws and brown tumors.
  • Bleeding: uremic toxins impair platelet adhesion and aggregation; hemodialysis adds heparin.
  • Infection risk and poor healing; drug clearance falls.
  • Oral: uremic stomatitis, xerostomia, altered or metallic taste, ammonia-like breath, pale mucosa from anemia, petechiae and ecchymoses, periodontal disease, renal osteodystrophy. Eyes: diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma, cataracts and macular degeneration.
  • Dialysis is started at eGFR under about 15 or with uremic symptoms.

Glomerular disease

  • Kidney disease can hit glomeruli, tubules, interstitium or vessels. Glomeruli are hurt mostly by immune mechanisms (circulating immune complexes, or antibodies against antigens in the glomerulus); tubules by toxins and infection. Primary glomerulopathy involves only the kidney; secondary comes from a systemic disease (diabetes, lupus, amyloidosis, drugs, infection, cancer).
Nephritic syndromeNephrotic syndrome
HallmarkHematuria (RBC casts), hypertension, oliguria (under 400 mL/day), mild azotemia; mild to moderate proteinuriaProteinuria over 3.5 g/day (normal under 300 mg/day), hypoalbuminemia (under 3 g/dL), severe edema, hyperlipidemia and lipiduria (fatty casts)
MechanismInflammation of the glomerulusPodocyte injury or GBM damage that lets protein through
ExamplesPost-streptococcal GN, IgA nephropathy, rapidly progressive GNMinimal change disease, FSGS, membranous nephropathy, MPGN; diabetes and amyloid (secondary)
  • Post-streptococcal GN: children, 1–4 weeks after group A strep throat or skin infection; cola-colored urine, edema, hypertension, low C3; hypercellular glomeruli with subepithelial "humps". Most children recover; adults more often progress.
  • IgA nephropathy: the most common glomerular disease worldwide; recurrent hematuria within a day or two of a respiratory infection; mesangial IgA. Benign in children, slowly progressive in adults.
  • Rapidly progressive GN: crescents of epithelial cells in Bowman space and loss of function over days to weeks; about 90% end up on long-term dialysis or with a transplant. Type I anti-GBM (linear IgG and C3), idiopathic or Goodpasture syndrome, where the antibody also binds the lung's alveolar basement membrane (lung hemorrhage with GN; plasmapheresis helps). Type II immune complex (post-streptococcal, lupus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura). Type III pauci-immune, ANCA-associated (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis).
  • Minimal change disease: the most common nephrotic syndrome in children; normal light microscopy, fused (effaced) podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy; about 90% respond to steroids.
  • FSGS: sclerosis of some segments (segmental) of some glomeruli (focal); about 10% of nephrotic syndrome; idiopathic or secondary to HIV, heroin use, diabetic nephropathy or nephron loss from other causes; poor steroid response, about half reach kidney failure in 10 years.
  • Membranous nephropathy: the classic most common nephrotic syndrome in adults (ages 30–50); subepithelial immune deposits that thicken the GBM, with spikes on silver stain; about 85% primary; slowly progressive.
  • MPGN: subendothelial deposits (type I, about two-thirds, tied to hepatitis B and C, lupus, infections and cancers) or dense deposits within the GBM (type II, dense-deposit disease); "tram-track" GBM; poor course, about 40% reach end-stage disease.

Where the injury sits names the disease: subepithelial deposits in membranous nephropathy (spikes on silver stain) and post-streptococcal GN (humps); subendothelial deposits in MPGN type I; mesangial IgA in IgA nephropathy; linear IgG along the GBM in anti-GBM disease; and no deposits, only effaced podocyte foot processes, in minimal change disease.

Tubules, stones and obstruction

  • Acute pyelonephritis: bacterial infection of the kidney and pelvis, usually ascending, most often E. coli (also Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas). Risks: instrumentation, obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux, female sex. Fever, chills, flank (costovertebral angle) pain, dysuria, frequency and urgency; WBC casts place it in the kidney. Complications: pyonephrosis, papillary necrosis (common in diabetics and with analgesic abuse), sepsis; untreated, it can become chronic.
  • Know two tubular diseases by name: acute tubular necrosis, where the tubular cells die, usually after ischemia (a long spell of low blood pressure) or a toxin; and interstitial nephritis, inflammation around the tubules from drugs or infection.
  • Urolithiasis: calcium oxalate/phosphate stones about 75%; magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) about 15%, from urease-making bacteria such as Proteus that keep the urine alkaline, and the cause of staghorn calculi; uric acid about 6% (gout); cystine 1–2% (an inherited defect of amino acid transport). Colicky flank pain to the groin, hematuria, infection behind an obstruction.
  • Hydronephrosis: dilated pelvis and calyces with atrophy from obstruction. Bilateral (obstruction below the ureters) leads to kidney failure if not relieved; unilateral can stay silent.

Cysts and tumors

  • ADPKD: adults, always bilateral, PKD1 (chromosome 16, about 85%) or PKD2 (chromosome 4); silent until the 40s, then flank pain and hematuria; hypertension, liver cysts (about 30%), berry aneurysms (10–30%); about 10% of chronic renal failure, usually end-stage by about 50. ARPKD: infants, PKHD1, small sponge-like cysts, congenital hepatic fibrosis.
  • Acquired cystic disease develops in kidneys on long-term dialysis; its worst complication is renal cell carcinoma in the cyst walls. Simple cysts are the most common and usually silent.
  • Renal cell carcinoma: about 2% of adult cancers and 80–90% of kidney cancers, mostly in men aged 40–70; risks are smoking, von Hippel-Lindau disease and adult polycystic disease. Hematuria, flank pain and a mass; a yellow-orange, vascular tumor that tends to invade the renal vein. Clear cell (70–80%, loss of VHL on 3p, cells full of lipid and glycogen); papillary (10–15%, not tied to 3p but to trisomies 7, 16 and 17); chromophobe (about 5%, best prognosis, perinuclear halos). Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (autosomal dominant) brings hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and pancreatic tumors. RCC spreads by blood, most often to lung and bone, and can surface as a metastasis in the jaw or gingiva.
  • Wilms tumor: children (about 2–5 years), a large abdominal or flank mass, sometimes with pain or hematuria; 5–10% bilateral; triphasic (blastemal, stromal, epithelial); about 90% long-term survival with nephrectomy and chemotherapy.
  • Benign: papillary adenoma, oncocytoma, and angiomyolipoma (tuberous sclerosis).

What's tested
  • The diuretic classes: site, mechanism, uses, main side effects and interactions (loop, thiazide, K+-sparing; mannitol, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors)
  • The CKD and dialysis patient in the dental chair: consult, timing around dialysis, the fistula arm, bleeding, infection; care by cause (diabetic, hypertensive and polycystic kidney disease, acute kidney injury)
  • Drug choice and dosing when kidney function is low: what to avoid, what to adjust, what is safe
  • Oral and radiographic signs of kidney failure, and the kidney transplant patient

Diuretics

  • Potency follows how much Na+ the segment handles: loop diuretics (25%) are the strongest ("high ceiling"); thiazides (5–8%) are moderate; K+-sparing drugs (2–3%) are weak.
  • Why loop and thiazide diuretics waste K+: more Na+ and fluid reach the collecting duct, ENaC reabsorbs more Na+, the lumen becomes more negative, and K+ is secreted. Volume loss also raises aldosterone. Adding a K+-sparing drug (spironolactone is the classic partner in heart failure) offsets it.
  • Braking: after the first Na+ and water losses, sympathetic activity, RAAS and ADH rise and limit further loss; on a steady dose, intake and excretion match again at a lower ECF volume.
  • Calcium: loop diuretics raise Ca2+ excretion; thiazides lower it, and the positive Ca2+ balance lowers fracture risk.
  • Interactions: NSAIDs blunt diuretic and antihypertensive effects (they block renal prostaglandins) and, with K+-sparing drugs, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, raise K+; thiazides and loop diuretics raise lithium levels, and so do NSAIDs; loop diuretics plus aminoglycosides add ototoxicity, and plus NSAIDs nephrotoxicity; low K+ makes digoxin toxic. Thiazides and loops are sulfonamides (ethacrynic acid is not).
  • In the chair: patients on diuretics are prone to orthostatic hypotension (sit them up slowly) and xerostomia; thiazides can cause lichenoid reactions. Plan bathroom breaks in a long appointment, and expect electrolyte losses to cause muscle cramps (a mouth prop helps the jaw). In a patient with healthy kidneys a short NSAID course is usually acceptable, but long use weakens blood pressure control.

The CKD and dialysis patient

  • Consult the physician or nephrologist: stage, cause, recent labs (eGFR, creatinine, BUN, CBC with hemoglobin and platelets, coagulation tests, electrolytes), blood pressure control, medications and the dialysis schedule. Ask the patient which days they dialyze, which arm holds the access, whether they get heparin, how they bleed and what they take for pain.
  • Hemodialysis runs about 3 times a week through an arteriovenous fistula or graft, usually in the forearm, with heparin. Treat on the day after dialysis: heparin's effect (a few hours) is gone and fluid, electrolytes and wastes are at their best. Avoid treating on a dialysis day.
  • Never take blood pressure, start an IV or draw blood on the fistula arm.
  • Bleeding: uremic platelet dysfunction makes bleeding likely even with a normal platelet count. Plan local hemostasis (pressure, sutures, hemostatic agents, tranexamic acid); the physician may give desmopressin before surgery.
  • Infection: wound healing is slow and immunity weak; dialysis patients have higher rates of hepatitis B and C. Antibiotic prophylaxis is not routinely recommended just for a fistula or graft; follow the nephrologist's advice when asked.
  • Peritoneal dialysis uses no systemic heparin; its main risk is peritonitis.
  • Hypertension, anemia (pallor, fatigue) and diabetes often come with CKD: check blood pressure each visit and keep appointments short and low-stress.
  • Diabetic kidney disease, the most common kind: more periodontal disease, infection and slow healing; check the HbA1c and glucose, and keep glucose on hand for hypoglycemia. Hypertensive kidney disease: blood pressure at every visit, watch for orthostatic hypotension, use epinephrine carefully and no NSAIDs.
  • Polycystic kidney disease: hypertension and intracranial (berry) aneurysms, so avoid swings in blood pressure and use epinephrine carefully. Glomerulonephritis with lupus or rheumatoid arthritis: immunosuppressed and often on long-term steroids, so major surgery may need a stress dose set with the physician.
  • Acute kidney injury: no NSAIDs, avoid high-dose acyclovir, lower the doses of renally cleared drugs and keep the patient hydrated; treat pain conservatively (for a toothache, a pulpectomy and a temporary) and defer elective care until the kidneys recover.

Drugs when the kidneys fail

  • A drug cleared by the kidney accumulates as GFR falls: lower the dose or lengthen the interval (usually once GFR is under about 50, and especially under 30 mL/min). Drugs removed by dialysis are given after the session.
  • Avoid: NSAIDs (they cut renal prostaglandins and GFR, raise K+ and blood pressure, add to bleeding), high-dose aspirin, tetracyclines other than doxycycline (they raise BUN), meperidine (its metabolite normeperidine accumulates and causes seizures), and nephrotoxic drugs.
  • Adjust: amoxicillin, penicillin VK and cephalexin (longer interval), ciprofloxacin, acyclovir and valacyclovir, gabapentin; codeine, hydrocodone, morphine and tramadol at the lowest dose (they or their active metabolites build up). Of the antifungals, fluconazole needs care (a lower dose and many drug interactions), ketoconazole is avoided (liver toxicity and interactions), and nystatin and clotrimazole are fine.
  • Usually no change: amide local anesthetics such as lidocaine (metabolized by the liver; articaine by plasma esterases) at normal doses, though long-acting bupivacaine is used with caution and epinephrine is kept low when blood pressure is high; clindamycin, azithromycin, metronidazole and doxycycline (cleared mainly by the liver or gut). Acetaminophen is the analgesic of choice, with a longer interval in severe disease.

Oral and radiographic signs

  • Uremic fetor (ammonia-like breath), uremic stomatitis (a red, sore, inflamed mouth and tongue, sometimes with white plaques or ulcers; eased with sips of water, good hygiene and soothing rinses), xerostomia (fluid limits, drugs), metallic or altered taste, pale mucosa, petechiae, ecchymoses and gingival bleeding, periodontal disease, parotitis, candidiasis and angular cheilitis. Children with CKD can show enamel hypoplasia and delayed eruption. Caries tends to be low (salivary urea raises pH), while calculus builds up.
  • Renal osteodystrophy from secondary hyperparathyroidism: loss of the lamina dura, a ground-glass trabecular pattern, demineralized jaws and brown tumors (giant cell lesions); soft tissue calcifications. Demineralized jaws raise the risk of fracture during extractions: the mandible around the lower molars, and the maxillary tuberosity with the upper molars; bone heals slowly.

The kidney transplant patient

  • Clear dental infection before transplant; defer elective care in the first months after and during any rejection episode, and coordinate with the transplant team. Antibiotic prophylaxis before invasive care is not in the ADA guidelines, but the transplant physician usually asks for it, so consult.
  • Immunosuppressants (tacrolimus or cyclosporine, mycophenolate, prednisone): infection, candidiasis, slow healing, and more oral cancer (screen at every visit and recall often); cyclosporine causes gingival overgrowth (worse with a calcium channel blocker such as nifedipine or amlodipine); long-term steroids can suppress the adrenals, so major surgery may need a stress dose set by the physician.
  • Interactions: erythromycin and clarithromycin and azole antifungals (fluconazole, ketoconazole) block the liver enzyme that clears cyclosporine and tacrolimus, raising their levels and their kidney toxicity; NSAIDs add nephrotoxicity.
full.he-axes:
What's tested
  • Hormone classes and their receptors (Gs, Gi, Gq, tyrosine kinase, JAK-STAT, nuclear)
  • Anterior vs posterior pituitary, feedback, and primary vs secondary lab patterns
  • Growth hormone regulation, IGF-1, gigantism vs acromegaly and the acromegalic jaw
  • Pituitary adenomas (prolactinoma, bitemporal hemianopsia), diabetes insipidus vs SIADH
  • Adrenal zones; Cushing vs Addison vs Conn; congenital adrenal hyperplasia; pheochromocytoma
  • Corticosteroid drugs (potency, taper, side effects) and the adrenal crisis in the chair

Hormones and their receptors

Peptides (insulin, GH, ACTH, PTH, ADH) are stored in granules, dissolve in plasma and bind surface receptors. Amines are epinephrine and norepinephrine (surface receptors) and thyroid hormone, the exception that crosses the membrane and binds a nuclear receptor. Steroids (cortisol, aldosterone, sex steroids, calcitriol) come from cholesterol, are made on demand, not stored, ride on binding proteins and act on intracellular receptors by changing gene transcription, so their effects start slowly and last.

PathwayWhat it doesHormones

JAK-STATCytokine-type receptor with JAK2GH, prolactin

Hypothalamus and pituitary

  • Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis, from Rathke pouch): hypothalamic releasing hormones reach it through the hypophyseal portal veins. Acidophils make GH and prolactin; basophils make FSH, LH, ACTH and TSH ("B-FLAT"); chromophobes have few granules.
  • Posterior pituitary (pars nervosa) makes nothing: ADH and oxytocin are made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, travel down axons, are stored in Herring bodies and released into blood (neuroendocrine secretion). Pituicytes are glia.
  • Dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin, so a stalk lesion or a dopamine blocker raises prolactin. TRH releases TSH (and prolactin); somatostatin inhibits GH (and TSH).
  • Negative feedback is the rule (long loop from the target hormone, short loop from the pituitary hormone). Primary (target gland) disease: the target hormone and the pituitary hormone move in opposite directions. Secondary (pituitary) disease: they move the same way.

Growth hormone

  • Pulsatile from somatotrophs, the biggest pulse in deep sleep soon after falling asleep. Up: GHRH (Gs), ghrelin, sleep, stress, exercise, hypoglycemia, amino acids. Down: somatostatin (Gi), glucose, free fatty acids, and GH and IGF-1 themselves (they raise hypothalamic somatostatin).
  • Linear growth runs mostly through IGF-1 (somatomedin) from the liver, acting on growth-plate chondrocytes. Metabolic effects: diabetogenic (anti-insulin, gluconeogenesis), lipolytic, builds muscle protein.
  • Fetal growth depends on insulin, not GH (big babies of diabetic mothers). Estrogen closes the growth plates in both sexes (and blunts GH's action on the liver's IGF-1): plan implants after growth stops.
  • Excess, usually a somatotroph adenoma: before the plates fuse, gigantism; after, acromegaly: coarse face, frontal bossing, big hands and feet, a growing mandible (Class I to Class III), new diastemas, macroglossia, glucose intolerance, hypertension. Screen with IGF-1; confirm when GH fails to fall after an oral glucose load.
  • Deficiency: short stature. Laron syndrome (GH receptor defect): GH high, IGF-1 low. Somatopause: GH falls from the 30s, mainly from less GHRH.

Pituitary disorders

  • Adenomas: micro under 10 mm, macro 10 mm or more. A macroadenoma presses on the optic chiasm: bitemporal hemianopsia and headache.
  • Prolactinoma, the most common functioning adenoma: amenorrhea and galactorrhea in women, low libido and infertility in men; treated with a dopamine agonist (bromocriptine, cabergoline). Corticotroph adenoma = Cushing disease; gonadotroph adenomas are usually silent.
  • Hypopituitarism needs about 75% loss: Sheehan syndrome (postpartum pituitary infarction: the first sign is failure to lactate), empty sella, surgery, radiation.
Central DINephrogenic DISIADH
ProblemNo ADH (trauma, surgery, tumor)Kidney ignores ADH (lithium, genetic)Too much ADH (small cell lung carcinoma, CNS disease, drugs)
UrineLarge volume, diluteLarge volume, diluteConcentrated
Serum sodiumHighHighLow (dilutional)
DesmopressinCorrects itNo effectNot given; restrict water

The adrenal gland

The cortex (about 90%) makes steroids in three zones, outside in, salt, sugar, sex: the glomerulosa makes aldosterone (driven by angiotensin II and high potassium; keeps sodium, excretes potassium and acid), the fasciculata (lipid-filled spongiocytes) makes cortisol under ACTH, and the reticularis makes androgens (DHEA). The medulla's chromaffin cells, modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons, release about 80% epinephrine on acetylcholine from preganglionic fibers; cortisol-rich blood draining from the cortex induces PNMT, the enzyme that turns norepinephrine into epinephrine.

Cortisol peaks in the early morning. It raises glucose (gluconeogenesis), breaks down muscle protein, mobilizes fat, increases bone resorption, suppresses inflammation and immunity and keeps vessels responsive to catecholamines. ACTH is its main regulator.

DisorderCause and labsFindings
Cushing syndromeExcess cortisol. Most often exogenous steroids. ACTH high: pituitary adenoma (Cushing disease) or ectopic ACTH (small cell lung). ACTH low: adrenal tumor or exogenousMoon face, buffalo hump, central obesity, purple striae, thin skin, bruising, hyperglycemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, infections, poor healing
Addison disease (primary insufficiency)Autoimmune destruction most often; cortisol and aldosterone low, ACTH highFatigue, weight loss, hypotension, salt craving, low sodium, high potassium, low glucose; skin and oral hyperpigmentation (ACTH and MSH share a precursor)
Secondary insufficiencyPituitary disease or stopping long-term steroids; ACTH lowLike Addison, but no pigmentation and aldosterone is spared
Conn syndromeAldosterone-secreting adenoma; aldosterone high, renin low (secondary hyperaldosteronism: renin high)Hypertension, hypokalemia
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia21-hydroxylase deficiency most often: cortisol and aldosterone low, ACTH and androgens highVirilization of girls, salt wasting; treated with glucocorticoid (and fludrocortisone)
PheochromocytomaChromaffin tumor making catecholamines ("rule of 10s")Episodic headache, sweating, palpitations, hypertension

Corticosteroid drugs

A corticosteroid crosses the membrane, displaces hsp90 from the cytoplasmic receptor, and the complex changes transcription in the nucleus. About 90% of cortisol rides on CBG; a high dose saturates it and the free fraction jumps. Names end in -sone or -solone.

DrugAnti-inflammatory potencySalt retentionNotes
Hydrocortisone (cortisol)11Short acting; replacement and the adrenal crisis
Prednisone4LessIntermediate; the common oral drug
Methylprednisolone5LessIntermediate; the Medrol Dosepak
DexamethasoneAbout 25–30Almost noneLong acting
FludrocortisoneAbout 10About 250Replaces aldosterone in Addison disease
  • Why a taper: an outside steroid suppresses CRH and ACTH, and the cortex goes into rest. Stopped abruptly, it cannot answer: adrenal insufficiency. Taken in the morning, like the natural peak, it disturbs sleep less.
  • Side effects: masked infection, oral candidiasis (inhaled steroids: rinse after), delayed healing, osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, hypertension, peptic ulcer (worse with NSAIDs), glaucoma and cataract, mood change and insomnia, hypokalemia, growth suppression in children, a cushingoid look.
  • Other adrenal drugs: ketoconazole and metyrapone (11β-hydroxylase) block cortisol synthesis for Cushing; mifepristone blocks the glucocorticoid receptor; spironolactone blocks aldosterone (hyperkalemia, gynecomastia), and eplerenone does the same with less gynecomastia.

In the dental chair

  • A patient on long-term steroids (about 20 mg prednisone a day for 3 weeks or more) should be assumed to have a suppressed axis. For routine care under local anesthesia: the usual morning dose, a morning appointment, and good anxiety and pain control. A long or stressful surgery, an infection or trauma, or a missed dose can trigger an adrenal crisis; extra steroid for a big procedure is set with the physician.
  • Adrenal crisis: severe hypotension, weakness, confusion, abdominal pain, loss of consciousness, shock. Stop, call 911, lay the patient supine with legs raised, give oxygen and 100 mg hydrocortisone IV or IM, and monitor vitals.
  • Addison disease: diffuse brown pigmentation of the gingiva, buccal mucosa and tongue. Acromegaly: a Class III bite, spacing, macroglossia, dentures that no longer fit.
full.he-thyroid:
What's tested
  • How thyroid hormone is made, stored and activated (TPO, colloid, T4 to T3)
  • Reading TSH and free T4; Graves vs Hashimoto; hyper vs hypo signs, in the mouth too; thyroid storm
  • Thyroid drugs: levothyroxine, methimazole vs propylthiouracil, radioactive iodine, iodide, beta-blockers, amiodarone
  • Thyroid cancers: papillary, follicular, medullary, anaplastic
  • PTH, vitamin D and calcitonin; hyper- and hypoparathyroidism and their labs; the jaw on the radiograph

Making thyroid hormone

  • The sodium-iodide symporter pumps iodide into the follicular cell; pendrin passes it into the colloid.
  • Thyroperoxidase (TPO), using H₂O₂, oxidizes iodide, attaches it to tyrosines on thyroglobulin (organification: MIT and DIT) and couples them: MIT + DIT = T3, DIT + DIT = T4. The hormone is stored in the colloid, the only hormone made and stored outside the cell.
  • TSH triggers endocytosis of thyroglobulin (through megalin); lysosomes free T4 and T3. The gland releases about 90% T4, a prohormone; 5′-deiodinase in the tissues makes the active T3, and inner-ring deiodination makes inactive reverse T3.
  • A large iodine load briefly blocks organification (Wolff–Chaikoff). In plasma T4 rides mostly on TBG; only the free fraction acts. Pregnancy and estrogen raise TBG: total T4 rises, free T4 stays normal.
  • Axis: TRH (Gq) → TSH (Gs) → T4 and T3; T3 is the main feedback. Actions: higher metabolic rate (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase), heat, more beta-1 receptors (fast, strong heart), brain development in infants, lower LDL cholesterol.
HyperthyroidismHypothyroidism
Commonest causeGraves disease: IgG that stimulates the TSH receptor; women far more oftenHashimoto thyroiditis (US): autoimmune destruction with anti-TPO antibodies and lymphocytes; iodine deficiency worldwide
Labs (primary)TSH low, free T4 highTSH high, free T4 low
BodyWeight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, tremor, anxiety, diarrhea; Graves adds exophthalmos and a diffuse goiterWeight gain, cold intolerance, bradycardia, fatigue, constipation, dry skin, myxedema, high cholesterol
MouthAccelerated tooth eruption in children; early loss of primary teethMacroglossia, delayed eruption, delayed wound healing; hoarseness
Dental cautionsUncontrolled: avoid excess epinephrine; stress, infection or surgery can set off thyroid stormMore sensitive to sedatives and opioids; untreated, risk of myxedema coma

Thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis) is rare and life-threatening: high fever, pulse 140 or more, agitation, delirium, vomiting, hypertension then shock, usually set off by stress, infection or surgery in a patient whose hyperthyroidism is not controlled. Stop, call 911, cool the patient; the hospital gives a beta-blocker, propylthiouracil, iodide and a glucocorticoid. Hypothyroidism is far more common in the chair than hyperthyroidism.

Thyroid development and cancer

The thyroid starts at the foramen cecum on the back of the tongue and descends: a lingual thyroid or a midline thyroglossal duct cyst that moves with swallowing are leftovers of that path. The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs behind the gland: injury in thyroid or parathyroid surgery leaves a hoarse voice.

Calcium and phosphate

About half of plasma calcium is ionized, the active part. Low calcium makes nerves too excitable: tingling lips, tetany, Chvostek sign (tapping the facial nerve twitches the face) and Trousseau sign (a blood pressure cuff sets off carpal spasm). High calcium causes lethargy, kidney stones and constipation.

full.he-diabetes:
What's tested
  • Islet cells and their hormones; how glucose releases insulin (the K-ATP channel)
  • What insulin and glucagon do; C-peptide
  • Type 1 vs type 2; the diagnostic cutoffs; HbA1c and control
  • Every diabetes drug class: mechanism, hypoglycemia risk, weight, key adverse effects; the insulin preparations
  • Diabetes in the mouth, the periodontal link, and hypoglycemia in the chair

The islets

Islets are 1–2% of the pancreas, mostly in the tail, with fenestrated capillaries and no ducts. Beta cells (about 70%) make insulin (with amylin and C-peptide), alpha cells (about 20%) glucagon, delta cells (5–10%) somatostatin, the paracrine brake on both; PP cells make pancreatic polypeptide and epsilon cells ghrelin.

  • Insulin release: glucose enters the beta cell through GLUT2 → glycolysis raises ATP → the ATP-sensitive K⁺ channel closes → the cell depolarizes → voltage-gated calcium channels open → insulin is released. Sulfonylureas and meglitinides close the same channel. Gut incretins (GLP-1, GIP) amplify release after a meal, only when glucose is up; amino acids and fatty acids also stimulate it.
  • Proinsulin is cut into insulin and C-peptide, released 1:1. C-peptide measures the patient's own insulin: low in type 1, low when hypoglycemia comes from injected insulin, high from a sulfonylurea or an insulinoma.
  • Insulin (receptor tyrosine kinase → IRS) moves GLUT4 to the membrane in muscle and fat, builds glycogen, fat and protein, blocks gluconeogenesis, lipolysis and ketogenesis, and drives potassium into cells. Brain and liver take up glucose without it.
  • Glucagon (Gs) acts on the liver: glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis. Low glucose and amino acids release it. Glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol and GH are the counter-regulatory hormones.
Type 1Type 2
CauseAutoimmune destruction of beta cells: absolute deficiencyInsulin resistance with high insulin at first ("ineffective, not deficient"), then failing beta cells
Typical patientYoung, lean, sudden onset with weight lossOlder, overweight, gradual; family history
C-peptideLowNormal or high
Acute crisisDiabetic ketoacidosis: high glucose, ketones, acidosis, Kussmaul breathing, fruity breathHyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
TreatmentInsulin to surviveLifestyle and metformin first, then other drugs, insulin later

Diagnosis (two abnormal results, or one with symptoms): HbA1c 6.5% or more, fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or more, 2-hour glucose tolerance 200 or more, or a random 200 or more with symptoms. Prediabetes: HbA1c 5.7–6.4%, fasting 100–125. HbA1c is glucose stuck to hemoglobin and reflects the last 2–3 months (red cell life): about 5% is normal, below 7% is well controlled, above 7% is poorly controlled. The classic triad is polyuria (osmotic diuresis), polydipsia and polyphagia. Gestational diabetes comes from human placental lactogen's anti-insulin effect.

Complications: microvascular (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) and macrovascular (heart attack, stroke, peripheral artery disease), with infections and poor healing from weak neutrophil function, a poor blood supply and impaired collagen.

Every drug that releases or adds insulin (insulin, sulfonylureas, meglitinides) causes hypoglycemia and weight gain. A patient with a weight problem: a GLP-1 agonist. Heart failure: an SGLT2 inhibitor (not a TZD). Regular and NPH insulin are sold without a prescription.

Diabetes in the mouth

Periodontitis is more frequent and more severe, and the link runs both ways: periodontal inflammation worsens glucose control, and periodontal treatment can lower HbA1c modestly. Also: xerostomia, candidiasis, burning mouth, caries, taste changes, enlarged parotids, delayed healing, postoperative infection, and more implant failure when control is poor.

In the dental chair

  • Before treatment ask the type, drugs, the last HbA1c and today's reading; confirm the patient ate and took the usual dose (metformin or insulin with a skipped breakfast is the classic setup for a low). Morning appointments, short visits, glucose within reach.
  • Hypoglycemia (glucose below about 70 mg/dL): sweating, tremor, tachycardia, anxiety, hunger, then confusion, slurred speech, seizure and loss of consciousness. It comes on fast; high glucose develops slowly.
  • Awake and able to swallow: 15–20 g of fast sugar by mouth (glucose tablets or gel, juice, regular soda), recheck in 15 minutes. On acarbose: glucose, not table sugar. On a GLP-1 agonist the response can be slow (slow gastric emptying).
  • Unconscious: nothing by mouth; glucagon 1 mg IM or subcutaneously (or nasal), or IV dextrose; call 911. A continuous glucose monitor may stop reading below its floor: confirm with a finger-stick.
full.he-repro:
What's tested
  • Sertoli vs Leydig cells (FSH vs LH), feedback, and reading testosterone, LH and FSH
  • The follicle, the two-cell model, the cycle's phases, the LH surge and the corpus luteum
  • Pregnancy: hCG, the placenta's hormones, labor; prolactin vs oxytocin and suckling
  • Hormonal contraception and the drugs that alter sex hormones: SERMs, aromatase inhibitors, GnRH analogs, 5α-reductase inhibitors, antiandrogens, testosterone
  • Pathology: cryptorchidism, testicular germ cell tumors, BPH vs prostate cancer, HPV and cervical neoplasia, endometrial carcinoma, vulvar lichen disorders, vaginitis, breast
  • Sex hormones and the mouth: puberty, pregnancy gingivitis and pyogenic granuloma, menopause

The male

Sertoli cellsLeydig cells
WhereInside the seminiferous tubule, basement membrane to lumenBetween the tubules (interstitium)
Driven byFSHLH
MakeAndrogen-binding protein (keeps testosterone high in the tubule), inhibin, anti-Müllerian hormone (fetus), aromataseTestosterone from cholesterol (rate-limiting: cholesterol desmolase)
AlsoTight junctions = blood-testis barrier; nourish germ cells; phagocytose shed cytoplasmTestosterone in the embryo, at puberty and through adult life
FeedbackInhibin turns down FSH (pituitary only)Testosterone turns down GnRH and LH
  • Spermatogenesis takes about 2–2½ months and needs a scrotal temperature (about 34–35 °C): spermatogonia → primary spermatocytes → meiosis → haploid spermatids → spermiogenesis (Golgi → acrosome, mitochondria → midpiece) → release. Sperm gain motility and mature in the epididymis and are capacitated in the female tract.
  • Route: tubules → tubuli recti → rete testis → efferent ductules → epididymis → vas deferens → ejaculatory duct → urethra. Seminal vesicles give about 70% of semen (fructose, prostaglandins); the prostate about 25% (PSA, citrate).
  • Erection is parasympathetic (NO → cGMP → smooth muscle relaxes); emission and ejaculation are sympathetic ("point and shoot"). Sildenafil blocks PDE5; never with nitrates (severe hypotension).
  • Development: SRY makes testes; AMH removes the Müllerian ducts; testosterone builds the Wolffian structures (epididymis, vas, seminal vesicles); DHT (5α-reductase) builds the penis, scrotum and prostate. Without them the female path is the default.
  • Labs: failing testes = testosterone low, LH and FSH high. Failing pituitary = all low. Outside testosterone = testosterone high, LH and FSH low, small testes, low sperm count.

The female cycle

  • Every follicle holds a primary oocyte arrested in prophase I; the LH surge completes meiosis I, and the ovulated secondary oocyte waits in metaphase II until fertilization.
  • Primordial follicle (flat cells) → primary (cuboidal granulosa, zona pellucida) → secondary (antrum, theca) → Graafian (about 20 mm). One dominant follicle ovulates; the rest become atretic.
  • Two cells, two gonadotropins: LH → theca cells → androgens; FSH → granulosa cells → aromatase → estradiol. (Theca is like Leydig; granulosa is like Sertoli.)
  • Follicular (proliferative) phase: estradiol rises and the lining grows; mucus thin and stretchy. When estradiol stays high (about 200 pg/mL), negative feedback flips to positive: the LH surge, then ovulation 24–36 hours later, about 14 days before menses.
  • Luteal (secretory) phase, a fixed 14 days: the corpus luteum makes progesterone (and estrogen): secretory glands, thick mucus, a slightly higher temperature. Without hCG it regresses to the corpus albicans; progesterone falls, spiral arteries constrict and the functionalis is shed, while the basalis stays to regrow it.
  • Three estrogens: estradiol (reproductive years), estriol (pregnancy), estrone (menopause, made in fat from adrenal androgens). Menopause: no follicles, so estradiol and inhibin fall and FSH and LH rise; hot flashes, bone loss, vaginal atrophy.

Pregnancy and lactation

  • Fertilization in the ampulla of the tube: sperm binding to ZP3 sets off the acrosome reaction; the cortical reaction blocks polyspermy. The blastocyst implants about day 6–7.
  • The syncytiotrophoblast makes hCG (detected by pregnancy tests, peaks about week 10), which rescues the corpus luteum so it keeps making progesterone through the first trimester; the placenta then takes over.
  • The placenta makes hCG, hPL (anti-insulin: the cause of gestational diabetes; breast growth), progesterone, estriol (it needs the fetal adrenal and liver first) and relaxin, but not oxytocin. hCG weakly stimulates the TSH receptor; estrogen raises TBG.
  • Labor: a rising estrogen-to-progesterone ratio, prostaglandins and oxytocin (posterior pituitary; positive feedback), which also limits bleeding after delivery.
  • Breast: estrogen grows the ducts, progesterone the alveoli; progesterone holds back full milk until delivery. Prolactin makes milk; oxytocin ejects it (myoepithelial cells). Suckling lowers dopamine (prolactin rises) and releases oxytocin; prolactin suppresses GnRH, so periods stop while nursing.

Reproductive pathology

Sex hormones and the mouth

Puberty and pregnancy exaggerate the gingiva's response to plaque: pregnancy gingivitis (second and third trimesters) and the pyogenic granuloma ("pregnancy tumor"), a red, bleeding, lobulated interdental mass that often shrinks after delivery. The second trimester is the best time for elective care. Menopause brings xerostomia, altered taste, burning mouth and osteoporosis.
full.he-heme:
What's tested
  • Recognizing the blood cells and their jobs; the white cells from most to least common
  • Innate vs adaptive immunity; B, T and NK cells; primary vs secondary lymphoid organs; thymus, lymph node and spleen
  • Anemias: microcytic vs macrocytic, sickle cell, and their oral signs
  • Leukemias: acute vs chronic, myeloid vs lymphoid; AML, ALL, CML, CLL; APL
  • Hodgkin vs non-Hodgkin lymphoma; Burkitt, follicular, mantle cell, MALT, diffuse large B-cell, mycosis fungoides; myeloma
  • Oral signs of blood disease and dental management

The blood cells

One pluripotent stem cell gives a myeloid line (red cells, megakaryocytes, granulocytes, monocytes) and a lymphoid line (B, T and NK cells). Red cells are most of the cells; they carry oxygen and carbon dioxide and live about 120 days. Platelets are fragments of marrow megakaryocytes that start clotting. White cells come in two classes and five types, most to least common: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils ("Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas").

CellShareLookJob
Neutrophil50–70%Multilobed nucleus, pale granules (myeloperoxidase, elastase)First line against bacteria; about 10 hours in blood
Lymphocyte20–40%Large round nucleus, thin rim of cytoplasmB cells (antibody), T cells, NK cells
Monocyte2–8%Single kidney-shaped nucleusBecomes the tissue macrophage; presents antigen (MHC II)
Eosinophil1–4%Bilobed nucleus, red granules (major basic protein)Parasites, allergy

  • Innate immunity is what the body simply does: skin and mucosa, low pH, lysozyme and thiocyanate in saliva, complement, interferons, phagocytes, NK cells. Adaptive immunity follows a first contact with an antigen, is specific and has memory: humoral (B cells → plasma cells → antibody) and cellular (T cells).
  • Helper T cells (CD4) see antigen on MHC II and help B cells; cytotoxic T cells (CD8) kill cells showing antigen on MHC I. NK cells have no B or T markers: a cell missing MHC I is killed, and in antibody-dependent killing their CD16 binds IgG.
  • Primary lymphoid organs are only the bone marrow (B cells) and the thymus (T cells). Secondary: lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils and MALT (Peyer patches in the ileum).
  • Thymus: behind the manubrium, large in infants, fat by the teens; dense cortex (positive selection), pale medulla with Hassall corpuscles (negative selection); its stroma is epithelioreticular cells (every other lymphoid organ uses reticular cells); most thymocytes die in selection. No thymus (DiGeorge): no T cells, and no parathyroids.
  • Lymph node: afferent lymphatic → subcapsular sinus → trabecular and medullary sinuses → efferent lymphatic. B cells in cortical follicles (germinal centers), T cells in the paracortex (high endothelial venules), plasma cells in the medulla.
  • Spleen: no afferent lymphatics; white pulp (the PALS, T cells around the central arteriole, and B-cell follicles) and red pulp (cords and sinusoids that cull old red cells and hold a third of the platelets). Without a spleen, encapsulated bacteria are the danger.

Anemias

Not taught as a lecture in this course, but tested on boards. Anemia shows in the mouth as pallor, a smooth sore tongue, angular cheilitis and slow healing.

Leukemias

Neoplastic cells replace the marrow and spill into the blood. Two axes: acute (blasts that don't mature, 20% or more blasts, rapid, fatal in months untreated) or chronic (cells that still mature, insidious, years), and myeloid or lymphoid. The consequences are marrow failure (anemia: fatigue, pallor; low platelets: petechiae and gingival bleeding; low neutrophils: infections and ulcers) and tissue infiltration (bone pain, spleen, liver and nodes, and gingival enlargement, where a dentist may be the first to notice).

Lymphomas

A lymphoma is a cancer of lymphocytes in nodes, spleen or any lymphoid tissue; the tissue makes the diagnosis (an excised node, fresh for flow cytometry). B symptoms: fever of 38 °C or more, drenching night sweats, loss of 10% of body weight in 6 months. A lymphoma node is firm, rubbery, painless and growing; an infected node is tender and soft. 85–90% of lymphoid cancers are B-cell.

In the dental chair

  • Unexplained gingival enlargement or bleeding, petechiae, pallor, nonhealing ulcers or a firm painless neck node: order a CBC with differential and refer promptly.
  • Before invasive care in leukemia or chemotherapy, get the counts and talk with the oncologist; elective care waits when neutrophils fall below about 1,000/µL or platelets below about 50,000/µL. Clear oral infection before chemotherapy; expect mucositis, candidiasis and herpes during it.
full.mg-giphys:
What's tested
  • The GI hormones: the cell that makes each, what releases it and what it does (gastrin, CCK, secretin, GIP, GLP-1, motilin, ghrelin), plus the paracrines (histamine, somatostatin) and neurocrines (VIP, NO, GRP, substance P)
  • Saliva: which gland makes what, isotonic primary saliva made hypotonic by the ducts, and autonomic control
  • Gastric acid: the parietal cell's pump, its three stimulants and its brakes, and the phases of secretion
  • Motility: slow waves, peristalsis vs segmentation, the migrating motor complex, gastric emptying, the colonic reflexes and defecation
  • Pancreatic and biliary secretion: secretin vs CCK, trypsin activation, bile salts and their recycling
  • Digestion and absorption of carbohydrate, protein and fat; where iron, calcium and B12 are absorbed; water and electrolyte transport, the kinds of diarrhea, and what vomiting and diarrhea do to acid-base balance
  • The liver: the proteins it makes, its zones, ammonia, drugs and alcohol, lipoproteins and bilirubin

How the gut is controlled

The gut has its own nervous system, the enteric nervous system, which can run without the brain: the submucosal (Meissner) plexus controls secretion and blood flow, and the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus, between the circular and longitudinal muscle, controls motility. Parasympathetic (vagus, pelvic) input generally speeds digestion; sympathetic input slows it. Chemical messengers act three ways: endocrine (into the blood: gastrin, CCK, secretin, GIP, GLP-1, motilin), paracrine (on neighbors: histamine, somatostatin) and neurocrine (released by nerves: VIP, NO, GRP, substance P, enkephalins). Digestion runs in four phases: cephalic/oral (sight, smell, taste and chewing act through the vagus: saliva, gastric and pancreatic secretion, gallbladder contraction and a relaxed sphincter of Oddi), gastric (distension and peptides: vagovagal and local reflexes, gastrin; acid, pepsinogen, mucus and contractions), small intestinal (chyme, its acid, fat and osmolarity: pancreatic juice and bile flow, gastric secretion is inhibited) and colonic (the ileocecal valve relaxes, water is absorbed, defecation).

HormoneCell and siteReleased byMain actions

Histamine comes from ECL cells, released by ACh and by gastrin, and acts on H2 receptors of parietal cells (cAMP), in synergy with both. Somatostatin from D cells (most importantly in the antrum) is the universal brake: released when antral pH falls below about 3, it inhibits gastrin and acid, and ACh inhibits its release, one way the vagus turns acid up. Among the neurocrines, the inhibitory nonadrenergic, noncholinergic (NANC) transmitters VIP (through cAMP) and its co-transmitter NO (through cGMP) relax smooth muscle (they open the LES), and VIP drives intestinal secretion (a VIPoma causes watery diarrhea, hypokalemia and achlorhydria). GRP carries the vagal signal to G cells, substance P (excitatory NANC, NK1 receptors) contracts muscle, and enkephalins slow transit by inhibiting ACh release (why opioids constipate).

Saliva

The parotid is the largest gland and is purely serous (amylase); the submandibular makes about 60-70% of resting saliva and is mixed; the sublingual makes about 5% and is mostly mucous. Acinar cells make primary saliva that is isotonic to plasma. The ducts reabsorb Na+ and Cl- and secrete K+ and HCO3-, but they let little water through, so final saliva is hypotonic. The faster it flows, the less time the ducts have, so high-flow saliva is closer to plasma and richest in HCO3-. About 1–1.5 L is made a day, and its control is entirely neural: no hormone drives it. Unusually, both autonomic divisions stimulate saliva: parasympathetic (ACh, Ca2+: copious, watery; blocked by atropine) and sympathetic (mainly β, cAMP: small volume, rich in protein and amylase). Saliva lubricates and buffers, starts starch digestion (α-amylase) and fat digestion (lingual lipase), and defends the mouth (lysozyme, lactoferrin, secretory IgA, mucins). In Sjögren syndrome, lymphocytes destroy the salivary and lacrimal glands: xerostomia, trouble chewing, swallowing and tasting, caries, enlarged glands and dry eyes.

Gastric secretion

Parietal cells make HCl and intrinsic factor (the one gastric product we can't live without: it is needed for B12 absorption in the terminal ileum). Inside the cell, carbonic anhydrase makes H+ and HCO3-; the H+/K+ ATPase pumps H+ into the lumen (the K+ it brings in leaks back out through apical K+ channels), Cl- follows through apical channels, and HCO3- leaves into the blood in exchange for Cl- (the "alkaline tide" after a meal). Three stimulants act directly: ACh (M3, Ca2+), gastrin (CCK-B receptor, Ca2+) and histamine (H2, cAMP). Histamine potentiates the other two, which is why an H2 blocker (famotidine, cimetidine, nizatidine) cuts acid from every stimulus; a PPI (omeprazole, lansoprazole, esomeprazole) blocks the final pump, so it works whatever the stimulus. Brakes: somatostatin, prostaglandins, low antral pH and, from the duodenum, secretin and GIP. At high secretion rates gastric juice becomes mostly HCl (100–200 mM, pH as low as 0.8–1) with little Na+ and no HCO3- to buffer it; at low rates more of it is the Na+-rich fluid of the other gastric cells. Chronic vomiting of this acid demineralizes the teeth. Chief cells make pepsinogen (released by vagal and enteric ACh and by secretin), which acid, and then pepsin itself, turns into pepsin, an endopeptidase. Surface and mucous neck cells make the mucus-bicarbonate layer that keeps the mucosal surface near pH 7; the vagus and prostaglandins drive it, which is why NSAIDs injure the stomach. Without intrinsic factor (pernicious anemia), B12 can’t be absorbed.

Phases of acid secretion: the cephalic phase (sight, smell, taste, about 30% of the acid) runs entirely through the vagus (direct ACh on parietal cells plus GRP on G cells), so vagotomy abolishes it; the gastric phase (distension, peptides, about 60%) acts through gastrin, vagovagal reflexes and local enteric reflexes; the intestinal phase is small and mostly inhibitory.

Motility

Interstitial cells of Cajal set slow waves, the basic electrical rhythm (about 3/min in the stomach, 12/min in the duodenum). The ICC sit between the circular and longitudinal muscle. A slow wave alone doesn't contract muscle; contraction happens when its peak passes threshold (about −40 mV) and spike potentials (Ca2+ entering through voltage-gated channels) fire on top of it: the more spikes, the stronger the contraction. Nerves, hormones and stretch decide how often that happens; inhibitory neurons release VIP and NO, which hyperpolarize the muscle and relax it. Swallowing is voluntary, then a medullary reflex (soft palate up, epiglottis down, UES relaxes), then primary peristalsis, with secondary peristalsis clearing what's left; the LES keeps a high resting tone (enteric nerves, vagal ACh and gastrin) and relaxes through vagal VIP and NO. In achalasia, those inhibitory (VIP/NO) myenteric neurons are lost, usually through autoimmunity or in Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi), so the LES can't relax and peristalsis fails: dysphagia to solids and liquids, regurgitation and a "bird's beak" on barium swallow; it is treated by cutting or dilating the LES, nifedipine, nitrates or botulinum toxin. GERD is not a primary motility disorder: most patients have a normal or even raised resting LES tone, and acid refluxes during transient LES relaxations (fatty meals, coffee, alcohol, nicotine, progesterone, anticholinergics, calcium channel blockers).

As a bolus arrives, the stomach relaxes to hold it (receptive relaxation, a vagovagal reflex through VIP). Antral contractions grind the meal against a nearly closed pylorus (retropulsion), and each wave squirts a little chyme into the duodenum. Gastric emptying is fastest for liquids (isotonic saline fastest) and slowest for fat (through CCK); acid in the duodenum, hypertonic or hypotonic chyme, amino acids and peptides, large particles and duodenal distension also slow it, as do secretin and GIP, which tighten the pylorus. In the small intestine (transit about 2 hours), segmentation mixes: the circular muscle contracts in the middle of the bolus, making pockets of chyme that move slowly aborally. Peristalsis propels: excitatory and inhibitory neurons fire together, so the muscle contracts behind the bolus and relaxes ahead of it. A peristaltic rush (from irritation) gives diarrhea; reverse peristalsis, vomiting. Between meals the migrating motor (myoelectric) complex (MMC, driven by motilin, about every 90 minutes) sweeps residue and bacteria into the colon; it starts about 3 hours after a meal, runs from mid-stomach to the terminal ileum, and eating stops it. Without it, bacteria overgrow. The colon (transit 30–40 hours) is the last place fluid is absorbed: the teniae coli form haustra that mix and store, and mass movements 1–3 times a day (vagus and pelvic nerves, gastrin and CCK) push feces into the rectum. Reflexes: gastrocolic (food in the stomach → colonic mass movements), gastroileal (food in the stomach → ileocecal valve relaxes; both through parasympathetic nerves, gastrin and CCK), coloileal (cecal stretch → the ileocecal valve closes, an intrinsic enteric reflex), and the defecation reflex (rectal stretch → rectum contracts and the involuntary internal anal sphincter relaxes, while the voluntary external sphincter, tonically contracted, decides when; the urge comes when the rectum is about 25% full). In Hirschsprung disease neural crest cells never reach the distal colon (RET mutations; more common in boys and in Down syndrome), so the aganglionic segment can't relax.

Pancreas and bile

Pancreatic acinar cells make enzymes (driven by CCK and ACh); duct cells make HCO3- through CFTR (driven by secretin). Secretin, CCK and ACh potentiate each other. Pancreatic juice (1–2.5 L a day, 80–90% of it from the ducts) is mostly water and NaHCO3; as flow rises, HCO3- rises and Cl- falls. Secretin answers duodenal pH below 4.5; CCK answers fat and the amino acids phenylalanine, methionine and tryptophan; the vagus adds a small cephalic part. Compared with saliva, both start as an acinar fluid that the ducts modify, but salivary ducts pull out NaCl and leave saliva hypotonic, while pancreatic ducts add HCO3- and water and the juice stays isotonic; and saliva is controlled only by nerves, the pancreas by nerves and hormones. Proteases are secreted inactive: brush-border enteropeptidase (enterokinase) turns trypsinogen into trypsin, and trypsin activates the rest (chymotrypsin, elastase, carboxypeptidase) and more trypsinogen. Amylase, lipase, RNase and DNase are secreted active; colipase is secreted as procolipase and activated by trypsin. Pepsin is a stomach enzyme, not a pancreatic one.

Hepatocytes make the primary bile acids (cholic and chenodeoxycholic) from cholesterol and conjugate them with glycine or taurine (bile salts), which lowers their pKa so they stay ionized in the lumen; gut bacteria deconjugate and dehydroxylate them into the secondary ones (deoxycholic and lithocholic). The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile between meals; CCK (with vagal input) contracts it and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi, and secretin adds water and HCO3- from the bile ducts. About 95% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum by a Na+-coupled transporter and return in portal blood (enterohepatic circulation): a pool of about 3 g cycles 4–12 times a day, and the 0.2–0.6 g lost in stool each day is replaced from cholesterol. Returning bile acids speed bile flow and slow new synthesis, and bile is the body’s only route for excreting cholesterol. Remove or inflame the ileum (Crohn disease) and bile salts are lost: steatorrhea, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency and gallstones, with B12 deficiency as well.

Bilirubin comes from the breakdown of hemoglobin. It travels in blood bound to albumin (unconjugated); the liver takes it up, conjugates it with glucuronic acid and secretes it in bile. Gut bacteria turn it into colorless urobilinogen, some of which is reabsorbed and leaves in urine as urobilin; the rest becomes stercobilin, which colors stool. Jaundice is prehepatic (hemolysis: sickle cell disease, thalassemia, hemolytic disease of the newborn), hepatic (poor uptake or conjugation: hepatitis, cirrhosis, neonatal jaundice) or posthepatic (blocked bile flow: gallstones, tumors).

NutrientDigested byAbsorbed as / how
CarbohydrateSalivary and pancreatic α-amylase, then brush-border lactase, sucrase, maltaseMonosaccharides only. Glucose and galactose: SGLT1 (secondary active, Na+-coupled); fructose: GLUT5; all exit by GLUT2
ProteinEndopeptidases (pepsin, trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase), then exopeptidases (carboxypeptidases A and B) and brush-border peptidasesAmino acids (Na+-coupled carriers) and di- and tripeptides (PepT1, driven by an H+ gradient; split to amino acids inside the cell); a little whole protein by endocytosis. Amino acids leave into blood by Na+-independent facilitated diffusion
