Short- and medium-chain fatty acids go straight into portal blood
Iron, calciumDuodenum (iron as heme or Fe2+; calcium helped by vitamin D)
Folate / B12Folate in the jejunum; B12 bound to intrinsic factor in the terminal ileum

Water, electrolytes and diarrhea

About 9 L of fluid enter the gut each day (2 L eaten, 7 L secreted): the small intestine absorbs about 7 L (the jejunum the most), about 2 L reach the colon, which absorbs about 1.9 L, and about 0.1 L is left in stool (about 99% absorbed). Water follows osmotic gradients in either direction. Plicae, villi and microvilli give the small intestine about 600 times the area of a plain tube; the colon has no villi. Villi absorb; crypts secrete. Na+ is absorbed with glucose and amino acids in the jejunum, as NaCl in the ileum, and through aldosterone-driven ENaC channels in the colon, which also secretes K+ (so diarrhea causes hypokalemia). Crypt cells secrete Cl- through CFTR when cAMP rises. Cholera toxin's B subunit binds the GM1 ganglioside and its A subunit locks Gsα on, so adenylyl cyclase makes huge amounts of cAMP and PKA opens CFTR: Cl-, with Na+ and water, pours out in a secretory diarrhea that goes on during fasting (VIP, irritant laxatives such as senna and many bacteria and viruses do the same). Oral rehydration works because Na+-glucose cotransport is untouched. Osmotic (malabsorptive) diarrhea comes from unabsorbed solute (lactase deficiency, celiac disease, magnesium laxatives) and stops with fasting. Diarrhea also comes from fast transit (more peristalsis, less segmentation) and from inflammation that breaks the epithelial barrier (Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis). Secretion is raised by VIP, ACh, serotonin, histamine, prostaglandins, bacterial toxins and bile acids; absorption is raised by aldosterone, glucocorticoids, somatostatin, norepinephrine and opioids (why opioids stop diarrhea).

Vomiting is run by the brainstem vomiting center, fed by the chemoreceptor trigger zone (area postrema, outside the blood-brain barrier: drugs and toxins), the gut (through 5-HT and dopamine), the inner ear and higher centers. Saliva pours out, reverse peristalsis brings intestinal contents back into the stomach, the glottis closes, the abdominal wall contracts and the LES and esophagus relax. Vomiting loses H+, Cl- and K+: a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (breathing slows and PCO2 rises), with more K+ lost in urine as aldosterone answers the volume loss. Diarrhea loses the HCO3- the lower gut secretes: a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (breathing speeds up and PCO2 falls), often with hypokalemia too.

The liver

The liver is the first stop for all blood leaving the gut; its jobs are exocrine (bile), endocrine (plasma proteins), metabolic, storage and protective. Hepatocytes make albumin (colloid osmotic pressure; carries hydrophobic drugs), transferrin (iron), ceruloplasmin (copper), α1-antitrypsin, complement, lipoproteins and most clotting factors (fibrinogen, prothrombin, V, VII, IX and X), but not factor VIII, which comes from endothelium. So cirrhosis lowers albumin and prolongs the PT/INR while factor VIII stays normal. The liver stores glycogen, iron and vitamins A, D and B12 (B12 for years); it makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D, which the kidney turns into the active 1,25 form. Kupffer cells lining the sinusoids eat the gut bacteria that reach portal blood. Between meals glucagon breaks down glycogen and drives gluconeogenesis (from lactate, pyruvate and amino acids), and epinephrine breaks down glycogen in fight or flight; glucose-6-phosphatase, which muscle and brain lack, lets the liver release free glucose. After a meal insulin drives glycogen storage.

The zones follow the blood from the portal triad to the central vein. Zone 1 (periportal, most oxygen): gluconeogenesis and glycogen breakdown, β-oxidation, cholesterol synthesis, plasma proteins and urea (carbamoyl phosphate synthetase: high capacity, low affinity). Zone 3 (around the central vein, least oxygen): glycolysis and glycogen made from glucose, lipogenesis, bile acid synthesis, glutamine synthesis (glutamine synthetase: low capacity, high affinity, catching the ammonia zone 1 missed) and most CYP450 drug metabolism, so zone 3 dies first in hypoxia and after acetaminophen. Ammonia comes mostly from the gut, where bacteria break down protein and urea; the liver turns it into urea for the kidneys, and a failing liver lets it reach the brain (hepatic encephalopathy).

Drugs go through phase I (CYP450 oxidation in the smooth ER: more polar, sometimes the active or a toxic form; induced by phenobarbital and smoking, inhibited by cimetidine), phase II (conjugation, most often with glucuronic acid) and phase III (secretion into bile or blood); what the liver removes on the first pass is why oral doses are larger than IV ones. Acetaminophen is safe at 1–4 g a day; about 5% becomes NAPQI through CYP450 (2E1 among others), which glutathione neutralizes. An overdose (above about 10–15 g, or less with chronic alcohol use or fasting) uses up glutathione and kills zone 3; N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione and protects about 90% of patients when given within 8–10 hours. Ethanol is oxidized by alcohol dehydrogenase, which saturates at low blood levels (below about 100 mg/dL), and above that by the microsomal system (CYP2E1). Alcohol causes fatty liver, and injured hepatocytes activate stellate (Ito) cells, which stop storing vitamin A and lay down collagen (TGF-β1): fibrosis, then cirrhosis.

Fat in the blood: chylomicrons lose triglyceride to lipoprotein lipase on capillary endothelium, and their cholesterol-rich remnants are taken up by the liver, which sends triglyceride back out as VLDL. VLDL shrinks to IDL and then LDL, rich in cholesterol and taken up through LDL receptors, while HDL collects cholesterol from tissues and brings it back to the liver (SR-B1) to become bile acids or be secreted in bile.
full.mg-gianat:
What's tested
  • Foregut, midgut and hindgut: their arteries and boundaries, the stomach's arteries and the main anastomoses
  • Peritoneum: visceral vs parietal pain, referred pain by gut region (appendicitis), retroperitoneal organs, the ligament of Treitz, SMA syndrome
  • Portal-caval anastomoses and what portal hypertension does at each one; the pectinate line
  • Abdominal wall: layers, rectus sheath and the arcuate line, dermatomes, inguinal hernias, diaphragm openings
  • Histology: the four layers and the two enteric plexuses, the esophagus, stomach glands and cells, duodenum vs jejunum vs ileum vs colon, oral mucosa, papillae and salivary glands
  • Liver, gallbladder and pancreas histology: the three lobule models, zones 1-3, the flow of blood, bile and lymph, sinusoids and their cells; centroacinar cells

Foregut, midgut, hindgut

RegionArteryExtentPain referred to
ForegutCeliac trunkAbdominal esophagus to the major duodenal papilla (2nd part of duodenum); liver, gallbladder, pancreas (part); spleen is supplied tooEpigastric region
MidgutSuperior mesenteric (SMA)Distal duodenum, jejunum, ileum, cecum, appendix, ascending colon, proximal 2/3 of transverse colonUmbilical region (T10)
HindgutInferior mesenteric (IMA)Distal 1/3 of transverse colon, descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, anal canal above the pectinate lineHypogastric (suprapubic) region

Celiac branches: left gastric (lesser curvature, abdominal esophagus), splenic (short gastrics to the fundus, left gastroepiploic to the greater curvature, pancreatic branches) and common hepatic. The common hepatic gives the proper hepatic (right and left hepatic, right gastric, cystic) and the gastroduodenal (right gastroepiploic, superior pancreaticoduodenals). So: lesser curvature = right and left gastric; greater curvature = right and left gastroepiploic; fundus = short gastrics. A posterior duodenal bulb ulcer erodes the gastroduodenal artery (major bleeding); an anterior one perforates into the peritoneal cavity.

SMA and IMA branches: the SMA leaves the aorta at L1 (the transpyloric plane), just below the celiac trunk and behind the neck of the pancreas, then crosses in front of the uncinate process, the left renal vein and the 3rd part of the duodenum. It gives the inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries, many jejunal and ileal (intestinal) branches from its left side, and from its right side the middle colic (proximal 2/3 of the transverse colon), the right colic (ascending colon) and the ileocolic (distal ileum, cecum and, through the appendicular artery in the mesoappendix, the appendix). The IMA leaves the aorta at L3, 3–4 cm above its bifurcation, and gives the left colic (descending colon), 2–5 sigmoid arteries and the superior rectal, its terminal continuation to the upper rectum.

Anastomoses: the superior (celiac, through the gastroduodenal) and inferior (SMA) pancreaticoduodenal arteries around the head of the pancreas, the only connection between the celiac trunk and the SMA; the marginal artery (of Drummond) along the edge of the colon, formed by the ileocolic, right, middle and left colic and sigmoid arteries, the collateral between SMA and IMA; superior epigastric (internal thoracic) with inferior epigastric (external iliac) inside the rectus sheath. The left colic (splenic) flexure, where SMA and IMA territories meet, has the least arterial supply (a watershed), so colonic ischemia shows there first.

Peritoneum and position

Parietal peritoneum lines the wall and has somatic nerves: sharp, well localized pain. Visceral peritoneum covers organs and has visceral afferents: dull, poorly localized pain referred by region. Appendicitis starts as periumbilical pain (midgut visceral afferents to T10) and moves to the right lower quadrant (McBurney point) once the inflamed appendix irritates the parietal peritoneum. McBurney point, two-thirds of the way from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine, marks the base of the appendix, which stays fixed even though the rest of the appendix varies in position. The lumen is usually blocked by lymphoid hyperplasia in young people and by a fecalith in older ones. A mesentery attached to the back wall is a "meso-"; a fold joining two organs or the front wall is a "ligament"; one attached to the stomach is an omentum. The falciform ligament holds the ligamentum teres (old umbilical vein); the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) holds the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, with the epiploic foramen behind it.

Retroperitoneal ("SAD PUCKER"): suprarenal glands, aorta and IVC, duodenum (parts 2-4), pancreas (not the tail), ureters, colon (ascending and descending), kidneys, esophagus, rectum. The transverse and sigmoid colon, jejunum, ileum and stomach are intraperitoneal. The ligament of Treitz (suspensory ligament of the duodenum) at the duodenojejunal flexure, left of L2, divides upper GI bleeding (hematemesis, melena) from lower (hematochezia, bright red blood per rectum). SMA syndrome: the 3rd part of the duodenum is squeezed between the SMA and aorta (often after rapid weight loss). Nutcracker syndrome: the left renal vein is squeezed there instead, backing up the left kidney, adrenal and gonadal veins: hematuria, proteinuria, abdominal pain and, in men, a painful left varicocele that shrinks when he lies down.

Intussusception: a proximal segment of bowel telescopes into the adjoining distal one, most often ileocolic (ileum into the colon). It is the main cause of bowel obstruction from 3 months to 6 years, can cut off the blood supply, and is fatal within days if untreated. Most cases have no known cause; a Peyer patch swollen after an infection can lead it in. Diverticula are outpouchings of the mucosa at weak points where arteries pierce the wall, mostly in the sigmoid colon of older people; they can become infected and rupture (sepsis).

Portal-caval anastomoses

Unpaired gut organs (the GI tract, spleen and pancreas) drain to the portal vein, which carries about 75% of the liver's blood (the hepatic artery the rest); the paired organs and the back wall drain straight to the IVC. The portal system lies ventral to the caval system: on a cross section the anterior of the two large veins is the portal vein and the posterior one the IVC. Normally the pressures in the two systems match and very little blood crosses the portal-caval anastomoses. When cirrhosis or a liver cancer blocks flow through the liver, portal pressure rises and, since the portal veins have no valves, blood takes these shortcuts, which dilate into varices:

SitePortal sideCaval sideResult
EsophagusLeft gastric veinEsophageal veins to the azygosEsophageal varices (life-threatening hematemesis)
UmbilicusParaumbilical veinsSuperficial epigastric veinsCaput medusae
RectumSuperior rectal vein (to the IMV)Middle and inferior rectal veins (to the internal iliac)Anorectal varices (the course's slides call them internal hemorrhoids)

Pectinate line: above it the canal is hindgut (endoderm): superior rectal artery (IMA), portal venous drainage, visceral nerves (painless internal hemorrhoids), adenocarcinoma. Below it, ectoderm: inferior rectal artery (internal iliac via internal pudendal), caval drainage, somatic pudendal nerves (painful external hemorrhoids), lymph to superficial inguinal nodes, squamous cell carcinoma.

Rectum and anal canal: the rectum begins at S3, lies on the sacrum as the most posterior pelvic organ, and widens into the ampulla, the fecal reservoir. Puborectalis holds the anorectal (perineal) flexure and relaxes with both sphincters for defecation. The pectinate line joins the anal valves at the lower ends of the anal columns. The internal anal sphincter is involuntary smooth muscle; the external is voluntary skeletal muscle. The lining runs from simple columnar (rectum) through a transitional zone to nonkeratinized stratified squamous, then keratinized skin at the anus; anal glands sit in the submucosa.

Abdominal wall

Superficial to deep: skin, superficial fascia (fatty Camper, membranous Scarpa), external oblique (down and in), internal oblique (up and in), transversus abdominis (horizontal), transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, parietal peritoneum. Their aponeuroses form the rectus sheath. Above the arcuate line the sheath has anterior and posterior layers; below it all three aponeuroses pass in front, so only transversalis fascia lies behind the rectus. Linea alba is the midline; linea semilunaris is the lateral edge of the rectus. Dermatomes: T4 nipple, T6 xiphoid, T10 umbilicus, L1 groin.

Inguinal canal: from the deep ring (in transversalis fascia, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels) to the superficial ring (external oblique aponeurosis); it carries the spermatic cord or the round ligament, plus the ilioinguinal nerve. An indirect hernia enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through a patent processus vaginalis (congenital, the most common type). A direct hernia pushes through Hesselbach triangle (inferior epigastric vessels, rectus edge, inguinal ligament), medial to the vessels, where the transversalis fascia is weak (older men). "MDs don't LIe": Medial = Direct, Lateral = Indirect. Umbilical folds: median (urachus; a patent urachus leaks urine at the umbilicus), medial (obliterated umbilical arteries), lateral (inferior epigastric vessels).

Diaphragm (phrenic nerve, C3-C5): IVC at T8, esophagus and vagal trunks at T10, aorta, thoracic duct and azygos at T12 ("I 8 10 eggs at 12"). The spleen sits under ribs 9-11 in the left upper quadrant, the organ most often injured in blunt left-side trauma.

GI histology

Four layers everywhere: mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae; it protects, absorbs and secretes), submucosa (dense irregular connective tissue, the larger vessels and lymphatics, the submucosal (Meissner) plexus, glands in the esophagus and duodenum), muscularis externa (inner circular, outer longitudinal, with the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus between them; the stomach adds an inner oblique layer), and serosa (free organs: mesothelium on connective tissue, the visceral peritoneum) or adventitia (fixed ones like the thoracic esophagus: connective tissue only). The enteric nervous system can run without the CNS. Meissner = mucosal functions: gland secretion, local blood flow and movement of the mucosa. Auerbach = action: the muscularis externa, coordinating peristalsis.

RegionSignature features
EsophagusNonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium in longitudinal folds; prominent muscularis mucosae; mucous esophageal glands proper in the submucosa (and esophageal cardiac glands in the lamina propria near the stomach); muscle skeletal in the upper third, mixed in the middle, smooth in the lower third; adventitia in the thorax; abrupt squamous-to-columnar Z-line at the stomach
StomachRugae (folds of mucosa and submucosa that flatten as it fills), gastric pits lined by surface mucous cells, no villi. Pits are shallow in the fundus and body and deepest in the pylorus. Cardia and pylorus: coiled mucous glands (G cells in the antrum). Fundus and body: long oxyntic glands with parietal cells (pink from their many mitochondria, upper and middle gland: HCl, intrinsic factor) and chief cells (basophilic from their rough ER, gland base: pepsinogen), mucous neck cells, ECL and D cells. Enteroendocrine granules sit at the cell base, toward the capillaries
DuodenumVilli plus Brunner glands in the submucosa (alkaline mucus); bile and pancreatic ducts open at the major papilla
JejunumTallest plicae circulares and long villi; no Brunner glands; the main site of absorption
IleumPeyer patches (lymphoid follicles) with M cells that sample antigens; most goblet cells of the small intestine
ColonNo villi or plicae; straight crypts full of goblet cells; teniae coli, haustra, epiploic appendages

Small intestine surface area is amplified by plicae circulares (permanent folds with a submucosal core, unlike rugae; tallest in the distal duodenum and jejunum, fewer and smaller in the ileum), villi (mucosa only, a core of lamina propria) and microvilli (the enterocytes' brush border, the largest gain). Each villus core holds capillaries, strands of smooth muscle and a central lacteal: long-chain fats leave the enterocyte as chylomicrons, too big for capillaries, into the lacteal. Villi absorb; the crypts of Lieberkühn, invaginations of the mucosa between the villi (not submucosal glands), hold stem cells and secrete, with Paneth cells (bright pink granules) at their base releasing lysozyme and defensins. Goblet cells increase from the duodenum to the ileum and on down the colon. Plasma cells in the lamina propria make the dimeric IgA that the epithelium carries into the lumen.

Appendix: colon-type mucosa with crypts and no villi, a small irregular lumen, and a nearly continuous ring of lymphoid nodules reaching into the submucosa; Paneth cells are present.

Oral mucosa: masticatory (gingiva, hard palate: keratinized or parakeratinized, bound to bone), lining (lips, cheeks, floor of mouth, ventral tongue, soft palate: nonkeratinized), specialized (dorsal tongue). Papillae: filiform (most numerous, heavily keratinized, bent backward for rasping, no taste buds), fungiform (mushroom-shaped, scattered, parakeratinized, taste buds on top), circumvallate (7–12 large ones in a V near the back of the tongue, each in a deep trench with taste buds in its side walls, flushed by serous von Ebner glands) and foliate (folds on the sides of the tongue, many in infancy but only a few in adults, taste buds in their side walls). Taste buds are pale, barrel-shaped groups that open at a taste pore: gustatory cells (apical microvilli, synapse with sensory nerves), supporting cells and basal (stem) cells that replace them. The lip has three surfaces: skin (keratinized, with hair follicles and glands), the vermilion (thin epithelium over tall connective tissue papillae that bring capillaries near the surface, its red color, and no glands) and the oral mucosa (nonkeratinized, with labial salivary glands), around a core of orbicularis oris.

Salivary glands: acinus → intercalated duct (simple cuboidal; adds HCO3-, takes up Cl-) → striated duct (simple columnar, inside the lobule; basal infoldings packed with mitochondria for ion transport: reabsorbs Na+, secretes K+ and HCO3-) → excretory ducts (in the connective tissue septa between lobules; columnar to stratified). The acinus, intercalated duct and striated duct form the salivon, the functional unit: acini make primary saliva, isotonic to plasma, and the ducts, letting little water follow, make it hypotonic. Myoepithelial cells, between the secretory cells and their basement membrane, contract to squeeze the acini and first ducts. Serous acini stain dark (rough ER, protein granules) with round nuclei and small lumens; mucous ones are pale (mucin washes out in processing) with flattened basal nuclei and wider lumens; serous demilunes cap mucous tubules.

GlandAciniShare of salivaClues
ParotidAlmost all serousAbout 30%; most of the amylaseThe largest; dark acini with scattered fat cells
SubmandibularMixed, mostly serous (about 90%)About 60%The longest striated ducts; serous demilunes on some mucous tubules
SublingualMixed, mostly mucousAbout 5%The smallest; pale, with well-developed serous demilunes; several small ducts, not one main duct

Minor glands: von Ebner glands (at the circumvallate papillae) are serous, posterior lingual glands (by the lingual tonsil) mucous and anterior lingual glands mixed. Secretory IgA: plasma cells around the secretory units make dimeric IgA joined by a J chain; the epithelium takes it up at its base, carries it across and releases it with secretory component, which protects it from enzymes. It stops microbes and toxins from attaching to the surface.

Liver, gallbladder and pancreas

Hepatocytes sit in plates between sinusoids, so blood passes close to nearly every cell. The liver has a dual supply: oxygen-rich blood in the hepatic artery and nutrient-rich blood in the portal vein, which mix in the sinusoids. Three ways to draw the lobule: the classic lobule (hexagon around a central vein, portal triads at the corners; blood flow), the portal lobule (triangle around a triad; bile flow) and the hepatic acinus (diamond between two central veins; the metabolic unit). In the acinus, zone 1 (periportal) gets the most oxygen; zone 3 (centrilobular) gets the least and has the most CYP450, so it is hit first by ischemia, acetaminophen and alcohol.

Three flows in three spaces: blood runs from the triad through the sinusoids to the central vein, then the sublobular, collecting and hepatic veins to the IVC. Bile runs the other way: hepatocytes secrete it into canaliculi, channels between neighboring hepatocytes sealed by tight junctions, with no lining of their own; then the canals of Hering; then bile ductules lined by cholangiocytes; then the bile ducts of the triad. Lymph forms as plasma fluid enters the space of Disse (between the sinusoid's endothelium and the hepatocytes' microvilli) and flows toward lymphatics in the portal tract. In a portal triad, the portal vein branch is the largest, with a thin wall; the hepatic artery branch is small with a thick wall; the bile duct is a ring of cuboidal cells. A central vein stands alone.

Sinusoids have fenestrated, discontinuous endothelium over the space of Disse. Kupffer cells, resident macrophages in the sinusoid lining, remove bacteria, debris and old red cells; stellate (Ito) cells in the space of Disse store vitamin A and fat and, when activated by chronic injury, lay down the collagen of fibrosis. The gallbladder stores bile and concentrates it up to 10 times, and contracts when CCK is released; it has tall, branching mucosal folds (not villi) of simple columnar cells with microvilli, a lamina propria, an irregular smooth muscle coat, and no muscularis mucosae or submucosa.

Pancreas: mostly dark exocrine acini (basal rough ER, apical zymogen granules) with pale, capillary-rich islets of Langerhans scattered among them. Pale centroacinar cells in the center of the acini are the start of the intercalated ducts, and there are no striated ducts and no myoepithelial cells: centroacinar cells mean pancreas, striated ducts mean salivary gland. Acinar cells release the enzymes, the proteases as inactive zymogens (stimulated by CCK and ACh); duct and centroacinar cells release bicarbonate-rich fluid (stimulated by secretin).
full.mg-gipath:
What's tested
  • Esophagus and stomach: GERD and its dental erosion, eosinophilic and infectious esophagitis, Barrett esophagus, varices, esophageal cancers, gastritis (H. pylori, chemical, autoimmune), peptic ulcers and NSAID injury, stomach tumors, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
  • Bowel: celiac disease and malabsorption in the mouth, Crohn disease vs ulcerative colitis, C. difficile and microscopic colitis, diverticular disease, appendicitis, ischemic bowel, Hirschsprung disease, colon polyps and colorectal cancer, and the polyp syndromes with oral signs
  • Liver: liver tests, injury patterns, hepatic failure and portal hypertension, the hepatitis viruses and hepatitis B serology, alcoholic, fatty, autoimmune and drug-induced liver disease, acetaminophen, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, liver tumors, jaundice and the biliary tract
  • The patient with liver disease in the dental chair: oral and eye signs, bleeding tests, the drugs the liver clears, infection control
  • GI drugs: PPIs, H2 blockers, antacids, misoprostol and bismuth; antiemetics and their side effects (extrapyramidal effects, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, long QT); antidiarrheals and laxatives; IBD drugs

Esophagus and stomach

Esophageal disease shows as dysphagia, odynophagia (painful swallowing), retrosternal pain, hematemesis and melena. GERD is reflux through an incompetent LES (low LES tone, transient relaxations, a sliding hiatal hernia, obesity, pregnancy, scleroderma) and the most common cause of esophagitis: heartburn, regurgitation, dysphagia, cough and hoarseness. Biopsy shows basal cell hyperplasia, long lamina propria papillae and intraepithelial eosinophils and neutrophils. Reflux esophagitis can lead to ulcers, a stricture, Barrett esophagus or cancer. In the mouth, GERD causes erosion of the palatal (lingual) surfaces of the maxillary teeth (2–4 times as common as in people without reflux), posterior occlusal cupping, sensitivity, halitosis, xerostomia and burning mouth (bulimia erodes the same surfaces), and GERD patients grind their teeth more at night. Care: refer for medical treatment, fluoride, diet counseling and brushing timed away from acid episodes. Eosinophilic esophagitis looks like reflux but has a normal pH, doesn't respond to acid drugs and causes food impaction; the epithelium is packed with eosinophils (microabscesses). Infectious esophagitis is Candida, herpes simplex or CMV; chemical esophagitis follows lye, acids, hot liquids, pills or radiation.

Barrett esophagus is intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells) above the gastroesophageal junction: velvety, salmon-colored mucosa in 5–15% of patients with chronic reflux symptoms, most often white men. It raises the risk of adenocarcinoma 30- to 100-fold, so every biopsy is reported for dysplasia. Adenocarcinoma, in the distal esophagus of older white men, is now over half of US esophageal cancer. Squamous cell carcinoma of the esophagus (upper and middle thirds), once far more common and now declining, follows tobacco, alcohol, nitrosamines and poor nutrition; the two carry a similar poor prognosis. Esophageal varices are dilated submucosal veins of the distal esophagus from portal hypertension (cirrhosis): silent until they rupture, and about 40% of ruptures are fatal. A Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal tear at the gastroesophageal junction after forceful vomiting.

Gastritis. H. pylori is the most common cause of chronic (active) gastritis. Reactive (chemical) gastropathy follows NSAIDs, alcohol and bile reflux, and iron pills can injure the mucosa too. Atrophic gastritis (autoimmune, or environmental metaplastic) destroys the parietal cells that make intrinsic factor, so B12 is no longer absorbed in the small intestine (pernicious anemia, with glossitis).

H. pylori is a curved, flagellated gram-negative rod whose urease makes ammonia that buffers the acid around it; it clings to the gastric mucosa and releases products that drive inflammation. It is found in about 42% of US patients with peptic ulcer disease (the share varies by population) and raises the risk of gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma. Ulcers cause epigastric pain, bleeding and anemia; duodenal ulcer pain tends to ease with food, gastric ulcer pain worsens with it. Diagnose with a urea breath test, stool antigen or biopsy. First-line eradication is bismuth quadruple therapy (PPI, bismuth, metronidazole, tetracycline) or rifabutin triple therapy (PPI, rifabutin, amoxicillin); vonoprazan with amoxicillin is another option. NSAIDs are the other main cause (about 4 times the ulcer risk, with more bleeding and perforation): they block COX-1 and COX-2, and the lost prostaglandins normally hold back acid secretion and keep up mucus, bicarbonate and blood flow. NSAIDs that block COX-1 more do more GI harm than COX-2-selective ones, and the risk climbs with anticoagulants, corticosteroids, SSRIs and age. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is a gastrin-secreting tumor (pancreas or duodenum, sometimes with MEN1): severe, multiple or jejunal ulcers and diarrhea, treated with high-dose PPI.

Stomach tumors. Benign: leiomyoma, lipoma, GIST (from the interstitial cells of Cajal, c-KIT; it can turn malignant) and polyps: fundic gland polyps (sporadic, or with FAP; possibly linked to PPIs), hyperplastic polyps (with chronic gastritis) and adenomas (older adults). Gastric adenocarcinoma is declining in the US and is more common in East Asia and in men. Its risks are H. pylori, atrophic gastritis, a diet of cured, smoked and pickled foods, smoking and genes. It is silent until late (weight loss, pain, anorexia, anemia, melena), spreads to the liver, lymph nodes and peritoneum, and fewer than 20% live 5 years; finding it early is what improves survival. It grows as a fungating, flat, ulcerating (it can mimic a peptic ulcer) or diffusely infiltrating mass; the diffuse, signet-ring cell type makes a rigid "leather bottle" stomach (linitis plastica). Gastric lymphoma is mostly MALT lymphoma, tied to H. pylori.

Bowel

Celiac disease is an immune reaction to gluten (wheat) in HLA-DQ2/DQ8 carriers: anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA, and a duodenal biopsy with villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and intraepithelial lymphocytes (in latent disease, the lymphocytes with normal villi). The lost surface area causes malabsorption: diarrhea with greasy, bulky stools, iron-deficiency anemia, dermatitis herpetiformis and, in the mouth, recurrent aphthous ulcers, symmetric enamel hypoplasia, delayed tooth eruption and glossitis; unexplained enamel defects can be the first sign. Treatment is a gluten-free diet.

Malabsorption shows in the mouth (celiac disease, Crohn disease, long-term PPIs): iron deficiency gives atrophic glossitis, angular cheilitis and pale mucosa; B12 deficiency a burning, smooth tongue and ulcers; folate deficiency glossitis and red mucosa.

Inflammatory bowel disease is an abnormal immune response to the normal gut flora and self antigens in genetically susceptible people; both kinds cause relapsing inflammation, mucosal destruction and intermittent bloody diarrhea. In dental care, their immunosuppressive drugs raise the infection risk, corticosteroids delay healing, and anemia and nutritional deficiencies are common.

Crohn diseaseUlcerative colitis
WhereAnywhere mouth to anus, most often terminal ileum; segmental, skip lesionsColon only: starts in the rectum and spreads continuously up the colon
DepthTransmural: fissures, fistulas, strictures, abscesses, adhesions, obstructionMucosa and submucosa: crypt abscesses, pseudopolyps; fibrosis, fistulas and perforation are rare
HallmarksNoncaseating granulomas (in about half), linear ulcers, cobblestone mucosa, creeping fat; smoking worsens itNo granulomas; bloody diarrhea, often with more bleeding and pain; toxic megacolon; slightly more common than Crohn disease
Outside the gutUveitis, polyarthritis, sclerosing cholangitis, kidney disordersPolyarthritis, sacroiliitis and ankylosing spondylitis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, primary sclerosing cholangitis (more often than with Crohn disease)
Colon cancerHigher risk than in the general populationHigher risk than in the general population
MouthMore common: cobblestoning, linear ulcers, mucosal tags, diffuse mucosal and lip swelling, orofacial granulomatosis, aphthous-like ulcers; can come before any gut symptomsLess common: aphthae; pyostomatitis vegetans ("snail-track" pustules)

C. difficile (pseudomembranous) colitis is overgrowth of toxin-making C. difficile after broad-spectrum antibiotics (clindamycin is the classic one, also cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones) and PPIs: toxins A and B, fever, cramps, watery diarrhea and gray-yellow pseudomembranes of necrotic exudate. Treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin and avoid antimotility drugs. Microscopic colitis (lymphocytic or collagenous) gives severe watery diarrhea with a normal-looking colonoscopy; only the biopsy shows it. Diverticulosis (outpouchings through weak muscle, mostly sigmoid, low-fiber diets) is mostly silent and can bleed; diverticulitis gives left lower quadrant tenderness, fever and sometimes an abscess. Appendicitis follows obstruction of its opening (a fecalith, tumor, parasites or a foreign body, though often none is found), with distention and bacterial invasion: periumbilical pain that moves to the right lower quadrant, nausea and vomiting, a low fever and a high white count; it can perforate. Ischemic bowel disease strikes the elderly with sudden abdominal pain, distention and bloody diarrhea and has a high mortality; ischemic colitis favors the splenic flexure, a watershed area. Hirschsprung disease: neural crest cells fail to reach the distal colon, the aganglionic segment can't relax, and the colon above it dilates (delayed meconium).

Colon polyps and cancer. A polyp is any raised mucosa, sessile or pedunculated. Hyperplastic polyps, mostly left-sided, are the most common serrated polyps; adenomas (tubular, tubulovillous, villous) are the precursors of cancer. Colorectal adenocarcinoma is the second leading cause of US cancer death (about 9%). Most follow the adenoma-carcinoma sequence (normal mucosa, aberrant crypt foci, adenoma, invasive carcinoma, metastasis; APC, then KRAS, then p53). Its risks are a high-fat, low-fiber diet, familial adenomatous polyposis, Lynch syndrome (HNPCC) and IBD. Cases under 50 are rising, so screening now starts at 45. It is silent for a long time; a left-sided (descending) cancer obstructs early (a change in bowel habits, crampy pain, an annular "napkin ring" tumor), and a right-sided (ascending) cancer bleeds slowly and shows as iron-deficiency anemia. Familial adenomatous polyposis (autosomal dominant APC) becomes cancer in every case without surgery. Syndromes a dentist may spot first: Gardner syndrome (an APC variant of FAP: jaw osteomas, supernumerary and impacted teeth, odontomas, epidermoid cysts) and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11: hamartomatous polyps and dark macules on the lips and buccal mucosa).

Liver

The liver's reserve is huge, so disease often stays silent until 80–90% of its function is lost, and the mouth and eyes may show it first. Liver tests fall into three groups: hepatocyte function (albumin, the prothrombin time/INR, ammonia), hepatocyte integrity (AST, ALT and LDH, which leak from damaged cells) and biliary excretion (alkaline phosphatase, total and direct bilirubin, urine bilirubin). AST and ALT up is a hepatocellular pattern; alkaline phosphatase up is a cholestatic one.

Injury patterns: ballooning, steatosis (stored triglyceride) and stored iron or copper; inflammation; necrosis and apoptosis, zonal (zone 3, by the central vein, first in ischemia) or focal, bridging, submassive or massive; and fibrosis. Acute hepatitis shows a swollen liver, ballooning hepatocytes and acidophil (Councilman) bodies, with AST and ALT 5–10 times normal; most infections are silent, symptomatic ones start flulike (malaise, nausea, low fever) and then turn jaundiced, most recover within weeks, and under 1% turn fulminant (about 80% of those die without a transplant). Chronic hepatitis is disease lasting more than 6 months: portal inflammation and, with time, portal then bridging fibrosis that ends in cirrhosis, the irreversible end stage of most chronic liver disease: regenerative nodules wrapped in bridging fibrous septa. Its causes are alcohol, viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease, biliary disease, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency and unknown ones (cryptogenic). How strongly the immune system answers a hepatitis virus sets the course: an adequate response clears it, an excessive one is fulminant, a marginal one becomes chronic and a failed one leaves a carrier.

VirusSpreadChronic?Notes
A (RNA)Fecal-oralNoAbout half of US acute hepatitis; about 4 weeks' incubation; clears within 8 weeks; IgM anti-HAV diagnoses it; vaccine
B (DNA)Blood, sex, birth, needlesticks4–10% of adults, about 90% of newbornsVaccine; about 1.5% of dental patients carry it; chronic infection leads to cirrhosis and HCC; serology below
C (RNA)Blood (IV drugs)Most (75–85%)No vaccine (its sequence keeps changing); often silent; cirrhosis in 20–40% of chronic infections, and HCC; 30% of liver transplants; PCR diagnosis; cured by direct-acting antivirals; linked to oral lichen planus and dry mouth and eyes
D (RNA)BloodWith BDefective: needs HBsAg, so it comes only as a coinfection or superinfection with B (suspect it when hepatitis B suddenly worsens); the B vaccine prevents it
E (RNA)Fecal-oral (water)NoEndemic in Asia and Mexico; mild, 1–4 weeks, but up to 25% die in pregnancy

Hepatitis B serology: HBsAg means infected now (acute or chronic); HBeAg means highly infectious; IgM anti-HBc means a recent, acute infection; IgG anti-HBc means a past or ongoing infection; anti-HBs means immune. A vaccinated person has anti-HBs alone (no anti-HBc, since the vaccine is surface antigen only); a person who cleared an infection has anti-HBs with IgG anti-HBc; a chronic carrier has HBsAg for more than 6 months, with anti-HBc and no anti-HBs.

Alcoholic liver disease is the most common liver disease in the US (over 60% of chronic cases, 40–50% of cirrhosis deaths, up to 45% of HCC); it affects 10–15% of heavy drinkers, at about 80 g of alcohol a day for men or 20 g for women over 10–12 years. It runs from reversible steatosis to alcoholic steatohepatitis (ballooning, necrosis, Mallory-Denk bodies, neutrophils, AST:ALT above 2) and perivenular fibrosis to cirrhosis; the treatment is abstinence. Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NAFLD/NASH) looks the same under the microscope without the alcohol: up to 5% of Americans, driven by insulin resistance and tied to obesity, diabetes and the metabolic syndrome, and it can go on to cirrhosis. Autoimmune hepatitis mostly affects women (about 78%): AST and ALT rise more than alkaline phosphatase, with ANA, anti-smooth muscle or anti-LKM antibodies, high globulins, often another autoimmune disease, and no viral, drug or alcohol cause; it responds dramatically to immunosuppression, so these patients are often on steroids (infection risk). Drugs and toxins cause about 10% of acute hepatitis but 10–20% of fulminant hepatitis: over 1100 drugs, among them antibiotics (erythromycin, isoniazid, nitrofurantoin), anticonvulsants, psychotropics, anesthetics, oral contraceptives and acetaminophen, with inherited differences in CYP450 metabolism.

Acetaminophen causes about 46% of acute liver failure, most of it by accident. At toxic doses CYP450 makes more NAPQI than glutathione can neutralize, and zone 3 dies; N-acetylcysteine restores glutathione and works best within the first 8–10 hours. Chronic alcohol use lowers the safe dose, and dental patients often already take it in several products, so add up every source before prescribing more.

Metabolic disease. Hemochromatosis deposits iron, a direct hepatotoxin, in the liver (cirrhosis, HCC), pancreas (diabetes), heart (failure) and skin (bronzing): "bronze diabetes." Labs: high serum iron and ferritin, low TIBC. Primary hemochromatosis is autosomal recessive (HFE) and shows in the 40s, in men more than women (menstrual blood loss protects women); secondary hemochromatosis follows transfusions or ineffective erythropoiesis. Treat with phlebotomy. Wilson disease (autosomal recessive, ATP7B) can't excrete copper into bile, so copper builds up in the liver (hepatitis, cirrhosis), the basal ganglia (psychosis, parkinsonism) and the cornea (Kayser-Fleischer rings, seen early with a slit lamp); it is usually diagnosed at 11–16 years, with low ceruloplasmin, and treated with copper chelation. Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (autosomal recessive): hepatocytes can't secrete this protease inhibitor, so it builds up in them (cirrhosis) while the unprotected lungs get emphysema.

Hepatic failure comes when 80–90% of function is lost, most often from long-standing chronic disease (hepatitis, alcohol, hemochromatosis) and acutely from massive necrosis (drugs, toxins, viral hepatitis). It brings jaundice, low albumin, high ammonia with hepatic encephalopathy (treated with lactulose and rifaximin; it can cloud consent and cooperation), coagulopathy (the liver makes most clotting factors, among them II, V, VII, IX and X; II, VII, IX and X also need vitamin K, which is poorly absorbed in cholestasis), hepatorenal syndrome, fetor hepaticus (a musty breath from mercaptans), palmar erythema, spider angiomas, and hypogonadism and gynecomastia (estrogen isn't cleared). Portal hypertension is prehepatic (portal vein thrombosis), intrahepatic (cirrhosis) or posthepatic (Budd-Chiari syndrome, a blocked hepatic vein outflow): varices and portosystemic shunts (caput medusae), ascites, and splenomegaly that traps platelets (thrombocytopenia). Cirrhosis also carries a high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma.

Liver tumors. Metastases (from the colon, among others) are the most common liver tumors, and hepatocellular carcinoma is the most common primary one. Only about 10% of HCCs arise in a normal liver; the rest follow cirrhosis from alcohol, hepatitis B or C, fatty liver disease, toxins, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease or glycogen storage disease. HCC grows into vessels, alpha-fetoprotein is its marker, and the prognosis is poor. Benign: hemangioma (the most common) and hepatocellular adenoma (oral contraceptives, glycogen storage disease).

Jaundice appears above about 2–3 mg/dL of bilirubin, in the sclera first: unconjugated from hemolysis or Gilbert syndrome; conjugated from obstruction (dark urine, pale stools, itching). Gallstones are mostly cholesterol stones (about 85%; female, over 40, obesity, pregnancy); pigment stones follow hemolysis. A stone in the cystic duct causes cholecystitis (acute from obstruction; chronic, nearly always with stones): right upper quadrant pain that can be referred to the right shoulder, vomiting and fever; in the common bile duct, jaundice; at the ampulla, pancreatitis (whose other big cause is alcohol). Cholangiocarcinoma is an adenocarcinoma of the bile ducts that shows late, with obstructive jaundice.

The dental patient with liver disease

  • Oral signs: jaundice of the soft palate and floor of the mouth; petechiae, ecchymoses and gingival bleeding (fewer clotting factors and platelets); fetor hepaticus; a smooth tongue, glossitis and cheilitis (poor nutrition); xerostomia, sialadenitis and Sjögren-like dryness; a crusted perioral rash; bruxism; and parotid enlargement in alcohol use. Oral lichen planus is a reason to ask about hepatitis C. In the eyes: scleral icterus (often the first visible jaundice) and Kayser-Fleischer rings.
  • Bleeding: before extractions, oral surgery or extensive periodontal work, consult the physician and check the PT/INR (clotting factor synthesis) and the platelet count (splenic sequestration); use local hemostatic measures.
  • Drugs the liver clears: amide local anesthetics (lidocaine, prilocaine, mepivacaine, bupivacaine), analgesics (aspirin, acetaminophen, ibuprofen, codeine, meperidine), sedatives (diazepam, barbiturates), antibiotics (erythromycin, clindamycin, tetracycline) and antifungals (ketoconazole, fluconazole). In significant liver disease, lower the doses, lengthen the intervals, stay well under local anesthetic maximums and work with the physician. The lecture lists erythromycin, clindamycin and tetracycline as antibiotics to avoid, and the general anesthetics halothane and thiopental as contraindicated. Acetaminophen at a reduced dose (about 2 g a day at most) is the usual analgesic; avoid NSAIDs in cirrhosis (bleeding, ulcers, kidney injury); sedatives last longer.
  • Infection control: about 1.5% of dental patients carry hepatitis B, and hepatitis C survives on surfaces for up to 5 days: standard precautions, instrument sterilization, hepatitis B vaccination for the whole team and a post-exposure plan. After a needlestick, HBV transmits far more readily than HCV, and HCV more than HIV.

GI drugs

Drug (clue)MechanismKey points
PPIs (-prazole): omeprazole, esomeprazole, pantoprazoleIrreversibly block the H+/K+ ATPase; weak-base prodrugs that collect and are activated in the acid canaliculus, so they act on secreting pumpsMost effective acid suppressors (80–95% of basal and stimulated acid): ulcers and H. pylori, GERD and erosive esophagitis, gastrinomas (ZE), NSAID ulcers, stress bleeding, dyspepsia. Take 30 min before a meal; full effect in 3–4 days. Long-term: low B12 (glossitis, anemia, neuropathy) and Mg, enteric infections such as C. difficile (fractures and pneumonia uncertain); rebound acid on stopping, so taper; less absorption of drugs that need acid; some CYP interactions

Steroids induce remission but don't maintain it (long-term: adrenal suppression, osteoporosis, cataracts, glaucoma, high glucose, delayed healing). Azathioprine: marrow suppression, pancreatitis, liver injury, lymphoma; low TPMT activity raises toxicity. Methotrexate (Crohn disease): mucositis and stomatitis (folic acid helps), liver and lung injury, teratogen; NSAIDs slow its elimination. Anti-TNF: screen for TB and hepatitis B and C; infections, heart failure, lymphoma. All raise infection risk and blunt vaccines; no live vaccines
full.mg-bone:
What's tested
  • Cartilage: the three types, appositional vs interstitial growth, type II collagen and aggrecan, poor repair
  • Bone: matrix (type I collagen, hydroxyapatite), the three cells, the osteoclast's acid machine, M-CSF, RANKL and OPG, why PTH acts on osteoclasts indirectly
  • Intramembranous vs endochondral ossification, the growth plate, remodeling, and calcium control by PTH, vitamin D, calcitonin and FGF-23
  • Bone disorders: osteogenesis imperfecta, achondroplasia, osteopetrosis, cleidocranial dysplasia, Paget disease, osteoporosis, osteomalacia and rickets, with their oral findings
  • Bone drugs: calcium and vitamin D, bisphosphonates, denosumab, teriparatide, romosozumab, raloxifene, and medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ)

Cartilage

Cartilage is avascular, aneural and alymphatic, fed by diffusion, so it repairs poorly. Chondroblasts from the inner perichondrium add matrix at the surface (appositional growth, girth); chondrocytes inside lacunae divide into isogenous groups (interstitial growth, length). Its matrix is type II collagen plus aggrecan, a bottle-brush proteoglycan on hyaluronan whose negative charge holds water and resists compression. SOX9 is the chondrocyte master gene; collagen hydroxylation needs vitamin C (scurvy).

TypeWhereFeatures
HyalineArticular surfaces, trachea, larynx, fetal skeleton, growth platesMost common; type II collagen; articular cartilage has no perichondrium and can't repair
ElasticExternal ear, epiglottisElastic fibers; has perichondrium
FibrocartilageIntervertebral discs, menisci, pubic symphysis, TMJ discTypes I and II collagen; no perichondrium; resists tension and compression

Bone and its cells

Bone holds 99% of the body's calcium and 85% of its phosphorus. It is about 30% organic (90% of that type I collagen, plus osteocalcin, osteopontin and osteonectin), 50% mineral (hydroxyapatite) and 20% water, and it grows only by apposition. Osteoblasts line bone surfaces, lay down osteoid (unmineralized matrix), make alkaline phosphatase, and end as lining cells, osteocytes or by apoptosis. Osteocytes (90-95% of bone cells) sit in lacunae, talk through canaliculi and sense load; they make sclerostin (brakes bone formation through Wnt) and FGF-23 (wastes phosphate). Osteoclasts come from the monocyte-macrophage line and fuse into giant multinucleated cells. A sealing zone walls off a Howship lacuna; carbonic anhydrase II and an H+ pump at the ruffled border make HCl (pH about 4) that dissolves mineral, and cathepsin K digests the collagen.

Coupling: osteoblasts and osteocytes make M-CSF and RANKL; RANKL binds RANK on precursors and makes osteoclasts. OPG is the osteoblast's decoy receptor that soaks up RANKL. Estrogen raises OPG, lowers RANKL and speeds osteoclast apoptosis, which is why bone loss accelerates after menopause. Osteoclasts have no PTH receptors: PTH acts on osteoblasts, which raise RANKL. Continuous PTH resorbs bone; intermittent PTH builds it.

Bone is laid down first as woven bone, then remodeled into lamellar bone: cortical (osteons around Haversian canals, joined by Volkmann canals) and trabecular. Don't confuse osteon (structural unit) with osteoid (new matrix).

Making bone and controlling calcium

Intramembranous ossification turns mesenchyme straight into bone: the skull vault, maxilla, most of the mandible and most of the clavicle (and an extraction socket heals the same way). Endochondral ossification replaces a hyaline cartilage model: long bones, vertebrae, pelvis, skull base. The growth plate runs reserve → proliferation → hypertrophy → calcification → ossification; estrogen closes it in both sexes. The mandibular condyle has its own secondary cartilage growth site. Remodeling never stops: activation, resorption (weeks), reversal, formation and mineralization (months).

When calcium falls, PTH raises it: bone (through osteoblast RANKL), kidney (keeps calcium, wastes phosphate, switches on 1α-hydroxylase) and gut (through calcitriol). Vitamin D is made in skin by UVB, 25-hydroxylated in the liver and 1α-hydroxylated in the kidney; calcitriol raises gut calcium and phosphate absorption. Calcitonin (thyroid C cells) lowers calcium. FGF-23 from osteocytes wastes phosphate; its excess causes hypophosphatemic rickets, which in the mouth gives large pulp chambers and abscesses of intact teeth.

Hypocalcemia (after parathyroid removal in thyroid surgery, vitamin D deficiency, CKD): perioral tingling, muscle cramps and tetany (Chvostek and Trousseau signs), long QT, cataracts; in children, enamel hypoplasia. Hypercalcemia (primary hyperparathyroidism, cancer): stones, bones, abdominal groans and psychiatric moans, constipation and weakness; hyperparathyroidism in the jaws shows loss of the lamina dura and brown tumors. Treat severe hypercalcemia with IV saline, then a bisphosphonate, denosumab or calcitonin.

Bone disorders

DisorderDefectWhat you see
Osteogenesis imperfectaType I collagen (COL1A1/COL1A2, dominant; CRTAP or P3H1, recessive)Too little bone: fractures, blue sclerae, hearing loss, dentinogenesis imperfecta
AchondroplasiaFGFR3 gain of function (dominant; most new mutations, older fathers)Endochondral growth fails, appositional is normal: short limbs, normal trunk, large head
OsteopetrosisOsteoclasts can't acidify (e.g. carbonic anhydrase II)Dense but brittle bone, marrow failure (anemia, infections), cranial nerve palsies, jaw osteomyelitis after extraction; cured by stem cell transplant
Cleidocranial dysplasiaRUNX2 (needed for osteoblasts)Absent or small clavicles, open fontanelles, many unerupted supernumerary teeth
Paget diseaseChaotic remodeling: osteolytic → mixed → osteoscleroticOver 50; skull, spine, pelvis, femur; very high alkaline phosphatase; mosaic bone; maxilla more than mandible: widening jaw, spacing, dentures stop fitting, "cotton wool" radiopacity, hypercementosis, bleeding at surgery; rarely osteosarcoma
OsteoporosisResorption exceeds formation; bone is normally mineralized but there is less of itPostmenopausal (trabecular: vertebrae, wrist) and senile (hip); DEXA T-score ≤ -2.5; glucocorticoids are the top drug cause
Osteomalacia / ricketsVitamin D deficiency: osteoid isn't mineralizedLow calcium and phosphate, high PTH and alkaline phosphatase; rickets: bowed legs, rachitic rosary, frontal bossing, delayed eruption, enamel hypoplasia

Fracture repair: hematoma, then a soft procallus (about week 1), a bony callus of woven bone (weeks 2-3), bridging, and remodeling. Osteoporosis in the dental patient means thinner alveolar bone, more ridge resorption after extraction, and patients on antiresorptives.

Bone drugs

DrugMechanismKey points
Calcium, vitamin DSupplementsCarbonate needs stomach acid (take with food); citrate absorbs without it; separate calcium by about 4 hours from tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, levothyroxine and bisphosphonates
Bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate oral; zoledronic acid IV)Pyrophosphate analogs that bind hydroxyapatite; resorbing osteoclasts take them up; nitrogen-containing ones block farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase (mevalonate pathway) and the cell diesFirst line for osteoporosis; also Paget, bone metastases, hypercalcemia of malignancy. Oral: empty stomach, plain water, upright 30 minutes (esophagitis). Stay in bone for years. Risks: MRONJ, atypical femur fractures, hypocalcemia
DenosumabMonoclonal antibody to RANKLInjected every 6 months; doesn't stay in bone, so stopping it brings rebound loss and vertebral fractures; hypocalcemia; MRONJ risk similar to or higher than bisphosphonates
Teriparatide (abaloparatide)Intermittent PTH-receptor activation: anabolicDaily injection, about 2 years (osteosarcoma in rats); can raise calcium; avoid in Paget disease, prior skeletal radiation and open growth plates; the osteoporosis drug not linked to MRONJ
RomosozumabAntibody to sclerostin: builds bone and slows resorption12 months; boxed warning for MI and stroke
RaloxifeneSERM: estrogen agonist in bone, antagonist in breastFewer vertebral fractures and breast cancers; raises clot risk
Calcitonin (salmon)Inhibits osteoclastsWeak; Paget disease, hypercalcemia

MRONJ

Medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw is exposed jawbone for more than 8 weeks in a patient on an antiresorptive (or antiangiogenic) drug who has had no jaw radiation. Antiresorptives stop the remodeling that repairs everyday microdamage, and the jaws carry heavy loads. The risk is highest with high-dose IV therapy for cancer (about 1-5%), far lower with oral drugs for osteoporosis, and rises with longer use, extractions and other bone surgery (the usual trigger), periodontal disease, steroids, diabetes and smoking; the mandible is hit more than the maxilla. Prevent it: finish extractions and remove infection before the drug starts, keep hygiene excellent, use atraumatic technique, and in high-risk patients prefer endodontics over extraction. Talk to the physician about timing; stopping the drug for surgery is not a settled practice.
full.mg-joints:
What's tested
  • Osteoarthritis vs rheumatoid arthritis (the lecturer's main point, with gout), including the TMJ; gout and pseudogout; HLA-B27 and the seronegative spondyloarthropathies
  • Autoimmune disease: how tolerance fails; Sjögren syndrome (the one most relevant to dentistry), lupus, scleroderma, Graves vs Hashimoto, myasthenia gravis and the rest
  • Nutrition: what each vitamin and mineral does and what its deficiency looks like, especially in the mouth; marasmus vs kwashiorkor
  • Bone and soft tissue tumors: metastases first, then each primary tumor's age, site and signature

Osteoarthritis vs rheumatoid arthritis

OsteoarthritisRheumatoid arthritis
NatureDegenerative cartilage failure; the most common joint diseaseSystemic autoimmune disease (CD4+ T cells, HLA-DR4); women 3:1
JointsWeight-bearing joints (hips, knees), DIP and PIP, first CMC, spine; often asymmetricSymmetric small joints: MCP, PIP, wrists; spares the DIP
Pain and stiffnessWorse with use, better with rest; morning stiffness under 30 minutesMorning stiffness over an hour, better with use; fatigue, low fever
PathologyLost proteoglycan first, then fibrillation, eburnation, subchondral cysts, osteophytes: Heberden (DIP) and Bouchard (PIP) nodesInflamed synovium creeps over the joint as a pannus that erodes cartilage and bone, then fibrous and bony ankylosis; ulnar deviation, swan-neck, boutonnière
LabsNormalRheumatoid factor (IgM against IgG Fc; about 80%, not the cause) and anti-CCP (more specific)
Beyond the jointNoneRheumatoid nodules, vasculitis, anemia, scleritis, secondary Sjögren syndrome
TMJCondylar flattening, osteophytes, crepitusBilateral condylar resorption: progressive anterior open bite and retrusion
TreatmentWeight loss, exercise, analgesics; nothing halts itNSAIDs, steroids, methotrexate (the anchor DMARD), anti-TNF biologics

If you see "pannus," think RA. The lecture called the RA mechanism, the JIA categories, the reactive-arthritis skin terms and the urate-handling genes low yield.

Gout is the most common inflammatory arthritis: monosodium urate crystals, seen as needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals in joint fluid. Hyperuricemia usually comes from under-excretion (kidney disease, thiazide and loop diuretics, low-dose aspirin, alcohol), less often overproduction (high cell turnover). The classic attack is sudden, excruciating and in one joint, the first MTP; untreated it becomes tophaceous gout with kidney damage. Acute attacks: NSAIDs, colchicine or steroids. Prevention: allopurinol or febuxostat (xanthine oxidase inhibitors) or probenecid (uricosuric). Pseudogout is calcium pyrophosphate: rhomboid, positively birefringent, usually the knee.

Seronegative spondyloarthropathies (RF-negative, HLA-B27, sacroiliitis, enthesitis, anterior uveitis): ankylosing spondylitis (young men, low back pain worse at night and better with exercise, bamboo spine; NSAIDs first), reactive arthritis (arthritis, urethritis and conjunctivitis 1-3 weeks after a GI or GU infection), psoriatic arthritis and enteropathic arthritis (with IBD). Juvenile idiopathic arthritis starts before 16, is often oligoarticular, RF-negative and ANA-positive, and threatens the eyes through chronic uveitis.

Autoimmune disease

Autoimmunity is a loss of self-tolerance. Central tolerance deletes self-reactive T cells in the thymus (AIRE makes thymic cells show self-antigens) and B cells in marrow. Peripheral tolerance catches escapees: anergy (antigen without a co-stimulatory second signal), regulatory T cells, activation-induced death through Fas-FasL, and hiding antigens in privileged sites (eye, testis, brain). Susceptibility genes (HLA) plus infection (molecular mimicry, released self-antigen) break it, and tissue damage exposes new epitopes (epitope spreading).

DiseaseTarget / antibodiesKey and oral findings
Sjögren syndromeLymphocytes destroy salivary and lacrimal glands; anti-SS-A (Ro), anti-SS-B (La), RF, ANAWomen 40-60; dry mouth and eyes, rampant cervical and root caries, candidiasis, parotid swelling; alone or with RA or SLE. Diagnose with a labial minor salivary gland biopsy. Watch for B-cell (MALT) lymphoma. Treat with fluoride, saliva substitutes, pilocarpine or cevimeline
SLEANA (sensitive, not specific); anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith (specific)Women 9:1; malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers, arthritis, serositis, nephritis, cytopenias. Drug-induced lupus: hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid (anti-histone). Dental: steroid cover, low platelets, infection risk
Systemic sclerosisVascular injury plus fibroblast collagen overproduction; limited (CREST, anticentromere) or diffuse (anti-Scl-70)Tight skin, Raynaud, dysphagia; microstomia and limited opening, xerostomia, uniform widening of the PDL space, resorption of the mandibular angle
Graves diseaseIgG that stimulates the TSH receptorHyperthyroid (low TSH, high T4), diffuse goiter, exophthalmos; the most common cause of hyperthyroidism
Hashimoto thyroiditisAnti-TPO and anti-thyroglobulin; cytotoxic T cellsPainless goiter, hypothyroid (high TSH), Hürthle cells, lymphoid germinal centers; lymphoma risk
Myasthenia gravisAntibodies that block the ACh receptorPtosis and diplopia first, weakness worse with use; thymoma; death from respiratory failure
Goodpasture syndromeAntibodies to type IV collagenLung hemorrhage plus glomerulonephritis; young men
Type 1 diabetes; multiple sclerosisT cells kill β cells; demyelinationMS: deficits separated in time and place

Nutrition

The lecturer's rule: know what each nutrient does and what happens without it. Fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) are stored, so deficiency is slow and usually means fat malabsorption; water-soluble ones need regular intake, except B12, which the liver stores for years.

NutrientJobDeficiency

DCalcium absorption, mineralizationRickets (children), osteomalacia (adults)
EMembrane antioxidantPosterior-column and spinocerebellar signs, hemolysis
KCarboxylates factors II, VII, IX, XBleeding (PT rises first); newborns get a shot; antibiotics and liver disease
B1 thiamineATP productionDry beriberi (neuropathy), wet beriberi (heart failure), Wernicke-Korsakoff in alcoholics: give thiamine before glucose
B2, B3, B6CoenzymesAngular cheilitis and glossitis (B2, B6); pellagra: dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia (B3); isoniazid neuropathy (B6)
FolateDNA synthesisMegaloblastic anemia without neurologic signs; glossitis; neural tube defects

ZincEnzymes, healingPoor taste and wound healing, periorificial rash, night blindness

Protein-energy malnutrition: marasmus is total calorie lack (over 60% weight loss, wasted muscle and fat, no edema); kwashiorkor is protein lack out of proportion to calories, and its discriminator is edema from low albumin, with a fatty liver.

Tumors of bone and soft tissue

Most tumors in bone are metastases, from breast, lung, thyroid, kidney and prostate ("BLT with a kosher pickle"); prostate metastases are blastic, most others lytic. In the jaw they favor the mandibular molar region and can numb the chin. Primary tumors cluster around the knee.

TumorWho and whereSignature
OsteochondromaTeens; metaphysis of long bonesMost common benign tumor: a cartilage-capped bony stalk; multiple = hereditary exostoses
Giant cell tumorAges 20-40; epiphysis around the kneeLytic "soap bubble," locally aggressive, recurs; osteoclast-type giant cells

OsteosarcomaTeens (and older adults with Paget disease or radiation); metaphysis of distal femur or proximal tibiaMost common primary malignant bone tumor; tumor cells make osteoid; Codman triangle, sunburst; lung metastases. In the jaws: patients in their 30s, symmetric PDL widening
ChondrosarcomaOver 50; pelvis, shoulder, ribsMalignant cartilage; second most common primary malignant bone tumor
