Soft tissue: benign tumors outnumber malignant ones about 100 to 1. Lipoma is the most common soft tissue tumor; liposarcoma (MDM2 amplification) grows deep in the thigh and retroperitoneum. Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft tissue sarcoma of childhood, often in the head and neck; cardiac rhabdomyoma goes with tuberous sclerosis. Leiomyoma (uterine fibroid) is the most common neoplasm in women.
full.mg-skin:
What's tested
  • Skin structure: the epidermal layers and cells, desmosomes vs hemidesmosomes, glands, Meissner vs Pacinian corpuscles
  • Dermatologic drugs: what raises absorption, topical steroids vs calcineurin inhibitors, isotretinoin, antifungals, scabicides, mupirocin
  • Skin and oral mucosal disease: pemphigus vs pemphigoid vs dermatitis herpetiformis, lichen planus, psoriasis, BCC vs SCC vs melanoma
  • Muscle contraction: the sarcomere, excitation-contraction coupling, the cross-bridge cycle
  • The neuromuscular junction: succinylcholine, nondepolarizing blockers and their reversal, malignant hyperthermia, spasmolytics, botulinum toxin

Skin structure

The epidermis is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, from the bottom up: basale (stem cells, melanocytes, Merkel cells), spinosum (keratinocytes joined by desmosomes; Langerhans cells), granulosum (keratohyalin and lamellar granules that seal the barrier), lucidum (thick skin of palms and soles only) and corneum (dead, flattened cells; the main barrier to drugs). The dermis is papillary (loose) over reticular (dense irregular) connective tissue; the hypodermis is fat.

  • Melanocytes (neural crest) make melanin from tyrosine (tyrosinase) and hand melanosomes to keratinocytes. Skin color depends on melanosome number, size and spread, not on the number of melanocytes. Albinism: normal melanocytes, no working tyrosinase. Vitiligo: melanocytes destroyed (autoimmune).
  • Langerhans cells present antigen (Birbeck granules); Merkel cells sense light touch.
  • Desmosomes join cell to cell through cadherins (desmoglein 1 and 3); hemidesmosomes anchor basal cells to the basement membrane through BP180 (type XVII collagen), BP230 and integrin.
  • Glands: eccrine sweat (everywhere, thermoregulation, sympathetic but cholinergic), apocrine (axilla and groin, into hair follicles, active from puberty), sebaceous (holocrine, into follicles; in the mouth as Fordyce granules).
  • Receptors: Meissner corpuscles in the dermal papillae of hairless skin (light, discriminative touch, rapidly adapting); Pacinian corpuscles deep in the dermis and hypodermis (vibration and deep pressure, rapidly adapting).
  • Oral mucosa vs skin: no stratum lucidum, no hair or sweat glands; keratinized on the gingiva, hard palate and dorsal tongue, nonkeratinized elsewhere.

Dermatologic drugs

Absorption through skin rises with a thinner stratum corneum (face, eyelids, scrotum vs palms and soles), hydration and occlusion, inflamed or broken skin, and in infants (more surface per kilogram). Topical means acting on the skin; transdermal means delivering through it into the blood (nicotine, fentanyl, scopolamine patches).

DrugHow it worksUse and the point to know
Topical corticosteroidsAnti-inflammatory; potency from very high to lowEczema, psoriasis, lichen planus. Atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, acne, HPA suppression with large areas or occlusion; low potency on the face
Tacrolimus, pimecrolimusTopical calcineurin inhibitors: block T-cell IL-2Eczema of the face and eyelids: no skin atrophy; burning; boxed warning about malignancy
IsotretinoinOral retinoid: shrinks sebaceous glandsSevere nodular acne. Teratogen (the iPLEDGE program); cheilitis, xerostomia, dry skin, high triglycerides, mood change; not with tetracyclines (intracranial hypertension)
Tetracyclines (doxycycline, minocycline)Protein synthesis (30S); anti-inflammatoryAcne, rosacea. Stain developing teeth (under 8, pregnancy), photosensitivity, chelated by antacids
TerbinafineBlocks squalene epoxidaseOral for onychomycosis; check the liver
AzolesBlock lanosterol 14α-demethylaseTinea, candidiasis; systemic azoles inhibit CYP3A4
PermethrinHolds open the parasite's nerve sodium channelsScabies and lice
MupirocinBlocks bacterial isoleucyl-tRNA synthetaseImpetigo; nasal MRSA carriage
Psoriasis systemicsMethotrexate (folate antagonist), biologics against TNF, IL-17 or IL-23Methotrexate: oral ulcers, liver toxicity; biologics: infection risk

Skin and oral mucosal disease

Pemphigus vulgarisBullous / mucous membrane pemphigoidDermatitis herpetiformis
Antibody targetIgG against desmoglein 3 (and 1): desmosomesIgG against BP180, BP230: hemidesmosomesIgA against epidermal transglutaminase
SplitIntraepidermal, suprabasal acantholysis ("tombstone" basal row)SubepidermalSubepidermal, neutrophils in the dermal papillae
ClinicalFlaccid bullae that rupture; Nikolsky positive; oral lesions usually come first; can kill untreatedTense bullae, Nikolsky negative, older adults. Mucous membrane form: desquamative gingivitis, eye scarringVery itchy vesicles on elbows and knees; celiac disease; dapsone and a gluten-free diet
ImmunofluorescenceNet-like, between cellsLinear along the basement membraneGranular IgA in the papillae
  • Lichen planus: purple, polygonal, itchy papules with Wickham striae on the skin; in the mouth, bilateral lacy white striae on the buccal mucosa (reticular) or painful erosions (erosive). A band of T lymphocytes along the junction destroys basal cells (sawtooth rete ridges, Civatte bodies). Topical steroids.
  • Psoriasis: well-demarcated plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces, nail pitting, Auspitz sign, Koebner phenomenon; parakeratosis, Munro microabscesses. In the mouth it is rare, but geographic tongue (migrating red patches with white borders) and fissured tongue go with it.
  • Lupus: oral ulcers and white striae; scleroderma: microstomia, uniform PDL widening (both in the autoimmune subsection).
  • Epithelial growths: seborrheic keratosis ("stuck-on," benign; a sudden crop suggests internal cancer); actinic keratosis (sun-damaged, premalignant; on the lower lip, actinic cheilitis); verruca vulgaris and squamous papilloma (HPV).
  • Basal cell carcinoma: the most common skin cancer; a pearly papule with rolled borders and telangiectasia on the face (the upper lip more than the lower), palisading basal cells, hedgehog pathway (PTCH); locally destructive, almost never metastasizes.
  • Squamous cell carcinoma: the second most common; sun-exposed skin and the lower lip; UV, immunosuppression, tobacco, alcohol; keratin pearls; can metastasize.
  • Melanoma: ABCDE (asymmetry, border, color, diameter over 6 mm, evolving); Breslow thickness is the strongest prognostic factor; BRAF V600E. Oral melanoma prefers the hard palate and maxillary gingiva and has a poor prognosis.

Skeletal muscle

The sarcomere runs Z line to Z line. Thin filaments (actin with tropomyosin and troponin) anchor at the Z line; thick filaments (myosin) sit in the A band, held at the M line; titin gives elasticity. During contraction the filaments slide: the A band stays the same length, while the I band and H zone shorten and the Z lines move closer.

Excitation-contraction coupling: the action potential runs down the T-tubule, where the voltage-sensing dihydropyridine receptor is mechanically linked to the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) of the sarcoplasmic reticulum (a triad: one T-tubule between two terminal cisternae). Calcium floods out and binds troponin C; tropomyosin rolls off myosin's binding sites. Cross-bridge cycle: myosin binds actin; release of Pi drives the power stroke; ATP binding detaches myosin from actin (no ATP: rigor mortis); ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the head. Relaxation needs ATP too, for SERCA to pump calcium back into the SR.

Type I fibers are slow, oxidative, red and fatigue-resistant (posture); type II fibers are fast, glycolytic and fatigue quickly. Duchenne muscular dystrophy: X-linked loss of dystrophin, boys, calf pseudohypertrophy, Gower sign.

The neuromuscular junction and its drugs

Calcium entry releases ACh, which opens the muscle's nicotinic receptors; acetylcholinesterase ends the signal. Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins so ACh isn't released (used for TMD pain, bruxism, cosmetic lines, spasticity).

  • Succinylcholine, the depolarizing blocker: fasciculations, then flaccid paralysis; fast onset and short action for intubation. Broken down by plasma pseudocholinesterase: a person with the atypical enzyme stays paralyzed for hours. Phase I block is worsened, not reversed, by neostigmine. Risks: hyperkalemia (burns, crush injury, denervation), bradycardia, and malignant hyperthermia.
  • Malignant hyperthermia: a RyR1 mutation; succinylcholine or a volatile anesthetic triggers uncontrolled calcium release: rigidity (masseter first), rising end-tidal CO2, tachycardia, hyperthermia, hyperkalemia. Treat with dantrolene, which blocks RyR1.
  • Nondepolarizing blockers (rocuronium, vecuronium, cisatracurium) compete with ACh. Reverse with neostigmine plus glycopyrrolate (the glycopyrrolate blocks neostigmine's muscarinic effects) or with sugammadex, which encapsulates rocuronium and vecuronium. Cisatracurium breaks down by Hofmann elimination, so organ failure doesn't prolong it.
  • Spasmolytics: baclofen (GABA-B agonist in the cord), tizanidine (α2 agonist), diazepam (GABA-A), dantrolene (RyR1 in the muscle itself). Cyclobenzaprine treats acute muscle spasm (including TMD), not spasticity; it is tricyclic-like, so drowsiness and dry mouth.
  • Myasthenia gravis is treated with pyridostigmine (a cholinesterase inhibitor), immunosuppression and thymectomy. Lambert-Eaton syndrome (antibodies to presynaptic calcium channels, small cell lung cancer) gets better with repeated use.

The jaw: the masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid close the mouth; the lateral pterygoid is the one muscle of mastication that helps open it and protrudes the mandible. TMD falls into muscle (myofascial pain, the most common), disc (displacement with reduction clicks; without reduction locks) and joint (arthralgia, arthritis) problems, managed with NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, splints and, for muscle pain, botulinum toxin.
full.et-ada:
What's tested
  • The five principles in Code order, their one-word meanings and the duty each states: patient autonomy (1), nonmaleficence (2), beneficence (3), justice (4), veracity (5)
  • Naming the principle and Code section a scenario turns on, and the ethical answer
  • How the Code is built: principles (aspirational), the Code of Professional Conduct (binding on members) and advisory opinions (interpretations); ethics versus law
  • The classic cases: records and transfer, impaired colleagues, abandonment, postexposure duties, abuse reporting, patient selection and HIV, emergency care, justifiable criticism, split fees, amalgam removal, insurance and fees, advertising and specialty claims

How the Code is built

The ADA Principles of Ethics and Code of Professional Conduct has three parts:

  • Principles of Ethics: five aspirational goals that justify the rest. They can overlap and compete, so at times they must be balanced.
  • Code of Professional Conduct: specific conduct that is required or forbidden, adopted by the ADA House of Delegates. It is binding on ADA members, and a violation can bring censure, suspension or expulsion.
  • Advisory opinions: the Council on Ethics, Bylaws and Judicial Affairs' interpretations of the Code in specific situations.

Ethics and law are related but not the same: ethical duties often go beyond legal ones. A complaint about a member goes first to the local (component) or state (constituent) dental society. Bioethics' usual four principles (Beauchamp and Childress) are autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence and justice; the ADA adds veracity.

SectionPrincipleIn a wordThe duty
1Patient autonomySelf-governanceRespect the patient's right to self-determination and confidentiality
2NonmaleficenceDo no harmRefrain from harming the patient
3BeneficenceDo goodPromote the patient's welfare
4JusticeFairnessTreat people fairly
5VeracityTruthfulnessCommunicate truthfully

Section 1: Patient autonomy

  • 1.A Patient involvement: tell the patient the proposed treatment and the reasonable alternatives in a way that lets them take part in the decision. This is the Code's basis for informed consent.
  • 1.B Patient records: keep records confidential. When the patient or the patient's new dentist asks, provide the information that will help future treatment, including copies of radiographs, free or for a nominal cost, whether or not the account is paid in full.
  • Sensitive information (HIV status, chemical dependency, sexual orientation) needs the patient's written permission before it is forwarded, unless you know the law allows it. If you must consult another practitioner and the patient can't stay anonymous, ask the patient first.

Section 2: Nonmaleficence

  • 2.A Education: keep knowledge and skills current. 2.B Consultation and referral: refer when the patient will benefit from someone's special skills; the specialist returns the patient to the referring dentist. A second opinion should come from someone with no stake in the treatment that follows.
  • 2.C Auxiliaries: delegate only duties that can legally be delegated, to qualified staff, and supervise them.
  • 2.D Personal impairment: practicing while impaired by alcohol or drugs is unethical. Urge an impaired colleague to seek treatment; with first-hand knowledge that a colleague is practicing impaired, report it to the dental society's professional assistance committee. A dentist with a disease that could endanger patients limits their practice on a physician's advice.
  • 2.E Postexposure: whatever the dentist's own status, tell an exposed patient at once of the need for postexposure evaluation and refer them; if the dentist is the source, share their status with the evaluating practitioner and be tested.
  • 2.F Patient abandonment: once treatment has started, don't stop it without adequate notice and a chance to find another dentist, and don't let the patient's oral health be jeopardized meanwhile.
  • 2.G Personal relationships: avoid relationships with patients that could impair judgment or exploit their trust.

Section 3: Beneficence

  • 3.A Community service, 3.B Governance (every profession regulates itself, so dentists join a professional society and follow its ethics), 3.C sharing research results, and 3.D patents never used to restrict research or practice.
  • 3.E Abuse and neglect: know the signs and report suspected cases to the proper authorities as state law requires. If an adult asks you not to report and the law doesn't require it, respect the wish and, with permission, look for other help.
  • 3.F Professional demeanor: dentists lead the team, and disruptive behavior undermines care and trust.
  • During a public health emergency, the duty to the public may outweigh a patient's request for elective care (3.A.1).

Section 4: Justice

  • 4.A Patient selection: dentists may use reasonable discretion, but may not refuse a patient because of race, creed, color, gender, sexual orientation, gender identity, national origin or disability. A patient with HIV, HBV or HCV is treated on the same basis as anyone else: refer only if another practitioner's skills or equipment are needed, and consult the physician if treatment might seriously compromise the patient's health.
  • 4.B Emergency service: make reasonable arrangements for the emergency care of patients of record, and of patients not of record who contact you in an emergency; afterward, return them to their regular dentist unless they prefer otherwise.
  • 4.C Justifiable criticism: tell patients their present oral health status without disparaging prior work, and check with the previous dentist where possible; a difference of opinion is not mistreatment. Report gross or continual faulty treatment to the reviewing agency the local or state society designates.
  • 4.D Expert testimony is allowed, but a fee that depends on the case's outcome is unethical.
  • 4.E Rebates and split fees are forbidden, including paying a marketer, social-coupon company or influencer a percentage of the fees collected.

Section 5: Veracity

  • 5.A Representation of care: removing sound amalgams from a non-allergic patient to rid the body of "toxins," at the dentist's recommendation, is unethical, and so is any claim to cure disease without scientific support.
  • 5.B Representation of fees: waiving a copayment without telling the insurer is overbilling; raising a fee because the patient has insurance is unethical; the full fee is the fee charged a patient without benefits. Reporting wrong treatment dates, misdescribing a procedure and recommending unnecessary services are all false representations.
  • 5.C Conflicts of interest: disclose a financial tie to a company whose product you present. 5.D: report a serious adverse drug or device reaction to the FDA; when selling products, verify the claims yourself and disclose your financial incentive.
  • 5.F Advertising is allowed unless it is false or misleading in a material respect (unsubstantiated claims of superior quality, results you can't promise). Advertising an HIV-negative test needs a statement that it can't guarantee current status.
  • 5.G Name of practice: a departing dentist's name may stay for up to one year. 5.H and 5.I: announce as a specialist only in a recognized specialty for which you are educated; a general dentist may list services such as implants or orthodontics but must say they are provided by a general dentist.

Working a scenario

Ask which duty is at stake and name its principle: a patient's choice or privacy (autonomy), a risk of harm (nonmaleficence), the patient's or the public's welfare (beneficence), fair treatment and dealings with colleagues (justice), or honesty in records, claims and advertising (veracity). Principles are prima facie duties that sometimes have to be weighed against each other, but the Code's specific rules (records released whether or not the bill is paid, no split fees) are not optional.

ScenarioPrincipleThe answer
A new dentist asks for records; the patient owes moneyAutonomy (1.B)Send copies anyway, free or at nominal cost
A colleague practices while impairedNonmaleficence (2.D)Urge treatment; report to the professional assistance committee
You want to dismiss a patient midway through a bridgeNonmaleficence (2.F)Adequate notice and time to find another dentist
A patient with HIV asks to become your patientJustice (4.A)Accept and treat on the same basis as others
A stranger calls with facial swelling on a weekendJustice (4.B)Arrange emergency care, then return them to their dentist
A new patient has poor crowns from another dentistJustice (4.C)Explain the findings without disparaging; report only gross or continual faulty work
A coupon site keeps half of each feeJustice (4.E)Fee splitting: not allowed
Copay waived without telling the insurerVeracity (5.B)Overbilling
full.et-pro:
What's tested
  • Informed consent: what must be disclosed, the reasonable-patient standard (Canterbury v. Spence), decision-making capacity, informed refusal and implied consent
  • Who consents for a minor or for an adult who lacks capacity
  • Confidentiality and HIPAA: what's protected, when you may share without authorization, the patient's rights, and the duty to warn (Tarasoff)
  • Records and the medical history: what to record and how to correct an entry
  • The duty to report suspected child abuse and neglect and its signs; disclosing errors; whistle-blowing
  • Infection control and bloodborne pathogens as professional duties: standard precautions, OSHA's rules, transmission risks and what to do after an exposure
  • Ethical reasoning: valid and sound arguments, the common fallacies and the main moral theories

Informed consent

Consent is a conversation, not a signature: the signed form only documents it. Valid consent needs a patient with capacity who understands and chooses freely after hearing the diagnosis; the nature and purpose of the proposed treatment; its benefits and material risks; the reasonable alternatives, including no treatment, and their risks; and the prognosis and costs, with a chance to ask questions.

Three court cases built it. Schloendorff (1914): every adult of sound mind has the right to decide what is done to their own body. Salgo (1957): the first use of the words "informed consent." Canterbury v. Spence (1972): disclose every risk that a reasonable person in the patient's position would find significant to the decision (the reasonable-patient standard), not just what other doctors customarily disclose.

  • Capacity is a clinical judgment, made decision by decision; competence is a legal finding by a court. Capacity means the patient can understand the information, appreciate that it applies to them, reason about the options and express a choice. Agreeing with the dentist is not one of them.
  • Informed refusal: a patient with capacity may refuse; explain the consequences, document the refusal and have it signed. But a patient can't require care below the standard of care: if a patient refuses the radiographs needed to diagnose, the dentist may decline that treatment.
  • Implied consent: a patient who opens for an examination implies consent to it, and an emergency in an unconscious patient implies consent to lifesaving care.
  • Mill's harm principle allows limiting liberty only to prevent harm to others. Paternalism, overriding a competent, informed adult for their own good (a Jehovah's Witness refusing blood), isn't justified: give your recommendation and reasons, then respect the choice.

Minors and patients who can't consent

  • For a minor, a parent or legal guardian consents. A grandparent, babysitter or stepparent can't, unless they are the legal guardian or hold written authorization. After a divorce, a parent with legal custody consents.
  • An emancipated minor (married, in the military, or self-supporting and living independently) consents for themselves. State law sets the details: Alabama's age of majority is 19, and Alabama lets a minor 14 or older consent to their own dental care.
  • Seek a child's assent (agreement) as well, but it doesn't replace the parent's consent. For an adult without capacity, a court-appointed guardian or a health care power of attorney consents.

Confidentiality and HIPAA

Confidentiality respects autonomy and an implied promise (deontological reasons) and lets patients disclose what the dentist needs to know (consequentialist reasons). HIPAA (1996):

  • The Privacy Rule protects protected health information (PHI), any individually identifiable health information, whether spoken, on paper or electronic. The Security Rule covers electronic PHI, and the Breach Notification Rule says when patients must be told of a breach.
  • PHI may be shared without written authorization for treatment, payment and health care operations, and where the law requires it (abuse reports, public health, court orders). Other uses, such as marketing or a patient's photo on social media, need written authorization.
  • The minimum necessary standard limits what is shared to what the purpose needs; it doesn't apply to sharing for treatment.
  • Patients receive a Notice of Privacy Practices and may see and get a copy of their records (within 30 days, for a reasonable cost-based fee), ask for corrections and get an accounting of disclosures. Discuss patients only with those caring for them, never in public spaces.

Tarasoff (1976): a therapist had a duty to protect an identifiable person whom his patient had threatened to kill. Confidentiality gives way to a serious, foreseeable threat to someone else.

Records and the medical history

  • The record is a legal document: medical history, findings, diagnosis, consent and refusal, treatment, prescriptions and communications.
  • Never erase, alter or backdate. Correct a paper entry with a single line, dated and initialed, so the original stays readable; in an electronic record, add a dated addendum.
  • The dentist owns the original, and the patient is entitled to a copy. Review the medical history at every visit and update it fully at least once a year.

The duty to report

  • Child abuse and neglect: dentists are mandated reporters in every state. Report a reasonable suspicion (proof isn't needed) to child protective services or the police. Good-faith reporters are immune from liability, and in most states failing to report is itself an offense.
  • More than half of physical abuse injuries are to the head, face, mouth or neck. Warning signs: bruises in different stages of healing, a torn labial frenum, bruises on the cheeks or ears, a story that doesn't fit the injury or keeps changing, delay in seeking care, and untreated disease the caregiver knows about (neglect).
  • Most states also require reports of elder or vulnerable-adult abuse; for a competent adult, follow the law and the patient's wishes (Code 3.E).
  • Errors: disclose them, since not disclosing is almost never justified. Disclosure keeps future consent informed and builds trust, and the fiduciary relationship demands it. A bad outcome isn't always bad work.
  • Whistle-blowing is permissible when serious harm is at stake, you have told your supervisors and nothing was done; it becomes obligatory when you also have documentation and good reason to think going public will prevent the harm. Use internal routes first.

Infection control as a professional duty

  • Standard precautions (CDC, 1996) apply to every patient, whatever their infection status. They grew out of universal precautions (1985), which treated blood and certain body fluids as infectious. In dentistry, saliva counts as potentially infectious material.
  • OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard: a written exposure control plan; engineering controls (sharps containers, self-sheathing needles) and work-practice controls (no two-handed recapping); PPE at no cost; the hepatitis B vaccine offered free within 10 working days of assignment (a refusal is signed); free, confidential follow-up after an exposure; and yearly training.
  • Risk of infection after a needlestick from an infected source: HBV about 30% (6–30%), HCV about 2%, HIV about 0.3%. HBV survives on dry surfaces for at least a week. There is a vaccine for HBV, but none for HCV or HIV.
  • After an exposure: wash with soap and water (flush the eyes or mouth with water), don't squeeze the wound or use bleach, report at once, and test the source with consent. HIV prophylaxis starts as soon as possible, ideally within 2 hours and no later than 72.

Thinking it through: arguments and theories

  • An argument offers premises as reasons for a conclusion. A deductive argument is valid when true premises would guarantee the conclusion, and sound when it is valid and its premises are true. An inductive argument is strong or weak; a strong one with true premises is cogent. Validity is about structure, not truth.
  • Valid forms: modus ponens (if p then q; p; so q) and modus tollens (if p then q; not q; so not p). Invalid: affirming the consequent (q; so p) and denying the antecedent (not p; so not q).
FallacyWhat it does
Straw manDistorts a view to attack it more easily
Ad hominemRejects a claim because of who made it
Appeal to ignoranceTrue because not proven false, or false because not proven true
Begging the questionUses the conclusion as its own support
Slippery slopeClaims one step will inevitably lead to disaster
TheoryWhat makes an act right
Utilitarianism (Bentham, Mill)Consequences: the greatest good for all affected (act or rule versions)
Kantian deontologyDuty and motive: act only on rules you could make universal; treat people as ends, never merely as means
Principlism (Ross; Beauchamp and Childress)Prima facie duties, weighed case by case
Virtue ethicsCharacter: what a good person would do
Ethics of careRelationships and responsibilities to particular people

  • Where to search: TRIP first, then PubMed Clinical Queries, then the Cochrane Library
  • Naming the design from a short description, and what case-control and cohort studies are each good and bad at
  • The evidence pyramid, and literature review versus systematic review versus meta-analysis versus clinical practice guideline (GRADE, AGREE)
  • Efficacy versus effectiveness, the study-context continuum, practice-based research networks and the three gaps between evidence and practice

The 5 A's

Evidence-based dentistry combines the best available research with the dentist's clinical expertise and the patient's needs and values. It runs as five steps, always in this order.

StepWhat you do
1. AskTurn the patient's problem into a focused, answerable question (PICO).
2. AcquireSearch for the best evidence: TRIP, PubMed, Cochrane.
3. AppraiseJudge it: is the design the strongest one for this question, is the study valid, are the results important?
4. ApplyCombine the evidence with your expertise and the patient's values, and decide together.
5. AssessCheck the result: did it work, did the patient follow through, what would you change next time?

Apply and assess are the pair people mix up: apply is using the evidence with this patient; assess is looking back at how it went.

Asking: PICO(T)

  • P (patient, population or problem): the few characteristics that matter (age, condition), neither so broad that it means nothing nor so narrow that no study fits.
  • I (intervention or exposure): the treatment, test or risk factor you are asking about.
  • C (comparison): ideally one alternative, such as standard care, a placebo or no treatment. It is sometimes only implied.
  • O (outcome): specific and measurable (new caries, pain score, implant survival), never "better care".
  • T (time): optional in the question and easy to forget, but every study answering it needs a time frame.

Template: "In [P], does [I], compared with [C], change [O] over [T]?" For example: "In children with primary teeth, does fluoride toothpaste, compared with non-fluoride toothpaste, lower caries incidence over one year?" A classic mistake is a population that makes the comparison impossible, such as comparing smokers with nonsmokers in a population defined as smokers.

BackgroundForeground
AsksGeneral knowledge about one condition or treatment (who, what, when, why, how)A comparison of two or more options for a specific patient or problem
Example"What are the side effects of ibuprofen?""After third-molar extraction, is ibuprofen plus acetaminophen as good as an opioid for pain?"
PICO?No: a textbook or review answers itYes
Question typeAsks aboutBest design
TherapyWhich treatment does more good than harmRandomized controlled trial
DiagnosisHow well a test identifies a diseaseCross-sectional comparison against a reference (gold) standard
PrognosisThe likely course of a disease, or what predicts itCohort
Etiology or harmCauses and risk factors; harm from an exposure or treatmentCohort or case-control (assigning a harm would be unethical)

Acquiring: where to search

  • TRIP first: one search returns guidelines, systematic reviews and primary studies, sorted by level of evidence.
  • PubMed (MEDLINE, from the National Library of Medicine) next: the largest biomedical database. Clinical Queries filters it by question type (therapy, diagnosis, etiology, prognosis) and pulls out systematic reviews.
  • Cochrane Library: rigorous systematic reviews, mostly of randomized trials.
  • Also: journals through the UAB library, the ADA's clinical practice guidelines and evidence-based journals. Expert opinion is the last resort.

Study designs

The first split is who decides the exposure. In an experimental study the investigator assigns it; in an observational study the investigator only watches exposures people already have. Observational studies are descriptive (no comparison group: case reports and series) or analytic (a comparison: ecological, cross-sectional, case-control, cohort).

DesignHow it worksGood forWeak spots
Case report or seriesOne unusual patient, or several with the same condition or treatment, describedNew diseases and side effects; ideas for trialsNo comparison group; the lowest inferential power of human studies
Ecological (correlational)Compares averages of groups (cities, countries)Cheap; uses existing dataEcological fallacy: the exposed people may not be the ones with the outcome
Cross-sectionalA snapshot: exposure and outcome measured at the same time in the same people, often by surveyPrevalence; quick and cheapNo time order, so no cause and effect
Case-controlStarts with the outcome: cases with the disease and controls without, then looks back for exposuresRare diseases, long latency, many risk factors at once; quick and cheapRecall and selection bias; poor for rare exposures; no incidence; gives an odds ratio
CohortStarts with the exposure: exposed and unexposed people followed for the outcome (prospective, or retrospective from records)Time order; incidence and relative risk; rare exposures; several outcomes of one exposureSlow and costly; loss to follow-up; poor for rare diseases
Controlled trialThe investigator allocates people to treatment or control without randomizingThe investigator controls the exposureAllocation can be biased
Randomized controlled trialRandom allocation to treatment or control, followed forwardThe only true experiment: randomization balances known and unknown factors, so it best shows cause and effectCostly; can't test a harmful exposure; strict entry rules limit whom it applies to

Clues in a stem: "looked back" from a disease is case-control; "followed" exposed and unexposed people is cohort; "surveyed once" is cross-sectional; cities or countries is ecological; "randomly assigned" is an RCT.

The evidence pyramid

From bottom to top, as the course draws it: animal and lab studies; case reports, case series and expert opinion; ecological; cross-sectional; case-control; cohort; randomized controlled trials; systematic reviews and meta-analyses; clinical practice guidelines. Higher means stronger evidence for a clinical decision, if the study is done well. Two twists: lab and animal studies control every variable, so they have the greatest inferential power (rigor) when done properly, yet they sit at the bottom because they apply least to patients. And many published pyramids put systematic reviews at the very top, where the course puts guidelines, which build their recommendations on those reviews.

Pre-appraised (filtered) evidence

Literature reviewSystematic reviewMeta-analysisClinical practice guideline
Summarizes the evidence?MaybeYesYesYes
Methods section?No: a narrative; the author picks the studiesYes: a full, reproducible search and a quality grade for each studyYes: a systematic review plus a summary statistic pooling the studies' dataYes: integrates the evidence to approach a clinical problem
Whose view?The author'sCollects and grades the evidenceCollects, grades and combines itEvidence, plus expert opinion where evidence is missing or weak
  • GRADE rates the certainty of a body of evidence as high, moderate, low or very low. Randomized trials start high and observational studies start low; risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness (surrogate outcomes), imprecision and publication bias rate it down.
  • AGREE (Appraisal of Guidelines for Research and Evaluation) judges the quality of clinical practice guidelines.
  • Reporting checklists: CONSORT for randomized trials, STROBE for observational studies, PRISMA for systematic reviews.
  • A forest plot shows each study as a square (bigger means more weight) on a line (its 95% confidence interval). The diamond at the bottom is the pooled result: its center is the estimate and its tips the 95% CI. A diamond that crosses the line of no effect (1 for a ratio) is not significant.

From research to practice

Study contexts run along a continuum: lab research (the treatment isn't ready for humans), clinical trials in academic settings (not ready for everyday patients; they test efficacy), practice-based research (not yet ready for all practices; it tests effectiveness) and community-based research (outside the health care system).

EfficacyEffectiveness
AsksDoes it work under ideal conditions?Does it work in the real world?
SettingAn academic health center, usually an RCTEveryday practices
PatientsHighly selectedTypical
CliniciansHighly trained, with no time or cost limitsTypical, with the usual time and money limits

A practice-based research network (PBRN) is a group of dental practices that join to answer research questions in daily practice, where most people get their care; a national dental PBRN has run since 2005.

GapWhat's wrongWhat closes it
Knowledge gapThe evidence doesn't exist yetEfficacy and effectiveness studies
Knowing gapThe evidence exists, but clinicians don't know itDissemination science
Knowing-to-doing gapClinicians know it but don't use it (patient acceptance, habit, cost)Implementation science

The "magic pill" example: if about half drop out at each step (hear of it, try it, prescribe it, the patient accepts it, the patient keeps taking it), very few patients end up helped.
full.eb-appraise:
What's tested
  • Internal versus external validity, and the three threats to validity: bias, confounding and chance
  • The kinds of bias and what randomization, blinding and intention-to-treat analysis do about them; what to check in an RCT
  • Standardization versus calibration, inter- versus intra-examiner reliability, precision versus accuracy, incidence versus prevalence
  • Types of data, mean versus median, and standard deviation
  • Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values from a 2×2 table, and which one a screening or a confirming test needs
  • Relative risk, odds ratio, absolute risk and the number needed to treat; reading a ratio with its 95% confidence interval
  • p-values, type I and II errors, power, and statistical versus clinical significance

Is the study valid?

Internal validityExternal validity
AsksWas the study well designed, run and analyzed?Was the study population well defined, and enrolled with that definition in mind?
MeansThe findings are believable for the people studiedThe findings apply (generalize) to your patients

Three things threaten validity: bias, any systematic error that skews the estimate of the link between exposure and outcome (a bigger sample doesn't fix it); confounding, a third factor tied to both the exposure and the outcome (studying soda and caries without accounting for oral hygiene); and chance, random variation in who was sampled (handled by sample size and statistics).

BiasWhat happensTypical design
SelectionThe way people are chosen makes the groups unlike each other or unlike the population (recruiting in a park for an exercise study)Any, especially case-control
RecallCases remember past exposures differently from controlsCase-control
Attrition (loss to follow-up)Those who drop out differ from those who stayCohort, RCT
Self-report (social desirability)People underreport smoking or overreport flossingSurveys, cross-sectional
Measurement (observer)An examiner who knows the group scores it differentlyUnblinded trials
PublicationPositive results are published more often than negative onesSystematic reviews (search the gray literature)

Confounding is controlled by randomization (the only method that also balances unknown factors), restriction, matching, stratification and statistical adjustment.

Appraising a randomized trial

  • Randomization done properly (for example, computer-generated and concealed), not circumvented, with the groups balanced at baseline.
  • Blinding (masking): in a double-blind trial neither the participants nor the clinicians and assessors know who got what. The groups must be treated alike apart from the intervention.
  • Intention-to-treat analysis: everyone is analyzed in the group they were randomized to, whether or not they finished or followed the treatment, which keeps randomization's balance. A per-protocol analysis counts only those who completed the treatment as planned and can overstate the benefit.
  • Subgroups planned at the start; a subgroup found afterward (reporting only the women because it worked better in them) is a red flag.
  • Sample size calculated beforehand, the trial registered on ClinicalTrials.gov and reported by CONSORT (enrollment, allocation, follow-up, analysis).
  • Applicability: patient-important outcomes rather than surrogate outcomes (a plaque index in place of tooth loss), an effect large enough to matter, long enough follow-up, benefits and harms both reported, good compliance, and participants like your patients.

Measuring well

  • Standardization: every examiner uses the same criteria, instruments and procedure. Calibration: examiners score the same patients and train until their scores agree; it takes longer.
  • Reliability (repeatability): inter-examiner, different examiners get the same score; intra-examiner, the same examiner gets the same score on the same patient at different times; test-retest, the same person answers the same questionnaire again 1–2 weeks later.
  • Precision is repeatability (reliability); accuracy is closeness to the truth (validity). An examiner who always records the same wrong probing depth is precise but not accurate.
  • Incidence is new cases over a period among people at risk (it needs follow-up: a cohort); prevalence is all existing cases at one time (a cross-sectional study).
  • A census measures everyone, so no inference is needed; a sample measures some and relies on statistics.

Data and the center

TypeWhat it isExamplesUsual graph
QuantitativeNumbers you can add or subtractAge, blood pressure, millimeters of bone lossHistogram, box plot
BinaryTwo categoriesDisease or no disease, treatment or controlBar chart
NominalNamed categories with no orderBlood type, occupationBar chart
OrdinalCategories with a rankCancer stage, light/moderate/heavy smokerBar chart

The mean is pulled by outliers; the median (the middle value) is the better center for skewed data. The standard deviation measures spread around the mean, and two data sets with the same mean can have very different SDs. In a normal curve about 68% of values fall within 1 SD and 95% within 2. A correlation coefficient runs from −1 (perfect negative) through 0 (none) to +1 (perfect positive); correlation doesn't prove cause.

Diagnostic tests

Disease presentDisease absent
Test positiveTrue positive (a)False positive (b)
Test negativeFalse negative (c)True negative (d)
  • Sensitivity = a/(a+c): of the people with the disease, the share who test positive (the true positive rate). A highly sensitive test misses few cases, so a negative result rules the disease out (SnNout). Screening tests need it.
  • Specificity = d/(b+d): of the people without the disease, the share who test negative (the true negative rate). A highly specific test has few false positives, so a positive result rules the disease in (SpPin). Use it to confirm before an irreversible step such as an extraction.
  • PPV = a/(a+b) and NPV = d/(c+d). Predictive values change with prevalence: where a disease is rarer, PPV falls and NPV rises. Sensitivity and specificity don't change with prevalence.
  • Moving a test's cutoff to catch more disease raises sensitivity and lowers specificity. That is why the class notes say a highly sensitive test "can lead to false positives": the false positives come from the specificity it gives up.

Example: a caries device tested on 100 decayed and 100 sound teeth is positive on 90 decayed and 20 sound teeth. Sensitivity 90/100 = 90%; specificity 80/100 = 80%; PPV 90/110 = 82%; NPV 80/90 = 89%.

Risk and the size of an effect

  • Absolute risk = events ÷ people in the group; odds = events ÷ non-events (200 of 600 with arthritis: risk 0.33, odds 0.5).
  • Relative risk (risk ratio) = risk in the exposed ÷ risk in the unexposed, from cohorts and RCTs. 1 means no difference, above 1 a harmful effect, below 1 a protective one (0.87 means 13% lower risk). A hazard ratio reads the same way over time.
  • Odds ratio = (a×d)/(b×c), the measure from case-control studies; it approximates the relative risk when the outcome is rare.
  • Absolute risk reduction (ARR) = control risk − treated risk, and NNT = 1/ARR, rounded up (NNH for a harm). Caries in 25% of controls and 15% of treated children: ARR 10%, NNT 10, though the relative risk reduction is 40%.
  • The lecture's pain NNT is how many patients must take an analgesic for one more to get at least 50% pain relief over 4–6 hours than with placebo: 1 is perfect and lower is better. Ibuprofen with acetaminophen (about 1.5) beats oxycodone 5 mg (about 5.5).
  • Relative risk can mislead when the event is rare: armor that makes you "8 times less likely" to be hit by a meteorite changes almost nothing in absolute terms.

Significance and errors

  • The p-value is the chance of a result at least this extreme if there were truly no difference. Below the chosen alpha (usually 0.05) the result is statistically significant. It doesn't measure how big or important the effect is.
  • The 95% confidence interval is the range of plausible true values. For a ratio, an interval that includes 1 is not significant (HR 0.92, CI 0.83–1.02); for a difference, one that includes 0. A narrower interval is a more precise estimate.
  • Type I error (alpha): a false positive, finding a difference that isn't real. Type II error (beta): a false negative, missing a real difference, most likely in a small study.
  • Power = 1 − beta (usually set at 80%), the chance of detecting a real difference. A larger sample, a bigger true difference, less variability and more accurate measurement raise it; a stricter alpha lowers it.
  • Statistical is not clinical significance: a huge trial can make a trivial difference significant. Judge the size of the effect, its interval, and whether it matters to patients.
full.rd-physics:
What's tested
  • X-ray production: cathode/anode, >99% heat vs ~1% x-rays, bremsstrahlung (primary) vs characteristic radiation
  • mA and time control photon quantity; kVp controls energy/penetration (beam quality); the inverse square law
  • Filtration (removes low-energy photons) and collimation (restricts beam, cuts scatter and dose)
  • Beam attenuation: photoelectric absorption (makes the image/contrast, ∝ Z³), Compton scatter (most common, adds fog), coherent
  • Image quality: density, contrast and spatial resolution, sharpness and receptors

Atoms, ionization and the kinds of radiation

Ionization is the gain or loss of an electron; it needs enough energy to overcome the electron's binding energy, which is higher for high-atomic-number elements and for tightly held inner-shell electrons. An atom that loses an electron becomes a positive cation; one that gains an electron becomes a negative anion. Ionizing radiation (alpha particles, beta particles, gamma rays, x-rays) carries enough energy to damage tissue and DNA; non-ionizing radiation (radio waves, microwaves) does not. X-rays and gamma rays are both electromagnetic and travel at the speed of light: x-rays are made outside the nucleus when electrons interact with other electrons (so they are easier to control and are the diagnostic form), while gamma rays come from inside the nucleus. Radiation behaves as both waves (different wavelengths for different energies) and photons (discrete bundles of energy); diagnostic dental photons run about 10–120 keV, and MR imaging instead uses radio waves.

The x-ray tube and how photons are made

  • Cathode (negative): a filament is heated and boils off electrons. Anode (positive): a tungsten target the electrons are accelerated toward and strike. The tube is a vacuum so the electrons are not deflected; oil insulates the housing; an aluminum filter and a collimator then shape the beam.
  • Focal spot size sets sharpness: a small focal spot gives a sharper image (but concentrates heat), a large one blurs the edges.
  • When the electrons hit the target, over 99% of their kinetic energy becomes heat and only about 1% becomes x-ray photons.
TypeMechanismNote
Bremsstrahlung ('braking')An electron is slowed or stopped near a tungsten nucleus and its lost kinetic energy leaves as a photon; a direct hit on the nucleus gives one high-energy photon, while the more common near miss gives several.The primary source of the beam; produces a continuous spectrum of energies.
CharacteristicAn incident electron knocks an inner-shell target electron out; an outer-shell electron drops into the vacancy and the energy difference leaves as a photon.Only a small fraction of the beam; produces discrete, element-specific energies.

Controlling the beam

SettingControlsEffect
Exposure timeNumber of photonsChanges quantity only; the range of photon energies is unchanged
Tube current (mA)Quantity of photonsDirect relationship with the number of photons produced
Tube voltage (kVp)Energy and penetration (beam quality)Raises the mean and maximal photon energy, and also the number of photons

Typical intraoral settings are about 7–10 mA and 65–70 kVp, with the exposure time varied for the region, the patient's size and the receptor. Filtration (usually 0.5–2.5 mm of aluminum; regulated at 1.5 mm Al at 70 kVp and 2.5 mm Al above 70 kVp) removes the weak, low-energy photons that would be absorbed in the patient and only add dose without reaching the receptor; by stripping them out it also raises the beam's mean energy. Collimation (a metal barrier with an aperture, often a lead diaphragm) restricts the beam's size and shape, cutting scatter and patient dose and improving image quality. The inverse square law states that intensity falls with the square of the distance from the source, so moving twice as far away leaves one quarter of the intensity.

How x-rays interact with tissue (attenuation)

As the beam passes through the patient it is reduced in intensity, a process called attenuation. The incident beam holds photons of many energies but is spatially uniform from center to edge. There are three interactions:

InteractionShareWhat it does
Compton scatter~57%A photon strikes a loosely bound outer-shell electron and scatters in a new direction, still energetic enough to reach the receptor as fog that reduces contrast; greater in bone than soft tissue
Photoelectric absorption~27%A photon is completely absorbed by an inner-shell electron, which is ejected as a photoelectron; this is the most important interaction for the image and for contrast, and its frequency varies with the cube of atomic number (Z³), so dense bone absorbs about 6.5× more than soft tissue
Coherent scatter~7%A low-energy photon (under 10 keV) briefly excites a whole atom, which re-emits a photon of the same energy in a new direction; adds little to the image

About 9% of photons pass through without interacting at all. The difference in photoelectric absorption between bone and soft tissue is exactly what makes a diagnostic radiographic image possible: without it, all tissues would look the same.

Image quality

  • Density is the overall darkness of the film.
  • Contrast resolution is the ability to tell different densities apart (for example bone from soft tissue), while spatial resolution is the ability to tell objects that are close together apart (for example enamel from dentin).
  • Sharpness is how crisply edges are defined; it is degraded by motion of the tube head, the patient or the receptor, and a blurred image is not diagnostic and must be retaken.
  • Receptors include film, PSP (photostimulable phosphor) plates and digital solid-state sensors; the attenuated beam strikes one of these after leaving the patient.
full.rd-biosafety:
What's tested
  • Direct vs indirect action (water radiolysis, free radicals H· and OH·); DNA double-strand breaks are the critical damage
  • Radiosensitivity by cell and organ; rapidly dividing/undifferentiated cells are most sensitive
  • Deterministic (threshold, dose-severity: xerostomia, ORN, cataracts) vs stochastic (no threshold, cancer and heritable effects)
  • ALARA/ALADA, justification, optimization, dose limitation; thyroid collar, rectangular collimation, selection criteria
  • Occupational limits (1 mSv dosimeter trigger), the 6-foot/90–135° rule, dental x-rays are a tiny dose

How radiation damages tissue

Linear energy transfer (LET) measures how much energy radiation deposits along its path: high LET (alpha particles, neutrons, heavy ions) deposits energy densely, while low LET (x-rays, gamma rays) spreads it out. Ionizing radiation injures cells in two ways:

ActionMechanism
DirectA photon ionizes a biologic macromolecule (DNA or protein) itself, creating unstable free radicals that leave the molecule altered.
IndirectA photon ionizes a water molecule; radiolysis produces free radicals (H· and OH·) that then damage DNA. With dissolved oxygen it also forms hydroperoxyl and hydrogen peroxide. This is the dominant pathway because the body is mostly water.

Both actions yield highly reactive, short-lived free radicals, and the presence of dissolved oxygen makes the damage worse by forming additional peroxide species. A single photon can cause a cluster of DNA damage within a short stretch of the molecule: base damage, single-strand breaks, double-strand breaks and DNA–DNA or DNA–protein cross-links. Single-strand breaks are usually repaired accurately using the opposite strand as a template, but the double-strand break is the hardest to repair and is the critical lesion behind radiation-induced cell death, heritable mutation and cancer.

Radiosensitivity

Not all cells are equally sensitive. Cells that divide rapidly and are undifferentiated are the most sensitive, and the extent of damage also depends on where the cell is in its cycle.

LevelCellsOrgans
HighBasal cells of oral mucosa, bone marrow stem cellsLymphoid organs, bone marrow, testes, intestines, mucosal lining
IntermediateFibroblasts, endothelial cells (connective tissue)Growing cartilage and bone, salivary glands, lungs, kidney, liver
LowNeurons, muscle cells (highly differentiated, non-dividing)Nerve, muscle

Deterministic vs stochastic effects

Deterministic (tissue reactions)Stochastic
ThresholdYes — below the threshold there is no effectNo threshold — any dose carries some risk
Dose relationshipSeverity rises with dose once past the thresholdProbability rises with dose; severity is all-or-none
MechanismCell killingA sublethal DNA mutation in a surviving cell
ExamplesXerostomia, osteoradionecrosis, cataracts, mucositisCancer (leukemia, thyroid cancer, salivary gland tumors), heritable disorders

Radiation-induced cancers are clinically and histologically identical to ordinary cancers, have a long latent period of years to decades, and the female breast and the thyroid gland are especially sensitive. A child's risk of tumor induction is roughly 3× that of an adult because of their rapidly dividing cells. Embryos and fetuses are more radiosensitive again, yet the thresholds for harm (for example about 100 mGy for pre-implantation death) are many thousands of times the dose of a dental film, so dental radiographs do not deliver enough dose to cause these effects on a fetus; even so, routine films for an asymptomatic pregnant patient may be deferred until after pregnancy. Patients who undergo head-and-neck radiotherapy can develop xerostomia, rampant radiation caries, mucositis, trismus and osteoradionecrosis of the jaw.

Dose units and sources of exposure

Three quantities matter. Absorbed dose (energy deposited per unit mass) is measured in gray (Gy); the older unit is the rad (1 Gy = 100 rad). Equivalent dose and effective dose, which weight for the type of radiation and the sensitivity of the tissue, are measured in sievert (Sv); the older unit is the rem. Because dental doses are small, they are quoted in milligray (mGy) and millisievert (mSv). Human exposure comes from three broad sources: background radiation (natural radon, cosmic and terrestrial sources), medical exposure (CT, nuclear medicine, fluoroscopy and plain films, of which dental is only about 0.26%), and consumer products. When counseling a worried patient, it helps to compare a dental film's dose with a familiar source such as a few days of background radiation or a short airline flight.

Radiation protection: the three principles

PrincipleMeaning
JustificationThe diagnostic benefit of an exposure must be likely to exceed its risk; use selection criteria based on the patient, not routine timing, to decide when to expose.
Optimization (ALARA/ALADA)As Low As Reasonably Achievable (or As Low As Diagnostically Achievable). Use rectangular collimation, fast receptors, a thyroid collar and good technique to keep dose down while still getting a useful image.
Dose limitationOccupational and public dose limits keep anyone from receiving an unacceptably high dose. These limits apply to staff, not to patients receiving necessary diagnostic exposures, who have no numerical dose limit.

Practical safety

  • Rectangular collimation shrinks the exposed area by about 60% compared with a round beam, and a longer source-to-skin distance produces a less divergent beam that irradiates less tissue.
  • Thyroid collar and lead apron shield sensitive tissues, which matters most in children.
  • Operator position: stand behind a protective barrier, or at least 6 feet (about 2 m) away at an angle of 90–135° to the primary beam and out of its path. Tilt the patient's head rather than a handheld device, and keep the device's backscatter shield in place.
  • Dental imaging is a tiny share of medical radiation (about 0.26%). The ADA recommends a personal dosimeter for any worker who might exceed 1 mSv per year.
  • A quality-assurance program keeps images diagnostic at minimum dose, and radiographs are best viewed in a semi-darkened room with light transmitted through the film.
full.rd-geometry:
What's tested
  • Paralleling (receptor parallel to tooth, beam perpendicular — preferred at UABSOD) vs bisecting angle
  • Geometric optics: small focal spot, long source-object distance, short object-receptor distance, parallel object/receptor
  • Vertical-angle errors: excessive = foreshortening, insufficient = elongation
  • Horizontal overlap, cone cut, missing crowns/incisal edges, blurring, PSP artifacts and their causes
  • XCP/RINN color coding (yellow posterior, blue anterior, red bitewing, green endo) and the position-indicating ring

What makes a radiograph diagnostic

A good intraoral film needs contrast resolution (telling densities apart, such as bone from soft tissue), spatial resolution (telling objects that are close together apart, such as enamel from dentin), sharpness (crisply defined edges) and minimal distortion. Because the x-ray beam is divergent it inherently magnifies the image, and the magnification can be unequal across the film, which distorts the shape of the object. Sharpness is lost to motion, so a film with low sharpness is never diagnostic and must be retaken. These metrics interact: pushing for very high resolution or contrast can raise the dose, so the goal is an image that is just good enough to answer the clinical question while keeping exposure low.

Four rules of geometric optics

The focal spot is the tungsten target where electron energy becomes x-rays. Photons leave different points of it and travel in straight lines, creating a blurred border called the penumbra or zone of unsharpness. Four factors control sharpness and magnification:

FactorFor a sharp, accurate image
Focal spot sizeUse the smallest effective focal spot — a small spot narrows the penumbra; angling the anode target makes a small effective spot while still spreading heat
Source-to-object distanceIncrease it (a longer tube or cone): the beam is less divergent, so there is less unsharpness and less magnification
Object-to-receptor distanceMinimize it: the closer the tooth is to the receptor, the narrower the penumbra and the less magnification
Object-to-receptor orientationKeep the object and the receptor parallel, with the beam perpendicular to both, to avoid distortion of shape

A shadow-puppet analogy helps: an object held close to the light (far from the wall) throws a large, blurry shadow, while an object held close to the wall throws a small, sharp one — so keep the tooth close to the receptor and the source far away. In practice the long cone and the receptor holder are what make this geometry repeatable from patient to patient.

Paralleling vs bisecting angle

TechniqueReceptorBeamNote
Paralleling (preferred at UABSOD)Parallel to the long axis of the toothPerpendicular to both the tooth and the receptorLeast distortion; needs a holder to keep the geometry
Bisecting anglePlaced close to the crown, angled to the toothPerpendicular to the imaginary bisector of the angle between the tooth and the receptorGives an accurate tooth length but causes unequal distortion of the alveolar crest relative to the CEJ

The XCP (extension cone paralleling) / RINN holders are color-coded by use: yellow for posterior periapicals, blue for anterior, red for bitewings (which show interproximal caries and bone levels between adjacent teeth), and green for endodontics. Their biting ridges hold the receptor, and the external ring is the position-indicating device: it sits outside the mouth and you align the collimator/tube to it so the beam is centered on the receptor and cone cuts are avoided. For placement, seat the patient upright with the maxillary plane parallel to the floor, use a cushion or a numbing spray for a strong gag reflex, and have the patient close slowly rather than bite so the PSP or sensor does not bend. Clear step-by-step communication with the patient reduces movement and repeat exposures, which is itself a form of dose reduction.

Sharpness and the other projections

Sharpness is the ability to define an edge precisely and is lost to any motion of the tube head, the patient or the receptor; an image with low sharpness is not diagnostic and must be retaken. Besides the periapical, the bitewing (red holder) shows the crowns of upper and lower teeth together to find interproximal caries and to judge bone levels, and the occlusal projection images a broad arch segment; each follows the same geometric rules of keeping the object close to a parallel receptor with the beam perpendicular.

Common errors and their causes

ErrorCause
Foreshortening (tooth looks too short)Excessive vertical angulation
Elongation (tooth looks too long)Insufficient (deficient) vertical angulation
Horizontal overlap of the contactsIncorrect horizontal angulation, so the beam does not pass through the contacts
Cone cut (an unexposed clear area)The beam or collimator was not centered on the receptor
Missing crown or incisal edgeThe receptor was placed too apically
Blurred imageMotion of the patient, the tube head or the receptor
Too light / too darkToo little / too much exposure time
PSP plate artifactsA damaged plate, or a plate not fully erased before reuse

Knowing which error goes with which cause lets you fix the technique on the retake instead of repeating the mistake.
full.rd-anatomy:
What's tested
  • Radiolucent vs radiopaque are relative; the egg-shell effect and the lamina dura
  • Maxillary radiopaque landmarks (anterior nasal spine, nasal septum/floor, zygomatic process = J/U, Y line of Ennis, maxillary tuberosity, hamulus)
  • Maxillary radiolucencies (incisive foramen, maxillary sinus, nasal fossa) and mandibular landmarks (genial tubercles, lingual foramen, mental foramen, mandibular canal, mylohyoid and external oblique ridges, coronoid process)
  • Panoramic basics: the focal trough, ghost images, and common positioning errors (chin up/down, tongue not on palate)
  • Diagnosis vs interpretation; radiographs are correlated with the clinical exam

Reading the film

Diagnosis is the clinician's synthesis of history, clinical examination and tests and is the responsibility of the clinician providing care; interpretation is the reading of one investigation, such as the radiograph, and may be done by a specialist or by the clinician, but it must be correlated with the clinical findings before a diagnosis is made. Radiolucent means dark, where x-rays pass through easily (less dense structures such as air, pulp and soft tissue); radiopaque means white, where x-rays are blocked (dense structures such as enamel, bone and metal). Both terms are relative: soft-tissue thickening in the maxillary sinus is more radiopaque than the air beside it but more radiolucent than the surrounding bone.

The egg-shell effect explains how curved structures appear: where the beam skims the edge of a curve it follows a longer, tangential path and is attenuated more, so the outer edge looks radiopaque, while the center, where the beam has a shorter path, looks radiolucent. The lamina dura is the dense cortical bone lining the tooth socket, seen as a thin, continuous radiopaque line around the root. An intact lamina dura and a normal periodontal ligament space around an apex confirm that a superimposed radiolucency, such as the mental foramen, is a normal structure and not periapical pathology.

The periodontal ligament (PDL) space appears as a thin radiolucent line between the root and the lamina dura; a uniform PDL space with an intact lamina dura is a sign of health, whereas widening or loss of these structures points to pathology. Ranking tissues from most radiolucent to most radiopaque runs roughly: air, soft tissue and pulp, then cementum and dentin, then enamel, cortical bone and metal restorations. Because the terms are relative, the same structure can look dark against one neighbor and light against another, which is why a landmark is always read in the context of what surrounds it.

Maxillary landmarks

LandmarkAppearance
Intermaxillary (median) sutureThin radiolucent vertical line between the central incisors
Anterior nasal spineV-shaped radiopacity at the midline of the nasal floor, above the central incisors
Incisive (nasopalatine) foramenRound or ovoid radiolucency between the central incisor apices
Nasal fossa and nasal septumLarge radiolucency above the incisors, divided by the radiopaque septum
Maxillary sinusLarge radiolucency above the premolar and molar roots; its floor is a thin radiopaque line
Y line of EnnisInverted 'Y' where the floor of the nasal fossa meets the anterior wall of the maxillary sinus
Zygomatic process of the maxillaJ- or U-shaped radiopacity superior to the molar roots; the zygoma extends posteriorly from it
Maxillary tuberosity and pterygoid hamulusRadiopaque bulge distal to the last molar, with the hamulus projecting below it

Mandibular landmarks

LandmarkAppearance
Genial tubercles and lingual foramenRadiopaque ring with a central radiolucent (lingual) foramen, at the midline lingual to the incisors
Mental foramenRound or ovoid radiolucency near the premolar apices; can mimic periapical pathology (check for an intact lamina dura)
Mandibular (inferior alveolar) canalRadiolucent band bordered by two thin radiopaque lines, below the molar apices
Mylohyoid and external oblique ridgesRadiopaque lines crossing the molar region (mylohyoid more lingual and inferior, external oblique more buccal and superior)
Submandibular gland fossaRadiolucent area below the mylohyoid ridge in the molar region
Coronoid process of the mandibleTriangular radiopacity superimposed over the maxillary tuberosity on a maxillary molar film, projected upward as the patient opens

Panoramic imaging

A panoramic image is a tomogram that captures a curved focal trough (image layer): structures that sit inside the trough are sharp, while those outside it are blurred, magnified, narrowed or missed altogether. Correct positioning keeps the teeth within the trough.

ErrorAppearance
Chin tipped up (too high)Flat or reverse smile line; the hard palate superimposes on the roots; condyles ride high or off the film
Chin tipped down (too low)Exaggerated 'frown' curve; the anterior teeth are blurred; condyles crowd the edges
Patient positioned too far forwardAnterior teeth look narrow and blurred
Patient positioned too far backAnterior teeth look wide and blurred; the spine overlaps the rami
Tongue not on the palateA dark radiolucent air shadow over the maxillary apices
Ghost imageA blurred, magnified radiopacity projected to the opposite side and higher up (for example the mandible, an earring or a necklace)

A ghost image forms when a dense structure (the opposite side of the mandible, an earring, a necklace or a dense palate) lies between the x-ray source and the center of rotation: it is projected across to the opposite side of the film, higher up, blurred and magnified. Recognizing a ghost image keeps it from being mistaken for real pathology. Because so much of panoramic interpretation depends on telling a positioning artifact from a true finding, knowing the normal anatomy and the typical errors is essential.

Success in radiology rests on knowing normal anatomy first, so that anything abnormal stands out against it.
full.em-prevent:
What's tested
  • The course's eight major themes and which emergencies happen most often in the dental office
  • Prevention: the medical history, risk assessment, and when to delay or change treatment
  • Your legal duty, the office emergency team and closed-loop communication
  • Basic life support: the C-A-B order, the pulse check, compressions, choking and the AED
  • The emergency kit: what each drug treats, its dose and route, and its catch

The eight themes

Dr. Kinard built the course around eight emergencies: anaphylaxis, hypoglycemia, asthma, chest pain, syncope, stroke, seizure and aspiration. For each one, know how it looks, what you do first, which drug (if any) you reach for, and when to call 911. On a dose question, pick the closest answer.

How often, and why

EmergencyShare of office emergencies
Syncope (fainting)About 50%, by far the most common
Mild allergic reactionAbout 8%
AnginaAbout 8%
Postural hypotensionAbout 8%
Seizures, asthma, hyperventilationAbout 4–5% each
Epinephrine reaction, hypoglycemiaAbout 3% each
Cardiac arrest, anaphylaxis, myocardial infarctionAbout 1% each
  • Most emergencies happen during or right after local anesthesia, most often in extraction and endodontic patients: stress and pain are the triggers.
  • Dr. Kinard names aspiration (crowns, burs, throat screens) as the top cause of serious trouble in the chair.
  • Malamed estimates that about 75% of office emergencies are preventable through patient evaluation, treatment modification and good management.
  • Alabama runs above the national average for smoking, obesity, diabetes and stroke, so expect sicker patients.

Prevention starts with the history

  • Take a full medical history, medication list and vital signs, and update them at every visit. The goal is to judge how much stress the patient can tolerate and whether treatment needs to change.
  • Recent heart attack or stroke: postpone elective care (the lecture says about 3 to 6 months) and plan it with the cardiologist.
  • Blood thinners: never stop an anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug yourself. Talk with the prescriber, who decides; most single extractions are done on the drug with local hemostasis.
  • "Medical clearance" is an outdated idea. The physician stratifies risk; the dentist interprets it, decides on the dental plan and stays responsible for it.
  • Delaying treatment until a condition is controlled is a valid way to lower risk.

Your duty and your team

  • The ADA expects dentists and staff to be trained to prevent, recognize and manage common emergencies, and to review those skills at least once a year.
  • The Alabama board expects you to respond to an emergency anywhere in your office, the waiting room included, to the level of your training.
  • Negligence is failing to do what a reasonably prudent dentist would do; gross negligence is willful or wanton disregard for the patient.
  • Five hazardous attitudes lead to mistakes: anti-authority, impulsivity, invulnerability ("it won't happen to me"), macho, and resignation ("what's the use?").
  • Use closed-loop communication: give a clear order to one person, who repeats it back ("0.3 mg epinephrine IM, drawing it up now").
MemberJob
1: the dentist (leader)Stays with the patient, positions them, directs the team, starts CPR
2Brings the kit, oxygen and AED; checks the tank; draws up drugs; helps with CPR
3Calls 911, meets EMS at the door and leads them in; relieves on CPR
4Recorder: times, vital signs, drugs and doses given

Basic life support

Every emergency comes down to keeping oxygenated blood going to the brain and heart. The class notes frame it as P-A-B-C-D: position, airway, breathing, circulation, then definitive care (drugs, defibrillation, diagnosis, EMS). Dr. Kinard: the order used to be airway-breathing-circulation and is now C-A-B: circulation first.

  • Make sure the scene is safe, tap and shout, call for help and send someone for the AED.
  • Check breathing and a pulse together for no more than 10 seconds. No pulse, or no breathing or only gasping: start CPR.
  • Compressions: 100–120 a minute, at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep, full recoil, pauses under 10 seconds, 30:2 with breaths.
  • A soft dental chair absorbs compressions: put a backboard under the patient or move them to the floor.
  • Head tilt-chin lift opens the airway: lifting the mandible pulls the genioglossus, and with it the tongue, off the back of the throat.
  • Pulses: the carotid can still be felt at the lowest pressure (systolic about 60), the femoral at about 70 and the radial at about 80. A pulse you can feel at the wrist means a reasonable pressure.
  • Choking: back blows and abdominal thrusts (5 and 5) for adults and children; infants get back blows and chest thrusts.
  • AED: when the AED is more than about 10 minutes away, survival from cardiac arrest is about 5%; within about 8 minutes, about 40%.
  • Keep backups for suction, power, oxygen and communication.

The emergency kit

DrugUseDose and routeWatch for
OxygenAlmost every emergency (not hyperventilation)Portable tank backs up wall oxygenKnow how to open the tank and set the flow
Epinephrine 1 mg/mLAnaphylaxis; bronchospasm that albuterol doesn't control0.3–0.5 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh, every 5–10 minutes; children 0.01 mg/kg (up to 0.3 mg)Glass ampule: snap it inside gauze; 23-gauge or larger needle; auto-injectors cost more and expire (about 20 months)
Albuterol (β2 agonist)Bronchospasm while the patient still moves air2 puffs (90 mcg each)Palpitations, tremor, nervousness
Diphenhydramine (H1 blocker)Mild allergy: hives, itching25–50 mg by mouth (up to an hour to work) or IM/IV (minutes)Sedation, dry mouth, urinary retention, fast heart rate; giving anything IM means calling 911
Nitroglycerin 0.4 mgAngina, chest painUnder the tongue, repeat every 5 minutesNot with systolic BP under 90 or an erectile dysfunction drug (sildenafil, tadalafil); brown bottle, lost to light, replace about 3 months after opening
Aspirin 325 mgSuspected heart attackChewed and swallowedNot with aspirin allergy, severe asthma or active GI bleeding
NaloxoneOpioid overdose4 mg in the nose, or 0.4 mg IV/IM; repeat every 2–3 minutesWears off in minutes while the opioid lasts hours: the patient can slip back, so call 911; patients often wake up agitated
GlucoseLow blood sugar in a conscious patientJuice, regular soda, glucose gelNothing by mouth if the patient can't swallow
Ammonia inhalantFaintingCrush and wave under the noseDr. Kinard calls it probably no longer needed: lay the patient back and raise the legs instead

Equipment: a pulse oximeter (two wavelengths of light; believe the number only with a good waveform; nail polish, cold hands, poor perfusion and bright light throw it off), a glucometer, a bag-valve-mask, oral and nasal airways (for unconscious patients only; they hold the tongue off the airway but don't clear a foreign body), backup suction, the AED and an emergency record to hand to EMS.
full.em-airway:
What's tested
  • Spotting a difficult airway before you start: history, Mallampati class, mouth opening, neck, weight, sleep apnea
  • Ventilation versus oxygenation, preoxygenation, pulse oximetry and bag-mask ventilation
  • Foreign-body aspiration: prevention, mild versus severe obstruction, what to do, where objects go and when to send the patient for X-rays
  • The airway ladder up to cricothyrotomy
  • Laryngospasm, asthma and bronchospasm, and hyperventilation
  • Allergy: a mild reaction versus anaphylaxis, and the drugs for each

Why the first minutes are yours

Dr. Squire: EMS takes about 7 minutes on average to arrive, and often twice that in rural areas, so you manage the airway until they come. Prevention is the best management. Smoking, COPD and asthma all raise the risk of breathing problems when patients are sedated. "It's never wrong to call EMS early. It's wrong every time to call them too late."

Ventilation and oxygenation

  • Ventilation is moving air in and out of the lungs (and CO2 out). Oxygenation is getting oxygen into the blood. A patient can move air and still be poorly oxygenated, and the reverse.
  • An adult uses about 250 mL of oxygen a minute. Preoxygenation fills the lungs' reserve with oxygen, which lengthens the time before saturation falls if breathing stops. Heart and lung disease, obesity and pregnancy shrink that reserve.
  • Pulse oximetry (finger, toe or earlobe) can't tell carbon monoxide-bound hemoglobin from oxyhemoglobin. Below about 88–90%, saturation falls fast.
  • Bag-mask ventilation: open the airway first (head tilt-chin lift or jaw thrust), seal the mask with the C-E grip, and give slow, gentle breaths. Too much pressure fills the stomach, which brings vomiting and aspiration, but getting air in comes first.
  • A color-change CO2 detector turns from purple to yellow when it sees exhaled CO2. No change: the tube is in the esophagus, or there is no circulation.

The difficult airway

ClassWhat you see with the mouth open and tongue out
ISoft palate, fauces, the whole uvula and the tonsillar pillars
IISoft palate, fauces and uvula
IIISoft palate and the base of the uvula
IVHard palate only

Classes III and IV predict a hard airway, though a class I patient can still be difficult. Other warning signs: limited mouth opening (trismus, deep neck infection, TMJ problems, scarring from past surgery), a beard, a short thick neck, BMI over 30, a short thyromental distance, a small or retruded mandible, limited neck extension (rheumatoid arthritis) and obstructive sleep apnea (screen with a questionnaire, confirm with a sleep study).

Foreign-body aspiration

  • The objects: crowns, implant parts and drivers, extracted teeth, burs, files, orthodontic brackets. Highest risk: sedated, elderly, anxious or intoxicated patients and those with stroke, Parkinson disease or brain injury, all of whom have weak protective reflexes.
  • Prevent it: a throat screen of unfolded 4x4 gauze (2x2s are small enough to aspirate), a rubber dam, floss tied to small parts and drivers, and suction.
  • Mild (partial) obstruction: the patient can cough, speak and move air, sometimes with high-pitched stridor. Encourage coughing and watch closely.
  • Severe (complete) obstruction: silent, can't speak or cough, hands to the throat, wide-eyed, turning blue. Ask "Are you choking?"; a nod without words means severe.
