Give abdominal thrusts (back blows plus thrusts is the Red Cross version). If the patient goes unresponsive, lower them, call 911 and start CPR, looking in the mouth before each set of breaths.
  • Never do a blind finger sweep: it pushes the object deeper. Remove only what you can see, with suction or forceps.
  • Aspirated objects usually go down the right main bronchus, which is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.
  • If an object disappears and you didn't see it come out, assume nothing, even if the patient looks fine: send them to the emergency room for chest and abdominal X-rays. An object in the airway comes out by bronchoscopy; one in the esophagus or stomach by endoscopy (EGD), and most swallowed objects pass on their own.

The airway ladder

Position (head tilt-chin lift, jaw thrust) → suction → oral or nasal airway → bag-mask → supraglottic airway (LMA) → endotracheal tube → surgical airway. When you can't intubate and can't oxygenate, the emergency surgical airway is a cricothyrotomy: through the cricothyroid membrane, between the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid below, with a vertical skin incision. A tracheostomy sits lower, near the thyroid gland, and bleeds more, so it isn't the emergency choice. Complications: bleeding, aspiration of blood, a false passage, esophageal injury, subcutaneous and mediastinal emphysema, vocal cord injury. Needle cricothyrotomy with jet ventilation buys time but doesn't protect the airway and isn't a first-line office tool.

Laryngospasm, bronchospasm, hyperventilation

  • Laryngospasm is the vocal cords clamping shut at the larynx, usually set off by blood, saliva, water or debris on the cords in a sedated patient. It is more likely in a lightly sedated patient than in one deeply asleep. Signs: high-pitched inspiratory stridor, or silence with chest movement but no air, and falling saturation. Treat: stop, suction the throat, 100% oxygen with positive pressure by bag-mask with a jaw thrust; if it doesn't break, a trained provider gives a small dose of succinylcholine.
  • Asthma and bronchospasm: wheezing (on breathing out), chest tightness, cough, using the neck muscles to breathe. Sit the patient up and give their own albuterol (2 puffs, repeat as needed) and oxygen. If they can't speak, the chest goes quiet or saturation falls, give epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg IM and call 911. Asthma patients bring their inhaler to every visit; avoid aspirin and NSAIDs in aspirin-sensitive asthma.
  • Hyperventilation: an anxious patient breathes fast, gets lightheaded, with tingling lips and fingers and sometimes hand spasms, from blowing off CO2 (respiratory alkalosis). Stop, sit them up, reassure and coach slow breathing (or breathing into cupped hands). Don't give oxygen.

Allergy and anaphylaxis

Mild allergic reactionAnaphylaxis
SignsSkin only: hives, itching, rash, flushingSkin signs plus wheeze, stridor or throat tightness, and/or low blood pressure and a fast pulse; minutes after the trigger
First drugDiphenhydramine 25–50 mg by mouth, or IMEpinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5–10 minutes
ThenWatch the patient; an IM dose means calling 911Call 911, lay the patient flat with legs raised (sitting up if breathing is hard), oxygen; albuterol and diphenhydramine only as add-ons

Office triggers include latex, antibiotics such as penicillin, NSAIDs and chlorhexidine. True allergy to an amide local anesthetic is rare. Diphenhydramine does nothing for airway swelling or shock, so never delay epinephrine to give it.
full.em-cardiac:
What's tested
  • Chest pain: telling angina from a heart attack, and the office steps (oxygen, nitroglycerin, aspirin, 911)
  • Heart failure and arrhythmias in the chair, and which rhythms the AED shocks
  • Infective endocarditis: which patients and which procedures need antibiotic prophylaxis, and the regimen
  • Hypertensive urgency versus hypertensive emergency
  • Bleeding: anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs, bleeding disorders and local hemostasis

Dr. Ying's focus is the workup and management: who is at risk, which drugs matter, what you do in the office.

Chest pain: angina and myocardial infarction

Plaque narrows the coronary arteries; chest pain comes when oxygen demand outruns supply. Stable angina comes with exertion or stress and eases with rest or nitroglycerin. Unstable angina is new, worsening or at rest. A myocardial infarction is a full blockage with muscle death (STEMI or NSTEMI, diagnosed in the hospital).

  • Signs: crushing, squeezing or burning pressure behind the sternum, spreading to the left arm, jaw or neck (referred pain: the heart's sensory fibers enter the same spinal levels as those skin areas), sweating, shortness of breath, nausea, anxiety; the pulse may be fast, slow or irregular. Women, older adults and people with diabetes may have only fatigue, nausea or jaw pain.
  • In the office: stop, sit the patient up comfortably, check vitals and give oxygen.
  • Nitroglycerin 0.4 mg under the tongue (the patient's own or the kit's), repeated every 5 minutes, if the systolic pressure is at least 90 and no erectile dysfunction drug was taken. Nitro paste on the skin is another form.
  • Pain that nitroglycerin doesn't relieve is a heart attack until proven otherwise: call 911, have the patient chew 325 mg of aspirin, keep them calm, monitor, and start BLS with the AED if they arrest. (Current AHA advice: call 911 if the pain isn't better 5 minutes after the first dose.)
  • Planning: ask about past heart attacks, stents and cardiac drugs; many cardiac drugs mean a sicker heart and a cautious hand with epinephrine.

Heart failure

The pump can't keep up, so fluid backs up. Left-sided failure floods the lungs: shortness of breath on exertion, orthopnea (can't lie flat; sleeps on pillows) and crackles. Right-sided failure shows as pitting edema of the legs and jugular venous distension. The hospital confirms it with a chest X-ray, an echo and BNP (released by an overstretched heart). In the chair: treat the patient sitting up, ask whether they took their diuretic, keep epinephrine to a minimum and stop if they get breathless. Heart failure alone doesn't call for antibiotic prophylaxis. If they decompensate: sit them upright, give oxygen and call 911.

Arrhythmias

  • Normal rate 60–100. Tachycardia is over 100, bradycardia under 60.
  • Atrial fibrillation is the common one: an irregularly irregular pulse, clots in the atria and a risk of stroke, so these patients are usually anticoagulated. With a rapid rate (130 to 150), pause and send the patient to their physician.
  • Supraventricular tachycardia: vagal maneuvers (Valsalva, cold water to the face) and, in the hospital, adenosine. Bradycardia: atropine. Rate control: β-blockers; amiodarone for AFib.
  • The AED shocks ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia. Asystole and pulseless electrical activity are not shockable: continue high-quality CPR.
  • Pacemakers and implanted defibrillators: ask what it does and when it was last checked.

Valve disease and endocarditis

A stenotic valve is stiff and narrow; a regurgitant valve leaks; atresia is a valve opening that never formed. Acquired causes: rheumatic fever after untreated strep throat, endocarditis, calcification with age, Marfan syndrome, lupus, scleroderma, trauma. Congenital lesions (bicuspid aortic valve, pulmonary stenosis, tetralogy of Fallot) are usually repaired in childhood, so ask about past heart surgery.

Infective endocarditis grows vegetations (clot full of bacteria) on the valves: fever, chills, weight loss, a new murmur, Osler nodes (painful nodules on the finger pads), Janeway lesions (painless flat red spots on the palms and soles), Roth spots (retinal hemorrhages) and splinter hemorrhages. Blood cultures and an echo confirm it. Injection drug use raises the risk.

Details
Who needs itProsthetic heart valve (mechanical or tissue) or prosthetic material used to repair a valve; past endocarditis; unrepaired cyanotic congenital heart disease; congenital heart disease repaired with prosthetic material (first 6 months, or for life with a leftover defect next to it); heart transplant with valve disease
Who doesn'tMitral valve prolapse, rheumatic heart disease without a prosthetic valve, bicuspid aortic valve, small atrial septal defect, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, Kawasaki disease, heart failure, stents, bypass grafts, pacemakers
Which proceduresAny that manipulate the gingiva or the periapical area or perforate the mucosa: extractions, periodontal surgery, scaling, implants, biopsies. Not an exam, radiographs, fluoride or a routine injection through healthy tissue
RegimenAmoxicillin 2 g by mouth 30–60 minutes before. Penicillin allergy: cephalexin 2 g (no history of anaphylaxis or hives), azithromycin or clarithromycin 500 mg, or doxycycline 100 mg. Can't swallow: ampicillin, cefazolin or ceftriaxone IV or IM

When a cardiologist recommends more or less than the guideline, you are still the treating provider: stay within the standard of care and document whom you spoke with.

Hypertension

High blood pressure is silent and damages the kidneys, heart, brain and eyes over years. A reading of 180 or more systolic or 120 or more diastolic is severe. It is a hypertensive emergency when there are signs of organ damage now (severe headache, chest pain, vision changes, confusion, weakness, shortness of breath): send the patient to the emergency room. Without them it is a hypertensive urgency: no elective care that day, a prompt visit to the physician or urgent care, and a note in the chart. Check blood pressure at every visit.

Bleeding

"Almost all bleeding can be stopped with gauze under pressure." Fold gauze over the socket and have the patient bite firmly, or hold it with your finger, for 10 to 15 minutes; replace it when soaked. Patients often bleed on because they place the gauze but don't press on the socket.

DrugActs onDental points
Warfarin (Coumadin)Vitamin K-dependent factorsMonitored by INR; the lecture's target for surgery is under 2.5, acceptable up to 3 with local measures; long-acting and slow to reverse (vitamin K)
Rivaroxaban (Xarelto), apixaban (Eliquis)Factor XaShort half-life (about 12 hours); reversal agent andexanet alfa
Dabigatran (Pradaxa)ThrombinReversal agent idarucizumab
AspirinCOX, irreversiblyEffect lasts the platelet's life, 7–10 days
Clopidogrel (Plavix)Platelet ADP (P2Y12) receptor, irreversiblyHeld about 5 days only if the prescriber decides

Stopping any of them is the prescriber's call. For simple extractions most patients stay on them and you use local measures: a stroke or stent clot is a worse outcome than an oozing socket.

  • Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder (about 1%) and often undiagnosed: the patient oozes for 2 or 3 days after surgery. Mild disease is treated with desmopressin (DDAVP), with the hematologist.
  • Hemophilia A (factor VIII) and hemophilia B (factor IX) are X-linked recessive; patients know their disease and get factor replacement through their hematologist before surgery.
  • Also think of ITP, leukemia, liver disease and kidney failure.

Local measures, cheapest first: pressure; local anesthetic with epinephrine injected at the site; packing with gelatin sponge (Gelfoam), oxidized cellulose (Surgicel) or collagen, with topical thrombin or fibrin glue; sutures for primary closure; bone wax pressed into a bleeding bony surface; electrocautery, ligatures and clips. Tranexamic acid (a 5% rinse or tablets) helps patients with bleeding disorders or ongoing oozing.
full.em-loc:
What's tested
  • The same first steps for anyone who loses consciousness: stop, position, airway, breathing, circulation, oxygen, vital signs, 911
  • Vasovagal syncope: why it happens, how it looks and how to treat it
  • Diabetes and hypoglycemia: the numbers, and juice versus glucagon versus IV dextrose
  • Oxygen delivery: nasal cannula, face mask and non-rebreather
  • Adrenal crisis and the rule of twos; thyroid storm
  • Seizures, stroke and local anesthetic overdose

Consciousness is being aware of and responsive to your surroundings. Check it by talking to the patient: name, place, day. Dr. Castro's message: prevention is the key, and know your drugs and equipment well enough to use them before the day you need them.

The common first steps

  • Stop the treatment and remove what's in the mouth.
  • Position: supine with the legs raised, so blood goes to the brain (sitting up instead for chest pain or a breathing problem).
  • Airway, breathing, circulation: head tilt-chin lift, look for breathing, feel for a pulse; start BLS if needed.
  • Oxygen and vital signs: blood pressure, pulse, oxygen saturation.
  • Call 911 if the patient doesn't quickly recover. Tell EMS what you gave in milligrams, not cartridges (2% lidocaine is 36 mg per 1.8 mL cartridge).

Vasovagal syncope

The most common office emergency (about half of them): a brief loss of blood flow to the brain from a vasovagal response to stress, fear, sudden pain, or the sight of blood or a needle. It usually lasts seconds to a few minutes. Before it comes the prodrome: lightheadedness, pallor, sweating, nausea; then the patient faints with a slow pulse.

  • Lay the patient back with the legs above the head (on the floor if it happens in the waiting room), loosen tight clothing, put a cold towel on the forehead, give oxygen and monitor.
  • Speak calmly; your voice steadies the patient.
  • An ammonia inhalant crushed under the nose rouses patients quickly; Dr. Castro uses it, Dr. Kinard thinks it's no longer needed.
  • Bradycardia that doesn't improve: atropine IV (the lecture's dose is 1 mg; the class notes give 0.5 mg every 3–5 minutes up to 3 mg).
  • Recovery should be quick once the patient is flat. If not, it isn't simple fainting: BLS and 911.

Postural hypotension is a drop in pressure when a patient sits up fast after lying back, more common with blood pressure drugs and diuretics: raise the chair slowly and let them sit a minute.

Diabetes

TestDiabetesControl (lecture)
Fasting glucose126 mg/dL or more
Random glucose200 mg/dL or more
HbA1c6.5% or moreAbout 7: good; 8.5–10: fair; over 10: poor

The classic signs are the three Ps: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia. Complications: retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy, heart attack and stroke, and infections, which are much more severe in the mouth. Infection is the most common trigger of diabetic ketoacidosis. A poorly controlled patient needs a medical consult before oral surgery. Ask every diabetic patient whether they ate and took their medicine, and what their last HbA1c was.

Hypoglycemia

The lecture's number: serum glucose under about 50–60 mg/dL (in diabetes care, under 70 is low and under 54 serious). Causes: insulin and sulfonylureas, a skipped meal, alcohol, sepsis, adrenal insufficiency, cirrhosis. Signs: hunger, shakiness, sweating, anxiety and a fast pulse, then confusion, odd or combative behavior, seizures and loss of consciousness. Low sugar is far more dangerous in the short term than high sugar, so when in doubt, give sugar.

  • Conscious: sugar by mouth: juice, regular soda, glucose gel or tablets. Check with a glucometer and repeat as needed.
  • Unconscious: nothing by mouth. Glucagon 1 mg IM (into the thigh, through clothing if necessary), or IV dextrose, 50 mL of 50% for an adult (25% for a child), and call 911. Glucagon makes the liver release stored glucose and brings the level to about 130 in 25–30 minutes.
  • Rule of thumb: each gram of fast sugar raises blood glucose about 3–5 mg/dL, so a 15 g gel raises it about 45–75.

Oxygen delivery

DeviceFlowOxygen delivered
Nasal cannula1–5 L/min (about 4% more per liter)24–40%; turning it higher adds nothing
Simple face mask5–7 L/minAbout 40–60%
Non-rebreather mask10–15 L/minThe highest without a tube (the lecture says about 100%)

Room air is 21% oxygen; the wall and tank give 100%. To breathe for a patient, use the bag-valve-mask with the C-E grip. If nothing else is at hand, the nitrous machine can deliver oxygen alone.

Thyroid storm

Hypothyroidism slows everything (cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, coarse hair); hyperthyroidism speeds everything up (tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, systolic hypertension, heat intolerance, weight loss, tremor, bulging eyes). A thyroid storm is a sudden, severe flare of hyperthyroidism set off by infection, surgery, trauma, pregnancy or stress: high fever, a racing heart, agitation, vomiting, confusion and possibly unconsciousness. Stop at once, call for help, oxygen, vitals, BLS as needed, and transport to a hospital.

Adrenal crisis and the rule of twos

The adrenal cortex makes steroids (cortisol, aldosterone, androgens); the medulla makes epinephrine and norepinephrine. Hydrocortisone is cortisol made in the lab; prednisone, dexamethasone and methylprednisolone are other synthetic glucocorticoids, and all of them raise blood sugar. Long-term steroids suppress the patient's own cortisol: secondary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease is the primary form; excess steroid causes Cushing syndrome).

An adrenal crisis is a sudden lack of cortisol when the body needs more, set off by infection, surgery, trauma or stopping long-term steroids abruptly: severe hypotension, vomiting, confusion and loss of consciousness. Rule of twos: a patient taking 20 mg of hydrocortisone (or the equivalent) a day for 2 weeks or more within the past 2 years may be suppressed. Most dental procedures under local anesthesia or nitrous oxide need no extra steroid; reduce stress and consult for major surgery. Treat a crisis: stop, lay the patient flat with the legs up, oxygen, 911, and hydrocortisone 100 mg (Solu-Cortef) IV or IM.

Seizures and stroke

  • Seizure: protect the patient from injury (clear instruments, lower the chair, don't restrain, nothing in the mouth), time it, then turn the patient on the side and give oxygen; confusion afterward (the postictal phase) is expected. A long or repeated seizure: 911 and a benzodiazepine (midazolam IM, lorazepam 2–4 mg IV, diazepam 5–10 mg IV).
  • Stroke: about 80% ischemic (thrombus or embolus), 20% hemorrhagic. Sudden one-sided weakness, facial droop, slurred speech; a sudden "worst headache of my life" suggests a subarachnoid bleed. Stop, call 911, note the time it started, support the airway and check the blood sugar (low sugar can look like a stroke).

Local anesthetic overdose

Keep count. Lidocaine with epinephrine allows about 7 mg/kg, so a 70-kg adult can have about 13 cartridges; when a patient isn't numb, the problem is usually technique, not volume. Risk rises with age extremes, low weight, liver, kidney or heart disease, pregnancy, and injection into a vessel. Mild to moderate signs: numbness around the mouth, talkativeness, confusion, slurred speech, tremor, twitching, nystagmus, rising heart rate and blood pressure. Severe: seizures, then CNS depression, hypotension, bradycardia and asystole. Treat: stop, position, airway and oxygen, 911, a benzodiazepine for seizures and, for severe toxicity, IV lipid emulsion 20% (Intralipid). Amides are cleared by the liver, except articaine, which is cleared mostly in the plasma, so it suits patients with liver disease.

plain.hn-neck:
What's tested
  • How spinal nerves and the two autonomic systems are laid out
  • Horner syndrome
  • What lives in the posterior and anterior triangles
  • The root of the neck, the thyroid and the nerves at risk in thyroid surgery
  • Neck fascia and how infection spreads

Each spinal nerve has a sensory back root and a motor front root. The sympathetic system starts in the spinal cord from T1 to L2; nerves for the head relay in the superior cervical ganglion and ride along the carotid arteries. The parasympathetic system leaves with cranial nerves III, VII, IX and X and the sacral cord; its head relay stations are the ciliary, pterygopalatine, submandibular and otic ganglia.

If the neck's sympathetic chain is cut or squeezed (for example by a lung-top tumor), you get Horner syndrome: a slightly droopy eyelid, a small pupil, and a face that is dry and flushed on that side.

The posterior triangle sits between the SCM, the trapezius and the clavicle. Its most famous content is CN XI, lying just under the fascia: cut it and the patient can't shrug. The skin nerves of the cervical plexus come out at the middle of the SCM's back edge; the great auricular nerve covers the skin over the angle of the jaw.

The anterior triangle holds the strap muscles, the carotid sheath (carotid artery inside, internal jugular vein outside, vagus behind), the carotid sinus (blood pressure sensor) and body (oxygen sensor), and the external carotid's eight branches. The hyoid is at C3 and the cricoid at C6.

At the root of the neck, the subclavian artery is split into three parts by the anterior scalene. The phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5) runs down that muscle to the diaphragm. The thoracic duct empties where the left internal jugular and subclavian veins meet.

In thyroid surgery, the nerve near the superior thyroid artery (external laryngeal) controls pitch, and the nerve near the inferior thyroid artery (recurrent laryngeal) controls most of the voice box; injuring it makes the voice hoarse. Removing the parathyroids by mistake drops calcium and causes muscle spasms.

Neck fascia forms tubes and spaces. The spaces behind the pharynx can carry an infection from a tooth or tonsil down into the chest.
plain.hn-skull:
What's tested
  • The bones and weak spots of the skull
  • What passes through the main skull openings
  • Dural sinuses and the cavernous sinus
  • Head bleeds
  • What each cranial nerve does and how it fails

The braincase is 8 bones; the face is built from the rest. The pterion, on the side of the head, is thin bone over the middle meningeal artery. A hard blow there can tear the artery and cause an epidural bleed: lens-shaped on CT, often with a period of feeling fine before the patient crashes.

Learn the openings in pairs: V2 through the foramen rotundum, V3 through the foramen ovale, the middle meningeal artery through the foramen spinosum; III, IV, V1 and VI through the superior orbital fissure; VII and VIII into the internal acoustic meatus; IX, X and XI through the jugular foramen; XII through its own canal.

Venous blood collects in the dural sinuses and leaves through the internal jugular vein. The cavernous sinus, next to the pituitary, holds the internal carotid and CN VI, with III, IV, V1 and V2 in its wall. Infection from the face or teeth can reach it; the first sign is often an eye that can't look outward (CN VI).

A subdural bleed comes from torn bridging veins (crescent shape, often older people after a small fall). A subarachnoid bleed comes from a burst aneurysm and gives a sudden, terrible headache.

Cranial nerve signs to know: the tongue points toward a bad XII; the uvula points away from a bad X; a bad III gives a droopy lid, a big pupil and an eye turned down and out; Bell palsy (VII nerve) paralyzes the whole half-face, but a stroke spares the forehead.

Two reflexes tie nerves together: touching the cornea is felt by V1 and answered by VII (blink); touching the throat is felt by IX and answered by X (gag).
plain.hn-face:
What's tested
  • The orbit and its fractures
  • How the eye muscles and pupil are controlled
  • Face muscles and facial nerve palsy
  • The danger triangle and the scalp
  • Tears and the parotid gland

The orbit's floor is the weakest wall. A punch to the eye can blow it out into the maxillary sinus, trapping the inferior rectus (the patient can't look up and sees double) and numbing the cheek.

Eye muscles: LR6, SO4, all the rest III. The superior oblique is tested by looking down and in. CN III also opens the eyelid and shrinks the pupil; the sympathetics widen the pupil. For close work, the ciliary muscle tightens and the lens gets rounder. Fluid made in the eye drains at the angle into the canal of Schlemm; when it can't, pressure rises (glaucoma).

All face muscles belong to VII, which splits into five branches inside the parotid. Feeling on the face comes from V1, V2 and V3. In Bell palsy the whole half-face is weak, forehead too. A dental block placed too far back can do this for a few hours.

Face veins around the nose link to the veins of the eye and on to the cavernous sinus, so infections in the danger triangle are serious. In the scalp, the loose layer under the aponeurosis is where blood and pus spread.

Tears come from a gland at the upper outer corner, run to the inner corner and drain into the nose (inferior meatus). The nerve signal for tears comes from VII and relays in the pterygopalatine ganglion.

The parotid is wrapped in tight fascia. The facial nerve runs through it but does not control it; spit from the parotid is driven by IX through the otic ganglion and the auriculotemporal nerve. Its duct opens opposite the upper second molar. After parotid surgery some people sweat on the cheek when they eat (Frey syndrome).
plain.hn-itf:
What's tested
  • What is in the infratemporal fossa
  • The four chewing muscles
  • V3 and its branches, and the blocks dentists give
  • The maxillary artery and the pterygoid plexus
  • How the TMJ moves and dislocates

The infratemporal fossa is the space behind and inside the ramus. It holds the two pterygoid muscles, the maxillary artery, the pterygoid venous plexus and V3, which enters from the foramen ovale.

Chewing muscles all come from arch 1 and all use V3. Three close the jaw (temporalis, masseter, medial pterygoid). The lateral pterygoid pulls the jaw forward and opens it. If V3 is cut on one side, the jaw swings toward that side when the mouth opens.

V3's front branch is mostly motor, except the buccal nerve to the cheek. The back branch gives the auriculotemporal nerve (temple, ear, TMJ), the lingual nerve (tongue feeling; it picks up the chorda tympani for taste) and the inferior alveolar nerve (lower teeth, then the mental nerve to the lip and chin).

An inferior alveolar block puts anesthetic in the space between the ramus and the medial pterygoid. It misses the buccal nerve. Too far back reaches the parotid and the facial nerve. A posterior superior alveolar block too deep can hit the pterygoid plexus and cause a sudden bruise-like swelling.

The maxillary artery has three parts: the first gives the middle meningeal and inferior alveolar arteries, the second feeds the chewing muscles, the third gives the arteries for the upper teeth, palate and nose. The pterygoid plexus links to the cavernous sinus, a path for dental infection.

The TMJ has a disc that makes two joints: the lower one hinges, the upper one slides. It dislocates forward, in front of the articular eminence, usually from a big yawn. The joint is fed by the auriculotemporal nerve, which also supplies the ear canal, so a sore TMJ often feels like an earache.
plain.hn-phx:
What's tested
  • What each pharyngeal arch and pouch builds
  • How the lip and palate form and how clefts happen
  • Neck cysts from development
  • The muscles and nerves of the pharynx and larynx
  • The parts of the ear and kinds of hearing loss

Each pharyngeal arch brings its own nerve: arch 1 is V (chewing muscles, malleus, incus), arch 2 is VII (face muscles, stapes, styloid), arch 3 is IX (stylopharyngeus), arches 4 and 6 are X (pharynx, palate and larynx). Pouch 3 makes the thymus and the lower parathyroids; pouch 4 makes the upper parathyroids.

The upper lip's middle (philtrum) and the front of the palate come from the joined medial nasal prominences. If the maxillary prominence doesn't meet them, you get a cleft lip. If the two palatal shelves don't meet each other, you get a cleft palate.

A lump on the side of the neck in front of the SCM may be a lateral cervical cyst, left over from the cervical sinus. A lump in the midline that rises when the tongue sticks out is a thyroglossal duct cyst, left along the path the thyroid took down from the tongue.

In the pharynx, the vagus moves every muscle except the stylopharyngeus (IX). IX feels the gag; X answers it. A fish bone stuck in the piriform recess can injure the nerve that lets the larynx feel food (internal laryngeal).

In the larynx, the recurrent laryngeal nerve runs every muscle except the cricothyroid. Only the posterior cricoarytenoid opens the vocal folds, so losing both recurrent nerves closes the airway. Emergency airway: cut through the cricothyroid ligament.

In the ear, the stapes sits in the oval window. The stapedius (VII) damps loud sound; without it, normal sounds hurt. Children get ear infections because their auditory tube is short and flat. Hearing loss is conductive (outer or middle ear) or sensorineural (cochlea or nerve).
plain.hn-oral:
What's tested
  • The openings of the pterygopalatine fossa
  • Where the sinuses drain and why the maxillary sinus matters to dentists
  • Nerves of the palate and tongue
  • The salivary glands
  • Where infections and lymph from the mouth go

The pterygopalatine fossa is a crossroads behind the upper jaw. V2 enters from the skull and sends branches to the upper teeth, palate, nose and face. Its ganglion relays signals from VII for tears and for nose and palate glands.

Most sinuses drain into the middle meatus. The tear duct drains into the inferior meatus. The maxillary sinus drains from high up, so it gets infected easily, and its floor sits on the roots of the upper back teeth: an extraction can leave a hole into the sinus, and sinusitis can feel like a toothache. Most nosebleeds start on the front of the septum.

For the palate, the greater palatine nerve covers the back of the hard palate and the nasopalatine nerve covers the front, behind the incisors. All soft palate muscles are run by X except the tensor veli palatini (V3).

For the tongue: front two-thirds feel through V3 and taste through VII (chorda tympani); back third feels and tastes through IX; XII moves it (except palatoglossus, X).

The submandibular gland makes most resting saliva and most salivary stones; its duct opens under the tongue. VII drives it and the sublingual gland; IX drives the parotid.

Lymph from the tongue tip and lower front teeth goes to the submental nodes; most other teeth drain to the submandibular nodes; everything ends in the deep cervical chain. A lower tooth whose root tip is below the mylohyoid line spreads infection under the jaw (submandibular space); above it, into the floor of the mouth (sublingual space). Both sides at once is Ludwig angina, an airway emergency.
plain.da-numbering:
What's tested
  • Writing any tooth in Universal, Palmer and FDI
  • When teeth come in, and in what order
  • When teeth start to harden and when roots finish
  • How baby teeth differ from adult teeth

Naming teeth

Universal numbers adult teeth 1 to 32, starting at the upper right third molar and going around to the lower right third molar. Baby teeth use letters A to T the same way. FDI uses two digits: the quadrant (1 upper right, 2 upper left, 3 lower left, 4 lower right; 5 to 8 for baby teeth), then the tooth counted from the midline. So #8 is 11, #19 is 36, #30 is 46, and baby tooth A is 55. Palmer uses a bracket for the quadrant and counts 1 to 8 (A to E for baby teeth) from the midline.

When teeth come in

Baby teeth: central incisors, lateral incisors, first molars, canines, then second molars, from about 6 months to 2 years. The lower teeth usually come first. Adult teeth: the first molars and lower central incisors arrive at about 6. The upper order is 6-1-2-4-5-3-7-8, so the upper canine comes after the premolars, at 11–12, and is the anterior tooth most likely to get stuck. The lower order is 6-1-2-3-4-5-7-8. The first adult tooth to replace a baby tooth is the lower central incisor. Adult molars replace nothing, so they are not "succedaneous".

Hardening and roots

Baby teeth start hardening before birth (about 4–6 months in the womb). The adult first molar starts at birth. Cusp tips and incisal edges harden first, and crowns before roots. An adult root finishes 2–3 years after the tooth comes in; baby roots finish by about age 3.

Baby versus adult teeth

Baby teeth are smaller and whiter, with thin enamel, big pulps and high pulp horns. Their crowns are short and bulge at the neck (cervical ridges), and their molar roots spread wide to leave room for the premolars. A few are one of a kind: the upper central is wider than it is tall, the upper canine has its longer slope on the mesial, and the lower first molar has a big transverse ridge and a bulge at the mesiobuccal. The second baby molars look like the adult first molars.
plain.da-anterior:
What's tested
  • Where the bulge of each surface is
  • Where teeth touch, and the exceptions
  • Telling the incisors apart
  • Upper versus lower canine

Bulges and contacts

Every tooth's facial bulge is in the cervical third. On the tongue side, front teeth bulge in the cervical third and back teeth in the middle third. A crown that is too bulky lets food skip the gum and collects plaque; one that is too flat pushes food into the gum. Teeth touch lower (more cervically) the farther back they are, and each tooth touches its back neighbor lower than its front one. The exceptions are the lower central incisor (both contacts level), the lower first premolar and the baby upper canine. The gap on the tongue side between teeth is bigger than on the cheek side. The CEJ dips most on the mesial of the central incisors.

Incisors

The upper central is the biggest incisor, with a sharp mesial corner and a rounded distal one. The upper lateral is a smaller, rounder copy with a deep lingual fossa; it can have a groove running onto the root that traps plaque, and it often comes in peg-shaped or not at all. The lower central is the smallest adult tooth and nearly symmetric. The lower lateral is a bit bigger, with its incisal edge twisted toward the distolingual.

Canines

The upper canine is the longest tooth with the longest root, a sharp cusp, a short mesial slope and a strong lingual ridge. The lower canine has the longest crown, a long distal slope, a smooth lingual side, and a mesial outline that runs straight into the root; its root can split in two. The upper canine is the last front tooth to come in, so it is the one that gets stuck. Its long root in thick bone also makes it the best tooth to guide the jaw sideways.
plain.da-posterior:
What's tested
  • Which premolar or molar is which
  • How many roots and canals each has
  • First versus second molars

Premolars

The upper first premolar is the one with two roots and a dip (concavity) on its mesial side. The upper second premolar has one root and two cusps of about the same height. The lower first premolar looks like a small canine: a big buccal cusp, a tiny lingual cusp, a crown leaning to the tongue, and a mesial marginal ridge lower than the distal one, which no other back tooth has. The lower second premolar usually has three cusps in a Y pattern with a pit in the middle; with two cusps its grooves look like an H or a U. Lower premolars lean toward the tongue; upper premolars sit straight over their roots.

Upper molars

The upper first molar is the biggest upper tooth. Its cusps from biggest to smallest are mesiolingual, mesiobuccal, distobuccal and distolingual, and the Carabelli cusp sits on the mesiolingual. A ridge (the oblique ridge) runs from the distobuccal to the mesiolingual cusp. It is the only molar wider on the tongue side. It has three roots: palatal longest, then mesiobuccal, then distobuccal. The mesiobuccal root usually holds two canals, so look for four. Its lingual groove and pit are where decay starts. The second molar has a smaller (or missing) distolingual cusp and roots that sit closer together.

Lower molars

The lower first molar has five cusps (three buccal, two lingual) and two buccal grooves; the distal cusp is the smallest. The lower second molar has four cusps in a plus-sign pattern. Both have two roots, mesial and distal; the mesial root is wider, more curved, and holds two canals. Lower molars lean toward the tongue, and their roots lean toward the distal, which helps you tell right from left on an extracted tooth.
plain.da-anomalies:
What's tested
  • Naming an anomaly from a description
  • Fusion versus gemination versus concrescence
  • Inherited versus acquired enamel and dentin defects
  • Types of wear
  • Tooth identification

Too few, too many, in the wrong place

Third molars are the teeth most often missing. Missing all teeth goes with ectodermal dysplasia. An extra tooth between the upper centrals is a mesiodens. Third molars and upper canines get impacted most.

Odd shapes

Gemination is one tooth trying to split: count it as one and the count is normal. Fusion is two teeth joined by dentin: count it as one and you are one short. Concrescence is two teeth joined only by cementum. A peg lateral is a small upper lateral. Notched incisors and many-cusped molars point to congenital syphilis. A talon cusp is a claw off the cingulum. Dens in dente is enamel folded into the tooth, usually an upper lateral. Taurodontism is a tall pulp chamber with the furcation pushed down. An enamel pearl at a furcation leaves a pocket.

Enamel and dentin defects

Inherited defects hit every tooth in both sets: amelogenesis imperfecta (bad enamel) and dentinogenesis imperfecta (bluish teeth, chipping enamel, pulps filled in). Fluoride causes white to brown mottling, tetracycline causes gray bands, and an infected baby tooth can spoil the one adult tooth below it (Turner tooth).

Wear

Attrition is tooth against tooth, abrasion is something else rubbing (hard brushing), erosion is acid (vomiting wears the inside of the upper front teeth), and abfraction is a V-shaped notch at the gumline from flexing.

Naming a tooth

Count the cusps for the class, use the roots and tilt for the arch, find the mesial landmark, then hold the face toward you with the mesial at the midline: that side is the patient's side. When two answers seem to fit, the root count and the crown's tilt usually decide it.
plain.da-occlusion:
What's tested
  • Angle Class I, II and III
  • Which cusps hold the bite
  • CR, MIP and CO
  • Canine guidance and group function, and bad contacts
  • What makes cusps taller or shorter

The basics

The upper tongue-side cusps and the lower cheek-side cusps are the "centric" cusps: they hold the bite height and land in the opposing grooves. The other cusps are sharper and guide and protect the cheek and tongue. Seen from the side, the lower teeth follow the curve of Spee; seen from the front, the curve of Wilson. Every tooth meets two opposing teeth except the lower central incisor and the upper third molar.

Angle classes

Class I (most people): the upper first molar's mesiobuccal cusp sits in the lower first molar's buccal groove. Class II: the lower jaw sits back. In division 1 the upper incisors flare forward; in division 2 the upper centrals tip back with a deep bite. Class III: the lower jaw sits forward.

CR, MIP and CO

Centric relation is a joint position: condyles up and forward against the eminences, discs in place. It does not depend on the teeth. MIP is where the teeth fit together best. Centric occlusion is the tooth contact you get with the condyles in CR. Most people (about 9 in 10) slide about 1 mm from CR contact into MIP.

Guidance

The ideal: all back teeth touch evenly when you close, forces go down the long axis, and when the jaw slides sideways or forward the front teeth separate the back teeth at once. Canine guidance means only the canines touch going sideways; they have the longest roots and quiet the closing muscles. Group function shares the guidance among the canine and premolars on the working side. A back-tooth contact on the nonworking side is the worst interference. Full dentures use balanced occlusion instead.

Cusp height

A steep joint path and a deep overbite allow tall cusps. A big overjet, a sharp curve of Spee and more sideways shift of the jaw call for short cusps. The front teeth can be changed by the dentist; the joint cannot.
plain.da-tmj:
What's tested
  • The joint's parts
  • Which muscles move the jaw
  • How far the jaw opens, and how
  • Articulators and the facebow
  • Jaw pain, loose teeth and wear

The joint

The jaw joint both hinges and slides. A disc sits between the condyle and the skull. Its middle is thin and has no blood vessels or nerves. Behind it, the retrodiscal tissue has both, so that is where pain comes from; its upper layer is elastic and pulls the disc back. Hinging happens below the disc and sliding above it. The temporomandibular ligament's outer part stops the pure hinge at about 20–25 mm; its inner part keeps the condyle from being pushed back.

Muscles

The temporalis, masseter and medial pterygoid close. The lower lateral pterygoid and the muscles under the chin open and push the jaw forward. To move the jaw right, the right temporalis and masseter pull while the left lateral and medial pterygoids push.

Movement

The jaw hinges for the first 20–25 mm and then slides forward to open 40–60 mm. In a side movement, the condyle on the side you move toward spins; the other one swings forward, down and in. The whole jaw may also shift sideways (Bennett movement).

Articulators

An articulator holds models and copies jaw movement. A facebow places the upper model in relation to the hinge axis. Models mounted in centric relation can find the bite, but models mounted in the bite can't find centric relation.

Problems

Most jaw pain is in the muscles. Stress, injury, other pain, clenching and grinding, and bite problems all play a part. Grinding starts in the brain, not in the bite. Start with reversible care such as a flat splint. Heavy bite forces can loosen a tooth but do not cause gum disease. Wear comes from teeth rubbing, brushing with gritty toothpaste, acid, and perhaps flexing.
plain.f1-biomol:
What's tested
  • Bonds, water, pH and buffers
  • Amino acids and the four levels of protein structure
  • Fibrous and globular proteins, and why proteins team up as groups of chains
  • Collagen and vitamin C; hemoglobin's oxygen binding
  • Sugars, fats and DNA's building blocks

The short version

Atoms bond to fill their outer shell of electrons. Covalent bonds share electrons and are the strongest. If two atoms pull on the electrons equally, the bond is nonpolar (C–C and C–H, the carbon backbones of biomolecules); if one pulls harder (it is more electronegative), the bond is polar (O–H) and the atoms carry partial charges; if one pulls so hard it takes the electron, the atoms become ions held by an ionic bond. Ionic bonds, hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces are weaker, can come apart again, and hold a protein's folded shape.

Water is polar. It dissolves charged and polar things by surrounding them, and it pushes oily things together, which is why fats form membranes. Its hydrogen bonds make ice float, let water soak up heat with little change in temperature (1 cal/g/°C), give it surface tension (water sticking to water is cohesion; to something else, adhesion) and a high boiling point. It can act as an acid or a base, and it splits into H3O+ and OH− only a little. Blood stays between pH 7.35 and 7.45. The body's main acid is CO2. A buffer works best at its pKa and only within a limited range; enough acid or base swamps it. The main blood buffer is bicarbonate: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−, sped up in red cells by carbonic anhydrase.

Proteins are chains of amino acids. The order is the primary structure. Local coils and sheets held by hydrogen bonds are secondary structure; the α-helix is a right-handed coil with 3.6 amino acids per turn. The whole folded shape is tertiary: a protein folds into its most stable shape by making many hydrogen bonds and tucking its oily parts inside, away from water. That shape is only just stable, so parts can bend and move, and that is how proteins grab things, work as enzymes and change shape. Big proteins (over about 250 amino acids) fold into two or more separate units called domains. Several chains working together is quaternary, as in hemoglobin. Teaming up makes the protein more stable (less surface touching water), saves genes and mistakes (small pieces are easier to make right), lets chains build an active site together, and lets the chains cooperate. The chains are mostly held together by oily (hydrophobic) contacts, not covalent bonds. Histidine is the amino acid whose side chain can pick up or drop a proton right around body pH.

Fibrous proteins are long, strong, insoluble and structural; globular ones are round and soluble. Hair keratin is two α-helices twisted around each other (a coiled coil). Silk is stacked β-sheets. Most globular proteins fit one of four groups: all helices, all sheets, helices and sheets mixed together (α/β), or helices and sheets in separate parts (α+β). Diseases of protein shape include osteogenesis imperfecta (bad collagen chains), sickle cell disease (hemoglobin that sticks together into long strands) and prion disease (a misfolded protein that makes normal ones misfold).

Collagen is the body's most common protein, made by fibroblasts, and type I (bone, dentin, skin) is most of it. Every third amino acid is glycine, the only one small enough for the center of the triple rope; the others are often proline and hydroxyproline. Each chain is a loose left-handed coil (3.3 amino acids per turn, not an α-helix), and three chains twist into a right-handed triple helix about 300 nm long. Enzymes inside the cell add OH groups to proline and lysine, and those enzymes need vitamin C. No vitamin C means weak collagen: bleeding gums, loose teeth and wounds that won't heal (scurvy). Sugars (galactose and glucose) go on the hydroxylysines. Outside the cell the ends are trimmed and the fibers are cross-linked by a copper enzyme. The molecules line up staggered, leaving 40 nm gaps that give collagen its striped look (a 68 nm repeat) and are where bone mineral is thought to start. Faulty type I genes (COL1A1, COL1A2) cause osteogenesis imperfecta: brittle bones and blue sclerae.

Hemoglobin has four chains and fills most of a red cell. Its iron is held by a histidine (His F8) and grabs oxygen. When one chain grabs oxygen, its iron moves into the heme ring, the chains shift from the tense to the relaxed shape, and the others grab oxygen more easily, so the binding curve is S-shaped: hemoglobin fills up in the lungs and lets go in the tissues. It is half full at 26 mmHg (its P50); a higher P50 means it holds oxygen less tightly. Acid, carbon dioxide, heat and 2,3-BPG make it let go of oxygen in working tissues (acid's effect is the Bohr effect). 2,3-BPG sits in a pocket between the two β chains. Fetal hemoglobin's γ chains have serine where the β chains have a positive histidine (number 143), so it binds 2,3-BPG less and holds oxygen tighter, letting the baby take oxygen from the mother. Myoglobin, in muscle, is a single chain that just stores oxygen. In sickle cell disease, hemoglobin without oxygen sticks together in long strands that block small vessels.

Sugars are aldoses or ketoses, named by their number of carbons. Glucose and galactose differ at one carbon (C-4): they are epimers. Mirror-image sugars (D and L) are enantiomers. In water, sugars close into rings (glucose a six-sided pyranose, fructose a five-sided furanose), which makes α and β forms (anomers) that flip back and forth. Sucrose is table sugar, glucose plus fructose; its bond uses up both sugars' reactive ends, so it is not a reducing sugar. It is what cavity bacteria (S. mutans) turn into acid and into sticky, insoluble glucans for plaque. Lactose (milk sugar) has a β-1,4 bond, broken by lactase; maltose comes from starch. Glycogen is the body's branched glucose store (α-1,4 chains with α-1,6 branches); cellulose (β-1,4) is fiber we can't digest. Glucose can stick to proteins without an enzyme (glycation), which is what HbA1c measures and part of how high sugar damages tissue in diabetes.

Sugars on proteins: adding sugars is the most common change made to a protein after it is built. N-linked sugars go on asparagine (at an Asn-X-Ser/Thr spot) in the ER, from a ready-made block carried on dolichol; O-linked sugars go on serine or threonine one at a time, mostly in the Golgi. ABO blood types are sugars too: the A gene's enzyme adds one sugar (GalNAc), the B gene's adds another (galactose), and the O gene's enzyme doesn't work. GAGs (hyaluronic acid, chondroitin, keratan, dermatan and heparan sulfate, and heparin) are long, negatively charged sugar chains that soak up water to make the gel between cells. On a core protein they make proteoglycans, which are about 95% sugar; in cartilage, many aggrecans hang on one hyaluronic acid without covalent bonds.

Fats (lipids) don't mix with water because they are mostly carbon and hydrogen. A fatty acid has an oily tail (usually 16–20 carbons) and an acid head, so it is amphipathic: part water-loving, part water-fearing. A triglyceride is glycerol plus three fatty acids and is the body's long-term energy store, in fat tissue (about 35% of the calories in a Western diet). Double bonds put kinks in fatty acids and keep fats liquid. Phospholipids make the cell membrane, glycolipids sit only on its outer face as name tags, and cholesterol, the stiffest membrane lipid, keeps it from getting too stiff or too runny. Steroids (four rings) and carotenoids (β-carotene, which the body turns into vitamin A) are built from isoprene units. Fatty acids are burned inside mitochondria.

DNA: DNA makes RNA, and RNA makes protein (the central dogma). A nucleotide is a sugar, a phosphate and a base; without the phosphate it is a nucleoside. Purines (A, G) have two rings and pyrimidines (C, T, U) have one, and every pair is one of each: A pairs with T using two hydrogen bonds; G pairs with C using three. Each strand runs from a 5′ end to a 3′ end, and the two strands run in opposite directions. RNA uses ribose, whose extra OH group makes it break down easily; it swaps U for T and is usually one strand. DNA is sturdier. About 6 feet of DNA in each cell wraps around histone spools (eight histones per nucleosome, like beads on a string), which coil tighter into chromosomes. Bacteria have one circular, supercoiled chromosome plus small DNA circles called plasmids.
plain.f1-cells:
What's tested
  • What each organelle does
  • How the body keeps its water and salts steady
  • How things cross the membrane
  • How a nerve fires and how drugs and toxins stop it
  • How synapses pass the signal on

The short version

Bacteria have no nucleus and no inner compartments; our cells (and fungi and parasites) do. Every cell has DNA, ribosomes and a membrane; viruses aren't cells at all. Bacterial walls are peptidoglycan and fungal walls chitin; our cells have no wall. The nucleus holds the DNA, and only proteins with a nuclear address tag get through its pores; the nucleolus builds ribosomes. The rough ER makes proteins that will be secreted or put in the membrane (a signal at the front of the protein brings its ribosome to the ER), the smooth ER makes lipids, clears drugs and stores calcium, the Golgi finishes and ships proteins, lysosomes digest things in acid (their enzymes carry a mannose-6-phosphate tag), peroxisomes break down very long fatty acids and use catalase on hydrogen peroxide, and the proteasome chews up proteins marked with ubiquitin. Mitochondria make ATP, store calcium and have their own DNA from the mother. Microtubules (the thickest fibers) build the spindle and the inside of cilia and carry cargo down axons; actin (the thinnest) lets cells change shape and, with myosin, contract; intermediate filaments are tough ropes. A cell that stops dividing rests in G0. Caspases carry out tidy, planned cell death (apoptosis), with no inflammation; necrosis from injury is messy and inflames. Gap junctions let small molecules and current pass straight from cell to cell, tight junctions seal neighbors together, and a signal only affects cells that have its receptor.

The body keeps its inside steady by negative feedback: sensors notice a drift from the set point and effectors push it back. About 60% of a man's weight is water, two-thirds of it inside cells; the fluid outside is salty (sodium, chloride), the inside is rich in potassium, and blood is about 290 mOsm/L. Things cross the membrane downhill on their own (diffusion: faster with more area, a steeper gradient and more fat-solubility, slower for big molecules and thick membranes), downhill through a channel or a carrier (a carrier can be saturated), uphill using ATP directly (the Na+/K+ pump: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in; ouabain and digoxin block it), or uphill by riding along with Na+ as it flows in (secondary active transport: moving with Na+ is cotransport, against it is exchange). Gases and small fat-soluble molecules slip through the membrane; ions, glucose and amino acids need a protein. Water moves toward more dissolved particles and is never pumped. What counts is the number of particles (NaCl splits into 2, MgCl2 into 3, glucose stays 1), and a solute that crosses freely pulls no water. In a dilute (hypotonic) bath a cell swells, in a concentrated one it shrinks. The pump also keeps cells from swelling: block it and salt and water seep in.

Channels are gated pores: they open to voltage, to a chemical outside or inside the cell, or to stretch, and leak channels are always open. In the gut lining, the pump on the blood side keeps sodium low in the cell, sodium coming in from the gut side drags glucose with it, and glucose leaves on the blood side through its own carrier. Tight junctions seal the cells together, and the voltage across the lining (the transepithelial potential) can pull charged ions between the cells.

A resting nerve is about −70 mV inside, close to potassium's balance point, because potassium leaks out through channels that are always open. Each tenfold difference in an ion's concentration is worth 60 mV. The pump builds the gradients but adds only a few millivolts itself, so stopping it lets the voltage fade only slowly. When a stimulus reaches threshold, sodium channels fly open and sodium rushes in: the spike, all or none. Each sodium channel has a fast door that opens and a slower one that then plugs it, so the sodium current stops on its own; potassium channels open more slowly to bring the voltage back down, and a little below. Right after a spike the nerve can't fire again at all, then only with a bigger push, which is also why the signal only travels forward. Myelin (from oligodendrocytes in the brain and spinal cord, Schwann cells in the nerves) makes the signal jump from gap to gap, where the sodium channels cluster, much faster.

Local anesthetics slip into the nerve uncharged and plug sodium channels from the inside. In infected, acidic tissue more of the drug stays charged outside, so less gets in and numbing is harder. Tetrodotoxin from pufferfish plugs sodium channels from outside; TEA plugs potassium channels, so the spike gets wider. Blood potassium (normally 3.5–5.0) matters: a little too much brings nerves closer to firing, but a lot jams the sodium channels shut, so muscles go weak; too little makes the inside more negative and the nerve harder to fire.

At an electrical synapse current flows straight through gap junctions, both ways (heart, some smooth muscle). At a chemical synapse, calcium entering the nerve ending makes the vesicles fuse (the SNARE proteins do it) and release the transmitter. It works through a receptor that is either a channel itself (fast) or works through a G protein (slower), and the receptor decides what the transmitter does. Small transmitters are made in the nerve ending; peptide transmitters are made in the cell body and shipped down the axon. Glutamate excites; GABA and glycine calm things down by letting chloride in (benzodiazepines boost GABA). Small inputs add up, one after another or from many synapses at once. At muscle, acetylcholine opens channels to start contraction, and acetylcholinesterase then breaks it down. Botulinum toxin cuts SNAP-25 so acetylcholine isn't released, and in myasthenia gravis the body makes antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor, so muscles tire quickly with use; drugs that block acetylcholinesterase help. Cocaine blocks the reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin, and SSRIs block serotonin's.
plain.f1-molbio:
What's tested
  • How DNA is copied, read into RNA and translated into protein
  • How genes are inherited and how to read a family tree
  • What kinds of mutations there are and which genes cause cancer

The short version

Copying DNA: the letters pair A with T and G with C, so DNA always has as much A as T and as much G as C (30% A means 30% T, 20% G and 20% C). Helicase unzips it, primase lays a short RNA starter, DNA polymerase adds new letters, always building in the 5′ to 3′ direction. The polymerase can't start without that starter and checks its own work as it goes, so it makes only about one mistake in 10 million letters. One strand is made in one long piece; the other in short Okazaki pieces that ligase glues together. Each new DNA keeps one old strand. Chromosome tips (telomeres) shrink each time, except where telomerase rebuilds them, as in sperm-making cells, some stem cells, skin cells, activated white cells and most cancers; without it, cells eventually stop dividing.

RNA has an extra OH on its sugar, which lets a weak base break it down while DNA holds up, and uracil in place of thymine. Most of a cell's RNA is ribosomal; a bacterial message lasts only a few minutes. Enzymes called nucleases cut DNA or RNA, either in the middle of a chain or from one end; pancreatic RNase A cuts right after a C or U. In bacteria, the σ part of RNA polymerase finds the start signal; the copy it makes has about one error in 10,000 letters, which is fine because each gene is read many times. The lac operon is switched on fully only when lactose is around and glucose is not, and a bacterium without a working lac repressor keeps it on all the time.

In our cells, RNA polymerase II makes messenger RNA. The message gets a cap on the front, its introns cut out (they start with GU and end with AG) and a poly(A) tail on the back, about 200–250 A's, that isn't copied from DNA. Small RNAs in the spliceosome do the cutting: U1 grabs the front of the intron, U2 the branch point, and the intron comes out as a loop (a lariat). Splicing the pieces in different ways gives one gene several proteins. Editing can change one letter afterward: in the gut a C becomes U and makes an early stop, so the gut makes the short apoB-48 while the liver makes the full apoB-100. The finished message leaves the nucleus front end first; in the cytoplasm the cap and tail protect it, and most of our messages last hours, bacterial ones only minutes. Acetylated histones open DNA up for reading; methylated DNA is shut off.

Translation: each tRNA carries one amino acid and matches a three-letter codon. AUG starts, UAA, UAG and UGA stop. The ribosome's own RNA makes the peptide bonds. Bacteria line up the ribosome with a Shine-Dalgarno sequence; our ribosomes slide from the cap to the first AUG.

Inheritance: two carriers' children come out 1 in 4 with two normal copies, 2 in 4 carriers and 1 in 4 affected. Dominant traits show up in every generation (Huntington disease, Marfan syndrome, neurofibromatosis); recessive ones skip generations and need two copies (sickle cell disease, cystic fibrosis, albinism). X-linked recessive diseases such as hemophilia A and Duchenne muscular dystrophy hit boys through carrier mothers. If your brother has a recessive disease and you don't, your chance of being a carrier is 2 in 3. To find out whether someone showing a dominant trait hides a recessive copy, cross them with someone showing the recessive trait (a test cross): any offspring with the recessive trait means they carry it.

Mutations: a single-letter change can be silent, swap an amino acid (sickle cell), make an early stop, or break a splice site so an intron stays in or an exon drops out. Adding or losing letters in numbers that aren't multiples of three scrambles everything after (frameshift). Growing repeats get worse each generation: Huntington disease, fragile X syndrome, Friedreich ataxia and myotonic dystrophy. Most mutations are copying errors (about 1 in 100,000 per gene per round); others come from chemicals and radiation: some chemicals damage a letter, acridine dyes add or drop one, X-rays break the strand and UV light makes thymine dimers. Known mutagens include aflatoxin from mold on peanuts and nitrosamines in cigarette smoke. The Ames test checks whether a chemical causes mutations, using bacteria that can't make histidine. Different mistakes in one gene can cause different diseases: β-globin mistakes give sickle cell disease or β-thalassemia, and collagen mistakes give osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bones, blue whites of the eyes, deafness), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (stretchy skin, loose joints) or Alport syndrome (deafness, kidney disease). Teeth have their own: amelogenesis imperfecta (bad enamel), dentinogenesis imperfecta (bad dentin: blue-gray or brown, see-through teeth) and ectodermal dysplasia (missing or small pointed teeth, with skin, hair, nail and sweat-gland problems).

Cancer builds up over years (often 20 or more) as one cell collects several mutations: a first change starts it dividing, its offspring keep dividing, and more changes make it malignant. Only about 1 in 10 cancers comes from a single gene. Benign tumors stay in a capsule and look like normal tissue; malignant ones invade, look immature and spread. Cancer genes: oncogenes are stuck gas pedals (one bad copy is enough), switched on by extra copies (HER2 in breast cancer, blocked by trastuzumab), a stuck-on protein (RAS) or a swapped piece of chromosome (BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukemia, blocked by imatinib). Tumor suppressors such as p53 and RB are brakes, and both copies have to be lost. BRCA1 and BRCA2 repair broken DNA. Inherited forms start with one bad copy in every cell: familial retinoblastoma (often both eyes, found earlier), Li-Fraumeni syndrome (p53; many cancers young), familial adenomatous polyposis (APC; hundreds of colon polyps) and Lynch syndrome (DNA repair genes; colon and other cancers). HPV causes throat cancer by knocking out p53 and RB. Cancer spreads through blood, lymph, along nerves and across body cavities, and a tumor outgrows its tissue because more of its cells are dividing.
plain.f1-enzhorm:
What's tested
  • How peptide and steroid hormones reach and act on cells
  • Insulin, cortisol, aldosterone and the calcium hormones
  • Which reactions release energy and which need it
  • How enzymes speed reactions, and what Km, Vmax and the inhibitor types mean

The short version

Peptide hormones (like insulin) dissolve in blood, can't get through the membrane, and so bind receptors on the outside of the cell. The signal is passed on inside by messengers such as cAMP (which turns on protein kinase A) or IP3 and calcium. They can't be swallowed as pills because the gut digests them. Insulin's receptor is a tyrosine kinase, and its job is to move GLUT4 glucose doors to the surface of muscle and fat cells.

Steroid hormones come in three types: glucocorticoids (cortisol: fuel and immunity), mineralocorticoids (aldosterone: salt and water) and sex steroids (testosterone and estrogen). The adrenal cortex and the gonads make them from cholesterol, the adrenal ones when the pituitary's ACTH tells them to. The first step, in the mitochondria, cuts off part of cholesterol's tail to make pregnenolone. Most of the enzymes are cytochrome P450s, and the reactions are oxidations that need oxygen and NADPH (from the pentose phosphate pathway). Steroids don't dissolve in blood, so they ride on carrier proteins (transcortin for cortisol, SHBG for the sex hormones), and only the free hormone can act. They slip through the membrane and switch genes on or off inside the nucleus. Cortisol raises blood sugar and calms the immune system; too much is Cushing syndrome, most often from steroid medicines. Aldosterone holds on to salt and water; too much is Conn syndrome (high blood pressure, low potassium), usually from an adrenal adenoma, a benign tumor. In Addison disease the adrenal glands fail, usually from autoimmune damage: low blood pressure, tiredness and dark patches in the mouth from high ACTH.

PTH raises blood calcium, active vitamin D helps the gut absorb it, and calcitonin lowers it by slowing osteoclasts.

Energy: metabolism is all of a cell's chemical reactions. Oxidation means losing electrons and reduction gaining them. Breaking things down (catabolism) is oxidation, releases energy and uses NAD+; building things (anabolism) is reduction, costs energy and uses NADPH. The main pathways: glycolysis, the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation burn fuel for ATP; gluconeogenesis makes new glucose; the urea cycle gets rid of ammonia; β-oxidation breaks down fatty acids; and the pentose phosphate pathway makes NADPH and the sugars for DNA and RNA. The brain and red blood cells live on glucose (red cells have no mitochondria, and fat can't get into the brain); heart and muscle mostly burn fat, and the liver is the hub that makes fuel for the rest of the body.

Thermodynamics: energy is never created or destroyed (first law), every real change makes the universe more disordered (second law), and a perfect crystal at absolute zero has no disorder (third law). Living cells are open systems: energy and matter go in and out. Enthalpy (ΔH) is heat; entropy (ΔS) is disorder. A reaction happens on its own when ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is negative, but that says nothing about how fast: speed depends on the activation energy (ΔG‡), which is what enzymes lower. Burning glucose releases 686 kcal per mole.

ATP is the go-between: breaking off its last phosphate releases about 30.5 kJ/mol (7.3 kcal/mol), and cells use that to power three kinds of work: mechanical (muscles), transport (pumps) and chemical (building molecules). In cells ATP is held by magnesium. You only have about 50 g of it, so each molecule is recycled about 1,300 times a day.

Enzymes are catalysts with three traits: huge catalytic power (up to 10^16 times faster), specificity (the right substrate fits the active site, the pocket where the reaction happens) and regulation. They speed reactions by lowering the energy hill (ΔG‡), not by changing where the reaction ends up (ΔG). The enzyme changes shape as the substrate binds (induced fit, a better model than the older lock and key): hexokinase closes around glucose. Their helpers: cofactors are usually metal ions, and coenzymes are usually made from vitamins (NAD+, FAD, TPP); a tightly bound one is a prosthetic group. The protein alone is the apoenzyme; with its helper it is the holoenzyme. A few enzymes are RNA (ribozymes, such as the ribosome's peptidyl transferase).

Km is the substrate level that gives half the top speed; a small Km means the enzyme grabs its substrate tightly. Vmax is the top speed, approached but never quite reached. The turnover number (kcat) is how many substrate molecules one enzyme converts per second when it is saturated, and kcat/Km is its efficiency, which can't beat how fast molecules bump into each other. With two substrates, either both bind before anything leaves (sequential) or the first product leaves before the second substrate binds (ping-pong, as in aminotransferases); on a Lineweaver-Burk plot, ping-pong gives parallel lines. A competitive inhibitor looks like the substrate and fights for the active site: Km goes up, Vmax stays (more substrate wins); malonate does this to succinate dehydrogenase. A noncompetitive inhibitor binds elsewhere: Vmax drops, Km stays. An uncompetitive one binds only the enzyme–substrate pair and lowers both, as lithium does. Irreversible inhibitors, such as penicillin, aspirin and organophosphates, put the enzyme out of action for good.
plain.f1-carbmet:
What's tested
  • Glycolysis: the ATP it spends and makes, its three irreversible enzymes, and PFK-1 control
  • Pyruvate's fates: lactate, the PDH complex and its five coenzymes, carboxylation
  • Citric acid cycle products and its rate-limiting enzyme
  • Electron transport chain: complexes, proton pumping, inhibitors and uncouplers; ATP per glucose
  • Glycogen synthesis and breakdown and their hormonal control
  • Gluconeogenesis: bypass enzymes, precursors, the Cori and alanine cycles

Cells burn glucose in stages. Glycolysis, in the cytosol, splits glucose into 2 pyruvate and nets 2 ATP and 2 NADH, even without oxygen. Its main control point is PFK-1: AMP and fructose 2,6-bisphosphate (raised by insulin) turn it on, while ATP, citrate and acid turn it off.

Without oxygen (or in red cells, which have no mitochondria) pyruvate becomes lactate, which frees NAD+ so glycolysis can keep going. With oxygen, pyruvate goes into the mitochondria, where the PDH complex (five coenzymes, B1 first among them) turns it into acetyl-CoA. That step is one-way: fat's acetyl-CoA can't make glucose. Plenty of acetyl-CoA, NADH or ATP switches PDH off, through a kinase that puts a phosphate on it.

The citric acid cycle strips acetyl-CoA's electrons onto carriers: 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP and 2 CO2 a turn. Its control point is isocitrate dehydrogenase, slowed by ATP and sped up by ADP; citrate synthase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase also slow down when NADH and succinyl-CoA pile up.

The electron transport chain passes those electrons to oxygen, pumping protons out as it goes; the protons flowing back through ATP synthase make ATP. The electrons run downhill to oxygen, which pulls on them hardest. ATP synthase works like a tiny motor: protons spin its rotor and its head makes ATP, about one for every 4 protons. So NADH gives about 2.5 ATP and FADH2 about 1.5 (it skips Complex I). NADH made in the cytosol can't get into the mitochondria, so shuttles carry its electrons in. One glucose gives about 32 ATP with the malate-aspartate shuttle (liver, heart, kidney) and 30 with the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle (muscle and brain). Cyanide and carbon monoxide block Complex IV, so cells can't use oxygen. Uncouplers such as DNP, and brown fat's thermogenin, let protons leak back, so energy turns into heat instead of ATP.

Glycogen is stored glucose. The liver packs in more per gram, but muscle holds about twice as much in all, because there is so much more muscle. Glycogen synthase builds it from UDP-glucose, starting on a primer protein, glycogenin, and the branching enzyme adds branches; phosphorylase takes it apart with phosphate (giving glucose 1-phosphate), and the debranching enzyme handles the branches. Glucagon and epinephrine switch breakdown on; insulin switches storage on. In working muscle, calcium and AMP speed breakdown. Only the liver can send glucose to the blood, because muscle lacks glucose 6-phosphatase.

Gluconeogenesis is the liver making new glucose once its glycogen runs low, 12–24 hours into a fast, for the brain, red cells and the few other tissues that need glucose. It uses lactate, alanine and most other amino acids (not leucine or lysine), and glycerol (not fatty acids). It goes around glycolysis's three one-way steps with pyruvate carboxylase and PEP carboxykinase, fructose 1,6-bisphosphatase, and glucose 6-phosphatase. The Cori cycle sends lactate from muscle and red cells back to the liver to be made into glucose again; it costs the liver more ATP than the tissues get back. In the alanine cycle muscle sends alanine instead, and the liver turns its nitrogen into urea. If glucose 6-phosphatase is missing (von Gierke disease), the liver can't release glucose: glycogen piles up and blood sugar falls in a fast.
plain.f1-innate:
What's tested
  • Innate versus adaptive immunity, how immune cells communicate (cytokines, chemokines); the innate cells and their jobs
  • Hematopoiesis and the cell markers (CD numbers); primary and secondary lymphoid organs, lymph and the lymphatics
  • Barriers, pattern recognition receptors (TLRs, NLRs, RLRs), PAMPs and DAMPs
  • Phagocytosis and the respiratory burst
  • Complement: the three pathways, what each fragment does, key deficiencies
  • Inflammation: mediators, leukocyte extravasation and the order cells arrive, kinds of cell death, M1 and M2 macrophages, fever and the acute phase response

The immune system has three layers: barriers, then innate immunity, then adaptive immunity. Its jobs are recognition, effector functions (killing and containing), regulation and memory. Infection means a microbe has invaded and is multiplying; disease means it is damaging tissue. Immune responses hurt our tissue too, so ending them (resolution) matters as much as starting them.

Innate immunity is the body's fast, built-in defense. It works within minutes to hours, in the tissues, with about 100 receptors that everyone inherits alike. They recognize larger shapes that many microbes share (PAMPs) or signs of damage (DAMPs), and the response is the same every time: no memory. Every immune cell except B and T cells is innate. Adaptive immunity (B and T cells) starts in lymphoid tissue and takes days the first time (10–14 to be fully working), but its receptors fit tiny pieces of an antigen (epitopes, such as 8–12 amino acids), and it improves and remembers.

Cells talk by touching (a receptor meeting its ligand) and by cytokines, small short-lived proteins that tell cells what to do; chemokines tell cells where to go. One cytokine can do many things (pleiotropy), several can do the same thing (redundancy), and they can boost (synergy) or oppose (antagonism) each other.

The first line is barriers. Skin is dry, salty and acidic (from its oil, sebum), and it keeps shedding dead cells. Mucosa is a layer of cells sealed by tight junctions under mucus (made of mucins). Cilia, tears and saliva sweep microbes away. The lining cells also make chemicals: defensins (punch holes in bacteria and in enveloped viruses such as flu and herpes), lysozyme in saliva, tears and airway mucus (breaks bacterial walls) and protease inhibitors such as α2-macroglobulin (stop a microbe's enzymes from digesting our tissue). Our normal microbes are a barrier too. Behind them are the cells. Neutrophils are the most common white cell and the first to arrive; they live a short time, and dead neutrophils make pus. Macrophages sit in the tissues as sentinels, eat microbes and debris, and are the main source of inflammatory cytokines. Dendritic cells carry antigen to lymph nodes to start adaptive immunity. Mast cells live a long time in tissue and release histamine; short-lived basophils do the same from the blood. Eosinophils fight worms too big to eat, and add to asthma. Neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils are the granulocytes (PMNs): cells with lobed nuclei and granules full of killing and signaling molecules. Mast cells have granules but a round nucleus. NK cells are lymphoid but innate: they kill cells that have lost MHC I, using granules of their own (they aren't granulocytes).

All blood cells come from stem cells in the bone marrow (their marker is CD34). Immune cells grow up in the bone marrow, except T cells, which grow up in the thymus. Lymphocytes meet antigen and are switched on in lymph nodes, the spleen and MALT (looser lymphoid tissue in the linings, such as the tonsils and Peyer's patches), which keep B cells and T cells in separate areas; other immune cells are switched on right where they live. Lymph is the fluid that drains out of the tissues: lymph vessels carry it, with lymphocytes, through the lymph nodes and back into the blood at the left and right subclavian veins. The spleen filters blood instead and isn't joined to the lymph vessels.

Labs tell cells apart by surface markers named with CD numbers: CD14 monocytes, CD11b macrophages, CD11c dendritic cells, CD16 and CD56 NK cells, CD19 and CD20 B cells and CD3 on every T cell (CD4 on helpers, CD8 on killers). B cells show antigen to T cells and make antibody, but they don't eat microbes. Plasma cells are B cells at their final stage: they lose their receptor, can't be switched on again and do nothing but make antibody.

Cells sense microbes with receptors such as TLRs (TLR4 senses LPS), NLRs in the cytosol (some build inflammasomes that make IL-1β), RLRs that sense viral double-stranded RNA in the cytosol, and C-type lectin receptors (CLRs) that grab microbial sugars. CLRs and TLRs are best at starting phagocytosis; TLRs, NLRs and RLRs switch on NF-κB, the master switch for inflammatory cytokines, and RLRs also make type I interferon against viruses. Neutrophils, macrophages and dendritic cells are the big eaters. After eating a microbe, phagocytes digest it in lysosomes and kill it with a respiratory burst made by NADPH oxidase; the oxygen radicals can leak out and hurt our own cells, and catalase limits that. Without NADPH oxidase (chronic granulomatous disease) infections keep coming back.

Complement is a set of blood proteins, made mostly by the liver, that is always on watch. It has three starting routes: alternative (C3 sticks to a microbe; it usually goes first because C3 is everywhere), lectin (mannose-binding lectin grabs microbial sugars) and classical (C1 grabs antibody or CRP). All meet at C3, the key step. C3b coats microbes so phagocytes eat them, C3a and C5a widen and open vessels, and C5b–C9 punches holes in bacteria, fungi and enveloped viruses. Missing C1 inhibitor causes hereditary angioedema, swelling that dental work can trigger.

In inflammation, macrophages in the tissue that spot a microbe release TNF-α and IL-1, which switch on the vessel lining, and IL-8, which calls neutrophils. Histamine, complement and two kinds of fats, prostaglandins and leukotrienes (made from arachidonic acid; NSAIDs block the prostaglandin step), add to it. Vessels widen and leak, and white cells roll along the vessel wall (selectins), stick hard (integrins: LFA-1 on neutrophils binding ICAM-1) and squeeze out toward the chemokines. Neutrophils come first, then monocytes, then basophils, eosinophils and lymphocytes. Early monocytes become inflammatory M1 macrophages; later ones become M2 macrophages that calm things down and repair. Inflammation that never resolves becomes chronic.

Apoptosis is a quiet death. Necrosis (a cell bursting after injury), necroptosis (when apoptosis is blocked), pyroptosis (after an inflammasome) and NETosis (neutrophils throwing out sticky DNA nets) all spill danger signals and inflame. Cytokines that cause fever are pyrogens. IL-6 makes the liver release acute phase proteins such as CRP.
plain.f1-adaptive:
What's tested
  • The five antibody isotypes: structure and jobs
  • How diversity is made: V(D)J recombination, class switching, somatic hypermutation
  • MHC class I versus class II: who has them, what they show, to whom
  • B-cell activation (T-dependent and T-independent) and T-cell activation (three signals)
  • CD4 helper subsets, CD8 killing, NK cells and interferons against viruses
  • Memory, vaccine types, active versus passive immunity
  • Mucosal immunity: barrier, antigen sampling, tolerance, secretory antibody and the microbiota

Adaptive immunity uses B cells, which make antibodies, and T cells, which help or kill. Each cell has one receptor, made at random before any infection by cutting and joining gene pieces (V(D)J recombination by RAG enzymes, with TdT adding extra letters at the joins).
