Light chains use only V and J. A B cell's antibody is its BCR, released: it binds exactly the same thing. A naive B cell carries IgM and IgD together because one RNA message is spliced two ways, not because its DNA changes again; splicing also decides whether the antibody stays on the cell or is released.

Antibodies come in five classes. IgM is a pentamer, the first made, and the best at activating complement. IgG is the most common in blood, rules the second response, and is the only one that crosses the placenta. IgA guards saliva, tears, milk and the gut as a dimer. IgE sits on mast cells and causes allergy. IgD sits on naive B cells. A B cell can switch class (from IgM to IgG, IgA or IgE) only with help from a T cell's CD40L, which turns on the enzyme AID; the T cell's cytokines pick the class, and a switch can't be undone. An antibody's tips (variable regions) decide what it binds; its stem (the heavy chain's constant region) decides its class and what it does. Antibodies don't kill on their own: they mark targets for other cells. IgG, which many cells can grab by its stem, is the most versatile.

B cells meet two kinds of antigen. T-independent ones work alone: repeating sugars that grab many BCRs at once (TI-2), or microbe parts such as LPS that also hit a TLR (TI-1, mitogens). They give weak, low-affinity IgM and little memory. T-dependent antigens are proteins: the B cell shows a piece to a Tfh cell (same antigen, different piece: linked recognition). In a germinal center the B cell's receptor mutates, follicular dendritic cells keep only the best binders (affinity maturation), and the cell switches class, making strong IgG and memory cells.

T cells only see protein pieces (peptides) held up by MHC, and only their own body's MHC. MHC I is on every nucleated cell and shows what's made inside it (such as a virus) to CD8 killer cells: the proteasome cuts the protein and TAP carries the pieces into the ER. MHC II is on antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells) and shows what they ate to CD4 helper cells: a blocker (the invariant chain, trimmed to CLIP) holds its groove until HLA-DM swaps in a peptide from the endosome. MHC needs a peptide to stay on the surface, so cells show their own pieces all the time. Unlike a BCR, a TCR is never released, has one binding site and never switches class. Most T cells are α/β and see protein; a few γ/δ T cells see other molecules such as lipids.

MHC genes (HLA, on chromosome 6) are polygenic (several genes: HLA-A, B, C and DP, DQ, DR), polymorphic (many versions in the population) and codominant (you use both parents' copies). That variety lets more peptides be shown to more T cells.

A naive T cell is switched on in a lymph node, usually by a dendritic cell. It needs its antigen plus a second signal (B7 on the presenting cell binding CD28), then IL-2 to multiply; without the second signal the cell shuts down (anergy). Helper cells then become types, steered by the dendritic cell's cytokines: Th1 (made under IL-12; its IFN-γ turns on macrophages and CD8 cells), Th2 (IL-4; makes IL-4, IL-5 and IL-13 for IgE, eosinophils and worms), Th17 (TGF-β, IL-6, IL-23; its IL-17 calls neutrophils against bacteria and fungi), Tregs (IL-2 and TGF-β; need FoxP3; their TGF-β and IL-10 calm things down) and Tfh (make IL-21 and IL-6; help B cells in germinal centers). CD8 cells are first primed in the lymph node (antigen, second signal and help from CD4 cells); after that they kill an infected cell just by seeing its peptide on MHC I, using perforin and granzymes or Fas.

Against viruses, infected cells release type I interferons that warn their neighbors (they stop making proteins) and turn on NK cells. NK cells need no TCR and no priming: they check how much MHC I a cell has, not which peptide it shows, and kill cells that hide their MHC I. They also kill antibody-coated cells through CD16, and their IFN-γ turns on macrophages.

Memory cells make the second response faster and stronger: there are more of them, they wait in the tissues too, memory T cells need no second signal, and memory B cells already make strong IgG. The innate system doesn't learn this way. Vaccines build active immunity; given antibody (passive) works at once but leaves no memory and can cause reactions. Live vaccines such as MMR are avoided in people with weak immune systems. The hepatitis B vaccine is a protein subunit; an antibody level of 10 or more after the series means you're protected. Protein, toxoid and conjugate vaccines need an adjuvant such as alum to wake up the innate system. Conjugate vaccines join a bacterial sugar to a protein so T cells can help, which lets babies make strong IgG against the sugar. mRNA and viral vector vaccines have your cells make the protein; the genes never enter your DNA.

Flu protection fades: the virus slowly changes (drift) or suddenly swaps gene segments with an animal flu (shift), and the body keeps making antibody against the first strain it met (original antigenic sin). Herd immunity means enough people are immune that a disease can't reach those who can't be protected.

Mucosal immunity guards the body's linings (gut, airways, mouth, eyes, urogenital tract), a far bigger surface than the skin and the way most infections get in. It works partly on its own, apart from the systemic immune system that guards the skin. Most of what we know comes from the gut; the mouth's and the eye's linings are built differently but use many of the same parts.

Goblet cells make mucus from mucins. Its sialic acid is negatively charged, so positively charged defenders stick in it: defensins and other antimicrobial peptides, which burst microbes, and secretory IgA, which blocks them. Tight junctions seal the gaps between the lining cells. Plasma cells under the lining make IgA in pairs joined by a J chain; the poly-Ig receptor grabs the J chain and carries the antibody across, leaving a piece of itself on it (secretory component) that protects it. Because it grabs the J chain, it can carry IgM (five units with a J chain) too, but not single IgA. IgA wins only because there are far more IgA plasma cells.

The lining samples what's in the gut all the time: M cells over Peyer's patches pass microbes and molecules to the immune cells below, and dendritic cells reach between the lining cells. Many defending cells wait in the tissue, ready, and the lining cells themselves sense microbes and send out antimicrobial peptides and signals. But the goal is tolerance: no inflammation unless it's truly needed, because inflammation damages the lining. Lining cells release calming signals (TGF-β, IL-10, retinoic acid, short-chain fatty acids); calm dendritic cells make TGF-β, which turns T cells into Tregs, and Tregs are everywhere here. Gut macrophages eat microbes but give no respiratory burst, make no inflammatory cytokines and show no second-signal molecules. Only when a pathogen breaks through do dendritic cells make Th1 and Th17 cells and macrophages start inflammation, as a last resort. Systemic immunity reacts after the fact and pays for it in damage; mucosal immunity is ready ahead of time and stays calm.

Our gut microbes (the microbiota; the microbiome is the list of them and their genes) help the gut's immune tissue develop and work: they make useful molecules, break down food, neutralize toxins, take up space that pathogens would need and keep the immune system calm. Oral tolerance means not reacting to a protein you eat. When the microbiota is thrown off (dysbiosis, for example by antibiotics), the mucus and lining break down and inflammation follows: Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, food allergy, asthma and C. difficile infection are linked to it. Selective IgA deficiency is the most common inborn immune defect; it's often mild (IgM carried out by the poly-Ig receptor can partly stand in), with a risk of reactions to blood products.
plain.f1-hyper:
What's tested
  • B-cell and T-cell development; positive and negative selection
  • Central and peripheral tolerance; AIRE, FoxP3 and Fas
  • How autoimmunity starts: molecular mimicry, bystander activation, cryptic antigens, epitope spreading, HLA links
  • The four hypersensitivity types: mechanism, timing and examples, dental ones included

B cells grow up in the bone marrow (and finish maturing in the spleen and lymph nodes) and T cells in the thymus. Each new cell is tested. A young T cell with both CD4 and CD8 must recognize the body's own MHC a little (positive selection, or it dies of neglect); once it keeps only CD4 or only CD8, it must not bind self too strongly (negative selection, or it is killed). A gene called AIRE lets the thymus show proteins from other organs, so cells that would attack them are removed; without AIRE, children get thrush and attacks on the parathyroid and adrenal glands. A self-reactive young B cell gets a chance to swap its light chain, and only its light chain (receptor editing), before it dies. Each B cell uses one heavy chain and one light chain (allelic exclusion), so it has one target. Mature B cells carry IgM and IgD together, made from one RNA cut two ways, not by changing the DNA. The thymus starts shrinking in the first year of life, but the T cells it already made last a long time; B cells keep being made for life. A T cell's receptor never changes after it leaves the thymus, while a B cell's can still change in germinal centers.

That is central tolerance, and it misses some cells. Peripheral tolerance deals with cells that slip through: naive T cells stay in the lymph nodes and spleen, a T cell that sees antigen without a second signal shuts down (anergy; ordinary cells such as kidney cells don't give that signal), late in a response B and T cells kill themselves through Fas, and Tregs (CD4, CD25 and FoxP3; made in the thymus, or from naive T cells with TGF-β and IL-2) calm the rest down. Some places, such as the brain, eye, testes and the pregnant uterus, are protected sites, mostly because they actively calm immune cells there (Fas ligand, TGF-β, IL-10), not because they shut them out.

Autoimmunity needs genes plus a trigger. Some HLA types raise the risk by deciding which peptides get shown, but they are a link, not a cause: about 90% of people with ankylosing spondylitis (a stiffening, fusing spine, sometimes with eye inflammation) have HLA-B27, and HLA-DR4 shows joint proteins changed to citrulline in rheumatoid arthritis. A germ can look like self (molecular mimicry: strep throat and rheumatic heart disease). An infection's inflammation can switch on dendritic cells that happen to be showing self, and they wake up a self-reactive T cell (bystander activation). Damage can expose hidden proteins, and the attack can spread to new targets (epitope spreading, as in pemphigus: desmoglein 3 in the mouth first, then desmoglein 1 in the skin).

Hypersensitivity is the immune system overreacting to something harmless (or, in autoimmunity, to self), in four types:

  • Type I: IgE on mast cells. The first meeting with the allergen makes the IgE (Th2 cells, IL-4); the next one sets it off. Histamine acts within 30 minutes (hives, swelling, wheezing); hours later eosinophils, kept alive by IL-5, bring a second wave. Asthma, hay fever, anaphylaxis (treat with epinephrine in the thigh muscle). The system is really meant for worms too big to eat. People prone to making IgE to allergens are called atopic.
  • Type II: antibodies, mostly IgG, against proteins on cells (the body's own, transfused cells or a baby's red cells), which kill the cells or block them. Transfusion reactions, Rh disease, drug-coated red cells, pemphigus, myasthenia gravis. In Rh disease the mother's first antibodies are IgM, which can't cross the placenta; only IgG can, so a later pregnancy is the one hurt. Anti-D shots prevent it.
  • Type III: small antibody–antigen clumps that aren't cleared, stuck in vessels and kidneys. The Arthus reaction in the skin at 4–8 hours, serum sickness (rash, joint pain, fever), lupus (anti-dsDNA antibodies).
  • Type IV: T cells and the macrophages they switch on, 1–3 days after contact, once at least a week has passed to become sensitized. Nickel or glove dermatitis, poison ivy, the TB skin test, granulomas, celiac disease and type 1 diabetes.

In the dental office, latex proteins can cause type I reactions and glove chemicals type IV, and penicillin can cause all four, because it sticks to the body's own proteins and makes them look foreign.
plain.f1-tissues:
What's tested
  • Microscopy and staining (H&E, basophilic versus acidophilic, PAS)
  • Germ layers and what they form; the four basic tissues
  • Cell junctions and adhesion molecules
  • Epithelium: features, classification, surface specializations, glands
  • Connective tissue: cells, fibers, ground substance and types; blood and adipose
  • Cartilage, bone, muscle and nerve at a glance

To make a slide, tissue is fixed so it won't break down (formalin for the light microscope; glutaraldehyde and osmium tetroxide for the electron microscope), its water is replaced with alcohol, it is cleared with xylene, set in wax (paraffin; epoxy resin for the electron microscope) and sliced thin: 5–10 µm for light and 50–100 nm for electron microscopes. Living, unstained cells are viewed with phase contrast. Immunohistochemistry tags an antibody so you can see where one molecule sits.

Under the microscope, H&E is the standard stain: hematoxylin colors acidic parts such as nuclei blue-purple (basophilic), and eosin colors most cytoplasm and collagen pink (acidophilic). PAS colors sugars magenta.

The body is built from four tissues: epithelium, connective tissue, muscle and nerve. They come from three germ layers, laid down at gastrulation (days 15–16): ectoderm (skin's surface, enamel, nerves, sensory placodes), mesoderm (connective tissue, muscle, blood, kidneys) and endoderm (the lining of the gut and airways, liver, thyroid).

Epithelium covers and lines, and makes glands. It can come from any of the three germ layers. Its cells are tightly joined, have a top (apical) side and a bottom (basolateral) side, have no blood vessels, and sit on a basement membrane (type IV collagen and laminin made by the epithelium, over a layer of reticular fibers; PAS stains it). The basement membrane holds the cells down, lets food in and waste out, and filters (the kidney's glomerulus). Epithelium protects, absorbs, secretes, excretes, lubricates (the linings of the chest and belly cavities), senses (taste buds) and makes sperm. Some renews fast (the gut lining, about every week) and some slowly (big glands); in layered epithelium only the bottom layer divides.

It is named by its layers and the shape of the top cells: simple squamous for fast exchange (alveoli, vessels), cuboidal for tubules and ducts (and the ovary's surface), columnar for the gut, pseudostratified for the airways, the smell area of the nose and the male reproductive tract, stratified squamous for wear (keratinized on the skin and attached gingiva), and transitional, only in the urinary tract, for the stretchy bladder: its dome-shaped "umbrella" cells flatten as it fills. Microvilli (actin, still) add surface; stereocilia are long, still microvilli (epididymis, inner ear); cilia (9+2 microtubules) beat to move mucus; a single still primary cilium on most cells senses the surroundings; and folds in the base of the cell, full of mitochondria, add surface.

Cells hold together with junctions: tight junctions seal, desmosomes weld cell to cell through keratin (attacked in pemphigus), hemidesmosomes anchor to the basement membrane (attacked in pemphigoid), and gap junctions let small molecules pass and spread contraction through heart and smooth muscle. A white blood cell leaving a vessel first rolls along on selectins, then grips with integrins and squeezes out.

Glands grow down from epithelium. Exocrine glands keep a duct; endocrine glands lose it and release into nearby capillaries. A simple gland has one unbranched duct and a compound gland a branched one; the secreting ends are tubes (tubular) or round sacs (acinar). Serous cells make a watery, enzyme-rich fluid and look dark and grainy; mucous cells make mucus and look pale. Glands release their product by exocytosis (most, including salivary glands), by pinching off a bit of the cell with its lipid (apocrine, the mammary gland's fat) or by shedding the whole cell (sebaceous glands).

Connective tissue is scattered cells in a lot of matrix, mostly from mesoderm. It carries the blood vessels and nerves (cartilage has none) and is the supporting frame (stroma) of each organ, around its working cells (parenchyma). Fibroblasts make the fibers and the gel between them, and rarely divide except to heal a wound: type I collagen for strength (bone, dentin, tendon), type III reticular fibers for soft frameworks such as lymph nodes, type IV in the basement membrane, type VII to anchor it, and elastic fibers (elastin on fibrillin) for stretch. Fibroblasts, fat cells, pericytes (around small vessels, setting blood flow), mast cells, macrophages and stem cells live there; white blood cells visit. Mast cells are full of dark-staining granules of histamine and heparin and release them when IgE on their surface meets its antigen.

Blood is a connective tissue too: about 5–6 L in an adult, 55% plasma and 45% cells. The hematocrit is about 39–50% in men and 35–45% in women; white cells and platelets are only about 1%. Albumin is the most common plasma protein. Serum is plasma without its clotting factors. White cells can leave the blood, but only lymphocytes come back. White fat stores energy and makes leptin, which curbs appetite; brown fat makes heat, most of all in newborns.

Cartilage has no blood vessels, nerves or lymphatics; its type II collagen and water-holding gel absorb shocks. Hyaline cartilage is the common kind (joints, ribs, nasal septum), elastic cartilage bends (ear, larynx), and fibrocartilage is tough (intervertebral discs, where tendons attach). Bone is type I collagen hardened by calcium phosphate, full of blood vessels and always remodeling: osteoblasts build it, osteocytes keep it and osteoclasts break it down. Muscle: skeletal muscle is striated, multinucleated and voluntary (also the tongue, pharynx and upper esophagus); cardiac muscle is striated and branched, joined by intercalated disks with gap junctions; smooth muscle is spindle-shaped, not striated and involuntary (gut, airways, vessels, bladder). Nerve: neurons carry signals, helped by Schwann cells and satellite cells outside the brain and spinal cord and by astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia inside.
plain.f2-genpath:
What's tested
  • Reversible versus irreversible cell injury, and the nuclear changes of cell death
  • The six necrosis patterns and the organ or disease each one belongs to (coagulative heart and kidney, liquefactive brain and abscess, caseous TB, fat necrosis pancreas)
  • Apoptosis versus necrosis, and the intrinsic (cytochrome c) and extrinsic (Fas) pathways, which both end in caspases
  • How cells are injured: ATP loss in hypoxia, free radicals and the enzymes that clear them, reperfusion injury
  • The four adaptations with an example of each, intracellular accumulations, and dystrophic versus metastatic calcification
  • Acute inflammation (vascular changes, exudate versus transudate, leukocyte recruitment, the main mediators, neutrophils versus macrophages) and chronic inflammation (M1 and M2 macrophages, granulomas, the morphologic patterns, repair and scar problems, the acute-phase response)
  • Neoplasia: naming, benign versus malignant, grade versus stage

Injured cells first swell. If the cause stops, they recover (reversible). If the mitochondria, membranes, lysosomes or DNA fail, the cell dies. A dying nucleus shrinks (pyknosis), breaks up (karyorrhexis) or fades (karyolysis). Proteins that leak out of dead cells, like troponin from the heart, help make the diagnosis. Heart cells without blood stop squeezing within 1–2 minutes and die at about 20–30 minutes, when troponin starts to show in the blood; the damage can be seen under an electron microscope at 2–3 hours and a light microscope at 6–12 hours. Brain cells last about 4 minutes without blood, heart cells about 30 minutes and skeletal muscle about 3 hours.

Necrosis is messy death with inflammation, and it always means disease. Learn the pattern with its place: coagulative in heart or kidney infarcts (ghost cells), liquefactive in abscesses and the brain (pus), caseous in TB (cheesy granuloma), fat necrosis in pancreatitis (chalky calcium soaps), fibrinoid in vessel walls hit by immune complexes (lupus) or malignant hypertension. Gangrene of a foot or hand is coagulative when dry and liquefactive when infected (wet); diabetes, smoking and frostbite raise the risk. Apoptosis is tidy, programmed death with no inflammation: the cell shrinks into membrane-wrapped pieces that phagocytes eat. It can be normal (the gut lining turning over, the endometrium shed each cycle, leukocytes dying off after an infection) or a sign of disease (DNA damage, misfolded proteins). The intrinsic path releases cytochrome c from mitochondria; the extrinsic path uses Fas ligand on a T cell binding Fas, a death receptor (the TNF receptor is another). Both switch on caspases.

Without oxygen or blood flow the cell runs out of ATP: the sodium pump stops (swelling), lactic acid builds up and protein making stops. Too little oxygen can come from high altitude, anemia or carbon monoxide; too little blood from a blocked vessel or bleeding. Free radicals hurt lipids, proteins and DNA. They come from normal mitochondrial breathing, the burst phagocytes use to kill, reperfusion and radiation; superoxide dismutase, catalase and glutathione peroxidase clear them. Bringing blood back to an ischemic organ (after a heart attack, a stroke or a transplant) can add injury (reperfusion). Some toxins harm directly (chemotherapy drugs, microbial toxins); others only after the body converts them (pesticides, carcinogens).

Adaptations: bigger cells (hypertrophy, like the heart in high blood pressure), more cells (hyperplasia, like an enlarged prostate), smaller cells (atrophy, like a muscle that isn't used), or a switch of cell type (metaplasia, like a smoker's bronchus turning squamous). Cells can also fill up with fat (a yellow, fatty liver with alcohol, which can lead to cirrhosis) or with pigment (melanin; carbon in a smoker's lung, called anthracosis; lead). Calcium in damaged tissue with normal blood calcium is dystrophic (plaques, damaged valves); calcium in normal tissue because blood calcium is high (an overactive parathyroid, cancer destroying bone, too much vitamin D, kidney failure) is metastatic.

Acute inflammation shows as pain, swelling, redness, heat and loss of function. It starts in minutes to hours and is mostly neutrophils. Histamine widens vessels, protein-rich exudate leaks out (edema), and neutrophils roll (selectins), stick (integrins), squeeze through (PECAM-1) and follow chemokines. The main messengers: histamine (wide, leaky vessels), prostaglandins (pain and fever; NSAIDs block them), leukotrienes (leaky vessels, drawing in leukocytes), the cytokines TNF, IL-1 and IL-6 (fever, and shock if severe), complement (draws and activates leukocytes) and bradykinin (pain, leaky vessels). Neutrophils act fast and live 1–2 days; macrophages are slower, live much longer, and make cytokines and nitric oxide. Phagocytes kill with oxygen radicals, nitric oxide and enzymes; myeloperoxidase makes bleach (hypochlorite). It ends in full healing, a scar, or chronic inflammation.

Chronic inflammation builds over days and brings macrophages (the main cell), lymphocytes and plasma cells; it destroys tissue and leaves fibrosis, so function is lost. Causes: infections that persist (TB), autoimmune disease and allergy, and long exposure to something harmful (silica, cholesterol). M1 macrophages kill; M2 macrophages (IL-4, IL-13) heal with IL-10 and TGF-β. T cells and macrophages keep switching each other on. Eosinophils fight parasites; mast cells release histamine in allergy. Granulomas wall off things the body can't clear: caseating in TB, noncaseating in sarcoidosis and Crohn disease, and foreign-body ones around sutures or splinters.

Patterns: serous (thin fluid with few cells, like a blister or an effusion), fibrinous (fibrin on the heart's sac or the lung's lining; it can leave adhesions), purulent (pus from bacteria such as staph and strep, as in appendicitis), abscess (pus walled off in a tissue), ulcer (a crater in the skin or the lining of the mouth or gut, as in acute necrotizing ulcerative stomatitis) and granulomatous.

Healing: a platelet plug comes first, then inflammation for 1–2 days, then for up to 1–2 weeks granulation tissue (new vessels and fibroblasts, little collagen) fills the wound, and then collagen gives the scar its strength. A mild injury can regrow without a scar (regeneration). Skin, gut lining and blood cells always divide; liver, kidney and pancreas cells can start dividing again; neurons and heart muscle can't regrow, so they scar. A clean, closed incision heals with little scar (first intention); a large wound fills in with more granulation tissue and shrinks (second intention). A keloid grows past the wound edges and doesn't shrink back; a hypertrophic scar stays inside them and can. Infection, steroids (weak scars), poor nutrition (protein, vitamin C), pressure, poor blood flow (diabetes) and foreign bodies slow healing.

The whole body reacts too: fever (IL-1 and TNF raise the brain's set point through prostaglandins; aspirin and other NSAIDs bring it down), a high white count (normal 4,500–11,000/µL; often 15,000–20,000/µL; 40,000–100,000/µL is a leukemoid reaction, which can look like leukemia) and liver proteins: CRP (also a heart-attack risk marker), fibrinogen (raises the sedimentation rate), serum amyloid A (amyloidosis if it lasts) and hepcidin (anemia of chronic disease). Sepsis is the severe form and can cause shock.

Tumors grow from one changed cell that ignores the body's growth signals; the tumor cells give it its name, and the supporting tissue holds it and feeds it. Benign ones end in "-oma" (lipoma, adenoma, papilloma, cystadenoma). Malignant epithelial tumors are carcinomas, malignant connective-tissue tumors are sarcomas, and lymphoma, melanoma, mesothelioma, seminoma and hepatoma are malignant despite their names. Whether a tumor is benign or malignant is the biggest question, because it sets the treatment. Benign tumors look like the normal tissue, grow slowly and often have a capsule; cancers look less normal (anaplasia), usually grow faster and invade. Metastasis proves malignancy. Cancer can cause wasting (cachexia) and paraneoplastic syndromes (in 10–15%: hormone effects such as SIADH, nerve and muscle problems, clots). A biopsy makes the diagnosis; tumor markers such as PSA only help screen for it or follow it. Grade is how abnormal the cells look; stage (TNM) is how far it has spread (0 = in situ; any distant spread makes it IV), and stage matters more for prognosis. Dysplasia, disordered growth in a lining such as the mouth's, raises the cancer risk but may never become cancer.
plain.f2-virology:
What's tested
  • What makes a virus a virus; enveloped versus naked viruses (stability, release by budding or lysis); how viruses cause disease and spread
  • The Baltimore classes, which viruses bring their own RNA polymerase or reverse transcriptase, and the six steps of the life cycle
  • The human herpesviruses HHV-1 to HHV-8: their diseases and where each stays latent
  • HPV, adenovirus, parvovirus B19 and the poxviruses; the RNA viruses (how positive- and negative-sense genomes make mRNA; picornaviruses, coronavirus, measles, RSV, rabies, influenza drift and shift, the hemagglutination inhibition test)
  • HIV: structure, entry, life cycle, stages and CD4 counts, tests, drug targets and oral signs
  • Hepatitis A to E (spread, chronicity, prevention) and hepatitis B serology
  • The oncogenic viruses and how they drive cancer (E6 and p53, E7 and Rb)

Viruses are genes (DNA or RNA, never both) in a protein shell that can only copy themselves inside a cell, using the cell's ribosomes and energy. They are built from parts rather than dividing, and they slip through filters that stop bacteria. The shell is a spiral (helical) or a 20-sided ball (icosahedral). Some wear a fatty envelope taken from the host's membrane; these break down when dry, in acid or with detergent, so they must stay wet, spread by blood, sex or droplets, and usually leave the cell by budding without killing it. Naked viruses (hepatitis A, HPV, polio) are tough, spread by the fecal-oral route or surfaces, and burst the cell open (lysis) to get out. Which cells a virus can infect (its tropism) depends on which cells carry the receptor its surface proteins grab.

The steps are always the same: attach, get in (naked viruses are swallowed by the cell; enveloped ones fuse their envelope with a membrane of the cell), take off the coat, copy the genes and make proteins, assemble, and get out. Right after a virus gets in, the amount of infectious virus drops, because it has taken its coat off (the eclipse period); new virus appears only once copies are assembled, and then each cell releases a burst of them. Bacteria simply divide and double.

DNA viruses copy themselves in the nucleus (poxviruses are the exception). Retroviruses (HIV) and hepatitis B use reverse transcriptase. Negative-sense RNA viruses (measles, rabies, influenza) must bring their own RNA polymerase.

Viruses are sorted into the Baltimore classes by how they make their mRNA. Our cells can't copy RNA from RNA, so RNA viruses carry or make their own copying enzyme.

Why viruses make us sick, and how they spread: a virus is selected to spread, not to kill, since a dead host is a dead end; much of the illness (fever, tiredness, rash) is the immune system fighting it. To start an infection a virus needs enough live virus, cells it can grow in, and defenses too weak to stop it at once. Symptoms come after an incubation period of days to years (years for HIV). Virus spreads near where it got in, then through the blood: a first wave (primary viremia) seeds organs such as the liver and spleen, and a second, larger wave (secondary viremia) carries it to its target. It passes between people by droplets (even from people without symptoms), the fecal-oral route, sex, saliva, skin, blood and from mother to baby (vertical spread; spread between other people is horizontal), and from animals by mosquitoes, ticks and bites (rabies). Isolation, hygiene, masks, mosquito control, education and, above all, vaccines stop it.

Herpesviruses never leave. HSV-1 (cold sores, herpetic gingivostomatitis) hides in the trigeminal ganglion, HSV-2 in the sacral ganglia, VZV (chickenpox, then shingles) in sensory ganglia, EBV (mono, oral hairy leukoplakia, Burkitt lymphoma) in B cells, CMV in white cells, HHV-6 and 7 cause roseola, and HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma.

Positive-sense RNA viruses have genes that are already mRNA, so the cell reads them at once and the bare RNA alone can start an infection. They make their copying enzyme first, then a mirror-image copy of the genome to use as a template, in protected "factories" in the cell. Picornaviruses (polio, rhinovirus, coxsackie, hepatitis A) read their whole genome as one long protein that is cut into pieces, so they make equal amounts of each protein, and they stop the cell making its own proteins. Polio reaches the brain and spinal cord in fewer than 2 in 100 infections and can paralyze; a vaccine has wiped it out of the United States. Coxsackie A causes herpangina and hand-foot-and-mouth disease. Coronaviruses are the biggest RNA viruses; SARS-CoV-2 grabs ACE2, starts in the lining of the nose and windpipe, makes its copying machinery from its full-length RNA and its structural proteins from shorter (subgenomic) mRNAs, and harms the lungs through clotting and inflammation in the air sacs (immunothrombosis).

Negative-sense RNA viruses (measles, RSV, rabies, influenza) all have an envelope and a spiral core, and their RNA can't be read directly, so the bare RNA isn't infectious: each virus brings its own copying enzyme. The enzyme starts at the same end (the 3′ end) every time, makes one mRNA per gene and often falls off between genes, so the genes nearest that end are made the most. While the coating protein (N) is scarce it makes mRNAs; once N builds up it makes full-length copies that become new genomes. One gene can still make two proteins, by splicing, by starting at a different spot or by the ribosome slipping (frameshifting).

Measles is extremely contagious (it hangs in the air up to 2 hours), spreads before symptoms, gives cough, runny nose and red eyes, then Koplik spots inside the cheek before the rash, and fuses cells together; the MMR vaccine is live. RSV causes bronchiolitis, the top cause of pneumonia in babies under 1; nearly every child has had it by 2, and a vaccine in pregnancy protects the baby for about 6 months. Rabies, bullet-shaped, goes from the bite into muscle and climbs the nerves to the brain (Negri bodies in the neurons); it is slow, so a vaccine after the bite works.

Influenza has 8 separate gene segments. Hemagglutinin grabs sialic acid on our cells to get in, and neuraminidase cuts it to let new virus out (oseltamivir blocks neuraminidase). Human strains grab one form of sialic acid (α2,6), bird strains another (α2,3), and pigs have both, so pigs can mix them. Influenza changes a little every year through small mutations (drift, all strains), and influenza A sometimes swaps whole segments with another strain (shift), which can make a virus nobody is immune to and cause a pandemic. The hemagglutination inhibition test checks immunity: the virus makes red cells clump into a mat, and antibody against hemagglutinin stops it; the more a person's serum can be diluted and still stop it (the titer), the better protected they are.

HIV binds CD4 and then CCR5 or CXCR4, turns its RNA into DNA and inserts it into our DNA. AIDS means a CD4 count under 200. Viral RNA testing is the most sensitive test. In the mouth look for candidiasis, hairy leukoplakia and Kaposi sarcoma.

Hepatitis: A and E are fecal-oral and don't become chronic (A is worse in adults than in young children; E is dangerous in pregnancy). B, C and D are bloodborne and can become chronic. C becomes chronic in about 80% of people but is now curable; B has a vaccine; D needs B to exist. For hepatitis B: surface antibody alone means vaccinated, surface antigen means infected, IgM core antibody means acute infection.

Cancer viruses (seven in all): HPV 16 and 18 (cervical and oropharyngeal cancer; E6 removes p53, E7 blocks Rb; the Gardasil vaccine prevents it), EBV (lymphomas, nasopharyngeal cancer), HBV and HCV (liver cancer), HTLV-1 (T-cell leukemia, spread by breast milk), HHV-8 (Kaposi sarcoma) and Merkel cell polyomavirus (a skin cancer).
plain.f2-bacteria:
What's tested
  • Gram-positive versus gram-negative envelopes and why they stain differently; acid-fast and wall-less exceptions
  • Structures outside the wall (capsule, pili, fimbriae, flagella, axial filaments), endospores, plasmids and 70S ribosomes as drug targets
  • Growth (binary fission, the growth curve), oxygen needs and the three ways to make ATP
  • Growth needs (temperature, pH, osmotic pressure), DNA replication (leading and lagging strands) and why oxygen kills anaerobes
  • Gene transfer: transformation, transduction and conjugation
  • Steps of pathogenesis, virulence factors, biofilms, and exotoxins versus endotoxin with the classic toxins
  • Types of infection (acute or chronic, localized or systemic), antibiotic resistance and its alternatives
  • Oral biofilms: coaggregation, the shift to caries, and how fluoride and arginine work
  • Staphylococcus (abscess, coagulase, MRSA, toxin syndromes) and Streptococcus (pyogenes, pneumoniae, mutans, viridans)
  • The gram-negative rods (Pseudomonas, Klebsiella, E. coli, Vibrio, Salmonella, H. pylori), MacConkey agar, the red complex and the spirochetes

The gram stain sorts bacteria by their wall. Gram-positive bacteria have a thick wall that keeps the purple dye. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin wall plus an outer membrane; the alcohol washes the purple out and they stain pink. Only gram-negatives have endotoxin (lipid A in LPS). Mycobacteria have waxy walls (acid-fast), and Mycoplasma has no wall at all.

The gram-positive wall is thick (20–80 nm), and its teichoic acids strengthen it and help bacteria stick to each other. Penicillins block wall cross-linking and vancomycin grabs the ends of the wall's peptides; MRSA resists penicillins with an altered binding protein (PBP2a, from mecA). Capsules stop phagocytosis, pili help bacteria stick and share DNA, flagella and axial filaments move them, and spores (only Bacillus and Clostridium) survive heat and disinfectants.

Bacteria split in two (binary fission), which means building new wall, so penicillins hit dividing cells. They copy their one circular chromosome in both directions from one starting point: one new strand is made in one piece (the leading strand), the other in short Okazaki pieces that DNA ligase joins (the lagging strand). They grow fastest in the log phase.

Bacteria need the right temperature, pH and salt. Most like body temperature and a neutral pH. The syphilis and leprosy bacteria like cool tissue, so their sores start on the lips, tongue, genitals, face and hands. H. pylori gets through stomach acid by making urease, whose ammonia neutralizes acid, and by hiding in the mucus. The wall protects bacteria from salt and water stress outside the body. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen as the last electron acceptor and makes 38 ATP, anaerobic respiration uses something like nitrate or sulfate and makes less, and fermentation makes only 2 ATP. Oxygen forms toxic radicals: aerobes clear them with superoxide dismutase and catalase, and obligate anaerobes, which lack those enzymes, die in air. Bacteria swap genes by taking up naked DNA (transformation), through viruses (transduction) or through a sex pilus (conjugation), which is how drug resistance spreads.

Toxins: exotoxins are proteins made by both groups, very potent, and can become vaccines (toxoids). Endotoxin is part of the gram-negative wall, heat-stable, and causes fever and septic shock; it sets off strong inflammation, but no vaccine can be made from it. Cholera toxin (and the toxin of enterotoxigenic E. coli, the cause of traveler's diarrhea) causes watery diarrhea, Shiga toxin bloody diarrhea and kidney failure, tetanus toxin spastic paralysis and botulinum toxin floppy paralysis.

S. aureus (clusters, coagulase-positive) makes abscesses that need draining, food poisoning, scalded skin and toxic shock. S. epidermidis grows as biofilm on implants. S. pyogenes causes strep throat and flesh-eating infections. S. pneumoniae, protected by its capsule, is the top cause of community pneumonia. S. mutans makes acid and sticky glucans from sugar, causing caries.

How infections behave. Normal flora protects us. An opportunist (Pseudomonas in the eye, Candida in the mouth) causes disease only when the host is weak, and a strict pathogen always does. Bacteria first stick (pili, adhesins, capsule), then invade and do damage (toxins, enzymes), then settle in as biofilms that shrug off drugs and immunity. Acute infections start fast and heal (a dental abscess, treated with antibiotics and a root canal); chronic ones creep, resist drugs and are often mixed (periodontitis). Localized means one place; systemic means spread through the body. Bacteria resist drugs by pumping them out (efflux pumps), changing the target (altered PBPs) or destroying the drug (β-lactamase), and they pass resistance genes on plasmids. Antibiotics kill only growing cells. Other options are phages, drugs against virulence factors, and vaccines.

Plaque is a layered community: species stick to each other (coaggregation, such as streptococci to Actinomyces), with the oxygen-hating bacteria inside. Caries starts when frequent sugar tips healthy plaque toward bacteria that make acid and like acid (S. mutans, lactobacilli). S. mutans arrives late, builds glucans outside the cell, stores sugar inside, and kills rivals with mutacin. Fluoride mainly protects enamel (less dissolving, more repair) and kills few bacteria; arginine and urea feed bacteria that make ammonia, which raises plaque pH. Tears carry lysozyme, which digests the bacterial wall.

Gram-negatives: Pseudomonas (can't ferment; the second most common cause of hospital infections; burns, cystic fibrosis, long-wear contact lenses; very drug-resistant; treated with aminoglycosides), Klebsiella (capsule, pneumonia with thick bloody sputum) and Acinetobacter (war wounds); four of the six ESKAPE superbugs are gram-negative. Gut bacteria: cholera and traveler's diarrhea toxins pull water into the gut (treat with fluids), EHEC's Shiga toxin causes bloody diarrhea and kidney failure, ordinary E. coli causes most UTIs, Salmonella causes typhoid fever and food poisoning, and H. pylori (urease, flagella) causes ulcers and stomach cancer. On MacConkey agar only gram-negatives grow and lactose fermenters turn pink; mannitol salt agar picks out S. aureus. The red complex of periodontitis is P. gingivalis, T. forsythia and T. denticola; A. actinomycetemcomitans causes localized aggressive periodontitis. Borrelia (ticks) causes Lyme disease, treated early with doxycycline.
plain.f2-fungi:
What's tested
  • The fungal cell (chitin wall, ergosterol membrane) and what antifungals target; yeast, mold and dimorphic forms
  • Endemic mycoses by region (Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides) versus opportunists (Candida, Aspergillus, Mucor, Cryptococcus, Pneumocystis); the five classes of mycoses; the medically important phyla
  • Tuberculosis: spread, latent versus active disease, the granuloma, IFN-γ and the macrophage, the skin test and the IGRA, why treatment takes months and the standard regimen; nontuberculous mycobacteria
  • Anaerobes: clinical clues, how to sample, the key organisms (Actinomyces, Fusobacterium, Bacteroides, Clostridium) and drugs
  • Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma (no wall), Rickettsia (Rocky Mountain spotted fever), Chlamydia (elementary and reticulate bodies), Neisseria (gonorrhea versus meningococcus) and syphilis
  • The five tissue reactions to infection and the lab tests (stains and preparations such as KOH, India ink and dark-field; culture, serology, antigen, skin test, PCR)

Fungi have a wall of chitin, glucans and mannoproteins, and ergosterol (not cholesterol) in their membrane. Remember: ergosterol is in the membrane, not the wall. Most antifungals go after ergosterol: polyenes (amphotericin, nystatin) bind it, and azoles and terbinafine stop the fungus making it; echinocandins go after the wall's glucan. Amphotericin also sticks a little to our own cholesterol, which hurts the kidneys. Yeasts are single cells that bud; molds grow as threads (hyphae) that form a mat. Dimorphic fungi are molds in the soil and yeasts in the body, and that switch marks the true pathogens. There are five kinds of fungal infection: superficial (the outer skin and hair, only cosmetic, like tinea versicolor), cutaneous (skin, hair and nails: the dermatophytes of ringworm and athlete's foot), subcutaneous (under the skin after a thorn or wound, like sporotrichosis), endemic and opportunistic. Most medically important fungi, and all the true pathogens, are sac fungi (Ascomycota); Cryptococcus is a club fungus (Basidiomycota, the group of most edible mushrooms); Mucor's group is rare but deadly; Microsporidia hit people with AIDS.

The true pathogens infect healthy people who breathe in spores in certain regions: Histoplasma (bird and bat droppings in caves and coops; small yeasts inside macrophages) and Blastomyces (big yeasts with wide-based buds; often spreads to skin and bone) along the Mississippi and Ohio rivers, and Coccidioides in the Southwest desert (valley fever). Itraconazole (or fluconazole for Coccidioides) treats them, for months. Most fungal infections, though, are opportunists that hit weak hosts and don't spread from person to person: Candida (thrush that wipes off; pus in tissue), Aspergillus and Mucor (invade vessels; Mucor in diabetic ketoacidosis can blacken the palate), Cryptococcus (meningitis in AIDS, seen with India ink) and Pneumocystis (pneumonia in AIDS).

Tuberculosis is a slow-growing rod so full of waxy fats that the gram stain doesn't work on it: it is acid-fast (it keeps a red dye through an acid wash). It spreads through the air, mostly to the lungs. Most infected people keep it in check for life (latent TB); about 5% get sick within 2 years and another 5% later. It can also spread through the body (miliary TB, meningitis, bone) or swell the lymph nodes of the neck (scrofula). It hides in macrophages until T cells make IFN-γ, and the fight builds a cheesy (caseating) granuloma. Two screening tests: the PPD skin test, and the IGRA blood test, which a past BCG shot doesn't turn positive. Its granulomas, its waxy wall that keeps drugs out, its sleepy persisters and its quick resistance to any one drug mean months of several drugs: four (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin for 4 more. Chlorhexidine doesn't kill it. Other mycobacteria come from the environment (water, soil), not from people, and are hard to treat, especially in cystic fibrosis.

Anaerobes can't live in oxygen (they don't have enough of the enzymes, such as superoxide dismutase, that clear away its harmful products). They are normal mouth and gut flora, so their infections come from our own flora and are mixed with other bacteria that use up the oxygen and destroy penicillin. Oral anaerobes can seed the brain or, when breathed in, the lungs. Think of them with foul pus, gas or an abscess near a mucosa. Collect pus with a needle (or a paper point for a gum pocket), not a swab, and keep it from the air; the lab grows them on rich plates without oxygen. Drain it, and use metronidazole, clindamycin or penicillin; aminoglycosides don't work. Actinomyces gives a jaw swelling with draining tracts and yellow "sulfur granules" after an extraction. Fusobacterium necrophorum gives Lemierre syndrome (a clot in the jugular vein after a sore throat), and F. nucleatum from poor teeth is linked to preterm birth. Tetanus toxin causes spasms and lockjaw; botulinum toxin causes floppy paralysis, in the US most often in infants, whose guts let swallowed spores make the toxin; C. perfringens causes gas gangrene; C. difficile causes colitis after antibiotics (PCR finds it, but also finds healthy carriers).

Mycoplasma has no wall, so penicillins don't work on its walking pneumonia, a slow, mild chest infection of children, teens and young adults; macrolides, tetracyclines or fluoroquinolones do. It can also cause rashes, mouth sores and red eyes, and PCR is the best test. M. salivarium lives in the mouth and can make gum disease worse in people with weak immunity; Ureaplasma and M. genitalium infect the genital tract. Rocky Mountain spotted fever (ticks) is the most common rickettsial illness in the US. The germ lives in the lining of blood vessels, and its rash starts on the wrists and ankles and reaches the palms and soles; give doxycycline right away, without waiting for tests. Chlamydia lives inside cells (elementary body infects, reticulate body divides), is the most common bacterial STI and is found by NAAT. Gonorrhea has no capsule and keeps changing its pili, so there is no vaccine; meningococcus has a capsule, spreads by droplets and needs antibiotics at once. Syphilis starts as a painless chancre and is treated with penicillin.

How tissue reacts: pus (neutrophils, as with S. aureus or Candida), granulomas (TB, fungi), cells changed by viruses (inclusions, giant cells) or made to grow (HPV), dead tissue from a toxin with little inflammation (gas gangrene), and scarring after a long infection (hepatitis B and C, syphilis). How the lab finds it: the acid-fast stain for TB, KOH or PAS and silver stains for fungi, India ink for Cryptococcus, dark-field for syphilis, blood antibodies (serology) for germs that are hard to grow (Rickettsia, Mycoplasma), the PPD skin test for TB, and PCR for chlamydia and gonorrhea.
plain.f2-pkpd:
What's tested
  • Potency versus efficacy, affinity and intrinsic activity, the kinds of agonists and antagonists, the therapeutic index and window, and pharmacodynamic interactions
  • The four receptor families and how fast each acts
  • Absorption and distribution: bioavailability, first-pass metabolism, ion trapping, protein binding, volume of distribution
  • Half-life, clearance, steady state, loading dose, first- versus zero-order elimination, AUC, Cmax and Tmax
  • What metabolism does, phase I and II, CYP450 inhibitors and inducers, CYP polymorphisms, drug transporters
  • Drug terms and kinds: indication, side effect and adverse event, generic and trade names, OTC and legend, orphan drugs
  • The phases of drug development, the IND and the NDA

The big picture

Pharmacodynamics is what a drug does to you; pharmacokinetics is what you do to the drug. Potency is how little drug it takes; efficacy is how big an effect it can make at most. A drug can be very potent and still weak at its best. How tightly a drug sticks to its receptor is its affinity (the smaller its KD, the tighter it sticks); how well it switches the receptor on is its intrinsic activity. Agonists and antagonists both stick; only agonists switch the receptor on. Often the full effect comes before every receptor is filled: the empty ones are spare receptors.

An agonist turns a receptor on. A partial agonist turns it on only partway, so next to a full agonist it acts like a brake. A competitive antagonist sits in the same spot and can be pushed out by more agonist, so the curve moves right but can still reach the top. An irreversible or allosteric antagonist lowers the top. The therapeutic index (toxic dose ÷ effective dose) says how much room there is: small for warfarin and lithium. The therapeutic window is the range of blood levels between the lowest level that works (MEC) and the lowest level that harms (MTC).

Tolerance means more drug for the same effect (the curve moves right); sensitization means less (it moves left). Dependence means stopping brings withdrawal; addiction is craving and not being able to stop despite the harm. Two drugs can simply add up (oxycodone with acetaminophen), do more than add up (synergism: alcohol with a benzodiazepine), boost another drug while doing nothing alone (potentiation) or work against each other (antagonism).

Getting in and getting around

Drugs cross membranes in their uncharged form; at a pH equal to the drug's pKa, half of it is charged. Alkaline urine traps a weak acid like aspirin so it leaves faster, and acid urine does the same for a weak base like amphetamine. Swallowed drugs lose some dose to the liver before reaching the blood (first pass), so oral bioavailability is below the 100% of IV. Bioavailability is how much gets in, not how fast; to switch an IV dose to one by mouth, divide it by F. Only drug that isn't stuck to albumin works, so low albumin makes warfarin stronger. A big volume of distribution means the drug hides in tissues (amiodarone, tricyclics); a small one (3–5 L) means it stays in the blood.

Getting out

Most drugs leave at a steady fraction per hour (first order); ethanol, phenytoin and high-dose aspirin leave at a steady amount (zero order). It takes about 4–5 half-lives to reach steady state. A loading dose (Vd × target level) gets there at once. A larger Vd or a lower clearance means a longer half-life. Clearance (ke × Vd) sets the maintenance dose. After stopping, each half-life halves the level. AUC is the total exposure, Cmax the peak, Tmax when it comes, and Cmin the trough at the end of a dose interval. If the kidney clears a drug faster than the GFR (about 120 mL/min), it is also secreting it. Drugs passed in bile can be soaked back up from the gut (enterohepatic recirculation).

Metabolism and interactions

Metabolism makes a drug more water-soluble, never more fat-soluble, and the liver does most of it. It can switch a drug off, leave an active product (diazepam to oxazepam), switch on a prodrug (codeine to morphine) or make a toxic one (acetaminophen to NAPQI). Phase I changes the drug, mostly with CYP450 and most often by adding an OH group. Phase II enzymes (transferases) attach a group such as glucuronic acid so the kidney can remove it. The genes that vary most are CYP2D6 (codeine), CYP2C9 (warfarin) and CYP2C19 (omeprazole). P-glycoprotein pumps drugs out of cells; OATP carries statins into liver cells. CYP inhibitors (clarithromycin, erythromycin, azoles such as ketoconazole and fluconazole, ritonavir, grapefruit) raise other drugs' levels; inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St. John's wort, smoking) lower them.

New drugs and drug words

A new drug is tested in two animal species (one not a rodent), then the company files an IND with the FDA before anyone takes it. Phase I tests safety in 20–100 healthy people; phase II tests whether it works in 100–500 patients; phase III confirms safety and efficacy in 1,000–5,000 patients and leads to the NDA, the request for approval; phase IV watches for rare harms and new uses after approval.

What makes something a drug is what it is meant for, not where it comes from. A poison does almost only harm; a toxin is a poison made by a living thing. An indication is a reason to use a drug; a contraindication is a reason not to. A side effect is an unintended effect of the drug, usually unwanted but sometimes useful (minoxidil grows hair); an adverse event is anything harmful that happens during or after use, caused by the drug or not. A boxed warning flags a serious danger on the label. The generic name (acetaminophen) is the official one and the trade name (Tylenol) the maker's. Over-the-counter drugs need no prescription; legend drugs do. Orphan drugs treat rare diseases (under 200,000 people in the US).
plain.f2-autonomic:
What's tested
  • How the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems are wired, and which receptor sits at each site
  • Cholinergic agonists, cholinesterase inhibitors and organophosphate poisoning
  • Antimuscarinic drugs, their uses and their side effects
  • Adrenergic agonists: epinephrine, norepinephrine, α1, α2 and β2 drugs, and indirect sympathomimetics
  • α- and β-blockers and their dental interactions

Two systems, a few receptors

The parasympathetic system ("rest and digest") uses ACh on muscarinic receptors: slower heart (M2), more saliva, small pupils, busy gut and bladder (M3). The sympathetic system ("fight or flight") mostly uses norepinephrine on α and β receptors: α1 squeezes vessels and opens the pupil, β1 speeds the heart, β2 opens the airways. Both systems pass through ganglia that use ACh on nicotinic receptors. Sweat glands are the odd one out: sympathetic, but they use ACh. At rest most organs are run by the parasympathetic side, but blood vessels are the exception: their tone comes from the sympathetic side through α1.

Turning the parasympathetic side up or down

Pilocarpine and cevimeline turn muscarinic receptors on and bring saliva back in Sjögren syndrome. Cholinesterase inhibitors make ACh last longer: pyridostigmine for myasthenia gravis, donepezil for Alzheimer disease. Pilocarpine and carbachol drops lower eye pressure in glaucoma by pulling open the drain, and the brain's own nicotinic reward receptors are where varenicline helps people quit smoking. Nerve agents and insecticides do the same thing permanently: tiny pupils, slow pulse, wheezing, drooling and sweating, treated with atropine and pralidoxime. Botulinum toxin stops ACh from being released.

Antimuscarinic drugs (atropine, scopolamine, oxybutynin, tiotropium) do the opposite: dry mouth, dry eyes, big pupils, fast heart, constipation, trouble urinating and confusion in older people. Dry mouth means more caries.

Turning the sympathetic side up or down

Epinephrine hits α and β receptors; at the small doses in dental cartridges it mostly speeds the heart. It is the drug for anaphylaxis. Norepinephrine squeezes vessels but doesn't open the airways. Albuterol opens the airways (β2). β2 receptors also tell the liver to raise blood sugar, which is why a nonselective β-blocker can blunt the body's rebound from a low sugar and hide its warning signs. Clonidine calms the sympathetic system from the brain and dries the mouth.

α1 blockers (terazosin, tamsulosin) make people dizzy when they stand: bring the chair up slowly. β-blockers slow the heart. Nonselective ones (propranolol) can tighten the airways, and with epinephrine they can cause a sharp rise in blood pressure, so keep epinephrine to about two cartridges and check vital signs.
plain.f2-painrx:
What's tested
  • The arachidonic acid cascade and what each eicosanoid does
  • COX-1 versus COX-2; aspirin, NSAIDs and acetaminophen, their harms and interactions
  • Opioid receptors, full and partial agonists and antagonists
  • Toxidromes and their antidotes
  • The parts of a prescription, common abbreviations and DEA schedules

Where pain and swelling come from

Injured cells free arachidonic acid. The COX enzymes turn it into prostaglandins (pain, fever, swelling, stomach protection), prostacyclin (keeps platelets from sticking) and thromboxane (makes platelets stick). COX-1 does the everyday jobs: protects the stomach and helps platelets. COX-2 is the inflammation enzyme, and it also keeps kidney blood flowing and helps the uterus contract. Aspirin leans toward COX-1, celecoxib strongly toward COX-2, and meloxicam, etodolac and diclofenac a little toward COX-2; most others hit both. Steroids act one step earlier and cut leukotrienes too. Some drugs copy prostaglandins: misoprostol protects the stomach from NSAIDs (and can cause an abortion), latanoprost-type eye drops lower eye pressure (and grow lashes), carboprost and dinoprostone act on the uterus, alprostadil treats erectile dysfunction, and epoprostenol-type drugs open the lungs' blood vessels.

The non-opioids

Aspirin knocks out platelet COX for good, so one dose thins the blood for about a week; that's why it is stopped 7–10 days before surgery with a high bleeding risk. Ibuprofen and naproxen block COX for a few hours: great for dental pain, but they can cause ulcers and bleeding, add to warfarin, hurt the kidneys with blood pressure drugs and blunt those drugs. Someone whose asthma flares with aspirin should skip the other NSAIDs too. Past the usual dose, more NSAID adds side effects, not relief. Long-acting ones (piroxicam, oxaprozin, nabumetone, meloxicam) are taken once a day, and ketorolac is limited to 5 days. Celecoxib spares the stomach and platelets but raises heart attack risk and still strains the kidneys. Acetaminophen isn't an NSAID: it eases pain and fever, not swelling, and is safe for the stomach and platelets; too much destroys the liver, especially with alcohol (antidote: N-acetylcysteine). Capsaicin cream or patch wears out the pain nerves' TRPV1 receptors; it doesn't fight swelling either. An NSAID plus acetaminophen beats most opioids for a toothache.

Opioids

Opioids act on mu receptors: pain relief, sleepiness and euphoria, but also slow breathing, tiny pupils and constipation, plus nausea, itching, trouble urinating and gallbladder pain. People get used to most effects but not the pupils or the constipation. Needing more drug (tolerance) or going into withdrawal when it stops (dependence) can happen to anyone and isn't addiction. Opioids with benzodiazepines or alcohol are the big danger. Full agonists (morphine, oxycodone, hydrocodone, fentanyl, methadone) switch the receptor fully on; partial agonists (buprenorphine, butorphanol, nalbuphine, pentazocine) only partway, and they can throw someone on full agonists into withdrawal; naloxone and naltrexone block it. By mouth, 30 mg of morphine matches about 20 mg of oxycodone, 30 mg of hydrocodone or 200 mg of codeine, and 10 mg of morphine IV. Tramadol also raises serotonin (dangerous with SSRIs). Methadone lingers and builds up for days, so its dose goes up slowly. Buprenorphine only half-activates the receptor; dissolved in the mouth, it causes caries. Naloxone reverses an overdose but wears off in an hour or two, so the person can stop breathing again. Loperamide (for diarrhea) and methylnaltrexone and naloxegol (for opioid constipation) work in the gut without reaching the brain.

Poisonings

Small pupils, slow breathing and stupor: opioids (give naloxone). Small pupils, drooling and sweating: organophosphates. Big pupils with hot, dry, red skin, a full bladder and confusion: antimuscarinics (diphenhydramine, cyclobenzaprine, tricyclics). Big pupils with sweaty skin: cocaine, amphetamines, MDMA or bath salts. Agitation, fever, sweating and twitchy, brisk reflexes soon after a second serotonin drug is added: serotonin syndrome (for example tramadol, methadone or fentanyl with an SSRI or SNRI).

Prescriptions

Heading (who: prescriber, patient, date), body (what drug, its strength, how much, how to take it) and closing (refills, warnings, signature, DEA number). Write the generic name and spell things out. "1 cap po q6h prn pain" means one capsule by mouth every 6 hours as needed. Always 0.5 mg, never 5.0 mg; write "units" and "micrograms" in full; write 5 mL, not a teaspoon (a tablespoon is 15 mL). Schedule II drugs (hydrocodone, oxycodone) can't be refilled; III and IV can be refilled up to 5 times in 6 months. Never presign a prescription or write a controlled drug for office use.
plain.f2-antiinf:
What's tested
  • Bactericidal versus bacteriostatic drugs, the goals of treatment, resistance and combinations
  • Cell wall drugs: β-lactams, β-lactamase inhibitors and vancomycin
  • Protein synthesis, DNA, folate, membrane and tuberculosis drugs: targets and signature harms
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental care
  • Antivirals (herpes, influenza, HIV, hepatitis) and antifungals: targets, uses and interactions
  • Chemotherapy principles, classic and targeted cancer drugs: mechanisms, dose-limiting toxicities and oral effects

How antibiotics work

Some antibiotics kill bacteria (penicillins, cephalosporins, vancomycin, gentamicin, ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, rifampin); others only stop them growing (tetracyclines, macrolides, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, linezolid). Killers are preferred when the immune system is weak. Penicillins break the cell wall while bacteria are growing, so pairing one with a growth-stopper can make it work less well.

Bacteria resist a drug by keeping it out or pumping it out, by destroying it with an enzyme (β-lactamase destroys penicillins), or by changing or overmaking the drug's target (MRSA's changed penicillin-binding protein). Treatment can be prophylactic (before any infection, in someone at high risk), pre-emptive (an infection found on testing, before symptoms), empirical (before the germ is known), definitive (aimed at the germ the culture found) or suppressive (keeping a treated or chronic infection quiet).

The ones to know

Penicillin and amoxicillin cover most mouth bacteria; clavulanate (like sulbactam and tazobactam) protects them from the bacteria's β-lactamase. Piperacillin-tazobactam is the penicillin for Pseudomonas. Vancomycin, bacitracin and fosfomycin also attack the cell wall but have no β-lactam ring, while aztreonam has one and covers only aerobic Gram-negative bacteria. Cephalosporins are relatives, avoided after a serious penicillin reaction. Vancomycin handles MRSA. Clindamycin is the classic cause of C. difficile diarrhea. Doxycycline stains developing teeth, so not in pregnancy or young children. Gentamicin can hurt the kidneys and ears. Metronidazole covers anaerobes and makes people sick if they drink alcohol. Erythromycin and clarithromycin raise levels of warfarin, statins and triazolam. Isoniazid causes tingling feet unless vitamin B6 is given; rifampin turns urine, tears and saliva orange; ethambutol can blur vision and dull red-green color vision; pyrazinamide raises uric acid. Tuberculosis takes all four drugs for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin for at least 4 more. Ciprofloxacin and doxycycline are both bound by calcium, iron and antacids, and ciprofloxacin can rupture tendons. Avoid trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Bactrim) in a sulfa allergy. Nitrofurantoin treats only bladder infections; polymyxin B breaks bacterial membranes.

Prophylaxis

Patients with an artificial heart valve, past endocarditis and a few other heart conditions take one dose before dental work that cuts or moves the gums: amoxicillin 2 g 30–60 minutes before. With a penicillin allergy: azithromycin, clarithromycin or doxycycline (cephalexin only if the reaction wasn't serious). Clindamycin is no longer used for this.

Viruses and fungi

Valacyclovir and acyclovir treat cold sores and shingles; the virus's own enzyme switches them on. Penciclovir and docosanol creams also treat cold sores. Flu drugs such as oseltamivir help only if started within 2 days; amantadine works only on influenza A, and inhaled zanamivir can tighten the airways. HIV drugs block reverse transcriptase (tenofovir), integrase (dolutegravir, kept apart from antacids and calcium) or protease (ritonavir), and everyone with HIV is treated. Ritonavir blocks liver enzymes, so triazolam is off limits. Hepatitis C drugs cure the infection; hepatitis B drugs (tenofovir, entecavir) only keep it in check. For oral thrush, nystatin rinses stay in the mouth and don't interact with other drugs; fluconazole pills work well but raise warfarin and statin levels. Amphotericin B and nystatin punch holes in the fungal membrane by binding ergosterol; azoles and terbinafine stop the fungus making ergosterol; echinocandins (caspofungin) block the cell wall.

Cancer drugs

Chemotherapy hits fast-dividing cells, so mouth sores and low blood counts are common: check counts before surgery. Small tumors have more dividing cells and respond better, so chemotherapy is given right after surgery (adjuvant) to clear what is left, or before it (neoadjuvant) to shrink the tumor, and drugs are combined that work in different ways and don't share side effects. Some drugs act in one phase of the cell cycle (methotrexate and 5-FU while DNA is copied; vincristine and paclitaxel during mitosis), while alkylating drugs such as cyclophosphamide and cisplatin act in any phase. Each drug has a signature problem: doxorubicin, the heart; bleomycin, the lungs; cisplatin, the kidneys and ears; cyclophosphamide, the bladder; vincristine, the nerves (even jaw pain). Busulfan also scars the lungs, carboplatin lowers counts, oxaliplatin damages nerves, irinotecan causes diarrhea and 5-FU sore hands and feet. Leucovorin protects normal cells from methotrexate. Vincristine stops microtubules from forming, while paclitaxel freezes them so they can't come apart. Targeted drugs: antibodies (names ending in -mab) bind a target outside the cell, such as cetuximab (EGFR, head and neck cancer), trastuzumab (HER2, breast cancer, hard on the heart), bevacizumab (VEGF, new blood vessels) and rituximab (CD20 on B cells); small molecules (-nib) such as imatinib (BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukemia) enter the cell and block a kinase. Checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) block PD-1, so the tumor can't switch T cells off and they attack it again.
plain.om-caries:
What's tested
  • The order of plaque formation: pellicle, reversible then irreversible attachment of pioneer streptococci, coaggregation (F. nucleatum as the bridge), maturation, dispersal
  • S. mutans virulence: adhesins to salivary Gp340, acid production and acid tolerance, glucosyltransferases (GTFs) that turn sucrose into sticky glucans, stored intracellular polysaccharide
  • Why sucrose is special, and soluble α1,6 versus insoluble α1,3 glucans
  • The Stephan curve, the critical pH of 5.5 and the ecological plaque hypothesis
  • Which organism goes with which lesion (S. mutans, Lactobacillus, Actinomyces, Candida) and fluoride's three actions

The big picture

Your mouth has about 700 kinds of microbes, and streptococci are the most common. Many can't be grown in a dish, so they are found by reading their 16S rRNA genes.

How plaque builds

First a thin film from saliva (the pellicle) coats a clean tooth. Friendly Gram-positive streptococci stick to it, loosely at first and then firmly. Other bacteria then stick to them; F. nucleatum is the bridge that lets the harmful Gram-negative anaerobes like P. gingivalis join later. The finished plaque is a biofilm, which shrugs off antimicrobials better than loose bacteria do.

Why S. mutans causes cavities

  • It sticks to the pellicle protein Gp340.
  • It makes lactic acid and survives in it.
  • It uses sucrose to build sticky, insoluble glucans with its GTF enzymes. Only sucrose has the high-energy bond it needs, so on glucose and fructose alone it can't stick.
  • It stores sugar inside the cell to keep making acid later.

Acid and the Stephan curve

After sugar, plaque pH falls below 5.5 within minutes and enamel starts to dissolve; saliva's bicarbonate brings it back up over about half an hour to an hour. Snacking often keeps the pH low, which favors acid-loving bacteria (the ecological plaque hypothesis).

Who goes with which cavity

  • S. mutans starts enamel caries.
  • Lactobacillus pushes deep, cavitated dentin caries.
  • Actinomyces goes with root caries.
  • S. mutans plus Candida drives early childhood caries.

Fluoride

Fluoride makes enamel tougher (fluorapatite), helps early lesions remineralize and blocks the bacterial enzyme enolase. It doesn't stop lactobacilli, so it helps most before a lesion cavitates.
plain.om-perendo:
What's tested
  • The red complex (P. gingivalis, T. forsythia, T. denticola) and its link to deep pockets and bleeding; the orange complex (F. nucleatum) as the bridge that comes first
  • The plaque hypotheses: nonspecific, specific, ecological/keystone (P. gingivalis as the keystone pathogen)
  • P. gingivalis traits and virulence factors (gingipains); A. actinomycetemcomitans and its leukotoxin in molar-incisor (localized aggressive) periodontitis
  • Host response and bone loss: antigen presentation, cytokines, RANKL and osteoclasts; the three routes to systemic disease
  • Pulp infection: routes, dentinal tubule size, the shift to obligate anaerobes, E. faecalis in persistent infection, and which treatment fits which stage

Gum disease bugs

Periodontitis is long-running inflammation under the gumline that eats away the bone holding the teeth. The red complex (P. gingivalis, T. forsythia, T. denticola) shows up in deep, bleeding pockets. The orange complex, with F. nucleatum, moves in first and acts as the bridge.

Today's view is the keystone idea: P. gingivalis is rare, but it confuses the immune system so the whole community grows out of control. It can't do it alone; it needs the other bacteria.

  • P. gingivalis: Gram-negative anaerobic rod, black colonies, needs iron, eats proteins instead of sugar, makes gingipain enzymes.
  • A. actinomycetemcomitans: the bug of aggressive disease in teens around first molars and incisors; its leukotoxin kills white cells.

Why bone is lost

Immune cells present the bacteria to T cells, which pour out inflammatory signals. These raise RANKL, which switches on osteoclasts; OPG is the brake. The inflammation and bacteria can also travel through the blood, the lungs and the gut, which ties gum disease to other illnesses.

Infected pulp

Bacteria mostly reach the pulp through the dentinal tubules, which are widest next to the pulp. Early on, bacteria that can live with or without oxygen win; once the pulp dies, strict anaerobes take over. E. faecalis is the tough survivor in root canals that fail.

Treatment by stage

  • Pulp barely reached: pulp cap.
  • Only the top of the pulp: pulpotomy.
  • Into the canals: root canal (pulpectomy).
  • Young tooth with an open apex: apexogenesis if the pulp is alive, apexification or regenerative endodontics if it's dead.
  • Spreading past the apex: antibiotics and extraction or drainage.

A pulp polyp is a red, bleeding, painless mass of pulp growing out of a big cavity in a young patient.
plain.om-viral:
What's tested
  • Culture media (blood agar, Rogosa SL, mitis-salivarius, Gold's agar) and Gram/colony features of common oral organisms
  • The herpesviruses: latency sites, oral signs and cancers (HSV-1, VZV, EBV, CMV, HHV-6/7, HHV-8)
  • HPV: papillomas, Heck disease, HPV-16/18 in oropharyngeal cancer, E6 and E7
  • RNA viruses with oral signs: coxsackievirus (hand, foot and mouth; herpangina), mumps, measles (Koplik spots), rubella
  • Cancer basics (oncogenes, tumor suppressors, two-hit) and bacteria tied to cancer (F. nucleatum, P. gingivalis, H. pylori)

Growing oral bacteria

Blood agar grows almost everything. Rogosa agar picks out lactobacilli, mitis-salivarius agar picks out streptococci, and Gold's agar (with extra sucrose and bacitracin) picks out S. mutans. S. mutans colonies look rough and frosted with a shiny glucan drop on top; S. salivarius looks like a big gumdrop.

Herpes family

  • HSV-1 hides in the trigeminal ganglion. First infection in a child: sore, swollen gums with blisters. Later: cold sores. On a finger: herpetic whitlow.
  • VZV causes chickenpox, then later shingles: a painful one-sided band of blisters that stops at the midline.
  • EBV causes mono and is tied to Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal cancer.
  • CMV passed to a fetus can leave thin enamel.
  • HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma: purple patches on the palate in people with weak immunity.

HPV

HPV makes small warty growths (papillomas) and Heck disease. Types 16 and 18 cause throat (oropharyngeal) cancer by switching off p53 (E6) and Rb (E7). Vaccines cover them.

RNA viruses

Coxsackie causes hand, foot and mouth disease and herpangina; mumps swells the parotids; measles gives Koplik spots inside the cheek; rubella in pregnancy can leave the baby with enamel defects or missing teeth.

Infection and cancer

Oncogenes are a stuck gas pedal (one bad copy is enough); tumor suppressors are lost brakes (usually both copies). Tobacco, alcohol and HPV are the big risks for mouth and throat cancer. F. nucleatum and P. gingivalis are found in tumors, and the mouth can reinfect the stomach with H. pylori.
plain.ns-anat:
What's tested
  • What each glial cell does
  • The three brain bleeds and the cavernous sinus
  • Ventricles, lobes and the main cortical areas
  • Neural tube, neural crest and their birth defects
  • Spinal cord layout, blood supply, cord syndromes and reflexes
  • Brainstem "rule of 4" and the cranial nerve lesion signs

Cells. Neurons carry signals. Astrocytes are the helpers: they clean up potassium and glutamate and help build the blood-brain barrier. Oligodendrocytes wrap CNS axons in myelin (MS attacks them); Schwann cells do it in the PNS (Guillain-Barré attacks them). Microglia are the brain's immune cells.

Bleeds. Epidural = artery (middle meningeal), lens shape, often after a blow to the temple with a lucid interval. Subdural = veins (bridging veins), crescent shape, often older people. Subarachnoid = aneurysm, sudden "worst headache". In the cavernous sinus, the carotid artery and CN VI run through the middle, and III, IV, V1 and V2 run in the wall.

Brain layout. CSF goes lateral ventricles → third ventricle → aqueduct → fourth ventricle → out. The central sulcus splits the motor strip (in front) from the sensory strip (behind). Broca (front, left) makes speech; Wernicke (temporal, left) understands it.

Development. The neural tube becomes the brain and cord; the neural crest becomes the peripheral nerves, ganglia, adrenal medulla and much of the face and teeth. If the top of the tube does not close: anencephaly. If the bottom does not close: spina bifida. Folic acid prevents both.

Spinal cord. It ends at about L1–L2, so needles go in lower. Front of the cord (anterior spinal artery) carries movement and pain; the back (posterior spinal arteries) carries fine touch and position sense. Cut half the cord and you lose movement and fine touch on the same side but pain and temperature on the other side. The knee-jerk is a one-synapse reflex.

Brainstem. Nerves I–IV sit above the pons, V–VIII in the pons, IX–XII in the medulla. Medial structures are motor; lateral ones are sensory and sympathetic. A PICA stroke (lateral medulla) numbs pain and temperature on the same side of the face and the opposite side of the body, with hoarseness and Horner syndrome.

Cranial nerve signs. The tongue (XII) and the jaw (V3) point toward the bad side; the uvula (X) points away. CN III palsy: eye down and out with a droopy lid and big pupil. Bell palsy (VII) droops the whole half of the face.
plain.ns-path:
What's tested
  • Fine touch versus pain pathways and where each crosses
  • The trigeminal pathway for the face and teeth
  • Upper versus lower motor neuron signs, and three nerve-muscle diseases
  • Cerebellum and basal ganglia problems
  • Which artery causes which stroke

Two sensory routes. Fine touch, vibration and position sense go up the back of the cord on the same side and cross in the medulla. Pain and temperature cross right away in the cord and go up the other side. So a half-cord injury loses fine touch on the same side and pain on the opposite side.

The face. Face and tooth sensation travels on CN V. Touch goes to the main sensory nucleus in the pons; pain and temperature go down to the spinal trigeminal nucleus; jaw-muscle and PDL position sense uses the mesencephalic nucleus, whose cell bodies are oddly inside the brain. All of it relays in the VPM of the thalamus.

Movement. Upper motor neurons run from the cortex and cross in the medulla. Damage gives stiff (spastic) weakness, brisk reflexes and an up-going big toe. Lower motor neurons run from the cord to the muscle; damage gives floppy weakness, lost reflexes, wasting and twitching. Guillain-Barré is weakness that climbs from the feet after an infection. Myasthenia gravis is weakness that gets worse with use (blocked ACh receptors). Lambert-Eaton gets better with use and goes with lung cancer.

Cerebellum. Problems show on the same side: clumsy reaching, shaking near the target, wobbly walking. Basal ganglia. Dopamine helps movement. Parkinson disease loses dopamine: slow, stiff, shaky at rest. Huntington disease is an inherited repeat that causes dance-like movements, mood change and dementia.

Strokes. ACA: opposite leg. MCA: opposite face and arm, plus language trouble on the left side or neglect on the right side. PCA: half the visual field. Small deep (lacunar) strokes give pure weakness or pure numbness. Clot-busting drugs work only in the first hours.
plain.ns-phys:
What's tested
  • Why the inside of a neuron is negative at rest
  • What each channel does during an action potential, and why myelin speeds things up
  • How a synapse releases transmitter, and the main receptor types
  • How local anesthetics work and what changes their onset, strength and duration
  • How general anesthetics and sedation levels work
