Resting voltage. At rest, potassium leaks out of the cell much more easily than anything else, so the inside sits near potassium's own voltage, about −70 mV. Add potassium outside the cell and the cell becomes less negative.

The spike. Sodium channels open and sodium rushes in (the upswing). Then sodium channels shut themselves off and potassium channels open, bringing the voltage back down. While sodium channels are shut off, the cell cannot fire again. Myelin lets the signal jump from node to node, so thick, myelinated fibers are fastest.

Synapses. The spike opens calcium channels; calcium makes vesicles fuse and dump transmitter. Fast receptors are channels; slow receptors use G proteins. The NMDA receptor opens only with both glutamate and a depolarized cell. Botulinum toxin stops ACh release.

Local anesthetics plug sodium channels from the inside. The uncharged form gets into the nerve; the charged form does the blocking. A pKa near body pH means fast onset; infected (acidic) tissue slows or stops it. More fat-soluble = stronger; more protein-bound = longer. Esters break down in the blood and make PABA (allergy); amides break down in the liver. Too much drug in the blood affects the brain first (tingling lips, ringing ears, seizures) and then the heart. Treat with oxygen, seizure control and lipid emulsion. A lidocaine cartridge holds 36 mg.

General anesthesia means asleep, no memory, no pain and no movement. Most drugs boost GABA (inhibition); ketamine blocks NMDA. MAC tells you potency: lower MAC, stronger gas. Moderate sedation: the patient still answers when you talk to them.
plain.ns-sens:
What's tested
  • How we hear, taste, smell and balance
  • Eye muscles, eye-nerve palsies and visual field cuts
  • Sympathetic versus parasympathetic
  • How pain travels and how drugs treat it
  • Face and head pain, and facial fracture basics

Hearing. The middle-ear bones boost sound. In the cochlea, bending hair cells lets potassium in, which fires CN VIII. The base of the cochlea hears high notes, the tip low notes. The route is ECOLIMA: eighth nerve, cochlear nucleus, olive, lateral lemniscus, inferior colliculus, medial geniculate, auditory cortex.

Taste and smell. Front of tongue: taste by VII, feeling by V3. Back of tongue: both by IX. Taste relays through the VPM of the thalamus. Smell is the only sense that skips the thalamus and goes straight to the piriform cortex and memory areas.

Balance and eyes. Canals sense turning; utricle and saccule sense straight-line movement and tilt. LR is CN VI, SO is CN IV, the rest are CN III. A pituitary tumor presses the chiasm and takes away both outer visual fields. A temporal lobe lesion takes the upper corner ("pie in the sky").

Autonomic. Sympathetic nerves start at T1–L2 and mostly use norepinephrine. Parasympathetic nerves start in the brainstem and sacral cord and use ACh. Parasympathetic stimulation makes lots of watery saliva.

Pain. Fast sharp pain rides Aδ fibers; slow aching pain rides C fibers. Rubbing the area helps by "closing the gate". The brain can turn pain down from the PAG. Injury makes nerves more sensitive (hyperalgesia) and can make touch hurt (allodynia). Tissue pain responds to NSAIDs and opioids; nerve pain responds better to gabapentin, tricyclics and carbamazepine.

Face pain. Trigeminal neuralgia is seconds of electric pain from a light touch; carbamazepine treats it. Pain in the lower face is most often dental. Jaw pain on chewing in an older person can be giant cell arteritis, an emergency for vision. Facial fractures. A fracture into the superior orbital fissure freezes the eye and numbs the forehead; add blindness and it is orbital apex syndrome.
plain.ns-dis:
What's tested
  • MS: who, which kinds, how it is found and treated
  • Seizure types, emergencies and drug side effects in the mouth
  • Alzheimer and Parkinson disease, their drugs and dental care
  • Sleep apnea, narcolepsy and the body clock
  • How addictive drugs work; schizophrenia and its drugs
  • How memories are made

MS strips myelin in the brain and spinal cord, usually in young women. It comes and goes in attacks at different times and places. MRI shows plaques; spinal fluid shows oligoclonal bands. Steroids shorten attacks. Trigeminal neuralgia in a young adult should make you think of MS.

Seizures look the same every time. Absence seizures are brief stares in children. Lip smacking and chewing suggest a temporal lobe seizure. Five minutes or more is an emergency: call for help and give a benzodiazepine such as midazolam. Phenytoin overgrows the gums; carbamazepine treats trigeminal neuralgia but can lower white cells; valproate can cause bleeding.

Alzheimer disease starts with forgetting new things. Amyloid plaques sit outside cells and tau tangles inside. Drugs (donepezil, memantine) help for a while but do not cure. Parkinson drugs replace or protect dopamine (levodopa with carbidopa). Patients get dizzy standing up, so sit them up slowly.

Sleep. Deep sleep comes early in the night, REM later. Sleep apnea: snoring, pauses in breathing and daytime sleepiness, mostly with obesity. CPAP is first line; a dental appliance that moves the jaw forward helps milder cases or people who cannot use CPAP. Narcolepsy: falling asleep in the day and going limp when laughing (cataplexy). The body clock (SCN) is set by morning light.

Addiction. Every addictive drug raises dopamine in the nucleus accumbens. Cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake; no epinephrine within 24 hours of cocaine. Schizophrenia needs 6 months of illness; drugs block D2 receptors. Older drugs cause movement side effects, including lip and tongue movements (tardive dyskinesia); clozapine can wipe out white cells.

Memory. The hippocampus files new facts; the cerebellum and striatum hold skills. Learning strengthens synapses through NMDA receptors, calcium and extra AMPA receptors (LTP).
plain.cr-cardiac:
What's tested
  • How cardiac and smooth muscle start a contraction, the sarcomere and the intercalated disc, and why the heart can't be tetanized
  • The heart's layers and the conduction pathway, with its slowest and fastest parts
  • Vessel walls and the three capillary types
  • Ventricular and SA node action potentials, and what the nerves do to them
  • ECG waves, heart rate from the strip and the AV blocks
  • The cardiac cycle, heart sounds, the dicrotic notch and the neck vein pulse
  • Flow, resistance, Poiseuille's law, velocity, compliance, MAP and pulse pressure
  • Cardiac output, stroke volume, ejection fraction, Frank–Starling, venous return and the two curves

The pump

The right heart pumps to the lungs at low pressure and the left heart to the body at high pressure (about 25 against 120 mmHg), so the left wall is thicker; both pump the same, about 5 L a minute. Arterioles set the resistance, capillaries (the biggest total cross-section) do the exchange, and veins hold about 70% of the blood.

Muscle

Heart and skeletal muscle use troponin as their calcium switch; its TnC part binds the calcium. In the heart, calcium coming in through L-type channels releases more from the SR. Smooth muscle has no troponin: calcium binds calmodulin, which turns on myosin light-chain kinase, and cAMP (from beta agonists) relaxes it; its thin filaments hold on to dense bodies instead of Z lines. Heart cells are joined by intercalated discs: desmosomes and fasciae adherentes hold them together and gap junctions pass the signal, so they beat together, and their long refractory period means they can't lock into a sustained contraction. In contraction the filaments slide but don't shorten, so the A band keeps its length. Heart cells barely divide, so dead heart muscle becomes scar; smooth muscle can make new cells. Digoxin blocks the sodium pump, which leaves more calcium in heart cells, so they beat harder. Right atrial cells store ANP and release it when stretched.

Heart and vessel walls

The heart wall is epicardium (the outer lining over fat and the coronary vessels), myocardium and endocardium (the inner lining, which forms the valves). Vessels have an intima, a media of smooth muscle and an externa. Arteries have a thick media, so the wall is thick for the lumen; in veins the externa is the thickest layer. Arterioles have only 1–3 muscle layers, the aorta's wall is full of elastic sheets, and limb veins have valves. The vasa vasorum feed the walls of big vessels, more in veins.

Pericytes wrap the capillaries. Lymph capillaries carry leaked fluid one way, back to the blood.

  • Continuous capillaries (no pores): muscle, nerves.
  • Fenestrated (pores): kidney, gut, endocrine glands.
  • Sinusoids (big gaps, very leaky): liver, marrow, spleen.

Electricity

The beat starts in the SA node, slows down in the AV node (the slowest spot, which gives the atria time to empty), then races through the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibers (the fastest). In ventricular muscle, sodium rushes in for the upstroke, calcium holds the plateau, and potassium brings the cell back down. Pacemaker cells drift up on their own through the "funny" sodium current, and their upstroke is calcium, which is why calcium channel blockers slow them. The SA node fires about 70–80 times a minute, the AV node on its own 40–60. Sympathetic nerves speed the drift and strengthen the beat; the vagus slows the drift and the AV node, and at rest it is in charge.

The ECG

  • P = the atria depolarize; QRS = the ventricles depolarize (atrial repolarization hides inside it); T = the ventricles repolarize. Normal: PR 0.12–0.20 s, QRS 0.06–0.10 s.
  • PR over 0.20 s = first-degree block. PR stretching until a beat drops = Mobitz I. Beats dropping without warning = Mobitz II, the more dangerous one. P waves and QRS complexes unrelated = complete block.
  • At 25 mm/s a small box is 0.04 s and a big box 0.20 s: heart rate = 1,500 ÷ small boxes between R waves. Over 100 is a tachycardia, under 60 a bradycardia; the rate rising as you breathe in (sinus arrhythmia) is normal.
  • Atrial fibrillation: no P waves, an irregular rhythm and a stroke risk. Ventricular tachycardia can stop the pumping and turn into fibrillation. Wolff–Parkinson–White: an extra pathway skips the AV node. A left axis shift suggests left ventricular hypertrophy, a right shift right ventricular hypertrophy.
  • A wave points up when the signal travels toward a lead's positive electrode. Lead II is the usual rhythm strip. The ECG says nothing about how well the heart pumps.

One heartbeat

The mitral and tricuspid valves shut (S1), pressure builds with every valve closed, the aortic valve opens and blood leaves, then the aortic and pulmonic valves shut (S2, the dicrotic notch) and pressure falls with every valve closed again before filling starts.

At 75 a minute a beat lasts 0.8 s, and a fast rate mostly cuts filling time; the atria's squeeze adds only 10–20% of the filling. S3 is normal in the young but means a failing ventricle in older adults; S4 means a stiff ventricle (hypertrophy, ischemia). Aortic stenosis leaves more blood behind and lowers stroke volume; aortic regurgitation swells the ventricle and its stroke volume. The neck vein pulse: a (the atrium squeezes), c (the tricuspid bulges back), v (the atrium fills).

Flow and pressure

  • Flow = pressure difference ÷ resistance. Resistance depends on the radius to the fourth power: half the radius, 16 times the resistance.
  • Pulse pressure = systolic − diastolic. Mean arterial pressure ≈ diastolic + one third of the pulse pressure.
  • Blood is slowest in the capillaries (the largest total cross-section), and pressure drops most across the arterioles. Veins stretch easily, so they store blood; stiff older arteries widen the pulse pressure, and stroke volume is the main thing that sets it.
  • Thick blood (polycythemia) resists flow; thin blood (anemia) flows more turbulently. Turbulence is the bruit or murmur you hear.

Output

Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. Stroke volume goes up with more filling (Frank–Starling) and stronger contraction, and down with a higher afterload. Ejection fraction = stroke volume ÷ end-diastolic volume. Breathing in pulls more blood back to the right heart.

Blood returns down a small gap (about 7 mmHg in the veins to 0 in the right atrium), helped by the muscle pump and breathing in and cut by straining (Valsalva) or a pregnant uterus on the vena cava. More blood volume raises output and right atrial pressure; a positive inotrope raises output and lowers right atrial pressure; higher resistance lowers output without changing right atrial pressure. The heart's oxygen use rises most with rate, contractility and afterload.
plain.cr-bp:
What's tested
  • The baroreceptor reflex: standing up, fainting and bleeding
  • The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, ADH and the natriuretic peptides
  • How organs control their own blood flow, and what causes edema
  • Hypertension, atherosclerosis, aneurysms, vasculitis and leg-vein clots
  • Shock: signs, types and treatment
  • Heart attacks, valve disease and endocarditis
  • Heart failure and heart muscle disease
  • Blood pressure cutoffs for dental care

Quick control

Pressure sensors in the carotid sinus (glossopharyngeal nerve) and the aortic arch (vagus) fire less when BP drops. The brain answers by speeding the heart and tightening vessels. Nerves to the heart and vessels do the work: sympathetic nerves speed and strengthen the heart and tighten arteries and veins; the vagus mostly slows the heart. Low oxygen or high CO2 (sensed in the carotid and aortic bodies and the brainstem), too little blood to the brain, and chest pain all raise BP the same way. Older patients on BP pills may not answer fast enough when they sit up, so they get dizzy or faint: raise the chair slowly. A simple faint (vasovagal syncope) is the most common dental emergency: both heart rate and BP drop, so lay the patient flat with the legs up.

Slow control

When the kidney gets too little blood, it releases renin. That leads to angiotensin II, which squeezes vessels and releases aldosterone, which keeps salt and water. Stretched atria release ANP, which does the opposite. ADH from the pituitary keeps water and, in large amounts, narrows vessels.

Local control

Organs also set their own flow. When pressure stretches an arteriole, its muscle tightens (the myogenic response), so flow stays steady (autoregulation, best in the kidney, heart and brain). A working tissue, or one whose blood supply was briefly cut off, builds up waste products that widen its arterioles (active and reactive hyperemia). The vessel lining releases nitric oxide, the main widener, and endothelin, which narrows vessels. Low oxygen widens vessels everywhere except the lungs.

Organs and edema

The heart muscle gets most of its blood between beats. Brain vessels widen when CO2 is high. Lung vessels tighten when oxygen is low. Resting muscle is held narrow by nerves, but in exercise its waste products open it up; skin flow is set by nerves to control temperature. Fluid leaves a capillary when the push of blood pressure beats the pull of the blood's proteins; about 20 L leaks out a day, most comes back, and 2–4 L returns as lymph. Edema comes from higher pressure in the capillaries, too little albumin in the blood, leaky vessels or blocked lymph.

Disease

  • Hypertension starts at 130/80 (stage 1); stage 2 is 140/90. Most of it has no single cause. It quietly damages the heart, brain, kidneys and eyes, and its drugs can dry the mouth or overgrow the gums.
  • Atherosclerosis: cholesterol gets into the artery wall and is swallowed by macrophages (foam cells). A plaque that breaks open can cause a heart attack or stroke.
  • A true aneurysm stretches all three layers of the wall. A port-wine stain never fades; a stork bite usually does. A tangle that joins arteries straight to veins (an arteriovenous malformation) can bleed badly during dental work.
  • Giant cell arteritis, in people over 50: headache, a sore temple and jaw pain when chewing. It can blind, so refer the same day.
  • A clot in a deep leg vein can travel to the lungs (a pulmonary embolism); lying still for a long time is the classic cause.
  • Shock means the tissues don't get enough oxygen: low BP, a fast pulse, little urine, confusion and a high lactate. Bleeding or a failing heart gives cold, clammy skin; widely opened vessels (distributive shock, the most common kind, usually from infection) give warm skin. Epinephrine comes first for anaphylactic shock.
  • An inferior heart attack (leads II, III, aVF) is usually the right coronary artery. Heart muscle starts to die 20–40 minutes after the artery closes, and the wall can tear 3–10 days after a heart attack. A clot from the heart can block the eye's artery: sudden, painless loss of sight in one eye, an emergency like a stroke.
  • Heart failure with a low ejection fraction (under 40%) is a big, weak ventricle, usually from coronary disease. With a normal ejection fraction, the ventricle is thick and stiff and can't fill, usually from high blood pressure. A failing left side backs fluid into the lungs; a failing right side backs it into the body (swollen legs, full neck veins). The left side usually fails first.
  • Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, an inherited thick septum, is the top cause of sudden death in young athletes. Fluid around the heart (tamponade) gives low BP, full neck veins and quiet heart sounds. Marfan syndrome (tall, a high-arched palate) weakens the aorta.
  • Aortic stenosis: a systolic murmur, fainting and chest pain on exertion. Mitral valve prolapse: a click.
  • Endocarditis after dental work is usually viridans streptococci. Prophylaxis is only for high-risk patients, such as those with artificial valves or past endocarditis; rheumatic heart disease or a prolapsed valve alone doesn't need it. Small red spots on the palate can be an early sign.

In the chair

At 180/110 or higher, don't do elective treatment: send the patient to a physician. After a heart attack, put off elective care: 6 months on Dr. Anderson's slides, about 30 days in newer guidance if the patient is stable. Never stop a patient's aspirin and clopidogrel after a stent without asking the cardiologist.
plain.cr-cvdrugs:
What's tested
  • How each blood pressure drug works and its main side effect
  • Diuretics and potassium
  • Heart failure drugs, and which ones help patients live longer
  • Heart rhythm drugs and amiodarone's side effects
  • Nitroglycerin for chest pain
  • Cholesterol drugs
  • How much epinephrine a heart patient can have

Blood pressure drugs

  • Water pills. Thiazides lower sodium, potassium and magnesium and raise sugar, fats, uric acid and calcium; chlorthalidone lasts longest. Loop diuretics (furosemide, torsemide) are stronger and work better when the kidneys are failing; they lower potassium, magnesium and sodium, send calcium into the urine (blood calcium usually stays normal) and can hurt hearing. Both are sulfa-type drugs. Spironolactone keeps potassium, so levels can get too high (more so with an ACE inhibitor or an NSAID), and it can cause breast growth in men.
  • ACE inhibitors (names ending in -pril, such as lisinopril and ramipril) cause a dry cough in up to 1 in 5 patients and, rarely, swelling of the lips and tongue, both from bradykinin. ARBs (-sartan) rarely do. Both raise potassium, can drop BP in a patient low on fluid, can harm the kidneys (worst when the arteries to both kidneys are narrowed) and can't be used in pregnancy.
  • β-blockers (-olol) slow the heart. The nonselective ones (propranolol) can make epinephrine push BP up and slow the heart. They can also hide the warning signs of low blood sugar in a diabetic on insulin and slow recovery from it, so make sure the patient has eaten. Carvedilol and labetalol (-alol, -ilol) block alpha receptors too.
  • Calcium channel blockers: amlodipine and nifedipine relax vessels, which can speed the heart and swell the ankles (water pills don't fix that swelling); verapamil and diltiazem slow the heart and can block the AV node or weaken the heart. Any of them can make the gums overgrow, in about 6–34% of patients: collagen breaks down more slowly and fibroblasts multiply. Treat it with careful plaque control, a drug switch by the physician and, if needed, surgery.
  • α1-blockers (-osin) make patients dizzy when they stand up.
  • NSAIDs taken for more than a few days make many BP drugs work less well and, with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, loop diuretics or spironolactone, raise the risk of kidney harm and high potassium.

Epinephrine

One cartridge of 1:100,000 has 0.018 mg of epinephrine. A heart patient's limit is 0.04 mg, about two cartridges; a healthy adult's is 0.2 mg.

Heart failure

ACE inhibitors or ARBs (or sacubitril–valsartan), certain β-blockers, spironolactone and SGLT2 inhibitors help patients live longer. Loop diuretics and digoxin only help symptoms. Sacubitril–valsartan pairs an ARB with a drug that keeps the body's own salt-losing natriuretic peptides around longer; it works better than an ACE inhibitor or ARB alone, but it can drop BP and can't be used in pregnancy or after lip and tongue swelling (angioedema) from an ACE inhibitor or ARB. SGLT2 inhibitors (-flozins) make the kidney's first segment spill sodium and sugar into the urine; they treat diabetes, heart failure and kidney disease, and can dry patients out, cause urinary tract infections and, rarely, harm the kidneys. Digoxin blocks the sodium–potassium pump to make the heart squeeze harder; it is now used less, and it doesn't help patients live longer. Low potassium and kidney failure make digoxin toxic: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, blurred vision and yellow halos around lights.

Rhythm drugs

Class I block sodium (procainamide, lidocaine, flecainide) and widen the QRS the most; class II are β-blockers (esmolol, metoprolol); class III block potassium (amiodarone, dofetilide, ibutilide) and lengthen the QT the most; class IV are verapamil and diltiazem. Adenosine, digoxin and magnesium sulfate are the others. Classes II and IV slow the heart rate in atrial fibrillation; classes I and III bring back a normal rhythm. Any of them can cause new arrhythmias, low BP and a slow heart. Amiodarone can scar the lungs, upset the thyroid, hurt the liver, turn the skin blue-gray and harm the eyes (corneal deposits, optic nerve damage). Epinephrine and albuterol speed the heart; β-blockers (eye drops too), calcium channel blockers and digoxin slow it. Amiodarone, some antibiotics (the macrolides), ondansetron and haloperidol lengthen the QT, so don't stack them. Lidocaine is a class I drug too, so it adds to flecainide's sodium block.

Chest pain in the chair

Nitroglycerin goes under the tongue, 0.4 mg. If the pain isn't better in 5 minutes, call EMS and give another dose, up to three. It causes headaches and low BP, and it can't be given after sildenafil or tadalafil.

Cholesterol drugs

Statins block the liver enzyme that makes cholesterol; LDL is what they lower most (by 20–60%), and they cut heart attacks, strokes and deaths. They can cause muscle pain and raise liver enzymes, and they can't be used in pregnancy or breastfeeding. Clarithromycin and erythromycin raise statin levels and the risk of muscle breakdown, so azithromycin is the safer macrolide. PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab, alirocumab) are injected antibodies that save LDL receptors from being broken down; they lower LDL more than any other drug and are added to a statin. Bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol, colesevelam) bind bile acids in the gut, cause constipation and bind other drugs, so those are taken 1–2 hours before or 4 hours after. Ezetimibe blocks cholesterol uptake from the gut. For triglycerides: fibrates (muscle breakdown, more so with a statin), niacin (also raises HDL; flushing, itching, liver enzyme rises) and omega-3 fish oils (more bleeding).
plain.cr-blood:
What's tested
  • How the platelet plug forms, and its disorders
  • The clotting cascade and the factors that need vitamin K
  • PT/INR versus aPTT, and the mixing study
  • Disorders that make blood clot too easily
  • Blood thinners: what each blocks, how it is checked and how it is reversed
  • Extractions in patients on blood thinners
  • Sickle cell disease, HbC and HbSC, and the thalassemias
  • Anemias, the drugs that lower B12, and the drugs that make blood cells

Stopping bleeding

First, platelets stick to the torn vessel with the help of von Willebrand factor (it links the platelet's GpIb to the vessel wall) and clump together through GpIIb/IIIa and fibrinogen. Problems here cause quick, oozing bleeding: gums, nosebleeds, heavy periods, tiny red spots (petechiae) and bruises. Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder. Two rare inherited platelet problems: Bernard–Soulier (no GpIb; giant platelets that don't clump with ristocetin) and Glanzmann (no GpIIb/IIIa; normal-sized platelets). Too few platelets is the most common cause of this kind of bleeding: platelets are given below 10,000/µL even without bleeding, below 20,000/µL when bleeding is likely, and below 50,000/µL for surgery. Vessel-wall causes, such as scurvy, are rare.

Then the clotting factors make fibrin to hold the plug. Problems here (such as hemophilia, mostly in boys) cause late bleeding and bleeding into joints and muscle. Tissue factor (factor III) and factor VII start the process ("37 cents"), and calcium is needed all along.

The tests

  • PT/INR checks factor VII and the common pathway. It is long with warfarin, liver disease and low vitamin K.
  • aPTT checks factors XII, XI, IX and VIII ("not $12.00 but $11.98"). It is long with heparin and the hemophilias A, B and C (factors VIII, IX and XI). Missing factor XII lengthens it but causes no bleeding.
  • A mixing study adds normal plasma: if the test corrects, a factor is missing; if it stays long, something is blocking the cascade.
  • The liver makes most factors, and factors II, VII, IX and X need vitamin K.

Clotting too easily

Factor V Leiden (factor V can't be switched off by protein C; the most common inherited cause), a prothrombin gene change that makes too much prothrombin, or a lack of protein C, protein S or antithrombin makes blood clot too easily. Immobility, surgery, pregnancy, estrogen, smoking and cancer add to the risk. In DIC (most often from sepsis) clots form inside the vessels and use up the factors and platelets, so the patient clots and bleeds at once.

Blood thinners

  • Warfarin blocks the recycling of vitamin K, so the liver makes fewer working factors II, VII, IX and X. It takes 2–7 days to work, and the first days can bring clots, so heparin covers the start. It is checked with the INR and reversed with vitamin K or prothrombin complex concentrate. Many drugs change it: metronidazole, fluconazole and some antibiotics raise the INR, NSAIDs add bleeding, and rifampin weakens it. It is the pill for a mechanical heart valve.
  • Heparin works through antithrombin. It is checked with the aPTT and reversed with protamine. Enoxaparin (LMWH) usually isn't monitored. On days 5–10 of heparin, some patients make antibodies that drop the platelets and cause clots (HIT): stop heparin and switch to a drug such as bivalirudin.
  • Dabigatran blocks thrombin (reversed by idarucizumab); the -xaban drugs block factor Xa (reversed by andexanet alfa or prothrombin complex concentrate). These pills are not for mechanical heart valves.
  • Aspirin knocks out each platelet for its whole life, 7–10 days. Clopidogrel and ticagrelor block the ADP receptor; ticagrelor must not be taken with clarithromycin.
  • Alteplase and tenecteplase dissolve clots (a heart attack, a large lung clot, a stroke). Tranexamic acid does the opposite and protects them.

In the chair

With an INR of 3.5 or less, a simple extraction usually goes ahead without stopping warfarin. Don't stop aspirin or other antiplatelets on your own. Use pressure, packing, sutures and a tranexamic acid rinse. Avoid NSAIDs: even a few days add bleeding; acetaminophen at usual doses is safer.

Hemoglobin problems

  • Sickle cell disease: one amino acid change (valine for glutamic acid) makes red cells sickle when oxygen is low. They block small vessels: pain crises, chest crises, stroke, and a scarred spleen that lets infections in. Keep visits short, keep the patient warm and well oxygenated, and treat infections fast. Sickle trait is the most common hemoglobin problem in the US and usually causes nothing.
  • HbC (lysine in the same spot) is mild, with target cells and no pain crises. HbSC disease is milder than sickle cell anemia but can damage the hip.
  • Thalassemias make too little of one globin chain. Losing one α gene causes nothing, two a mild anemia, three HbH disease; losing all four is fatal before birth (Hb Barts holds on to its oxygen). β-thalassemia minor (one bad gene) is mild; major (two) needs transfusions, can enlarge the upper jaw and overloads the body with iron.

In the mouth, hemoglobin disorders can show pale mucosa, late tooth eruption, weak enamel and dentin, tongue changes, extra cementum, and gum disease unusual for a child.

Anemia

Iron deficiency gives small red cells, a sore smooth tongue, cracked mouth corners, ice craving and spoon nails; a low ferritin shows it best. It is treated with ferrous sulfate by mouth (IV iron if that fails); deferoxamine removes extra iron. Low B12 or folate gives large cells; only B12 fixes the nerve damage, which can become permanent. B12 needs stomach acid, intrinsic factor and the end of the small bowel to be absorbed, so acid blockers lower it, and so do metformin and nitrous oxide. B12 is given as a shot (for nerve symptoms), by mouth or as a nasal spray. Folic acid in early pregnancy prevents spine defects. Epoetin raises red cells (used in kidney disease; it can raise blood pressure), filgrastim and sargramostim raise white cells but cause bone pain, and romiplostim and eltrombopag raise platelets.
plain.cr-resp:
What's tested
  • Chest and airway anatomy, and the cells of the airways and alveoli
  • Lung volumes and capacities
  • How the lungs inflate: pressures, stiffness and surfactant
  • Ventilation, gas exchange and V/Q
  • How blood carries oxygen and CO2
  • What controls breathing
  • Obstructive versus restrictive disease, lung diseases and infections
  • Asthma, antibiotic and allergy drugs

Anatomy

Swallowed or inhaled objects usually go down the right main bronchus, which is wider and straighter. The nerve and vessels between the ribs run under each rib, so needles go over the top of a rib. The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) runs the diaphragm; if one is paralyzed, that side of the diaphragm moves up instead of down when you breathe in.

The lung's own covering (visceral pleura) doesn't feel sharp pain; the lining of the chest wall (parietal pleura) does. Pain from the chest-wall part is felt over the ribs (intercostal nerves); pain from the part on the diaphragm is felt in the neck and above the collarbone, because the phrenic nerve (C3–C5) carries it. Fluid in the chest pools in the lowest gutter, the costodiaphragmatic recess.

The right lung has three lobes and two fissures; the left has two lobes, one fissure and the lingula. Each lung has about 10 bronchopulmonary segments, each with its own bronchus, so one can be removed alone. Bronchial arteries from the aorta feed the airways themselves, not the alveoli.

The diaphragm and the external intercostals breathe in; neck muscles help in a hard breath. The abdominal muscles and internal intercostals push air out hard. The T4 skin band is at the nipple and T10 at the belly button.

Cells

The airways that only carry air (the nose down to the terminal bronchioles, about 150 mL) are the anatomic dead space; gas exchange starts at the respiratory bronchioles. Each branching adds surface, so the alveoli spread over about 70 m².

Most airways are lined by ciliated cells with mucus-making goblet cells, on basal stem cells; the cilia sweep the mucus up and out, and smoking stops them. The trachea is held open by C-shaped cartilage rings. The smallest airways (terminal bronchioles) have no cartilage or goblet cells; their club cells protect and detoxify. Big particles stop in the nose, middle-sized ones get swept out, and the smallest reach the alveoli, where macrophages eat them.

Type I cells are flat and line the alveoli for gas exchange. Type II cells are plump, store surfactant in lamellar bodies, keep small alveoli from collapsing and replace type I cells. Babies born before about 35 weeks don't have enough surfactant and get respiratory distress syndrome.

Volumes

Vital capacity = everything you can breathe in and out. Residual volume is the air that never leaves, so spirometry can't measure it, or FRC and total lung capacity, which include it; helium dilution or a body box (plethysmography) does. Air trapped behind closed airways, as in COPD, shows up only in the body box.

FEV1 is how much you can blow out in the first second; healthy lungs blow out more than 70% of their forced vital capacity in that second. A total lung capacity under 80% of the predicted value suggests small, stiff lungs (restrictive); over 120% suggests trapped air (obstructive).

Breathing in

The diaphragm pulls down, the pressure around the lungs gets more negative, and air flows in. Breathing out at rest needs no muscles: the lungs spring back. If air gets between the lung and the chest wall (pneumothorax), the lung collapses. Stiff lungs (fibrosis) are hard to inflate. Floppy lungs (emphysema) inflate easily but don't spring back, so their airways collapse when the patient blows out hard; breathing out through pursed lips helps hold them open.

Surfactant makes the lungs easier to inflate, keeps small alveoli from emptying into big ones and keeps fluid out. The narrower an airway, the much higher its resistance, but there are so many small airways that most of the resistance is in the larger ones. The vagus nerve tightens the airways; sympathetic (beta-2) signals open them.

Gas exchange

  • Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − dead space) × breaths per minute. Dead space is air that never meets blood: about 150 mL in the airways plus a little in alveoli with poor blood flow. Double the breathing and CO2 halves; halve it and CO2 doubles. Make twice the CO2 (exercise) and you must breathe twice as much to keep CO2 normal.
  • Alveolar oxygen ≈ 0.21 × (760 − 47) − CO2 ÷ 0.8 ≈ 150 − 50 = 100 mmHg. Blood reaches the lung with oxygen at 40 and CO2 at 45 and leaves with 100 and 40.
  • The top of the lung has the highest V/Q and the base the lowest. A blood clot in the lung makes dead space, where the alveolar air stays like fresh air; a blocked airway makes a shunt, where the alveolar air turns like venous blood, and extra oxygen can't fix it.
  • Blood flows through the lung at low pressure. At the very top, if blood pressure drops or a ventilator pushes air in, the alveoli can squeeze the capillaries shut (zone 1, no flow); the base gets the most flow (zone 3). Vessel resistance is lowest at a normal resting lung volume.
  • Oxygen loads easily at rest; in hard exercise blood rushes through so fast it may not fully load.

Oxygen in the blood

Almost all oxygen rides on hemoglobin; very little dissolves. Each oxygen that binds makes the next bind more easily, so the curve is S-shaped: blood stays nearly full of oxygen until PO2 falls below about 60, then lets go quickly in the tissues. Heat, acid, CO2 and 2,3-BPG (2,3-DPG) make hemoglobin let go more easily (right shift); cold, alkalosis, fetal hemoglobin and carbon monoxide make it hold on (left shift). Carbon monoxide grabs hemoglobin tightly; the pulse oximeter can look normal even though the tissues are starving.

CO2 travels mostly as bicarbonate (made in red cells by carbonic anhydrase, then traded out of the cell for chloride), some on hemoglobin and a little dissolved. Too much CO2 makes the blood acid (respiratory acidosis, from breathing too little); blowing off too much makes it alkaline (respiratory alkalosis, from anxious overbreathing or high altitude).

Control

The medulla sets the rhythm of breathing. In the pons, the pneumotaxic center cuts breaths short and helps set the rate, and the apneustic center is thought to lengthen them, but their exact jobs aren't settled. You can also override all of it on purpose, as when you hold your breath.

The brain mostly watches CO2: CO2 slips into the fluid around the brain and makes it acidic, and breathing speeds up. If CO2 stays high for months (severe COPD), that fluid gets extra bicarbonate and the brain gets used to the high CO2. The carotid and aortic bodies watch for low oxygen, but they only push hard once oxygen falls below about 60 mmHg. Stretch receptors stop a breath that is too big; irritant receptors make you cough. In exercise you breathe much more, but blood oxygen and CO2 stay about normal.

Disease

  • Obstructive (asthma, COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis): air can't get out, so it gets trapped; FEV1/FVC is low. Asthma reverses with an inhaler; COPD doesn't. COPD is chronic bronchitis (a wet cough 3 months a year, 2 years running) plus emphysema (destroyed air sacs). Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency gives emphysema young, with liver disease, even without smoking. Cystic fibrosis makes thick mucus, lung infections and a high caries risk.
  • Some people with asthma (often with nasal polyps) get a severe attack from aspirin or NSAIDs such as ibuprofen; give them acetaminophen.
  • Restrictive (fibrosis, sarcoidosis, dust diseases): the lungs are small and stiff; FEV1/FVC is normal or high. Silica dust raises the risk of TB; asbestos causes mesothelioma.
  • Sarcoidosis makes granulomas without caseation, mostly in young adults and African American women, with high ACE and calcium. In the mouth: swollen parotids on both sides, enlarged gums, nodules and jaw lucencies. Swollen parotids + uveitis + facial palsy = Heerfordt syndrome.
  • "Strawberry" gums (red, grainy, bleeding) with sinus and kidney disease mean granulomatosis with polyangiitis: biopsy and refer quickly, because the kidneys can fail.
  • Lung cancer: adenocarcinoma is the most common and the one in nonsmokers; squamous and small cell sit centrally and come from smoking (small cell can make hormones such as ADH and ACTH; squamous can raise calcium). A droopy eyelid and small pupil in a smoker can mean a tumor at the top of the lung (Pancoast).
  • Tuberculosis: put off elective care and refer; urgent care needs N95 masks and isolation.
  • The most common pneumonia germ is S. pneumoniae; pneumonia caught in the hospital needs drugs that cover MRSA and Pseudomonas. Ear and sinus infections get amoxicillin, with or without clavulanate (a macrolide for penicillin allergy). Flu drugs only help if started within 48 hours; inhaled zanamivir can tighten the airways, and amantadine works only on flu A.

Drugs

Albuterol is for attacks; have it at hand at every visit. Inhaled steroids prevent attacks but can cause thrush, so patients should rinse and spit. Tiotropium and ipratropium (mainly for COPD) dry the mouth and raise caries risk. Patients with COPD sit partly upright in the chair and don't get nitrous oxide; people whose asthma is well controlled can.

Tetracyclines stain developing teeth, so not in pregnancy or before age 8. Fluoroquinolones can tear tendons and are a last choice. TB is treated with four drugs for 2 months, then two for at least 4 more; ethambutol can harm vision and rifampin turns body fluids orange.

Diphenhydramine gets into the brain, so it makes people sleepy and dries the mouth; loratadine, cetirizine and fexofenadine mostly don't. For anaphylaxis, lay the patient flat and give epinephrine 0.3 mg into a muscle right away; antihistamines only help the itch afterward.
plain.rn-filtration:
What's tested
  • What the kidneys do and where they sit
  • The parts of a nephron and the filter that keeps protein in the blood
  • How the bladder fills and empties
  • How much blood the kidneys get, how much they filter, and what speeds or slows filtering
  • Clearance and the markers inulin, creatinine and PAH
  • Where the body's water is, and what happens when you lose or gain fluid

The kidneys clean the blood, keep water, salt, potassium and acid in balance, set blood pressure, and make three hormones: erythropoietin (for red cells), active vitamin D, and renin. Active vitamin D is finished in the kidney by an enzyme called 1α-hydroxylase; its full name is 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol. The kidney makes more of it when calcium is low, PTH is high or phosphate is low; the 24,25 form is the inactive one.

Four words run through the whole course: filtration (plasma pushed out of the glomerulus into the tubule), reabsorption (taken back from the tubule into the blood), secretion (added from the blood into the tubule) and excretion (what leaves in the urine). What is excreted = what is filtered − what is reabsorbed + what is secreted.

Where they are

They sit behind the peritoneum at about T12 to L3. The right one is lower because the liver sits above it. Blood goes in through the afferent arteriole to the glomerulus and leaves through the efferent arteriole. Urine runs from the papilla to the calyces, the pelvis, the ureter and the bladder. Several nephrons empty into each collecting duct.

The filter

The glomerulus filters plasma through three layers, all negatively charged: leaky endothelium, a basement membrane, and podocyte feet. Big, negative proteins like albumin stay in the blood. Near the glomerulus, the macula densa tastes the salt in the tubule and sends out adenosine, and the JG cells release renin.

The bladder

Sympathetic nerves hold urine in (detrusor relaxed, internal sphincter closed). Parasympathetic nerves from S2–S4 empty it (detrusor contracts). The pudendal nerve keeps the external sphincter shut until you choose to go. At about 300 mL, stretch sets off the micturition reflex. The pontine micturition center in the brainstem decides whether now is a good time: if not, it holds the reflex back; if so, the pudendal nerve lets go of the external sphincter and parasympathetic nerves squeeze the bladder.

Filtering

The kidneys get about a fifth of the cardiac output and filter about 100–125 mL a minute: the course's slides say about 100 mL a minute (144 L a day) in one lecture and 180 L a day in another. About 20% of the plasma that arrives is filtered. Glomeruli filter so much because their capillaries are about 100 times leakier to water than other capillaries and their pressure stays high all the way along. As plasma is filtered, the protein left behind pulls back harder until filtering stops; faster plasma flow puts that off, so more is filtered. Squeezing either arteriole lowers the plasma flow, but they move the pressure inside the glomerulus opposite ways: squeezing the afferent arteriole lowers it and lowers filtering; squeezing the efferent arteriole (angiotensin II) raises it and keeps filtering going when blood pressure is low. A blocked ureter (a stone) or more protein in the plasma (multiple myeloma) lowers filtering without changing the plasma flow; less protein in the blood (nephrotic syndrome) raises it. Between about 80 and 200 mmHg the kidney keeps its flow steady by itself; one way is the macula densa sending adenosine to tighten the afferent arteriole. Caffeine blocks adenosine, which is one reason coffee makes you urinate.

Clearance

Clearance = urine concentration × urine flow ÷ plasma concentration. Inulin's clearance equals GFR. Creatinine is the everyday marker: when GFR halves, blood creatinine doubles. But creatinine comes from muscle, so big muscles, creatine supplements or a lot of meat push it up (and make the kidneys look worse than they are), and a vegan diet pulls it down. PAH measures renal plasma flow; divide that by (1 − hematocrit) to get renal blood flow. A substance cleared faster than inulin is secreted; slower, it's reabsorbed. Albumin (held back by the filter) and glucose (filtered, then all taken back) normally have a clearance of zero.

Body water

Water is about 60% of body weight (less in women and older adults, who carry more fat, and more in infants): 40% inside cells and 20% outside. Of the outside water, about a fifth is plasma (the course's 20%; some books say a quarter); the rest bathes the cells. A kilogram of water is a liter, so losing 2 kg overnight means losing about 2 L of water. Sodium is the main positive ion outside the cells, with chloride and then bicarbonate as the negative ones; potassium rules inside. Normal body fluid is about 275–290 mOsm. Fluid is gained or lost from the outside water first; then water moves into or out of cells until both sides have the same osmolarity. Darrow-Yannet diagrams draw this as two boxes (inside cells on the left, outside on the right): wider means more volume, taller means higher osmolarity, and the dashed line is the new state. Normal saline stays outside the cells and fills the blood vessels; half-normal saline lets some water into the cells; D5W ends up as plain water that goes everywhere. Plain water is never put into a vein, because it would burst red cells.
plain.rn-tubule:
What's tested
  • How salt, water, glucose and bicarbonate get back into the blood
  • What each part of the tubule does
  • How the kidney makes concentrated urine
  • What aldosterone and ADH do
  • Where each diuretic works

Every tubule cell has a lumen side (apical) and a blood side (basolateral). A sodium pump on the blood side keeps sodium low inside the cell, so sodium rushes in from the lumen and carries other things with it. The carriers on the lumen side spend no energy of their own: the pump's sodium gradient pays for them (secondary active transport). When you look at a drawing of a tubule cell, find the lumen side first.

Proximal tubule: the bulk reabsorber

It takes back about two-thirds of the salt and water and almost all the glucose, amino acids and bicarbonate. Water simply follows the salt. Glucose rides in with sodium on SGLT2. Those carriers can fill up: above about 200 mg/dL of blood sugar some glucose starts to spill into the urine, and by about 350 mg/dL every carrier is full (the transport maximum). The "-flozin" drugs block SGLT2 on purpose; they don't cause low blood sugar on their own and also help in heart failure, but they invite yeast infections and UTIs. Early in the tubule, sodium goes back with bicarbonate and glucose rather than chloride, so chloride builds up in the tube; later it is taken back too, partly between the cells. Sodium itself stays at the same concentration as in plasma along the whole tubule, because water follows it. When the body has extra fluid, the proximal tubule takes back less, so the extra is passed; when it is low on fluid, it takes back more. Acetazolamide works here too: you lose bicarbonate, the urine turns alkaline and potassium falls. Mannitol is given into a vein and holds water in the tube.

Loop of Henle: building the salty medulla

Going down, the tube lets water out (and urea in) but not salt, so the fluid gets more concentrated. Going up, it lets salt out but not water. The thick part pumps salt out with the NKCC2 carrier and makes the fluid dilute. Furosemide blocks NKCC2; the same kind of carrier in the ear and the salivary glands explains ringing ears and a dry mouth. It is used for swelling (edema) in heart failure and to bring down a high calcium or potassium, and it can raise uric acid. The loop and the slow blood flow of the vasa recta keep the deep medulla very salty: about 1,200 with ADH and about 600 without it, half of it salt and half urea.

Distal tubule

It takes back a little more salt through NCC, the carrier thiazides block. Thiazides also make the kidney keep calcium.

Collecting duct: the fine tuning

Several nephrons empty into each collecting duct, and hormones fine-tune it. Principal cells take in sodium through ENaC and put potassium out into the urine. Aldosterone turns this up. ADH (through V2 receptors) puts water channels (aquaporin-2) into these cells so water can leave the urine and the urine gets concentrated. The duct takes back only 4–5% of the filtered sodium, but anywhere from about 5% of the filtered water (after a lot of drinking) to more than 24% (in dehydration). Intercalated cells handle acid: the alpha type pumps out acid, the beta type pumps out bicarbonate.

Amiloride blocks ENaC and spironolactone blocks aldosterone. Both keep potassium in the body, so they can raise it too high. Because the duct handles so little sodium, they are weak diuretics and are mostly given with a stronger one.
plain.rn-balance:
What's tested
  • How ADH and thirst keep the blood's water right, and what goes wrong (SIADH, diabetes insipidus)
  • How the body senses and fixes its volume with salt
  • Potassium: what pushes it into and out of cells, and how the kidney gets rid of it
  • Calcium, phosphate and magnesium, and the hormones PTH, vitamin D and FGF23
  • Acids and bases: the four disorders and how the body makes up for each

Water

Blood sodium tells you about water. Low sodium (under 135) means too much water; high (over 145) means too little. ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. Sensors in the brain (the OVLT and subfornical organ) notice the blood getting salty; ADH comes first, then thirst, through the brain's thirst areas. ADH puts water channels in the collecting duct (V2 receptors) and squeezes arterioles (V1 receptors). A big drop in blood volume also releases ADH, and volume wins over salt. Nausea, pain and drugs like morphine and ecstasy turn ADH on; alcohol turns it off.

Too much ADH (SIADH, often from lung cancer) gives low sodium; restrict fluids, or in a sudden case give furosemide and 3% saline. Low sodium that comes on fast from drinking a lot of water (with ecstasy, or in marathon runners) swells the brain and can cause seizures; it needs 3% saline right away. No ADH (central diabetes insipidus) gives lots of dilute urine; give desmopressin. Kidneys that ignore ADH (nephrogenic, usually from lithium) don't respond to desmopressin; thiazides help.

Salt and volume

Total sodium sets how full the blood vessels are. When volume is low, the pressure sensors make the kidney's sympathetic nerves fire, and renin rises (it is released for low pressure in the arteriole entering the glomerulus, for sympathetic signals, and when little salt reaches the macula densa); angiotensin II and aldosterone rise, and the kidney keeps salt and water. Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex fine-tunes salt in the collecting duct to match what you eat. When the atria are stretched, they release ANP, which makes the kidney dump salt.

In heart failure the extra fluid sits in the tissues, where the pressure sensors can't feel it. The blood vessels seem underfilled, so the kidney keeps holding salt and the swelling gets worse.

Potassium

Almost all potassium is inside cells; normal blood level is 3.5–5.0. Insulin, epinephrine's β2 effect, aldosterone and alkalosis push it into cells; acidosis, β-blockers, epinephrine's α effect, low insulin and broken cells let it out. Too much aldosterone lowers potassium; too little (Addison disease) raises it. The collecting duct decides how much leaves in urine: aldosterone and diuretics make you lose more; spironolactone, kidney failure and acidosis make you keep more. Aldosterone works mostly by pulling sodium in, which pushes potassium out. In kidney disease, NSAIDs lower renin and aldosterone and can push potassium too high, so these patients eat less potassium and avoid NSAIDs.

Calcium, phosphate, magnesium

Most calcium is taken back early in the tubule; the distal tubule does the fine tuning under PTH. Loop diuretics make you lose calcium and magnesium, because the TAL's voltage that pulls them back is lost; thiazides make you keep calcium (sometimes too much). Magnesium is mostly taken back in the thick ascending limb. PTH raises blood calcium and makes the kidney dump phosphate. Active vitamin D, made in the kidney, mainly pulls calcium in from the gut. FGF23 from bone makes the kidney dump phosphate and lowers active vitamin D and PTH.

Acid and base

The lungs control CO2; the kidneys control bicarbonate; the pH follows the balance of the two. To tell which one started it, look at the arrows: if CO2 and bicarbonate move the opposite way to the pH, it's respiratory; the same way, it's metabolic. The kidney takes back filtered bicarbonate and makes new bicarbonate each time it gets rid of acid as ammonium or on phosphate. Metabolic acidosis (low bicarbonate, as in diabetic ketoacidosis) → fast breathing. Metabolic alkalosis (vomiting) → slow breathing; it lasts while the patient is dehydrated, because the volume-saving hormones make the kidney keep bicarbonate. Diarrhea loses bicarbonate and potassium: acidosis with low potassium. Respiratory acidosis (too little breathing, as with too much opioid or sedation, or lung disease) or alkalosis (too much, as in an anxious patient or at altitude) → the kidneys adjust over days; the lungs can't compensate for a problem they caused.
plain.rn-disease:
What's tested
  • What chronic kidney disease is, its causes and its five stages
  • Azotemia versus uremia
  • What failing kidneys do to the blood, bones, mouth and bleeding
  • Nephritic versus nephrotic kidney disease and their classic examples
  • Infections, stones, cysts and tumors of the kidney

CKD

Chronic kidney disease means the kidneys have been damaged or underperforming for at least 3 months. Diabetes is the top cause, then high blood pressure. Chronic glomerulonephritis and polycystic kidneys can also end in kidney failure. Doctors stage it by eGFR: stage 1 is 90 or more (with other signs of damage), 2 is 60–89, 3 is 30–59, 4 is 15–29, and 5 is under 15, which means dialysis or a transplant. A urine albumin test can show damage early. The kidneys keep up until about half the nephrons are gone. To slow it down: control sugar and blood pressure, eat less protein and salt, and take an ACE inhibitor or ARB, an SGLT2 inhibitor, finerenone or semaglutide.

Azotemia and uremia

Azotemia is a lab result: high BUN and creatinine. Uremia is the sick patient: nauseated, vomiting, tired, with muscle cramps, and with problems in almost every part of the body; the mouth and eye signs are the ones to know. It comes from wastes building up, some hormones running high, and the kidney's own hormones (erythropoietin, vitamin D) going missing.

What CKD does

Anemia (no erythropoietin), high blood pressure, high potassium, acid buildup and heart disease. Diabetics on insulin have more low-sugar spells, because the kidney clears less insulin. Albumin lost in the urine lets fluid leak out of the vessels, so the legs swell. Phosphate builds up and active vitamin D falls, so calcium drops and the parathyroids work overtime; the bones, jaws included, lose mineral (renal osteodystrophy). Platelets work poorly, so patients bleed more. In the mouth: dry mouth, odd taste, ammonia breath, pale gums, bruises and gum disease. In the eyes: retinopathy, glaucoma, cataracts and macular degeneration.

Glomerular disease

Nephritic means an inflamed filter: blood in the urine, high blood pressure, little urine. Examples: post-strep glomerulonephritis in kids a few weeks after strep, IgA nephropathy (the most common worldwide, blood in the urine right after a cold), and rapidly progressive disease with crescents, which can ruin the kidneys in weeks. In Goodpasture syndrome the same antibody attacks the lungs, so patients cough up blood. Nephrotic means a leaky filter: lots of protein in the urine, low albumin, swelling and high cholesterol. Minimal change disease is the common one in children; membranous in adults. FSGS, linked to HIV and heroin, responds poorly to steroids.

Where the immune deposits sit in the filter names the disease: on the podocyte side of the basement membrane (subepithelial) in membranous disease (spikes) and post-strep disease (humps); on the blood side (subendothelial) in MPGN type I; IgA in the central support cells (the mesangium) in IgA nephropathy; and a smooth line of antibody along the membrane in anti-GBM disease. Minimal change disease has no deposits, only flattened podocyte feet.

Other problems

Kidney infections (pyelonephritis) are usually E. coli, with fever and flank pain. Most stones are calcium; big staghorn stones are struvite, from a urine infection with bacteria such as Proteus. Acute tubular necrosis means the tubule cells die, usually after a long drop in blood pressure or a toxin; interstitial nephritis is inflammation around the tubules from drugs or infection. A blocked ureter swells the kidney (hydronephrosis). Adult polycystic kidney disease is dominant and comes with brain aneurysms. Years of dialysis can also fill the kidneys with cysts, and cancer can grow in them. Clear cell carcinoma is the common adult kidney cancer (smoking and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome raise the risk); Wilms tumor is the childhood one, and about 90% of children survive it.
plain.rn-dental:
What's tested
  • The diuretic families, where they act and their side effects
  • How to treat a patient on dialysis safely, and patients with diabetic, hypertensive or polycystic kidney disease or a sudden kidney injury
  • Which drugs to avoid, adjust or use freely when the kidneys are failing
  • What kidney failure looks like in the mouth and on X-rays, and the transplant patient

Diuretics

Loop diuretics like furosemide block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. They are the strongest, used for fluid overload and pulmonary edema. They make you lose potassium, magnesium and sodium, push calcium into the urine and can damage hearing. They still lower blood pressure when the kidneys are failing, where thiazides stop working. Thiazides like hydrochlorothiazide block NCC in the distal tubule. They are first-line for high blood pressure; they lose potassium, lower sodium more often than any other diuretic, keep calcium (which lowers fracture risk), and raise sugar, lipids and uric acid. Spironolactone and amiloride spare potassium, so they can push it too high; spironolactone can cause breast growth and impotence in men and irregular periods in women. Acetazolamide causes a mild acidosis and is avoided with a sulfonamide allergy; mannitol pulls water into the urine and out of a swollen brain or eye. SGLT2 inhibitors (the flozins) send sugar into the urine; they help diabetes, heart failure and kidney disease but bring genital yeast infections and UTIs.

Patients on diuretics get dizzy when they stand up fast and often have a dry mouth. Plan bathroom breaks, and expect muscle cramps (a mouth prop helps the jaw). NSAIDs weaken diuretics and blood pressure drugs, and diuretics and NSAIDs both raise lithium levels.

The dialysis patient

Talk to the kidney doctor first, and ask the patient which days they dialyze and which arm has the fistula. Hemodialysis is done about three times a week through a fistula in the arm, using heparin. Book dental work for the day after dialysis, when the heparin has worn off and the patient feels best. Never put a blood pressure cuff or needle on the fistula arm. These patients bleed more because their platelets don't work well, so plan good local hemostasis. They have more hepatitis B and C.

Diabetic kidney disease, the most common kind, brings gum disease, infections and slow healing; check blood sugar control. With high blood pressure or polycystic kidneys, keep blood pressure steady and go easy on epinephrine. Lupus or arthritis patients may be on steroids and need extra for surgery. With a sudden (acute) kidney injury, give no NSAIDs, use lower doses, ease the pain and put off elective work until the kidneys recover.

Drugs

Drugs the kidney clears build up, so use smaller doses or space them out. Avoid NSAIDs (no ibuprofen or naproxen), tetracycline and meperidine; avoid ketoconazole and take care with fluconazole. Space out amoxicillin, penicillin and cephalexin, and keep opioids such as codeine, hydrocodone and tramadol at the lowest dose. Lidocaine and most local anesthetics, clindamycin, azithromycin, metronidazole, doxycycline and acetaminophen are generally fine; use bupivacaine and epinephrine with care. Give dialyzable drugs after the session.

In the mouth

Ammonia breath, dry mouth, odd taste, pale gums, bruises, gum disease, yeast infections and uremic stomatitis: usually a red, sore mouth and tongue, sometimes with white sores; sips of water and soothing rinses help. On X-rays the jaw can lose its lamina dura, look like ground glass and show brown tumors, all from overactive parathyroids; the weakened jaw can break during an extraction. After a transplant, patients are immunosuppressed and get more oral cancer, so screen them at every visit; cyclosporine grows the gums, and erythromycin or clarithromycin can raise its blood level.
plain.he-axes:
What's tested
  • How hormones signal and how the pituitary is controlled
  • Growth hormone and acromegaly
  • Pituitary tumors, diabetes insipidus and SIADH
  • The adrenal gland: Cushing, Addison, Conn
  • Steroid drugs and the adrenal crisis

The big picture

The hypothalamus tells the pituitary what to do, and the pituitary tells the other glands. When a gland makes enough hormone, that hormone turns the hypothalamus and pituitary down (negative feedback). So if the gland itself is broken, its hormone is low and the pituitary hormone is high (they move opposite ways). If the pituitary is broken, both are low.

The front (anterior) pituitary makes GH, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, FSH and LH. The back (posterior) pituitary only stores ADH and oxytocin, which nerve cells in the hypothalamus make. Dopamine keeps prolactin down.

Growth hormone

GH comes out in bursts, mostly in deep sleep. It works through IGF-1 from the liver to make bones grow. It also raises blood sugar and breaks down fat. Too much in a child makes a giant; too much in an adult is acromegaly: a jaw that keeps growing into an underbite, spaces between the teeth, a big tongue. The test that proves it: GH does not drop after drinking glucose.

Pituitary problems

A big pituitary tumor squeezes the crossing optic nerves, so people lose the outer half of vision in both eyes. The most common hormone-making tumor makes prolactin (no periods, milky discharge). No ADH, or kidneys that ignore it, means lots of watery urine and high blood sodium (diabetes insipidus). Too much ADH holds water and drops sodium (SIADH), often from small cell lung cancer.

The adrenal gland

The outer layers make salt (aldosterone), sugar (cortisol) and sex (androgen) hormones; the center makes epinephrine. Too much cortisol (Cushing, most often from steroid pills): round face, hump, high sugar, thin skin, slow healing. Too little (Addison): tired, low blood pressure, and dark patches in the mouth, because ACTH is high. Too much aldosterone (Conn): high blood pressure and low potassium.

Steroid drugs

Prednisone and similar drugs calm inflammation but shut down the body's own cortisol. That is why you taper them, and why a patient on them can crash under stress. Side effects: thrush, slow healing, weak bones, high sugar, hidden infections. If a steroid patient becomes pale, confused and very hypotensive in the chair, call 911 and give 100 mg hydrocortisone.
plain.he-thyroid:
What's tested
  • How the thyroid makes its hormone and which lab moves which way
  • Too much vs too little thyroid hormone, and the drugs for each
  • Thyroid cancers
  • PTH, vitamin D and calcitonin, and what goes wrong

The thyroid

The thyroid grabs iodine, sticks it onto a protein in its colloid, and stores the hormone there. It mostly releases T4, which the body turns into the active T3. TSH from the pituitary pushes the thyroid; thyroid hormone pushes TSH back down. So a sick thyroid shows TSH and T4 moving opposite ways.

Too much (Graves disease, an antibody that acts like TSH): thin, hot, shaky, fast heart, bulging eyes; TSH low, T4 high. Children's teeth come in early. Don't load an uncontrolled patient with epinephrine, and know thyroid storm: high fever, very fast pulse, confusion. Call 911.

Too little (Hashimoto, the immune system destroying the gland): tired, cold, slow heart, weight gain; TSH high, T4 low. A big tongue, late teeth, slow healing. Babies born without enough hormone develop cretinism.

The drugs

Levothyroxine (T4) is the replacement: on an empty stomach, morning, away from calcium and iron; it takes weeks to settle, and if TSH stays high the dose goes up. For an overactive gland, methimazole, except early in pregnancy, when propylthiouracil is used. Watch for fever, sore throat and mouth ulcers on these drugs: white cells may have crashed. Radioactive iodine destroys the gland (never in pregnancy). Beta-blockers calm the shaking. Amiodarone is full of iodine and can push the thyroid either way.

Cancer

Papillary is the most common and the gentlest, spreading to neck nodes. Follicular invades vessels and spreads by blood. Medullary comes from C cells, makes calcitonin and runs in MEN 2 families. Anaplastic is fast and deadly.

Calcium

PTH raises calcium: it frees it from bone, keeps it in the kidney, throws out phosphate, and activates vitamin D so the gut absorbs more. Calcitonin lowers calcium, a little. Too much PTH, usually one benign tumor: high calcium, kidney stones, and on dental X-rays the lamina dura disappears and "brown tumors" appear. Too little PTH, often after thyroid surgery: low calcium, twitching and cramps. Kidney failure lowers active vitamin D, so PTH climbs.
plain.he-diabetes:
What's tested
  • What the islet cells make and how insulin gets released
  • Type 1 vs type 2 and the numbers that diagnose them
  • What each diabetes drug does and which ones cause lows
  • Diabetes in the mouth and a low blood sugar in the chair

Insulin and glucagon

Beta cells make insulin, which moves sugar into muscle and fat and stores it. Alpha cells make glucagon, which makes the liver release sugar. Somatostatin from delta cells slows both. When blood sugar rises, it enters the beta cell, makes more ATP, closes a potassium channel, and the cell releases insulin. Sulfonylurea pills close that same channel. C-peptide is made along with your own insulin, so a low C-peptide means your pancreas isn't making much.

The two types

Type 1: the immune system destroys the beta cells, usually in a young, thin person, who needs insulin to live and can go into ketoacidosis. Type 2: the body stops responding well to insulin, usually in an older, heavier person; it starts with lifestyle and metformin. Diabetes is diagnosed by an HbA1c of 6.5% or more, or a fasting sugar of 126 or more. HbA1c shows the average of the last 2–3 months: under 7 is good control; above 7 is poor, with more infections, gum disease and failed implants.

The drugs

Metformin is first: it stops the liver making sugar, doesn't cause lows, but upsets the stomach and is stopped in severe kidney disease. Insulin, sulfonylureas and meglitinides can cause lows and weight gain. GLP-1 drugs (semaglutide) cause weight loss. DPP-4 drugs (gliptins) are mild pills. SGLT2 drugs (gliflozins) dump sugar in the urine, which brings yeast and urinary infections. Pioglitazone causes fluid retention and can worsen heart failure.

In the chair

Diabetes worsens gum disease, and gum disease worsens diabetes. Expect dry mouth, thrush and slow healing. Book mornings and make sure the patient ate. A low blood sugar looks like sweating, shaking, a fast heart and confusion. If awake, give sugar by mouth (juice, glucose gel); if unconscious, give glucagon and call 911.
plain.he-repro:
What's tested
  • Which testicular and ovarian cells answer to FSH and LH
  • The phases of the cycle and what triggers ovulation
  • The hormones of pregnancy and nursing
  • The sex hormone drugs and their big side effects
  • The main tumors and infections of the reproductive tract

Testes and ovaries

In the testis, FSH works on Sertoli cells, which feed developing sperm and make inhibin; LH works on Leydig cells, which make testosterone. The ovary copies this: LH tells theca cells to make androgen, and FSH tells granulosa cells to turn it into estrogen. Someone injecting testosterone shuts off his own LH and FSH, so his testes shrink and his sperm count drops.

The cycle

In the first half, estrogen grows the uterine lining. When estrogen stays high long enough, it flips to triggering a burst of LH, and ovulation follows. In the second half the corpus luteum makes progesterone to ready the lining. No pregnancy: progesterone falls and the lining sheds. After menopause there are no follicles, so estrogen is low and FSH and LH are high.

Pregnancy and nursing

The early embryo makes hCG, which keeps the corpus luteum making progesterone until the placenta takes over. That's what a pregnancy test detects. The placenta also makes hPL, which fights insulin (gestational diabetes). Oxytocin drives labor. After birth, prolactin makes milk and oxytocin squeezes it out.

The drugs

Birth control pills stop the LH surge. Estrogen drugs, tamoxifen and raloxifene raise the risk of blood clots. Tamoxifen blocks estrogen in the breast but acts like it in the uterus. Aromatase inhibitors stop estrogen being made. Leuprolide, given nonstop, shuts the pituitary down, which lowers testosterone in prostate cancer. Finasteride blocks DHT for an enlarged prostate. Testosterone can harm the liver.

Disease

An undescended testis needs surgery early, but its cancer risk stays. Testicular cancer hits young men and is very curable; seminoma is the most common. BPH grows around the urethra and blocks urine; prostate cancer grows at the edge and spreads to bone. HPV 16 and 18 cause cervical cancer at the transformation zone; 6 and 11 cause warts. In the mouth, pregnancy brings swollen gums and pyogenic granulomas.
plain.he-heme:
What's tested
  • The blood cells and what each does
  • How the immune system is organized and where its cells mature
  • Anemias and what they do to the tongue
  • The four leukemias and the main lymphomas
  • What a dentist should notice and do

Blood cells

Red cells carry oxygen; platelets start clots; white cells fight infection. Of the white cells, neutrophils are the most common and go after bacteria first; lymphocytes are B, T and NK cells; monocytes become macrophages; eosinophils fight parasites and allergy; basophils carry histamine.

Immune organs

B cells mature in the bone marrow and T cells in the thymus: those two are the primary organs. Lymph nodes, the spleen and the tonsils are secondary organs, where the cells meet germs. In the spleen, T cells wrap around the small arteries (the PALS). NK cells kill cells that hide their MHC I "ID badge."

Anemias

Low iron (small red cells) and low B12 or folate (big red cells) both make the tongue smooth, red and sore, with cracked mouth corners. B12 lack also causes numbness. Sickle cell disease makes red cells sickle and block vessels; keep visits short and the patient warm, hydrated and oxygenated.

Leukemias

Acute leukemias are full of immature blasts and move fast; chronic ones have more mature cells and move slowly. AML is the adult acute one (Auer rods); ALL is the child's. CML has the Philadelphia chromosome and is treated with imatinib. CLL is the old person's slow leukemia with smudge cells. Leukemia crowds out normal marrow: anemia, bleeding gums and infections, and the gums can swell with leukemic cells.

Lymphomas

Hodgkin lymphoma has Reed-Sternberg cells, starts in central nodes and spreads in order; it is very curable. Non-Hodgkin lymphomas are mostly B-cell, scattered, and often outside nodes. Burkitt grows very fast and can start in a child's jaw. MALT lymphoma grows from long-standing inflammation, such as Sjögren in the salivary glands. Myeloma punches holes in bone, jaws included.

For the dentist

Swollen, bleeding gums, tiny red spots and pale tissue need a blood count and a referral. Check counts before surgery on a patient with leukemia.
plain.mg-giphys:
What's tested
  • The GI hormones: who makes them, what releases them, what they do
  • How saliva and stomach acid are made and controlled
  • How the gut moves, and how the pancreas and bile digest food
  • Where each nutrient is absorbed, the kinds of diarrhea, and what vomiting and diarrhea do to the blood's acid-base balance
  • What the liver makes, stores and clears

The messengers

Gastrin (stomach G cells) turns acid up; protein and stretch release it, and acid shuts it off through somatostatin. CCK (I cells) answers fat and protein: it squeezes the gallbladder, calls for pancreatic enzymes and slows the stomach. Secretin (S cells) answers acid in the duodenum by calling for bicarbonate. GIP and GLP-1 (both answer sugar, protein and fat) tell the pancreas to release insulin; GLP-1 also slows the stomach and curbs appetite, which is how semaglutide (Ozempic, Wegovy) works, and tirzepatide (Mounjaro, Zepbound) copies both hormones. Motilin starts the "housekeeper" waves between meals. Ghrelin makes you hungry. Histamine and somatostatin act on neighbors: somatostatin is the brake that acid turns on and the vagus (ACh) turns off. VIP and NO relax muscle; substance P contracts it; enkephalins slow it down. Digestion runs in four phases: head (seeing, smelling, tasting and chewing, through the vagus), stomach, small intestine and colon.

Saliva and acid

The parotid is the biggest gland, but the submandibular makes most resting saliva. Saliva starts out like plasma; the ducts pull out salt but not water, so it ends up watery (hypotonic). Only nerves control it (no hormones), and both the parasympathetic (lots of watery saliva) and sympathetic (a little protein-rich saliva) nerves turn it on. In Sjögren syndrome the immune system destroys the glands: dry mouth, caries and dry eyes. In the stomach, parietal cells pump acid with the H+/K+ pump and make intrinsic factor for B12. ACh, gastrin and histamine turn the pump on; histamine boosts the other two. PPIs (omeprazole) block the pump itself; H2 blockers (famotidine) block histamine. The faster the stomach secretes, the more its juice is pure acid, strong enough to erode teeth with repeated vomiting. Chief cells make pepsinogen, which acid turns into pepsin. Mucus and bicarbonate, kept up by prostaglandins, protect the lining, which is why NSAIDs hurt the stomach. The vagus runs the "thinking about food" phase.

Movement

Pacemaker cells (Cajal) set slow waves; muscle contracts only when a wave passes threshold and spikes ride on it. The stomach relaxes to take in a meal, grinds it against a nearly closed pylorus and lets a little out with each wave. Segmentation squeezes the middle of a bolus and mixes; peristalsis squeezes behind it, relaxes ahead and pushes. Liquids leave the stomach fastest and fat slowest (CCK); acid, protein pieces and too-strong or too-weak chyme in the duodenum slow it too. Between meals, starting about 3 hours after eating, motilin's migrating waves clear out bacteria; eating stops them. The colon is slow (30–40 hours): its haustra mix and store, and mass movements 1–3 times a day fill the rectum. Eating triggers colonic mass movements (gastrocolic reflex) and opens the ileocecal valve (gastroileal reflex); a stretched cecum closes it (coloileal reflex). Rectal stretch relaxes the internal sphincter by reflex; you control the external one. If the LES can't relax (its VIP/NO nerves are lost), that's achalasia; in GERD the LES tone is usually normal, but it relaxes for moments and lets acid up. In Hirschsprung disease the nerves never reached the end of the colon.

Digestion

The pancreas makes enzymes (CCK) and bicarbonate (secretin). Unlike saliva, its juice stays as strong as plasma, and both nerves and hormones control it. Enteropeptidase switches on trypsin, and trypsin switches on the other proteases and colipase; amylase and lipase come out already active. Only single sugars are absorbed. Protein goes in as amino acids (with sodium) or as pieces two or three long (with H+). Fat travels in micelles made with bile salts; long fatty acids leave the gut cell as chylomicrons into lymph, skipping the liver, while short ones go straight into portal blood. Only the small intestine has villi; the colon has none. Bile salts are recycled from the terminal ileum, which is also where B12 is absorbed; iron and calcium go in at the duodenum. Gut bacteria turn the liver's bile acids into secondary ones. Bilirubin from old red cells is made water-soluble (conjugated) by the liver and leaves in bile; jaundice comes from too much red cell breakdown, a sick liver, or a blocked duct.

Diarrhea

Secretory diarrhea (cholera) keeps going even when fasting: the toxin opens chloride channels. Osmotic diarrhea (lactose intolerance) stops when you stop eating the cause. Sugar-and-salt drinks work because the sodium-glucose carrier still works. Inflammation (Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis) and fast transit cause diarrhea too. Vomiting loses acid, chloride and potassium, so the blood turns alkaline; diarrhea loses bicarbonate, so it turns acidic. Both can lower potassium.

The liver

All blood from the gut goes through the liver first. It makes albumin and most clotting factors (not factor VIII), so a failing liver means swelling and bleeding (a high INR). It stores sugar as glycogen and releases it between meals, makes new glucose, and stores vitamins A, D and B12 (B12 for years). Kupffer cells eat gut bacteria. The cells near the incoming blood (zone 1) make glucose and urea; the cells by the central vein (zone 3) get the least oxygen, clear drugs with CYP450 and mop up leftover ammonia, so they die first in shock or an acetaminophen overdose. Glutathione neutralizes acetaminophen's toxic product, NAPQI; N-acetylcysteine refills it and works best within 8–10 hours. Alcohol is broken down by alcohol dehydrogenase and, at high levels, by CYP2E1; stellate cells turn a damaged liver to scar (cirrhosis). The liver also sends fat out as VLDL, which becomes LDL; HDL brings cholesterol back to the liver, and bile is its only way out of the body.
plain.mg-gianat:
What's tested
  • Which artery feeds each part of the gut, and where gut pain is felt
  • Portal hypertension's shortcut veins, the pectinate line, the abdominal wall and hernias
  • How to tell each part of the gut apart under the microscope, plus the mouth, salivary glands, liver and pancreas

Blood supply and pain

Celiac trunk: stomach to the middle of the duodenum (pain in the upper belly). SMA: the rest of the small bowel to two-thirds of the way across the transverse colon (pain at the navel). IMA: the rest of the colon down to the pectinate line (pain low in the belly). The SMA's branches are the middle colic, right colic and ileocolic, which gives the appendix its artery; the IMA's are the left colic, the sigmoid arteries and the superior rectal. Only the pancreaticoduodenal arteries, around the head of the pancreas, link the celiac trunk to the SMA; the marginal artery along the colon links the SMA to the IMA. The splenic flexure, where the SMA's and IMA's areas meet, has the weakest blood supply, so it is the first part of the colon to go ischemic. Organ pain is vague until the inflamed organ touches the body-wall lining, which is why appendicitis moves from the navel to McBurney point in the right lower belly (two-thirds of the way from the navel to the front point of the hip bone).
