The appendix is usually blocked by swollen lymphoid tissue in young people and by a hard lump of stool in older ones. A bleeding ulcer on the back of the duodenum hits the gastroduodenal artery.

Bleeding above the ligament of Treitz (where the duodenum meets the jejunum) usually shows as vomited blood; below it, as blood in the stool. The SMA and the aorta can pinch the third part of the duodenum between them (SMA syndrome), or the left renal vein (nutcracker syndrome: blood in the urine and, in men, a left varicocele that shrinks lying down). In intussusception the bowel telescopes into the next stretch, usually the ileum into the colon; it is the main cause of blocked bowel from 3 months to 6 years and can cut off the blood supply. Diverticula are pouches of the lining, mostly in the sigmoid colon of older people, at the weak spots where arteries pass through the wall.

Portal hypertension and the wall

Blood from the gut, spleen and pancreas goes to the liver in the portal vein, which lies in front of the IVC (on a scan, the front one of the two big veins is the portal vein). Normally almost no blood crosses the links between the portal veins and the body's other veins. When the liver is scarred, portal pressure rises and blood detours through them: esophageal varices (left gastric to azygos), caput medusae (around the navel) and rectal varices (the slides call them internal hemorrhoids). Above the pectinate line the anal canal is painless and drains to the liver; below it, it hurts and drains to the body's veins. Hernia rule: "MDs don't LIe": medial to the inferior epigastric vessels is direct, lateral is indirect (through the deep ring, the common kind). Below the arcuate line, only transversalis fascia lies behind the rectus. The umbilicus is T10. Diaphragm holes: IVC T8, esophagus T10, aorta T12.

Under the microscope

The gut wall has four layers: mucosa, submucosa, the muscle coat and serosa (or adventitia where the gut is fixed). Two nerve nets run in it: the submucosal (Meissner) plexus runs the lining's secretion and blood flow, and the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus, between the two muscle layers, runs peristalsis. Meissner is for the mucosa, Auerbach for action.

Esophagus: flat, non-keratinized lining, a thick muscularis mucosae and mucous glands in the submucosa; skeletal muscle on top, smooth at the bottom. Stomach: pits and glands, no villi; the pits are deepest in the pylorus. Parietal cells (pink, full of mitochondria) make acid; chief cells (purple, full of rough ER, at the bottom of the glands) make pepsinogen. Duodenum: Brunner glands. Jejunum: tallest folds. Ileum: Peyer patches. Colon: no villi, lots of goblet cells. A fold (plica) has submucosa inside it; a villus has only mucosa, with a lymph vessel (lacteal) that takes up fat as chylomicrons. Paneth cells at the bottom of the crypts make lysozyme and defensins. The appendix looks like colon wrapped in a ring of lymphoid nodules. The anal canal's lining goes from column-shaped cells to layered flat cells, then skin; its inner sphincter is smooth muscle you don't control, the outer one skeletal muscle you do.

Mouth: filiform papillae have no taste buds; fungiform papillae have them on top, and the circumvallate (7–12 big ones in a V at the back) and foliate (a few on the sides) have them in their side walls, with serous von Ebner glands rinsing the circumvallate trench. The red part of the lip has thin epithelium with blood vessels close to the surface and no glands. Saliva runs acinus → intercalated duct → striated duct → excretory duct; the ducts take back salt and let little water follow, so saliva ends up hypotonic. Myoepithelial cells squeeze the acini. Parotid: the biggest, all serous, about 30% of saliva and most of the amylase. Submandibular: mixed, mostly serous, about 60%, with the longest striated ducts. Sublingual: the smallest, mostly mucous, about 5%.

Liver, gallbladder and pancreas

Blood runs from the portal triad through the sinusoids to the central vein. Bile runs the other way, in tiny channels between hepatocytes (canaliculi), to the bile ducts in the triad. Lymph forms in the space of Disse, between the sinusoid wall and the hepatocytes, and also flows toward the triad. The three stay apart. Zone 1 sits by the incoming blood and gets the most oxygen; zone 3, by the central vein, gets the least and is damaged first by low blood flow and acetaminophen. Kupffer cells are the liver's macrophages; Ito cells store vitamin A and make scar. The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile and squeezes it out when CCK arrives; its wall has folds but no villi, no muscularis mucosae and no submucosa.

Pancreas: dark acini that make enzymes, with pale islets among them. Pale centroacinar cells in the middle of the acini start its ducts, and it has no striated ducts and no myoepithelial cells: that is how to tell it from a salivary gland.
plain.mg-gipath:
What's tested
  • Reflux and Barrett esophagus, ulcers and H. pylori, gastritis and stomach cancer; celiac, Crohn and ulcerative colitis; C. diff, appendicitis and colon cancer
  • Liver tests, the hepatitis viruses and hepatitis B blood tests, alcohol, fatty and autoimmune liver disease, iron and copper overload, acetaminophen, liver failure, liver tumors and gallstones
  • Treating a patient with liver disease safely; the main GI drugs and their side effects

Gut diseases

Reflux is the most common cause of an inflamed esophagus. In the mouth it erodes the palate side of the upper teeth and cups the back teeth; refer the patient, give fluoride and advise on diet and when to brush. Over years it can turn the lower esophagus into Barrett lining (intestine-type cells with goblet cells), which raises the risk of adenocarcinoma 30 to 100 times; that cancer is now the most common esophageal cancer in the US. Squamous cell cancer of the esophagus comes from smoking and alcohol. Eosinophilic esophagitis looks like reflux, but acid drugs don't help and food gets stuck. Swollen veins at the bottom of the esophagus (varices) come from a scarred liver and can bleed to death.

H. pylori survives acid by making ammonia with urease. It is the most common cause of long-lasting stomach inflammation, is found in about 4 in 10 US ulcer patients, and raises the risk of stomach cancer and MALT lymphoma. The first-line cure is four drugs: a PPI, bismuth, metronidazole and tetracycline. NSAIDs cause ulcers by removing the prostaglandins that hold down acid and keep up the protective mucus. Autoimmune gastritis destroys the cells that make intrinsic factor, so B12 can't be absorbed. Stomach cancer is found late; one kind stiffens the whole stomach (a "leather bottle").

Celiac disease flattens the small intestine's villi; it causes greasy diarrhea, anemia, mouth ulcers, enamel defects, late tooth eruption and a sore tongue. Poor absorption shows in the mouth: a smooth, sore tongue and cracked mouth corners (iron, B12, folate). Crohn disease can hit anywhere from mouth to anus, goes through the whole wall and skips around; in the mouth it causes cobblestoning, swelling and ulcers, sometimes before any gut symptoms. Ulcerative colitis starts in the rectum, stays in the lining of the colon and is continuous. Both raise colon cancer risk, and their drugs lower resistance to infection and slow healing.

C. diff colitis follows antibiotics such as clindamycin; it is treated with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin. Appendicitis starts as pain around the navel that moves to the lower right. Colon cancer is the second biggest cancer killer in the US, and screening starts at 45. On the left side it blocks the bowel; on the right side it bleeds slowly and causes iron-deficiency anemia. FAP always turns into cancer without surgery; jaw osteomas plus extra teeth can mean Gardner syndrome, a form of FAP.

Liver

The liver can lose most of its function before anyone notices, so the mouth and eyes may give the first clue. Liver tests come in three groups: how well the liver makes things (albumin, PT/INR), whether its cells are leaking (AST, ALT) and whether bile is flowing (alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin). Hepatitis that lasts more than 6 months is chronic, and its scarring can end in cirrhosis.

Hepatitis A and E come from food and water and clear up; E can be deadly in pregnancy. B and C come from blood and can last for years, leading to cirrhosis and liver cancer. B has a vaccine; C doesn't but can be cured. D infects only people who already have B. In hepatitis B blood tests, the surface antigen means infected, the surface antibody means immune, and the core antibody means the virus itself was there (IgM: recently); a vaccinated person has only the surface antibody.

Alcohol is the most common cause of liver disease in the US; fatty liver without alcohol goes with obesity and diabetes; autoimmune hepatitis mostly affects women and responds to steroids. Hemochromatosis piles up iron (bronze skin, diabetes); Wilson disease piles up copper in the liver, brain and eyes of young people; alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency damages the liver and the lungs. Acetaminophen overdose is the top cause of sudden liver failure and kills the cells around the central vein; N-acetylcysteine is the antidote, best in the first 8–10 hours.

A failing liver makes fewer clotting factors and less albumin, lets ammonia build up (confusion) and gives jaundice, a musty breath, red palms and spider veins. High pressure in the portal vein causes varices, fluid in the belly and a big spleen that traps platelets. Most liver tumors have spread from elsewhere; the main one that starts there, hepatocellular carcinoma, grows in scarred livers. Most gallstones are cholesterol, and gallbladder pain can spread to the right shoulder.

In the dental chair

Look for yellow mucosa and eyes, bleeding gums, bruises and petechiae, a smooth tongue, dry mouth and a musty breath; oral lichen planus is a reason to ask about hepatitis C. Before surgery on a patient with cirrhosis, talk to the physician and check the INR and platelets. The liver clears local anesthetics, pain relievers, sedatives and some antibiotics and antifungals, so use lower doses and keep local anesthetic well under its maximum; avoid erythromycin, clindamycin and tetracycline. Use acetaminophen at a lower dose and skip NSAIDs. Hepatitis B is the main infection risk to the team: vaccinate everyone and use standard precautions.

Drugs

PPIs shut off the acid pump for good (take them 30 minutes before a meal; they take a few days to work fully). Over years they can lower B12 and magnesium and let C. diff in, and stopping them suddenly brings the acid back. H2 blockers work faster but are weaker; cimetidine interacts with many drugs and can cause breast growth in men. Antacids work fastest; they bind tetracyclines and other antibiotics, so give them hours apart. Misoprostol protects against NSAID ulcers but can't be used in pregnancy. Bismuth fights H. pylori and traveler's diarrhea and turns the tongue black; avoid it with an aspirin allergy.

For motion sickness, use scopolamine or an antihistamine such as meclizine (dry mouth, drowsiness). Ondansetron blocks serotonin to stop nausea but can lengthen the QT interval. Dopamine blockers such as metoclopramide and prochlorperazine can cause movement problems (treated with diphenhydramine) and, rarely, a dangerous fever with stiff muscles (neuroleptic malignant syndrome). Loperamide slows the gut without reaching the brain.

For IBD, steroids calm a flare but aren't for the long term; mesalamine keeps ulcerative colitis quiet. Methotrexate for Crohn disease can cause mouth sores (folic acid helps), and NSAIDs make it build up. Azathioprine and TNF blockers lower resistance to infection, and people are checked for TB and hepatitis before a TNF blocker.
plain.mg-bone:
What's tested
  • The three cartilages and the three bone cells
  • How osteoclasts are switched on (RANKL) and off (OPG), and how PTH and vitamin D control calcium
  • The bone diseases and their mouth findings, and the bone drugs with their jaw risk (MRONJ)

Cartilage and bone

Cartilage has no blood supply, so it heals poorly. Hyaline cartilage covers joints, elastic cartilage shapes the ear, and fibrocartilage (discs, menisci, the TMJ disc) has no outer layer. Cartilage uses type II collagen; bone uses type I. Osteoblasts build bone, osteocytes sense load, and osteoclasts dissolve bone with acid. Osteoblasts make RANKL to switch osteoclasts on and OPG to block it. PTH works on osteoblasts, not directly on osteoclasts.

Growth and calcium

Skull bones, the upper jaw and most of the lower jaw form straight from tissue (intramembranous); long bones form from a cartilage model (endochondral). Low calcium releases PTH, which pulls calcium from bone, keeps it in the kidney and activates vitamin D in the kidney. Too little calcium causes tingling and cramps; too much causes stones, bone pain, belly pain and confusion.

Diseases

Brittle bone disease (OI) is a type I collagen problem: fractures, blue whites of the eyes, weak see-through teeth. Achondroplasia (FGFR3) gives short limbs. In osteopetrosis, osteoclasts can't dissolve bone, so it is dense but breaks, and a jaw infection after extraction is a real risk. Missing collarbones and many extra unerupted teeth suggest cleidocranial dysplasia. Paget disease remodels bone chaotically: a growing jaw, spaced teeth, loose dentures and "cotton wool" X-rays. Osteoporosis is too little normal bone; osteomalacia is soft, poorly mineralized bone from low vitamin D.

Drugs and the jaw

Bisphosphonates stick to bone and kill the osteoclasts that eat them. Denosumab blocks RANKL; its effect fades fast if stopped. Teriparatide builds bone and isn't linked to jaw necrosis. Jaw necrosis (MRONJ) is most likely with high-dose IV drugs for cancer plus an extraction, so do the dental work before the drug starts.
plain.mg-joints:
What's tested
  • Telling osteoarthritis from rheumatoid arthritis, and gout
  • The autoimmune diseases, especially Sjögren syndrome
  • What each vitamin does and what goes wrong without it
  • Which bone tumor fits which age and spot

Joints

Osteoarthritis is wear and tear: big weight-bearing joints and the finger-tip joints (Heberden nodes), pain after use, short morning stiffness, normal blood tests. Rheumatoid arthritis is the body attacking its joints: both hands the same, the knuckles rather than the finger tips, long morning stiffness, a "pannus" that eats bone, and anti-CCP antibodies. In the jaw, RA can slowly open the front bite. Gout is uric acid needles in one joint, often the big toe; allopurinol prevents attacks. HLA-B27 points to ankylosing spondylitis and its relatives.

Autoimmune

Sjögren syndrome dries the mouth and eyes, causes rampant decay and raises lymphoma risk; a lip biopsy confirms it. Lupus brings a cheek rash, mouth ulcers, kidney disease and anti-dsDNA antibodies; some drugs cause it. Scleroderma tightens the skin, shrinks the mouth opening and widens the PDL space on X-rays. Graves antibodies switch the thyroid on; Hashimoto disease wears it down. Myasthenia gravis antibodies block the muscle's ACh receptors.

Nutrition

No vitamin C: bleeding gums and poor healing (collagen can't be finished). No thiamine: nerve, heart and brain trouble in alcoholics, so give thiamine before sugar. Folate and B12 both make big red cells, but only B12 hurts the nerves. B vitamins and iron show up as a sore, smooth tongue and cracked mouth corners. Swelling (edema) separates kwashiorkor from marasmus.

Tumors

Most bone tumors are spread from breast, lung, thyroid, kidney or prostate. In teens, osteosarcoma sits near the knee; Ewing sarcoma sits in the shaft. A small tumor whose night pain goes away with aspirin is an osteoid osteoma. Giant cell tumor sits at the end of the bone in young adults. Lipoma is the most common soft lump.
plain.mg-skin:
What's tested
  • The skin's layers and cells, and what holds them together
  • Which skin drug does what
  • Blistering diseases, lichen planus and the three skin cancers
  • How a muscle contracts and how anesthesia drugs block the nerve-muscle junction

Skin

The top layer is the dead stratum corneum, the main barrier to drugs. Below it, cells hold on to each other with desmosomes and the bottom row holds on to the basement membrane with hemidesmosomes. Everyone has about the same number of pigment cells; darker skin just makes and spreads more pigment. Meissner corpuscles feel light touch near the surface; Pacinian corpuscles feel vibration deep down.

Skin drugs

Thin, wet, covered or inflamed skin, and a baby's skin, absorb more. Strong steroid creams thin the skin; tacrolimus doesn't, so it suits the face. Isotretinoin clears severe acne but causes birth defects and dry lips and mouth. Terbinafine treats nail fungus, permethrin treats scabies, mupirocin treats impetigo.

Skin and mouth disease

Pemphigus attacks desmosomes, so the blister forms inside the epidermis, breaks easily and usually starts in the mouth. Pemphigoid attacks hemidesmosomes, so the blister forms under the epidermis and stays tense; in the mouth it peels the gums. Dermatitis herpetiformis goes with celiac disease. Lichen planus makes lacy white lines inside both cheeks. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer and rarely spreads; squamous cell carcinoma likes the lower lip and can spread; melanoma's outlook depends on how deep it goes.

Muscle and anesthesia drugs

Calcium released inside the muscle binds troponin so myosin can pull actin. ATP lets myosin let go; without it the muscle locks (rigor). Succinylcholine paralyzes fast; people missing the enzyme that breaks it down stay paralyzed for hours, and in some people it triggers malignant hyperthermia, treated with dantrolene. Sugammadex or neostigmine reverses the other paralytics. Only the lateral pterygoid helps open the jaw.
plain.et-ada:
What's tested
  • The five principles in Code order, their one-word meanings and the duty each states: patient autonomy (1), nonmaleficence (2), beneficence (3), justice (4), veracity (5)
  • Naming the principle and Code section a scenario turns on, and the ethical answer
  • How the Code is built: principles (aspirational), the Code of Professional Conduct (binding on members) and advisory opinions (interpretations); ethics versus law
  • The classic cases: records and transfer, impaired colleagues, abandonment, postexposure duties, abuse reporting, patient selection and HIV, emergency care, justifiable criticism, split fees, amalgam removal, insurance and fees, advertising and specialty claims

Three parts

The ADA Code has principles (the ideals), a Code of Professional Conduct (the rules ADA members must follow, or face discipline) and advisory opinions (how the rules apply to real situations). Ethics often asks more of you than the law does.

The five principles, in order

  • 1. Patient autonomy (self-governance): involve patients in decisions and keep their information private. Send records to a new dentist when asked, even if the patient still owes you money.
  • 2. Nonmaleficence (do no harm): stay current, refer when needed, don't work impaired, and don't abandon a patient in the middle of treatment. Help an impaired colleague get treatment and report them to the dental society's assistance committee. After a needlestick, tell the patient and send them for care.
  • 3. Beneficence (do good): serve the community, regulate your own profession, and report suspected abuse as the law requires.
  • 4. Justice (fairness): don't turn patients away because of race, gender, disability or HIV status; arrange emergency care even for people who aren't your patients; don't badmouth other dentists' work (but report gross or repeated bad work); never split fees.
  • 5. Veracity (truthfulness): no removing healthy amalgams to "detox," no misleading ads, no fudging insurance claims or dates, no unnecessary treatment, and say when you profit from a product you recommend.

How to answer a scenario

Find the duty at stake, name the principle, then pick the answer that protects the patient while staying honest and fair. Answers that hold records for payment, refuse patients with HIV, disparage colleagues or bend a claim are always wrong.
plain.et-pro:
What's tested
  • Informed consent: what must be disclosed, the reasonable-patient standard (Canterbury v. Spence), decision-making capacity, informed refusal and implied consent
  • Who consents for a minor or for an adult who lacks capacity
  • Confidentiality and HIPAA: what's protected, when you may share without authorization, the patient's rights, and the duty to warn (Tarasoff)
  • Records and the medical history: what to record and how to correct an entry
  • The duty to report suspected child abuse and neglect and its signs; disclosing errors; whistle-blowing
  • Infection control and bloodborne pathogens as professional duties: standard precautions, OSHA's rules, transmission risks and what to do after an exposure
  • Ethical reasoning: valid and sound arguments, the common fallacies and the main moral theories

Consent

Before treatment, tell the patient what's wrong, what you plan, its risks and benefits, the other options (including doing nothing) and the cost, so they can choose. The signature only records that the talk happened. Since Canterbury v. Spence, you disclose what a reasonable patient would want to know. A patient can say no (document it), but can't make you give care below the standard. Capacity means they understand, see that it applies to them, can weigh the options and can state a choice.

Children

A parent or legal guardian consents for a child; a grandparent or babysitter can't unless they have legal authority. Ask the child to agree too.

Privacy

HIPAA protects any health information that identifies a patient, spoken, written or electronic. You may share it for treatment, payment and running the practice, and when the law requires (such as abuse reports); for most other uses you need written permission. Patients can get copies of their records. If a patient seriously threatens a specific person, the duty to protect that person (Tarasoff) outweighs confidentiality.

Records

Never change or backdate a record; cross out an error with one line, date and initial it. Check the medical history every visit.

Reporting

If you suspect child abuse (bruises of different ages, a torn lip frenum, a story that changes), you must report it; you don't need proof, and an honest report is legally protected. Tell patients about your mistakes.

Infection control

Treat every patient with standard precautions. After a needlestick, wash, report right away and start HIV medicine within hours if needed. Hepatitis B is the most contagious by needlestick (about 30%), then hepatitis C (about 2%), then HIV (about 0.3%); only hepatitis B has a vaccine, which employers must offer free.

Reasoning

A valid argument's conclusion must follow if its premises are true; a sound one is valid with true premises. Watch for slippery slopes, straw men and attacks on the person. Utilitarians judge by results; Kantians by duty and respect for persons.
plain.eb-ask:
What's tested
  • The 5 A's in order (ask, acquire, appraise, apply, assess) and what each step does
  • Building a PICO(T) question and picking P, I, C, O and T out of a case; background versus foreground questions; the four kinds of clinical question and the design that best answers each
  • Where to search: TRIP first, then PubMed Clinical Queries, then the Cochrane Library
  • Naming the design from a short description, and what case-control and cohort studies are each good and bad at
  • The evidence pyramid, and literature review versus systematic review versus meta-analysis versus clinical practice guideline (GRADE, AGREE)
  • Efficacy versus effectiveness, the study-context continuum, practice-based research networks and the three gaps between evidence and practice

The big picture

Evidence-based dentistry means deciding with three things together: good research, your own clinical skill, and what the patient wants. The 5 A's are the steps: ask a clear question, acquire (find) the evidence, appraise (judge) it, apply it with your patient, then assess how it went.

Asking a good question

PICO(T) keeps a question focused: who the patient is (P), what you're thinking of doing (I), what you're comparing it with (C), the result you care about (O), and over how long (T). Only "which is better?" questions (foreground questions) fit PICO; simple fact questions such as "what causes dry socket?" (background questions) don't need it.

Finding the evidence

Start with TRIP, then PubMed's Clinical Queries, then the Cochrane Library of systematic reviews.

Telling the designs apart

  • Case report or series: describes patients, with no comparison group.
  • Ecological: compares whole groups, such as cities.
  • Cross-sectional: one snapshot in time; gives prevalence.
  • Case-control: starts with people who have the disease and looks back; good for rare diseases; gives an odds ratio.
  • Cohort: starts with an exposure and follows people forward; gives incidence and relative risk; good for rare exposures.
  • Randomized controlled trial: people are randomly put into groups; the best single study for "does this treatment work?"

The pyramid

Lab and animal studies sit at the bottom (very controlled but far from real patients), then case reports and expert opinion, then the observational designs, then RCTs, then systematic reviews and meta-analyses, with clinical practice guidelines on top. A systematic review searches for every study in a planned, repeatable way; a meta-analysis also pools their numbers; a plain literature review has no method and reflects the author's picks.

Ideal versus real world

Efficacy is whether a treatment works in a perfect study setting; effectiveness is whether it works in ordinary offices with ordinary patients. Evidence also has to reach practice: if it doesn't exist yet, that's a knowledge gap; if dentists haven't heard of it, a knowing gap; if they know but don't use it, a knowing-to-doing gap.
plain.eb-appraise:
What's tested
  • Internal versus external validity, and the three threats to validity: bias, confounding and chance
  • The kinds of bias and what randomization, blinding and intention-to-treat analysis do about them; what to check in an RCT
  • Standardization versus calibration, inter- versus intra-examiner reliability, precision versus accuracy, incidence versus prevalence
  • Types of data, mean versus median, and standard deviation
  • Sensitivity, specificity and predictive values from a 2×2 table, and which one a screening or a confirming test needs
  • Relative risk, odds ratio, absolute risk and the number needed to treat; reading a ratio with its 95% confidence interval
  • p-values, type I and II errors, power, and statistical versus clinical significance

Can you trust the study?

Internal validity means the study was done right; external validity means its results apply to your patients. Three things spoil a result: bias (a built-in tilt, such as people misremembering the past), confounding (a hidden third factor, such as brushing habits in a soda study) and chance (the luck of who was sampled).

A good trial

People are put into groups at random, nobody knows who got the real treatment (blinding), and everyone is counted in the group they were assigned to, even if they quit (intention to treat).

Measuring

Standardization means everyone uses the same tools and rules; calibration means examiners practice on the same patients until their scores agree. Precision is getting the same answer each time; accuracy is getting the right answer. Incidence counts new cases over time; prevalence counts everyone who has it now. For skewed numbers, the median is a better middle than the mean.

Tests

Sensitivity is how well a test catches people who have the disease: good for screening, and a negative result rules the disease out. Specificity is how well it clears people who don't: wanted before something you can't undo, and a positive result rules the disease in. How much a positive or negative result means (PPV, NPV) depends on how common the disease is.

Risk numbers

A relative risk or odds ratio of 1 means no difference, above 1 more risk, below 1 less risk. Case-control studies give odds ratios; cohorts and trials give relative risks. The NNT is how many people you treat for one to benefit (1 ÷ the absolute risk reduction): smaller is better.

Significance

p below 0.05 is "significant"; a ratio's confidence interval that includes 1 is not. A type I error is a false alarm; a type II error misses a real effect; power, the chance of finding a real effect, grows with bigger samples. A significant result can still be too small to matter to patients.
plain.rd-physics:
What's tested
  • X-ray production: cathode/anode, >99% heat vs ~1% x-rays, bremsstrahlung (primary) vs characteristic radiation
  • mA and time control photon quantity; kVp controls energy/penetration (beam quality); the inverse square law
  • Filtration (removes low-energy photons) and collimation (restricts beam, cuts scatter and dose)
  • Beam attenuation: photoelectric absorption (makes the image/contrast, ∝ Z³), Compton scatter (most common, adds fog), coherent
  • Image quality: density, contrast and spatial resolution, sharpness and receptors

Making x-rays

Inside the tube, the cathode (the negative side) heats a filament that gives off electrons. They speed across to the anode (the positive tungsten target) and crash into it. Over 99% of that energy turns into heat and only about 1% turns into x-rays. Most of the photons come from bremsstrahlung ('braking') radiation, made when electrons are slowed near a nucleus; a few come from characteristic interactions. X-rays and gamma rays are both electromagnetic, but x-rays are made outside the nucleus and are easier to control.

The knobs on the machine

  • mA and exposure time change how many photons you make (the quantity).
  • kVp changes how much energy the photons have and how far they penetrate (the quality).
  • Filtration (aluminum) removes weak photons that would only add dose; collimation shrinks the beam to cut scatter and dose.
  • Inverse square law: double the distance and the intensity drops to one quarter.

What happens inside the patient

Three things can happen to a photon: Compton scatter (the most common, about 57%, which adds fog that lowers contrast), photoelectric absorption (about 27%, which makes the image and its contrast; bone absorbs about 6.5× more than soft tissue), and a little coherent scatter. That difference between how bone and soft tissue absorb is the whole reason we can see an image.

Telling a good image from a bad one

Sharpness is how crisp the edges are, and it is ruined by any movement. A blurry image isn't diagnostic, so it has to be retaken. The image is captured on film, PSP plates or digital sensors.
plain.rd-biosafety:
What's tested
  • Direct vs indirect action (water radiolysis, free radicals H· and OH·); DNA double-strand breaks are the critical damage
  • Radiosensitivity by cell and organ; rapidly dividing/undifferentiated cells are most sensitive
  • Deterministic (threshold, dose-severity: xerostomia, ORN, cataracts) vs stochastic (no threshold, cancer and heritable effects)
  • ALARA/ALADA, justification, optimization, dose limitation; thyroid collar, rectangular collimation, selection criteria
  • Occupational limits (1 mSv dosimeter trigger), the 6-foot/90–135° rule, dental x-rays are a tiny dose

How radiation hurts cells

Radiation can hit DNA directly (direct action), but most damage is indirect: the photon splits a water molecule into free radicals (H· and OH·) that then wreck the DNA. The body is mostly water, so this is the main pathway. The worst injury is a double-strand break, which cells struggle to repair, and it underlies cell death, mutation and cancer.

Which cells care most

Cells that divide fast and are immature are the most sensitive: bone marrow, the gut lining, the mouth's mucosa and reproductive cells. Fully grown nerve and muscle cells are the least sensitive.

Two kinds of effect

  • Deterministic effects have a threshold and get worse as the dose goes up — xerostomia (dry mouth), osteoradionecrosis and cataracts.
  • Stochastic effects have no threshold; more dose just means more chance, not worse disease — cancer and heritable effects.

Children are about 3× more at risk than adults, and dental x-ray doses are far too small to harm a fetus, though routine films can still be put off during pregnancy.

Staying safe

ALARA means keeping the dose as low as reasonably achievable. Use rectangular collimation (about 60% less area), a thyroid collar and fast receptors, and only take films that are justified. The operator stands at least 6 feet away at 90–135° from the beam. Dose limits apply to staff, not patients. Wear a dosimeter if you might go over 1 mSv a year.
plain.rd-geometry:
What's tested
  • Paralleling (receptor parallel to tooth, beam perpendicular — preferred at UABSOD) vs bisecting angle
  • Geometric optics: small focal spot, long source-object distance, short object-receptor distance, parallel object/receptor
  • Vertical-angle errors: excessive = foreshortening, insufficient = elongation
  • Horizontal overlap, cone cut, missing crowns/incisal edges, blurring, PSP artifacts and their causes
  • XCP/RINN color coding (yellow posterior, blue anterior, red bitewing, green endo) and the position-indicating ring

Getting a sharp, true-size image

Four things control how sharp and how magnified an image is:

  • Use the smallest focal spot.
  • Increase the distance from the source to the object (a longer cone).
  • Shorten the distance from the object to the receptor.
  • Keep the tooth and the receptor parallel, with the beam perpendicular to both.

Think of a shadow puppet: hold your hand near the light and the shadow is big and blurry; hold it near the wall and the shadow is small and sharp.

Two techniques

Paralleling (used at UABSOD) puts the receptor parallel to the tooth and aims the beam straight at both, giving the least distortion. Bisecting angle aims the beam at the imaginary line that splits the angle between the tooth and the receptor; it gets the length right but distorts the bone. The XCP/RINN holders are color-coded — yellow posterior, blue anterior, red bitewing, green endo — and the ring is the part you line the tube up to.

Angle mistakes

  • Too much up-and-down angle → the tooth looks short (foreshortening).
  • Too little up-and-down angle → the tooth looks long (elongation).
  • Wrong side-to-side angle → the teeth overlap.
  • Beam off-center → a cone cut (a blank area).
  • Receptor placed too low → a missing crown.
  • Any movement → a blur, so you retake it.

Other films

Besides periapicals, bitewings (the red holder) show the crowns to catch cavities between teeth and check bone levels.
plain.rd-anatomy:
What's tested
  • Radiolucent vs radiopaque are relative; the egg-shell effect and the lamina dura
  • Maxillary radiopaque landmarks (anterior nasal spine, nasal septum/floor, zygomatic process = J/U, Y line of Ennis, maxillary tuberosity, hamulus)
  • Maxillary radiolucencies (incisive foramen, maxillary sinus, nasal fossa) and mandibular landmarks (genial tubercles, lingual foramen, mental foramen, mandibular canal, mylohyoid and external oblique ridges, coronoid process)
  • Panoramic basics: the focal trough, ghost images, and common positioning errors (chin up/down, tongue not on palate)
  • Diagnosis vs interpretation; radiographs are correlated with the clinical exam

Dark versus white

Radiolucent means dark, where x-rays pass through (air, pulp, soft tissue). Radiopaque means white, where x-rays are blocked (enamel, bone, metal). They are relative terms — something can be more radiopaque than one neighbor but more radiolucent than another. The lamina dura is the white line around a tooth's socket; if it stays intact around the apex, a dark spot over the root (like the mental foramen) is normal, not disease.

Maxilla landmarks

White (radiopaque): the anterior nasal spine (a V shape), the zygomatic process (a J or U over the molars) and the Y line of Ennis. Dark (radiolucent): the incisive foramen between the central incisors, the nasal fossa and the maxillary sinus.

Mandible landmarks

The genial tubercles are a white ring with a dark lingual foramen at the midline. The mental foramen is a dark spot near the premolars. The mandibular canal is a dark band with two white lines, and the mylohyoid and external oblique ridges are white lines across the molar area.

Panoramic basics

A panoramic film only shows things that sit inside its curved focal trough; anything outside it blurs or disappears. Tipping the chin too high flattens the smile line; tipping it too low makes a big frown and blurs the front teeth; not putting the tongue on the roof of the mouth leaves a dark shadow over the upper teeth. A ghost image is a blurry white shadow thrown to the opposite side and higher up.
plain.em-prevent:
What's tested
  • The eight big emergencies and which ones happen most
  • How a good medical history prevents emergencies
  • Your duty to act, and who does what on the team
  • CPR basics and the AED
  • What each drug in the kit is for

The big eight

The course is built on eight emergencies: anaphylaxis, low blood sugar, asthma, chest pain, fainting, stroke, seizure and aspiration (breathing in an object). Fainting is the most common emergency by far, about half of all of them, and most emergencies happen around the time of the local anesthetic shot. About three out of four can be prevented.

Prevention

Take a full history, drug list and vital signs at every visit. Put off elective work for months after a heart attack or stroke and plan it with the cardiologist. Never stop a patient's blood thinner yourself; the doctor who prescribed it decides. The physician tells you the risk, but you make the dental plan and you are still responsible for it.

Your duty and your team

You must help in any emergency in your office, even in the waiting room, as far as your training goes. Train your staff and practice at least once a year. The dentist leads. One helper brings the kit, oxygen and AED; another calls 911 and meets the ambulance; another writes down times and drugs. When you give an order, the helper repeats it back so nothing gets lost.

CPR

The order is now circulation, airway, breathing. Check for a pulse and breathing for no more than 10 seconds. If there is no pulse, push hard and fast: 100 to 120 a minute, at least 2 inches deep, 30 pushes to 2 breaths. Get the patient onto a hard surface first. Tilting the head back and lifting the chin pulls the tongue off the back of the throat. Use the AED as soon as it arrives; every minute without it lowers survival.

The kit

  • Oxygen for almost everything.
  • Epinephrine shot into the thigh muscle for a severe allergy (anaphylaxis).
  • Albuterol inhaler for an asthma attack.
  • Diphenhydramine (Benadryl) for a mild allergy like hives.
  • Nitroglycerin under the tongue for chest pain, but not with low blood pressure or erectile dysfunction pills.
  • Aspirin to chew for a suspected heart attack.
  • Naloxone for an opioid overdose; it wears off fast, so call 911.
  • Sugar by mouth for low blood sugar if the patient can swallow.
plain.em-airway:
What's tested
  • Spotting a patient whose airway will be hard to manage
  • Moving air versus getting oxygen in, and the oxygen tools
  • A swallowed or inhaled object: what to do and where it goes
  • Cord spasm, asthma attacks and fast anxious breathing
  • A mild allergy versus a severe one

You're on your own for the first minutes

An ambulance takes about 7 minutes on average, longer in the country, so you handle the airway until it arrives. Call 911 early rather than late.

Air and oxygen

Breathing moves air in and out; oxygenation is oxygen getting into the blood. Giving oxygen before a procedure fills the lungs with extra so the patient lasts longer if breathing stops. When oxygen saturation drops below about 88%, it falls quickly. If you have to breathe for a patient with a bag and mask, open the airway first and squeeze gently; too much air goes to the stomach and causes vomiting.

The hard airway

Have the patient open wide and stick out the tongue. If you can see only part of the uvula or only the hard palate (Mallampati class III or IV), the airway may be hard to manage. A small jaw, a short thick neck, a beard, obesity, sleep apnea and limited mouth opening also warn you.

Objects in the airway

Crowns, burs, screws and teeth get dropped and inhaled, especially by sedated or elderly patients. Use an unfolded 4x4 gauze throat screen, a rubber dam and floss tied to small parts. A patient who can cough and talk should keep coughing. A patient who can't talk or breathe needs abdominal thrusts right away, and CPR if they pass out. Never sweep blindly with a finger; it pushes the object deeper. Inhaled objects usually end up in the right lung's main airway. If something disappeared and you didn't see it come out, send the patient to the emergency room for chest and belly X-rays, even if they feel fine.

Other breathing problems

  • Laryngospasm: the vocal cords snap shut, often from blood or water in a lightly sedated patient. Suction and give 100% oxygen with the bag and mask.
  • Asthma attack: sit the patient up and give their albuterol inhaler; if it doesn't work, give epinephrine and call 911.
  • Hyperventilation: fast breathing with tingling fingers from anxiety. Calm the patient and slow their breathing. No oxygen.

Allergies

Hives and itching alone: give diphenhydramine and watch. Hives plus wheezing, a tight throat or low blood pressure is anaphylaxis: give epinephrine into the thigh muscle right away and call 911.
plain.em-cardiac:
What's tested
  • Chest pain and a heart attack in the chair
  • Heart failure, irregular heartbeats and the AED
  • Who needs antibiotics before dental work, and which ones
  • Very high blood pressure: when to send the patient to the ER
  • Bleeding: blood thinners, bleeding disorders and how to stop it

Chest pain

Angina is chest pain when the heart muscle isn't getting enough blood; it eases with rest or nitroglycerin. A heart attack is a full blockage. The pain feels crushing or squeezing, often spreads to the left arm or jaw, and comes with sweating and shortness of breath. Stop, sit the patient up, give oxygen and nitroglycerin under the tongue (not if the blood pressure is low or they took an erectile dysfunction pill). If the pain doesn't go away, call 911 and have them chew an aspirin.

Heart failure and heartbeats

In heart failure the patient gets short of breath lying flat, and has swollen legs and swollen neck veins. Treat them sitting up and go easy on epinephrine. A normal heart rate is 60 to 100. Atrial fibrillation is an irregular rhythm that can throw clots, so these patients take blood thinners. The AED shocks ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia without a pulse; for a flat line, keep doing CPR.

Antibiotics before dental work

Give antibiotics before work that makes the gums bleed (extractions, scaling, surgery) only to patients with a prosthetic heart valve, a past heart infection (endocarditis), certain congenital heart problems or a heart transplant with valve disease. The usual dose is 2 g of amoxicillin by mouth 30 to 60 minutes before. Mitral valve prolapse, stents, pacemakers and heart failure don't need it.

High blood pressure

A reading of 180 over 120 or higher is severe. With symptoms like a bad headache, chest pain or vision changes, it is an emergency: send the patient to the ER. Without symptoms, do no elective work and send them to their doctor soon.

Bleeding

Almost all mouth bleeding stops with firm pressure on gauze for 10 to 15 minutes. Don't stop a patient's blood thinner yourself; most simple extractions are done without stopping it. Warfarin is checked with the INR. Aspirin's effect lasts about a week. Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding problem and often isn't known until after surgery. Hemophilia patients usually know how to manage their disease with their hematologist. If pressure isn't enough, use an anesthetic with epinephrine, packing material like Gelfoam or Surgicel, stitches, bone wax for bleeding bone, and tranexamic acid rinses.
plain.em-loc:
What's tested
  • What to do first when anyone passes out
  • Fainting, the most common emergency
  • Low blood sugar: juice, glucagon or IV sugar
  • How much oxygen each device gives
  • Steroid patients and adrenal crisis; thyroid storm
  • Seizures, stroke and too much local anesthetic

First steps, every time

Stop working and clear the mouth. Lay the patient back with the legs up so blood reaches the brain. Open the airway, check breathing and a pulse, give oxygen and take vital signs. If the patient doesn't wake up quickly, call 911, and tell the paramedics exactly how many milligrams of each drug you gave.

Fainting

About half of all office emergencies are simple fainting from fear, pain, or seeing blood or a needle. The patient feels dizzy, turns pale and sweaty, then passes out for a few seconds with a slow pulse. Lay them flat with the legs up, put a cold towel on the forehead and give oxygen. They should wake up quickly. If the heart rate stays very slow, atropine speeds it up.

Low blood sugar

Diabetes is a fasting sugar of 126 or more, or an HbA1c of 6.5% or more; an HbA1c over 10 means poor control. Blood sugar under about 50 to 60 causes shaking, sweating, confusion, seizures and passing out. Low sugar is more dangerous than high sugar, so if unsure, give sugar. If the patient can swallow, give juice, soda or glucose gel. If they can't, give a glucagon shot into the thigh or sugar through an IV, and call 911. Each gram of sugar raises the blood level by about 3 to 5.

Oxygen

A nasal cannula works up to about 5 liters a minute and gives up to about 40% oxygen; turning it higher does nothing. A face mask gives up to about 60%. A non-rebreather mask at 15 liters gives the most.

Steroids and the thyroid

Patients who took steroids for a long time may not make enough of their own cortisol when stressed. The rule of twos: 20 mg of hydrocortisone a day (or the equivalent) for 2 weeks within the last 2 years. Most routine dental work needs no extra steroid. A crisis looks like very low blood pressure, vomiting and confusion; treat it with 100 mg of hydrocortisone and call 911. A thyroid storm is a dangerous flare of an overactive thyroid with fever and a racing heart: stop and get help.

Seizures, stroke, overdose

During a seizure, keep the patient from getting hurt and put nothing in the mouth; for a long seizure, call 911 and give a benzodiazepine. A stroke causes sudden weakness on one side, a drooping face or slurred speech: call 911 right away. Too much local anesthetic causes numb lips, talkativeness, twitching and then seizures. Keep count of your cartridges (about 13 of lidocaine for a 70-kg adult). Severe cases get IV lipid emulsion.

What's tested

1 Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis and flushing from a cervical sympathetic lesion

Objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • To the head: presynaptic fibers from T1–T2 ascend the trunk and synapse in the superior cervical ganglion; postsynaptic fibers ride the internal and external carotid arteries (periarterial plexuses) to the dilator pupillae, superior tarsal muscle, sweat glands and vessels.

Horner syndrome (cervical sympathetic chain cut or compressed, classically by an apical lung, or Pancoast, tumor): ptosis (superior tarsal muscle, so the droop is partial), miosis (unopposed sphincter pupillae, so the pupil is small), anhidrosis and flushing (warm, red skin) on the same side.

2 Nerves at risk in thyroid surgery and the carotid sheath and its neighbors

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

External carotid branches (SALFOPSM): superior thyroid, ascending pharyngeal, lingual, facial, occipital, posterior auricular, and the two terminal branches, superficial temporal and maxillary. The internal carotid has no branches in the neck. The carotid sinus (dilation of the proximal ICA) holds baroreceptors; the carotid body (at the bifurcation) holds chemoreceptors; both report through the carotid sinus branch of IX, so pressure on the sinus can slow the heart. The carotid sheath holds the common/internal carotid (medial), IJV (lateral) and vagus (posterior, between them), with the deep cervical nodes along the IJV; the sympathetic trunk lies behind the sheath, in the prevertebral fascia. The IJV begins at the jugular foramen as the continuation of the sigmoid sinus. Key nodes: jugulodigastric (tonsil, back of the tongue) and jugulo-omohyoid (tongue).

  • Thyroid: isthmus over tracheal rings 2–4, inside the pretracheal fascia (so it moves with swallowing). Superior thyroid artery (ECA) runs with the external laryngeal nerve (injury: can't raise pitch, weak monotone voice); inferior thyroid artery (thyrocervical trunk) is close to the recurrent laryngeal nerve (injury: hoarseness). A thyroid ima artery is present in about 10%. Superior and middle thyroid veins go to the IJV, the inferior to the brachiocephalic veins. The four parathyroids sit on the back of the lobes; removing them causes hypocalcemia and tetany.

3 Root of the neck: subclavian branches, phrenic nerve, thoracic duct and the superior thoracic aperture

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

The superior thoracic aperture (T1, first ribs, manubrium) passes the trachea, esophagus, great vessels, vagus and phrenic nerves, thoracic duct and the lung's cupula (a stab wound here can cause a pneumothorax). The brachial plexus and subclavian vessels go over the first rib to the axilla instead.

  • Thoracic duct: from the cisterna chyli to the left venous angle; drains everything except the right upper quadrant, which the right lymphatic duct drains. Injury leaks chyle (chylothorax).

4 Posterior triangle: CN XI and the cervical plexus at the nerve point

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • CN XI crosses it superficially on the levator scapulae, so a lymph node biopsy here can cut it: the shoulder droops and the patient can't shrug (trapezius). The SCM is often spared because its branch leaves earlier.
  • Cervical plexus (C1–C4 ventral rami) cutaneous branches emerge at the nerve point (Erb's point) at the middle of the SCM's posterior border, the site of a cervical plexus block: lesser occipital (C2), great auricular (C2–C3; skin over the parotid and the angle of the mandible, which is not trigeminal), transverse cervical (C2–C3; front of the neck), supraclavicular (C3–C4).

1 Parotid: what runs through it, the duct opposite the maxillary second molar, IX–otic–auriculotemporal secretion, Frey syndrome

Objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Secretomotor path: inferior salivatory nucleus → IX → tympanic nerve and plexus → lesser petrosal nerve → synapse in the otic ganglion → auriculotemporal nerve (V3) → gland. VII passes through but gives it no secretory fibers. Frey syndrome: after parotid surgery, cut parasympathetic fibers regrow into the sweat glands of the overlying skin (great auricular and auriculotemporal territory), so eating causes sweating and flushing of the cheek. A parotid tumor with facial weakness suggests malignancy.

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Signs: the inferior rectus is trapped (can't look up, double vision), numbness of the cheek, side of the nose and upper lip (infraorbital nerve), sunken eye.

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

S-C-A-L-P: skin; dense connective tissue with vessels held open when cut (scalp wounds bleed freely); epicranial aponeurosis (frontalis and occipitalis); loose connective tissue, the "danger zone" where blood and pus spread and emissary veins lead into the skull; pericranium. Fluid in the loose layer can't spread back or to the sides but can run forward into the eyelids (black eyes). Supply: in front of the ears V, behind them C2–C3 (greater and lesser occipital); arteries from the ECA (superficial temporal, occipital, posterior auricular) and ICA (supraorbital, supratrochlear).

Study guide + review guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Groove 1 becomes the external acoustic meatus; membrane 1 the tympanic membrane. Grooves 2–4 are buried by arch 2 as the cervical sinus; if it persists, a lateral cervical (branchial) cyst or fistula appears along the anterior border of the SCM, often in a young adult.

The front two-thirds of the tongue come from arch 1 (two lateral lingual swellings over the tuberculum impar), so general sensation is V3 (lingual nerve); taste there runs in the chorda tympani (VII). The back third comes from the hypopharyngeal eminence of arches 3 and 4: IX, with X at the base. Tongue muscles come from occipital myotomes and bring XII with them (the palatoglossus, a palate muscle, is X). The thyroid grows down from the foramen cecum along the thyroglossal duct, in front of the hyoid. A thyroglossal duct cyst is in or near the midline and rises with swallowing and tongue protrusion; a leftover piece can form a pyramidal lobe or a lingual thyroid.

1 Globular protein classes (all α, all β, α/β, α+β), what stabilizes a fold, and the advantages of quaternary structure

Slides + objectives · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Quaternary structure's four advantages: stability (less surface facing water), genetic economy and efficiency (small subunits made accurately), catalytic sites formed between subunits, and cooperativity.
  • Quaternary: the arrangement of several chains (subunits), as in hemoglobin, a tetramer. A single-chain protein has none. Identical subunits make a homo-oligomer and different ones a hetero-oligomer (the Greek letters that name subunits have nothing to do with α-helices or β-sheets). Globular subunits are held together noncovalently, mostly by hydrophobic interactions; fibrous proteins are often joined covalently. Its advantages: stability (a lower surface-to-volume ratio buries surface that would face water), genetic economy and efficiency (small subunits are made more accurately than one huge chain), catalytic sites built where subunits meet, and cooperativity and regulation.

5 Carbohydrate isomers, glycosidic bonds, sucrose and S. mutans, GAGs and glycation

Slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Simple carbohydrates are (CH2O)n with n of 3 or more, named by their number of carbons (triose, pentose, hexose) and by their carbonyl: aldoses (aldehyde) or ketoses (ketone). Glycosidic bonds join them: two units make a disaccharide, 3–10 an oligosaccharide, more than 10 a polysaccharide. Isomers share a formula: positional isomers differ in where a group sits, geometric isomers in the arrangement at a rigid part, and optical isomers at a chiral carbon (one with four different groups). Enantiomers are mirror images (D and L) with the same physical and chemical properties but different biological ones; they turn polarized light in opposite directions. Epimers differ at only one chiral carbon (not the carbonyl carbon): glucose and galactose at C-4, glucose and mannose at C-2. In solution the carbonyl reacts with one of the sugar's own OH groups to close a ring (a hemiacetal, or a hemiketal for a ketose): a six-membered pyranose (glucose in solution, a C-1–O–C-5 ring) or a five-membered furanose (fructose, C-2–O–C-5). The open chain is under 0.01%. Ring closure makes C-1 a new chiral, anomeric carbon, giving the α and β anomers, which interconvert (mutarotation, sped by acid or base). Sugars with a free anomeric carbon are reducing sugars. A reducing sugar's carbonyl can join the amino group of a protein's lysine as a Schiff base: glycation, which is nonenzymatic and distinct from enzymatic glycosylation. Glycation products cross-link proteins, build up when blood glucose runs high and are thought to underlie some of diabetes's damage (HbA1c is glycated hemoglobin).

  • Sucrose (glucose α1→β2 fructose) is nonreducing, since its bond ties up both anomeric carbons. Streptococcus mutans ferments it to lactic acid and uses it to build sticky, water-insoluble extracellular glucans (dextran-based, with α-1,3 bonds) for plaque.

6 Lipid structure, base pairing and buffers

Slides + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Blood pH is held at 7.35–7.45, since small changes disturb protein structure. Metabolism makes mostly acid, and CO2 is the main acidic product. A buffer resists pH change best when the pH equals its pKa, works only over a limited range, and too much acid or base overwhelms it. The bicarbonate system is the main buffer of blood and extracellular fluid: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−. The first step can happen without an enzyme, but carbonic anhydrase in red cells and other tissues speeds it.

Also flagged in class

  • Most globular proteins are all α, all β, α/β (helices and strands intermingled) or α+β (separate α-helical and β-sheet domains).
  • A fold is stabilized by many intramolecular hydrogen bonds and by burying hydrophobic side chains away from water; it is only marginally stable, so parts flex, which binding, catalysis and shape changes need.

You can skip

  • Skip the electronegativity cutoff numbers; know that a growing electronegativity difference moves a bond from nonpolar covalent to polar covalent to ionic.
  • Skip how much of the body is water and how much we drink a day; know water's properties and why they come from its hydrogen bonds.
  • For this lecture, know the bicarbonate buffer: CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−, with carbonic anhydrase in red cells speeding the first step.
  • Skip the bases' ring structures; know adenine and guanine are purines and cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines.
  • Skip the chart of lipid structures; know that lipids are defined by their low solubility in water, and the main kinds: triglycerides, phospholipids and steroids.

What's tested

1 Potassium and excitability: hyperkalemia depolarizes (a mild rise nears threshold; enough locks Na+ channels inactivated), hypokalemia hyperpolarizes

Hint + review + slides · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • A mild rise in K+ brings the membrane closer to threshold, but enough hyperkalemia depolarizes it so far that the Na+ channels stay inactivated: nerve and muscle can't fire, so muscles go weak. Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes and also lowers excitability.

Plasma K+ is normally 3.5–5.0 mmol/L. Hyperkalemia shrinks the K+ gradient, so E(K+) and the resting potential become less negative (raising outside K+ from 4.5 to 5.2 mM moves E(K+) from about −85 to −81 mV). A mild rise brings the membrane closer to threshold, but enough hyperkalemia locks the Na+ channels in the inactivated state, so nerve and muscle can't fire: weakness or paralysis (as in hyperkalemic periodic paralysis) and dangerous heart rhythms. Hypokalemia hyperpolarizes (2.2 mM outside gives about −104 mV), so a bigger stimulus is needed to reach threshold and excitability also falls.

2 The action potential: Na+ channel activation and inactivation gates, delayed-rectifier K+ channels, refractory periods and one-way conduction

Review + slides + objectives · 1 question in the bank

During the absolute refractory period the Na+ inactivation gates are closed and no stimulus can fire another action potential. The relative refractory period follows and overlaps the afterhyperpolarization: some Na+ channels are still inactivated and K+ channels are still open, so only a larger-than-normal stimulus works. An action potential spreads by local currents that bring the next patch of membrane to threshold; the patch behind it is refractory, so conduction runs one way, from the cell body to the terminals. Myelin (about 80% lipid, 20% protein) insulates the axon. It is made by oligodendrocytes in the CNS (one cell wraps segments of many axons, up to about 30) and by Schwann cells in the PNS (one cell, one segment of one axon). The action potential jumps from one node of Ranvier, where the voltage-gated Na+ channels are concentrated, to the next (saltatory conduction); larger diameter also speeds it.

3 Drugs and toxins on the action potential: local anesthetics (from inside, weak in acidic tissue), tetrodotoxin (Na+ channels, from outside) and TEA (K+ channels)

Review + slides · 2 questions in the bank

Tetrodotoxin (pufferfish) blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels from outside, so threshold is never reached. Tetraethylammonium (TEA) blocks voltage-gated K+ channels: the action potential broadens, repolarizes more slowly and loses most of its afterhyperpolarization. Local anesthetics such as lidocaine cross the axon membrane as the uncharged base, pick up a proton inside, and the charged form blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels from the cytoplasmic side: a low dose slows the upstroke, a higher one stops action potentials. In inflamed, acidic tissue more of the drug is charged outside the nerve and less gets in, so the block is weaker.

5 Resting potential: Nernst (a tenfold gradient = 60 mV), the K+ leak, and the pump-leak model (the pump adds little voltage)

Hint + review + slides + objectives · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • The resting potential comes from the K+ leak (K+ conductance far above Na+, so it sits near E(K+)); the pump builds the gradients and adds only a few millivolts directly.

A membrane permeable to several ions sits between their equilibrium potentials, nearest the one it conducts best. A resting nerve's K+ conductance (through K+ leak channels that are always open) far exceeds its Na+ conductance, so the resting potential (about −70 mV; −10 to −100 mV across cell types) sits close to E(K+). In the pump-leak model the Na+/K+ pump builds the gradients and the leaks spend them; its own electrogenic current adds only a few millivolts, so blocking the pump lets the potential fall only slowly, as the gradients run down.

6 Osmosis and tonicity: particles per molecule (NaCl 2, MgCl2 3, glucose 1), the reflection coefficient, swelling and shrinking

Hint + review + slides + objectives · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • Osmotic pressure counts particles: multiply the concentration by g (NaCl 2, MgCl2 3, glucose 1) and by the reflection coefficient (0 = crosses freely, draws no water; 1 = impermeant, full effect).

Diffusion is passive and downhill, driven by random thermal motion; with no gradient there is no net flux. For an uncharged solute (Fick's law) the rate rises with surface area, the concentration gradient and lipid solubility, and falls with molecular size and membrane thickness; a voltage across the membrane doesn't affect it. Gases and small uncharged or lipid-soluble molecules cross the bilayer easily; ions, other charged molecules and hydrophilic molecules larger than about 4 Å (glucose, amino acids) need a protein. A charged solute follows its electrochemical gradient (concentration and voltage together), so it doesn't always move down its concentration gradient. Osmosis is water moving toward the side with more osmotically active particles; it is always passive (there are no water pumps), through the bilayer and aquaporins. Osmotic pressure (van't Hoff: π = gσRTC) depends on the number of particles, not their size or mass (g, particles per molecule: NaCl 2, MgCl2 3, glucose 1), and on how well they cross, the reflection coefficient σ: 0 means the solute crosses freely and draws no water; 1 means it is impermeant and exerts its full pressure. Normal saline (0.9% NaCl, 154 mM) is about 286 mOsm/L.

Know this
  • Secondary active transport runs on the Na+ gradient the Na+/K+ pump makes: cotransport moves the solute with Na+ (SGLT1, Na+–K+–2Cl−), countertransport against it (Na+/Ca2+, Na+/H+).

8 Synapses: electrical versus chemical, ionotropic versus metabotropic, EPSPs, IPSPs and summation, glutamate, GABA-A (Cl−) and glycine

Hint + review + slides + objectives · 2 questions in the bank

EPSPs depolarize (Na+ entry, usually glutamate); IPSPs hyperpolarize (Cl− entry, usually GABA or glycine; K+ exit does the same). Both are graded (their size follows the amount of transmitter) and local, and they add up at the axon hillock: temporal summation adds potentials that arrive one after another at one synapse; spatial summation adds potentials that arrive at the same time from different synapses. At skeletal muscle a motor unit is one motor neuron and all the fibers it supplies (a few for fine eye movements, hundreds or more for postural and power muscles). Acetylcholine opens nicotinic receptors at the motor end plate, and the graded end-plate potential triggers the muscle action potential.

You can skip

  • Skip which neuropeptides go with which small-molecule transmitter. Know the classes: amino acids (glutamate, GABA, glycine), biogenic amines, purines and acetylcholine are made in the terminal; neuropeptides (3–36 amino acids, such as substance P and enkephalin) are made in the cell body.
  • Skip the receptor-family figure. Know that only cells with the matching receptor respond, and that a signal is relayed by phosphorylation and second messengers (cAMP, Ca2+), often to transcription factors that change which proteins the cell makes.

2 Oncogenes versus tumor suppressors (two hits), p53, RB, BRCA and HPV, inherited cancer syndromes, and benign versus malignant

Slides + study guide · 3 questions in the bank

  • Tumor suppressors ("removing the brakes"; over 30 are known): both copies must be lost, Knudson's two-hit hypothesis; the loss is usually a deletion, sometimes a point mutation, and DNA tumor viruses (HPV, SV40, adenovirus) bind their proteins. RB (retinoblastoma: sporadic cases need two somatic hits; inherited cases need one more hit beside the inherited one, so they are found earlier and are often in both eyes, and the susceptibility passes to half of an affected parent's children), p53 (stops the cycle or triggers apoptosis after DNA damage; abnormal in over half of cancers; an inherited TP53 mutation is Li-Fraumeni syndrome, many cancers at young ages), APC (colon: an inherited APC mutation is familial adenomatous polyposis, hundreds to thousands of polyps).
  • An inherited first hit is in every cell, gametes included, so cancer comes earlier and more often, and the tumor grows wherever the second hit happens. High-risk HPV (types 16 and 18) causes oropharyngeal and cervical cancer: its E6 protein degrades p53 and E7 inactivates RB.

3 Chargaff's rule, replication enzymes, leading and lagging strands, and telomerase

Slides + study guide · 3 questions in the bank

The two strands are antiparallel and complementary, so double-stranded DNA always has as much A as T and as much G as C (Chargaff's rule): DNA that is 30% A is also 30% T, and the other 40% is 20% G and 20% C. Replication is semiconservative (each daughter has one old and one new strand) and happens in S phase. It starts at origins (one in bacteria, many in eukaryotes) and runs both ways from each. Polymerases add only to a free 3′-OH, so new DNA grows 5′ → 3′. The leading strand is made continuously toward the fork; the lagging strand is made away from it in short Okazaki fragments, each also built 5′ → 3′.

4 Transcription: σ and promoters, the lac operon, the three eukaryotic polymerases and epigenetic switches

Slides + study guide · 1 question in the bank

The lac operon: lacZ, lacY, lacA share one promoter and operator. Negative control: the lacI repressor binds the operator; allolactose (from lactose) pulls it off. A lacI mutant with no working repressor makes the lac enzymes all the time (constitutive expression). Positive control: when glucose is low, cAMP rises and the CAP–cAMP complex binds upstream, bends the DNA and recruits polymerase. Transcription is highest with lactose present and glucose absent; glucose and lactose together give only low expression (catabolite repression).

5 RNA versus DNA, RNA processing and translation

Slides + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • 5′ cap: 7-methylguanosine joined by a 5′–5′ triphosphate bond. Needed for export, translation and stability. RNA polymerase I and III products are uncapped.

6 Types of mutation, mutagens and the inherited diseases of the teeth

Core of the slides · 2 questions in the bank

  • Point mutations: a transition swaps purine for purine or pyrimidine for pyrimidine; a transversion swaps a purine for a pyrimidine. By effect: silent (a synonymous codon: AAA and AAG both code lysine), missense (another amino acid, with a severe, mild or no effect; sickle cell, Glu → Val, mRNA GAG → GUG, a transversion), nonsense (premature stop, truncated protein; some cystic fibrosis alleles) and splice-site (an intron is kept in the message or an exon is skipped).

Inherited diseases of the teeth: amelogenesis imperfecta (abnormal enamel: small, discolored, pitted or grooved teeth that wear and break), dentinogenesis imperfecta (abnormal dentin: blue-gray or yellow-brown, translucent, weak teeth) and ectodermal dysplasia (skin, hair, nails, sweat glands and teeth: missing teeth, or small, pointed ones).

You can skip

  • Skip how many hours each cell type takes to divide. Know the point: some cancers divide more slowly than some normal cells, and a tumor outgrows its tissue because a larger share of its cells are dividing.

1 Enzyme definitions: catalytic power, specificity and regulation; the active site; cofactors, coenzymes, prosthetic groups, apoenzyme and holoenzyme; lock and key versus induced fit

Objectives + slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • The definitions: an enzyme's catalytic power, specificity and regulation; coenzyme, cofactor, holoenzyme, apoenzyme and active site; how enzymes affect a reaction's thermodynamics; Km and Vmax; the turnover number (kcat) and catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km); single- versus double-displacement reactions; lock and key versus induced fit.
  • ΔG, the overall free energy change, is related to the equilibrium constant (how far a reaction goes); ΔG‡, the free energy of activation, is related to the rate constant (how fast). Enzymes lower ΔG‡ only.

Enzymes have catalytic power (the ratio of the catalyzed to the uncatalyzed rate, up to about 10^16), specificity (choosing the right substrate and giving yields often above 95%, set by the structure of the active site, the pocket where the substrate binds and the reaction happens) and regulation (substrate and cofactor supply, allosteric control, how much enzyme is made and broken down). They lower the activation energy (ΔG‡) by binding the transition state most tightly; they don't change ΔG or the equilibrium. Keep the two apart: ΔG is related to the equilibrium constant (how far a reaction goes), ΔG‡ to the rate constant (how fast). Lock and key was the first model of specificity (a rigid site that fits the substrate); induced fit is more accurate: substrate binding changes the enzyme's shape and favors the transition state; in hexokinase two domains close around glucose to form the catalytic site. Enzymes work in a pH range (ionizable side chains) and speed up with temperature, roughly doubling every 10 °C, until they denature (activity falls above about 50–60 °C). Not all enzymes are proteins: ribozymes are catalytic RNAs (RNase P, the ribosome's peptidyl transferase), and abzymes are antibodies raised against a transition state.

  • Cofactors are usually metal ions (Mg2+ for hexokinase, K+ for pyruvate kinase, Zn2+ for DNA polymerase). Coenzymes are organic, often from vitamins (NAD+ from niacin, FAD from riboflavin, TPP from thiamine), and carry groups or electrons. A tightly bound one is a prosthetic group. The protein alone is the apoenzyme; with its cofactor or coenzyme it is the holoenzyme.

2 How enzymes affect a reaction's thermodynamics: they lower ΔG‡ (the rate constant), never ΔG (the equilibrium constant)

Objectives + slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

ΔG = ΔH − TΔS at constant temperature and pressure. ΔG < 0: exergonic, spontaneous. ΔG > 0: endergonic, needs coupling to an exergonic process. ΔG = 0: equilibrium. A process is spontaneous when the system gives up energy (ΔH negative), gains disorder (ΔS positive) or both, and the more negative ΔG, the more work it can do: oxidizing glucose to CO2 and water has ΔG = −686 kcal/mol (−2,870 kJ/mol); photosynthesis, the endergonic reverse, runs on sunlight. ΔG says nothing about speed: ΔG°′ = −RT ln K′eq links it to the equilibrium constant, while the free energy of activation (ΔG‡) sets the rate constant. Unfolding a protein absorbs heat (ΔH positive) and raises entropy.

3 Km, Vmax, the turnover number (kcat) and catalytic efficiency (kcat/Km)

Objectives + slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Michaelis-Menten (E + S ⇌ ES → E + P): v = Vmax[S] / (Km + [S]). Km = (k−1 + k2)/k1 is the [S] that gives half of Vmax and, under true Michaelis-Menten conditions, estimates the enzyme–substrate dissociation constant; a low Km means tight binding (high affinity). At low [S] the rate is first order in substrate; at saturating [S] it is zero order and approaches Vmax, a theoretical maximum that is approached but never reached (it would need every enzyme molecule bound to substrate) and that rises with the amount of enzyme. kcat (turnover number) = Vmax / [enzyme]: substrate molecules converted per enzyme per second at saturation. kcat/Km is catalytic efficiency at low [S]; its ceiling is the diffusion limit (about 10^8–10^9 per molar per second). The ES complex reaches a steady state.

4 Single- versus double-displacement (ping-pong) two-substrate reactions and their Lineweaver-Burk patterns

Objectives + slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Bisubstrate reactions: single-displacement (sequential: both substrates bind before any product leaves; ordered or random, as in creatine kinase) and double-displacement (ping-pong: the first product leaves before the second substrate binds, through a covalently modified enzyme, as in glutamate–aspartate aminotransferase). On Lineweaver-Burk plots, sequential reactions give lines that cross to the left of the 1/v axis; ping-pong reactions give parallel lines.

5 Thermodynamic systems, the three laws, enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs free energy (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS)

Objectives + slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • What a thermodynamic system is (isolated, closed, open), the three laws, enthalpy and entropy, Gibbs free energy (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS), ATP's ionization states and its free energy of hydrolysis, and the kinds of biological work.

Systems are isolated (no exchange), closed (energy only) or open (energy and matter: living cells). First law: energy is neither created nor destroyed; ΔE = q + w (the heat absorbed plus the work done on the system), and internal energy is a state function (it depends on the state, not the path). Second law: every real energy transfer increases the entropy of the universe. Third law: a perfect crystal has zero entropy at 0 K. Energy units: joules (SI) or calories (1 cal = 4.184 J).

6 ATP: its free energy of hydrolysis, Mg2+, and energy coupling to the cell's three kinds of work

Objectives + slides · 1 question in the bank

ATP is the cell's energy shuttle: ATP + H2O → ADP + Pi has ΔG°′ of about −30.5 kJ/mol (−7.3 kcal/mol). The energy comes from the products' lower free energy, not from the phosphate bonds themselves. ATP has four ionizable protons and in cells is bound to Mg2+, which stabilizes its phosphates. Phosphoryl transfer has a high activation energy (200–400 kJ/mol), so ATP keeps until an enzyme uses it. Energy coupling: an exergonic process (ATP hydrolysis) drives an endergonic one, for the cell's three kinds of work: mechanical (muscle contraction, cilia), transport (across membranes) and chemical (nonspontaneous synthesis, such as making proteins). The body holds only about 50 g of ATP and ADP but turns over about 65 kg of ATP a day, so each molecule is recycled nearly 1,300 times a day.

7 Steroid hormones: the three types and what they do, synthesis from cholesterol (mitochondrial P450 side-chain cleavage with NADPH and O2), carriers, intracellular receptors and the adrenal disorders

Objectives + slides + study guide · 4 questions in the bank

Know this
  • The three types (glucocorticoids, mineralocorticoids, sex steroids) and what each does; synthesis from cholesterol in the adrenal cortex and gonads, starting in mitochondria, by P450 oxidations that need NADPH and O2; examples with their disorders (Cushing, Conn, Addison); and the mechanism: carrier proteins, then an intracellular receptor that changes transcription.
  • Steroid synthesis is oxidative: mitochondrial P450 side-chain cleavage uses NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway and O2 to turn cholesterol into pregnenolone.

Three types: glucocorticoids (carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism; immunosuppression), mineralocorticoids (salt and water recovery by the kidney) and sex steroids (androgens and estrogens: the sex organs and their function; pregnancy). Made in the adrenal cortex (glomerulosa: aldosterone; fasciculata: cortisol; reticularis: androgens) and the gonads (testosterone mostly from the testes, with some from the ovaries and adrenals; estrogen mostly from the ovaries, with smaller amounts from fat, liver and breast). ACTH from the anterior pituitary drives the adrenal synthesis of cortisol and androgens. The first and rate-limiting step, in mitochondria, cleaves cholesterol's side chain (side-chain cleavage, desmolase) to make pregnenolone. Over a dozen enzymes take part, most of them cytochrome P450 mixed-function oxidases whose main job is to modify cholesterol's tail: the synthesis is an oxidation that needs O2 and NADPH (from the pentose phosphate pathway).
