8 Enzyme inhibition on a Lineweaver-Burk plot: competitive, noncompetitive, uncompetitive and irreversible, with examples (malonate, lithium, penicillin)

Slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Examples. Competitive: malonate at succinate dehydrogenase (the classic case: it resembles succinate), methotrexate with dihydrofolate at dihydrofolate reductase, statins at HMG-CoA reductase, and sildenafil, which resembles cGMP, at phosphodiesterase 5 (more cGMP relaxes vascular smooth muscle). Uncompetitive: lithium at inositol monophosphatase, its target in bipolar disorder. Pure noncompetitive inhibition (equal binding to E and ES) is uncommon. Irreversible inhibitors bind for good, usually covalently: penicillin is a suicide inhibitor of the bacterial transpeptidase that cross-links the cell wall, aspirin acetylates cyclooxygenase, organophosphates block acetylcholinesterase. Allosteric enzymes give sigmoidal curves, not Michaelis-Menten.

9 Catabolic versus anabolic pathways, oxidation and reduction, NAD+ versus NADPH, and which tissues burn which fuel

Objectives + slides · 1 question in the bank

  • Catabolic pathways break molecules down: oxidative, exergonic, and they reduce NAD+ to NADH. Anabolic pathways build: reductive, endergonic, and they spend NADPH and ATP.

10 Peptide versus steroid hormones, the second-messenger pathways and insulin

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Chemical classes: amino acid–derived (thyroxine and catecholamines from tyrosine), peptides and proteins (insulin, oxytocin, growth hormone), steroids (from cholesterol), fatty acid–derived (eicosanoids).
  • Gs stimulates adenylyl cyclase → cAMP → protein kinase A. PKA is two regulatory and two catalytic subunits; cAMP binds the regulatory subunits (four sites in all) and frees the active catalytic ones. Phosphodiesterase breaks cAMP down (caffeine blocks it). Gs examples: glycogen breakdown in liver, fat breakdown in adipose tissue, water conservation in the kidney (ADH). Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase (slows the heart).
  • Gq activates phospholipase C, which splits PIP2 into IP3 (releases Ca2+ from the ER) and DAG (with Ca2+ activates protein kinase C).

Also flagged in class

  • Lineweaver-Burk is the reciprocal of Michaelis-Menten: 1/v = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax, so the y-intercept is 1/Vmax, the x-intercept −1/Km and the slope Km/Vmax.

You can skip

  • Skip the metabolic map's details. Know the major pathways and what each one does: glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, gluconeogenesis, the urea cycle, fatty acid β-oxidation and the pentose phosphate pathway.

5 Glycogen synthesis and breakdown: glycogenin, branching and debranching, phosphorolysis

Objectives + slides + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Synthesis: glucose 6-phosphate → glucose 1-phosphate (phosphoglucomutase) → UDP-glucose ("activated glucose", made from UTP; hydrolysis of the pyrophosphate released makes the step irreversible) → glycogen synthase (rate-limiting; adds glucose in α-1,4 links to the nonreducing ends of chains, starting from glycogenin, a primer protein that attaches the first glucose residues to one of its own tyrosines) → branching enzyme (once a chain is at least 11 residues long, moves a block of about 7 to make each α-1,6 branch).
  • Breakdown: glycogen phosphorylase (rate-limiting) cleaves α-1,4 links at the nonreducing ends with phosphate (phosphorolysis, unlike the gut's α-amylase, which hydrolyzes them), releasing glucose 1-phosphate, and stops 4 residues from a branch (the limit dextrin). The debranching enzyme moves 3 of them, then frees the last as free glucose (α-1,6-glucosidase). Liver's glucose 6-phosphatase releases glucose to the blood; muscle has none.

6 Pyruvate's fates and the PDH complex: lactate dehydrogenase, the five coenzymes, and regulation by phosphorylation

Objectives + slides · 1 question in the bank

  • With oxygen: pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix, where the pyruvate dehydrogenase (PDH) complex makes acetyl-CoA, CO2 and NADH. The step is irreversible, so acetyl-CoA can't become glucose. Five coenzymes: thiamine pyrophosphate (B1), lipoic acid, CoA (B5), FAD (B2), NAD+ (B3). It is three enzymes in one complex. Its products acetyl-CoA and NADH, and ATP, turn it off, mainly by activating PDH kinase, which phosphorylates the E1 enzyme (phosphorylated PDH is inactive); a phosphatase turns it back on, and pyruvate, ADP, NAD+ and CoA keep it active. Thiamine deficiency and arsenic (which binds lipoic acid) block it.

Study guide + slides · 1 question in the bank

  • NK cells (large granular lymphocytes, CD16 and CD56) have no TCR and need no priming by an APC. Their receptors are inhibitory (ITIM motifs) or activating (ITAM motifs), and they kill when activating signals outweigh inhibitory ones. Many inhibitory receptors bind MHC I, so a cell that loses MHC I ("missing self") is killed; NK cells sense how much MHC I a cell has, not which peptide it shows. CD16 (an FcγR) lets them kill IgG-coated cells (ADCC). They kill with the same perforin, granzymes and Fas–FasL as CTLs. IFN-α/β and IL-12 activate them; they make IFN-γ, which activates macrophages, an inflammatory feedback loop.

7 Mucosal immunity keeps tolerance: M cells and dendritic cells sample the lumen; epithelial TGF-β, IL-10, retinoic acid and short-chain fatty acids keep dendritic cells and macrophages calm; Tregs abound; mucosal macrophages give no respiratory burst; the poly-Ig receptor binds the J chain, carrying dimeric IgA and pentameric IgM into secretions

Objectives + slides · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Tregs (CD4+, CD25+, FoxP3+) can't form without FoxP3; their TGF-β and IL-10 suppress self-reactive cells and calm inflammation.
  • Secretory antibody: plasma cells in the lamina propria make dimeric IgA. The poly-Ig receptor on the epithelium binds the J chain of polymeric antibody and carries it across the cell; part of the receptor stays on as secretory component, protecting it from proteases. So pentameric IgM, which also has a J chain, can be carried out too, while monomeric IgA, with no J chain, can't. IgA dominates secretions only because most mucosal plasma cells make IgA. TGF-β drives IgA switching.
  • Tolerance (inflammation only when absolutely needed, to spare the barrier): epithelial cells release TGF-β, IL-10, retinoic acid and short-chain fatty acids, which keep dendritic cells and macrophages tolerant. Tolerant dendritic cells secrete TGF-β, which drives naive CD4 T cells to become Tregs (CD4+, CD25+, FoxP3+); Tregs are plentiful and make IL-10. Mucosal macrophages are highly phagocytic but hyporesponsive to PAMPs and DAMPs: they destroy what they eat in lysosomes with no respiratory burst, make no proinflammatory cytokines, carry no activation or costimulatory molecules and favor Tregs. Monocytes recruited to replace them take on the same anti-inflammatory character.

1 IgG crosses the placenta and IgM does not: Rh hemolytic disease of the newborn in a later pregnancy, prevented by anti-D (RhoGAM)

Core of the slides · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • In Rh disease the mother's first anti-RhD is IgM, which stays on her side; in a later Rh-positive pregnancy her memory B cells switch to IgG, which crosses the placenta and destroys fetal red cells. Anti-D (RhoGAM) prevents the first sensitization.
  • Type II: mostly IgG on a cell-surface protein. The cell dies by complement's membrane attack complex (IgG or IgM), by phagocytosis or ADCC through Fc receptors (NK cells), or it loses function. Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn: a first Rh-positive pregnancy sensitizes an Rh-negative mother, whose first anti-RhD is IgM, which can't cross the placenta; in a later pregnancy her memory B cells switch to IgG, which does, and destroys fetal red cells. Anti-RhD is the most dangerous; other blood-group antigens (Kell, Rh c and E) can do it too if they raise IgG. Anti-D immune globulin (RhoGAM) is anti-RhD IgG: fetal red cells coated with it don't activate her naive B cells. A drug such as penicillin stuck to red cells makes a neoantigen (drug-induced hemolytic anemia). In myasthenia gravis the antibody blocks the acetylcholine receptor without complement or Fc receptors: loss of function.

2 HLA links to autoimmunity are a correlation, not a cause: HLA-B27 (about 90% of ankylosing spondylitis), DR4 (rheumatoid arthritis), DQ2/DQ8 (celiac disease)

Slides + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • An HLA allele raises the risk of an autoimmune disease by deciding which peptides are shown, but it doesn't cause it: about 90% of people with ankylosing spondylitis carry HLA-B27, and DR4 goes with rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Genes: MHC (HLA) differences sit mostly in the peptide-binding groove, so an allele decides which peptides are shown and how strongly T cells respond. HLA-B27: ankylosing spondylitis, carried by about 90% of patients: inflamed entheses (where ligaments and tendons insert) of the spine, which fuses, and uveitis in about half. HLA-DR4 (DRβ1*04): rheumatoid arthritis. Peptidyl arginine deiminases (PADs) turn arginine into citrulline as cells die; the immune system normally never sees it because phagocytes clear apoptotic cells, but when clearance fails, citrullinated joint proteins (vimentin, collagen, fibrinogen) bind DR4's groove better and CD4 T cells respond. HLA-DQ2/DQ8: celiac disease (gluten deamidated by tissue transglutaminase). DR3/DR4: type 1 diabetes. Each is a correlation, not a cause. Sex and hormones matter too: most autoimmune diseases are more common in women.

  • Type III: IgG binds soluble antigen, and the small complexes are cleared poorly, lodge in small vessels and fix complement; the inflammation makes vessels leaky and destroys the tissue around them, and phagocytes can't engulf complexes stuck to a wall (frustrated phagocytosis), so it is hard to resolve. Localized: the Arthus reaction, 4–8 hours after antigen enters the skin of someone who already has IgG to it: a large red, swollen area (some insect bites; rarely a tetanus or diphtheria vaccine). Systemic: serum sickness, from foreign serum proteins (antivenom in the past, drugs now): an itchy rash, arthritis and fever days to weeks later; and SLE, where antinuclear antibodies (probably from poorly cleared apoptotic cells; anti-dsDNA is highly specific) form complexes that deposit in tissues.
  • Type IV: T-cell initiated, mostly Th1 cells (IFN-γ activates macrophages), with CD8 CTLs that lyse cells. Sensitization takes at least 7 days; the effector reaction comes 24–72 hours after re-exposure. Contact hypersensitivity, the most common type IV: small chemicals (nickel, urushiol from poison ivy, glove accelerators) bind skin proteins and make neoantigens; Langerhans cells carry them to the node. The tuberculin test is read at 48–72 hours; its firm red lump is mostly macrophages, not neutrophils. Persistent microbes (M. tuberculosis) keep macrophages activated: they turn epithelioid and fuse into multinucleated giant cells, forming granulomas that wall the organism off but damage tissue. Celiac disease: CD4 T cells react to deamidated gluten peptides (a neoantigen) in the gut's lymphoid tissue, and the macrophages they activate destroy the epithelium. Type 1 diabetes: CD8 T cells lyse the insulin-making β cells, helped by CD4 T cells and macrophages.

6 Lymphocyte development and tolerance: positive and negative selection, AIRE, Tregs, anergy

Slides + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Double positive (CD4+CD8+) cells undergo positive selection in the cortex: the TCR must bind self-MHC weakly. No binding → death by neglect (most thymocytes). Binding class I → CD8; class II → CD4.
  • Negative selection, at the single-positive stage, mainly in the medulla (epithelial cells using AIRE, a transcription factor that switches on proteins from tissues all over the body, and dendritic cells): binding self peptide or self-MHC too strongly → apoptosis, or for some, becoming a Treg.
  • Central tolerance happens in the primary organs as lymphocytes develop. AIRE lets the thymus show proteins normally made elsewhere (insulin, parathyroid and adrenal proteins). AIRE loss = APS-1 (APECED): chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency.

7 Triggers of autoimmunity: molecular mimicry, bystander activation, cryptic antigens and epitope spreading in pemphigus

Slides + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Bystander activation: an infection's inflammation activates dendritic cells that are presenting self peptides, and with their new costimulation they activate self-reactive T cells in the lymphoid tissue by mistake.
  • Epitope spreading: the response starts on one epitope of a molecule and moves to other epitopes of the same molecule, then to other molecules. Pemphigus vulgaris, the most serious bullous disease (type II: IgG and C3 on the cadherins of keratinocyte desmosomes; oral ulcers and skin blisters), starts with antibodies to desmoglein 3 (mouth) and later adds desmoglein 1 (skin); the spread tracks the disease getting worse.

8 Dental reactions: glove and nickel dermatitis (type IV) versus latex and penicillin anaphylaxis (type I)

Study guide + slides · 1 question in the bank

  • Gloves: natural rubber latex proteins cause type I reactions (hives, swelling, wheezing in minutes); accelerators in gloves cause type IV contact dermatitis (1–2 days later); irritant dermatitis isn't immune at all.

You can skip

  • Skip the poly-A and splice sites; know that one RNA transcript spliced two ways, not DNA recombination, lets a mature naive B cell carry IgM and IgD together.

1 Epithelium classification and where each type lines the body, oral mucosa included

Slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Epithelium covers body surfaces and lines cavities, a border between two environments, and forms glands. It comes from all three germ layers (the epidermis from ectoderm, endothelium and mesothelium from mesoderm, the gut lining from endoderm). It is polarized (an apical domain facing the lumen and a basolateral domain on the basement membrane), avascular (fed by diffusion from the connective tissue), tightly joined, and sits on a basement membrane: the basal lamina (lamina lucida with laminin; lamina densa with type IV collagen), made by the epithelial cells, plus a reticular lamina of type III collagen from the connective tissue. Seen together by light microscopy, the two layers are the PAS-positive basement membrane. In the glomerulus and the lung's alveolar wall, two cell layers share one fused basal lamina.

2 Reversible versus irreversible injury: swelling comes first; nuclear changes, membrane rupture and necrosis mean the cell has died

Slides + objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Reversible injury goes back to normal if the cause is removed. The first sign is cell swelling (the ATP-driven sodium pump fails and water follows sodium in). Others: plasma membrane blebs, dilated ER with ribosomes falling off, swollen mitochondria, fatty change, myelin figures and clumped chromatin. The organ is heavier and firmer.

3 Apoptosis versus necrosis, and the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways

Slides + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Swelling is the first, reversible change. Karyorrhexis, karyolysis, a ruptured membrane, leaking contents, enzymatic digestion and necrosis with inflammation all mean the injury is irreversible.
  • Apoptosis can be physiologic or pathologic and causes no inflammation; necrosis is always pathologic and brings inflammation.
ApoptosisNecrosis

  • Intrinsic (mitochondrial): loss of survival signals, DNA damage or radiation → sensors block BCL2 → mitochondrial channels open → cytochrome c leaks out → caspases.
  • Extrinsic (death receptor): the cell carries death receptors (Fas, the type I TNF receptor); Fas ligand on a cytotoxic T cell binds Fas on the target cell → death domain adaptors → caspases.

4 Acute inflammation: leukocyte recruitment steps, the main mediators, neutrophils versus macrophages

Slides + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

TNF and IL-1 from macrophages make the endothelium put out selectins and integrin ligands; chemokines raise the integrins' grip and set the leukocyte's direction. Most mediators come from macrophages, dendritic cells and mast cells at the site and are short-lived.

5 Acute versus chronic inflammation, M1 and M2 macrophages, granulomas and the morphologic patterns (serous, fibrinous, purulent, abscess, ulcer)

Slides + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Acute: neutrophils, congestion and edema, tissue preserved, can resolve. Chronic: macrophages, lymphocytes and plasma cells, tissue destroyed and replaced by fibrosis, with loss of function.
  • Serous = cell-poor fluid (blister, effusion); fibrinous = fibrinogen leaks and fibrin coats the pericardium or pleura (adhesions if not cleared); purulent = neutrophils and liquefied debris, which can wall off into an abscess; ulcer = a surface defect from sloughed necrotic tissue.

Morphologic patterns (acute and chronic): serous (cell-poor fluid under a surface epithelium or in a serous cavity: a blister, an effusion), fibrinous (fibrinogen leaks and fibrin lines the pericardium or pleura; fibrinolysis and macrophages clear it, or it leaves adhesions), purulent (suppurative: neutrophils and liquefied debris of necrotic cells, from pyogenic bacteria such as staphylococci and streptococci; e.g., acute appendicitis, bacterial meningitis), abscess (pus localized in a tissue: a necrotic center with a rim of inflammatory cells), ulcer (a crater where inflamed necrotic tissue sloughs off a surface: mouth, gut, genitourinary tract, and the legs with poor circulation; acute and chronic inflammation together, a scar if it lasts; e.g., acute necrotizing ulcerative stomatitis) and granulomatous (below).

  • Causes: persistent infection (mycobacteria, some viruses, fungi, parasites), hypersensitivity (autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis or multiple sclerosis; allergy such as asthma), long toxic exposure (silica in silicosis; cholesterol in atherosclerosis). Histology: lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells, tissue destruction and fibrosis, so function is lost (acute = neutrophils, congestion and edema, tissue preserved, can resolve). Macrophages are the dominant cell: they phagocytose, secrete cytokines and growth factors (TNF, IL-1), activate T cells, and both drive inflammation and start repair.

6 Tumor naming, benign versus malignant, grade versus stage

Slides + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Grade = differentiation under the microscope (1 = well differentiated). Stage = extent: TNM (T = tumor size and invasiveness, N = nodal metastases, M = distant metastases), AJCC stage 0 (carcinoma in situ) to IV; any distant metastasis makes it stage IV. Stage predicts prognosis better than grade.

7 Repair and scar problems (granulation tissue, collagen, keloid versus hypertrophic scar) and acute-phase proteins

Slides + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Slow healing: infection (prolongs inflammation), protein or vitamin C deficiency, steroids (less TGF-β and fibrosis, so a weak scar), pressure or torsion, poor blood flow (arteriolosclerosis, diabetes), foreign bodies. Scar problems: hypertrophic scar (raised, inside the wound, can regress), keloid (grows past the wound edges, doesn't regress), exuberant granulation, contracture (the wound shrinks too much and deforms, as after burns).
  • Acute-phase response (cytokine-driven, whole body): fever (exogenous pyrogens such as bacterial lipopolysaccharide → endogenous pyrogens IL-1 and TNF → prostaglandins set the hypothalamus higher; NSAIDs such as aspirin block it; with a faster pulse, higher blood pressure, shivering, poor appetite and sleepiness), leukocytosis (normal white count 4,500–11,000/µL; often 15,000–20,000/µL in inflammation; 40,000–100,000/µL is a leukemoid reaction, which can mimic leukemia: first the marrow releases stored cells, including immature ones, then colony-stimulating factors make more), and liver proteins: CRP (binds microbial walls and complement, an opsonin; heart-attack risk marker), fibrinogen (sticks red cells together, raising the sedimentation rate), serum amyloid A (opsonin; long exposure causes secondary amyloidosis), hepcidin (holds iron: anemia of chronic disease). Sepsis is a severe acute-phase response to bacterial infection that can bring septic shock: low blood pressure, disseminated intravascular coagulation, metabolic trouble such as insulin resistance.

Know this

ATP falls: the Na+/K+ pump fails (swelling) and protein synthesis stops; severe, lasting ischemia finally breaks the mitochondrial and lysosomal membranes (necrosis)

Made by mitochondrial respiration, the phagocytes' respiratory burst, reperfusion and ionizing radiation; they damage lipids (peroxidation), proteins and DNA. 9 Adaptations with an example of each, and dystrophic versus metastatic calcification

Slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Metastatic calcification: high serum calcium (bone destroyed by cancer, hyperparathyroidism, vitamin D excess, kidney failure) deposits in normal tissue. Dystrophic: normal calcium, damaged tissue (atheroma, damaged valves).
  • Dystrophic calcification: normal serum calcium, deposits in damaged tissue (atheroma, old heart valves, necrosis).
  • Metastatic calcification: high serum calcium (hyperparathyroidism, bone destroyed by cancer such as metastatic carcinoma, vitamin D excess, kidney failure), deposits in normal tissue (vessels, kidneys, the lungs' alveolar septa, stomach).

Also flagged in class

  • Know an example of each adaptation: disuse atrophy of skeletal muscle, hypertrophy of the heart in hypertension, hyperplasia (more cells, as in the prostate) and metaplasia (columnar to squamous in a smoker's bronchus). Anthracosis is carbon in the lung; alcohol makes a yellow fatty liver that can go on to cirrhosis.
  • Neutrophils are first and fast and live 1–2 days in tissue (degranulation, respiratory burst). Macrophages dominate chronic inflammation, live days to weeks (tissue-resident ones for years) and make nitric oxide and cytokines after new gene transcription.
  • Granulation tissue (new vessels, fibroblasts, little collagen) comes first; collagen laid down in remodeling gives the scar its strength. A keloid is scar overgrowth past the wound's edges.
  • Whether a tumor is benign or malignant sets the treatment: conservative or wide excision, lymph node staging, chemotherapy or radiation. Metastasis is the hallmark of malignancy; benign tumors are well differentiated, slow, often encapsulated and don't invade.

5 Influenza: hemagglutinin and neuraminidase, drift versus shift, and the hemagglutination inhibition assay

Objectives + slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Influenza (orthomyxovirus; spherical; 8 segments; RdRp and the nuclear export protein are packaged in the virion): hemagglutinin (HA) binds sialic acid to attach; neuraminidase (NA) cleaves sialic acid to free new virus (blocked by oseltamivir, zanamivir and peramivir). HA and NA are the main antigens. The sialic acid–galactose link differs by species: human strains bind α2,6, bird strains α2,3, and pigs carry both, so they can be infected by both and mix them; the HA sequence decides which species a strain infects. Drift = point mutations, above all in the antigenic sites around HA's receptor-binding site; gradual, in all strains, yearly epidemics and the reason the vaccine is updated. Shift = segments swapped (reassortment) between strains; sudden, a new HA or NA, influenza A only, pandemics.
  • Hemagglutination inhibition (HI): red cells alone settle into a tight dot (a button) at the bottom of a well; influenza HA cross-links them into a diffuse mat (hemagglutination). Antibody against HA in a serum sample blocks that, so the dot comes back. The HI titer is the highest dilution of serum that still blocks hemagglutination: a high titer against a strain means neutralizing antibody and protection, and a low titer against a new strain (after drift or shift) means vaccinated people are poorly protected.

6 Negative-sense RNA viruses: the packaged RdRp, the 3′ gradient and the N switch; measles and Koplik spots

Objectives + slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • (−)ssRNA: all enveloped with helical nucleocapsids; the genome is linear (paramyxo-, pneumo- and rhabdoviruses) or segmented (influenza). It can't be read as mRNA, so the genome alone is not infectious: humans have no RdRp, and the virion carries its own (L, with its cofactor P) on the genome, which nucleocapsid protein (N) coats; matrix (M) lines the envelope and the glycoprotein (G) attaches. mRNA is made in one step. The RdRp starts at the genome's 3′ end and makes one capped, polyadenylated mRNA per gene, stopping at each gene junction (stuttering there adds the poly(A) tail) and scanning on for the next start. It often falls off at a junction and must restart at the 3′ end (attenuation), so genes near the 3′ end make the most mRNA: gene position sets expression. Nonsegmented viruses cap their own mRNAs; influenza takes caps from host mRNAs (cap snatching). While free N is low, the polymerase makes mRNAs; once N builds up, it makes full-length, N-coated antigenomes, the templates for new genomes. One gene can make more than one protein by alternative splicing, alternative initiation (leaky scanning) or ribosomal frameshifting (−1 at an RNA fold, +1 at a rare codon; not only in these viruses).
  • Measles (paramyxovirus; H and F glycoproteins; nonsegmented; kills cells and fuses them into syncytia): extremely contagious by aerosols and droplets (it stays in the air up to 2 hours) and infectious before symptoms; the "3 Cs" (cough, coryza, conjunctivitis), then rash; Koplik spots (blue-white specks on red buccal mucosa) come first; MMR live attenuated vaccine, with outbreaks where vaccination is low.

7 Positive-sense RNA viruses: infectious genomes, the picornavirus polyprotein and coronavirus subgenomic mRNAs

Objectives + slides · 1 question in the bank

  • (+)ssRNA: naked (icosahedral: picornaviruses, norovirus) or enveloped (coronavirus, rubella); every genome is linear, with a 5′ cap or a VPg protein on its end. The genome is mRNA, so it is infectious by itself and is translated as soon as it enters; no polymerase comes in the virion. It is self-replicating: it encodes its replication enzymes (RdRp first), proteins that block the innate immune response and the structural proteins. Then two steps: RdRp copies the genome into a full-length (−) antigenome, the template for new genomes and mRNAs; some (coronaviruses) also make shorter subgenomic mRNAs for single genes. Replication runs in cytoplasmic "viral factories" (inclusion bodies that shield it from host defenses); its dsRNA intermediates are what the sensors RIG-I and MDA5 detect.
  • Coronaviruses: the largest RNA viruses (26–32 kb genomes), enveloped, with a helical nucleocapsid. SARS-CoV-2 first infects ciliated cells of the nasopharynx and trachea; its spike binds ACE2 and is cut by TMPRSS2. The genomic mRNA is translated into the ORF1a and ORF1b polyproteins, cut into 16 nonstructural proteins that build the replication complex (with RdRp); the structural and accessory proteins come from subgenomic mRNAs. Severe disease comes from immunothrombosis in the alveoli.

8 Virus basics: enveloped versus naked, the Baltimore classes and the life cycle

Objectives + slides · 1 question in the bank

Life cycle: attachment (adsorption) → entry → uncoating → transcription, replication and translation (every virus uses host ribosomes) → assembly → release. Entry: naked viruses enter by receptor-mediated endocytosis; enveloped ones fuse their envelope with the plasma membrane or, after endocytosis, with the endosome's membrane, where the low pH changes the shape of the viral proteins. Uncoating frees the genome, sometimes with the help of host endosomal proteases. DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus, except the poxviruses, which bring their own enzymes and replicate in the cytoplasm. Most RNA viruses stay in the cytoplasm. Assembly (building the capsid and packaging the genome) is usually spontaneous. Naked viruses assemble in the cytoplasm or nucleus and are usually released by lysis; enveloped ones take their envelope at the plasma membrane (released by budding) or at the ER or Golgi (released by exocytosis), usually without killing the cell.

You can skip

  • Skip the step-by-step scheme of how SARS-CoV-2 replicates its genome and makes its mRNAs. Know that its genomic mRNA makes the ORF1a and ORF1b polyproteins (the replication proteins) and that its structural proteins come from subgenomic mRNAs.
  • Know the Baltimore classes and the main virus families, not the ICTV realm, kingdom, phylum, class and order names.

1 Oxygen needs, the growth curve and the three ways to make ATP

Slides + objectives + study guide · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Obligate aerobes need O2 and can't ferment; facultative anaerobes respire with or without O2 or ferment; obligate anaerobes die in O2 because they lack superoxide dismutase and catalase to clear its radicals.
  • Lag (adjusting), log (exponential division; antibiotics, which need growing cells, work best), stationary (nutrients run out; division equals death), death. Bacteria divide by binary fission, which needs new wall.
  • Aerobic respiration (glycolysis, TCA cycle, electron transport at the plasma membrane, O2 as final acceptor) gives 38 ATP; anaerobic respiration ends on nitrate, sulfate or another acceptor and gives less; fermentation (glycolysis only, an organic acceptor) gives 2. Every route needs a final acceptor to regenerate NAD+ and FAD.

Bacteria divide by binary fission: the chromosome (and plasmids) is copied and split between two daughter cells, and the wall is remodeled with new peptidoglycan, which is why β-lactams act on dividing cells. DNA replication starts at one origin and runs both ways around the circle (about 40 minutes in E. coli): the leading strand is made continuously and the lagging strand in Okazaki fragments, whose RNA primers are removed (RNase H) before DNA ligase joins them; topoisomerase separates the two finished chromosomes. Growth curve: lag → log (exponential; drugs work best) → stationary → death.

  • Aerobic respiration: glycolysis (in the cytoplasm), TCA cycle and electron transport (at the plasma membrane); final electron acceptor O2; most ATP (38 per glucose). Every route needs a final electron acceptor to regenerate NAD+ and FAD.
  • Why oxygen kills obligate anaerobes: O2 forms toxic superoxide, hydrogen peroxide, hydroxyl radicals and singlet oxygen. Aerobes and facultative anaerobes turn them into water and O2 with superoxide dismutase, catalase and peroxidase; obligate anaerobes lack these enzymes.

3 Gram-positive versus gram-negative envelope and the gram stain

Slides + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Gram stain: crystal violet → iodine → alcohol (decolorizer) → safranin. The alcohol step decides it: a thick peptidoglycan wall holds the violet (gram-positive, purple); a thin wall under an outer membrane lets it wash out, and the counterstain makes it pink (gram-negative). Shape and arrangement (cocci in clusters or chains, rods, spirals) complete the first identification.

5 S. aureus virulence, abscess and MRSA; S. epidermidis biofilm; S. pneumoniae capsule

Slides + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Staphylococci: clusters, catalase-positive, tough on fomites. S. aureus is coagulase-positive; carried by most people at some point; invades through broken skin or mucosa. Virulence: coagulase (fibrin wall), protein A (binds the Fc of antibody, blocking opsonization), leukocidin (kills neutrophils), hemolysins. When neutrophils can't clear it, the body walls it off: an abscess (liquefactive necrosis in a fibrous capsule) that must be drained, since drugs can't get in. About 90% of strains make β-lactamase; methicillin resists that, but mecA (PBP2a) gives MRSA, treated with vancomycin.

6 Gram-negative rods, MacConkey agar and the periodontal pathogens (red complex, A. actinomycetemcomitans)

Slides + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa: gram-negative rod and non-fermenter (it respires with O2, or with nitrate when O2 is absent; the course's slide calls it a facultative anaerobe), everywhere in the environment, opportunistic, multidrug-resistant; the second leading cause of nosocomial infection (catheters, endoscopes, ventilators); cystic fibrosis lungs, third-degree burns, ICU infants, diabetes, HIV, and long-wear soft lenses (the leading cause of contact-lens ulcerative keratitis); aminoglycosides, which block protein synthesis.
  • Periodontitis (chronic): gram-negative subgingival anaerobes; chronic inflammation, bone loss and tissue damage. The red complex = Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, Treponema denticola. T. denticola (a strict anaerobic spirochete) destroys gingival tissue with proteases and hydrogen sulfide. Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans: localized aggressive periodontitis.

1 Tuberculosis: acid-fast (not gram-positive), latent versus active, the caseating granuloma, the skin test and IGRA, and why treatment takes months of several drugs (the 2 + 4 month regimen)

Slides + study guide · 4 questions in the bank

Know this
  • A cavity holds about 10^9 bacilli and resistance to any one drug arises in 1 in 10^5–10^8, so TB is always treated with several drugs at once: four for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin for 4.
  • For bacterial virulence, know the lecture's own examples; in this part: M. tuberculosis blocking phagolysosome maturation (the granuloma), Rickettsia in endothelium (vasculitis, DIC) and the clostridial toxins (alpha toxin, tetanus, botulinum).
  • Pathogenesis: alveolar macrophages in the airways take up the bacilli first and carry them into the lung tissue; the bacilli block phagolysosome maturation and grow inside a modified phagosome; they later escape by killing the cell (necroptosis). CD4 Th1 cells make IFN-γ (driven by IL-12), which activates the macrophages (M1) to acidify the phagosome to about pH 4.5 and make ROS and NO. The result is the caseating granuloma. Defects in the IL-12/IFN-γ loop, HIV, malnutrition, age, male sex and immunosuppression allow disease or reactivation of latent infection.
  • Tests: the tuberculin skin test (purified protein derivative, PPD: a delayed-type hypersensitivity) and the interferon-γ release assay (IGRA), a blood test whose antigens (ESAT-6, CFP-10) are missing from BCG, so a past BCG vaccine doesn't make it positive; it also needs one visit, gives a result within 24 hours and doesn't boost later tests. For disease: the acid-fast smear, culture and PCR (to confirm M. tuberculosis).
  • Why treatment takes months, with several drugs at once: bacilli hide in granulomas, out of the drugs' reach; the waxy outer membrane has very low fluidity and permeability, the main reason for its intrinsic resistance (β-lactams such as penicillin, vancomycin, macrolides, tetracyclines and sulfonamides don't work); slow, drug-tolerant persisters; and resistance. A lung cavity holds about 10^9 bacilli, while resistance to one drug arises in 1 in 10^5–10^8 (rifampin 1 in 10^8), so any single drug selects resistant mutants (streptomycin alone failed within a year); resistance to isoniazid and rifampin together arises in only 1 in 10^13–10^14. Standard regimen for drug-susceptible TB: isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol and pyrazinamide for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin for 4 months (about 90% cured; about 50% of MDR-TB, 25% of XDR-TB and 70% of TB with HIV). A vaccine (BCG) exists.

2 Fungi: ergosterol in the membrane (not the wall), thermal dimorphism of the true pathogens, the five classes of mycoses, endemic mycoses by region, Candida and the vessel-invading molds

Slides + study guide · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Thermal dimorphism marks the true (endemic) pathogens, Histoplasma, Blastomyces and Coccidioides: mold in the soil, yeast in the body. Most opportunists aren't dimorphic.
  • Yeasts: single oval or round cells that reproduce asexually by budding (the buds are blastoconidia); buds that stretch out and stay attached are pseudohyphae. Molds: multicellular filaments (hyphae, which grow at their tips; septate, with cross walls, or coenocytic, without them and multinucleate) forming a mat, the mycelium; they reproduce by spores (teleomorph = sexual, anamorph = asexual). Fleshy fungi are the mushrooms. Most fungi keep one form (monomorphic); dimorphic fungi switch with temperature: mold in the environment (the saprobic phase), yeast at body temperature (the parasitic phase). Thermal dimorphism is the mark of the true pathogens.

Endemic (true) pathogens infect healthy people who breathe in spores, are limited to certain regions (Histoplasma and Blastomyces follow the Mississippi River and its tributaries) and are thermally dimorphic. Most fungal infections are opportunistic: they come from our own commensals or the environment, strike the immunocompromised (almost any fungus can), are usually not dimorphic and are mostly not communicable. (Histoplasma is a true pathogen that is much worse in the immunosuppressed.) How fungi reach us: inhaled (Histoplasma), inoculated into the skin (Sporothrix), invading from our own flora (Candida) or by contact with an infected host (dermatophytes). How tissue reacts: an acute pyogenic abscess (Candida), a chronic granuloma (Histoplasma), a mixed pus-and-granuloma reaction (Blastomyces), a chronic localized infiltrate in the dermis (dermatophytes), vessel invasion with thrombosis and infarction (Mucor; Aspergillus too), or allergy without a tissue reaction (Aspergillus). Oral candidiasis: white plaques that wipe off leaving a red base, or red atrophic forms under dentures and in angular cheilitis; risks are antibiotics, steroid inhalers, dentures, diabetes, dry mouth and HIV. With S. mutans it raises caries risk.

3 How the lab finds the organism (acid-fast, KOH, PAS and silver, India ink, dark-field, serology, antigen tests, PPD, PCR/NAAT) and the five tissue reactions to infection

Objectives + slides · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Match each test to what it finds: acid-fast stain (TB), KOH, PAS and silver (fungi), India ink (Cryptococcus), dark-field (T. pallidum), serology (hard-to-grow organisms such as Rickettsia and Mycoplasma), antigen tests, the PPD skin test (TB) and PCR (chlamydia and gonorrhea).

Lab, each test with what it finds: the gram stain (gram-positive cocci such as Staphylococcus, gram-negative rods); the acid-fast stain for M. tuberculosis; a KOH preparation for fungi in a scraping (oral thrush); India ink for Cryptococcus's capsule in CSF; dark-field microscopy for Treponema pallidum; on biopsy, PAS and silver (GMS) for fungi (silver also H. pylori); culture, on media chosen for the organism sought (tell the lab when you suspect something unusual); serology (antibodies: exposure), most useful for organisms that can't be grown or grow slowly (Rickettsia, Mycoplasma, hepatitis viruses); antigen detection by ELISA, immunofluorescence or immunohistochemistry (Histoplasma, Aspergillus, Cryptococcus, Legionella, SARS-CoV-2); skin testing (PPD, a delayed-type hypersensitivity, for TB); PCR/NAAT, the test of choice for genital chlamydia and gonorrhea ("CT/NG"), also used for respiratory viruses, C. difficile, Trichomonas and to confirm M. tuberculosis.

5 Neisseria and Chlamydia: capsule, antigenic variation, the EB/RB cycle, NAAT

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Chlamydia: obligate intracellular, cannot make its own ATP; gram-negative-type envelope without much peptidoglycan, so penicillins fail. Cycle: the elementary body (infectious) enters by endocytosis → becomes a reticulate body that divides inside an inclusion → turns back into elementary bodies released at about 48-72 hours. C. trachomatis: the most common bacterial STI, mostly silent, causes infertility; serovars A-C trachoma (a leading infectious cause of blindness), L1-L3 lymphogranuloma venereum (painless ulcer, buboes, proctitis). Test with NAAT; treat with doxycycline (azithromycin in pregnancy). C. pneumoniae: atypical pneumonia; C. psittaci: from bird droppings (psittacosis).

6 Mycoplasma (no wall) and Rocky Mountain spotted fever (doxycycline now)

Slides + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Mycoplasma and Ureaplasma (class Mollicutes): smallest free-living bacteria (0.2–2 µm), permanently without a cell wall (sterols stiffen the membrane), so most stains miss them and β-lactams and vancomycin are useless; they also resist trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and rifampin. Use macrolides, tetracyclines or fluoroquinolones (about 15% of M. pneumoniae in the US now resists macrolides). M. pneumoniae: "walking," atypical pneumonia, mostly in children and adolescents (peak 5–15 years; children, often mildly ill, are the reservoir) and the main syndrome in young adults; droplets, with high household spread; incubation 9–13 days (up to 3 weeks); gradual onset, low fever, headache, myalgia, dry cough, patchy infiltrates rather than lobar consolidation; P1 adhesin binds sialic acid; CARDS toxin strips cilia. Outside the lungs: the skin in about 25% (rashes up to Stevens-Johnson syndrome), mucositis (oral erosions) and conjunctivitis, meningoencephalitis, Bell palsy, myocarditis and cold-agglutinin hemolysis. NAAT/PCR is the most sensitive test (better than antigen tests); serology needs paired sera (antibodies at about 1 week, peaking at 3–6 weeks); culture takes 3 weeks or more. M. salivarium is normal oral flora that can worsen gingivitis and periodontitis in the immunocompromised (also a submasseteric abscess and TMJ pain). Genital: M. genitalium (sexually transmitted urethritis, often silent; about half resist azithromycin) and Ureaplasma (urease-positive: urethritis, epididymo-orchitis, stones) are linked to miscarriage, stillbirth and preterm birth; M. hominis to bacterial vaginosis and postpartum fever; newborns are often colonized at birth.
  • Rickettsia: tiny obligate intracellular gram-negative bacteria (peptidoglycan and LPS) that stain poorly with the gram stain but show with Giemsa; spread by arthropods (ticks, lice, fleas, mites). They infect endothelial cells, escape the phagosome and spread cell to cell on actin tails (the spotted fever group; the typhus group lyses the cell instead), causing necrotizing vasculitis, leaky vessels and possibly DIC, with damage to the brain, eyes, muscles, joints and lungs. Rocky Mountain spotted fever (R. rickettsii, dog and wood ticks; the most common rickettsial illness in the US): about a week after the bite, fever, headache, myalgia, then a petechial rash starting at the wrists and ankles that spreads inward and reaches the palms and soles late; about 23% fatal untreated. Tests (NAAT of blood or a skin biopsy, IgM and IgG serology, immunohistochemistry) need a sample taken while the patient is sick; give doxycycline at once, since confirmation by rising titers comes too late to wait for. Murine typhus (R. typhi, rats and rat fleas) is milder: a rash in only about 18%, on the trunk and limbs, sparing palms and soles.

Also flagged in class

  • Ergosterol is in the fungal plasma membrane: polyenes bind it, and azoles and terbinafine block its synthesis. The wall is chitin, β-glucans and mannoproteins; echinocandins block glucan.
  • M. tuberculosis is found with the acid-fast stain (red fuchsin, acid alcohol, methylene blue): its lipid-rich, mycolic-acid envelope doesn't take the gram stain reliably.

2 Potency versus efficacy, affinity and intrinsic activity, and the kinds of agonists and antagonists

Review + slides + objectives + study guide · 3 questions in the bank

Two properties of a drug decide what it does at a receptor. Affinity is how tightly it binds, measured by the dissociation constant KD, the concentration that fills half the receptors (affinity = 1/KD, so the smaller the KD, the higher the affinity). Intrinsic activity (α) is how well the bound drug activates the receptor: 1 for a full agonist, between 0 and 1 for a partial agonist, 0 for an antagonist. So full agonists, partial agonists and antagonists all have affinity, and a partial agonist has high affinity but low intrinsic activity. Potency reflects both and largely sets the dose. For most drugs the maximal response comes before every receptor is filled; the receptors left unbound are spare receptors.

3 Half-life, clearance, steady state, loading dose and zero-order elimination

Review + slides + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • First-order kinetics: a constant fraction is removed per unit time (most drugs). Zero-order: a constant amount per unit time, because the enzymes are saturated (ethanol, high-dose aspirin, phenytoin). In first order the half-life stays the same at every level; in zero order it has no fixed meaning.
  • With regular dosing, steady state comes after about 4–5 half-lives. After stopping, each half-life halves the level (50%, 25%, 12.5%, 6.25%, about 3% left), so about 4–5 half-lives clear about 94–97% of the drug, and falling to a quarter of a level takes two half-lives.
  • Loading dose = Vd × target concentration (÷ F). Maintenance dose rate = clearance × target concentration (÷ F).

4 Bioavailability, ion trapping, protein binding and volume of distribution

Review + slides + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Most drugs cross membranes by passive diffusion of the un-ionized, lipid-soluble form. At a pH equal to a drug's pKa, half of it is ionized. A weak acid (aspirin) is un-ionized in acid, so much of an oral dose is uncharged in the stomach; a weak base (local anesthetics, amphetamine) is un-ionized in alkaline fluid.
  • Ion trapping: alkalinizing the urine with sodium bicarbonate ionizes a weak acid so it can't be reabsorbed, which speeds the clearance of aspirin and phenobarbital. Acidifying the urine does the same for a weak base such as amphetamine. Inflamed, acidic tissue ionizes local anesthetics, which is why they work poorly in an abscess.
  • Bioavailability (F) is the fraction that reaches the circulation unchanged, the extent of absorption rather than its rate: 100% for IV by definition, 75–100% for IM or subcutaneous, anywhere from 5% to nearly 100% by mouth. Poor absorption and first-pass metabolism in the gut wall and liver lower it (oral nitroglycerin and lidocaine lose most of the dose). Sublingual, IV, inhaled and transdermal routes avoid first pass, and rectal partly does. Switching IV to oral: oral dose = IV dose ÷ F.

5 Drug terms: what makes a drug, indication and contraindication, side effect versus adverse event, generic names

Hint + review + slides + objectives · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • An indication is an approved reason to use a drug and a contraindication (relative or absolute) a reason not to; a side effect is an unintended effect of the drug, while an adverse event is any harm during or after use, caused by the drug or not; a poison has almost only harmful effects.
  • A side effect is an unintended effect of the drug at a usual dose, predictable from its actions: usually unwanted, sometimes useful and a reason for off-label use (minoxidil, an antihypertensive, grows hair). An adverse event is any harmful occurrence during or after use, whether or not the drug caused it.

7 The therapeutic index and window, and the concentration–time curve

Review + slides + objectives · 1 question in the bank

A quantal curve plots the share of a group that responds at each dose. From it come the ED50, the TD50 and, in animals, the LD50. The therapeutic index is TD50/ED50 (LD50/ED50 in animal work): the larger it is, the safer the drug. Warfarin, lithium, digoxin, phenytoin and theophylline have narrow indexes and need blood levels or monitoring (the INR for warfarin). The therapeutic window is the range of plasma levels from the minimum effective concentration (MEC) to the minimum toxic concentration (MTC): the range in which most patients get the effect with few adverse effects.

  • AUC (the area under the concentration–time curve) is the total exposure. Cmax is the peak level and Tmax the time it comes; Cmin is the trough, the lowest level, at the end of a dosing interval. After an IV dose the level falls fast at first as the drug moves into tissues (distribution), then more slowly as it leaves the body (elimination).

  • Direct muscarinic agonists: bethanechol (urinary retention, ileus), carbachol (glaucoma drops, and miosis during eye surgery), pilocarpine (glaucoma drops; in open-angle glaucoma they lower pressure by contracting the ciliary muscle, which opens the trabecular meshwork so aqueous humor drains out, and the small pupil is only a side effect), and pilocarpine and cevimeline tablets for dry mouth from Sjögren syndrome or radiation, as long as some gland tissue remains. Side effects follow DUMBBELSS: diarrhea, urination, miosis, bradycardia, bronchospasm, emesis, lacrimation, salivation, sweating.

3 Cholinesterase inhibitors and organophosphate poisoning

Slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Reversible cholinesterase inhibitors: neostigmine and pyridostigmine (charged, stay out of the brain: myasthenia gravis, reversing neuromuscular block), physostigmine (enters the brain: antimuscarinic poisoning), donepezil, rivastigmine and galantamine (Alzheimer disease).
  • Organophosphates (insecticides, nerve agents) inhibit cholinesterase irreversibly: DUMBBELSS plus twitching, then paralysis, and seizures. Treat with atropine for the muscarinic effects and pralidoxime to regenerate the enzyme before the bond "ages".

4 α- and β-blockers and central α2 agonists

Slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • α1 blockers (-osin): prazosin, terazosin, doxazosin (hypertension, BPH), tamsulosin (α1A, BPH). Main problem: orthostatic hypotension, worst after the first doses, so raise the chair slowly. Phentolamine (reversible, nonselective) treats epinephrine extravasation and reverses soft-tissue numbness after dental work. With an α blocker, epinephrine can lower blood pressure (β2 effect unopposed: "epinephrine reversal").
  • β-blockers (-olol): β1-selective atenolol, metoprolol, bisoprolol, esmolol, betaxolol; nonselective propranolol, nadolol, timolol; α1 plus β carvedilol and labetalol. Uses: hypertension, angina, after MI, heart failure, arrhythmias, migraine prevention, tremor, performance anxiety, glaucoma. Harms: bradycardia, bronchospasm (nonselective), fatigue, masked warning signs of hypoglycemia, rebound if stopped abruptly.

5 The receptor map, resting vascular tone and the autonomic eye

Core of the slides · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Most blood vessels have sympathetic nerves only, so resting vascular tone is α1-mediated vasoconstriction; the endothelial M3 receptors are not innervated and answer only circulating ACh.
  • Who sets the tone at rest: most organs that get both supplies are run by the parasympathetic side at rest, and the two sides usually oppose each other. The exceptions: the heart's ventricles are mainly under sympathetic tone, and most blood vessels have sympathetic nerves only, so resting vascular tone is set by α1. The muscarinic (M3) receptors on vessel endothelium make nitric oxide, which relaxes the muscle beneath; they have no parasympathetic nerves and answer only ACh carried in the blood.

2 Antiviral and antifungal targets: influenza, HIV classes, hepatitis B and C goals, ergosterol drugs

Slides + review guide · 4 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Start a neuraminidase inhibitor (oseltamivir by mouth, zanamivir inhaled, peramivir IV) within 48 hours of the first symptoms, as a 5-day course: it shortens the illness and viral shedding. Amantadine and rimantadine work only on influenza A.
  • Everyone with HIV is offered treatment, whatever the CD4 count, starting with an integrase inhibitor plus 1 or 2 NRTIs. NRTIs (tenofovir, abacavir) can cause lactic acidosis; integrase inhibitors are bound by antacids, calcium and iron; protease inhibitors (ritonavir) inhibit CYP3A4, so no triazolam or oral midazolam.
  • Influenza: the neuraminidase inhibitors oseltamivir (by mouth), zanamivir (inhaled; can trigger bronchospasm) and peramivir (IV) stop new virions from leaving infected cells; started within 48 hours, a 5-day course shortens the illness and viral shedding. Amantadine and rimantadine block the M2 ion channel, so they work only on influenza A (influenza B has no M2), with CNS side effects. Baloxavir, one dose by mouth, blocks the viral polymerase complex.
  • HIV: nucleoside or nucleotide reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs: tenofovir, emtricitabine, abacavir; can cause lactic acidosis), non-nucleosides (NNRTIs: efavirenz, nevirapine), integrase inhibitors (-tegravir: dolutegravir, bictegravir; bound by antacids, calcium and iron, so doses are taken apart) and protease inhibitors (-navir: lopinavir, ritonavir). Entry blockers: maraviroc (the CCR5 co-receptor), ibalizumab (binds CD4 and blocks entry after attachment) and enfuvirtide (fusion). Treatment is offered to everyone with HIV, whatever the CD4 count; a first regimen is an integrase inhibitor with 1 or 2 NRTIs, and it needs over 95% adherence. Ritonavir strongly inhibits CYP3A4: no triazolam or oral midazolam. Oral signs that suggest poorly controlled HIV: candidiasis, hairy leukoplakia, Kaposi sarcoma, linear gingival erythema and necrotizing periodontal disease.
  • Hepatitis: hepatitis C is treated to eradicate it. Direct-acting antivirals aimed at the virus's own proteins (NS3/4A protease inhibitors, -previr; NS5A inhibitors, -asvir, such as ledipasvir and velpatasvir; the NS5B polymerase inhibitor sofosbuvir) cure most cases in 8–12 weeks and replaced interferon with ribavirin. Hepatitis B is rarely cured: the goal is to suppress its DNA to undetectable levels, with nucleoside or nucleotide analogs (tenofovir, entecavir, lamivudine) or pegylated interferon. Hepatitis A needs only supportive care. Ask about liver function before giving acetaminophen or other drugs the liver clears.

3 Bactericidal versus bacteriostatic drugs and the goals of treatment

Slides + review guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Bactericidal drugs kill: β-lactams, vancomycin, aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, metronidazole, rifampin and the membrane disruptors (polymyxin B, daptomycin). Bacteriostatic drugs stop growth and leave the rest to the immune system: tetracyclines, macrolides, clindamycin, chloramphenicol, sulfonamides, linezolid. Bactericidal drugs are preferred in immunocompromised patients, and killing matters most in endocarditis and meningitis too. Combine like with like: two bactericidal drugs or two bacteriostatic ones.
  • Goals of treatment: prophylactic treatment prevents infection in someone at high risk (immunosuppressed patients; amoxicillin before dental care for a prosthetic valve); pre-emptive treatment starts when an infection is found on monitoring, before symptoms (cytomegalovirus after a transplant); empirical treatment covers the likely organisms before the cause is known; definitive (targeted) treatment aims at an identified, susceptible organism, often narrowing an empirical start once cultures return; suppressive treatment (secondary prophylaxis) keeps a treated or chronic infection from flaring, as in AIDS and after transplants.

6 Targeted cancer drugs and how checkpoint inhibitors reactivate T cells

Slides + objectives · 1 question in the bank

Checkpoint inhibitors: immune checkpoints keep T cells from attacking indiscriminately. PD-1 on activated T cells binds PD-L1, which many tumors overexpress, and CTLA-4 on T cells binds B7 on antigen-presenting cells; both switch the T cell off. 4 Plaque formation sequence and which organism goes with which lesion

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

StageWhat happens
1. Acquired pellicleWithin minutes a film of salivary glycoproteins, mucins, immunoglobulins and enzymes (under 1 µm thick) coats a clean tooth. Gp340 is the key receptor.
2. Reversible attachmentPioneer bacteria carried by saliva are held by weak, long-range forces (van der Waals).
3. Irreversible adhesionAdhesins on the pioneers bind pellicle receptors. The pioneers are commensal Gram-positive streptococci (S. sanguinis, S. oralis, S. mitis) and Actinomyces.
4. CoaggregationSecondary colonizers bind bacteria already attached, often through lectin-like adhesins. F. nucleatum is the bridge between early colonizers and the Gram-negative late colonizers.
5. MaturationThe matrix thickens, oxygen falls and Gram-negative anaerobes such as P. gingivalis (tertiary colonizers) settle in.
6. DispersalCells detach, often by degrading their own adhesins, and seed new sites.

2 Ester versus amide metabolism and allergy; prilocaine and articaine

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Every local anesthetic has a lipophilic aromatic ring, an intermediate chain (ester or amide link) and a hydrophilic amine. Naming trick: amides have an "i" before "-caine" (lidocaine, mepivacaine, prilocaine, articaine, bupivacaine); esters do not (procaine, benzocaine, tetracaine, chloroprocaine, cocaine).

True amide allergy is very rare; reactions are usually to the preservative methylparaben or to sodium bisulfite, the antioxidant in cartridges with a vasoconstrictor. No cross-allergy between the classes.

3 Local anesthetic systemic toxicity

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

LAST (local anesthetic systemic toxicity), usually from intravascular injection or overdose: the CNS goes first: circumoral numbness, metallic taste, tinnitus, dizziness, twitching, then seizures, then CNS depression; at higher levels the heart: hypotension, arrhythmia, arrest. Potency tracks toxicity; acidosis makes it worse. Treatment: stop injecting, airway, oxygen, a benzodiazepine for seizures, and 20% lipid emulsion (the "lipid sink").

Risks: obesity (strongest), male over 50, postmenopause, thick neck, retrognathia or micrognathia, crowded oropharynx, alcohol and sedatives. Diagnosed by polysomnography. Treatment: weight loss, avoid sleeping supine, CPAP (first line), and a mandibular advancement oral appliance for snoring and mild to moderate OSA, or moderate to severe OSA when CPAP is refused or not tolerated (best in thin patients whose OSA is worse supine). 5 Reward circuitry and drugs of abuse; antipsychotics; LTP

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Reward runs on dopamine from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens (the mesolimbic pathway). Every drug of abuse raises dopamine there. Cocaine blocks the dopamine (and norepinephrine and serotonin) transporters; amphetamine reverses them. Opioids act on mu receptors (Gi/o) of GABA interneurons, releasing VTA dopamine neurons from inhibition. Alcohol boosts GABA-A and blocks NMDA; nicotine acts on α4β2 nicotinic receptors; marijuana on CB1 (anandamide). Addiction: tolerance, craving, withdrawal, use despite harm; genetic risk is polygenic. Treatment: behavioral therapy (CBT, contingency management, 12-step), nicotine replacement and varenicline, naltrexone or disulfiram for alcohol, methadone, buprenorphine or naltrexone for opioids. Dental: no epinephrine within 24 hours of cocaine use (arrhythmia, hypertensive crisis); methamphetamine causes rampant caries; for patients recovering from opioid use, plan non-opioid analgesia.

1 Stroke volume and cardiac output: preload (Frank–Starling), afterload and contractility, with the SV, CO, EF and MAP arithmetic

Objectives + slides + review guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Preload (end-diastolic stretch): more filling, more forceful ejection. This is the Frank–Starling law: within limits the heart pumps out what comes in, which keeps the two sides matched.

At steady state cardiac output equals venous return: the point where the cardiac function curve (cardiac output against right atrial pressure, the Frank–Starling curve) and the venous return curve cross. More blood volume shifts the venous return curve right, so cardiac output and right atrial pressure both rise (blood loss: both fall). A positive inotrope, a faster rate or less afterload lifts the cardiac function curve: cardiac output rises and right atrial pressure falls. A higher TPR lowers the cardiac curve and rotates the venous return curve down: cardiac output falls with right atrial pressure unchanged. Myocardial O2 demand rises with heart rate, contractility and afterload, much less with preload; when supply falls short, ischemia brings angina and, if it lasts, infarction.

6 Vessel walls: the three tunics, the arteries' thicker tunica media against the veins' tunica externa, and the three capillary types

Slides + objectives · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • Arteries and arterioles have a thick smooth-muscle tunica media (a high wall-to-lumen ratio); veins and venules have a thin media, and their thickest layer is the tunica externa.

Vessels larger than capillaries have three layers: the tunica intima (endothelium; arteries add an internal elastic lamina), the tunica media (smooth muscle) and the tunica externa or adventitia (collagen and elastic fibers). Arteries have the thicker tunica media, so their wall is thick for their lumen (a high wall-to-lumen ratio); a vein of the same size has a thin wall, a wide lumen and its thickest layer in the externa. The vasa vasorum feed the outer wall of large vessels and are better developed in veins, whose blood carries less O2.

7 The sarcomere and the intercalated disc: filaments slide without changing length, and what each part of the disc does

Slides + objectives · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • Contraction is the filaments sliding: their overlap grows and the I and H bands narrow, but neither filament shortens, so the A band keeps its length.

The sarcomere runs from Z line to Z line: the A band is the length of the thick (myosin) filaments, the H band thick filaments alone and the I band thin filaments alone. The thin filament is actin with tropomyosin and troponin: TnC binds Ca2+, TnI inhibits the actin–myosin bond and TnT attaches to tropomyosin. In contraction the filaments slide, so the I and H bands narrow, but neither filament changes length and the A band stays the same. Each cardiac fiber contracts all-or-none. Heart cells, packed with mitochondria, burn mainly fatty acids, aerobically. Right atrial myocytes store atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) in granules and release it when stretched.

  • Prophylaxis is for the highest-risk hearts only: a prosthetic valve or valve repair material, past endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease and a heart transplant with valve disease. Amoxicillin 2 g by mouth 30–60 minutes before a procedure that manipulates the gingiva or the periapical tissue. Rheumatic heart disease, mitral valve prolapse or a murmur alone doesn't qualify.
  • Infective endocarditis: damaged endothelium or turbulent flow collects a sterile platelet–fibrin clot, and bacteremia (a dental procedure) seeds it into an infected vegetation. Viridans streptococci from the mouth on damaged valves (subacute, after bleeding dental care); S. aureus on normal valves (acute; the tricuspid valve in people who inject drugs); S. epidermidis on prosthetic valves; the HACEK group. Signs: fever, a new murmur, splinter hemorrhages, Janeway lesions (painless, palms and soles: septic emboli), Osler nodes (painful, finger pads: immune complexes), Roth spots, an embolic stroke, and petechiae, including on the palate, which can be the first sign. The mitral valve is most often involved.
  • Antibiotic prophylaxis before dental care that manipulates the gingiva or the periapical tissue (current AHA guidance): prosthetic valves or valve repair material, previous endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease, and a heart transplant with valve disease. Not for rheumatic heart disease, mitral valve prolapse or a murmur alone. Adult dose: amoxicillin 2 g by mouth 30–60 minutes before.

2 Atherosclerosis's risk factors and steps (foam cells, fibrous plaque, rupture and thrombus), and hypertension's stages and damage

Slides + objectives + review guide · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Know the risk factors (hypertension, high LDL, diabetes, smoking, obesity, inactivity, family history) and the steps: endothelial injury, oxidized LDL taken up by macrophages as foam cells (the fatty streak), a fibrous plaque, then rupture and a thrombus (MI or stroke).
  • Stages (2017 ACC/AHA, unchanged in 2025): normal, under 120/80; elevated, 120–129 with diastolic under 80; stage 1, 130–139 or 80–89; stage 2, 140/90 or higher; crisis, above 180/120. It is the "silent killer": many patients don't know they have it or have stopped their drugs. About 90–95% is primary (essential): genes, salt, obesity, inactivity, smoking, diabetes and aging vessels, with the kidney excreting less Na+ than is taken in. Secondary causes: kidney disease, renal artery stenosis, primary aldosteronism, Cushing syndrome, pheochromocytoma, hypothyroidism, preeclampsia, coarctation of the aorta, sleep apnea.
  • Atherosclerosis, the main cause of cardiovascular disease: endothelial injury → LDL enters the intima and oxidizes → monocytes become macrophages and then foam cells (the fatty streak) → smooth muscle migrates in, collagen and calcium are laid down, and a fibrous cap forms over a lipid core that can become necrotic. A cap that ruptures → thrombus → MI or stroke. Risk factors: hypertension, high LDL, diabetes, smoking, obesity, inactivity and family history. A calcified carotid plaque can show on a panoramic radiograph, xanthelasma (yellow plaques at the inner eyelids) and corneal arcus point to high cholesterol, and periodontal disease is linked to atherosclerotic events. Most often hit: abdominal aorta, coronary, popliteal and carotid arteries.

3 The baroreceptor reflex (carotid sinus on CN IX, aortic arch on CN X) and orthostatic hypotension in the chair

Slides + objectives + review guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Standing up: blood pools in the legs, venous return and BP fall, and the reflex speeds the heart and constricts vessels. When that fails (older patients, α1-blockers, diuretics and other antihypertensives, dehydration, a long reclined appointment), the patient gets orthostatic hypotension. Raise the chair slowly and let the patient sit for a minute before standing.

4 Long-term BP control: renin from juxtaglomerular cells, angiotensin II, aldosterone, ANP and BNP

Slides + objectives + review guide · 2 questions in the bank

Renin comes from the juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole when renal perfusion falls, the macula densa senses less NaCl, or sympathetic nerves fire (beta-1). Renin turns angiotensinogen (from the liver) into angiotensin I, and ACE, mostly on lung capillary endothelium, makes angiotensin II. Angiotensin II constricts arterioles (and the efferent arteriole, holding GFR), releases aldosterone (Na+ and water kept, K+ and H+ lost at the collecting duct) and ADH, and causes thirst. ACE also breaks down bradykinin, which is why ACE inhibitors cause cough and angioedema.

ANP from stretched atria and BNP, mainly from the ventricles, do the opposite: Na+ and water loss, vasodilation (through cGMP), and less renin, angiotensin II and aldosterone. Neprilysin breaks ANP down, so blocking it (sacubitril) lowers BP. BNP is a blood test for heart failure. ADH (vasopressin) from the posterior pituitary rises with high plasma osmolality, low atrial stretch, angiotensin II and sympathetic input: through V2 receptors the kidney keeps water, and through V1 receptors, at high levels, vessels constrict.

2 Calcium channel blockers: gingival overgrowth (how it arises and how it's treated), and dihydropyridines (vessels) versus verapamil and diltiazem (heart)

Slides + objectives + review guide · 1 question in the bank

Two dental interactions come up again and again. NSAIDs taken for more than a few days block renal prostaglandins and blunt ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics and β-blockers; with an ACE inhibitor, ARB, loop diuretic or spironolactone they also raise the risk of acute kidney injury and high K+. A short course for dental pain is generally fine. Nonselective β-blockers leave epinephrine only alpha-1 receptors to act on, so BP rises and the baroreceptors slow the heart; with propranolol, nadolol or timolol use fewer cartridges, aspirate and inject slowly. A rough guide to selectivity: A to M are beta-1 selective (atenolol, bisoprolol, esmolol, metoprolol), N to Z nonselective (nadolol, propranolol, timolol). β-blockers also hide the warning signs of hypoglycemia and slow recovery from it in a diabetic patient on insulin, the nonselective ones most: make sure the patient has eaten. Drug-influenced gingival overgrowth comes from calcium channel blockers (nifedipine most), phenytoin and cyclosporine. With a calcium channel blocker it affects about 6–34% of patients, mild to severe: collagen breakdown slows (less matrix metalloproteinase activity) and fibroblasts multiply. Treatment is meticulous plaque control, a drug change by the physician and surgical excision when needed.

3 Heart failure: the front-line drugs that lower mortality (ACE inhibitor, ARB or sacubitril–valsartan, select β-blockers, aldosterone antagonists, SGLT2 inhibitors) and digoxin's toxicity with low K+

Slides + objectives + review guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Drugs that lower mortality (reduced ejection fraction): an ACE inhibitor, ARB or sacubitril–valsartan; an evidence-based β-blocker (carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol); an aldosterone antagonist (spironolactone, eplerenone); an SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin); hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate in Black patients.
  • Sacubitril–valsartan (an ARNI) pairs the ARB valsartan with sacubitril, a neprilysin inhibitor that raises the natriuretic peptides (more Na+ and water lost, less fibrosis). It beats an ACE inhibitor or ARB alone on death and heart failure admissions. Adverse effect: hypotension. Contraindicated in pregnancy and after angioedema from an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
  • Digoxin inhibits the Na+/K+-ATPase, so Na+ builds up inside the cell, the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger removes less Ca2+, and contraction is stronger. It also raises vagal tone, slowing the AV node (rate control in atrial fibrillation). Its window is narrow: low K+ (from diuretics), low magnesium, high calcium, kidney failure, and drugs such as amiodarone, verapamil and the macrolides raise toxicity. Signs: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, yellow-green halos and blurred vision, arrhythmias. Antidote: digoxin immune Fab. Now seldom used; it doesn't lower mortality but may improve quality of life.

4 Antiarrhythmic classes with one key drug each, their class effects (QRS, QT, rate versus rhythm control) and amiodarone's toxicity

Slides + objectives · 2 questions in the bank

Rate control in atrial fibrillation uses class II and IV drugs (β-blockers, verapamil, diltiazem); rhythm control uses class I and III drugs (dofetilide, ibutilide, propafenone, amiodarone, flecainide); either way with an anticoagulant. Any antiarrhythmic can cause new arrhythmias (proarrhythmia), hypotension and bradycardia. Amiodarone has a very long half-life and inhibits CYP enzymes, raising warfarin and digoxin levels. Epinephrine and albuterol speed the sinus rate; β-blockers (timolol eye drops too), calcium channel blockers and digoxin slow it. Amiodarone, dofetilide, sotalol, some antibiotics (the macrolides), ondansetron and haloperidol lengthen the QT and can bring on torsades de pointes; avoid stacking them. Lidocaine is itself a class IB drug, so its Na+ channel block adds to a class I antiarrhythmic's.

5 Statin mechanism and myopathy with CYP3A4-inhibiting macrolides; the other lipid drugs, for cholesterol or for triglycerides

Slides + objectives + review guide · 1 question in the bank

The dental interaction: clarithromycin and erythromycin strongly inhibit CYP3A4, which clears simvastatin, lovastatin and atorvastatin, so statin levels and myopathy risk rise. Azithromycin barely affects CYP3A4; pravastatin and rosuvastatin depend least on it. Grapefruit and azole antifungals raise those statins too. Two more for the chair: omega-3 fatty acids add to bleeding, and bile acid sequestrants bind drugs taken at the same time. Statins, ezetimibe, bile acid sequestrants and PCSK9 inhibitors are the cholesterol (LDL) drugs; fibrates, niacin and omega-3 fatty acids are the triglyceride drugs.

6 β-blocker selectivity and the epinephrine interaction, and the 0.04 mg epinephrine limit for cardiac patients

Objectives · 1 question in the bank

1:100,000 epinephrine is 0.01 mg/mL, so a 1.8 mL cartridge holds 0.018 mg (1:200,000 holds 0.009 mg; 1:50,000 holds 0.036 mg). The usual ceiling is 0.2 mg for a healthy adult and 0.04 mg for a patient with significant heart disease, about two cartridges of 1:100,000. Avoid it in unstable angina, an MI in the last 30 days or so, uncontrolled arrhythmia or uncontrolled hypertension, and keep it out of retraction cord in cardiac patients.

  • One drug per class: IA procainamide, IB lidocaine, IC flecainide; II esmolol, metoprolol; III amiodarone; IV verapamil, diltiazem; others digoxin and magnesium sulfate.

1 Primary versus secondary hemostasis: platelet and vessel bleeding (mucosal, petechiae) against factor bleeding (joints, deep, delayed); vWF with GpIb and GpIIb/IIIa, von Willebrand disease, Bernard–Soulier and Glanzmann

Slides + objectives + review guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Von Willebrand disease: the most common inherited bleeding disorder, usually autosomal dominant. vWF in the vessel wall binds platelet GpIb (and GpIIb/IIIa once platelets are activated); type 1 is a mild lack of vWF, type 2 a faulty vWF, type 3 a severe lack. Mucosal bleeding; desmopressin (DDAVP) releases stored vWF.
  • Bernard–Soulier syndrome (no GpIb, so platelets can't bind vWF) and Glanzmann thrombasthenia (no GpIIb/IIIa, so they can't bind fibrinogen): rare (about 1 in a million), autosomal recessive and usually severe. Platelet aggregation studies tell them apart: Bernard–Soulier has giant platelets and no response to ristocetin (which makes vWF bind GpIb); Glanzmann has normal-sized platelets that respond to ristocetin and to nothing else. Platelet granule (storage pool) defects are rare; dense granule defects are mild unless aspirin is added.

2 Warfarin: vitamin K epoxide reductase, PT/INR, the early clot risk, why it interacts (metronidazole, antibiotics, acetaminophen, NSAIDs, rifampin), its reversal, and extractions at an INR of 3.5 or less

Slides + objectives + review guide · 2 questions in the bank

Why warfarin interacts so much: it is 99% protein-bound, broken down in the liver (CYP2C9; CYP2C9 and VKORC1 gene variants change the dose), long-acting and narrow. Metronidazole and fluconazole block CYP2C9 and raise the INR, and macrolides raise it too; some antibiotics (2nd- and 3rd-generation cephalosporins; also amoxicillin) raise it by cutting the gut bacteria's vitamin K; regular acetaminophen near 4 g a day raises it; NSAIDs, antiplatelets and other anticoagulants add bleeding; rifampin induces the liver enzymes and weakens it.

  • Warfarin: check the INR within 24 hours of surgery (up to 72 hours if it has been stable). At an INR of 3.5 or less, most office extractions go ahead without stopping the drug; above that, consult the physician. Target INRs: 2–3 for atrial fibrillation and venous clots, 2.5–3.5 for a mechanical mitral valve.

6 Sickle cell disease, HbC and HbSC, and the thalassemias; anemias and the hematopoietic drugs

Slides + objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Sickle cell disease: valine replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of β-globin (HbS). Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes into rigid crystals; the cells sickle, block small vessels and hemolyze. Autosomal recessive and most common in people of African ancestry: sickle trait (HbAS) is usually silent and is the most common hemoglobinopathy in the US (about 8% of African Americans); the disease (HbSS) shortens life (median survival into the 40s). Vaso-occlusive crises: pain (sickling in bone), acute chest syndrome, stroke, priapism, and autosplenectomy, which leaves infection (pneumococcus, Salmonella osteomyelitis) and sepsis. Triggers: low O2, dehydration, acidosis, cold, fever, infection, stress. Radiographs: a stepladder trabecular pattern and a "hair-on-end" skull. In the chair: short morning visits, good pain control, stay well oxygenated, treat infection promptly. Treatment: transfusion, red cell exchange and hydroxyurea, which raises HbF. Carriers of sickle trait or thalassemia get milder malaria.
  • HbC (lysine for glutamic acid at β6) forms crystals and target cells: mild hemolytic anemia and splenomegaly, no pain crises, usually no treatment. HbSC disease is milder than HbSS: mild hemolysis, fewer and less painful crises, a modestly shorter life, and hip pain from aseptic necrosis of the femoral head; the smear shows target and sickle cells.

Also flagged in class

  • Mucosal oozing, petechiae and bleeding from small cuts point to platelets or vessels (von Willebrand disease, low platelets, aspirin); delayed, deep and joint bleeding points to a clotting factor (hemophilia, warfarin, liver disease).

You can skip

  • Skip how blood is collected for clotting tests (the citrate tube and its blood-to-citrate ratio); know that the PT follows the extrinsic pathway (III and VII, "37 cents") and the aPTT the intrinsic (XII, XI, IX, VIII, "$11.98").

1 Obstructive versus restrictive spirometry: emphysema, fibrosis, and reversibility in asthma

Slides + objectives + study guide + review guide · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Asthma's obstruction reverses with a bronchodilator; COPD's (chronic bronchitis plus emphysema) doesn't.
