2 Lung volumes and capacities (RV, FRC and TLC need more than spirometry), alveolar ventilation and PaCO2

Slides + objectives + review guide · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • The alveolar ventilation equation: alveolar PCO2 varies inversely with alveolar ventilation. Halve ventilation and PaCO2 doubles; double CO2 production and ventilation must double to hold PaCO2 at 40 mmHg.
  • Minute ventilation = tidal volume × rate (a normal rate is 12–20 a minute). Alveolar ventilation = (tidal volume − physiologic dead space) × rate. Physiologic dead space = anatomic (about 150 mL) + alveolar dead space (ventilated but poorly perfused alveoli, about 20–50 mL), about 175 mL in a healthy adult. By the alveolar ventilation equation (alveolar ventilation = CO2 production × 863 ÷ PACO2), PaCO2 varies inversely with alveolar ventilation: double the ventilation, halve the PaCO2; halve it, and PaCO2 doubles. If CO2 production doubles (exercise), alveolar ventilation must double to hold PaCO2 at 40 mmHg.

3 Oxyhemoglobin curve shifts and carbon monoxide; V/Q from apex to base, shunt and dead space with their gas values; the diffusion barrier

Slides + objectives + study guide + review guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • V/Q: for the whole lung, about 4 L/min of alveolar ventilation over 5 L/min of blood gives a V/Q of about 0.8. In an upright lung the apex alveoli are already stretched (pleural pressure is more negative there) and expand little, while the base alveoli start small and ventilate best; perfusion rises toward the base even faster. So ventilation and perfusion are both greatest at the base, but perfusion more so: V/Q is lowest at the base and highest at the apex. V/Q of zero is a shunt (blocked airway: atelectasis, pneumonia, a mucus plug): alveolar gas comes to the mixed venous values (PO2 40, PCO2 45), and the hypoxemia barely responds to 100% O2. An anatomic shunt (a septal defect, an artery-to-vein connection) bypasses the alveoli altogether. V/Q near infinity is dead space (pulmonary embolism): alveolar gas stays at inspired values (PO2 about 150, PCO2 0). Low alveolar O2 constricts pulmonary arterioles (hypoxic vasoconstriction), matching blood to air.

4 Control of breathing: central versus peripheral chemoreceptors, the pontine centers; surfactant and neonatal RDS

Objectives + study guide + review guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Central chemoreceptors in the medulla, behind the blood–brain barrier, control breathing at rest. CO2 crosses the barrier but H+ and bicarbonate don't; in the CSF, CO2 forms H+, and the CSF has little protein to buffer it, so a small rise in PaCO2 drives breathing hard. CO2 is the main minute-to-minute drive: ventilation rises in a straight line as PaCO2 rises above its resting 40 mmHg, and falls when PaCO2 drops below 40. In chronic CO2 retention (severe COPD), the choroid plexus secretes bicarbonate into the CSF, its pH returns toward normal, and the center resets to the higher PaCO2. Peripheral chemoreceptors (type I glomus cells of the carotid bodies, signaling by CN IX, and of the aortic bodies, by the vagus) sense PaO2, PaCO2 and pH. A fall in PaO2 from 100 to 60 mmHg changes breathing little, because the CO2 drive dominates; below about 60 mmHg they drive breathing hard. Chronic CO2 retainers depend more on this hypoxic drive.

5 Respiratory drugs and lung disease in the dental chair: inhaled steroids and candidiasis, aspirin-sensitive asthma, tetracycline staining, antihistamines, TB precautions

Slides + objectives + study guide · 3 questions in the bank

  • Asthma and COPD: albuterol (short-acting beta-2 agonist; tremor and a fast heart rate) for attacks and the emergency kit; inhaled steroids as the main asthma controller, which cause oral candidiasis (white plaques on the palate or oropharynx) and hoarseness (use a spacer, rinse and spit); salmeterol and formoterol never alone in asthma; ipratropium and tiotropium (antimuscarinics, the mainstay for COPD), which, like the long-acting beta-2 agonists, dry the mouth and raise caries risk; montelukast (blocks leukotrienes); theophylline, with a narrow window (erythromycin and fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin raise it); omalizumab (anti-IgE). High-dose or systemic steroids also bring cataracts, glaucoma, delayed healing and bone loss, and a recent prednisone burst can suppress the adrenals.
  • Antibiotics: β-lactams cover the typical organisms; macrolides, tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones the atypical ones. Tetracyclines and doxycycline (protein synthesis, bacteriostatic) stain developing teeth (avoid in pregnancy and under age 8), are chelated by calcium, aluminum and magnesium, and can harm the vestibular system and liver. Respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin; DNA gyrase) carry boxed warnings for tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy and CNS effects such as seizures, so they are a last resort; they also lengthen the QT, are avoided in children (cartilage) and in myasthenia gravis. Macrolides (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin) lengthen the QT, and erythromycin and clarithromycin inhibit CYP3A4. Vancomycin covers MRSA. TB: rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol for 2 months, then isoniazid and rifampin for at least 4 more; rifampin turns secretions orange and, as a CYP inducer, weakens warfarin and oral contraceptives; isoniazid causes hepatitis and neuropathy; ethambutol causes optic neuritis (lost acuity, red-green color vision).

6 Thoracic wall and pleura: pleural nerve supply and referred pain, the costodiaphragmatic recess, the thoracic dermatomes (T4 nipple, T10 umbilicus)

Core of the slides · 1 question in the bank

  • Pleura: visceral pleura covers the lung and has only visceral (autonomic) afferents, so it isn't sensitive to sharp pain. Parietal pleura lines the chest wall and is somatic, so pleuritis gives sharp pain with each breath: the intercostal nerves supply its costal part (pain felt over the chest wall), and the phrenic nerve its mediastinal and central diaphragmatic parts (pain referred to the C3–C5 dermatomes, the side of the neck and above the clavicle). In an upright patient, fluid collects in the costodiaphragmatic recess, which the lung enters only in deep inspiration. Air in the space is a pneumothorax; fluid is an effusion (drained by thoracentesis); lymph is a chylothorax.

7 Granulomatous disease with oral signs: sarcoidosis (noncaseating granulomas, ACE and calcium, parotid enlargement, Heerfordt syndrome) and strawberry gingivitis in granulomatosis with polyangiitis

Core of the slides · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Sarcoidosis: noncaseating granulomas, high ACE and calcium, young adults and African American women; in the mouth, parotid and gingival enlargement and radiolucent jaw lesions; Heerfordt syndrome = parotid enlargement + uveitis + facial nerve palsy.
  • Red, granular, friable gingival overgrowth with sinusitis and kidney disease is granulomatosis with polyangiitis: biopsy and refer, don't treat it as periodontitis.
  • Sarcoidosis: noncaseating granulomas in many organs (lungs and hilar nodes, eyes, skin, liver, CNS), most often in young adults and African American women; high serum ACE, hypercalcemia (granuloma macrophages activate vitamin D) and high lysozyme; systemic steroids when an organ is threatened. In the mouth: parotid enlargement (consider it with unexplained swelling of both parotids), gingival enlargement, mucosal nodules and radiolucent jaw lesions. Heerfordt syndrome = parotid enlargement + uveitis + facial nerve palsy. Uveitis in a young adult calls for a chest film and an ACE level.
  • Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA): a vasculitis of small and medium vessels in the upper airway, lungs and kidneys. "Strawberry" gingivitis (red, granular, friable gingival overgrowth) + sinusitis + kidney disease = GPA: biopsy and refer rather than treating it as periodontitis, because the kidneys can fail within weeks. Its treatment (rituximab or cyclophosphamide with steroids) leaves the patient immunosuppressed.

Also flagged in class

  • Capacities are sums of volumes: inspiratory capacity = TV + IRV; vital capacity = IC + ERV (IRV + TV + ERV); FRC = ERV + RV; TLC = VC + RV. Anything that contains RV needs helium dilution or plethysmography.
  • Humidified inspired air: PO2 about 145 mmHg (760 × 19.7%) and PCO2 about 0. Against mixed venous blood (PO2 40, PCO2 45), they set the gradients that bring alveolar gas and arterial blood to 100 and 40.
  • Thoracic dermatomes: T2 at the sternal angle, T4 at the nipple, T10 at the umbilicus. The intercostal nerves are T1–T11 and the subcostal nerve T12; the names of their cutaneous branches matter less.
  • Sinusitis and otitis media: amoxicillin or amoxicillin–clavulanate. Influenza: oseltamivir, zanamivir, amantadine, rimantadine, baloxavir. Bronchitis: azithromycin, clarithromycin, TMP-SMX. Pneumonia: doxycycline, levofloxacin, vancomycin, piperacillin–tazobactam. TB: rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol.
  • First-generation H1 blockers (diphenhydramine, hydroxyzine) cross the blood–brain barrier and block muscarinic and alpha receptors, so they sedate; second generation (cetirizine, fexofenadine, loratadine) barely do; topical: azelastine, olopatadine, ketotifen. Epinephrine for anaphylaxis is given by injection, never by mouth.

You can skip

  • Skip the percentages of nitrogen, oxygen, argon and CO2 in air; know that air holds far more O2 than CO2 (inspired PCO2 is about 0).
  • Skip the names of the lymph node groups around the trachea and lungs; know only that they exist and are named by where they sit.

1 Starling forces and what changes GFR: afferent versus efferent constriction, a blocked ureter, plasma protein, filtration equilibrium; angiotensin II, prostaglandins and autoregulation

Recording + slides + objectives + study guide · 4 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Constricting either arteriole lowers renal plasma flow; afferent constriction lowers glomerular pressure and GFR, efferent constriction raises them.
  • Know the What changes GFR table: afferent constriction, RPF and GFR down; efferent constriction, RPF down and GFR up; a blocked ureter, GFR down with RPF unchanged; plasma protein up, GFR down; plasma protein down, GFR up.
  • Oncotic pressure rises along the capillary (from about 19 to about 35 mmHg) as protein-free fluid leaves, until it matches the net hydrostatic pressure (45 − 10 = 35 mmHg) and net pressure reaches zero (filtration equilibrium). A higher renal plasma flow makes it rise more slowly, so filtration goes on along more of the capillary and GFR rises; a lower flow does the opposite. The protein-rich blood leaving in the efferent arteriole gives the peritubular capillaries a high oncotic pressure, the main force for proximal reabsorption.

Efferent arteriole constricts (angiotensin II)↓↑ (moderate)Pressure builds up in the glomerulus; filtration fraction rises

  • Autoregulation keeps RBF and GFR nearly constant from about 80 to 200 mmHg (below about 80 they fall steeply) by adjusting afferent and efferent tone, through two mechanisms: the myogenic response of the afferent arteriole and tubuloglomerular feedback – more NaCl at the macula densa → adenosine → afferent constriction → GFR back down. Sustained changes in NaCl delivery also change renin release. Caffeine blocks the adenosine (A1) receptors: the afferent arteriole stays open and tubular Na+ reabsorption falls, so urine flow and Na+ excretion rise.

2 Body fluid compartments (60–40–20), ECF and ICF ions, normal osmolarity 275–290, water shifts read on Darrow-Yannet diagrams, and IV fluids

Recording + slides + objectives + study guide · 4 questions in the bank

Know this
  • 0.9% saline expands only the ECF; 0.45% saline lowers osmolarity and moves some water into cells; D5W is free water that expands both compartments the most.
  • ECF: Na+ the main cation, Cl− the main anion and HCO3− second. ICF: K+, then Mg2+, with organic phosphates and proteins as the anions.
  • Every gain or loss happens in the ECF first; if ECF osmolarity changes, water moves into or out of cells until ICF and ECF osmolarity match again.
  • Read a Darrow-Yannet diagram (ICF left, ECF right; width is volume, height is osmolarity; dashed line the new state). Diarrhea: ECF smaller, same height. Sweating: both smaller, higher. Adrenal insufficiency: ECF smaller, ICF larger, lower. Saline: ECF larger, same. Salt: ECF larger, ICF smaller, higher. SIADH: both larger, lower.
  • ECF ions: Na+ (main cation), Cl− and HCO3−. ICF ions: K+ and Mg2+, with proteins and organic phosphates (ATP, ADP) as the anions.
  • Darrow-Yannet diagrams draw these shifts as two boxes, ICF on the left and ECF on the right: width is volume, height is osmolarity; the solid line is the normal state and the dashed line the new one. Work them in three steps: what changed in the ECF; whether ECF osmolarity rose, fell or stayed the same; which way water then moves so that ICF and ECF osmolarity match. Volume contraction moves the ECF edge in, expansion moves it out; a line above normal is hyperosmotic, below it hypo-osmotic.
  • IV fluids: normal saline (0.9%, 154 mEq/L NaCl, about 308 mOsm/L) stays in the ECF, the best plasma volume expander (volume depletion, maintenance); half-normal saline (0.45%) is hypotonic: it lowers ECF osmolarity, so some water enters cells (used when ICF is depleted, as in diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemia); D5W becomes free water once the glucose is used, spreads over both compartments, expands them more than half-normal saline does, and treats hypernatremia from a water deficit. Plain water is never given IV: it would lyse red cells.

3 Bladder innervation and the micturition reflex: the pontine micturition center

Flagged in the recording · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • Bladder stretch at about 300 mL sets off a spinal reflex; the pontine micturition center holds it back or lets voiding go ahead (pudendal inhibited so the external sphincter relaxes; parasympathetic contracts the detrusor and relaxes the internal sphincter). Sympathetic stores; parasympathetic voids.
  • Micturition reflex, a spinal reflex: at roughly 300 mL (the bladder holds about 500–600 mL), stretch receptors signal the sacral cord and the detrusor starts to contract. The pontine micturition center (PMC) decides: if voiding is inconvenient, it suppresses the reflex; if voiding is allowed, the pudendal nerve is inhibited (the external sphincter relaxes) and parasympathetic output contracts the detrusor and relaxes the internal sphincter.

4 Clearance: inulin = GFR, PAH = RPF and RBF, plasma creatinine varies inversely with GFR and its limits, clearance ratios and the two zero clearances (albumin, glucose)

Recording + slides + objectives + study guide · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • At steady state, double the plasma creatinine means half the GFR. Creatinine slightly overestimates GFR because a little is secreted; inulin is the gold standard.
  • Albumin (not filtered) and glucose (filtered, then all reabsorbed) have a clearance of 0; PAH's clearance is the highest possible, equal to renal plasma flow.
  • Creatinine: made from creatine phosphate by muscle at a steady rate and freely filtered, with a little secretion, so its clearance slightly overestimates GFR; it's the clinical marker (eGFR also uses cystatin C). Plasma creatinine varies inversely with GFR: if GFR halves, plasma creatinine doubles at steady state. Normal plasma creatinine is about 0.6–1.2 mg/dL in men and 0.5–1.1 mg/dL in women.
  • Its limits: production depends on muscle mass, so age and sex change what is normal. Creatine supplements and a high-meat diet raise plasma creatinine and make eGFR read low without kidney disease; a vegan diet lowers it. Inulin, the ideal marker, has to be infused.
  • Clearance ratio (Cx / Cinulin): = 1, filtered only; > 1, filtered and secreted (PAH, organic acids and bases); < 1, filtered and reabsorbed (Na+, Cl−, K+, urea) or not filtered. Two substances normally have a clearance of 0: albumin, which the filter holds back, and glucose, which is filtered and then all reabsorbed. The highest possible clearance equals renal plasma flow (PAH).

5 Nephron parts in order, the paths of blood and urine, and the four processes: filtered − reabsorbed + secreted = excreted

Recording + slides · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Filtration (glomerulus into Bowman space), reabsorption (tubule back to the blood), secretion (blood into the tubule) and excretion (urine): excreted = filtered − reabsorbed + secreted.

The four processes: filtration (glomerular capillaries into Bowman space), reabsorption (tubular fluid back to the peritubular blood), secretion (peritubular blood into the tubular fluid) and excretion (what leaves as urine). Key relationship: filtered − reabsorbed + secreted = excreted.

  • Blood path: renal artery → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular (cortical radiate) → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries (and vasa recta for juxtamedullary nephrons) → renal vein.

6 Juxtaglomerular apparatus: the distal tubule touches its own glomerulus; JG cells hold renin, the macula densa releases adenosine (tubuloglomerular feedback); the filtration barrier

Recording + slides + objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • Each nephron's distal tubule comes back to touch its own glomerulus: the macula densa, where the thick ascending limb meets the DCT, lies against the renin-making JG cells of the afferent arteriole (the juxtaglomerular apparatus).
  • JG (granular) cells in the afferent arteriole wall hold renin; macula densa cells sense NaCl and release adenosine, which constricts the afferent arteriole (tubuloglomerular feedback); a sustained change brings renin release.
  • Juxtaglomerular apparatus: the macula densa (tubule cells where the thick ascending limb meets the distal convoluted tubule, touching its own glomerulus) senses NaCl (mainly the Cl− entering through NKCC2) and releases adenosine; JG (granular) cells in the afferent arteriole wall secrete renin; extraglomerular mesangial cells lie between them.

7 Active vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol) is made in the kidney

Flagged in the recording · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • Active vitamin D is made in the kidney: 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol, by 1α-hydroxylase, turned on by low Ca2+, high PTH and low phosphate; 24,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol is inactive.
  • Make hormones: erythropoietin from interstitial cells of the cortex when local O2 falls; renin from juxtaglomerular cells; and active vitamin D. Cholecalciferol (from skin exposed to UV light, or the diet) is 25-hydroxylated in the liver; the kidney then makes either the inactive 24,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol or, by 1α-hydroxylase in the proximal tubule, the active 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol). Low plasma Ca2+, high PTH and low phosphate turn 1α-hydroxylase on (FGF23 turns it down).

Also flagged in class

  • Total body water, ICF, ECF, plasma and interstitial fluid, and the 60–40–20 rule: 42, 28 and 14 L in a 70-kg adult.
  • Know the nephron in order (renal corpuscle, proximal tubule, thin descending, thin ascending and thick ascending limbs, distal convoluted tubule, collecting duct) and the four processes: filtered − reabsorbed + secreted = excreted.
  • Urine: collecting duct → papilla (the tip of a pyramid) → minor calyx → major calyx → renal pelvis → ureter → bladder. Blood: renal → segmental → interlobar → arcuate → interlobular arteries → afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries.
  • GFR = Kf × [(glomerular capillary hydrostatic − Bowman space hydrostatic) − glomerular capillary oncotic pressure]; Bowman space oncotic pressure is about 0. The class numbers: 45 − 10 − 19 = 16 mmHg.
  • Normal osmolarity is 275–290 mOsm/kg, the same inside and outside cells; estimate plasma osmolarity as 2[Na+] + glucose/18 + BUN/2.8.

You can skip

  • Know what the clearance, osmolarity and Starling equations mean and which way each term moves things; the worked numbers in this part are practice for that, not arithmetic to drill.
  • Skip the outer medulla's stripes; know the cortex, outer medulla and inner medulla, and that short loops stay in the outer medulla while long loops reach the inner medulla.
  • Skip the slit diaphragm's proteins; know the barrier's three layers (fenestrated endothelium, negatively charged basement membrane, podocyte foot processes) and that it holds back large, negative proteins.
  • Skip the names of the pelvic and hypogastric nerves that carry the bladder's stretch signal; know what sympathetic, parasympathetic and pudendal (somatic) activity each do to the detrusor and the two sphincters.
  • Skip the hematocrit and plasma Na+ columns of the fluid-shift summary; know what happens to ECF volume, ICF volume and osmolarity.

1 Where each transporter and channel sits (apical or basolateral, which cell, which segment), and the exact segment and target of each diuretic

Recording + objectives + study guide · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • For each channel know its side, cell and segment: SGLT2 apical and GLUT basolateral (proximal tubule); NKCC2 apical (TAL); NCC and TRPV5 apical (DCT); ENaC and ROMK apical (principal cells); H+-ATPase and H+-K+-ATPase apical, AE1 basolateral (α-intercalated); pendrin apical (β-intercalated).
  • α-intercalated cells secrete H+ (apical H+-ATPase and H+-K+-ATPase, which takes K+ back) and return HCO3− to the blood through basolateral AE1; β-intercalated cells secrete HCO3− through apical pendrin.
  • Early proximal tubule: the apical Na+/H+ exchanger secretes H+, which reclaims filtered HCO3− with the help of carbonic anhydrase; HCO3− leaves basolaterally on a Na+-HCO3− cotransporter. Glucose enters with Na+ on SGLT2 and leaves on GLUT transporters; other apical Na+ cotransporters carry amino acids, phosphate, lactate and citrate. Bringing Na+ in without Cl− makes the early lumen slightly negative.
  • Late proximal tubule: early on, Na+ went back with HCO3− and organic solutes rather than Cl−, and water followed, so Cl− is now concentrated in the lumen. It is reabsorbed with Na+ through apical Na+/H+ and Cl−/formate exchangers (Cl− leaves the cell through a basolateral Cl− channel) and paracellularly, down its gradient. The lumen here is positive, which also pushes Na+ between the cells.
  • Intercalated cells (about 40%): α-intercalated cells secrete H+ (apical H+-ATPase and H+-K+-ATPase, which also reabsorbs K+) and return HCO3− to the blood through the basolateral Cl−/HCO3− exchanger AE1; β-intercalated cells secrete HCO3− through apical pendrin (a Cl−/HCO3− exchanger) and put H+ into the blood through a basolateral H+-ATPase. Both types are rich in carbonic anhydrase II.

2 Apical and basolateral sides of every tubule cell: the Na+-K+-ATPase powers secondary active transport

Recording + slides + objectives · 1 question in the bank

  • Everything is powered by the basolateral Na+-K+-ATPase (3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in), which keeps cell Na+ low so Na+ flows in across the apical membrane and drags other solutes with it. The apical carriers use no ATP of their own: Na+ moving down its gradient carries the other solute up its gradient, which is secondary active transport.

3 Loop of Henle: water leaves the descending limb, not the ascending limbs; the corticopapillary gradient (about 600 mOsm/kg without ADH, 1,200 with it) and urea recycling

Recording + objectives + study guide · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • ADH puts aquaporins into the outer and inner medullary collecting ducts and urea transporters into the inner medullary duct only; urea concentrates in the duct, leaves into the inner medulla and recycles into the thin descending limb.
  • Thin descending limb: permeable to water (aquaporin-1; about 10% of filtered water) and to small solutes such as urea, not to NaCl. Water leaves into the salty medulla and urea enters, so the fluid becomes more concentrated going down.
  • Urea recycling: ADH makes the cortical and outer medullary collecting ducts permeable to water but not urea, so urea concentrates in the duct; in the inner medullary collecting duct ADH also inserts urea transporters, urea diffuses into the interstitium and supplies much of the inner medulla's osmolarity. Some urea re-enters the thin descending limb from the ascending vasa recta and is recycled. A low-protein (vegan) diet makes less urea, so the urine can't be concentrated as much.

4 Glucose reabsorption: SGLT2 and GLUT, the threshold (about 200 mg/dL), splay and the transport maximum (about 350 mg/dL), glycosuria and the flozins

Recording + slides + objectives + study guide · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • SGLT2 (apical) and GLUT (basolateral) reabsorb all filtered glucose until the carriers saturate: glycosuria starts at about 180–200 mg/dL (splay), and all carriers are full (Tm) above about 350 mg/dL.
  • The flozins (empagliflozin, canagliflozin, dapagliflozin) block SGLT2 in the apical membrane of the proximal tubule, causing glycosuria; SGLT1 in the gut is untouched.
  • Glucose transport maximum (Tm): there are only so many SGLT2 carriers, so reabsorption saturates. Below about 200 mg/dL of plasma glucose, all filtered glucose is reabsorbed. Above about 200 mg/dL (the threshold) some carriers are full and glucose starts to appear in the urine; at about 350 mg/dL every carrier is saturated and reabsorption levels off at Tm. The bend between the two is splay, which is why glucose spills before Tm is reached. What isn't reabsorbed is excreted – glycosuria with an osmotic diuresis.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors (the "-flozins": empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) block SGLT2 but not the gut's SGLT1, causing glycosuria on purpose to treat type 2 diabetes. On their own they don't cause hypoglycemia; they also lower weight and blood pressure and are used in heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction, with or without diabetes. Watch for genital yeast infections, UTIs (rarely Fournier's gangrene), volume loss and euglycemic ketoacidosis.

5 The proximal tubule's bulk reabsorption: tubular fluid along it, and ECF volume (expansion lowers it, contraction raises it)

Recording + slides · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Along the proximal tubule, tubular fluid ÷ plasma for Na+ stays about 1 (iso-osmotic); glucose, amino acids and HCO3− fall toward 0; Cl− rises, because HCO3− is taken first, until the late segment takes Cl− back.
  • ECF volume expansion lowers proximal reabsorption (peritubular hydrostatic pressure up, oncotic pressure down); contraction raises it. With glomerulotubular balance, a rise in GFR raises proximal reabsorption so the fraction stays about the same.
  • Along the proximal tubule (tubular fluid ÷ plasma concentration): Na+ stays at about 1, because water follows it, so osmolarity stays about 1 too; glucose, amino acids and HCO3− fall toward 0 as they are taken back; Cl− rises above 1, because HCO3− is reclaimed first.
  • Glomerulotubular balance: when GFR rises, the proximal tubule reabsorbs more, keeping the fraction reabsorbed about constant (a higher filtration fraction raises peritubular oncotic pressure, which pulls more fluid back). ECF volume expansion works the other way: peritubular hydrostatic pressure rises and oncotic pressure falls (dilution), so the proximal tubule reabsorbs less and the extra NaCl and water are excreted; volume contraction raises proximal reabsorption.

6 Collecting duct: several nephrons per duct; principal cells (ENaC, ROMK, aldosterone, ADH) and α- and β-intercalated cells

Recording + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Several nephrons drain into one collecting duct: their connecting tubules merge at the cortical collecting duct (how many per duct doesn't matter).
  • The collecting duct reabsorbs only about 4–5% of filtered Na+ but is the segment hormones tune: principal cells respond to aldosterone (more ENaC and Na+-K+-ATPase) and ADH (aquaporin-2).
  • The collecting duct system: connecting tubule, then the cortical, outer medullary and inner medullary collecting ducts. Several nephrons drain into one collecting duct: their connecting tubules merge at the cortical collecting duct. It reabsorbs only about 4–5% of filtered Na+, but it is the segment hormones tune.
  • Principal cells (about 60%): Na+ in through apical ENaC, K+ out to the lumen through apical ROMK (renal outer medullary K+ channel); respond to aldosterone and ADH. Na+ entry makes the lumen strongly negative (about −50 mV), which drives K+ secretion and paracellular Cl− reabsorption, so the more Na+ is reabsorbed, the more K+ is secreted.

7 What each segment reabsorbs: its share of filtered Na+ and water

Slides + objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • Know each segment's share. Na+: proximal tubule about 65%, loop 25%, DCT 5%, collecting duct 4–5%. Water: proximal tubule about 65%, thin descending limb 10%, collecting duct about 5% to more than 24% with ADH.
  • Name each diuretic's exact segment and target: acetazolamide, carbonic anhydrase (proximal tubule); loop diuretics, NKCC2 (thick ascending limb); thiazides, NCC (distal convoluted tubule); amiloride and triamterene, ENaC, and spironolactone, the aldosterone receptor (principal cells).

Also flagged in class

  • For every cell drawing, find the apical (lumen) side and the basolateral (blood) side with its Na+-K+-ATPase, then ask whether each solute is reabsorbed or secreted and whether it crosses through the cell or between cells.
  • The proximal tubule takes back about two-thirds of filtered water, Na+ and Cl− and nearly all glucose, HCO3− and amino acids, iso-osmotically.
  • Thin descending limb: water out (and urea in), so the fluid concentrates. Thin and thick ascending limbs: no water; NaCl leaves, so the fluid dilutes (the TAL through NKCC2: the diluting segment).
  • The corticopapillary gradient runs from 300 mOsm/kg to about 600 at the papilla without ADH and up to about 1,200 with it; ADH raises NKCC2 activity in the TAL and water and urea permeability in the collecting duct.

1 SIADH, central and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and ADH control

Recording + slides + objectives + study guide · 4 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Volume wins: a 5–10% fall in blood volume or pressure releases ADH even when the plasma is dilute.
  • In SIADH, ADH stays high and unregulated (often from a tumor such as small cell lung cancer): water is kept, sodium falls and the urine is inappropriately concentrated.
  • ADH (arginine vasopressin) is made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. Its three actions: through V2 receptors it raises the collecting duct's water permeability (aquaporin-2) and the inner medullary duct's urea permeability; through V1 receptors on vascular smooth muscle it constricts arterioles and raises blood pressure.
  • Non-osmotic control: a 5–10% fall in blood volume or pressure, sensed by the left atrium, carotid sinus and aortic arch, releases ADH. Volume wins: hypovolemia resets the osmostat so ADH is released even at a low osmolarity. Nausea, pain, motion sickness, hypoxia, insulin-induced hypoglycemia, strenuous exercise and drugs (morphine, nicotine, MDMA) also release ADH; alcohol and opiate antagonists such as naloxone suppress it. Thirst also rises with a 10–15% fall in blood volume and with angiotensin II acting on the subfornical organ.

2 Reading a blood gas: the four simple disorders and their compensation

Recording + objectives + slides + study guide · 6 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Compare arrows: PCO2 and HCO3− moving opposite to the pH means a respiratory disorder; moving the same way as the pH means a metabolic one.
  • A vomiting (contraction) alkalosis lasts while the patient is volume depleted, because angiotensin II and aldosterone keep HCO3− high; rehydration lets it correct.
DisorderPrimary changeCompensationExamples
Metabolic acidosisHCO3− ↓Hyperventilation (PCO2 ↓)Diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, renal failure, aspirin overdose (high anion gap); diarrhea, acetazolamide (normal gap)
Metabolic alkalosisHCO3− ↑Hypoventilation (PCO2 ↑)Vomiting, loop and thiazide diuretics (contraction alkalosis), excess aldosterone, antacid or bicarbonate intake
Respiratory acidosisPCO2 ↑Kidneys make and keep HCO3− (days)Hypoventilation: COPD, pneumonia, pulmonary edema; airway obstruction (aspiration, sleep apnea); weak respiratory muscles (ALS); opioids, sedatives or anesthetics depressing the medullary respiratory center

  • To read a blood gas: look at the pH; find which of PCO2 or HCO3− moved in the direction that explains it (the primary change); the other one moving the same direction is compensation. A quick check by the arrows: when PCO2 and HCO3− move opposite to the pH, the disorder is respiratory; when they move the same way as the pH, it is metabolic.
  • Acid-base and K+ move together: acidosis drives K+ out of cells (hyperkalemia); alkalosis drives it in (hypokalemia). Vomiting gives metabolic alkalosis with hypokalemia, kept going by volume contraction: proximal HCO3− reabsorption rises, angiotensin II and aldosterone drive H+ secretion, so the alkalosis lasts until volume is restored. Without volume contraction the kidney corrects an alkalosis by excreting HCO3− (β-intercalated cells secrete it). Severe diarrhea does the opposite: a normal-gap metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia (K+ lost in the stool, aldosterone up).

3 Potassium: the shift table, aldosterone's ENaC effect on secretion, and NSAIDs and hyperkalemia in CKD

Recording + objectives + study guide · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Know the K+ shift table: insulin, β2 agonists, α blockers, alkalosis and aldosterone move K+ into cells; insulin deficiency, β-blockers, α agonists, acidosis, hyperosmolarity, cell lysis and hard exercise move it out.
  • Aldosterone adds ENaC channels; more Na+ reabsorbed makes the lumen more negative and drives K+ secretion.
  • NSAIDs block the macula densa's prostaglandins, so renin and aldosterone fall and K+ is retained: in CKD this causes hyperkalemia, so these patients limit K+ and avoid NSAIDs.
  • Out of cells (plasma K+ rises): insulin deficiency (type 1 diabetes), β-blockers, α-adrenergic agonists (epinephrine's α effect, mainly in the liver), acidosis, hyperosmolarity, cell lysis (burns, rhabdomyolysis, hemolysis, chemotherapy), strenuous exercise (hyperkalemia in someone on a β-blocker or with poor kidney function). Low aldosterone (Addison disease) causes hyperkalemia.
  • Aldosterone raises K+ secretion mostly through its effect on Na+: more ENaC channels let more Na+ into the principal cell, the lumen turns more negative, and K+ is secreted. It also adds Na+-K+-ATPase pumps and apical K+ channels.
  • NSAIDs and CKD: NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that signal renin release at the macula densa, so renin and aldosterone fall and less K+ is secreted. With a low GFR, and more so with ACE inhibitors or spironolactone, this causes hyperkalemia, so CKD patients limit K+ intake and avoid NSAIDs.

4 Renin release (low afferent pressure, sympathetic β1, low macula densa NaCl) and ANP's inhibition of RAAS

Recording + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Renin is released for low perfusion pressure in the afferent arteriole, sympathetic β1 stimulation and low NaCl at the macula densa (signaled by prostaglandins).
  • ANP inhibits: renin, aldosterone, ADH and Na+ reabsorption in the collecting duct all go down, so Na+ and water are excreted.
  • Renin is released by JG cells for low afferent pressure, sympathetic (β1) activity and low NaCl at the macula densa (signaled by prostaglandins); a rise in afferent pressure inhibits it. This macula densa signal to renin is separate from tubuloglomerular feedback, where the macula densa adjusts the afferent arteriole through adenosine. Renin: angiotensinogen → angiotensin I; ACE (on the endothelium of the lungs and kidneys) → angiotensin II.
  • ANP from atrial myocytes, released by atrial stretch (volume expansion): dilates the afferent and constricts the efferent arteriole (GFR up), inhibits renin, aldosterone and ADH, and reduces Na+ reabsorption in the collecting duct → natriuresis. It opposes RAAS.

5 Loop diuretics waste Ca2+ and Mg2+; thiazides keep Ca2+

Recording + slides + objectives · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • Loop diuretics remove the TAL's lumen-positive voltage, so Ca2+ and Mg2+ are lost in the urine; thiazides lower Ca2+ excretion.
  • Loop diuretics raise Ca2+ and Mg2+ excretion: blocking NKCC2 stops K+ recycling, so the lumen-positive voltage that drives their paracellular reabsorption in the TAL is lost. Thiazides lower Ca2+ excretion: with less Na+ entering the DCT cell, the cell reabsorbs more Ca2+ (hypercalcemia can follow). ECF volume expansion raises Ca2+ excretion.

6 Heart failure edema: interstitial fluid the baroreceptors can't sense keeps the kidney retaining Na+

Recording + objectives · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • In heart failure the extra fluid is interstitial, where the baroreceptors can't sense it; the effective circulating volume is low, so the kidney keeps retaining Na+.
  • Heart failure: the excess fluid is Na+ and water retained in the interstitial compartment (about three-quarters of the ECF), where the baroreceptors can't sense it, and blood pressure is often low from the weak heart. The effective circulating volume is low, so the sensors keep signaling depletion, the kidney keeps retaining Na+ and the edema worsens. Cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome do the same.

Also flagged in class

  • ADH is made in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei; the OVLT and subfornical organ send axons to them and to the cortex's thirst areas (insula, anterior cingulate gyrus); hyperosmolarity releases ADH and stimulates thirst.
  • A 1–2% rise in plasma osmolarity releases ADH; thirst needs about 2–3%, so the kidney starts saving water before you feel thirsty.
  • Low volume → baroreceptors → renal sympathetic nerves: the arterioles constrict, renin is released and Na+ reabsorption rises.

You can skip

  • Skip the anatomy in the hypothalamus diagram; know where ADH is made, where the osmoreceptors are and that hyperosmolarity releases ADH and stimulates thirst.
  • Skip the long lists of causes of hypo- and hypernatremia; know why each happens: too much water for the sodium, or too little.
  • Skip how the ADH precursor is packaged and cleaved on its way down the axon; know where ADH is made and released.
  • Skip the full lists of causes of central and nephrogenic DI; know the big picture: too little ADH (central) versus kidneys that ignore it (nephrogenic, most often lithium), and how each is treated.
  • Skip the rare causes of hypokalemia such as Liddle syndrome; know the big causes: K+ shifting into cells, renal loss (diuretics, excess aldosterone) and low intake.
  • Skip the names of the Ca2+, Mg2+ and phosphate channels and transporters; know where along the nephron each ion is reabsorbed and what moves it (paracellular in the proximal tubule and TAL, PTH and thiazides in the DCT).
  • Skip the equation itself; know that pH follows the ratio of HCO3− to CO2: more HCO3− raises it, more CO2 lowers it.
  • Skip the details of ammonia handling in the collecting duct; know that acidosis drives K+ out of cells (hyperkalemia) and alkalosis drives it in.

1 Nephritic versus nephrotic syndrome and the classic glomerular diseases

Recording + objectives + slides + study guide · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Rapidly progressive GN: crescents of epithelial cells in Bowman space and loss of function over days to weeks; most patients end up on dialysis or with a transplant.
  • Rapidly progressive GN: crescents of epithelial cells in Bowman space and loss of function over days to weeks; about 90% end up on long-term dialysis or with a transplant. Type I anti-GBM (linear IgG and C3), idiopathic or Goodpasture syndrome, where the antibody also binds the lung's alveolar basement membrane (lung hemorrhage with GN; plasmapheresis helps). Type II immune complex (post-streptococcal, lupus, Henoch-Schönlein purpura). Type III pauci-immune, ANCA-associated (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis).
  • Minimal change disease: the most common nephrotic syndrome in children; normal light microscopy, fused (effaced) podocyte foot processes on electron microscopy; about 90% respond to steroids.
  • Membranous nephropathy: the classic most common nephrotic syndrome in adults (ages 30–50); subepithelial immune deposits that thicken the GBM, with spikes on silver stain; about 85% primary; slowly progressive.

2 Pyelonephritis, casts and stones

Slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Acute pyelonephritis: bacterial infection of the kidney and pelvis, usually ascending, most often E. coli (also Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas). Risks: instrumentation, obstruction, vesicoureteral reflux, female sex. Fever, chills, flank (costovertebral angle) pain, dysuria, frequency and urgency; WBC casts place it in the kidney. Complications: pyonephrosis, papillary necrosis (common in diabetics and with analgesic abuse), sepsis; untreated, it can become chronic.
  • Urolithiasis: calcium oxalate/phosphate stones about 75%; magnesium ammonium phosphate (struvite) about 15%, from urease-making bacteria such as Proteus that keep the urine alkaline, and the cause of staghorn calculi; uric acid about 6% (gout); cystine 1–2% (an inherited defect of amino acid transport). Colicky flank pain to the groin, hematuria, infection behind an obstruction.

3 Classification of renal tumors: clear cell RCC (VHL) versus Wilms tumor

Objectives + slides · 1 question in the bank

  • Renal cell carcinoma: about 2% of adult cancers and 80–90% of kidney cancers, mostly in men aged 40–70; risks are smoking, von Hippel-Lindau disease and adult polycystic disease. Hematuria, flank pain and a mass; a yellow-orange, vascular tumor that tends to invade the renal vein. Clear cell (70–80%, loss of VHL on 3p, cells full of lipid and glycogen); papillary (10–15%, not tied to 3p but to trisomies 7, 16 and 17); chromophobe (about 5%, best prognosis, perinuclear halos). Von Hippel-Lindau syndrome (autosomal dominant) brings hemangioblastomas, renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and pancreatic tumors. RCC spreads by blood, most often to lung and bone, and can surface as a metastasis in the jaw or gingiva.
  • Wilms tumor: children (about 2–5 years), a large abdominal or flank mass, sometimes with pain or hematuria; 5–10% bilateral; triphasic (blastemal, stromal, epithelial); about 90% long-term survival with nephrectomy and chemotherapy.

4 Glomerular hallmarks: crescents in RPGN, mesangial IgA in IgA nephropathy, and where the deposits sit

Recording + slides · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Mesangial IgA on immunofluorescence is IgA nephropathy (Berger disease): recurrent hematuria a day or two after a respiratory infection.
  • Know where each deposit sits: subepithelial (membranous spikes, post-streptococcal humps), subendothelial (MPGN type I), mesangial (IgA), linear along the GBM (anti-GBM); none in minimal change disease.
  • IgA nephropathy: the most common glomerular disease worldwide; recurrent hematuria within a day or two of a respiratory infection; mesangial IgA. Benign in children, slowly progressive in adults.

Where the injury sits names the disease: subepithelial deposits in membranous nephropathy (spikes on silver stain) and post-streptococcal GN (humps); subendothelial deposits in MPGN type I; mesangial IgA in IgA nephropathy; linear IgG along the GBM in anti-GBM disease; and no deposits, only effaced podocyte foot processes, in minimal change disease.

Also flagged in class

  • Know the oral signs of kidney disease (pale mucosa, petechiae and ecchymoses, uremic stomatitis, periodontal disease, altered taste, xerostomia; enamel hypoplasia and delayed eruption in children) and the eye signs (diabetic retinopathy, macular degeneration, glaucoma, cataracts).

You can skip

  • Skip the renal lab table's cutoffs by stage; know which way each moves as the kidneys fail: BUN, creatinine and the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio rise, GFR and creatinine clearance fall.
  • Skip the system-by-system list of uremic signs; know that uremia touches nearly every system, and learn the oral and eye signs of CKD.
  • Interstitial nephritis: know only that it is inflammation around the tubules, from drugs or infection.
  • Acute tubular necrosis: know only that the tubular cells die, usually after ischemia or a toxin.
  • Know only that kidney failure can be pre-renal, renal or post-renal; the lecture's diseases are the renal causes.
  • Skip the classification of kidney diseases into groups; learn the diseases themselves.
  • Skip the syndromes that link the kidney and the eye; know the common oral and eye signs of kidney disease instead.
  • Skip normal lab values (BUN, serum creatinine, creatinine clearance): the lab report prints them. Know which way each moves as the kidneys fail, the eGFR stage cutoffs (90, 60, 30, 15) and the albuminuria categories (under 30, 30–300, over 300 mg/g), which are stages, not reference ranges.

1 Dialysis patient: the day after dialysis, the access arm, bleeding and hepatitis

Recording + objectives · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Treat a hemodialysis patient the day after dialysis: the heparin has worn off and fluid and electrolytes are at their best.
  • Consult the physician or nephrologist: stage, cause, recent labs (eGFR, creatinine, BUN, CBC with hemoglobin and platelets, coagulation tests, electrolytes), blood pressure control, medications and the dialysis schedule. Ask the patient which days they dialyze, which arm holds the access, whether they get heparin, how they bleed and what they take for pain.
  • Hemodialysis runs about 3 times a week through an arteriovenous fistula or graft, usually in the forearm, with heparin. Treat on the day after dialysis: heparin's effect (a few hours) is gone and fluid, electrolytes and wastes are at their best. Avoid treating on a dialysis day.

2 No NSAIDs in kidney disease: acetaminophen first, opioids at the lowest dose, renally cleared antibiotics adjusted

Recording + objectives · 3 questions in the bank

Know this
  • In kidney disease, no NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen): acetaminophen is the analgesic, with opioids such as codeine, hydrocodone or tramadol at the lowest dose.
  • Clindamycin, azithromycin and metronidazole usually need no dose change in kidney failure; amoxicillin, penicillin VK and cephalexin get longer intervals.
  • Acute kidney injury: no NSAIDs, avoid high-dose acyclovir, lower the doses of renally cleared drugs and keep the patient hydrated; treat pain conservatively (for a toothache, a pulpectomy and a temporary) and defer elective care until the kidneys recover.
  • Adjust: amoxicillin, penicillin VK and cephalexin (longer interval), ciprofloxacin, acyclovir and valacyclovir, gabapentin; codeine, hydrocodone, morphine and tramadol at the lowest dose (they or their active metabolites build up). Of the antifungals, fluconazole needs care (a lower dose and many drug interactions), ketoconazole is avoided (liver toxicity and interactions), and nystatin and clotrimazole are fine.
  • Usually no change: amide local anesthetics such as lidocaine (metabolized by the liver; articaine by plasma esterases) at normal doses, though long-acting bupivacaine is used with caution and epinephrine is kept low when blood pressure is high; clindamycin, azithromycin, metronidazole and doxycycline (cleared mainly by the liver or gut). Acetaminophen is the analgesic of choice, with a longer interval in severe disease.

4 Oral and radiographic signs of kidney failure

Recording + slides + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Know the oral signs of CKD: uremic stomatitis, xerostomia, taste changes, mucosal petechiae and ecchymoses, pale mucosa from anemia, mucosal lesions, periodontal disease and renal osteodystrophy (demineralized jaws that can fracture during treatment); and the eye signs: retinopathy, glaucoma and cataracts.
  • Uremic fetor (ammonia-like breath), uremic stomatitis (a red, sore, inflamed mouth and tongue, sometimes with white plaques or ulcers; eased with sips of water, good hygiene and soothing rinses), xerostomia (fluid limits, drugs), metallic or altered taste, pale mucosa, petechiae, ecchymoses and gingival bleeding, periodontal disease, parotitis, candidiasis and angular cheilitis. Children with CKD can show enamel hypoplasia and delayed eruption. Caries tends to be low (salivary urea raises pH), while calculus builds up.
  • Renal osteodystrophy from secondary hyperparathyroidism: loss of the lamina dura, a ground-glass trabecular pattern, demineralized jaws and brown tumors (giant cell lesions); soft tissue calcifications. Demineralized jaws raise the risk of fracture during extractions: the mandible around the lower molars, and the maxillary tuberosity with the upper molars; bone heals slowly.

5 The diuretic patient in the chair: orthostatic hypotension, bathroom breaks, cramps and electrolytes

Recording + objectives · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • Diuretic patients: orthostatic hypotension, dry mouth, bathroom breaks, cramps and low K+ (loop, thiazide) or high K+ (K+-sparing).
  • In the chair: patients on diuretics are prone to orthostatic hypotension (sit them up slowly) and xerostomia; thiazides can cause lichenoid reactions. Plan bathroom breaks in a long appointment, and expect electrolyte losses to cause muscle cramps (a mouth prop helps the jaw). In a patient with healthy kidneys a short NSAID course is usually acceptable, but long use weakens blood pressure control.

6 Transplant immunosuppression and diabetic or hypertensive kidney disease in the chair

Flagged in the recording · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • Diabetic kidney disease: periodontal disease, infection and slow healing, glucose control. Hypertensive kidney disease: blood pressure every visit, careful epinephrine, no NSAIDs.
  • Diabetic kidney disease, the most common kind: more periodontal disease, infection and slow healing; check the HbA1c and glucose, and keep glucose on hand for hypoglycemia. Hypertensive kidney disease: blood pressure at every visit, watch for orthostatic hypotension, use epinephrine carefully and no NSAIDs.

Also flagged in class

  • Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the TAL; thiazides block NCC in the DCT; K+-sparing drugs act on the collecting duct's principal cells (ENaC or the aldosterone receptor).
  • Transplant immunosuppressants: infection, candidiasis, slow healing, cyclosporine gingival overgrowth, more oral cancer, and adrenal suppression from steroids.

1 The patient on long-term steroids in the chair: a suppressed axis, the adrenal crisis and 100 mg hydrocortisone, and why steroids are tapered

Recording + slides + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Why a taper: an outside steroid suppresses CRH and ACTH, and the cortex goes into rest. Stopped abruptly, it cannot answer: adrenal insufficiency. Taken in the morning, like the natural peak, it disturbs sleep less.
  • A patient on long-term steroids (about 20 mg prednisone a day for 3 weeks or more) should be assumed to have a suppressed axis. For routine care under local anesthesia: the usual morning dose, a morning appointment, and good anxiety and pain control. A long or stressful surgery, an infection or trauma, or a missed dose can trigger an adrenal crisis; extra steroid for a big procedure is set with the physician.
  • Adrenal crisis: severe hypotension, weakness, confusion, abdominal pain, loss of consciousness, shock. Stop, call 911, lay the patient supine with legs raised, give oxygen and 100 mg hydrocortisone IV or IM, and monitor vitals.

1 Motility: segmentation vs peristalsis, slow waves, the migrating motor complex and motilin, and achalasia

Slides + objectives · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Segmentation contracts the circular muscle in the middle of the bolus and mixes; peristalsis contracts behind the bolus and relaxes ahead of it, and propels.

As a bolus arrives, the stomach relaxes to hold it (receptive relaxation, a vagovagal reflex through VIP). Antral contractions grind the meal against a nearly closed pylorus (retropulsion), and each wave squirts a little chyme into the duodenum. Gastric emptying is fastest for liquids (isotonic saline fastest) and slowest for fat (through CCK); acid in the duodenum, hypertonic or hypotonic chyme, amino acids and peptides, large particles and duodenal distension also slow it, as do secretin and GIP, which tighten the pylorus. In the small intestine (transit about 2 hours), segmentation mixes: the circular muscle contracts in the middle of the bolus, making pockets of chyme that move slowly aborally. Peristalsis propels: excitatory and inhibitory neurons fire together, so the muscle contracts behind the bolus and relaxes ahead of it. A peristaltic rush (from irritation) gives diarrhea; reverse peristalsis, vomiting. Between meals the migrating motor (myoelectric) complex (MMC, driven by motilin, about every 90 minutes) sweeps residue and bacteria into the colon; it starts about 3 hours after a meal, runs from mid-stomach to the terminal ileum, and eating stops it. Without it, bacteria overgrow. The colon (transit 30–40 hours) is the last place fluid is absorbed: the teniae coli form haustra that mix and store, and mass movements 1–3 times a day (vagus and pelvic nerves, gastrin and CCK) push feces into the rectum. Reflexes: gastrocolic (food in the stomach → colonic mass movements), gastroileal (food in the stomach → ileocecal valve relaxes; both through parasympathetic nerves, gastrin and CCK), coloileal (cecal stretch → the ileocecal valve closes, an intrinsic enteric reflex), and the defecation reflex (rectal stretch → rectum contracts and the involuntary internal anal sphincter relaxes, while the voluntary external sphincter, tonically contracted, decides when; the urge comes when the rectum is about 25% full). In Hirschsprung disease neural crest cells never reach the distal colon (RET mutations; more common in boys and in Down syndrome), so the aganglionic segment can't relax.

4 Parietal cell acid secretion: the H+/K+ pump, its three stimulants, its brakes and the vagal cephalic phase

Objectives + slides + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Parietal cells make HCl and intrinsic factor (the one gastric product we can't live without: it is needed for B12 absorption in the terminal ileum). Inside the cell, carbonic anhydrase makes H+ and HCO3-; the H+/K+ ATPase pumps H+ into the lumen (the K+ it brings in leaks back out through apical K+ channels), Cl- follows through apical channels, and HCO3- leaves into the blood in exchange for Cl- (the "alkaline tide" after a meal). Three stimulants act directly: ACh (M3, Ca2+), gastrin (CCK-B receptor, Ca2+) and histamine (H2, cAMP). Histamine potentiates the other two, which is why an H2 blocker (famotidine, cimetidine, nizatidine) cuts acid from every stimulus; a PPI (omeprazole, lansoprazole, esomeprazole) blocks the final pump, so it works whatever the stimulus. Brakes: somatostatin, prostaglandins, low antral pH and, from the duodenum, secretin and GIP. At high secretion rates gastric juice becomes mostly HCl (100–200 mM, pH as low as 0.8–1) with little Na+ and no HCO3- to buffer it; at low rates more of it is the Na+-rich fluid of the other gastric cells. Chronic vomiting of this acid demineralizes the teeth. Chief cells make pepsinogen (released by vagal and enteric ACh and by secretin), which acid, and then pepsin itself, turns into pepsin, an endopeptidase. Surface and mucous neck cells make the mucus-bicarbonate layer that keeps the mucosal surface near pH 7; the vagus and prostaglandins drive it, which is why NSAIDs injure the stomach. Without intrinsic factor (pernicious anemia), B12 can’t be absorbed.

5 Saliva: isotonic primary saliva made hypotonic by the ducts, control by nerves alone, and dual autonomic control

Objectives + slides + study guide · 1 question in the bank

The parotid is the largest gland and is purely serous (amylase); the submandibular makes about 60-70% of resting saliva and is mixed; the sublingual makes about 5% and is mostly mucous. Acinar cells make primary saliva that is isotonic to plasma. The ducts reabsorb Na+ and Cl- and secrete K+ and HCO3-, but they let little water through, so final saliva is hypotonic. The faster it flows, the less time the ducts have, so high-flow saliva is closer to plasma and richest in HCO3-. About 1–1.5 L is made a day, and its control is entirely neural: no hormone drives it. Unusually, both autonomic divisions stimulate saliva: parasympathetic (ACh, Ca2+: copious, watery; blocked by atropine) and sympathetic (mainly β, cAMP: small volume, rich in protein and amylase). Saliva lubricates and buffers, starts starch digestion (α-amylase) and fat digestion (lingual lipase), and defends the mouth (lysozyme, lactoferrin, secretory IgA, mucins). In Sjögren syndrome, lymphocytes destroy the salivary and lacrimal glands: xerostomia, trouble chewing, swallowing and tasting, caries, enlarged glands and dry eyes.

6 Vomiting vs diarrhea: hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis vs hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis

Objectives + slides · 1 question in the bank

Vomiting is run by the brainstem vomiting center, fed by the chemoreceptor trigger zone (area postrema, outside the blood-brain barrier: drugs and toxins), the gut (through 5-HT and dopamine), the inner ear and higher centers. Saliva pours out, reverse peristalsis brings intestinal contents back into the stomach, the glottis closes, the abdominal wall contracts and the LES and esophagus relax. Vomiting loses H+, Cl- and K+: a hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis (breathing slows and PCO2 rises), with more K+ lost in urine as aldosterone answers the volume loss. Diarrhea loses the HCO3- the lower gut secretes: a hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis (breathing speeds up and PCO2 falls), often with hypokalemia too.

7 The liver's plasma proteins: albumin and the clotting factors, but not factor VIII

Objectives + slides · 1 question in the bank

The liver is the first stop for all blood leaving the gut; its jobs are exocrine (bile), endocrine (plasma proteins), metabolic, storage and protective. Hepatocytes make albumin (colloid osmotic pressure; carries hydrophobic drugs), transferrin (iron), ceruloplasmin (copper), α1-antitrypsin, complement, lipoproteins and most clotting factors (fibrinogen, prothrombin, V, VII, IX and X), but not factor VIII, which comes from endothelium. So cirrhosis lowers albumin and prolongs the PT/INR while factor VIII stays normal. The liver stores glycogen, iron and vitamins A, D and B12 (B12 for years); it makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D, which the kidney turns into the active 1,25 form. Kupffer cells lining the sinusoids eat the gut bacteria that reach portal blood. Between meals glucagon breaks down glycogen and drives gluconeogenesis (from lactate, pyruvate and amino acids), and epinephrine breaks down glycogen in fight or flight; glucose-6-phosphatase, which muscle and brain lack, lets the liver release free glucose. After a meal insulin drives glycogen storage.

Also flagged in class

  • The small intestine, where most nutrients, electrolytes and water are absorbed, is lined with villi (with plicae and microvilli, about 600 times the area of a plain tube); the colon has no villi.

1 The two enteric plexuses: Meissner (submucosal) for secretion and blood flow, Auerbach (myenteric, between the muscle layers) for motility; the gut wall's four layers

Slides + objectives · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • The submucosal (Meissner) plexus runs secretion and local blood flow; the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus, between the circular and longitudinal muscle, runs peristalsis.

Four layers everywhere: mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae; it protects, absorbs and secretes), submucosa (dense irregular connective tissue, the larger vessels and lymphatics, the submucosal (Meissner) plexus, glands in the esophagus and duodenum), muscularis externa (inner circular, outer longitudinal, with the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus between them; the stomach adds an inner oblique layer), and serosa (free organs: mesothelium on connective tissue, the visceral peritoneum) or adventitia (fixed ones like the thoracic esophagus: connective tissue only). The enteric nervous system can run without the CNS. Meissner = mucosal functions: gland secretion, local blood flow and movement of the mucosa. Auerbach = action: the muscularis externa, coordinating peristalsis.

The left colic (splenic) flexure, where SMA and IMA territories meet, has the least arterial supply (a watershed), so colonic ischemia shows there first.

4 Pancreas vs salivary gland: centroacinar cells and islets, no striated ducts or myoepithelial cells

Slides + objectives · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • Pancreatic acini have centroacinar cells (the start of the intercalated duct) and no striated ducts or myoepithelial cells; salivary glands have striated ducts and myoepithelial cells.

Pancreas: mostly dark exocrine acini (basal rough ER, apical zymogen granules) with pale, capillary-rich islets of Langerhans scattered among them. Pale centroacinar cells in the center of the acini are the start of the intercalated ducts, and there are no striated ducts and no myoepithelial cells: centroacinar cells mean pancreas, striated ducts mean salivary gland. Acinar cells release the enzymes, the proteases as inactive zymogens (stimulated by CCK and ACh); duct and centroacinar cells release bicarbonate-rich fluid (stimulated by secretin).

5 Liver: blood to the central vein, bile and lymph toward the portal tract; the acinus zones; Kupffer and stellate cells

Slides + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Hepatocytes sit in plates between sinusoids, so blood passes close to nearly every cell. The liver has a dual supply: oxygen-rich blood in the hepatic artery and nutrient-rich blood in the portal vein, which mix in the sinusoids. Three ways to draw the lobule: the classic lobule (hexagon around a central vein, portal triads at the corners; blood flow), the portal lobule (triangle around a triad; bile flow) and the hepatic acinus (diamond between two central veins; the metabolic unit). In the acinus, zone 1 (periportal) gets the most oxygen; zone 3 (centrilobular) gets the least and has the most CYP450, so it is hit first by ischemia, acetaminophen and alcohol.

6 Foregut, midgut and hindgut: boundaries, referred pain and appendicitis (T10 to McBurney point), the stomach's arteries

Slides + objectives + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Parietal peritoneum lines the wall and has somatic nerves: sharp, well localized pain. Visceral peritoneum covers organs and has visceral afferents: dull, poorly localized pain referred by region. Appendicitis starts as periumbilical pain (midgut visceral afferents to T10) and moves to the right lower quadrant (McBurney point) once the inflamed appendix irritates the parietal peritoneum. McBurney point, two-thirds of the way from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine, marks the base of the appendix, which stays fixed even though the rest of the appendix varies in position. The lumen is usually blocked by lymphoid hyperplasia in young people and by a fecalith in older ones. A mesentery attached to the back wall is a "meso-"; a fold joining two organs or the front wall is a "ligament"; one attached to the stomach is an omentum. The falciform ligament holds the ligamentum teres (old umbilical vein); the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) holds the portal vein, hepatic artery and bile duct, with the epiploic foramen behind it.

7 Abdominal wall layers and the arcuate line, inguinal hernias (MDs don't LIe), dermatomes and diaphragm openings

Objectives + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Inguinal canal: from the deep ring (in transversalis fascia, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels) to the superficial ring (external oblique aponeurosis); it carries the spermatic cord or the round ligament, plus the ilioinguinal nerve. An indirect hernia enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through a patent processus vaginalis (congenital, the most common type). A direct hernia pushes through Hesselbach triangle (inferior epigastric vessels, rectus edge, inguinal ligament), medial to the vessels, where the transversalis fascia is weak (older men). "MDs don't LIe": Medial = Direct, Lateral = Indirect. Umbilical folds: median (urachus; a patent urachus leaks urine at the umbilicus), medial (obliterated umbilical arteries), lateral (inferior epigastric vessels).

Also flagged in class

  • Portal-caval anastomoses (esophagus, umbilicus, rectum) carry almost nothing until portal pressure rises, as in cirrhosis; then they dilate into esophageal varices, caput medusae and rectal varices.
  • On a cross section or scan, the anterior of the two large veins is the portal vein and the posterior one the IVC.
  • Blood runs in the sinusoids to the central vein; bile in canaliculi between hepatocytes out to the portal bile ducts; lymph in the space of Disse out to portal lymphatics.

  • The liver clears amide local anesthetics, aspirin, acetaminophen, ibuprofen, codeine, meperidine, diazepam, barbiturates, erythromycin, clindamycin, tetracycline, ketoconazole and fluconazole. In significant liver disease, lower the doses, lengthen the intervals, stay well under local anesthetic maximums and work with the physician. The lecture lists erythromycin, clindamycin and tetracycline as antibiotics to avoid, and the general anesthetics halothane and thiopental as contraindicated. Acetaminophen at a reduced dose (about 2 g a day at most) is the usual analgesic; avoid NSAIDs in cirrhosis (bleeding, ulcers, kidney injury); sedatives last longer.

6 GERD's dental erosion and Barrett esophagus, and how colorectal cancer presents

Core of the slides · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • Smooth, shiny erosion of the palatal surfaces of the maxillary teeth, with posterior occlusal cupping and sensitivity, points to reflux: refer for medical care, give fluoride and advise on diet and brushing times.

Esophageal disease shows as dysphagia, odynophagia (painful swallowing), retrosternal pain, hematemesis and melena. GERD is reflux through an incompetent LES (low LES tone, transient relaxations, a sliding hiatal hernia, obesity, pregnancy, scleroderma) and the most common cause of esophagitis: heartburn, regurgitation, dysphagia, cough and hoarseness. Biopsy shows basal cell hyperplasia, long lamina propria papillae and intraepithelial eosinophils and neutrophils. Reflux esophagitis can lead to ulcers, a stricture, Barrett esophagus or cancer. In the mouth, GERD causes erosion of the palatal (lingual) surfaces of the maxillary teeth (2–4 times as common as in people without reflux), posterior occlusal cupping, sensitivity, halitosis, xerostomia and burning mouth (bulimia erodes the same surfaces), and GERD patients grind their teeth more at night. Care: refer for medical treatment, fluoride, diet counseling and brushing timed away from acid episodes. Eosinophilic esophagitis looks like reflux but has a normal pH, doesn't respond to acid drugs and causes food impaction; the epithelium is packed with eosinophils (microabscesses). Infectious esophagitis is Candida, herpes simplex or CMV; chemical esophagitis follows lye, acids, hot liquids, pills or radiation.

Also flagged in class

  • About 1.5% of dental patients carry hepatitis B: vaccinate the whole team, use standard precautions, have a post-exposure plan, and read the serology (HBsAg infected, IgM anti-HBc acute, IgG anti-HBc past or chronic, anti-HBs immune).
  • Acetaminophen causes about 46% of acute liver failure, most of it accidental; N-acetylcysteine works best in the first 8–10 hours, and every product a patient already takes counts toward the daily total.

You can skip

  • Learn the words for each liver injury pattern and what each means (ballooning, acidophil bodies, steatosis, bridging fibrosis, regenerative nodules, Mallory-Denk bodies); reading a liver biopsy image isn't expected.
  • Cholangiocarcinoma: know that it is an adenocarcinoma of the bile ducts that shows late, with obstructive jaundice.
  • Know each antiemetic's receptor (H1 and muscarinic for motion sickness, D2, 5-HT3) and its side effects, not which brainstem site (chemoreceptor trigger zone or solitary tract nucleus) holds which receptor.

3 Osteoclast biology: RANKL, OPG and M-CSF, and PTH acting through osteoblasts

Recording + slides · 1 question in the bank

Coupling: osteoblasts and osteocytes make M-CSF and RANKL; RANKL binds RANK on precursors and makes osteoclasts. OPG is the osteoblast's decoy receptor that soaks up RANKL. Estrogen raises OPG, lowers RANKL and speeds osteoclast apoptosis, which is why bone loss accelerates after menopause. Osteoclasts have no PTH receptors: PTH acts on osteoblasts, which raise RANKL. Continuous PTH resorbs bone; intermittent PTH builds it.

4 Intramembranous vs endochondral ossification; cartilage types and collagen types

Recording + slides · 1 question in the bank

Intramembranous ossification turns mesenchyme straight into bone: the skull vault, maxilla, most of the mandible and most of the clavicle (and an extraction socket heals the same way). Endochondral ossification replaces a hyaline cartilage model: long bones, vertebrae, pelvis, skull base. The growth plate runs reserve → proliferation → hypertrophy → calcification → ossification; estrogen closes it in both sexes. The mandibular condyle has its own secondary cartilage growth site. Remodeling never stops: activation, resorption (weeks), reversal, formation and mineralization (months).

5 Calcium balance: hypocalcemia after thyroid surgery and the osteoporosis risk factors

Recording + slides · 1 question in the bank

Hypocalcemia (after parathyroid removal in thyroid surgery, vitamin D deficiency, CKD): perioral tingling, muscle cramps and tetany (Chvostek and Trousseau signs), long QT, cataracts; in children, enamel hypoplasia. Hypercalcemia (primary hyperparathyroidism, cancer): stones, bones, abdominal groans and psychiatric moans, constipation and weakness; hyperparathyroidism in the jaws shows loss of the lamina dura and brown tumors. Treat severe hypercalcemia with IV saline, then a bisphosphonate, denosumab or calcitonin.

4 Excitation-contraction coupling, troponin C, ATP in the cross-bridge cycle, sarcomere bands

Recording + slides · 1 question in the bank

Excitation-contraction coupling: the action potential runs down the T-tubule, where the voltage-sensing dihydropyridine receptor is mechanically linked to the ryanodine receptor (RyR1) of the sarcoplasmic reticulum (a triad: one T-tubule between two terminal cisternae). Calcium floods out and binds troponin C; tropomyosin rolls off myosin's binding sites. Cross-bridge cycle: myosin binds actin; release of Pi drives the power stroke; ATP binding detaches myosin from actin (no ATP: rigor mortis); ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the head. Relaxation needs ATP too, for SERCA to pump calcium back into the SR.

5 Succinylcholine (pseudocholinesterase, malignant hyperthermia), reversal with neostigmine or sugammadex, spasmolytics

Recording + slides · 1 question in the bank

  • Succinylcholine, the depolarizing blocker: fasciculations, then flaccid paralysis; fast onset and short action for intubation. Broken down by plasma pseudocholinesterase: a person with the atypical enzyme stays paralyzed for hours. Phase I block is worsened, not reversed, by neostigmine. Risks: hyperkalemia (burns, crush injury, denervation), bradycardia, and malignant hyperthermia.
  • Malignant hyperthermia: a RyR1 mutation; succinylcholine or a volatile anesthetic triggers uncontrolled calcium release: rigidity (masseter first), rising end-tidal CO2, tachycardia, hyperthermia, hyperkalemia. Treat with dantrolene, which blocks RyR1.

Study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Three court cases built it. Schloendorff (1914): every adult of sound mind has the right to decide what is done to their own body. Salgo (1957): the first use of the words "informed consent." Canterbury v. Spence (1972): disclose every risk that a reasonable person in the patient's position would find significant to the decision (the reasonable-patient standard), not just what other doctors customarily disclose.

2 Bloodborne pathogens: transmission risks, the steps after a needlestick, and OSHA's hepatitis B vaccine rule

Review guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • OSHA's Bloodborne Pathogens Standard: a written exposure control plan; engineering controls (sharps containers, self-sheathing needles) and work-practice controls (no two-handed recapping); PPE at no cost; the hepatitis B vaccine offered free within 10 working days of assignment (a refusal is signed); free, confidential follow-up after an exposure; and yearly training.
  • Risk of infection after a needlestick from an infected source: HBV about 30% (6–30%), HCV about 2%, HIV about 0.3%. HBV survives on dry surfaces for at least a week. There is a vaccine for HBV, but none for HCV or HIV.
  • After an exposure: wash with soap and water (flush the eyes or mouth with water), don't squeeze the wound or use bleach, report at once, and test the source with consent. HIV prophylaxis starts as soon as possible, ideally within 2 hours and no later than 72.

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

Typical intraoral settings are about 7–10 mA and 65–70 kVp, with the exposure time varied for the region, the patient's size and the receptor. Filtration (usually 0.5–2.5 mm of aluminum; regulated at 1.5 mm Al at 70 kVp and 2.5 mm Al above 70 kVp) removes the weak, low-energy photons that would be absorbed in the patient and only add dose without reaching the receptor; by stripping them out it also raises the beam's mean energy. Collimation (a metal barrier with an aperture, often a lead diaphragm) restricts the beam's size and shape, cutting scatter and patient dose and improving image quality. The inverse square law states that intensity falls with the square of the distance from the source, so moving twice as far away leaves one quarter of the intensity.

2 Direct versus indirect action and the DNA double-strand break

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

Both actions yield highly reactive, short-lived free radicals, and the presence of dissolved oxygen makes the damage worse by forming additional peroxide species. A single photon can cause a cluster of DNA damage within a short stretch of the molecule: base damage, single-strand breaks, double-strand breaks and DNA–DNA or DNA–protein cross-links. Single-strand breaks are usually repaired accurately using the opposite strand as a template, but the double-strand break is the hardest to repair and is the critical lesion behind radiation-induced cell death, heritable mutation and cancer.

2 Lamina dura, the mental foramen mimic, and the egg-shell effect

Study guide · 1 question in the bank

The egg-shell effect explains how curved structures appear: where the beam skims the edge of a curve it follows a longer, tangential path and is attenuated more, so the outer edge looks radiopaque, while the center, where the beam has a shorter path, looks radiolucent. The lamina dura is the dense cortical bone lining the tooth socket, seen as a thin, continuous radiopaque line around the root. An intact lamina dura and a normal periodontal ligament space around an apex confirm that a superimposed radiolucency, such as the mental foramen, is a normal structure and not periapical pathology.

3 Panoramic focal trough, ghost images and positioning errors

ELCS D2 notes + study guide · 1 question in the bank

A panoramic image is a tomogram that captures a curved focal trough (image layer): structures that sit inside the trough are sharp, while those outside it are blurred, magnified, narrowed or missed altogether. Correct positioning keeps the teeth within the trough.

1 Basic life support in the office: C-A-B, the 10-second breathing and pulse check, compressions, the AED

Recording + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • BLS is C-A-B: a 10-second breathing and pulse check, then compressions first.
  • Check breathing and a pulse together for no more than 10 seconds. No pulse, or no breathing or only gasping: start CPR.
  • Compressions: 100–120 a minute, at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep, full recoil, pauses under 10 seconds, 30:2 with breaths.

1 Foreign-body aspiration: mild versus severe, abdominal thrusts, no blind finger sweep, right main bronchus, ER for X-rays

Flagged in the recording · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Aspirated objects go to the right main bronchus: wider, shorter and more vertical.
  • Mild (partial) obstruction: the patient can cough, speak and move air, sometimes with high-pitched stridor. Encourage coughing and watch closely.
  • Severe (complete) obstruction: silent, can't speak or cough, hands to the throat, wide-eyed, turning blue. Ask "Are you choking?"; a nod without words means severe. Give abdominal thrusts (back blows plus thrusts is the Red Cross version). If the patient goes unresponsive, lower them, call 911 and start CPR, looking in the mouth before each set of breaths.
  • Aspirated objects usually go down the right main bronchus, which is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left.

2 Mallampati classes and the difficult airway

Flagged in the recording · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • Mallampati classes I to IV by what you see; III and IV predict a difficult airway.

Classes III and IV predict a hard airway, though a class I patient can still be difficult. Other warning signs: limited mouth opening (trismus, deep neck infection, TMJ problems, scarring from past surgery), a beard, a short thick neck, BMI over 30, a short thyromental distance, a small or retruded mandible, limited neck extension (rheumatoid arthritis) and obstructive sleep apnea (screen with a questionnaire, confirm with a sleep study).

3 Laryngospasm in the lightly sedated patient

Flagged in the recording · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Laryngospasm is more likely in a lightly sedated patient than in one deeply asleep.
  • Laryngospasm is the vocal cords clamping shut at the larynx, usually set off by blood, saliva, water or debris on the cords in a sedated patient. It is more likely in a lightly sedated patient than in one deeply asleep. Signs: high-pitched inspiratory stridor, or silence with chest movement but no air, and falling saturation. Treat: stop, suction the throat, 100% oxygen with positive pressure by bag-mask with a jaw thrust; if it doesn't break, a trained provider gives a small dose of succinylcholine.
