5 The surgical airway: cricothyrotomy

Flagged in the recording · 1 question in the bank

Position (head tilt-chin lift, jaw thrust) → suction → oral or nasal airway → bag-mask → supraglottic airway (LMA) → endotracheal tube → surgical airway. When you can't intubate and can't oxygenate, the emergency surgical airway is a cricothyrotomy: through the cricothyroid membrane, between the thyroid cartilage above and the cricoid below, with a vertical skin incision. A tracheostomy sits lower, near the thyroid gland, and bleeds more, so it isn't the emergency choice. Complications: bleeding, aspiration of blood, a false passage, esophageal injury, subcutaneous and mediastinal emphysema, vocal cord injury. Needle cricothyrotomy with jet ventilation buys time but doesn't protect the airway and isn't a first-line office tool.

Also flagged in class

  • A blind sweep pushes the object deeper; remove only what you can see.
  • EMS takes about 7 minutes or more; call as soon as an airway problem isn't resolving.

Details

Flagged in the recording · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Most patients stay on their anticoagulant or antiplatelet for simple extractions; you control bleeding locally.

Stopping any of them is the prescriber's call. For simple extractions most patients stay on them and you use local measures: a stroke or stent clot is a worse outcome than an oozing socket.

4 Hypertensive urgency versus emergency

Flagged in the recording · 1 question in the bank

High blood pressure is silent and damages the kidneys, heart, brain and eyes over years. A reading of 180 or more systolic or 120 or more diastolic is severe. It is a hypertensive emergency when there are signs of organ damage now (severe headache, chest pain, vision changes, confusion, weakness, shortness of breath): send the patient to the emergency room. Without them it is a hypertensive urgency: no elective care that day, a prompt visit to the physician or urgent care, and a note in the chart. Check blood pressure at every visit.

Also flagged in class

  • Firm, direct pressure on folded gauze over the socket for 10–15 minutes comes before anything else.
  • Know who is at risk, which drugs matter and what you do in the office, more than the pathophysiology.
  • A physician's opinion doesn't shift responsibility: follow the standard of care and document whom you spoke with.

1 Hypoglycemia: the numbers, juice versus glucagon versus IV dextrose

Recording + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

  • Conscious: sugar by mouth: juice, regular soda, glucose gel or tablets. Check with a glucometer and repeat as needed.
  • Unconscious: nothing by mouth. Glucagon 1 mg IM (into the thigh, through clothing if necessary), or IV dextrose, 50 mL of 50% for an adult (25% for a child), and call 911. Glucagon makes the liver release stored glucose and brings the level to about 130 in 25–30 minutes.

2 Rule of twos and adrenal crisis (hydrocortisone 100 mg)

Recording + study guide · 2 questions in the bank

Know this
  • Rule of twos: 20 mg of hydrocortisone (or equivalent) daily, for 2 weeks or more, within 2 years.

An adrenal crisis is a sudden lack of cortisol when the body needs more, set off by infection, surgery, trauma or stopping long-term steroids abruptly: severe hypotension, vomiting, confusion and loss of consciousness. Rule of twos: a patient taking 20 mg of hydrocortisone (or the equivalent) a day for 2 weeks or more within the past 2 years may be suppressed. Most dental procedures under local anesthesia or nitrous oxide need no extra steroid; reduce stress and consult for major surgery. Treat a crisis: stop, lay the patient flat with the legs up, oxygen, 911, and hydrocortisone 100 mg (Solu-Cortef) IV or IM.

3 Vasovagal syncope: prodrome, legs up, recovery

Recording + study guide · 1 question in the bank

  • Recovery should be quick once the patient is flat. If not, it isn't simple fainting: BLS and 911.

4 Local anesthetic overdose: maximum dose, signs, IV lipid emulsion

Recording + study guide · 1 question in the bank

Know this
  • Severe local anesthetic toxicity is treated with IV lipid emulsion 20%.

Keep count. Lidocaine with epinephrine allows about 7 mg/kg, so a 70-kg adult can have about 13 cartridges; when a patient isn't numb, the problem is usually technique, not volume. Risk rises with age extremes, low weight, liver, kidney or heart disease, pregnancy, and injection into a vessel. Mild to moderate signs: numbness around the mouth, talkativeness, confusion, slurred speech, tremor, twitching, nystagmus, rising heart rate and blood pressure. Severe: seizures, then CNS depression, hypotension, bradycardia and asystole. Treat: stop, position, airway and oxygen, 911, a benzodiazepine for seizures and, for severe toxicity, IV lipid emulsion 20% (Intralipid). Amides are cleared by the liver, except articaine, which is cleared mostly in the plasma, so it suits patients with liver disease.

Also flagged in class

  • Hypoglycemia (the lecture's number): serum glucose under about 50–60 mg/dL, with confusion, seizures and coma.
  • A nasal cannula runs 1–5 L/min (up to about 40%); for more oxygen, switch to a mask.
